AL-MAQRIZI
TOPOGRAPHICAL AND HISTORICAL DESCRIPTION OF EGYPT
(Description topographique et historique de l'Egypte) -- Parts 1 and 2
French translation from the Arabic by Urbain Bouriant.

COMPLETE ENGLISH TRANSLATION (in progress)
================================================================================

NOTE ON THIS EDITION
--------------------
This is a complete English rendering of Urbain Bouriant's French translation of
al-Maqrizi's "Khitat" (the Mawa'iz wa-l-i'tibar fi dhikr al-khitat wa-l-athar).
The source is the Bibliotheque nationale de France (Gallica) scan.

The printed volume contains, at its front, both Bouriant's preface and a sample
of an older partial translation by Quatremere. The full Bouriant translation of
the work itself begins after these (at the section headed "In the name of God,
the Compassionate..."). This English edition translates the work proper in full,
in order.

Conventions: Arabic names and terms keep Bouriant's transliteration. Footnotes
are gathered at the foot of each page block. Markers like [PDF p. NN] and, where
printed, [printed p. NN] are given for cross-reference against the scan. Hijri
dates carry Bouriant's Western equivalents where he supplied them.

================================================================================


THE WORK OF AL-MAQRIZI

[Maqrizi's Preface]

[PDF p. 34]

In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.

Praise be to God, creator of knowledge and intelligence, who has taught men what
they did not know. He has heaped upon his servants material and spiritual
benefits; through his growing goodness he has spread over them goods ever greater
and ever repeated. He has sent them upon the earth, where for a time they spread
abroad, granting them as their portion his riches, which they enjoy. To some he
has given to pursue knowledge and learning, urging them to range the fields of
meditation and to traverse the plains of the intellect; to others he has inspired
the thought of renouncing created things to devote themselves to him, prompting
them to lean upon him in all things. He has kept some far from every generous and
fine action, surrounding them with companions who drag them toward all that is
shameful and base. He has obstructed the hearts of others to the point that they
can scarcely understand a word; he has set them far from the path of virtue, so
that they have neither strength nor power. Then all of them, without distinction,
he has destined to vanish and to leave the abode of tribulation and trial for the
domain of death and affliction; and he will make them all enter the abode of
recompense,

[PDF p. 35]

where each will have to answer for his acts and will be questioned on what was
given and granted to him, as well as on the state in which he presents himself
before Him (may he be adored!) and on what he has prepared for that presentation.
God will not be questioned on his acts, but men will be questioned on theirs.

I praise him, and my praise is that of a man who knows that one serves no God but
him, sole creator of creatures; my praise demands of him a redoubling of
benefits, and my gratitude grows as his benefits are renewed.

May God grant his blessing to our lord Mohammed, his servant and his apostle, his
prophet and his beloved, the lord of men and the best of those who have passed and
are no more; he who united in his person the perfection of character and of acts;
he who, above all men, merited the name of the Perfect! He was [a prophet while
Adam was still between water and clay; God sent him to all mankind and sealed
through him the line of the prophets, and blessed his family and his companions
until the day of judgment.]

[PDF p. 36]

The science of history is one of the most important of sciences, and the one that
enjoys the greatest consideration among intelligent people, because of its merit
and its value; for it contains examples and lessons, teaching man that he must
leave this world for the other; it recounts noble actions so that one may model
oneself on them, and makes known shameful acts so that intelligent people may
avoid them. Always generous souls are drawn toward it, and elevated minds take
pleasure in it and love it. The sages have composed a number of works on this
subject, and the writers of the elite have inserted in their books a quantity of
passages relating to it.

Egypt is my native land; it is there that my comrades played and that my family
was gathered; it is the abode of my friends and my companions, the homeland of
those dear to me and of my passing acquaintances; the nest in which my wings grew
and where my poverty perched; and it is of that nest alone that the soul loves to
remember. Since knowledge touched me and God gave me reason and intelligence, I have never
ceased to attach myself to the knowledge of the accounts concerning Egypt and to
take pleasure in drawing from its wells, questioning travelers about the
inhabitants of its regions. I have written in my own hand over long years, and
from all I have written I have drawn useful observations that will be found in no
book and that no binding holds, so rare and strange are they. But all this is
presented without methodical arrangement and has not the regularity of a cloth on
the weaver's loom. I wished to give an overview of what the regions of Egypt
contain in the way of monuments left to us by vanished peoples and bygone ages;
of what survives at Fostat-Masr in the way of monuments, not to speak of those
that time and age have nearly destroyed, whose faint still-visible traces will
soon be the prey of destruction and oblivion.

[PDF p. 37]

I speak also of the remains of magnificent palaces met with in the city of Cairo,
of the quarters and grounds that compose it, of its superb buildings, with an
overview of the illustrious people who founded them and a notice on the great and
venerable persons who completed them. I have strewn the whole with pleasant
anecdotes and with noble, elevated reflections, without lengthening or amplifying,
but without too much abridging or cutting short either, which would have made me
miss the aim; I have instead kept the just mean between these extremes and traced
my path there.

For all these reasons, I have named my book: THE BOOK OF COUNSELS AND EXAMPLES
CONCERNING THE QUARTERS AND THE MONUMENTS. I hope, God willing, that it will be
welcomed by kings and not rejected by the common people and the poor. The
accomplished scholar will praise it, and it will be admired by the beginning
student; it will find favor with the pious believer and be listened to kindly by
the heedless and brazen young man; the idle and the rich will receive it as a
diversion, while sensible and wise people will take it as instruction and as
example -- for they will see in it the proof of God's admirable power in the play
of vicissitudes, and will learn the marvels of the operations the Lord sets in
motion in moving things from one fortune to another.

[PDF p. 38]

If I have succeeded in my compilation, if I have brought my undertaking to a good
end, I owe it to the great munificence of God, to the excellence of his goodness,
to the abundance of his benefits toward me, to the extent of his favors. If, on
the contrary, I have failed in my design, if I have committed errors in my work --
for who, more than man, is subject to err and to falter, if he is not guided and
sustained by him who knows the most hidden things?

    I do not conceal from myself that I am a man
        who sins and errs if Providence does not preserve him.
    And you will find no one easier to excuse, among people liable to error,
        than him who makes this confession: "I am a man."

Let the reader of this book cast over the author the hem of his robe, if some
error passes before his eyes; let him show himself indulgent and obliging if he
meets there some misstep or some chip. What horse, however excellent, does not
stumble? What sword, were it of the best steel of the Indies, does not grow dull
and chip? Especially when the mind is preoccupied with a thousand things, when
resolution gets entangled in difficult affairs, when the intelligence is darkened
by the misfortunes of this somber time, and when the heart is oppressed by the
succession of woes and the redoubling of calamities.

    My time persecutes me like an enemy,
        and each day it presents itself to me with a terrible blow;
    if I desire a thing, it is the contrary it brings me,
        and if it smiles on me one day, the next it is somber toward me.

O my God, I ask your pardon; it is not out of bitterness

[PDF p. 39]

that I complain, nor out of revolt against fate: it is the groan of the sick man
and the sigh of the wounded man, who relieves himself by exhaling his pain and his
laments and finds a soothing of his ills by sharing with others his sobs and his
complaints.

    If one looked between my ribs and my entrails,
        one would see traced upon my liver a line from the book of love.
    And if one felt what I have met with of love,
        one would excuse me, or I would find an excuse for others.

Of God I ask that he grant this book a good reception among intelligent and
learned people; that he preserve it from passing through the hands of the envious
and the ignorant; that, for this work and for others, he guide me in the best
path, for he is my support -- and what better protector can I have? In him, in his
power, is my consolation in all misfortunes; in him my confidence in every event.
There is no God but him! He alone is to be revered!

   INTRODUCTION

   OF THE EIGHT PRINCIPLES

[PDF p. 40]

Before beginning a work, the ancient masters were accustomed to set out eight
principles, namely: the aim of the book, its title, its usefulness, its category,
the names and qualities of its author, its genre, the number of its parts, and
the various sources of information used to compose it. We will therefore say:

The aim of this work is to gather the scattered documents concerning the land of
Egypt and the vicissitudes of its inhabitants, and to form, by this assembling, a
whole that allows one to know the totality of the history of the provinces of
Egypt -- so that an intelligent man, having become acquainted with it, will be
able at all times to recall the monuments that still survive in Egypt and those
that have disappeared; he will be able to recount the fortunes of its earliest
occupants and its inhabitants, the course of their history and all that attaches
to it, and that in a continuous manner, according to the general usefulness that
can be drawn from these monuments.

Title of this book (that is, the name I have given it). -- Having collected the
documents on Egypt, documents I found scattered and confused, it was very
difficult for me, once they were gathered, to classify them either in
chronological order -- because of the uncertainty of the period in which each fact
occurred, especially for the earliest period -- or in alphabetical order, for
other reasons,

[PDF p. 41]

which anyone who goes through this book will readily perceive. That is why I have
dispersed them within the accounts relating to the quarters and the monuments; in
this way, each part of this work contains all that concerns it and relates to it.
Having adopted this method, I have gathered what was scattered on all sides in the
way of documents on Egypt, without fear of repeating myself when the occasion
required it, according to a plan that will please the learned man; nor will it be
disagreeable to the intelligent and cultivated man to find in each chapter all
that relates to it, without having to resort to the others. For all these reasons,
I have named this work: THE BOOK OF COUNSELS AND EXAMPLES, CONCERNING THE QUARTERS
AND THE MONUMENTS.

The usefulness of this book emerges clearly from the proposed aim and from its
title; I mean by this that in a very short time a man will be able to gain an
overview of the events that took place on the land of Egypt and of all the changes
that occurred there over long periods of time and over many years; in reflecting
on them, his soul will be purified, his character will become better; he will love
the good and put it into practice; he will hate evil and flee it. He will
recognize the fragility of this world and learn to detach himself from it to turn
toward what is imperishable.

Category of this work. -- It belongs to the whole of one of the two divisions of
the sciences, which are the intellectual and the positive. One should therefore
take pleasure in reading it and reflecting on the lessons it presents only after
having well grasped what it is necessary to know of these two sciences: the
intellectual and the positive. For every man whose heart God does not blind and
whose eyes he does not darken will, by reflecting, come to know how men like
himself, after having possessed riches and armies, arrived at death and nothingness.
This work therefore takes its place after the knowledge of the intellectual and
positive sciences, for through it one learns how those who came before us ended.

Name and quality of the author. -- His name is Ahmed ben Ali ben Abd el-Qader ben
Mohammed, but he is known under the name of El-Maqrizi. He was born at Cairo, in
the land of Egypt, after the year 760 [3 December 1358 to 22 November 1359] of the
era of the hijra of

[PDF p. 42]

Mohammed. As for his rank in the sciences, it is sufficiently established by this
book and by other works he has composed and written.

Science to which this book relates. -- It belongs to the historical science, whose
aim is to make known the dogmas established by God, to preserve the traditions of
his prophets and apostles, and to record their maxims, by which those whom God
assists are led to serve him, to obey him, and are preserved from disobedience
toward him. This science transmits the annals of the kings of old and of the
pharaohs; it explains how the divine wrath was unleashed upon them for having
performed acts forbidden to them; it is through it that creatures -- that is, men
-- have been able to know the sciences and arts set down in writing, and to learn
what happened in distant regions, in the most far-off countries, and many other
things whose value is undeniable. Every people, Arab or foreign, despite the
diversity of customs and the divergence of religions, possesses annals known to
all, very widespread and celebrated among them; in every inhabited country events
have occurred that are always known to the scholars of that country. Had I wished
to investigate all that has been written on this subject by Arab and foreign
scholars, the number would have been so great that merely to enumerate it would
have far exceeded the limits of human power.

The number of the parts of this work is seven. The first comprises the general
history of the land of Egypt, the various states of its Nile, its taxes, its
mountains; the second embraces a great number of its towns and the races that
inhabit it; in the third is set out the history of Fostat-Masr and of its kings;
the fourth turns on the history of Cairo, of its founders and the monuments they
raised; the fifth contains the description of the various states through which
Cairo and its surroundings have passed; the sixth treats of the citadel of the
mountain and of its kings; finally, in the seventh are enumerated the causes that
brought about the ruin of the provinces of Egypt. Each of these seven parts is
divided into a certain number of chapters.

Sources of information used for this work. -- I have, for my part, followed three
methods: extracts from scholarly books, accounts of elders or high personages I
was able to meet, and the relation of facts of which I was an eyewitness. For the
extracts from the compilations composed by the doctors on all sorts of

[PDF p. 43]

sciences, I note, at each citation, the work from which I drew it, to safeguard my
responsibility and protect myself from all reproach; many people, my contemporaries
and living in the same city as I, by reason of their slight scientific culture, the
narrowness of their historical knowledge, and the ignorance in which they are of
what men have repeated, bitterly deny what they do not know; in fairness they ought
to recognize that the ignorance is on their side. Besides, the science treated in
this book is not a decisive science nor indispensable to religion. It suffices for
the scholar to know what has been said on this subject and to base himself on it. --
When it is a matter of accounts from people of quality or from elders I was able to
converse with, I have most often given the name of the narrator, unless it seemed to
me useless or I had forgotten it -- but these circumstances are rare. -- As for what
I have seen myself, I hope, thank God, that no one will charge me with falsehood or
suspect my good faith.

Concerning the eight principles, I have said all that it was necessary to say. It
remains only for me to march toward my goal. My plan is to condense (in a single
chapter) all that can be said on any quarter or any monument; in this way, the
knowledge of the facts relating to it will be more complete and therefore more
useful, being easier to grasp. God leads whom he pleases in the straight path, and
more than all the learned he is learned.

The first who occupied himself with the quarters and monuments of Egypt and treated
of their origins in a special book was Abou Omar Mohammed ben Youssef el-Kandi;
after him, the cadi Abou Abd Allah Mohammed ben Salamat ben el-Qoda'i wrote his book
entitled: Selection of Accounts on the Quarters and the Monuments. This writer died
in 457 [13 December 1064 to 2 December 1065], before the years of misery. Most of
the monuments he mentions have disappeared, and there remain only ruins and deserted
spots; this disaster was the consequence of the years of misery of Mostanser, from
the year 457 to 464 [29 September 1071 to 17 September 1072], during which raged
famine

[PDF p. 44]

and plague. The inhabitants perished, the country became uncultivated, the situation
of Egypt changed. Desolation spread over Amal Foq (the upper district), from one end
to the other and on both sides of Fostat, to the west and the east: to the west,
from the bridge of the Beni-Ouaïl, where the Ouaraqat (paper-mills) are today, near
the Gate of the Bridge, outside the city of Masr, as far as the hill known under the
name of Er-Rased, going toward the great cemetery; to the east, from the point of
the Birket-el-Habech that borders the cemetery as far as the vicinity of the mosque
of Ahmed ibn Touloun. Shortly after, the emir el-gouïouch Badr el-Gemali entered
Masr in the year 466 [6 September 1073 to 27 August 1074]. The buildings were
destroyed; the country was empty of its inhabitants, of those who had lately
animated it; famine and plague had annihilated them; death and devastation had
dispersed them. There remained in Masr only remnants of men, like the dead, with
pale faces and features altered (by hunger) because of the exaggerated price of
food, of the fear the soldiers inspired in them, and of the ravages caused by the
tribes of negroes and of the Maliha; no one was found to sow the lands, and
moreover the roads were cut off by river and by land, and one could travel only
under good escort and at great expense. Cairo too was deserted and in ruins; Badr
el-Gemali authorized the men of the army, the Maliha and the Armenians, as well as
all who could do so, to build as they saw fit in Cairo with the materials coming from
the houses of Fostat, left empty by the death of their inhabitants. They therefore
set about demolishing the dwellings of Fostat and, with the materials thus obtained,
building others in Cairo. That was the first time Cairo was divided into quarters. --
The one who, after El-Qoda'i, occupied himself with the quarters and their description
was his disciple Abou Abd Allah Mohammed ben Barakat, in an excellent work in the
course of which he makes known to El-Afdal Abou-l-Qassem, son of the emir el-gouïouch
Badr el-Gemali, certain sites that, formerly waqf properties, had been usurped and
occupied by private persons. Later the sharif Mohammed ben As'ad el-Gouani wrote a
book entitled: The Point of Elucidation of the Most Unknown Quarters. In this book he
gives the description of unknown buildings and ruined monuments. -- The last who
treated of the matter was the cadi Tag ed-din Mohammed ben Abd el-Ouahab ben
el-Mou-

[PDF p. 45]

tawwag. In his work entitled: Instruction of the One Who Meditates and Awakening of
the One Who Sleeps, concerning the quarters, he gives a general overview of the
various states of Masr and its quarters down to the year 720 and some. The localities
he describes were, subsequently, for the most part destroyed by the scourge of the
year 749 [1 April 1348 to 21 March 1349], then by that of the year 761 [23 November
1359 to 11 November 1360] and the famine of 776 [12 June 1374 to 2 June 1375]. -- The
cadi Mahi ed-din Abd Allah ben Abd ez-Zaher wrote the book entitled: The Verdant and
Flowering Garden concerning the Quarters of the Cairo of Moez, in which he opens a
quite necessary door. Since the time of this writer, the population of Cairo and its
suburbs became such, in the time of En-Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun, that the city
could scarcely contain its inhabitants. So it remained until the unleashing of the
scourges of the year 749 and of the year 761 and the famine of 776. A great number of
dwellings fell into ruins, and when the calamities and trials of the year 806 [21
July 1403 to 9 July 1404] arrived, devastation spread over Cairo, over Masr, and over
the generality of the provinces of Egypt. And if it please God, in speaking of each
quarter, I will set out as best I can what concerns it.

================================================================================
PART ONE
CONTAINING THE GENERAL HISTORY OF THE LAND OF EGYPT, THE VARIOUS STATES OF ITS
NILE, THE ENUMERATION OF ITS REVENUES, AND THE DESCRIPTION OF ITS MOUNTAINS
================================================================================

CHAPTER I
A GLANCE AT THE FIGURE OF THE HEAVENS

[PDF p. 46]

Egypt being only a fraction of the earth, it is well, before speaking of its
situation on the earth and of the place the earth occupies in the universe, to
cast a glance at the universe itself; after which I will speak of the form of the
earth, of the distribution of its climes; then I will treat of the situation of
Egypt on the earth, of the place it holds among the climes, of its limits, its
origins, its relations with religion, its marvels, its treasures, the character of
its inhabitants, its Nile, its canals, its nomes, its revenues -- in short, all
that touches it -- and all this before arriving at the subject of the book, which
is to describe the quarters of Masr and of Cairo.

The science of the stars comprises three parts: (1) the knowledge of the structure
of the heavens, of the number of the stars, of the constellations of the Zodiac,
of their relative distances, their extent, their movement -- this science bears
the name of astronomy; (2) the science of the astronomical tables and that of the
calendar; (3) the knowledge of the influences exerted by the celestial revolutions
and the rising of the zodiacal constellations on future events -- this science is
called astrology. My intention is to present here the few notions of astronomy
necessary for understanding what is to follow.

[PDF p. 47]

The heavenly bodies are spherical bodies; according to the observations of the
scholars, one counts a thousand and twenty-nine of them, dividing into two
categories: the moving stars and the fixed stars. The moving stars (planets) are
seven in number: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon;
their names have been combined in a single verse. [Footnote: this verse has, in
reality, no meaning; it is an example of the mnemonic devices used among the
Arabs, such as were once current among us. Quatremere, in his fragment of
translation of Maqrizi reported above, thought fit to render it thus: "Saturn
(Jupiter) has bought his Mars from his Sun, and Moons (Venus) have been lit by
Mercury." According to Maqrizi's own explanation, the word khanis has the complex
sense of "to slip away and reappear."]

These seven heavenly bodies are called el-khounnas (the fugitives), and it is of
them, it is said, that God meant to speak when he said: "Truly, I swear by the
fleeing ones (that is) the skiffs that hide themselves" (Koran, LXXXI, 15), and in
this other passage: "the regulators of things" (Koran, LXXIX, 5). They are called
fugitives because of the straightness of their back-and-forth movement, and it is
said that they hide themselves because they run across the constellations then
hide, that is, slip away as the gazelle does. This name of fugitives who slip away
is given to five planets, those other than the Sun and the Moon. This name comes
to them from the word khunus (the act of slipping away), synonymous with ikhtifa'
(disappearance). In the traditions it is said: "When Satan suggests something to a
believer, if the latter pronounces the name of God, Satan flees (yakhnis)," that
is, disappears, then returns. The name of khanis was therefore given to these
heavenly bodies to signify their return. They were named khunnas from the
expression "the gazelle slipped away" when it has returned to its lair, that is,
its dwelling. This name was therefore given to these bodies because of their
disappearance into the light of the Sun. These bodies are also called "the
bewildered," because at times they apparently abandon their movement from east to
west to move from west to east, and this backward march makes them resemble madmen.
The name given to each of the planets is drawn, it is said, from its own essence.
Saturn comes from the expression "so-and-so lingered" when he has stayed

[PDF p. 48]

behind. It was so named because of the slowness of its march. It is said that the
word also signifies "hatred," and, according to common opinion, Saturn
predisposes to that passion. It is of it, it is said, that this word of God
concerns: "By the heaven and the nocturnal star. How will you recognize the
nocturnal star? It is the star that hurls darts." (Koran, LXXXVI, 1-3.)

The name of Jupiter comes to it from its beauty, as if it had bought beauty for
itself alone, or because it is the star of commerce. It influences, it is said,
success and wealth. -- The name of Mars comes from the word markh (a kind of tree
whose wood, by rubbing two pieces against each other, produces fire); it was so
named because of its reddish glow. One also calls "marikh" a barbless arrow which,
once shot, does not follow a straight line; so it is with Mars, whose course is
very twisting; that is why it is claimed to have an influence on slyness (?). --
The Sun was so named because it occupies the middle between the three superior
planets above it and the three inferior planets below it. This name was given to
it for the reason that the middle of a necklace is called shams. -- The name of
Venus is drawn from the word zaharah, which means "the most dazzling white." --
Mercury (Otared) means "the one who accomplishes all things"; that is why this
name was given to the planet; it is also called "the scribe," for it has a great
influence on the heavenly bodies that neighbor it or are in relation with it. The
name of the Moon (qamar) is drawn from the word qumrah, which means "the white"
(noun), aqmar meaning "white" (adjective).

Saturn also bears the name of Kiouan; Jupiter those of Tebr and Bergis; Mars that
of Bahram; the Sun that of Mohr; Venus those of Aïahid and Sadaht; Mercury that of
Hermes; and the Moon that of Mah. All these names have been combined in a single
distich, which is this:

    You will never cease to subsist and to rise
        as long as the heavens last, for the seven regulators:
    Mohr, Mah, Kiouan, and Tebr too,
        and Hermes, and Aïahid, and Bahram.

[PDF p. 49]

They are given this title because these seven heavenly bodies surpass the other
stars of the sky, which are called the fixed stars because of their fixity in one
same point of the sky, or, according to others, because of the slowness of their
march -- for, it is claimed, they need thirty-six thousand solar years to complete
their revolution in the firmament; whereas each of the seven planets has its
particular firmament. The firmaments are spherical bodies, transparent and
concentric. They are nine in number, of which the nearest to us is the firmament
of the Moon; after it comes the firmament of Mercury, then that of Venus, that of
the Sun, those of Mars, of Jupiter, of Saturn; then comes the firmament of the
fixed stars, which comprises all the heavenly bodies visible in the sky except the
seven planets; and beyond the firmament of the fixed stars is the enveloping
firmament, which is the ninth; this last is given the name of Atlas, or of the
firmament of firmaments, or firmament of the universe. There is no agreement about
the firmaments: some call them "heavens," and, according to others, the two are
quite different things; in the view of some, they are spherical; not at all,
according to the view of others.

The eighth firmament bears the name of "throne," and the ninth that of "canopy."
Many other things are said. This ninth firmament turns continually like a
pivoting cabinet and completes one turn in exactly twenty-four hours. This turn is
always made from east to west and carries along in its movement the eight other
firmaments and the heavenly bodies they comprise; this rotation is determined by
the circular movement of the ninth firmament, which produces night and day. The
day is the span of time during which the Sun remains above the horizon of the
Earth, and the night the span of time during which the Sun remains below that same
horizon.

The firmament of the fixed stars is divided into twelve parts, like the slices of
a watermelon. Each of these divisions bears the name of a sign of the Zodiac
(constellation). These signs are: the Ram, the Bull, the Twins, the Crab, the Lion,
the Ear (of grain / Virgo), the Balance, the Scorpion, the Bow (Archer), the
Capricorn, the Bucket (Aquarius), and the Whale (Pisces). Each of these twelve
constellations is divided into thirty parts named "degrees"; each of these thirty
degrees is divided into sixty parts called "minutes"; each of these sixty minutes
is divided into sixty parts named "seconds," and so on into "thirds," "fourths,"

[PDF p. 50]

"fifths," up to "twelfths" and beyond. A series of three constellations forms a
season, and it is according to this division that time is divided into four seasons:
spring, summer, autumn, and winter. The points of orientation are also four: east,
west, north, and south. Likewise there are four elements: fire, air, water, and
earth, and four states: the hot, the cold, the humid, and the dry. One counts also
four humors: bile, black humor, phlegm, and blood, and four winds: the east wind,
the west wind, the north wind, and the south wind. Three constellations belong to
spring; they are ascending in the north, and during their span the days are longer
than the nights: these are the Ram, the Bull, and the Twins. Three others belong to
summer; they are descending in the north, and during their span the nights gain on
the days: these are the Crab, the Lion, and the Ear. The next three belong to
autumn; they are descending in the south, and during their span the nights are
longer than the days: these are the Balance, the Scorpion, and the Bow. Finally, the
last three belong to winter; they are ascending in the south, and during their span
the days gain on the nights: these are the Capricorn, the Bucket, and the Whale.

The enveloping firmament, as we have said, turns continually like a reel, always
moving from east to west above the Earth and from west to east below it; there is
always above the Earth half the sky, that is, six constellations comprising 180
degrees, the other half, with the six other constellations and 180 degrees likewise,
remaining below. And each time one of these degrees -- whose total number is 360 --
rises above the terrestrial horizon in the east, the one diametrically opposite it,
belonging to the seventh constellation, descends below the western horizon. So that
always six constellations appear during the day and the six others during the night.
The horizon is the terrestrial line that separates the apparent part from the hidden
part of the sky. The firmament turns on two poles, north and south, as the millstone
turns supported by two supports. A circular line divides it into two parts, situated
at equal distance from the two poles; this circle is called the equinoctial circle;
it cuts the circle of the constellations, and the latter cuts the equinoctial circle
in such a way that one of the halves of the first circle inclines about 24 degrees
toward the north. In this half are found

[PDF p. 51]

the six northern constellations, from the Ram to the Ear. The other half, on the
contrary, moves away from it and inclines as much toward the south; in this one are
comprised the six southern constellations, from the Balance to the Whale. The two
points of intersection of the two circles -- that is, of the equinoctial circle and
the circle of the sky of the constellations -- are the two equinoctial points:
these are the initial point of the Ram and the initial point of the Balance. The
revolution of the Sun, the Moon, and all the stars is accomplished parallel to the
circle of the firmament of the Zodiac (the ecliptic) and not to the equinoctial
circle. The Sun passes to the equinoctial circle only on its arrival at the two
equinoctial points, which are the points of intersection of the two circles. It
thus traces the equatorial line, beneath which the time is invariable, the night
not prevailing over the day nor the day over the night. For on this line the Sun
radiates at equal distance from north and south. The Sun traverses the firmament
and crosses the twelve signs of the Zodiac in about 365 1/4 days; this span of time
forms the solar year. It sojourns in each of these signs for thirty days and a
fraction of a day. During the day it remains constantly above the Earth; it is the
contrary during the night. As long as it stays in the six northern constellations
-- that is, the Ram, the Bull, the Twins, the Crab, the Lion, and the Ear -- it
rises in the atmosphere very near the zenith; this is the time of spring and summer.
When it is in the southern constellations -- that is, the Balance, the Scorpion, the
Bow, the Capricorn, the Bucket, and the Whale -- it is the time of autumn and
winter; the Sun lowers and moves away from the zenith.

Ouahb ben Monabbeh claims that the first of the four seasons created by God was
winter, and that he made it cold and humid; that he next created spring, which he
made hot and humid, then summer, which he made hot and dry, and finally autumn,
which he made cold and dry. For our contemporaries, the first season is spring,
which begins at the moment when the Sun leaves the constellation of the Whale. The
ancients did not agree on the initial season. Some held for spring and chose it to
begin the year; others made it start from the summer solstice, others from the
autumn equinox, others finally from the winter solstice. When the Sun arrives at
the initial point of the Ram, the day is equal to the night, the weather is in
equilibrium: winter gone, spring arrives softening the air, the zephyr blows, the
ice melts, the valleys are furrowed with streams [...]

[PDF p. 52]

... the rivers swell (except in Egypt), the grasses grow, the harvests rise, the
plants increase, the flowers begin to bud, the trees clothe themselves in leaves,
the buds half-open, the surface of the earth turns green, the cattle give birth,
the udders swell, the earth adorns itself with its most brilliant ornaments, as a
young girl adorns herself for those who look at her. God! what an admirable breast
nourished the poet el-Hafiz Gemal-ed-din Youssef ben Ahmed el-Ya'mouri, who said:

    Breathe the air of spring, for it
        is the best zephyr and the most beneficent.
    Its breath nourishes bodies, like
        a spirit enclosed in a transparent substance.

Ibn Qotaïbah says: "As for spring, people declare that it is the season following
winter, and that with it appear the buds and the flowers; they know no other
spring. The Arabs, however, do not agree on this. Some claim that spring is the
season when the fruits ripen (autumn) and that winter comes after it, summer coming
after winter -- this is the season commonly called spring -- and finally comes the
season of great heat that others call summer. Others call 'first spring' the
temperate season when the fruits ripen (that is, autumn) and 'second spring' the
season that follows winter and in which the buds and flowers appear. But all agree
in saying that spring is autumn." -- When the Sun arrives at the end of the Twins
and the beginning of the Crab, the day is at its maximum and the night at its
minimum. Then the days begin to decrease while the nights increase. Spring ends,
one enters the season of summer: the heat becomes stronger, the air is burning, the
simooms blow, the waters fall (except in Egypt), the grasses dry up, the grains are
ready, the harvest is made, the fruits are ripe, the cattle grow fat, bodies become
more vigorous, the udders of the animals swell, the earth appears like a bride. --
When the Sun reaches the end of the Ear and the beginning of the Balance, the night
is equal to the day for the second time, and the night begins to gain on the day,
which decreases. Summer is past, one enters the season of autumn:

[PDF p. 53]

the air becomes cooler, the wind blows, the weather changes, the rivers run dry, the
springs are exhausted, the leaves of the trees yellow, the fruits fall, the
threshing-floors are busy, the grains are stored, the grasses gathered, the soil
becomes dusty (except in Egypt), the animals grow lean, the insects die, the
reptiles burrow, the birds and beasts migrate toward warmer countries, men lay up
provisions for winter. The world resembles a woman of mature age whose youth has
fled. And what an admirable poet is the imam Az ed-din Abou-l-Hosan Ahmed ben Ali
ben Mo'aqqal el-Azdi el-Mohabbi el-Homsi, who expressed himself thus:

    Admirable is the season of autumn, by which one enjoys
        the freshness of the air; it brings us marvels,
    covering the earth with the gold of its leaves --
        and yet it is the earth that usually gives gold.

The same said again:

    Admirable is the season of autumn, season
        of delicate flanks and limpid.
    The water escapes from a resigned heart,
        and the tears flow on the face of the lover.
    The coldness of the first, the pallor of the second,
        are sweet -- the one to him who tastes, the other to him who loves.

And:

    Come is the season of autumn with all sorts of sweetnesses
        and a beauty that enchants the heart and the eyes.
    It shows us the foliage yellowing and gold-colored,
        the water more limpid, white as silver;
    it heaps upon us every benefit
        and grants us every favor.

Another, an adversary of autumn, said:

    Take your heavy garments in autumn, for
        it is dangerous and its breath is harmful;
    it penetrates bodies, like life;
        like a friend -- but of a friend one must beware.

[PDF p. 54]

Another said:

    O you who incriminate the season of autumn, you are far
        from being its equal, in blaming this season.
    There is nothing sweeter to me than it:
        if it makes the boughs leave off their shirt,
    it spreads its garments beneath them.
        Admire then its compassion and the excess of its pity.
    And the most delicious hours of intimacy are those when the moment of parting
        arrives, and when this season draws near.

When the Sun arrives at the end of the sign of the Bow and the beginning of the sign
of the Capricorn, the night is at its maximum and the day at its minimum: the day
begins to increase while the night decreases. Autumn is past, one enters the season
of winter. The cold becomes more severe, the air is sharper, the leaves of the trees
fall, most of the plants die, the animals sink beneath the earth, bodies become
weaker, the surface of the earth strips itself of its ornaments, the clouds gather,
the dew increases, the atmosphere darkens, the soil is laid bare (except in Egypt),
men can no longer go about their labors, the world becomes like an old woman whose
death is near. When the Sun reaches the end of the Whale and the beginning of the
Ram, the weather becomes again what it was the preceding year, and so on. Thus it
was ordered by the Most High, the Almighty, and decreed by the Omniscient. There is
no other God but him!

Ptolemy compared spring to childhood, summer to youth, autumn to mature age, and
winter to old age. -- It is the movements of the Sun and its passage through the
twelve constellations indicated above that regulate the periods of the year and
divide the day into day and night, and these latter into hours. The movements of the
Moon in these same constellations determine the months and the lunar year. The Moon
traverses the twelve constellations and makes the complete circuit of the sky in 28
days and a fraction, and sojourns in each constellation for about 2 1/3 days,
remaining in each of the 28 lunar mansions 1 day and 1 night. It appears at its
rising in the west, after the disappearance of the disk of the Sun, and its light
increases each night by a half-seventh until its light is complete, which happens on
the

[PDF p. 55]

14th night from its appearance. From the 15th night it decreases, and its light
diminishes each night by a half-seventh, as it had increased, until its light reaches
its minimum on the 28th night of its appearance. And during the time elapsed from its
separation from the Sun and its rising in the west until its conjunction with it, it
crosses 28 mansions, which are: the Crab, the Little Belly (e, d, ? of the Ram), the
Pleiades, Aldebaran, the Little Circle (l of Orion), the Brand-Mark (g and n of the
Twins), the Arm (a and b of the Twins), the Thorax (e of the Crab), the Point (k of
the Crab and l of the Lion), the Forehead (z, g, e and o of the Lion), the Mane (th
and o of the Lion), the Coils (b of the Lion), the Howler, the Support (a of the Ear),
the Strands of Hair, the Two Claws (a and b of the Balance), the Crown (b, d, p of the
Scorpion), the Heart (Antares), the Tail (l and u of the Scorpion), the Ostriches (g,
d, e, e, s, t of the Archer), the City (starless part of the Archer), the Fortune of
the Combatant (a and b of the Capricorn), the Voracious Fortune (k, n, e of the
Water-Carrier), the Fortune of Fortunes (b and j of the Water-Carrier), the Fortune of
the Tents (g, z, ch and e of the Water-Carrier), the Anterior Spout (a and b of
Pegasus), the Posterior Spout (a of Andromeda and g of Pegasus), and the Belly of the
Fish (b of Andromeda). The reckoning relating to all this is reported in the special
works, but what we have said suffices. God knows all, and you know nothing.
[Footnote: the translation of the names of the lunar mansions and their identification
are drawn from the Memoire sur les instruments astronomiques des Arabes, by
L.-Am. Sedillot, published in the Memoires presented by various scholars to the Royal
Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres, 1st series, vol. I, Paris, 1844.]

[PDF p. 56]

CHAPTER II
OF THE FORM OF THE EARTH AND THE DISTRIBUTION OF ITS CLIMES

Now that, from what has just been said of the Universe, the man to whom God has
allotted intelligence can understand how the movement that produces day and night is
brought about, and how these two form the months and the years, we can speak of the
Earth.

The points of orientation are six in number: the east, which is the place where the
Sun, the Moon, and all the stars rise at the different points of the horizon; the
west, which is the side where these bodies set; the north, which is the place where
the Capricorn and the two Calves (b and g of the Little Bear) move; the south, which
is the side where Canopus moves; the zenith, which is above, in the direction of the
sky; and the nadir, below, in the direction of the center of the Earth.

The Earth is a body round like a sphere; some, however, claim that it is not
spherical. It is placed in the air with its whole array of mountains and seas, of
inhabited countries and desert expanses. It is enveloped by the air on all sides, like
the yolk inside the egg; it is situated at equal distance from all the points of the
sky. The lower point of the Earth is in reality determined by its thickness, from the
surface to the center, wherever one may be, the general opinion being that the Earth
is like a sphere placed in the middle of the air and similar to the yolk of the egg in
the shell, the Earth occupying the middle and being at equal distance from all the
points of the sky.

"Beneath the Earth," asserts Hecham ben el-Hakam, "is a body endowed with the property
of rising; it is this body that prevents the Earth from falling; as for itself, it
needs no support, since it never tends to fall but on the contrary to rise." The same
writer says also: "God established the Earth without support." According to Democritus,
the Earth rests on water, and this water is so tightly pressed beneath the Earth that
it finds no outlet by which it might escape.

[PDF p. 57]

-- According to another, the Earth is placed at the center (of the Universe), at equal
distance from all the points of the sky, which attracts it from all sides; that is why
the Earth inclines neither toward one side nor the other, for the force of attraction
is everywhere equal.

It is the same phenomenon as that of the lodestone attracting iron; by its nature, the
sky is the magnet of the Earth and attracts it, but the Earth maintains itself at the
center because of the rapidity of the movement of the sky, which from all sides pushes
the Earth back toward the center. If one puts dust in a bottle and spins it sharply,
the dust will remain at the center of the vessel. Mohammed ben Ahmed el-Khouarezmi says
that the Earth is situated at the center of the sky -- that is, at the bottom of the
sky in reality; that it is round and full of irregularities at the surface, because of
the mountains that jut out and the valleys that lie deep; these irregularities,
moreover, do not prevent it from being round, if one takes account of its whole, for
the height of the mountains -- and I speak of the highest -- is nothing in comparison
with the circumference of the Earth. If, for example, on a ball one or two cubits in
diameter there is some protrusion or some depression, these accidents will not prevent
that ball from being spherical. If, by misfortune, the water surrounded it on all
sides, so as to drown everything and no protrusion were seen anymore, it would be the
end of the special properties enjoyed by minerals, plants, and animate beings (?). Let
us therefore give glory to Him whose mysterious decisions no one but he can penetrate.

The outer surface of the Earth, bathed by the air on all sides, occupies the upper
part; the air holds itself above it, envelops it, and attracts it from all sides. Above
the air are the firmaments of which we spoke above, one above the other up to the ninth
firmament, which is the highest of all and forms the limit of the created Universe.
Opinions are divided on what is beyond: some claim it is the void, others that it is the
plenum, others that it is neither plenum nor void. -- At whatever point of the Earth a
man stands upright, his head is always directed toward the sky and his feet toward the
center of the Earth; he sees continually one half of the sky, while the other half
remains constantly hidden from him by the curvature of the Earth, and [...]

[PDF p. 58]

... however far he moves from one point to another, he always sees of the sky a part
equal to that which is hidden from him.

The Earth is immersed in water like a grape floating on a liquid; about half of it is
visible, while the other half remains plunged in the water. The visible portion of the
Earth is divided into two parts and, as it were, cut by a line parallel to the
equinoctial line and passing below that line. All the countries situated on this line
are without latitude; for them the two poles remain indeterminate and are situated, for
these countries, at the two extremities of the circle of the horizon. Any country
situated off this line on the north side, by the value of one degree, sees the north
pole -- that is, the point of revolution of the Capricorn -- rise by one degree for its
inhabitants, and the south pole, point of revolution of Canopus, lower by one degree,
and so on. Likewise for the south side, it is the south pole that rises and the north
pole that lowers. It is by this that the latitude of a place has been determined. The
latitude of a place, in effect, is the inclination of the equinoctial circle relative
to the zenith of the people of that place and the elevation of the pole at their
horizon; in other words, the latitude of a place is expressed by the difference between
the zenith of the people of that place and the zenith of the people who have no
latitude. -- The visible part of the Earth situated south of the equator is
uninhabited; the other part, north of the equator, represents the inhabited quarter of
the Earth, that is, the peopled part of the Earth.

The equatorial line does not exist in reality; it is a hypothesis of our mind, an
imaginary line that goes from east to west below the circle of revolution of the
initial point of the Ram; it was so named because in the localities it crosses, the
nights are equal to the day, without excess or diminution of one over the other,
throughout the whole course of the year. Of this line, the two points that touch the
horizon: the one is directed on the circle of revolution of Canopus in the south, the
other on the circle of revolution of the Capricorn in the north.

The inhabited Earth counts, from east to west, 180 degrees, and from north to south --
that is, from Khat-Arin (the equator) to Banat-Na'ach (the Daughters of the Bier, the
two Bears), 48 degrees representing twice the value of the inclination of the Sun, and
beyond Khat-Arin 16 degrees; the extent of the inhabited Earth is therefore (from north
to south)
   ---
   [Footnote: the equator. Cf. Reinaud, Geographie d'Aboulfeda (Paris, 1848), vol. I,
pp. ccxl ff.]

[PDF p. 59]

about 70 degrees, which is due to the regularity of the Sun's march and its passage,
twice a year, into the regions situated beyond the Ram and the Balance. The extreme
north and the extreme south are touched by the Sun only once a year; but, as the
culminating point of the Sun is reached by that body twice in the northern hemisphere,
it is in this hemisphere that the inhabited part of the Earth is found, thanks to the
elevation of the Sun, too far off to harm the inhabitants. The contrary taking place in
the southern hemisphere, the Earth is not inhabited there. [Footnote: in contradiction
with what is said further on, p. 34.]

There is no agreement on the extent of the Earth. According to some, it is 500 years'
march, of which one third is inhabited, a second third desert, and the last third
occupied by the seas. According to others, the inhabited part of the Earth is 120
years' march: 90 for Gog and Magog, 12 for the land of the Negroes, 8 for Roum
(Byzantium), 3 for the Arabs, and 7 for all the other peoples. It is said moreover that
the world is divided into 7 parts, of which 6 are for Gog and Magog and 1 for all the
rest of mankind; that the Earth is 500 years' march, of which 300 for the seas, 100 for
the desert regions, and 100 for the inhabited lands; that the extent of the earth is
24,000 parasangs, of which 12,000 for the land of the Negroes, 8,000 for Roum, 3,000
for the Persians, and 1,000 for the Arabs. According to Ouahb ben Mounabbeh, the
inhabited part of the Earth would be, in comparison with the uninhabited part, like a
tent in the desert. Ardechir ben Babek says that the Earth comprises four parts, of
which one belongs to the Turks, another to the Arabs, the third to Persia, and the
last to the Negroes. The climes are 7 in number, the cardinal points 4; there are 45
regions, 10,000 towns, and 256,000 villages; the towns and fortresses number 21,600.
In the first clime one counts 3,100 great towns; in the second, 2,713 towns and great
villages; in the third, 3,079 towns and villages; in the fourth, which is that of
Babel, 2,974 towns; in the fifth, 3,006 towns; in the sixth, 3,408 towns; and in the
seventh, 3,300 towns distributed among the islands. El-Khouarezmi says that the
diameter of the Earth is 7,000 parasangs, which represents the half-sixth of the
Earth, including the mountains, the deserts, and the seas; the rest is uninhabited and

[PDF p. 60]

one meets there neither plants nor animals. -- The inhabited portion of the Earth
resembles, it is said, a bird whose head would be represented by China, the right wing
by the Hind and the Sind, the left wing by the land of the Khazars, the breast by
Mecca, Iraq, Syria, and Egypt, and the tail by the West. It is also recounted that the
diameter of the earth is 7,414 miles and its circumference 20,400 miles, including
everything, lands and seas. Abou Zeid Ahmed ben Sahl el-Balkhi says that the length of
the Earth, from the eastern extremity to the western extremity, is about 400 stages,
and its breadth, from the northern limit of the inhabited earth, abode of Gog and
Magog, to the southern limit, abode of the Blacks, 220 stages; that the part stretching
from the desert of Gog and Magog to the ocean surrounding the Earth in the north, as
well as the part going from the desert of the Blacks to the ocean enveloping the Earth
in the south, are uninhabited; that no living being is met there and that their total
extent is 5,000 parasangs. But all this is only words resting on no proof.

The means of knowing the extent of the Earth is the following: by moving from south to
north along the meridian, the equator will be found to the south of our zenith; if then
we advance by the value of one celestial degree -- that is, the 360th part (of the
celestial circle) -- the pole will rise for us by a degree equivalent to the degree of
displacement. We will then know that we have traversed the 360th part of the
circumference of the terrestrial globe corresponding to the same division of the sky;
measuring the distance separating our point of departure from our point of arrival when
the pole rises by one degree, we will find that one celestial degree represents in
reality on the Earth a distance of 56 2/3 miles, or 25 parasangs. And if we multiply the
value of a single degree -- that is, the number of miles we have just indicated -- by
360, we will obtain as result 20,400 miles, which is the length of the terrestrial
circumference; dividing this last number by 3 1/7, we will obtain as quotient 6,440
miles, the length of the terrestrial diameter; multiplying, moreover, this diameter by
the circumference, one will have the total surface of the Earth, which is about
132,600,000 square miles. From this surface one can derive the evaluation of the
inhabited quarter of the Earth, which would be 33,150,000 square miles; the breadth of
the inhabited part of this quarter is equal to the distance separating the circle of
revolution of the Crab from the

[PDF p. 61]

pole -- that is, 55 1/2 degrees -- which represents the sixth of the terrestrial circle.
The inhabited Earth ends at the island of Thule in Britain; it is the last inhabited
point in the north. This sixth makes, in miles, 3,764; if we multiply this sixth, which
represents the breadth of the Earth, by its half, which is its length, the inhabited
Earth will equal the half of the sixth of the Earth. As for the breadth of the
inhabited Earth, it goes always decreasing because of the narrowing of the divisions of
the circles (of latitude). Its value is equal to the fifth of the circle and is about
4,080 miles. In the inhabited quarter of the earth there are seven great seas, each of
which comprises a certain number of islands; one also counts there 15 lakes, some salt,
others not, 200 high mountains, and 240 great rivers. It is divided into seven climes,
which contain 17,000 great towns.

One reads in the book of Orosius: After Julius, surnamed Caesar, had quelled the
sedition and taken the government of the universe, he chose four philosophers -- whose
names Orosius gives -- and prescribed that the four of them divide among themselves the
description of the limits of the world and the enumeration of its seas and its
provinces; to one was assigned the description of the east, to the second that of the
west, to the third that of the north, to the fourth fell the south. Their work was
completed in about thirty years. The total of the seas known in the universe was
twenty-nine, of which eight for the east, eight for the west, eleven for the north, and
two for the south. The number of the principal islands was seventy-one, of which eight
for the east, sixteen for the west, thirty-one for the north, and sixteen for the
south. The great mountains known were thirty-six in number, all high mountains, whose
names they gave in their work; seven of them were in the east, fifteen in the west,
twelve in the north, and two in the south. One counted also sixty-three great regions,
of which seven in the east, twenty-five in the west, nineteen in the north, and twelve
in the south; they likewise gave the names of these regions. The great known regions
[smaller divisions] amounted to two hundred and nine, of which seventy-five in the east,
sixty-six in the west, six in the north, and sixty-two in the south. The great known
rivers throughout the whole earth were fifty-six in number, of which seventeen for the
east, thirteen for the west, nineteen for the north, and seven for the south.

Each of the seven climes is like an outspread carpet whose length would be measured
from east to west, and the breadth from north to south; these climes are

[PDF p. 62]

of different lengths and breadths. The first of these climes has its middle crossed by
the line beneath which the longest days are 13 hours, while the countries found on the
line passing through the middle of the seventh clime have for their longest days days
of 16 hours. The territory stretching beyond the southern limit of the first clime is
composed of sea and desert; as for that found beyond the northern limit of the seventh
clime, it is not known whether it is inhabited or not. The length of each of the seven
climes, from east to west, equals 12 hours of the revolution of the sky; their breadths
differ by a half-hour according to the count of the hours of their longest days. The
longest and broadest of these climes is the first, which has in length, from east to
west, about 3,000 parasangs, and in breadth, from north to south, 150 parasangs. The
smallest, in length and breadth, is the seventh clime, which has, from east to west,
only a length of 1,500 parasangs and a breadth of 70 parasangs, from north to south.
The five other climes are found between the two we have just spoken of; their limits are
imaginary lines, not existing in reality, and invented by the ancient travelers who
traversed the earth, to recognize its exact limits, fix the location of each region,
and survey the roads that furrow it. So much for the inhabited quarter.

As for the three other quarters, they are deserts. The north is situated under the
circle of revolution of the Capricorn: the cold there is severe, the night lasts six
months without interruption -- it is then the season of winter in those regions; during
this time there is no daylight there, the air is charged with an intense darkness, the
water is solid thanks to the extreme rigor of the cold, and one meets there neither
plants nor animals. This region is diametrically opposite to the south, which is the
place where the revolution of Canopus is carried out; there the day is six months,
without night; it is for this region the time of summer; the air there is burning, the
wind torrid, and the intensity of the heat there makes the animals and plants perish;
one can neither cross it nor sojourn there. As for the west, the enveloping ocean
prevents one from going there, so agitated are its waves and so thick the darkness
there; as for the east, very high mountains forbid the passage. That is why all men have
grouped themselves on the inhabited quarter of the earth; and the greater part of the
earth -- that is, the three quarters other than the inhabited quarter -- is known to no
one.

[PDF p. 63]

The entire earth, with all it contains of mountains and seas, is, in comparison with
the universe, only as a point in comparison with the circle. -- The limits of the
climes have been deduced from the hours of the day, because, when the Sun stands at the
initial point of the Ram, the days and nights are equal throughout all the climes; but
if it moves, continuing its course in the Ram, the Bull, and the Twins, the hours of
the day become unequal for all the climes; when it reaches the end of the Twins and the
beginning of the Crab, the length of the day in the middle of the first clime is 13
hours precisely; it is 13 and a half hours in the middle of the second; 14 hours in the
middle of the third; 14 and a half hours in the middle of the fourth; 15 hours in the
middle of the fifth; 15 and a half hours in the middle of the sixth; and 16 hours in
the middle of the seventh, and so on, increasing up to the 90th (degree), where the day
is continual.

The longitude of a place is the distance separating it from the extreme point of the
inhabited Earth in the west, and its latitude is the distance separating it from the
equator. The equator, as we said above, is a line such that all the countries found on
this line have, at all times, the days equal to the nights. All these countries are
without latitude, and all the countries situated at the extreme west are without
longitude. From the extreme west to the extreme east there are 180 degrees; all the
places whose longitude is 90 degrees are at equal distance from the west and the east.
Any place whose longitude is less than 90 degrees is nearer to the west than to the
east, and any place whose longitude is greater than 90 degrees is nearer to the east
than to the west.

The ancients claimed that the terrestrial world was divided into seven parts called
climes. The clime of India depends on Saturn, that of Babel depends on Jupiter; that of
the Turks, on Mars; that of Roum, on the Sun; that of Egypt, on Mercury; and that of
China, on the Moon. Others say that the Ram and Jupiter are allotted to Babel; the
Capricorn and Mercury to India; the Lion and Mars to the Turks; the Balance and the
Sun to Roum; moreover, that the year is divided among twelve constellations, of which
the Ram and its associates belong to the east; the Bull and its associates to the
south; the Twins and their associates to the west; the Crab and its associates to the
north. -- It is also said that, in each clime, there are two great towns corresponding
to the double [...]

[PDF p. 64]

mansions of each planet, except in the clime of the Sun and that of the Moon, these
two latter possessing only a single great town. The towns and fortresses of the seven
climes number 21,600, corresponding to the number of the minutes of the circle of the
sky. Hermes claims that if, instead of the number of minutes, one took that of the
fourths, one would have the total number of men peopling the climes, for each time a
man dies he is replaced by another. It is asserted that the number of great towns and
villages of the first clime, from the point where the Sun rises, is 3,100; that in the
second there are 2,713; in the third 3,079; 2,974 in the fourth, that of Babel; in the
fifth, 3,006; in the sixth 3,508; and in the seventh 3,300, distributed over the
islands.

On the median line of the first clime are situated the countries where the longest day
is 13 hours. For these places the north pole rises above the horizon by 16 2/3 degrees,
which represents the latitude. It extends in breadth as far as the places where the
longest day is 13 1/4 hours and where the pole rises by 20 1/2 degrees, which is the
latitude of those places; its total breadth is 440 miles. It begins at the extremity of
the land of China, crosses it in the southern part, passes to the shores of the Hind,
then to the lands of the Sind, and, crossing the sea, cuts the Arabian peninsula and the
land of Yemen, crosses the sea of Qolzoum, embraces the land of the Abyssinians, cuts
the Nile of Egypt north of Abyssinia, at the town of Dongola in Nubia, and extends over
the land of the west, south of the country of the Berbers, as far as the enveloping
Ocean. In this clime there are twenty mountains, whose height varies from 20 to 1,000
parasangs; one counts there also thirty great rivers whose course, too, varies between
1,000 and 20 parasangs, and fifty great towns. Most of the peoples inhabiting this clime
are of black color. The constellations that govern it are the Ram and the Bow, and it is
placed under the influence of the planet Jupiter. Despite the intensity of the heat, one
meets in this clime an abundance of water and pastures; maize and rice are cultivated
there; but, as there is never a moderate temperature, the vine produces no grapes there
nor the wheat ears. Cattle are very numerous there because of the considerable quantity
of pastures. -- To the east of this clime is the sea, which extends to the 13th degree
beyond the equator; to the west, the Nile and the sea

[PDF p. 65]

of the west. It is from this clime that the Nile of Egypt comes. The east of this clime
is bathed by the eastern sea, which is none other than the sea of India and of Yemen.

In the second clime, the longest day is 13 1/2 hours; the north pole rises there by 24
1/10 degrees, which is the latitude of this point; it extends in length from the limit
of the first clime to the point where the longest day is 13 3/4 hours and where the
elevation of the north pole is 27 1/2 degrees, and this breadth represents a distance of
400 miles. It begins at the lands of the east, crossing China and heading toward the
lands of the Hind and the Sind; then it crosses the Green Sea and the sea of Basra, cuts
the Arabian peninsula in the region of the Negd and of Tehamah; in this clime are
comprised the towns of El-Iamama, El-Bahraïn, Hagar, Mecca, Medina, Et-Taïf, and the
land of the Hedjaz; from there, heading over the sea of Qolzoum, it embraces Upper
Egypt, crosses the Nile, comprises the towns of Qous, Akhmim, Esneh, Antinoe, and
Assouan, extends over the land of the west in the middle of the land of Ifrikiah, and,
passing to the land of the Berbers, ends at the western sea. In this clime there are
seventeen mountains, seventeen great rivers, and four hundred and fifty great towns. The
color of the inhabitants holds the middle between brown and black. Its special
constellation is the Capricorn and its planet Saturn. It is the abode of the nomads,
whose western tribes are the Hadalah, the Sanhagah, the Lamtunah, and the Masoufah, to
whom are attached the nomads of Egypt who inhabit the oases. It is also in this clime
that are comprised the towns of Yahl, Mecca, and Medina, as well as all the land
stretching between the Samaouah of Iraq and the Turkish nomads.

On the median line of the third clime are situated the places where the longest day is
14 hours, and where the pole rises by 30 1/2 1/5 degrees, the latitude of those places;
it extends in breadth from the northern limit of the second clime to the point where the
longest day is 14 1/4 hours, there where the pole rises by 33 degrees, the latitude of
that point; this breadth is 350 miles. It begins in the east, passes north of China and
the lands of India, comprising the town of Kandahar; it embraces the northern Sind, the
lands of Caboul, of Caramania, of Sagestan, as far as the coast of the sea of Basra; the
towns of Istakhar, Sabour, Shiraz, Siraf; extends over the Ahouaz

[PDF p. 66]

and Iraq, the towns of Ouasit, Basra, Bagdad, El-Koufa, El-Ambar, Heit; over Syria as
far as Salamiah, Tyre, Acre, Damascus, Tiberias, Caesarea, Jerusalem, Ascalon, Gaza,
Madian, Qolzoum; over Middle Egypt from north of Antinoe to Fostat-Masr and the shores
of the sea, comprising the Fayoum, Alexandria, Farmah, Tanis, and Damietta; over the
land of Barca as far as Ifrikiah, with Cairouan, and ends at the sea of the west. One
counts in this clime thirty-three high mountains, twenty-two great rivers, and one
hundred and twenty-eight towns. The inhabitants are of brown color. Its constellation is
the Scorpion and its planet Venus. This clime is inhabited without interruption from one
end to the other.

In the middle of the fourth clime are the countries where the longest day is 14 1/2
hours and where the elevation of the north pole -- that is, the latitude -- is 36 1/5
degrees. It extends, in breadth, from the northern limit of the third clime to the point
where the longest day is 14 1/2 1/4 hours, and the latitude 39 1/3 degrees. [Footnote:
the text erroneously reads 29 1/3.] The extent of this clime is 300 miles. It begins in
the east, comprises Tibet and Khorassan, Hagandah, Farghanah, Samarkand, Bokhara, Herat,
Merw, Er-Roud, Sarakhs, Tous, Nisapour, Gourgan, Qoumes, Tabaristan, Qazwin, Deïlem,
Raï, Ispahan, Hamadan, Nehaouend, Dinawa, Mossoul, Nosibeïn, Amad, Ras-el-Aïn,
Shouméisat, Er-Raqqah; crosses Syria; embraces Baies, Moseh, Malatiah, Alep (Aleppo),
Antioch, Tripoli, Es-Sisah, Hamah, Saïda, Tarsus, Amouriat, and Laodicea; cuts the sea
of Syria; extends over the islands of Cyprus and Rhodes; arrives at the land of Tangier,
to end at the sea of the west. In this clime one meets twenty-five high mountains,
twenty-five great rivers, and two hundred and twelve towns; the color of its inhabitants
holds the middle between brown and white; it has for its constellation the Twins and for
its planet Mercury. This clime comprises all the sea of Roum from the west to
Constantinople; it is in this clime that the prophets and apostles appeared and that the
scholars and sages shone; it occupies, indeed, the middle of the climes, three being
situated to its north and three to its south, and it belongs to the domain of the Sun.
After it come, in importance, the third and fifth climes, which are both its neighbors.
As for the other climes, their inhabitants are far inferior in qualities and far less
elevated in virtues, by reason of the deformity of their bodies and the

[PDF p. 67]

wickedness of their nature; such are the Zings and the Abyssinians. Most of the peoples
spread through the first, second, sixth, and seventh climes are Gogs, Magogs, Tatars,
and Saqalibahs (Slavs) or other people of the same kind.

In the middle of the fifth clime are situated the places where the longest day is 15
hours, places where the elevation of the pole -- that is, the latitude -- is 41 1/3
degrees. It extends from the extreme latitude of the fourth clime to the point where the
longest day is 15 1/4 hours, a point whose latitude is 43 degrees. Its extent is 250
miles. It begins in the east, embraces the lands of Gog and Magog, extends north of the
land of Khorassan, embracing Khouarezm, Asbigab, Azerbaijan, Bourda'ah, Sagestan, the
Jordan, and Khalat; passing over the land of Roum, it heads toward Rome the Great and
Spain and ends at the sea of the west. In this clime one counts thirty high mountains,
fifteen great rivers, and two hundred great towns. Most of its inhabitants have white
skin; its constellation is the Water-Carrier and its planet the Moon.

In the middle of the sixth clime are the places where the longest day is 15 1/2 hours,
places where the elevation of the north pole -- that is, the latitude -- is 45 2/5
degrees. It extends from the northern limit of the fifth clime to the point where the
longest day is 15 1/2 1/4 hours, a point whose latitude is 47 1/4 degrees: the extent of
this clime is 210 miles. It begins in the east, crosses the land of the Turks from the
sea of Kheir and of the Tartars to the region of the Khazars, passes north of their
encampments, comprises Allan, El-Sherir, the land of Borgan, Constantinople, and
northern Spain, and ends at the enveloping Ocean. In this clime there are twenty-two
high mountains, thirty-two great rivers, and ninety great towns. Most of its inhabitants
are of a color intermediate between white and blond; its constellation is the Crab and
its planet Mars.

The middle of the seventh clime is occupied by the places where the longest day is 16
hours exactly; in these places the elevation of the north pole -- that is, the latitude
-- is 48 2/3 degrees; this clime extends from the northern limit of the sixth clime to
the points where the longest day is 16 1/4

[PDF p. 68]

hours, points whose latitude is 50 1/2 degrees; its extent is 185 miles. From this it is
easy to see that the space between the southern limit of the first clime and the
northern limit of the seventh is 3 1/2 hours, representing an elevation of the pole of
38 degrees, or in miles 2,140. The seventh clime begins in the east at the land of Gog
and Magog, extends over the region occupied by the Turks, skirts the sea of Gourgan to
the north, cuts the sea of Roum at the land of Gourgan and of the Saqalibah, and extends
as far as the enveloping sea in the west. This clime contains ten high mountains, forty
great rivers, and twenty-two great towns; its inhabitants are of blond color; its
constellation is the Balance and its planet the Sun.

In each of these seven climes, the peoples differ in language and color as well as in
nature, manners, opinions, religion, mind, habits, acts, industry, customs, and worship,
and none of them resembles another. It is the same for the animals, minerals, and
plants, whose form, taste, color, and scent are diverse, by reason of the differences of
the atmosphere, the aspect of the region, the nature of the soil, the sweetness or the
bitterness of the waters -- things that vary according to whether such or such
constellation rises on the horizon of the country, or whether such or such planet passes
to the zenith of such or such point of the earth, sending its rays there, as is very well
explained in the scientific books. Let the sensible man therefore reflect! Let the
intelligent man guide himself by God's decisions regarding his creature, by the laws it
has pleased him to fix, and by the acts it seems good to him to accomplish! There is no
God but him!

It must be said further that the inhabited quarter of the earth, with its various
regions, was divided among seven great peoples, who are: the Chinese, the Indians, the
Blacks, the Berbers, Roum, the Turks, and the Persians. The southeast of the earth is the
Chinese's, the northeast the Turks', the full south the Indians', the full north Roum's,
the southwest the Blacks', the northwest the Berbers'; as for Persia, it occupies the
center and is surrounded by the six other peoples.

[PDF p. 69]

CHAPTER III
OF THE SITUATION OF EGYPT ON THE EARTH AND OF ITS PLACE AMONG THE SEVEN CLIMES

Since God has made easy for us the task of describing the general state of the earth and
of setting out what concerns each of its climes, let us now speak of the position of
Egypt in relation to both.

A part of Egypt belongs to the second clime and the rest to the third. All the upper
part of the Said, with Qous, Akhmim, Esneh, Antinoe, Assouan, is situated in the second
clime; while all the part of Egypt situated north of Antinoe -- that is, the lower Said
from Siout to Fostat-Masr, the Fayoum, Cairo, Alexandria, Farmah, Tanis, Damietta --
belongs to the third clime. [Footnote: there is an error here, Siout being not north of
Antinoe but rather about 20 leagues to the south.] The longitude of the city of
Masr-Fostat and of Cairo -- that is, their distance from the extreme western point of the
inhabited earth -- is 55 degrees; their latitude -- that is, their distance from the
equator -- is 30 degrees; the longest day there is 14 hours, and the maximum elevation of
the Sun in the sky is 83 1/3 1/4 degrees. Fostat-Masr and Cairo have Mecca to the
southeast quarter. The upper Said, being situated to the south of Fostat and several days'
march away, is for this reason directly to the west of Mecca, which is separated from
Egypt by impracticable regions; for to the east of Egypt, beyond the eastern mountain, is
the sea of Qolzoum. To the west extends the western desert, to the south the desert of
Nubia and Abyssinia, to the north the sea of Syria and the sands covering the space
between the sea of Roum and the sea of Qolzoum. Ibn Khordadhabah, in his book entitled The
Regions and the Roads, says that between Masr and Bagdad there are 1,710 miles, or 570
parasangs, or 140-odd post-stages. Between Masr and Syria -- I mean

[PDF p. 70]

Damascus -- there are 365 miles, or 121 2/3 parasangs, or 30-and-a-fraction post-stages.
Ibn Khordadhabah adds that the extent of Abyssinia and of the Soudan is seven years' (of
march), that Egypt is only the sixtieth part of the Soudan, and the Soudan a fraction of
the earth. In the book of Orosius it is said that the lower Said has, to the east,
Palestine, and, to the west, the land of Libya; that Upper Egypt extends in the direction
of the east; that its limits are to the north the Canal of the west, to the south the
Great Sea, to the west Middle Egypt, and to the east the sea of Qolzoum, and that in this
country there are twenty-eight different peoples.
   ---
   [Footnote: this name is written "Ourious" in the Boulaq edition. In a preceding
passage (see above, p. 28) the name of the same author is spelled "Ourosious."]

[PDF p. 71]

CHAPTER IV
LIMITS AND ORIENTATION OF EGYPT

Delimitation is the figuration of the bounded country with all it contains; the limit is
the end of a thing. The limits are more or less extensive according to the thing bounded.
The directions serving to delimit dwellings and localities are four in number: the north,
in the direction of the celestial north pole, recognizable by its constellation, the
Capricorn, and by the Farqadeïn (b and g of the Little Bear); diametrically opposite to
the north is the south, situated on the side of the celestial south pole, to which Canopus
and the stars of the Ship that neighbor it are very close; the third side is the east,
where the Sun rises at the two equinoxes -- that is, at the initial point of the Ram at
the beginning of the spring season, and at the initial point of the Balance at the
beginning of the autumn season. The fourth side is the west, where the Sun sets at the two
equinoxes of which we have just spoken. These four points are fixed in the firmament and
remain invariable despite the changes of the seasons, and it is by them that one delimits
the lands and the dwellings they contain; it is on them that men guide themselves in their
travels, and by them that they determine the direction of their mihrabs. -- The east and
the west are well known; the north and the south, joined to the east and the west, form
the equal sides of a square embracing the sky. The line that joins the two points north
and south is called the meridian and cuts at a right angle the line passing through the
points east and west, which is called the equator. The spaces intercepted by these two
lines are equal.
