A man facing the south has constantly behind him the north, to his right the west, and the
east to his left. These four points serve to delimit the countries, the lands, the
houses. However the Egyptians, in their orientation, instead of the term "south," employ
the expression qibli (direction of the qiblah) and say, for example: "the qibli limit
ends at such a place" and not "the

[PDF p. 72]

south limit." Likewise, they say: "the bahari (direction of the sea) limit ends at such a
place," meaning by the word bahari the north direction. These two terms of orientation are
for certain countries a source of error. Thus, for a place situated on the same latitude
as Mecca but on a lesser longitude, the direction of the qiblah will be exactly to the
east; on the contrary, for a place situated on the same latitude as Mecca but on a greater
longitude, the direction of the qiblah will be exactly to the west; hence, if one wishes
to give the delimitation of something, land or house, in these localities, using the four
cardinal points, two of these points will merge into one. Likewise for the expression
bahari, which among the Egyptians is the direction opposite to qibli, so that they express
the orientation of the lands and dwellings situated between these two points by means of
these two terms habitual to them -- which is also at times a source of error, the
direction of the qiblah being for certain countries the same as that of the sea.

This being established, know that the limit of Egypt starts from the sea of Roum, at
Alexandria -- or according to others at Barca -- crosses the mainland, passes behind the
oases, and continues as far as Nubia; there it bends, follows the frontier of Nubia and
the limit of the (district) of Assouan, and, skirting the territory of the Beggahs situated
south of Assouan, reaches the sea of Qolzoum; then, coasting this sea, it passes Qolzoum in
the direction of Sinai and, crossing the desert of Tih of the Beni Israïl, arrives at the
sea of Roum near the land of Gefar, beyond El-Arich and Raphah; finally, returning along
the shore, it follows the sea of Roum as far as Alexandria and ends at the point from
which it started, in the vicinity of Barca.

Abou-s-Salt Omayah ben Abd el-Aziz, in his opuscule on Egypt, says that this country is
situated entirely in the inhabited earth, partly in the second clime, partly in the third,
but in this last for the greater part. Those who have occupied themselves with the annals
and history of Egypt report that its limit extends, in length, from the town of Barca on
the south coast of the sea of Roum to Aïlat on the gulf formed by the sea of Abyssinia, of
the Zings, of India, and of China. This distance represents about forty days'
   ---
   [Footnote: that is, from one longitude to another.]

[PDF p. 73]

march; its breadth is comprised between Assouan and the lands of the High Said situated on
the same latitude along the land of Nubia, and Rosetta and the mouths of the Nile that
empty into the sea in the vicinity of that town. This breadth corresponds to about thirty
days' march.

Egypt is bounded, in its breadth, by two mountains, of which one, situated to the east of
the Nile, bears the name of Moqattam, and the other extends to the west of the river;
between the two flows the Nile. These are two sterile mountains, not very high and very
close together from Assouan to Fostat. From this point, they separate and move gradually
away from each other, the Moqattam heading toward the east and the other mountain toward
the west, the space intercepted by these two mountains going always enlarging. In
consequence, Egypt widens from Fostat to the shore of the sea of Roum, on which are
situated Farma, Tanis, Damietta, Rosetta, and Alexandria. It is at the sea that its
breadth ends -- that is, the distance between its most southerly point and its most
northerly point. In more precise terms, this distance does not reach thirty days but falls
short of it by an inappreciable quantity, for the space between the latitude of Assouan,
the most southerly point of Egypt, and that of Tennis, its most northerly point, is about
nine divisions (of the circle) and a tenth (9 deg 6'). Between its two extreme longitudes
there is, give or take a little, the same distance; it is about 520 miles, representing
twenty days' march; travelers, in average march, divide the route separating these two
points into as many stages, or a little more, because of the sinuosity of the roads and
the absence of direct routes.

According to El-Qoda'i, the name of Egypt is given to all the country stretching from
El-Arich to the confines of Libya and of Maraqia: beyond the land of Maraqia is the
Pentapolis, otherwise called the land of Barca. To go there, starting from El-Arich,
forty nights are needed, the route constantly following the shore of the sea of Roum, the
northern limit of Egypt and the point from which the north wind blows for it in the
direction of the qiblah or nearly so. Having reached the

[PDF p. 74]

extreme limit of the land of Maraqiah, one turns to the left and, facing south, one crosses
the sands and heads toward the qiblah, leaving on the right the sands of Africa and on the
left the land of Egypt, until one has passed the Fayoum and the four oases; this part of
the route followed forms the western limit of Egypt. At the extremity of the land of the
oases, one faces east and marches in the direction of the Nile; after eight stages one
arrives at the river, which one follows by going up the bank; having then reached the
extreme limit of the Muslim lands, which in this region are bounded by Nubia, and crossing
then the Nile, one marches from Assouan toward the east, turning one's back on Assouan and
heading toward Aïdab, a town situated on the sea of the Hedjaz. From Assouan to Aïdab there
are fifteen stages; this is what is called the southern frontier of Egypt and the point
from which the south wind blows for it; crossing the sea at Aïdab, one lands on the
territory of the Hedjaz, at El-Haura, a locality where the land of Egypt begins, and which
is situated on the same latitude as the city of the Prophet. The fraction of sea thus
delimited is the sea of Qolzoum, which penetrates into the land of Egypt, bathing it on the
east, the west, and the north; on the eastern shore of this sea is the territory of
El-Haura, then Tensa, En-Nabq, the districts of Madian and of Aïlat, and beyond this last
country, the waters extend as far as the Moqattam of Egypt (?). To the west, they bathe the
territory stretching from Aïdab to the sea of the Ostriches and to the Moqattam. To the
north, they reach the town of Qolzoum and the mountain of Tor. From Qolzoum to Farmah there
are a day and a night of march; this stretch of land constitutes the barrier separating the
two seas, that of the Hedjaz and that of Roum. All this route forms the eastern limit of
Egypt, from El-Haura to El-Arich; it is the point from which the east wind blows for the
Egyptians. Such are the limits of Egypt -- but all the territories situated beyond the
western frontier were conquered by the Egyptians, as well as all the ports from Barca to
Spain.
   ---
   [Footnote: I suspect the text is faulty here; however, as will be seen further on, the
Moqattam, according to Maqrizi, extends from Cairo into the Arabian peninsula and beyond.
There would be nothing astonishing, in that case, in the sea of Qolzoum bathing the foot of
some spur of this mountain.]

[PDF p. 75]

CHAPTER V
OF THE SEA OF QOLZOUM

The word qolzoum signifies "anguish" and "constriction." This word was given to the sea of
Qolzoum because it is constricted between mountains. Now, Egypt being constricted between
two seas, that of Qolzoum to the east and that of Roum to the north, and the sea of Qolzoum
penetrating into the land of Egypt, as was explained above, it is fitting for our book to
give a description of it.

This sea bears the name of Qolzoum only in the land of Egypt, because, to the east of Egypt
and to the west of this sea, is a town named Qolzoum, destroyed today, as will be explained,
God willing, in the part of this book where we will treat of the villages and the towns. The
name of the town was therefore given to the sea, the word Qolzoum being employed in the
genitive; it is called in Hebrew yom souf. In sum, this sea is only a gulf detached from the
great sea that envelops the earth and is called the Ocean, or again the Sea of Darkness,
because of the thickness of the fogs that rise from it and the powerlessness of the sun to
dissipate them; thus these mists are very dense and the obscurity impenetrable; the waves of
this ocean are enormous and increase its horror still more. Of it one knows only what is
known of a few points of its shore and of some of its nearest islands. Near the western shore
of this sea, from which issues the sea of Roum -- of which, God willing, we will soon speak
-- are the Khaledat islands which, it is said, are six in number, inhabited by a savage
people; to the east, on the side of China, are six other islands, named the Sabali islands,
in which, in the first times of Islam, some Alids fleeing death landed. From this ocean issue
six seas; God meant to speak of the two greatest of them [...]

[PDF p. 76]

... when he said: "He has separated the two seas that touch" (Koran, LV, 19) and: "He
has placed a barrier between the two seas" (Koran, XXVII, 62). One of these seas is to
the east and the other to the west. The eastern sea bears the names of sea of China,
Indian sea, Persian sea, sea of Yemen, sea of Abyssinia, according to the regions it
bathes; that of the west is named the sea of Roum. The sea of India -- that is, the one
that takes its origin in the east -- begins to the east of China, 13 degrees beyond the
equator, and heads toward the west, bathing China, India, then Kanbana and Et-Taïr of
the land of Karman. At the land of Karman it divides into two branches, of which one
bears the name of Persian sea and the other that of sea of Yemen. The latter begins at a
mountainous cape named the Cape of the Skull. From this point it advances toward the
town of Tafar, skirts El-Masgar and the land of Hadramaout as far as Aden and
Bab-el-Mandeb. The total length of the Indian sea (from the beginning to Bab-el-Mandeb)
is 8,000 miles, and its breadth 1,700 miles in some places, but at times its breadth is
less. Arrived at Bab-el-Mandeb, it forms the sea of Qolzoum. The Mandeb is a mountain 12
miles long, and the breadth of the strait is such that a man placed on one of its banks
can make out a man placed on the opposite bank. From Bab-el-Mandeb, this sea heads toward
the north between the two shores of Zebid and El-Heroun as far as Athr, formerly a royal
residence. From there, passing Hala, it arrives at 'Asfan and Anmar, port of the city of
the Prophet; from there it skirts the region facing El-Hagfa, a locality named today
Rabarh, arrives at El-Haura, Madian, Aïlat, Tor, Faran, and the town of Qolzoum. At
Qolzoum it returns toward the south, passes Qoseïr, port of Qouss, then from Qoseïr to
Aïdab, port of the Begahs, and from Aïdab to the land of Zeila, on the coast of
Abyssinia, which serves Berber. The length of this sea is 1,500 miles and its breadth
400 miles, and often less. It is a sea disagreeable to the sight and to the smell. It is
this sea that receives the Tigris and the Euphrates; it bathes the lands of India and
of Yemen, peninsulas that the water surrounds on three sides; it bars the course of the
river Mahran as the sea of Roum obstructs the course of the Nile. In this sea, between
Qolzoum and Aïlat, is a place named Faran, near which rises a mountain that it is very
difficult for ships to avoid, because of the frequency of the shifts of wind and the
violence with which it blows in the channel formed by

[PDF p. 77]

two mountains there; it is a kind of lake, 6 miles wide, named the lake of Garandal; it
is there, it is asserted, that Pharaoh drowned; when the south wind blows it is
impossible for ships to cross this lake. The Garandal is, it is said, the name of a
statue placed there formerly to close the exit from Egypt to those who had incurred the
disgrace of the king or who wished to escape him. When Moses, at the head of the
Israelites, left Egypt heading toward the east, God ordered him to stop facing this
statue. The news of the flight of the Hebrews having reached Pharaoh, he thought that
the statue, according to its habit, would prevent Moses and his people from continuing
their route; he therefore set out, with his armies, in pursuit of Moses and the Hebrews,
hoping to seize the fugitives. God has recounted to us how he drowned. As for the story
of Moses, it will be spoken of, in connection with the church of Dimouah, in the part of
this book that treats of the churches of the Jews.

The sea of Qolzoum contains fifteen islands, of which four are peopled: the island of
Dahlak, the island of Souakin, the island of Na'man, and the island of Samry. This sea
gives birth to two straits, one minuscule, in the land of India, and the other which
separates the Soudan from Yemen and whose breadth, at its narrowest part, is about two
parasangs. The shortest distance from this sea to the sea of Roum, across the
territories of Syria and Egypt, is hardly more than a day's march.

[PDF p. 78]

CHAPTER VI
OF THE SEA OF ROUM

Since several towns of Egypt are situated on the coast of the sea of Roum -- such as
Alexandria, Damietta, Tanis, Farma, El-Arich, and others -- and since Egypt is bathed on
the north by this sea into which the Nile empties, it is well to give some information on
it.

As we have already said, the sea of Roum takes its origin in the west, in the fourth
clime, between Spain and Morocco, and extends as far as Constantinople. It is recounted
that it was Alexander the Great who dug it and brought it from the western ocean.
Formerly, it is said, the peninsula of Spain and the land of the Berbers formed but a
single land inhabited by the Berbers and the Spaniards, who plundered one another. This
lasted until the reign of Alexander the Great, son of Saliqus (Philip), son of Aricos,
son of Douban. The Spaniards begged this prince to establish between them and the Berbers
an arm of the sea that would prevent these two peoples from passing into each other's
land. Alexander therefore dug a ditch 18 miles long and 12 wide; on each side he built
masonry on which a bridge was placed allowing passage. On this bridge guards were posted,
charged with preventing the Berbers from crossing it without permission. Now, the level
of the Ocean being higher than the ceiling of this canal, the water invaded it, covered
the masonry as well as the bridge, flooded a quantity of lands in its passage, and
destroyed a number of countries. The legend adds that the sailors assert that at certain
times, despite a favorable wind, they cannot continue their route, because of the
obstacles they meet, and because the hull of the ships gets caught between the
battlements crowning the parapets of the bridge, or between the two parapets themselves.
Subsequently, the ditch lengthened and

[PDF p. 79]

widened to the point of becoming a sea 18 miles wide. At low tide, it is claimed, one can
still today see the bridge -- but all these sayings seem to me pure fables. For this sea
was known as bathing the coasts of Egypt many centuries before Alexander, whether it was
formed by human hand in primitive times, or whether this human origin is fabulous. In any
case, the era in which Alexander lived is recent compared with the existence of this sea.
And God knows it better than we!

This strait, difficult for navigation, is, moreover, of a frightful horror because of the
agitation of its waves. The sea, having passed this strait, skirts the land of the
Berbers, the north of the far west to the middle of the lands of the setting sun, bathes
Ifrikiah (Tunisia), Barca, Alexandria, the north of the desert of Tih, Palestine, the
coast of Syria; then, making a bend, it heads toward El-Alaïa and Antioch, passes outside
Constantinople, and ends at the enveloping Ocean from which it issued. The length of this
sea is 5,000 miles according to some, 6,000 miles according to others, and its breadth
varies between 700 and 300 miles. One meets there 170 islands inhabited by numerous and
known peoples, but whose description does not enter into the plan of this book. Among
these islands are Sicily, Sourqa, and Crete.

Facing the sea of India, to the west, is a sea starting from the enveloping Ocean, to the
west of the land of the Zings, and ending in the vicinity of the mountain of Qomor; it is
into this sea that empties the Nile crossing Abyssinia, and, at the bottom of this sea,
are the Khaledat islands where the extreme western meridian passes. Opposite the sea of
Syria to the east are the sea of Gergan, which, it is said, rejoins the enveloping Ocean
by passing between high mountains, and the sea of Saqalba, a sea that begins in the west
between the 6th and 7th climes. It is a very vast sea, containing numerous islands, among
others the island of Andalusia; but this last is attached to the continent by a mountain
shaped like an arm, which links Spain to the continent at the height of Barcelona. To
these seas is attached that of Gog and Magog, an immense sea containing marvelous things
whose description does not enter into the scope of this work. The extent of the shore of
the sea of Roum is, it is said, four months' march.

Abou'r-Rihan Mohammed ben Ahmed Albirouni, in his book entitled Delimitation and
Orientation of Dwellings for Determining the Extent of Inhabited Countries, recounts

[PDF p. 80]

that certain kings of Persia, during their domination over Egypt, conceived the idea of
digging the space intercepted by the seas of Qolzoum and of Roum, and of suppressing the
barrier separating them; the first was Shasis, son of king Tarates, then king Darius. But
the enterprise failed, because the level of the sea of Qolzoum is higher than that of
Egypt. In the time of Greek domination, Ptolemy III entrusted the enterprise to
Archimedes, on condition that no harm should result from it; but the Roman emperors had
this canal filled in to prevent their enemies from reaching them. The philosophers who
have occupied themselves with history claim that the space between the territory of
Alexandria and Constantinople was formerly a land planted with sycamores and peopled, but
unhealthy; that the inhabitants were Greeks; that it was Alexander who brought the sea
there, and that since then this land has been under the waters. It is there that dwelt, it
is said, the bird Cycnos -- a bird whose magnificent voice becomes more beautiful as death
approaches: during the last seven days of its life, the voice of this bird is such that no
one can hear it, for the charm of its song captivates the heart of the one who listens to
it, to the point that the latter dies of it; for during these days, full of well-being and
joy and taking no rest, he follows the bird that is going to die. It is recounted that the
inventor of music was a philosopher who wished to hear the voice of the swan at that
precise moment. But fearing that too sudden a hearing would kill him, he stopped his ears
hermetically, then, approaching the animal, reopened them little by little, taking three
days to unstop them completely; he wished by this means to come gradually to hear it, so
as not to be seized abruptly by the beauty of the bird's song and die. This bird was, it
is asserted, destroyed, and there remained no trace either of it or of its young, because
the water submerged it in its nest, along with its brood, during the night, and absolutely
nothing of it remained. It is recounted that a king, wishing to put a philosopher to
death, gave him a poisoned cup to drink and warned him of it. The philosopher at once
showed great joy and lively gladness. "O sage," asked the king, "why is this?" "What
then," answered the philosopher, "am I not worth as much as a swan!"

[PDF p. 81]

CHAPTER VII
OF THE ORIGIN OF THE NAME OF MASR, OF ITS MEANING, AND OF THE DIFFERENT NAMES OF EGYPT

In primitive times, before the flood, Egypt bore, it is said, the name of Gezlah;
subsequently it was called Masr; the scholars do not agree on the reason that caused this
name to be given to Egypt. Some say it comes to it from Masr, son of Mourkabil, son of
Douabil, son of Ariab, son of Adam; that one is the first Masr. Others claim, on the
contrary, that it comes to it from the second Masr, son of Misraïm, son of Ya'rouch the
mighty, son of the first Misraïm; this second Masr gave his name to Masr, son of Bensar,
son of Cham, after the flood. According to others, finally, its name would come to it from
the third Masr, son of Bensar, son of Cham, son of Noah. For some, it is a foreign word
that does not take the nunnation; for others, it is derived from Arabic. Those who plead
in favor of the foreign origin of the name of Masr rely on the accounts collected by the
historians on the arrival in Egypt of Masr, son of Bensar, son of Cham, and on the
division of the soil among his children; hence its name.

Here is what one reads in El-Hassan ben Ahmed el-Hamdani: "Masr, son of Cham, is the same
as Misraïm," and he adds that Bensar, son of Hermes, son of Herdous, is the forefather of
Alexander. He affirms also that Louma, son of Cham, married a daughter of Shouaïl, son of
Yaphet, son of Noah, who gave him as sons Bouqir and Qobt, father of the Copts of Egypt;
this is what made it believed that Masr was son of Cham, while in reality he is the son of
Hermes, son of Herdouch, son of Bitoum, son of Raoua, son of Lithi, of Younnan. It is
from him that Egypt took its name of Masr, which is a Macedonian word (?).

Abou-l-Hassan el-Maçaoudi, in his book on The News of the Times, recounts that, discord
having arisen among the sons of Adam, and the sons of Qabil (Cain), son of Adam, having
set about molesting their brothers, Naqraouch the mighty, son of

[PDF p. 82]

Misraïm, son of Mourkabil, son of Douabil, son of Ariab, son of Adam, set out, with
seventy horsemen all valiant, in search of a corner of land where they could live safe
from the aggressions of their brothers. They continued their march until they had arrived
at the Nile; they skirted the river and, seeing the extent and beauty of the valley, were
marveled and said: "This country is good to inhabit and to cultivate." And they settled
there, peopled it, built there magnificent constructions and admirable edifices, and
Naqraouch founded the city of Masr, to which he gave the name of his father Misraïm.
Naqraouch was powerful and strong, and moreover possessed knowledge. The genies seconded
him in the destruction of his brothers and obeyed him always thereafter. He had learned
some of the sciences formerly taught by Zouamil to Adam, and that is what gave him
superiority over the great ones and the kings who preceded him. When he was master (of
Egypt), he had a city built at the spot where he had pitched his tent; the stones of the
mountains were cut, the lead mines worked, and a city was built to which was given the
name of Amsous, and where towers were raised, each a hundred cubits high; then, the
country becoming fertile and peopled, he had towns and villages built and occupied all the
points of the country that seemed to him good to occupy. Then the Nile was dug to bring
the water of the river toward all the inhabited points. Before this time, there was no
regularity in the course of the river; it went at random, spread over the lands, and the
water returned toward Nubia; it was embanked, canals were derived from it that watered
most of the towns that had been founded. A special canal passed by the city of Amsous,
which it crossed through its middle.

After the flood, Egypt took the name of Masr, son of Bensar, son of Cham, son of Noah,
because the priest Qlimoun, having left Egypt, had taken refuge with Noah and had adopted
his religion -- he, his family, his son, and his disciples -- and because, having gone up
with Noah into the ark, his daughter married Bensar, son of Cham, son of Noah. On leaving
the ark, Noah divided the earth among his children. Now the daughter of Qlimoun had given
Bensar a son named Misraïm, and Qlimoun said to Noah: "O prophet of God, send my son with
me, that I may take him to my country, show him my treasures, and teach him the sciences
and the secrets he must know." And he took him with him, as well as all the people of his
house. He was then a young boy accustomed to comfort. On approaching

[PDF p. 83]

Egypt, Qlimoun had a shelter built for him of tree branches covered with grasses of the
land. Later a city was raised there that was named Darsan -- that is, "gate of paradise."
The land was cultivated, trees and gardens were planted from Darsan to the sea, and in
this space there were nothing but fields, gardens, and dwellings. The companions of
Misraïm were vigorous; they cut the rocks, raised towers and edifices, and led the
happiest life. It is recounted that the Egyptians chose for their king Misraïm, son of
Bensar, in the time of Talegh, son of Amer, son of Shamekh, son of Arphaxad, son of Sem,
son of Noah; he reigned in Masr, a powerful city on the Nile to which he had given his
name. Misraïm, it is said, planted with his own hand trees whose fruits were prodigious,
so much so that an orange cut in two formed the load of a camel and the cucumbers reached
the length of fourteen spans. Misraïm is also, it is said, the first to have built boats
on the Nile, and the first of these boats was 300 cubits long by 100 cubits wide.
According to tradition, Misraïm married a daughter of the caste of priests, by whom he had
a son named Qobtim. The latter, at the age of seventy, married a woman by whom he had four
sons: Qobtim, Ashmoun, Atrib, and Sa; then they multiplied and spread over the land, which
was blessed for them. It is recounted that on their arrival they were thirty men, and that
a city was built to which was given the name of Nafat, a word that in their language means
"thirty"; it is the same as Memphis. [Footnote: there must be a printing error; the name
of the city should have been "Nisafat," the word "thirty" being rendered in Egyptian.] The
companions of the priest Qlimoun discovered the treasures of Egypt and unveiled its
sciences: they worked the mines, learned the sciences of talismans and alchemy, built
towns elsewhere than on the river -- among others Raqoudat, where Alexandria later rose.
Near death, Misraïm designated as his successor his son Qobtim. He had already divided the
land among his sons, leaving to Qobtim the territory between Qouft and Assouan; to Ashmoun
the part stretching from Ashmoun to Memphis; to Atrib the whole Haouf; and to Sa the space
stretching from the region of Sa northward to Barca. Qobtim therefore said to his brother:
"Take for your share, from Barca to the setting sun"; and the latter became the possessor
of Africa and

[PDF p. 84]

the master of the peoples with the cleft lip. Qobtim ordered each of his sons to build
himself a city in the place assigned to him; moreover, he prescribed that they should, after
his death, dig him an underground chamber, pave it with white marble, deposit his body
there, bury there all the gold and gems that were in his treasures, and engrave there the
name of God to prevent his body from being carried off. They therefore dug him an
underground chamber 150 cubits long, placed in the middle a pedestal plated with leaves of
gold, and traced four doors each guarded by a statue of gold, crowned with a crown set with
gems and seated on a throne of gold inlaid with emeralds; on the chest of each statue were
engraved verses to protect the corpse. Then they deposited the body of Misraïm in a marble
coffin plated with gold, and they engraved this inscription on the pedestal: "Misraïm, son
of Bensar, son of Cham, son of Noah, died seven hundred years after the flood. He never
worshiped the idols; thus he was never old, nor sick, nor sorrowful, nor morose; his
strength resided in the name of God Most High. None will approach him but a king, issued
from seven kings faithful to the religion of the God of the faiths, who will have believed
in the mission of the one who, at the end of time, will come with the Book and invite men
to convert to the true faith." And they placed near him, on this pedestal, a thousand cut
emeralds, a thousand statuettes of precious stones, a thousand vessels filled with
magnificent pearls, and a quantity of divine works, perfumes, marvelous talismans, and
ingots of gold; then they covered the whole with rocks, spread sand over it between two
mountains, and his son Qobtim took the reins of the kingdom.

Abou Mohammed Abd el-Melek ben Hecham, in his book of the Precious Gifts, says that Abd
Shams was son of Yachkhob, son of Ya'rab, son of Qahtan, son of Houd, brother of Ad, son
of Amer, son of Shalekh, son of Arphaxad, son of Sem, son of Noah; that the true name of
this Abd Shams was Amer, but that he was called Abd Shams because he was the first man to
worship the sun; he was also named Saba, for he is the first who gave himself over to
pillage. That one is Saba the Ancient, father of Himyar and of Kahlan, who reigned after
his father Yachkhob over the land of Yemen, gathered the Beni Qahtan and the Beni Houd,
and set out with them on an expedition. With them he arrived in the land of Babel,
conquered it, and killed all that opposed his passage; from there he reached Armenia,
seized the land of the descendants of Yaphet, son of Noah, and wished

[PDF p. 85]

next to go to Syria and Mesopotamia. As he was told: "For that you must retrace your
steps," he had a bridge built over the sea, by means of which he was able to reach Syria,
and seized that country as far as Ed-Darb. In that time there were no inhabitants beyond
Ed-Darb; he therefore formed the design of conquering the land of the Arabs, stopped at
the edge of the Nile, and gathered his council: "I have resolved," he said, "to build a
city in the isthmus separating the two seas of Roum and of Qolzoum, a city that will
serve as a separation between the East and the West." "O king," answered the councilors,
"the design is excellent." And he built a city that he named Masr; he established as
governor of it his son Babilioun, then continued his route toward the land of the
descendants of Cham, son of Noah, who inhabit the desert as far as Yamouniat and
Ya'mouniat of the Copts. He attacked the confederation of these tribes, carried off their
children, as he had done in the East; that is why he was given the name of Saba. Then he
returned to Egypt, crossed it to go to Syria and from there reach the Hedjaz. At the
moment of departing, he gave these counsels to his son Babilioun:

    Here is what must be said to Babilioun, and it is a wise word:
        Since you have taken the reins of the East and the West, be a good prince
    toward the sons of Cham; take in all things the just mean;
        and if they turn one day from the truth, draw near to them.
    If, in their words, and through obedience, they show themselves just,
        desiring what is just and equitable, be just also.
    In critical moments do not let your designs appear,
        one would take boldness from it against you; act with decision.
    Do not levy the tax unjustly,
        and, when it comes in, do not keep it for yourself, but be generous.
    Correct with the sword those who hate you, for,
        seeing decision in you, the hateful one will make himself agreeable.
    Be gentle and firm toward the man of elevated sentiments;
        do not show yourself violent toward him, but agreeable.
    For those who implore you, be the refuge and the clemency,
        for it is the generous man who is invoked.
    Beware of short expeditions; for,
        in all circumstances, God knows how to dispense wealth.

Then, having returned to Yemen, he built the dam of Mareb, intended to close the reservoir
into which empty seventy rivers that water a space three months long by as much in width,
and died at the age of five hundred years. After [...]

[PDF p. 86]

him reigned his son Himyar, son of Saba. The sons of Cham revolted against Babilioun and
attempted to ravage Egypt. Babilioun called to his aid his brother Himyar, who went to
Egypt, marched as far as the lands of the West, and remained there a hundred years,
building towns and raising edifices. Babilioun, son of Saba, died at Masr and was replaced
by his son Amri'l-Qaïs, son of Babilioun. Then Himyar, son of Saba, died at the age of
four hundred and forty-four years, after four hundred years of reign. After him reigned
Ouaïl, son of Himyar, who, after his death, was replaced by his son Saksak, son of Ouaïl.
It is that one who was surnamed Mouqa'qa' el-Hamd (the shaker of glory). Discord having
arisen in the kingdom of Himyar, Saksak fought the rebels, marched as far as Syria, met,
at Ramleh, 'Amer, son of Amri'l-Qaïs, son of Babilioun, son of Saba, who had taken the
government after the death of his father, and went to meet him with presents. He confirmed
him in Egypt, where he remained until the arrival of Abraham, the Beloved of God, to whom
he made a present of Hagar. [Footnote: this entire passage, up to the words "Abou-l-Qassem
... says," is missing from most of the manuscripts. Perhaps it was interpolated by one of
the readers of the work. (Note of the Boulaq edition.)]

Abou-l-Qassem Abd er-Rahman ben Abd Allah ben Abd el-Hakem, in his book of the Conquests
and Chronicles of Egypt, says, on the authority of Abd Allah ben Abbas: Noah had four
children -- Sem, Cham, Japhet, and Yokhtan -- and he supplicated God, asking him to grant
his gifts to his sons and their posterity, which would multiply by the favor of God and
his blessing. God consented to it. Then Noah called his children, who were asleep, for it
was daybreak. He began with Sem, who answered him by running up and who called his children
also, among whom Arphaxad alone answered; the two went to Noah, who, placing his right hand
on Sem and his left on Arphaxad, son of Sem, asked God to grant Sem the most magnificent
of his blessings and to choose the kings and prophets from among the descendants of
Arphaxad. -- Then Noah called Cham, turning right and left, but Cham did not answer and did
not run up to his father, neither he nor any of his children. Then Noah asked God to make
the descendants of Cham wretched and to make them the servants of the descendants of Sem.
Now Masr, son of Bensar, son of Cham, was sleeping near the latter and, having heard the
curse pronounced by Noah on

[PDF p. 87]

his grandfather and his line, rose, ran toward Noah, and said to him: "O my forefather, if
my grandfather, nor any other of his children, has answered you, I at least run up;
address therefore to God one of your prayers for me." Noah, much rejoiced, placed his hand
on the head of Masr and said: "O my God, this one has answered my call; bless him as well
as his posterity, and give him for an abode the blessed land, mother of regions and refuge
of the servants of God, the land whose river is the most admirable of the rivers of the
world. Put in it the best of your blessings; make it humble for this child and his
posterity; submit it to them, and let them be its powerful masters." -- And he called his
son Yaphet (who did not answer), nor any of his children. Then Noah implored God against
them, asking that he make them the worst of creatures. -- And Sem lived blessed until his
death, as did Arphaxad his son; and royalty, beloved of God, and prophecy and blessing
remained in the house of Arphaxad, son of Sem.

The eldest of the children of Cham was Chanaan, the one whose mother was pregnant at the
time of the avenging cataclysm (the flood). Noah having cursed him, he became black; he
had as his share strength, violence, and harshness; it is he who was the father of the
Blacks and the Abyssinians. The second son of Cham was Qouch, father of the inhabitants of
India and the Sind; the third Phut, son of Cham, ancestor of the Berbers; and the youngest
Bensar, son of Cham, stock of all the Copts. Bensar, son of Cham, had in turn four sons:
the eldest Masr, son of Bensar, for whom Noah made the prayer we have reported; then Farek,
son of Bensar; then Mah, son of Bensar; and finally Yah, son of Bensar. The children of
Masr were also, it is said, four in number: Qoft, son of Masr, Ashmoun, son of Masr, Atrib,
son of Masr, and Sa, son of Masr. -- According to Ibn Lahia and Abd Allah ben Khaled, the
first to inhabit Egypt was Bensar, son of Cham, son of Noah, who went there after God had
made his people perish by the flood. The first city built in Egypt was Memphis, in which
dwelt Bensar and his family, thirty persons in number; four of them grew up and married --
these were the four sons of Bensar, Masr, Farek, Yah, and Mah, of whom the eldest was Masr,
by whom the city of Masr was built. Previously the Egyptians inhabited the flanks of the
Moqattam, where they had cut for themselves numerous shelters. Noah had asked God to make
Masr dwell in the excellent and blessed land, mother of nations and

[PDF p. 88]

refuge of the servants of God, whose river is the most admirable of the rivers of the
earth, and to spread there for him the best of his blessings, to make this land humble for
him and his descendants, to submit it to them, and to make them its powerful masters. Masr
having questioned Noah about this land, Noah described it to him and gave him some
information about it.

Masr, son of Bensar, was, it is said, with Noah in the ark when the latter made this prayer
for him. Bensar was already old and weak; he sent his children, Masr and all his brothers,
to Egypt, where they stopped and to which they gave the name of Masr. When Bensar and his
sons were solidly installed in Egypt, Farek, Yah, and Mah, sons of Bensar, said to their
brother Masr: "We know that you are our eldest and the best among us. Now this land, in
which your forefather Noah made you dwell, we find too narrow for you (and they spoke thus
because the children of Masr and their descendants had multiplied). We therefore ask of you
the blessing that our forefather Noah put in you, so that this blessing may follow us into
the land where we will stop and where we will dwell, and that it may remain with us and
with our children." "Your aim is wise," said Masr; "but stay in a country near mine and do
not move far from me. My land has an extent of a month's march in every direction; I will
therefore keep it for myself, my children, and their posterity." And Masr, son of Bensar,
kept for himself the space between the region of the two Trees, near El-Arich, and Assouan
in length, and between Barca and Aïlat in breadth. Farek attributed to himself the space
between Barca and Ifrikiah; his descendants were the Africans and the country took the name
of Ifrikiah; the extent of this territory is a month's march. -- Mah had for his share the
space stretching from the region of the two Trees, limit of Egypt, to Mesopotamia, over a
length of a month's march; he is the father of the Copts of Syria. Finally, Yah took for
himself all the part beyond Mesopotamia, from the sea to the East, over an extent of a
month's march. He is the stock of the Copts of Iraq. Bensar, son of Cham, died and was
buried at the spot where later rose the convent of Amba-Hermes, to the west of the
Pyramids: it is the first place where anyone was buried in Egypt. The children of Masr
multiplied; the first were Qoft, Atrib, Ashmoun, and Sa. The Copts are the descendants of
this Masr. It is said that Qoft was the brother of the Qoft whom they call in their
language Qoftim, Qobtim, and Misraïm.

[PDF p. 89]

Bensar, son of Cham, therefore died, after having designated as his successor Masr and
having assigned to each of Masr's brothers a part of the land equal in extent to Egypt,
which Masr had reserved for himself and his children. And when the children of Masr and the
children of his children had multiplied, he divided Egypt among each of his sons and
assigned them a territory for themselves and their descendants; the Nile was divided
likewise. His son Qobt had for his lot the city of Qoft, where he resided and to which he
gave his name, as well as the territory stretching south of Qoft to Assouan, and north to
Ashmoun, and all the towns comprised in this space, to the east and west (of the Nile). To
Ashmoun were attributed the country and the towns from Ashmoun to Memphis, east and west;
Ashmoun inhabited the city of Ashmoun, to which he gave his name. Atrib had as his share
the country situated between Memphis and Sa (Saïs) and inhabited Atribis, which took his
name. Sa was put in possession of the land between Sa and the sea, and inhabited the city
of Sa, to which he gave his own name. Thus Egypt was divided into four parts, of which two
comprised Upper Egypt and two Lower Egypt.

According to El-Bakhri, Masr is a feminine word. It is said in the Koran: "Am I not the
master of Masr?" (Koran, XLIII, 50) and: "Enter into Masr" (Koran, XII, 100). 'Amer ben
Abou Ouathilat el-Kinani said to Moawiah: "As for Amr ben el-As, you have given him Masr as
his share"; and as for the verse: "Enter into a Masr" (Koran, XII, 100), God, in this
passage, meant by Masr any town whatever. The reading of Selim el-'Amach is: "Enter into
Masr," saying that this Masr is the country over which Selim ben Ali governed; thus he does
not give it the nunnation. El-Qoda'i reports that Bensar, son of Cham, having become old
and weak, his son Masr took him, as well as all his brothers, to Egypt, where they stopped,
and which from this took the name of Masr. It is, he adds, a word that does not take the
nunnation, for it is a masculine substantive by which this city was designated. In this
way, it unites the two qualities of feminine and proper noun, which prevents it from taking
the nunnation. [Footnote: the word masr is a common noun of the masculine gender; but,
designating a particular city, it becomes feminine and a proper noun.] One designates by
the name of Masr all the great towns where travelers

[PDF p. 90]

stop; if it is one of these towns you wish to designate, then the word Masr takes the
nunnation, for one of the two reasons opposing this nunnation no longer exists, the word no
longer being a proper noun. In the verse of the Koran where God says to Moses: "Go down into
Masr, for you will find there what you desire" (Koran, II, 58), the word Masr takes the
nunnation according to all the readings, except those of El-Hassan and El-Amach. The
partisans of the nunnation rely on two reasons: (1) God, they affirm, meant to say: Go down
into a town, because the Israelites were then in the desert of Tih; (2) even if God had
meant to designate the town of Masr, the nunnation would be necessary because it is a
masculine word, derived from a masculine noun, which does not prevent the nunnation. Their
adversaries understand, in this passage, the town of Masr, and refer to the passage relating
to Joseph, where it is said: "Enter in safety into Masr, God willing!" (Koran, XII, 100) and
the word of Pharaoh: "Am I not the master of Masr?" (Koran, XLIII, 50), understanding by
this word Masr nothing other than Egypt. The word masr, in Arabic, has the sense of "line of
demarcation between two lands"; and the people of Hegr commonly say, it is asserted: "I have
bought the house masran," that is, "with its limits."

In his book entitled In Praise of Egypt, El-Gahez says that Egypt received the name of Masr
because men head there and gather there; likewise one has named masir el-gouf (internal
passage, or intestine), masir (path), or masran the path followed by food. The word masr, in
the sense of locality, makes in the plural amsar, and the plural of the masir of food is
masran. But the Masr that occupies us (Egypt) has no plural, for it designates a unique
thing.

"I was, El-Akhtal said one day, on the point of embracing Islam, when I gave it up." "Why
was that?" he was asked. "I had come to my wife; I was very hungry and asked her for
something to eat. She said to the servant: Put on the fire for Abi Malek a masir (a piece of
tripe). Which she did. A moment later I again asked to eat. My wife cried: Hey! servant,
where is the masir of Abi Malek? -- On the fire, answered the servant. -- I considered this
reply a bad omen and, although on the point of converting to Islam, I gave it up." [The
joke turns on masir meaning both "tripe" and "destiny/end."] El-Gouhari, in his book Of
Exact Terms, says: Masr designates a particular town [...]

[PDF p. 91]

and is of the masculine gender as well as the feminine, according to Ibn Sareg. One calls
Masran the two towns of El-Koufat and Basrat. Ibn Khalouïat, in one of his books, says:
"No one has yet explained to us why Egypt was formerly called Maqdouniah, unless this word
comes from Hebrew; for Maqdouniah in that language means 'refuge,' and this name will have
been given to Egypt because Bensar, son of Cham, withdrew there. The Greeks claim that all
of Macedonia forms a religious property belonging to the great church of Constantinople,
and they give the name of land of Maqdouniah to the region of El-Ausofia, a region that,
for them, comprises Alexandria with all its dependencies -- that is, all of Egypt, except
the upper Said." Masr has also been given the name of Omm-Khannour (mother of benefits),
the word khannour meaning benefit. The word masr also means "line of demarcation between
two things"; thus the poet, describing (the work) of God, said:

    He set the sun as a visible separation
        between day and night, to delimit them.

This verse is by 'Adi ben Zeïd el-'Abadi; others attribute it to El-Ommyah ben es-Solt
eth-Thaqfi. It is part of the piece that begins thus:

    Listen to an account that one day you will recite
        by heart, if someone comes to question you.
    How the world was in the beginning, then
        how God spread his benefits upon it, and showed us, from the first, his generosity.
    There was then only the wind, the foaming torrent,
        and the darkness that left empty neither hole nor cleft.
    God commanded the black darkness and it withdrew,
        and he removed the water from the places where it was spread.
    He spread the earth like a carpet and placed it
        under the sky, well balanced and without the least deviation.
    Then he set the sun, as a visible limit
        between day and night, to separate them.
    He placed in the sky the torches that light us,
        without their costing us either oil or wick.
    In six days he completed his creation,
        whose last work was the formation of man.

[PDF p. 92]

    God took the clay and formed it (man),
        and, when he saw it finished and well proportioned,
    he called it aloud: Adam! and the man answered him.
        Then he breathed the soul into the body he had created,
    and gave man paradise as his abode,
        and created him a companion from a rib drawn from his flank.
    God forbade man but one single thing:
        to taste nothing and eat nothing of the excellent tree.
    The spotted serpent was, when it was created,
        similar in its form to a she-camel or a camel.
    And God cursed it because it had tempted his creature:
        through all the nights -- and this curse will have no end --
    it will drag its belly on the earth as long as it lives,
        and it will eat dust, whether on mountain or on plain.

El-Hafiz Abou-l-Khattab Magd ed-din Omar ben Dahiat says that Egypt is the most fertile of
the lands of God. God gave it the name of Masr, and this name, according to all the
readings -- and if one neglects the nunnation -- applies to no other country. This word
does not take the nunnation, for it is a proper noun derived from a masculine noun. It
unites therefore two qualities: it is proper and feminine, and cannot, in consequence,
take the nunnation. For us, it derives from the expression "the ewe was milked," which is
used to say that the milk was taken from its udder. And Egypt was named Masr because of the
abundance of the goods it contains and that are not found elsewhere; its inhabitants enjoy
all the goods it produces, and it is with it as with the ewe whose milk, wool, and young
are used. According to Ibn el-'Arabi, the word masr means "vessel"; thus the intestines are
named masir, in the plural masran and masarin; likewise Egypt, which is like the treasury
of the earth.

Abou Zarr el-Ghafari, one of the companions of the Prophet, says that Egypt is the treasury
of the whole earth. Do you not see what Joseph says: "Place me at the head of the treasury
of the land, for I am a wise guardian" (Koran, XII, 55). God then gave him Egypt as his
share, and its treasures belonged to all, as El-Houfi explains in his commentary. El-Bakri
says: Omm-Khannour, with a fatha on the first letter, a tashdid on the second, and an
unpointed re, is a name of Egypt. Artah ben Shahbat said: "O tribe of Zabian, preserve your
blood and be not like the people of Omm-Khannour," meaning: Be not cowards, do not remain
exposed to the attacks of whoever

[PDF p. 93]

wishes to attack you, and do not let them take from you what pleases them, as happens with
the tax in Egypt -- that is, in Omm-Khannour. Kora says: "Omm-Khannour means benefit; it is
for this reason that Egypt was named Omm-Khannour, because of the abundance of its goods."
-- Ali ben Hamzah says: Egypt was surnamed Omm-Khannour because it draws to itself all those
whose life is short. The hyena also bears the name of khannour (or khannouz), with a re or a
zeïn. -- Ibn Qoteibah, in his Marvels of the Traditions, says that masr means "limit," and
that the people of Hegr write in their contracts: "I have bought the house masran," meaning
with its limits. El-'Adi ben Zeïd said:

    He set the sun as a visible barrier
        between day and night, to separate them.

[PDF p. 94]

CHAPTER VIII
A GLANCE AT THE RELATIONS OF EGYPT WITH RELIGION
[Footnote: the word manaqib properly means "virtues, qualities," but has a wider sense than
the French word and applies to all that touches, closely or remotely, on the Koran and the
traditions of Islam.]

Egypt has considerable advantages, and among others that of having been cited by God, in
his venerated book, some twenty times, sometimes directly, sometimes indirectly and by
allusion.

God said: "Go down into Masr, for you will find there what you ask" (Koran, II, 58). Abou
Mohammed Abd el-Haq, son of Atiah, says on this subject, in his commentary: "Most people
read Masr with the tanwin (nunnation), which is the reading of all the Korans, except a few
copies of Osman." According to Mogahed and others, those who give this word the nunnation
understand by Masr any town whatever, relying on the context of the Koran which, according
to them, signifies that it is enjoined (on the Israelites) to enter into the village, and
on the tradition which says that on leaving Tih they inhabited Syria. A certain number of
the partisans of the nunnation claim that God, in this passage, meant to designate Pharaoh's
own Masr, and rely on the passage of the Koran where God allotted to the Beni Israel the
dwellings of Pharaoh and his monuments. In this case the nunnation would be admitted because,
according to El-Akhfach, the pronunciation of this word is in common use, similar to that of
the words Hind and Da'd. Sibaouya is not of this opinion, and others besides El-Akhfach
recognize that God meant any place of dwelling and apply the tanwin, while El-Hassan, Abou
ben Taleb, and others read: "Go down into Masr," without nunnation. Such is the reading of
Abaï ben Ka'b, who declares: "This Masr is the Masr of Pharaoh." -- "This Masr," says
El-'Amach, "is the Masr of which Saleh ben Ali is governor." --

[PDF p. 95]

"Malek said to me," recounts Achhab, "For me it is a question of Masr your country, the
abode of Pharaoh."

God said: "Enter into Masr, and, God willing, you will be in safety there" (Koran, XII,
100). Abou Ga'far Mohammed ben Garir et-Tabari, in his commentary, says, on the authority
of Farqad es-Sabakhi: "Joseph went to meet Jacob, and the Egyptians escorted him,
acclaiming him. When Joseph and Jacob were in sight of each other, the latter was going on
foot, leaning on one of his sons named Juda, to whom he said, seeing the horses and the
crowd: 'O Juda, it is the Pharaoh of Egypt.' 'No,' answered Juda, 'it is your son.' And when
they were near each other, Jacob said to Joseph: 'Greeting to you who remove sorrow from
me,' using the expression: 'O you who remove sorrow from me.'" [Footnote: Maqrizi dwells on
the expression used by Jacob, which is unusual; regularly it should be otherwise phrased.]

God said: "We gave this order to Moses and his brother: Take for your people houses in Masr
and make of your houses places of prayer where you may pray" (Koran, X, 87). Et-Tabari
reports, on the authority of Ibn Abbas and others, that the Beni Israïl feared Pharaoh and
that they received the order to make of their houses oratories to pray in. Qotadah says that
this happened at the time when Pharaoh prevented the Israelites from praying, and that they
received the order to install their oratories in their houses and to turn (in praying)
toward the qiblah. According to Mogahed, the expression "your houses as qiblah" means: in
the direction of the Kaaba; as Moses and his people, for fear of Pharaoh, dared not pray in
public temples, they received the order to install in their houses oratories turned toward
the Kaaba, to pray there in secret. According to Mogahed, in the phrase "Take for your
people dwellings in Masr," Masr means Alexandria.

God said, speaking of Pharaoh: "He said: Does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me, is it
not under my authority that these canals flow? Do you not see it?" (Koran, XLIII, 50) Ibn
Abd el-Hakem and Abou Saïd Abd er-Rahman ben Ahmed ben Younes and others say, on the
authority of Abou Zahm es-Samal, that, in the verse "Does not the kingdom of Egypt belong to
me? Is it not under my authority that these canals flow," God meant to give to understand
that there [...]

[PDF p. 96]

was then on earth no king more powerful than the king of Egypt, and that all the peoples of
all countries had need of Egypt; as for the canals, they were furnished with bridges and
dams wisely and skillfully arranged, so that the water flowed at the foot of the houses and
courtyards, the Egyptians directing it as they pleased.

Such are the verses where God speaks directly of Egypt in his august book; as for the
allusions he makes to this country, in other verses of this same book, they are very
numerous.

God said: "We assigned to the Beni Israïl a delightful place" (Koran, X, 93); and again:
"We gave them (Moses and Aaron) for an abode a fertile place full of springs" (Koran,
XXIII, 52). Ibn Abbas, Saïd ben el-Mosib, and Ouahb ben Monabbah say that by this one must
understand Egypt. Abd er-Rahman ben Zeïd ben Aslam says, on the authority of his father,
that it is a question of Alexandria.

God said: "We made them go out of gardens, of springs, of treasures, of a delightful
abode" (Koran, XXVI, 57-58); and again: "How many gardens they abandoned, how many springs,
how many cultivated fields, what a delightful and beneficent abode in which they resided
and which they enjoyed!" (Koran, XLIV, 24-26). Ibn Younes, concerning the verse "We made
them go out of gardens, springs, treasures, a delightful abode," says that, according to
Abou Zahm, these gardens were situated on the two banks of the Nile, from one end of Egypt
to the other, from Assouan to Rosetta; that there were seven canals: the canal of
Alexandria, that of Sakha (Xoïs), those of Damietta, of Serdous, of Memphis, of the Fayoum,
and the Menhi, all linked together and in no way separated; that the cultivated lands
covered the space between the two mountains from one extremity of Egypt to the other, which
the waters (of the inundation) reached; and that, at that time, the whole land of Egypt was
covered by the waters when the flood reached a height of sixteen cubits, so well arranged
were the barrages and dams. As for the places of comfort, they are, says the same author,
the minbars (pulpits for preaching), for there were a thousand of them in Egypt. Mogahed
and Saïd ben Gabir explain the words "places of comfort" by the word "pulpits." Qotadah
understands by this expression "the good and delightful things they enjoyed." And he adds:
"Indeed, by God! God made Pharaoh go out of his garden, his springs, his cultivated lands,
to cast him into the sea." Saïd ben Katir ben 'Afir recounts this:

[PDF p. 97]

"We were at Qobbat-el-Haoua, with El-Mamoun, at the time of his arrival in Egypt. The
caliph said to us: 'I do not know why Pharaoh was so marveled at Egypt when he cried: Does
not the kingdom of Egypt belong to me?' I spoke up: 'May I be permitted to speak, O
commander of the Faithful?' I asked. 'Speak,' he said to me. 'You no longer see,' I then
said, 'anything but ruined remains. For God said: We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people
had made and what they had built (Koran, VII, 133).' 'You are right,' answered El-Mamoun,
and he kept silent."

God said: "We wished to be benevolent toward those who, because of religion, were oppressed
on the earth; we made of them imams and our heirs, we made them powerful on the earth, and
through them we made Pharaoh, Haman, and their army come to what they dreaded" (Koran,
XXVIII, 4-5). And again, speaking of Pharaoh: "He said: O people, to you belongs the empire
today, you are the masters of the world" (Koran, XL, 30). And again: "The word of your
excellent master was accomplished for the Beni Israïl because of their patience, and we
destroyed what Pharaoh and his people had made and what they had built" (Koran, VII, 133).
And again, speaking of the people of Pharaoh: "Will you let Moses and his people destroy the
land (that is, the land of Egypt)?" (Koran, VII, 124); concerning Joseph, God reports that
he said: "Place me over the treasures of Egypt, for I am a wise guardian" (Koran, XII, 55).
According to the tradition reported by Ibn Younes, who had it from Abou Basra el-Ghafari,
Egypt is the treasury of the whole earth and its king is the king of the whole earth. Do
you not see what Joseph says to the king of Egypt: "Place me at the head of the treasures of
the land." Which was done, and Joseph made of Egypt a refuge, and its treasures were then
those of the inhabitants and the peoples of the whole earth.

God said: "Thus we made Joseph powerful on the earth, able to choose a dwelling wherever he
wished" (Koran, XII, 56). And Joseph, being king of Egypt, all the other kings of the whole
earth had need of him and of the things he administered.

God said, speaking of Moses: "He said: O our Lord, you have given Pharaoh and his subjects
splendor and riches in this world, that they may turn away from your path. O Lord, annihilate
their riches and harden their hearts, that they may not believe until they undergo the
terrible punishment!" (Koran, X, 88). And again: "Perhaps your Lord will make your enemies
perish and will install you as masters of the land, and he will see how you act" (Koran,
VIII, 126). And again: "Pharaoh said: Let

[PDF p. 98]

me kill Moses and let him invoke his God! for myself I fear that he will change your religion
and bring corruption upon the land (that is, the land of Egypt)" (Koran, XL, 27). And again:
"Pharaoh raised himself up on the land (that is, the land of Egypt)" (Koran, XXVIII, 35). And
again, speaking of one of Joseph's brothers: "I will not leave the land (that is, the land of
Egypt)" (Koran, XII, 80).

God said: "You wish then to be a tyrant on the land (that is, the land of Egypt)" (Koran,
XVIII, 18). Ibn Abbas says that Egypt is named "the whole land" in ten passages of the Koran.
Such are, as far as I recall, all the passages of the holy book of God where Egypt is
mentioned.

The virtues of Egypt are cited also in a number of traditions. Abd Allah ben Lahiat reports
this fact in the traditions relating to 'Amr ben el-As: "The commander of the Faithful Omar
told me that he had heard the Messenger of God say: When, after my death, God has opened for
you the land of Egypt, you will raise there a considerable army that will be the best of the
armies of the earth. 'And how is that, O Messenger of God?' asked Abou Bekr. 'Because they
will be in the vanguard until the day of resurrection.'" -- According to 'Amr ben el-Hamq,
the Prophet is said to have said: "There will be a sedition during which the most just and
the best of men will be (the warriors of) the army of the West; and that is why," he added,
"Egypt must be for you in the first rank." -- According to Tabi' ben 'Amer el-Kala'i: "I had,
he said, set out from Es-Saïfat and I met Abou Moussa el-Acha'ri, who asked me: Where do you
come from? -- From the land of Egypt, I answered. -- From the army of the West? -- Yes. --
The pitiful army! -- Is it so weak? I asked. -- Indeed, he said, no one can attack it without
God defending it! Go to Mo'az ben Gebal that he may teach it to you. -- I went to Mo'az ben
Gebal, who asked me: What did the old man tell you? I recounted it to him: What better thing
can you carry back to your country than this saying! he cried; write it on your tablets. And
when I had returned to Mo'az he informed me that this saying came from the Prophet of God."

Ibn Ouahb, among other traditions on Safouan ben 'Assal, reports this one: "I heard (it is
Safouan who speaks) the Prophet of God say: God has opened for repentance a gate situated to
the west, seventy years (of march) wide, which will not close until the sun rises from that
side."

[PDF p. 99]

Ibn Lahia, in his traditions on 'Amr ben el-As, recounts: "The commander of the Faithful
Omar told me that he had heard the Prophet of God say: After my death, God Most High and
sublime will open Egypt for you. Treat well the Copts who inhabit it, for between them and you
there is alliance and kinship."

Ibn Ouahb says: "Harmalat ben 'Amran en-Nagibi told me, on the authority of Abd er-Rahman ben
Shemasat el-Mahri, that Abou Zarar used to say: I heard the Prophet of God say: You will
conquer a land where they count by qirats; treat its inhabitants well, for there is between
them and you kinship and alliance; and when you see there two men disputing over the location
of a brick, then leave it." Now, having passed near Rabiat and Abd er-Rahman, the two sons of
Sharhabil, he saw them disputing over the location of a brick, and he left Egypt. According to
another tradition, this is what the Prophet is said to have said: "You will conquer Egypt, the
land where they count by qirats; when you have conquered it, treat its inhabitants well, for
there is between them and you kinship and alliance"; and, according to other texts, "alliance
and consanguinity." The traditions of Malek and El-Leits add: "treat the Copts well." Mouslim
put in his book Of the Authentic Traditions these accounts, which he had borrowed from
Abou-t-Taher, who had them from Ouahb.

Ibn Shehab reports the opinion that makes the mother of Ismaïl a woman of this nation.
El-Leits ben Sa'd recounts: "I asked Ibn Shehab: What is this kinship? -- The mother of
Ismaïl, son of Ibrahim, was of this people, he answered me." -- "I asked Ez-Zahari," recounts
Mohammed ben Ishaq, "what was this kinship of which the Prophet spoke, and he said to me:
Hagar, mother of Ismaïl, was of this nation."

Among other traditions relating to Abou Salam el-Gishani, Ibn Lahi'at recounts that one of
the companions of the Prophet had heard him say: "You will possess armies, but the best of
your armies will be composed of the men of the West. Fear God therefore concerning the Copts,
and do not devour them like vegetables." According to Mouslim ben Yesar, the Prophet is said
to have said: "Treat the Copts well, for you will find them your best auxiliaries for fighting
your enemies."

Abou Salamat ben Abd er-Rahman, says Yezid ben Abou Habib, told me that at the moment of his
death, the Prophet of God recommended making the

[PDF p. 100]

Jews go out of the Arabian peninsula, adding: "Fear God, fear God concerning the Copts of
Egypt, for you will subdue them and they will be for you excellent auxiliaries in the ways of
God."

Ibn Ouahb reports, on the authority of Moussa ben Ayoub el-Rhafeqi, who had it from a man of
Rend, that the Prophet of God, being ill, fainted, then, coming to himself, cried: "Treat
well the people of brown skin and curly hair." A second time he fainted and, on waking,
repeated the same thing. A third time he lost consciousness and, having come to himself,
repeated the same words. And those present said to one another: "What if we asked the Prophet
what he means by the people of brown skin and curly hair?" And they asked him on his waking.
"They are," said the Prophet, "the Copts of Egypt, for they are your uncles and your
fathers-in-law, and they will help you against your enemies in the accomplishment of your
religion." "And how," it was asked, "will they help us in the accomplishment of our religion,
O Prophet of God?" "They will spare you," he answered, "the labors of this world, and your
time will be free for prayer. Those who let them be ill-treated will be as if they ill-treated
them themselves, and those who hate their oppressors will be as if they had removed oppression
from them."

Amr ben Harib and Abd er-Rahman el-Halebi assert that the Prophet is said to have said: "You
will be the masters of a people with curly heads; treat them well, for, with God's permission,
they will be for you a strength and a help against your enemies." This is a question of the
Copts of Egypt.

A servant of Afrat, reports Ibn Lahi'at, told me that the Prophet of God had said: "Fear God,
fear God concerning the people of the black land who have brown skin and curly hair, for there
is between them and you kinship and alliance." The alliance, added 'Amr, the servant of Afrat,
means that the Prophet of God took among them a concubine, and the kinship that the mother of
Ismaïl was of their race.

Ibn Ouahb says: "Ibn Lahi'at told me that the mother of Ismaïl, Hagar, was of Omm-el-Arab, a
village situated opposite Farma, in Egypt."

Merouan el-Qosas (the shearer) says that three prophets had Copts for fathers-in-law: Abraham,
the Beloved of God, took Hagar for a concubine; Joseph married the daughter of the lord of
'Aïn-Shams; and the Prophet of God took for [...]

[PDF p. 101]

a concubine, Maria. According to Yezid ben Abou Habib, the birthplace of Hagar was the
village of Baq, in the vicinity of Omm-Danin. The Arabs, asserts Hecham, say indifferently
Hagar and Agar, exchanging the he and the alif, just as one says (two forms for "to pour
water") and other analogous examples.

According to Omar ben el-Khattab, there are, it is said, seven Masr: the town that is also
called a masr, Syria which is a masr, Egypt (whose name is Masir), Mesopotamia, El-Bahraïn,
Basrah, and Koufah. Mokhoul reports that the first region destroyed was Armenia and the
second Egypt. -- "The Copts," says Abd Allah ben Omar, "are the most generous of the
barbarians (the non-Arabs), those whose hand is most widely open, and whose origin is the
most illustrious; by alliance, they are also, of all men, the closest to the Arabs in
general and to the Qoreïchites in particular. Let whoever wishes to have an idea of Paradise,
or to see something approaching it in this world, cast his eyes on the land of Egypt, when
the crops are green and the fruits begin to form!" -- "He who wishes to see something
resembling Paradise," says Ka'b el-Ahbar, "has only to look at Egypt in the season of autumn"
-- or, according to another reading, "when it is in flower."

[PDF p. 102]

CHAPTER IX
OF THE PARTICULARITIES FOUND IN EGYPT

Among the inhabitants of Egypt were those magicians who all, at the same hour, converted;
and one knows of no mass conversion more important than that of the Copts. According to Yezid
ben Abou Habib and other authors, there were twelve chief magicians, each commanding twenty
lieutenants, each lieutenant having under his orders a thousand sorcerers; the number of
sorcerers thus amounted to two hundred forty thousand two hundred fifty-two, including the
chiefs and the lieutenants. And when they saw what was given them to see [the prodigies
worked by Moses before Pharaoh; cf. Koran, ch. XX, verses 60-78], they recognized that this
came from heaven and that magic could do nothing against the orders of God. The twelve chiefs
fell prostrate, their lieutenants imitated them, followed by all the others. And all cried:
"We believe in the Master of men, in the Lord of Moses and Aaron" (Koran, XX, 73). Tabi'
reports that these magicians accompanied Moses and that none of them followed in their
perjury the unfaithful Israelites who worshiped the (golden) calf; the same author says that
no people converted at once in as great a number as the Copts.

According to Ka'b el-Ahbar, the Copts of Egypt may be compared to a garden which, the more
it is pruned, the more it produces; it is through them and their stratagems that God will
annihilate the islands of Roum.

Abd Allah ben 'Amr says that the world was created according to five forms recalling the five
parts of the bird: the head, the breast, the two wings, and the tail. The head is represented
by Mecca, Medina, and Yemen; the breast by Syria and Egypt; the right wing by Iraq, the
people of the Ouak beyond Iraq, and the people of the Ouakouak beyond the Ouak, and finally,
beyond these last, by peoples known to God alone; to the left wing

[PDF p. 103]

correspond the Hind, and beyond the Hind, the Sind; beyond the Sind, the people of the Nasek;
beyond the Nasek, the Mounsek; and beyond the Mounsek, peoples known to God alone. The tail
extends from Zat-el-Homam to the setting sun; and the tail is the most detestable part of the
bird.

According to El-Gahez, there are ten (qualities or defects attributed to ten) towns: industry
at Basrah, eloquence at Koufah, gentleness at Bagdad, stammering at Er-Raï, envy at Nisapour,
beauty at Herat, braggadocio at Samarkand, virility at Balkh, commerce in Egypt, and avarice
at Merw. -- The word (braggadocio) means "word not followed by action."

Yahia ben Dakher el-Haferi recounts having heard 'Amr ben el-As say in a speech: "Know that
you will be under arms until the day of judgment, for you will be ceaselessly surrounded by
enemies whose hearts will be constantly jealous both of you and of your dwelling-place, a
mine of harvests and riches, of abundant goods and growing blessings." Abd er-Rahman ben
Ghanem el-Acha'ri reports that, having come from Syria to Abd Allah ben 'Amr ben el-As, the
latter asked him: "Why have you come to our country?" "You had told me," answered El-Acha'ri,
"that Egypt was, of all the countries of the earth, the most ruined, and I see you taking
lands, raising palaces, and installing yourself there more and more." "It is," said Abd
Allah, "that the time of ruin is past for Egypt since the conquest of Bokht-Nasr
(Nebuchadnezzar), who left there only lions and hyenas. Today it is the country of the earth
that possesses the best soil and whose ruin is the most distant. Never will the blessing
cease there as long as there is any blessing on the earth."

Egypt occupies, it is said, the center of the world and does not have to suffer from the heat
of the first two climes nor the cold of the last two. Situated in the third clime, the air
there is healthy, the heat temperate, and the cold not very rigorous. Its inhabitants are
preserved from the winters of El-Ahouaz, the summers of Oman, the storms of Tehamat, the
pustules of Mesopotamia, the scabies of Yemen, the plagues of Syria, the pleurisies of Iraq,
the scorpions of Askar-Mokram, the splenitis of El-Bahraïn, the fevers of Kheïbar; they are
safe from the incursions of the Turks, the armies of Roum, the depredations of the Arabs,
the trickeries of the Dilemites, the razzias of the Carmathians, as well as from the
drying-up of the rivers or the famine caused by the lack of rain.

[PDF p. 104]

Egypt is divided into eighty districts; and there is not a single one that does not contain
astonishing and marvelous things -- in the way of products, monuments, things good to drink
or eat, objects useful to man or worthy of being deposited in the treasury of kings. These
things are renowned both within the district and outside it, and everything a district
produces bears its name.

The Said (Upper Egypt) is a terrain similar to that of the Hedjaz; the heat there is the
same as in Iraq; it produces the date-palm, the acacia, the doum-palm, and the achr.
[Footnote: Kazimirski renders this word as Asclepias gigantea. It is a broad-leaved shrub
still found in quantity at Gebel-Silsileh. The wood, somewhat spongy, dries very quickly and
readily gives fire by friction; the inhabitants of Silsileh use it for that purpose.] Lower
Egypt resembles Syria; it rains there as in Syria, and the fruits of Syria ripen there, such
as the vine, the olive, the almond, the fig, the walnut, and all sorts of fruits, vegetables,
and flowers. Snow and hail also fall there. The districts of Alexandria, of Libya, of
Maraqiah are only deserts, mountains, and gardens where the vine and the olive grow; these
are lands of camels and sheep, of honey and milk.

Each district of Egypt possesses a town containing magnificent constructions of stone or
marble and marvelous objects. Its Nile is furrowed with boats, each of which can carry the
load of five hundred camels. Each of the villages of Egypt may be considered a town; this is
what God said: "Send into the towns messengers to gather (troops)" (Koran, XXVI, 35). Various
industries are common in Egypt, among others that of the ovens in which hen's eggs are
hatched. The oven is given the normal heat of the brooding hen, and the chicks come out of
these ovens; it is thus that most of the chickens of Egypt are produced, and it is only in
Egypt that this industry is practiced.

Omar ben Maïmoun recounts that, the day after the departure of Moses with the Beni Israel,
Pharaoh had a ewe brought to him, and, the ewe having come, had it slaughtered, declaring
that they would not finish skinning it until he had gathered around him five hundred thousand
Egyptians; this number of men having been gathered, Pharaoh said: "Indeed, these people are
very few!" The companions of Moses numbered only six hundred seventy thousand.

[PDF p. 105]

A writer [Maçaoudi, Meadows of Gold, ed. Barbier de Meynard, vol. II, p. 235], wishing to
give an idea of Egypt, said: "For three months it is like a white pearl; for three months,
like a piece of black musk; for three months, like a green emerald; for three months, like
an ingot of red gold. The white pearl is Egypt during the months of Abib, Mesari, and Thoth,
during which it is covered by the waters; the land is then all white, and the villages, on
the tops of the mounds and hills, are like stars; the water surrounds them on all sides and
one can reach them only by boat. -- The black musk is Egypt during the months of Babah,
Hathor, and Kihak, when the water withdraws from the land, which appears black; it is at this
moment that the sowing is done. -- The green emerald is Egypt during the months of Tobah,
Amchir, and Barmahat; the plants then come out of the earth, it is spring, and Egypt is green
as an emerald. -- The red ingot is Egypt during the months of Bermoudah, Bachons, and Baounah;
the plants flower, the harvests are ripe and good to reap, and Egypt becomes like an ingot of
gold in aspect and in value."

A caliph asked El-Leits ben Sa'd what was the best moment of Egypt. "It is," he said, "when
the waters have withdrawn, the diseases have ceased, the land has dried, and the pastures are
ready."

Another said: "Its Nile is a marvel, its soil is gold, its goods are (a source of) profit;
its possession enriches like plunder [that is, without trouble and without long cares], its
riches are envied, its people are unsubmissive and obey only through fear, and its treaties
are without consistency; they make war to plunder; it belongs to whoever seizes it."

Another said: "Egypt counts among the mistresses of the villages and the queens of the
towns."

Zeïd ben Aslam, concerning the verse "If he does not water it with heavy rains, he will moisten
it with light rains" (Koran, II, 267), says that it is a question of Egypt; indeed, if it does
not rain there, it is at its apogee, and if it rains there, it weakens. This is what Maçaoudi
says in his history [Meadows of Gold, ed. Barbier de Meynard, vol. II, p. 36]: [...]

[PDF p. 106]

It is reported that God, having created Adam, showed him the world to the east and the west
-- its plains, its mountains, its rivers, its seas, its constructions, its desert parts, the
peoples who were to inhabit it, the kings who were to govern it; and when he saw Egypt, a
plain crossed by a river issued from Paradise and carrying blessing within it; when he saw
one of its two mountains resplendent with light and ceaselessly favored with the sight of the
Lord, by his mercy, having at its foot trees laden with fruit while its summit was lost in
Paradise, watered by the waters of compassion, Adam invoked God that he might bless the Nile,
and be merciful to the land of Egypt and grant it felicity and strength; and he blessed seven
times the Nile and the mountain, saying: "O mountain full of mercy, your foot is Paradise,
your soil is a musk in which are buried the planters of the garden of Paradise; preserving,
obedient, and pitiful land, O Egypt, may blessing never cease in you, may preservation never
cease for you, and may royalty and power never move away from you! O land of Egypt, in you
are wealth and treasures, to you belong felicity and prosperity. May your Nile flow like
honey! may God multiply your crops; may he swell your udders, may he make your plants grow!
may the blessing that is in you grow! Be fertile, and may your goods never cease for you as
long as you are neither violent, nor proud, nor treacherous! But if you become such, may your
enemies treat you with violence and may your goods vanish!" And Adam was the first who prayed
God to grant Egypt pity, fertility, mercy, and blessing.

According to Ibn Abbas, Noah invoked God for Masr, son of Bensar, son of Cham, saying: "O my
God, this one has answered my call, bless him as well as his posterity, give him for a domain
the blessed land, mother of nations and refuge of the servants of God; the one whose river is
the most excellent of the rivers of the earth, and put in this country the best of blessings.
Subdue it for Masr and for his descendants; submit it to them and make them strong over it."

Ka'b el-Ahbar said: "If I did not have the desire to inhabit Jerusalem, I would wish to
inhabit no other country than Egypt." And as he was asked why, he answered: "Because it is a
country safe from sedition, and those who wish to harm it are repulsed by God himself; it is a
blessed country, as are those who inhabit it."

[PDF p. 107]

One reads in Ibn Ouahb: Yahia ben Ayoub, who had it from Khaled ben Yezid, who had heard it
from Ibn Abou Halal, told me that Ka'b el-Ahbar is said to have said: "I love Egypt and its
inhabitants, for Egypt is a country protected (by God) and its inhabitants are generous, which
distinguishes them from other peoples." -- It is said, in certain books that treat of the
divine sciences, that Egypt is the treasury of the whole earth, and that those who wish to
attack it are broken by God himself.

"The general government of Egypt," 'Amr ben el-As used to say, "is by itself worth the
