caliphate." By "general government" must be understood the union of the financial
administration and the military command of the country. [Footnote: these two functions were
most often filled by two distinct persons. See on this subject Casanova, Notice sur quelques
poids de verre (Bulletin de l'Institut egyptien, 1891), where the distinction between the two
powers is clearly determined.]

According to Ahmed ben Modabber, Egypt could put under cultivation twenty-eight million
feddans, but it cultivates only one million. [Footnote: a feddan is a measure of surface area
equivalent to about 4,000 square meters.] And, he adds, after having traversed Egypt, I
recognized that the uncultivated part of Egypt is by far more considerable than the cultivated
part; if the sultan applied himself to putting the whole into productive use, he would draw
from it a revenue equal to the yield of the whole world.

Someone said that the revenue of Iraq was never higher than in the time of Omar ibn Abd
el-Aziz, the period when it reached one million seventeen thousand dirhems, and that the
revenue of Egypt was never lower than in the time of 'Amr ben el-As, the period when it
nevertheless reached twelve million dinars. The provinces of Syria yielded fourteen million,
not counting the revenue of the frontier towns.

Egypt counts, among other merits, that of having given birth to three prophets: Moses, Aaron,
and Joshua. And it is recounted that Jesus, son of Mary, going to Syria, was skirting the foot
of the Moqattam when, turning to his mother, he said to her: "O my mother, here is the
cemetery of the people of Mohammed." It is reported that Jesus was born at the village of
Ahnas in the region of the Said of Egypt, and that there is a palm tree there that would be
the palm tree cited in the Koran in the verse where it is said: "Shake the trunk of the palm
tree" (Koran, XIX, 25). This account is erroneous, for

[PDF p. 108]

everyone agrees -- both the priests of the Bible and the wisest of the Muslims -- in
recognizing that Jesus was born at the village of Bethlehem, in the district of Jerusalem.

The prophets who came to Egypt are Ibrahim, the Beloved of God, whose story will be found in
this book in the chapter of the Canal of Cairo; Jacob; Joseph; and the patriarchs whose
history is reported in the chapter of the Fayoum. Jeremiah also came there.

He was an Egyptian too, that member of the family of Pharaoh who converted (to the true
faith), and to whom God, in the Koran (XL, 29), accords such great praise. He was, it is said,
the very son of Pharaoh, but I believe this assertion false.

They were Egyptians too, those councilors of Pharaoh whose superior intelligence God praises,
and the wise advice they gave when Pharaoh consulted them about Moses and Aaron. Here is what
God says: "Pharaoh said to the great ones around him: That one is a skillful sorcerer who, by
his magic, will compel you to leave your country. What do you advise me to do? -- And the
great ones answered: Defer him and his brother and send into all the towns messengers who will
bring you back the most skillful sorcerers" (Koran, XXVI, 33-36). What a difference with what
the companions of Nimrod said about Ibrahim, when they advised him to put him to death. Here
is what God says of it: "They said: Burn him and give the victory to your gods, if you wish"
(Koran, XXI, 68).

She was Egyptian, the wife of Pharaoh whom God praises in his holy book, when he says: "God
has given an example in the wife of Pharaoh, who said: Lord, build me near you a house in
Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his acts, save me from the people of iniquity" (Koran,
LXVI, 11).

She was Egyptian, the hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter who believed in Moses, whom Pharaoh
had combed with an iron comb, as one combs flax, and who remained firm in her faith in God.

Sa'd el-Loghaoui, in his book Of the Biography of Peoples, reports that all the sciences known
before the flood had been taught by the first Hermes, who dwelt in the upper Said of Egypt.
This Hermes was the first to treat of the celestial substances and the movement of the stars;
he was the first to raise temples to worship God in; he was the first to occupy himself with
the science of

[PDF p. 109]

medicine and composed for his contemporaries well-measured poems on terrestrial and celestial
things. It is said also that he was the first to foresee the flood, and to sense that a
celestial cataclysm was going to fall upon the earth, in the form of fire or water; so,
fearing the annihilation of the sciences and the disappearance of the industrial processes, he
built the pyramids and the temples of Upper Egypt, represented there the trades and the tools,
and engraved there the explanation of the sciences, with the aim of transmitting them to those
who would come after him and for fear of seeing them disappear from the world. This Hermes is
the same as Edris.

Abou Mohammed el-Hasan ben Ismaïl ben el-Farat, in his Chronicles of Egypt, says that El-Khidr
crossed the sea with Moses, with whom he was in favor.

In Egypt have been found a host of sages who, by their words, their wisdom, and their counsels,
civilized the world. Among other sciences they cultivated medicine, astronomy, geometry, the
science of engineers, chemistry, and the science of talismans. Formerly, it is said, the
seekers of knowledge came to Egypt to broaden their intelligence, fortify their reason, enlarge
their mind, and refine their perspicacity.

Among other merits, Egypt has also that of abundantly supplying provisions to the inhabitants
of the two holy cities (Mecca and Medina). Egypt is the port of the world and exports its
riches everywhere. By Suez, it ships to the two holy cities, to Yemen, to the Hind, to China,
to the Sind, to Oman, and to Chahr; by Tams, Damietta, and Farma, to the lands of Roum and of
the Franks, to the coasts of Syria and, by the frontier towns of this last country, as far as
the confines of Iraq. Alexandria communicates with Crete, Sicily, and [the lands of the
setting sun]. By [the Nile it reaches] Nubia, the land of the Beggas [and Yemen]. There are in
Egypt a number of frontier-posts constantly under arms for the safety of the religion; these
are Bourlos, [Rosetta,] Alexandria, Zat-el-Homam, Beherah, Akhna, Damietta, Shata, Tad,
Achtoum, Farma, Ouaradah, El-Arich, Assouan, Qous, and the oases. [In Egypt are] the pyramids,
the temples, the convents, the churches, and

[PDF p. 110]

its inhabitants can do without all other countries, to such a point that if a wall were raised
between Egypt and the rest of the earth, Egypt, thanks to its riches, would allow its
inhabitants to do without all other countries.

It is in Egypt that the essence of balsam is prepared, whose usefulness is considerable. The
kings of the earth send to fetch it in Egypt and preserve it with care. The Christian kings
seek it ardently, and the Christians attribute to it so great a virtue that they would not
believe themselves truly Christian if a little of this essence were not mixed with the
baptismal water in which the neophyte is plunged.

It is there too that one finds the soqonqour (skink), whose usefulness is undeniable; one also
meets there the ichneumon and the weasel, great destroyers of serpents; it is said even that
without the ichneumons and the weasels, the serpents would render Egypt uninhabitable. One
finds there too the trembling fish (electric catfish), marvelously effective for restoring
health to the feverish, if it is suspended above the patient. Egypt also produces an acacia
wood that has no equal in its property; if one burns it for a whole day under a cauldron, no
ashes remain; it is very easy to break; it kindles easily but is extinguished only with the
greatest difficulty. It is, it is said, the same tree as the ebony, whose color the soil of
Egypt is said to have changed, making it red.

Egypt produces opium, an extract of the poppy whose usefulness is contested only by the
ignorant. One also met there the henbane, a kind of berry the size of a green almond; it was
one of the best products of Egypt, but it disappeared before the year 700 of the hijra [16
September 1300 to 1301].

There one also finds the citron. The historian Abou Daoud, in his book Of Alms, says: "I
measured in Egypt a cucumber of thirteen spans, and I saw a citron which, cut in two, sufficed
to make the double load of a camel." Maçaoudi, in his history, says: The round citron was
brought from India after the year 300 of the hijra [18 August 912 to 6 August 913]; it was
first planted at Oman, whence it was transported to Basrah, into Iraq and Syria; it spread
first to Tarsus and the other Syrian ports, then to Antioch, on the coasts of Syria, in
Palestine [...]

[PDF p. 111]

and in Egypt, where it was not yet known. There it lost its magnificent bright red color, the
color it has in India and that is the best; for in Egypt it is deprived of the air, the soil,
and the properties of its native land.

There are found in Egypt mines of emerald, of naphtha, of alum, and of beram [Footnote: a
kind of fireproof stone from which pots and cauldrons were made], and quarries of marble.
There were in Egypt thirty kinds of metals, it is said.

The Egyptians feed on the product of the fishing of the sea of Roum and the sea of Qolzoum,
which always give them fresh fish, for the distance separating these two seas, from Qolzoum
to Farma, is only a day's and a night's march. This space forms the separation spoken of in
the Koran: "He has put a barrier between the two seas" (Koran, XXV, 53) -- that is, between
the sea of Roum and the sea of Qolzoum -- and in this other passage: "He has prevented the
two seas from rejoining, casting between them a barrier that opposes their union" (Koran, XXV,
53). According to the commentators, this barrier is the space between Qolzoum and Farma.

One of the particularities of Egypt is that in each of the months of the Coptic year, one
finds some food or some perfume peculiar to that month and unknown in the others. Thus one
says: the dates of Thoth, the pomegranates of Babah, the bananas of Hathor, the fish of
Kihak, the water of Tobah, the mutton of Amchir, the milk of Barmahat, the roses of
Barmoudah, the nobaq [the fruit of the jujube, very widespread in Egypt -- Zizyphus spina
Christi] of Bachons, the figs of Boonah, the honey of Abib, the grapes of Mesori.

One may say that the summer of this country is an autumn, so much fruit is found there, and
that its winter is a spring, for it is the season when clover and flax are harvested. Egypt,
moreover, enjoys this advantage of producing fruits when there are none in other countries.
Another advantage is that during the summer the Egyptians have no need to pitch tents or dig
shelters in the earth, as one is obliged to do at Bagdad, nor, during the winter, to wear
furs or to heat themselves, as one must do in Syria. In Egypt one has no need either to use
ice in summer.

[PDF p. 112]

One commonly says: the emerald of Egypt, the caftans of Egypt, the asses of Egypt, the
serpents of Egypt. The usefulness of these last in theriac is considerable.

One of the merits of Egypt is to have furnished the piece of marble placed in the wall of the
Kaaba. It was shipped by Mohammed ben Ta'rif, freedman of Abbas ben Mohammed, in the year 241
[22 May 855 to 9 May 856], with another piece of green marble; both were sent as a gift to
the Stone, and one of them is placed on the exterior of the wall surrounding the Kaaba. They
are the two finest pieces of green marble in the mosque; their keeper, Abd-Allah ben Mohammed
ben Daoud, gives the measure of one of them, which reaches a cubit and three fingers; this at
least is what El-Fakhri reports in his history of Mecca.

Another merit of Egypt is to have furnished a concubine to the Prophet, who had children by
the Egyptian woman, while his other wives, non-Arab, remained sterile.

Here is what Ibn Abd el-Hakem recounts on this subject. In the year 6 of the hijra of the
Prophet [23 May 627 to 10 May 628], when the latter was returning from El-Hadibiah, he sent
messages to the kings. Hateb ben Abou Balta'ah also set out with a letter from the Prophet.
Arrived at Alexandria, he found El-Maqoqos seated in a pavilion overlooking the sea; Hateb
took a boat, advanced over the sea, and, when he was in sight of the pavilion, made a sign to
El-Maqoqos with the Prophet's letter between his fingers. El-Maqoqos, having seen him, had the
letter brought to him; it was taken. Then El-Maqoqos had the messenger brought to him also,
who went to him. After reading the letter, El-Maqoqos said to Hateb: "What prevents Mohammed,
if he is a prophet, from invoking God against me and vanquishing me?" "What then," answered
Hateb, "prevented Jesus, son of Mary, from invoking God against those who misknew him and
doing with them what he would have wished?" El-Maqoqos was silent a moment, then asked Hateb
to repeat what he had just said: Hateb repeated it, and El-Maqoqos kept silent. Hateb resumed:
"Before you there existed a man who had himself called the Lord Most High; God used him for
his vengeances, and then took vengeance on him.

[PDF p. 113]

Take example from others than yourself and not from yourself. If you have a religion, leave it
only for a better -- that is, for Islam, by which God compensates everything else. Moses
prophesied Jesus, as Jesus prophesied Mohammed, and we invite you to believe in the Koran only
as you yourself have invited the people of the Torah to believe in the Gospel; we do not
forbid you to follow the religion of Christ -- on the contrary, we invite you to conform to
it." El-Maqoqos then reread the letter of Mohammed. It was conceived thus: "In the name of God
the Compassionate and Merciful, from Mohammed, the Prophet of God, to El-Maqoqos, the lord of
the Copts; greeting be upon all who follow the good path! I invite you to that to which Islam
invites; embrace Islam and you will be saved and God will give you twice your reward. O people
of the Bible, come to us. A single word separates us, here it is: We worship only God and give
him no associates. We choose no other master than God (Koran, III, 57). And if you refuse (to
follow us), at least attest that we are Muslims." And having finished his reading, El-Maqoqos
took the letter and put it in an ivory casket that he sealed.

According to Aban ben Saleh, El-Maqoqos, having with him only an interpreter, sent for Hateb
during the night and said to him: "Will you not answer the questions I shall put to you? I know
that your master did not send you without having chosen you." "To all you ask," said Hateb, "I
will answer frankly." "What then does Mohammed require?" "He asks that you worship God, that you
give him no associates, and that you reject all that is not him; he prescribes also prayer."
"How many times do you pray?" "Five times during the day and night; moreover, we fast during
the month of Ramadan; we must make the pilgrimage to the Kaaba, keep our promises, and abstain
from meat not slaughtered and from blood." "Who are his followers?" "The most valiant of his
people and others besides." "Is his word accepted?" "Yes." "Describe him to me." "I described
him," reports Hateb, "but incompletely." "There are other things you do not speak of," said
El-Maqoqos: "the redness of his eyes, a redness that rarely disappears, and the seal of
prophecy placed between his two shoulders; he rides an ass, clothes himself in a mantle and,
for food, contents himself with dates and a piece of bread, without concerning himself with who
passes near him, whether it be his uncle or his cousin." "That is exact," said Hateb. "I knew,"
resumed El-Maqoqos, "that a prophet

[PDF p. 114]

remained to come, but I thought he would appear in Syria, the country where the prophets who
preceded him appeared. And here he comes out of Arabia, land of affliction and misery. The
Copts will not follow me if I rally to him, and I am anxious that you not divulge our
conversation. He (the Prophet) will conquer the country, and his companions, after his death,
will occupy this land that is ours and will be masters of all that is here. I will not say a
word of all this to the Copts. As for you, return to your master." Then, calling a secretary,
El-Maqoqos had him write in Arabic a letter conceived thus: "To Mohammed, son of Abd Allah,
from El-Maqoqos, prince of the Copts, greeting. I have read your letter and understood its
meaning, as well as the invitation it contains; I knew that a prophet remained to come, but I
thought he would appear in Syria. I have treated your messenger well, and I send you two of
the noblest slaves among the Egyptian women; at the same time, I have a mantle delivered to
you and a mule that will serve you as a mount. Greeting."

According to Abd er-Rahman ben Abd el-Qari, when Hateb presented the Prophet's letter to
Maqoqos, the latter kissed it; then he treated Hateb generously and granted him the widest
hospitality. He sent him back to the Prophet of God, to whom he made a gift of a garment, a
mule with its saddle, and two slaves -- one of whom was the mother of Ibrahim, the other,
given by the Prophet to Gahem ben Qeïs el-Abdari, was the mother of Zakaria ben Gahem, who
succeeded 'Amr ben el-As in the government of Egypt. Others claim that she was given by the
Prophet to Mohammed ben Mouslimat el-Ansari, or to Dahiah ben Khalifat el-Kalbi, or, according
to a last version, to Hassan ben Thabet.

According to Yezid ben Abou Habib, Maqoqos, on receiving the Prophet's letter, pressed it
against his chest and said: "Here is the time when the Prophet announced and described in the
book of God must come. Among the traits that characterize him, we find that he will not take
two sisters either as wives or as concubines; he will receive presents and not alms; he will
choose the poor for his councilors, and the seal of the prophets will be imprinted between his
two shoulders." Then, calling a wise man -- as there were not in Egypt young girls more
beautiful or prettier than Maria and her sister, both originally from the land of Gafn, in the
district of Antinoe -- he sent the two of them to the Prophet, to whom he made a gift in
addition of a gray mule and a gray

[PDF p. 115]

ass, a garment of Egyptian cloth, honey of Benha, and silver for alms. It is said that
Maqoqos gave as a present to the Prophet four slaves -- two according to others -- a mule
named Douldoul, an ass named Yafour, a mantle, a thousand mithqals of gold, twenty garments
of Egyptian cloth, a eunuch named Mabour who, it is said, was the cousin of Maria, a mare
named El-Korrar, a glass cup, and honey of Benha; the Prophet was marveled at it and called
upon him the blessing of God, saying: "The wicked man showed himself miserly with what he
possessed, and nothing of what he possessed will remain to him. El-Maqoqos has said good
things and has treated Hateb ben Abou Balta'at well; he has almost accomplished what he ought
to do, but he has not embraced Islam."

Ibn Sa'd says: Mohammed ben Omar el-Ouaqedi Abou Ya'qoub ben Mohammed ben Abou Sa'sa'at told
me, on the authority of Abd Allah ben Abd er-Rahman ben Abou Sa'sa'at, that El-Maqoqos, lord
of Alexandria, had sent as a present to the Prophet, in the year 7 of the hijra [11 May 628
to 30 April 629], Maria and her sister Sirin, a thousand mithqals of gold, twenty garments,
the mule Douldoul, the ass 'Afira, and the eunuch Mabour. Hateb taught Islam to Maria, who
converted, as did her sister; after them, the eunuch embraced Islam. The man whom Maqoqos had
sent to accompany Maria was named Ibn Abd Allah el-Qobti, freedman of the Beni 'Afar.
El-Maqoqos, according to Ibn Abd el-Hakem, had prescribed to his messenger to see who sat with
the Prophet and to look whether, on his back, there was a large mole covered with hairs, which
the messenger did. And when he arrived before the Prophet, he presented him the two sisters
and the two mounts, the honey and the garments, and told him that all this was the presents of
Maqoqos. The Prophet received the presents, for he had the habit of refusing the gifts of no
one. And, looking at Maria and her sister, they pleased him, but he did not wish to take the
two of them. As they resembled each other, he said: "O my God, choose for your prophet," and
God made him choose Maria in this manner: when the Prophet said to the two of them, "Confess
that there is no god but God and that Mohammed is his servant and his apostle," Maria hastened
to pronounce the confession and believed before her sister, who reflected a moment, then
pronounced the formula [...]

[PDF p. 116]

and believed. The Prophet made a gift of Maria's sister to Moslema Ibn Mohammed el-Ansari --
or, according to others, to Dahiat ben Khalifat el-Kalbi.

Yezid ben Abou Habib recounts, on the authority of Abd er-Rahman ben Shamat el-Mahri, who had
it from Abd Allah ben Omar, that the Prophet, having entered to the mother of Ibrahim, the
Egyptian, mother of his son, found with her a relative who had come with her from Egypt and
who often visited her. Grief fell upon the heart of the Prophet, who, on going out, met Omar
ben el-Khattab. The latter recognized, from the Prophet's face, that there was something; he
questioned him, and the Prophet told him everything. Omar seized his sword, entered to Maria;
the relative was still there. Omar advanced on him with his sword raised, but the latter,
seeing the gesture, lifted his robe; he was a eunuch and had nothing between his legs. At this
sight, Omar returned to the Prophet and told him how it was. The Prophet then said: "Gabriel
came to me and announced that Maria was innocent, as was her relative, and informed me that
she bore in her womb a son of mine who would resemble me, and he ordered me to call him
Ibrahim, and he greeted me by the name of Abou Ibrahim."

Ez-Zaheri, on the authority of Anas, says that, when the mother of Ibrahim brought Ibrahim
into the world, grief fell upon the heart of the Prophet until Gabriel came to him and said:
"Greeting be upon you, O Abou Ibrahim." El-Maqoqos had sent, it is said, with Maria a eunuch
who often went to see her. It is said also that Maqoqos made a gift to the Prophet of several
slaves, of whom one, Maria, was the mother of Ibrahim, the second was given to Abou Gahem ben
Hazifah, and the third to Hassan ben Thabet.

Maria gave the Prophet Ibrahim, the most cherished of men until his death -- a death that
caused the Prophet great grief. On the day of his death, he was sixteen months old.

The mule and the ass [sent by El-Maqoqos] were the favorite mounts of the Prophet. He gave the
mule the name of Douldoul and the ass that of Ya'four. He found the honey delicious and called
the blessing of God on the honey of Benha. He kept the garments, some of which served to bury
him. The name of Maria's sister was Qisar, according to others Sirin, or, according to a third
reading, Hamanah.

El-Hassan ben Aly asked Moawiah ben Abou Safian to exempt from tax

[PDF p. 117]

the inhabitants of the village of the mother of Ibrahim, out of veneration for her. Moawiah
consented to it: they were exempted from the tax, and none of them had any due to pay. All the
people of the village were either relatives or allies of Maria; they are extinct today.

According to the traditions, the Prophet is said to have said: "If Ibrahim had lived, I would
have exempted all the Copts from the tax." Maria died at Medina, in Moharrem of the year 15
[the month of Moharrem of the year 15 runs from 14 February to 14 March 636].

Ibn Ouahb says: Yahia ben Aïoub and Ibn Lahi'at told me, on the authority of Aqil, who had it
from Ez-Zahari, to whom the thing had been told by Ya'qoub ben Abd Allah ben el-Morhirat ben
el-Akhfash, who had it from Ibn Omar, that the Prophet used to say: "Iblis entered Iraq and
did there what he wished; then he entered Syria, where he was pursued until he had taken
refuge in the mountain of Shaq; then he entered Egypt and laid eggs there. His eggs hatched
and his young spread." This is an authentic tradition but little known.

Some authors have disparaged Egypt. All that it has of beauty, they say, comes to it from
outside, even the four elements: the water, brought by the Nile, comes to it from the south;
the earth is carried by the water, without which the soil would be only pure sand producing
nothing; fire? one finds no tree in Egypt fit to maintain it; as for the wind, it blows there
only from the two seas, now from the sea of Roum, now from the sea of Qolzoum. The author, in
this, shows an exaggerated bias.

Ka'ab el-Ahbar said: Mesopotamia will be preserved from ruin as long as Armenia is not
destroyed; Egypt will be preserved from ruin as long as Mesopotamia is not ruined; and
El-Koufa will be preserved from ruin as long as the universal cataclysm has not come.

[PDF p. 118]

CHAPTER X
OF THE MARVELS THAT EXISTED IN EGYPT, IN THE WAY OF TALISMANS, TEMPLES, AND OTHER SUCH THINGS

It is recounted, in the book of the Curious Facts of History and Marvels of Events, that there
was in Egypt a stone such that whoever clenched it in his hands voided everything he had in
his body.

El-Qoda'i says: El-Gahez and others report that the marvels of the world numbered thirty, of
which ten for all countries (other than Egypt), which are: the mosque of Damascus, the church
of Er-Rouha (Edessa), the bridge of Sandjar, the palace of Rhamdan, the church of Rome, the
statue of the Olives, the halls of Chosroes at Modaïn (Ctesiphon), the temple of the Winds at
Palmyra, the two palaces of Khouarneq and Sadir at Herat, and the three stones of Baalbek
which are, it is said, a temple of Jupiter and Venus -- there was there, it is asserted, a
temple for each of the seven planets, but they have been destroyed. The twenty other marvels
belong to Egypt. Of this number are the TWO PYRAMIDS, among the greatest and most astonishing
constructions; there is on the surface of the earth no monument, made by human hand and stone
by stone, greater than they. On seeing them, one would take them for two mountains rising up;
this is what made an author who had seen them say: "There is nothing for which I do not dread
the effect of time, except the two pyramids; as for them, I dread rather their effect upon
time." [Footnote: this somewhat convoluted phrase means simply that time, which wears away all
things, will be worn away by the two pyramids.] -- the STATUE OF THE TWO PYRAMIDS, also called
Balhouiah or Balhit. It is, it is said, a talisman raised against the sands, intended to
prevent them from invading the cultivated lands of Gizeh; -- the TEMPLE OF SAMANHOUD, one of
the most marvelous things of Egypt.

[PDF p. 119]

Abou Amr el-Kandi recounts this: "I visited it at the time when the governor was having the
fruits of the season stored there. At the moment when the camels approached the door with
their loads, all the flies settled on the fruits fell, and none of them entered the temple."
It was destroyed around 350 [20 February 961 to 8 February 962]; -- the TEMPLE OF AKHMIM,
marvel of marvels, full of figures and prodigious things, and presenting the portrait of the
kings who were to reign over Egypt. Dhou'n-Noun el-Akhmimi, who read the berabi (hieroglyphic
writing), noted an extraordinary wisdom in it, and he effaced the greater part of it; -- the
TEMPLE OF DENDERAH, a marvelous temple, pierced with one hundred eighty windows. Each day the
sun entered by one of these windows, the next day by the following one, and so on to the last,
after which it retreated from window to window to its point of departure; -- the WALL OF THE
OLD WOMAN, which extended from El-Arich to Assouan and went around Egypt, from east to west; --
ALEXANDRIA AND ITS MARVELS, among which must be cited the TOWER (lighthouse), the COLUMN, and
the CIRCUS where people gathered on a certain day of the year; then a ball was thrown into the
air, and the one in whose lap it fell was to reign one day over Egypt. Amr ben el-As attended
one of these festivals, and the ball fell into his lap, and indeed he later reigned over the
country in the time of Islam. This circus held a million persons, each of whom could easily
see the faces of the others. If a reading was made, everyone heard it, and if some game was
played, each could follow it with the eyes without having to raise himself on his tier,
whether he was above or below; -- the TWO OBELISKS, which are like two mountains placed on
pedestals of bronze, each angle of the mass resting on a column. One could pass beneath them,
from one side to the other, whatever one wished; -- the TWO COLUMNS OF FATIGUE are two
overturned columns, behind each of which is a mountain of pebbles, similar to the heaps of
stones one throws at Mina. If someone is tired and exhausted, he has only to approach them,
holding in his hand seven pebbles; arrived near one of these columns, he throws the seven
pebbles behind him, rises again without turning around, and returns to his work; whatever
burden he carries, he feels no fatigue at all;

[PDF p. 120]

-- the GREEN CUPOLA, a surprising cupola clad in copper like pure gold, which time cannot
destroy and which the centuries leave intact; -- the PORT OF AQABAH, the PALACE OF FARES, and
the UNDERGROUND CHURCH; this last is like a town raised upon another town, and there is no
town like it on the surface of the earth. It is, it is said, the same as Iram-dhat-el-Amad
(Iram of the Columns), to which this name was given because its columns and its (walls of)
marble are of violet-colored stones (?), alternated with bands in height and in width;
[Footnote: the phrase is difficult to understand; I do not know what two of the terms are.]
-- the MOUNTAINS OF THE SAID that skirt the Nile. These mountains, three in number, bear the
names of mountain of Kahf (or of Kaf), of Tilmoun, and of mountain of Zemagir the sorceress.
In this last is found, it is said, a peak that one sees from the Nile but that no one can
reach. There are writings traced there in your name, O my God; -- the DEFILE OF THE BIRDS,
Bouqir, in the vicinity of Ashmoun, in the Said; it is a crevice in the mountain where there
is a fissure to which, on a certain day of the year, the Bouqirs (cattle egrets) come; they
approach the crack, each bird puts its beak in it then turns back, until the crack closes on
the beak of one of them and holds it prisoner. All escape, and the captive remains suspended
until, dead, it finally falls; -- AÏN-SHAMS (Heliopolis), which is a temple of the Sun. One
sees there those two columns (obelisks) that nothing surpasses nor even equals in marvels.
They rise toward the sky to a height of about fifty cubits; they rest on the ground, and one
sees represented on them figures on mounts. At their summit are cones of copper, from the
point of which, when the Nile rises, water falls drop by drop; one easily ascertains this on
examining it. The water flows thus to the foot of these columns, where jujube trees and other
plants grow. When the sun is at the initial point of the Capricorn, the time of year when the
day is shortest, that body reaches the more southerly of the two columns and appears above its
summit; [when the sun is at the initial point of the Crab, the time of year when the day is
longest, that body reaches the more northerly of these two columns and appears above its
summit;] [Footnote: I have added the bracketed clause from the description of Aïn-Shams.] they
are the two extreme points of the two declinations, and the equinoctial line passes between
the two and [...]

[PDF p. 121]

then the sun moves between them, both going and returning, throughout the whole year. This at
least is what is said by the people who occupy themselves with this kind of science; --
MEMPHIS, ITS MARVELS, its statues, its monuments, its hypogea, its treasures; one finds there
an incalculable number of vestiges of kings, sages, and prophets. This cannot be denied; --
FARMA, richer still in marvels and monuments; -- the FAYOUM; -- the NILE; -- the stone known
by the name of the STONE OF VINEGAR, which remains at the surface of that liquid and moves in
it like a fish. One finds also in Egypt a stone such that whoever presses it in his hands
voids all he has in his body. One also met with a pearl that women wore at the hip so as not
to become pregnant, and a stone which, placed at the door of an oven, made the bread fall out
of it. In the Said were found soft, brittle stones that one kindled like torches. -- There was
also, among other marvels, a STONE VAT, into which one and even four persons could climb who,
agitating the water with some instrument, passed from one bank of the river to the other. No
one knows who had made it. Kafour el-Ikhshidi had it transported to Masr, examined it, and had
it drawn out of the water. It was placed on the shore, and writings were seen traced in its
bottom that no one could understand. The virtue of the vat ceased from then on. Another of the
marvels of Egypt was an acacia found in a village of the Said named Dechneh. If one threatened
to cut it, this tree withered, shrank, and curled up; if one said to it, "We spare you and let
you live," it returned to life. What is true is that one still finds at present in the Said an
acacia which, if one puts the hand on it, withers, and, if one withdraws it, revives. It was
brought to Cairo, and, after examination, it was recognized that its wood goes to the bottom
of the water like ebony. In Egypt one also meets the acacia, which furnishes a wood used to
heat great cauldrons for a long time. This wood leaves no ashes. -- Ibn Naser el-Masri reports
that there was, at the gate of the great palace called the Gate of the Basil, near the
suspended church, a bronze statue representing a camel, mounted by a man wearing a turban,
holding under his arm an Arab bow and shod in babouches. The Greeks, the Copts, and the other
people of the country, if they did themselves some wrong or some injury, would approach this
statue and, holding themselves between the camel's feet, the offended party would say to the
offender: "Render me justice before

[PDF p. 122]

the man with the camel makes you render it willy-nilly." This rider was none other than the
prophet Mohammed. When 'Amr ben el-As came to Egypt, the Greeks destroyed this camel for fear
it would testify against them. Ibn Lahiat says: "I was told that this statue remained a number
of years in the same place without anyone knowing who had made it."

Such are, says El-Qodaï, the twenty marvels of Egypt, several of which are even the union of a
great number of marvels; and, if one had to enumerate them one by one, the number would become
immense. It is said that there is in no country a thing so marvelous that there is not found in
Egypt something similar or approaching it. And moreover, Egypt surpasses other countries by the
marvels peculiar to it, which are not met with elsewhere.

According to the book entitled Gifts of the Hearts, there was in Egypt an underground chamber
where Christian monks lived. In this chamber was a wooden bed, beneath which lay the body of a
dead child, wrapped in leather and bound with cords. On the bed was placed a kind of jar
traversed by a copper tube fitted with a wick. When the wick was lit, and as long as it gave
light, there came out of the tube a pure, delicious, and excellent oil that filled the jar and,
by its very abundance, extinguished the wick. As soon as the wick was out, nothing more came
out of the tube, and if one withdrew the body of the child from under the bed, the oil ceased
to flow. This jar was examined without finding anything beneath it, not even the smallest hole.
The monks lived on this oil, which people bought for their use.

Master Ibrahim ben Ouasif Shah recounts that the king 'Adim, son of Naqtarim, was a violent and
proud prince, of high stature; it was he who ordered the rocks to be cut to make pyramids of
them, as the ancients had done. In his time lived the two angels driven from heaven, who
inhabited the well of Aftarah; these two angels taught the Egyptians magic, and it is claimed
that Adim, son of El-Budchir, learned most of their sciences; after which the two angels went
to Babel. The Egyptians, the Copts especially, assert that these were two demons named Mahla
and Bahala, and not the two angels; that the two angels are at Babel in a well, where the
sorcerers gather, and that they will remain there until the day of judgment. It is since that
time that idols are worshiped; it is Satan, it is said, who made them known to men and raised
them for them;

[PDF p. 123]

according to others, the first to raise idols was Badoura, and the first idol erected was that
of the Sun; others, finally, claim that the first Nimrod ordered the kings to raise the idols
and worship them. It was also, it is said, 'Adim who first made use of the punishment of the
cross, on this occasion: a woman married to a personage of the court had adulterous relations
with a man of the artisan class. The king had them crucified on two posts, the back of one of
the guilty facing the back of the other. And there was written on each post the name of the
guilty, their crime, and the date of the punishment. From then on, adultery ceased. This king
built four cities where all sorts of marvelous objects and talismans were deposited; he buried
there considerable treasures. In the east, he raised a tower at the summit of which was placed
a statue turned toward the rising sun, the two hands extended to prevent the animals of the
sea and of the desert from passing its limit; on its chest was engraved the date of its
erection. This statue is, it is said, still standing to the present; had it disappeared, the
waters of the eastern sea would have invaded the land of Egypt. The same king also had a bridge
thrown over the Nile, at the point where Nubia begins; on this bridge, he raised four statues
turned toward the four cardinal points; each of them was armed with two javelins to strike
those who would advance toward its side. These statues remained standing until the day they
were destroyed by the Pharaoh of Moses. This king also had raised, at the gate of Nubia, a
temple that has remained standing to our days. He also had cut, in one of the four cities of
which we have just spoken, a vat of black granite, filled with water, which never throughout
the course of time diminished or spoiled, for the builder had brought into it the humidity of
the air; the people of the region as well as the inhabitants of the city drank of this water
without its diminishing. The king had had this vat made because the city was very far from the
Nile. Some Coptic priests hold that this water remained thus persistent because of the
proximity of the sea, whose mists the heat of the sun pumped up, which, whether by mechanical
means or by magic, were resolved partly into water that was brought to this vat, by means of
elements such as coolness, or by using the force of the wind; in any case, despite time, this
water did not diminish, however much the people might drink of it. This king also had made a
pretty cup that enjoyed the same properties, and that Houamel offered to king Alexander the
Great. 'Adim

[PDF p. 124]

reigned over the Egyptians for one hundred forty years, and died at the age of seven hundred
thirty years. He was buried in one of his marvelous cities or, according to others, in the
desert of Qoft.

Certain Copts recount that the tomb of 'Adim had been built in the desert of Qoft at the
surface of the ground, under a cupola of brilliant green glass, at the summit of which was
placed a ball of gold surmounted by a bird of gold inlaid with gems, with outspread wings,
charged with defending the entrance of the cupola. The dimensions of the monument were a
hundred cubits square. In the middle, the body of the king was deposited, the face uncovered,
on a bed of plaited gold, and there were spread over him garments of woven gold interwoven with
gems arranged with art. The height of the cupola was forty cubits; there were deposited inside
one hundred seventy manuscripts of scientific works, and seven tables with their service: a
table of pearls of pomegranate-red color with a similar service; a table of gold of Qlimoun,
with a service of the same metal; a table of brilliant sun-stone with its service (this stone
is the emerald that makes the eyes of vipers that look at it run); a table of worked red sulfur,
with its service; a table of worked, shining white salt, with its service; and a table of solid
mercury. There were also enclosed in the cupola numerous gems, vessels of magnificent
workmanship and, around the body, seven swords and cuirasses of iron of a brilliant white and
beautiful workmanship, statues of horses in gold harnessed with saddles of gold, and seven gold
sarcophagi of dinars on which was figured the image of the king; there were also deposited with
him all sorts of drugs, poisons, and medicines enclosed in vessels of stone. People who have
seen this mausoleum claim to have remained days and days without being able to reach it, and
that finally, having approached it to a distance of eight cubits, the cupola began to turn right
and left; and, among other marvelous facts, they recounted that passing from vault to vault,
they never saw any image other than the one they had seen from the preceding vault; they said
also that they had seen the face of the king a cubit and a half long, and his beard very long
and uncovered; they measured the length of his body, which reached ten cubits and more. These
people who saw the mausoleum say that, having gone out for some work, they had discovered it by
chance, that they had questioned the people of Qoft about it, and that only one old man had been
able to answer them.

[PDF p. 125]

The king 'Adim recommended to his son Shedab ben 'Adim to raise in each province of his empire a
column on which he would write his name. Shedab therefore went to Ashmounein, erected a column
there, and inscribed his name on it. He also built circuses there, and in the desert of
Ashmounein he raised a tower surmounted by a two-headed statue dedicated to the two planets that
were in conjunction at the time of its erection. From there he went to Athrib and built there a
magnificent cupola raised on columns and pillars set one above the other; at the summit of the
cupola was placed a small statue of gold; he built besides a temple to the planets and set out
for the district of Sa. There he raised a tower surmounted by a mirror made of mixed substances
in which one could see each province, then he departed. Shedab ben 'Adim also built the temple
of Erment in which were erected statues in the name of the planets and made of all sorts of
metals; this temple was magnificently decorated: it was inlaid with gems and colored glass,
hung with silk and brocade. In the towns of the interior, starting from Antinoe, he built a
temple and constructed another at Athribis, his residence; it was he again who raised the
temple situated east of Alexandria. He also raised a statue of black granite on the western
bank of the Nile, and on the eastern bank he built several cities: in one of them was a standing
statue representing a man with his penis: if some impotent or bewitched man, incapable of
performing the virile act, approached it and rubbed it with his hand, his virility reappeared
and he could accomplish coitus. In another of these cities was the image of a cow with enormous
udders: if a woman's milk dried up, she had only to approach the cow and rub it with her two
hands for her milk to reappear. The same king also made, in the district of Assiout, a talisman
to attract the crocodiles; these animals came in throngs by the Nile as far as Akhmim, where
they were killed, and from their skins boats and other utensils were made.

The king Menqaous built a house surrounded by statues assigned to all the infirmities. On the
head of each of them, he wrote the name of the disease it cured. People used them for a long
time, until the day when a certain king overturned them. He also made the statue of a woman with
a smiling face that an afflicted person could not look at without being delivered from his grief
and his pain. People approached her one after another, went around her, [...]

[PDF p. 126]

worshiping it, and this statue became one of the divinities they honored thereafter. He also
raised another statue of gilded bronze, fitted with two wings, near which neither male nor
female fornicators could pass without showing their nakedness; it was by means of this statue
that adulterers were discovered, and this crime was no longer committed, for fear of the
statue. Under the reign of Kalkoun, one of the women of this prince was seized with desire for
one of his servants, but she feared being discovered by the statue. So, one day, conversing
with the king, she brought the conversation around to adulteries, overwhelming them with
invectives and sarcasms. Kalkoun then spoke to her of the statue and its virtue. "The king
speaks truly," answered the queen, "but Menqaous was not very wise, for he took, along with his
sages, much trouble for the well-being of his people, and not for his own. It would have been
better had he erected the statue in the royal palace, there where his women and slaves are, and
if any of them had committed adultery, it would have been known, and the apprehension of this
statue would have been a curb to the desires that might have fallen into their hearts." "You
are right," said Kalkoun, who believed the queen's advice sincere; and he had the statue
removed from the place it occupied to transport it to his palace; but it lost its virtue and
the woman accomplished her desire.

The same Menqaous also had built on the mountain of Qoçeïr a temple where magicians resided
who did not permit the winds to favor the passage of ships until the latter had paid the tax
the magicians levied on them on the king's account.

Menaous, son of Menqaous, built in the western desert a city, near the city of the magicians;
it was called Qantarat and was filled with marvels. In the middle of the city, the king had
raised a cupola above which was a kind of cloud that let fall, summer as in winter, a light
rain; beneath the cupola was a reservoir filled with a green water that served to treat and
cure all diseases. In the east, he built a superb temple fitted with four double-leaved doors.
On each leaf was represented a head that conversed with its neighbor about the events of the
day. On whoever entered this temple in a state of impurity the two faces of the door blew, and
the impure one was seized with a violent trembling that left him only when he fell dead. It is
recounted that in the middle of this temple light descended in the form of a column, and
whoever

[PDF p. 127]

managed to embrace it could distinctly perceive the spirits, hear their words, and see their
actions. At each of the gates of this city was the statue of a monk holding in his hands a
manual treating of some one of the sciences. Those who wished to know that science had only to
approach the monk and rub the book with his two hands, which he then passed over his chest; at
that instant this science fixed itself in his breast. These two cities were, it is said, built
in the name of Hermes, who is the same as Mercury, and still subsist in the same state. -- It
is recounted that a man came one day to Abd el-Aziz ben Merwan, emir of Egypt, and informed him
that, having lost his way in the eastern desert, he had come upon a ruined city where there was
a tree producing all sorts of fruits, that he had eaten of them and gathered a provision of
them. A Copt assured him that it was one of the two cities of Hermes and that there must be
considerable treasures there. Abd el-Aziz sent the man with an escort and provisions of water
and food, but they beat the desert for months without finding traces of the city.

The mother of king Milatus had dug in the western desert an immense basin in the middle of
which rose a column thirty cubits high surmounted by a stone bowl from which water flowed
constantly; around this basin were placed images of stones of various colors representing
animals -- wild and domestic beasts, birds; and every animal that approached the image
representing it remained attached to it in such a way that one could take it with the hand and
make use of it. -- She also had built for her son a pavilion. This prince was very fond of the
chase. The queen put in this pavilion seats raised on pedestals of marble plated with gold and
inlaid with gems and enamels. The pavilion was entirely adorned with marvelous designs and
engravings. Water escaped from gushing springs and flowed through canals paved with silver
toward gardens adorned with magnificent furnishings. Around the pavilion were ranged statues
that whistled in all sorts of languages, and before the seats were hung curtains of brocade.
The queen chose for her son his most beautiful cousins and the most beautiful princesses; she
married him and installed him in this garden, around which were seats for the viziers, the
priests, and the chiefs of the artisans, who came to render him account of all their acts;

[PDF p. 128]

the report finished, food and drink were served to them. Milatus, having become king at the
death of his father Marqouah, was still only a child, and the kingdom was directed by his
mother, a judicious and prudent woman, who conducted affairs as in the time of Milatus's
father, in an admirable way, treating her subjects with justice and relieving them of several
taxes. His whole reign was happy; he spread abundance and happiness among men, as well as
justice.

Milatus had one day devoted to the chase; when he returned, he had presents distributed to his
companions and had food and drink served to them. The other days, he spent one sitting,
examining the situation of his subjects and providing for their needs, and the next he spent
with his women. He reigned thirteen years and died of smallpox.

Farsoun ben Qjlmoun ben Athrib raised at the edge of the sea of Qolzoum a tower surmounted by a
mirror that drew ships to the shore and did not let them leave unless they paid the tithe; the
tithe paid, the mirror was veiled until the ships had passed. Farsoun reigned two hundred sixty
years and had built for himself a tomb behind the black mountain of the East; at the center was
a cupola surrounded by twelve chapels containing marvels all different from one another, and
there was inscribed on this cupola the name of the king and the duration of his reign.

The king Marqonos was a sage, a friend of astronomy, science, and philosophy. In his time a
singular dirhem was struck; if the owner of this dirhem wished to buy something, he agreed with
the merchant to weigh the merchandise bought simply at the weight of the dirhem, without
demanding anything more. Seduced by this proposition, the merchant accepted, and the bargain
concluded, the dirhem came to weigh a number of rotls equal to ten times double its weight, and
even twice that number of rotls if the owner of the dirhem desired it. This dirhem was found in
the treasury of the people of that age, and later in the treasury of the Omayyads. Other
dirhems were found, struck, it is said, under the same reign: if, wishing to buy something, one
placed this dirhem in the scale of some merchant, one had only to kiss it, saying: "Remember the
agreement," and one bought what one wished; returned home with the merchandise bought, the buyer
found his dirhem again, which had preceded him to his dwelling; as for the merchant, he no longer
found in the place

[PDF p. 129]

of this dirhem anything but a myrtle leaf, a piece of paper, or some other thing round like the
dirhem. It is from the time of this king also that the glass vessels were made that served as
weights; filled with water or some other thing, they weighed no more than empty. In his time
also were made those vessels that transformed water into true wine in color, perfume, and effect.
One of these vessels was found at Alfih during the vizierate of Haroun ben Khamarawiah ben Ahmed
ben Touloun; they were goblets of onyx closed with a blue stopper streaked with white. Those who
found it were Abou-l-Hasan the jeweler, of Khorassan, and his companions. As they were eating on
the bank of the Nile, they drank water from this goblet and found it to be wine; they got drunk
and began to dance; the goblet fell and broke into pieces. Abd el-Hasan was very grieved and went
to Haroun with the pieces of the vessel. Haroun, much afflicted, cried: "Had this goblet been
intact, I would have paid for it a part of my kingdom!" As for the copper vessels that changed
water into wine, they are attributed to Cleopatra, daughter of Ptolemy, queen of Alexandria;
these are numerous. It is from the time of Marqonos that the images of reptiles, toads, beetles,
flies, scorpions, and other insects were made. If one put in any place one of these images, all
those of its species gathered there and could no longer separate from the image, and they were
easily killed. This king seems to have regulated himself, in all he did, by the celestial
constellations, according to their names and their appearance, and in this way he accomplished
all he desired. He also established in the western desert a circus of colored glass, in the
middle of which was a cupola of transparent green glass. When the sun was above this cupola, the
rays were sent back to a great distance. On the four sides of the circus he installed four high
seats of glass, each of them of a different color, and on each seat were traced in glass, of a
color different from the ground, marvelous magic formulas, strange designs, and extraordinary
figures, all in limpid and transparent glass. The king spent whole days in this circus and
established three festivals there per year. At each festival the people came running, made
sacrifices, and remained seven days; and they came willingly, for this circus had no equal, no
similar circus existed in the universe; it was finally destroyed by a king furious at not being
able to make a similar one.

[PDF p. 130]

The mother of Marqounos was the daughter of the king of Nubia; her father worshiped the star
Souha, to which he gave the name of god; she asked her son to build her a particular temple. He
built it, plated it with gold and silver, and installed there an idol veiled by a curtain of
silk; the queen entered it with her slaves and her suite and prostrated herself before the idol
three times a day; she instituted a monthly festival in which victims were slaughtered and
incense was burned before the statue night and day; she enthroned a Nubian priest charged with
watching over the idol, making the sacrifices, and burning the perfumes; and she gave her son no
rest until he in turn worshiped the idol and invited (his people) to worship it. When the priest
saw that the king professed a perfect cult for the star, he wished to give the star Souha
representatives on the earth in the form of an animal that would be worshiped. For this he acted
by cunning, and waited until, by chance, the vultures, having multiplied in Egypt, caused great
damage to the people. The king summoned this priest and asked him the cause of the increase of
the vultures. "It is," said the priest, "your god who has sent them, so that you may make in
their image a statue that will be worshiped." "If that is to satisfy the God, I will do it," said
the king. "The God will be satisfied," said the priest. The king therefore had made a vulture
two cubits high and a cubit wide, of cast gold; its eyes were two rubies; two necklaces of pearls
fitted on tubes of green stone were put around its neck, and a pearl suspended at its beak; its
thighs were adorned with red pearls. It was placed on a pedestal of chased silver, itself set on
a support of blue glass, and it was installed under a vault to the right of the temple; before it
was hung a curtain of silk; it was prescribed to burn for it aromatics and odoriferous gums, and
there were consecrated to it a black calf, the firstborn of the chicks, and the first of the
fruits and flowers. After seven days, the king invited the people to come worship the idol, and
the people came running. The priest, ever preoccupied with the cult of this statue, had a festival
instituted for it. Forty days later, the devil spoke through the mouth of the idol. The first
thing it asked was that sandalwood be burned for it at each middle of the month, and that the
temple be sprinkled with old wine taken from the surface of the jars; moreover, it announced to
the people that it was it who had driven away the vultures and made the harm they caused cease,
and that in the future it would preserve them from all they had to fear. The priest, delighted,
went to find the king's mother to inform her of what was happening; she went to the [...]

[PDF p. 131]

temple, heard the words of the vulture and, all joyful, worshiped it. The king, informed in
turn, went on horseback to the temple; the statue conversed with him, prescribing certain
things to him and forbidding him others. The king worshiped it, gave it servants, and had the
temple decorated with the finest ornaments. And Marqounos remained in the temple worshiping the
statue and questioning it about what he should do, and the statue answered him.

In the matter of chemistry, he did what no king until then had yet done; it is said that he
buried in the western desert five hundred treasures. It is said also that he raised at the
gate of the city of Sa a column surmounted by a statue representing a woman seated and holding
a mirror in which she looked. If a sick person came to her and looked into this mirror, or if
someone looked for him, if he was to die of that disease, he was seen dead; if he was to live,
he was seen living. Likewise for a traveler: if he was seen from the front, it was known that
he would return; if he was seen from the back, it was known that he would linger on the road.
Was he sick or dead, he was seen such in the mirror. He also made at Alexandria the image of a
monk seated on a seat, the head covered with a kind of burnous and holding a staff in his hand.
If some merchant passed near him, he had to deposit in his hands a part of his money
proportioned to his merchandise; if he wished to pass, even far from the statue, without
handing it money, he could not do so and remained there fixed to the spot. By this means
considerable sums were gathered, which were distributed among the incurable, the infirm, and
the poor. There were executed, in his time, all sorts of marvelous things on which he had his
name engraved; it was inscribed also on all the scientific objects, on the talismans and the
statues. He had made for himself an underground tomb near the mountain of Sedam; this tomb was
vaulted, and the vault was, it is said, a hundred cubits long, thirty cubits high, and twenty
wide. It was paved with marble and colored enamels, and the ceiling was made of stones. All
around were ranged benches of glass on each of which was placed a marvelous object. In the
middle of the vault was a gallery of glass, at the four corners of which rose an image charged
with preventing people from approaching; between each two statues was a column surmounted by a
luminous stone, and in the middle of the gallery was placed a vat of gold in which was
deposited the body of the king, after he had been embalmed with all sorts of preservative
aromatics; there were enclosed

[PDF p. 132]

with him all his treasures -- gold, gems, and the rest -- and the door of the corridor was
closed with rocks and lead, over which sand was spread; he had reigned seventy-three years and
was two hundred forty years old. He was handsome, his hair was magnificent; after his death,
his women led a life full of piety and guarded the temple.

After him reigned Aïsad, then Sa, son of Aïsad (some claim that Sa was the son of Marqounous,
brother of Aïsad). This prince had built in the city of Memphis a mirror in which one saw the
times when Egypt was to be either prosperous or barren; he raised, in the interior of the
oases, a city and erected near the sea numerous towers; he also raised, behind the Moqattam, a
statue called the statue of Cunning; whoever had an entangled affair came to this statue,
burned incense to it, and his affair was found cleared up. By his orders was built, on the
shore of the sea, a tower from which one could recognize the state of the sea and know what was
happening there as far as the gaze reached -- that is, at a distance of several days' march --
and he was the first to make use of it. It was he, it is said, who built the greater part of
the city of Memphis and all the important constructions of Alexandria.

When Badares ben Sa took the government of the states of his father and his royalty was well
established in Egypt, he built, to the west of Memphis, an admirable temple to the planet
Venus; in this temple he raised a magnificent statue of gilded lapis lazuli, bearing a crown
of bluish gold, and enclosed it between two walls of green emerald. The statue represented a
woman with two tresses of worked black gold; at her legs were two rings of transparent red
stone, at her feet sandals of gold, and in her hand a scepter of coral. She moved her fingers
as if to greet those who were in the temple. Facing this statue was erected a second
representing a cow with two horns and two udders of gilded red bronze and a necklace of lapis.
The face of the cow was turned toward the face of Venus, and between the two statues, on a
pillar of onyx, was placed a basin made of a mixture of all sorts of stones and containing a
prepared water that cured all diseases. The temple was strewn with herb of Venus, renewed every
seven days; there were arranged for the priests seats plated with gold and silver, and there
were sacrificed to this idol a thousand heads of ewes, goats, wild beasts, and

[PDF p. 133]

birds. On the day of Venus, the king went around the temple, which he had furnished and hung
with curtains. He also had placed there, under a cupola, the image of a man mounted on a winged
mare and holding in his hand a javelin from whose point hung a human head. This temple lasted
until it was destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar, in the time of Maliq ben Tedares. This prince was a
monotheist according to the religion of Qobtim and Misraïm. He set out with a numerous army, by
land and sea, and made war against the Berbers, Africa, Spain, the land of the Franks, as far
as the Ocean; there he raised towers on which he engraved his name and the account of his
campaign; then he returned, dreaded by the kings of the earth.

To the west of Egypt was a city named Qarmidah whose inhabitants had for queen a sorceress;
Maliq made war on them but without success and returned to Egypt. The queen of Qarmidah wished
to destroy Egypt and, calling magic to her aid, she had fabricated (a talisman) that was thrown
into the Nile. The water swelled and flooded the crops, which perished; the crocodiles teemed,
as did the toads; diseases spread among the Egyptians, and the serpents and scorpions
multiplied. Maliq gathered the priests and sages in the palace of their sessions and engaged
them to occupy themselves with this affair. They therefore looked into their stars and saw that
this spell came to them from the west, that a woman was its author, and that it had been thrown
into the Nile; they knew from then on whence this spell came and applied themselves to repel it
by their own science, so that they got rid of the corrupted water and destroyed the dangerous
beasts. A general was sent with an army against this city, but only a single man was found
there; an incalculable number of riches, gems, and statues were seized -- among others the
statue of a priest, made of green emerald set on a pedestal of stone, and the figure of a genie,
in gold, whose head was of a red stone and the two wings of pearls, and which held in its hand
a volume containing a great part of the sciences of this people; the two boards of this book
were inlaid with gems; there was taken, besides, a basin of sapphire on a pedestal of green
enamel, in which was a water that drove away diseases; finally a mare of silver which, if
someone pronounced over it a certain formula and, after having burned for it certain perfumes,
mounted its back, flew off with its rider. There were brought to Egypt all

[PDF p. 134]

these objects and many other marvelous things and other magical works such as statues,
treasures, gems, and at the same time was brought the man (taken prisoner in the city). The king
asked him what was the most marvelous thing they had done. "One day," he said, "a king of the
Berbers, dragging after him an immense army and frightful engines, attacked us. The people of
the city closed their fortresses and went to pray to the idols. The high priest went to a great,
very deep pond, where the inhabitants quenched their thirst, and, having sat on the shore,
ordered the priests to place themselves around the basin; then he began to murmur over the
water, which began to bubble, and from the middle of the lake came out a fire, in the center of
which appeared a figure similar to the disk of the sun and all luminous. The assembly fell
prostrate before this apparition, which continued to grow until it had passed the cupola, and it
was heard to say: 'You are safe from the harm (your enemies wished to do you).' They rose, and
the enemies were dead, as were all those who accompanied them. And this because the image of
the sun, come out of the basin, had passed by, uttering a cry that had made them perish."

Kalkoun reigned over Egypt after the death of his father Khariba. It is in his time that Nimrod
lived, who, having heard of the wisdom and magical power of Kalkoun, asked this prince
permission to pay him a visit, begging him to come to meet him. Nimrod then inhabited the
countryside of Iraq and had subjugated a great number of peoples. Kalkoun went to meet him,
borne by four winged steeds, surrounded by a kind of fire and ringed with frightful images. He
was in their midst, wearing slung across him a serpent whose extremity served him as a belt;
this serpent had its mouth open. Kalkoun held in his hand a wand of green myrtle and, each time
the serpent agitated its head, he struck it with his wand. Nimrod, when he saw him, was seized
with terror and recognized the greatness of his wisdom. The Copts claim that Kalkoun rose into
the air and sat at the summit of the western pyramid, under a canopy arranged above his head. If
there befell the people of the country some painful affair, they gathered around the pyramid.
It is recounted also that he remained for days at the summit of the pyramid without drinking or
eating, and that once he disappeared for a certain time, so that he was believed dead; the kings
then had a desire to take Egypt, and one of them, a king of the West,

[PDF p. 135]

named Sadoum, attacked it with a numerous army and arrived as far as Ouadi-Haïbab. Kalkoun went
to meet the aggressors, spread by magic above their heads a cloud charged with a stifling heat,
and they remained for days under this cloud without knowing which way to go. Kalkoun then rose
into the air and went to Egypt to inform the Egyptians of what he had done; on his orders, they
went out and found the army destroyed, men and mounts. All the priests dreaded him, and they
engraved his image in all the temples. This king raised to Saturn a temple of black granite, in
the western province, and instituted a festival for it.

In the time of Darem ben er-Raian, who is the fourth pharaoh, named by the Copts Drimous, a
silver mine was discovered three days' march from the Nile; a considerable quantity of metal was
drawn from it. This prince had a statue executed in the name of the Moon, for he was born at the
moment when this planet was in conjunction with the Crab, and he raised it above the alabaster
palace his father had built in the eastern desert; around it he raised statues, all of silver,
which he clothed in red silk, and instituted for it a festival celebrated each time the Moon
entered the sign of the Crab.

When Aksaïs, the sixth pharaoh, took power after his father Mo'dan ben Mo'adious ben Darem ben
Drimous, he had erected around Memphis numerous towers; above these towers were raised columns
from one of which to another one could go; he also made at Raqoudah, at Sa, and in the towns of
Upper and Lower Egypt constructions and towers that were illuminated, and a host of talismans;
he fabricated a block of silver on which was engraved the image of the planets; this block,
plated with porcelain, was placed atop a column in the middle of Memphis; he raised in his
father's temple a statue of Saturn in worked black gold. It is from his time that the balance
intended to counsel men was fabricated: its two pans were of gold, the beam of silver, and the
chains of gold; it was suspended in the temple of the Sun, and on one of the pans was engraved
the word "truth," and on the other the word "falsehood"; below were placed stones bearing the
name of the planets. Was there a dispute between two persons, the offender and the offended
entered the [...]
   ---
   [Footnote: the Arab historians call Pharaohs the kings we name the Shepherds (Hyksos); they
count seven of them and give them an Arab origin. See El-Aïas.]

[PDF p. 136]

temple, each took a stone and pronounced over it some words, then placed one of them in one of
the pans of the balance and the other in the other; the pan of the offender sank and that of
the offended rose. Did a man wish to undertake a journey, he took two stones, giving one the
name of "departure" and the other that of "stay," and placed each of them in a pan. If the two
pans sank, neither rising above the other, he stayed; if both rose, he departed; and if only
one pan rose, he delayed his journey but ended by departing. This balance was likewise consulted
for a debt, for absent persons, and to know whether an affair was good or bad. -- Bokht-Nasr
(Nebuchadnezzar), it is said, among other objects he took to Babylon after the conquest of
Egypt, carried off this balance, which he placed in one of the temples of fire. During the reign
of Aksaïs there was also fabricated an oven that roasted and cooked without fire, and a knife
which, set in place, attracted the animals that saw it, which came to slaughter themselves on it
of their own accord; this prince also prepared a water that transformed itself into fire, and a
glass that changed itself into air, and many other magical objects; he even left the necessary
prescriptions for fabricating them.

As for the temples, it was Sourid, the builder of the pyramids, who, according to Ibn Ouasif
Shah, raised them all, deposited treasures in them, wrote in them the precepts of science, and
established a genie charged with protecting them against whoever would wish to destroy them. In
the book of El-Fihrist it is said that one finds in Egypt constructions named Berabi (temples)
built of stones of an extraordinary size. These Berabi are of different forms. One sees there
chambers for grinding, others for pounding, for condensing, for disaggregating, for filtering --
which proves that they were intended for the practices of chemistry. In these monuments are seen
engravings and unknown writings, and there have been found buried there formulas of science
traced on sheets of gold and silver, and on stone. According to El-Hassan ben Ahmed el-Hamdani,
the construction of the Berabi is attributed to Berab ben Darmesil ben Nahouil ben Khanoukh ben
Qâr ben Adam.

Abou-r-Rihan Mohammed ben Ahmed el-Birouni, in his book entitled Vestiges of the Past Centuries,
reports that in a village of Egypt is a church, visited by trustworthy people whose opinions
prevail

[PDF p. 137]

and on whose accounts one relies. This church possesses an underground chamber reached by a
staircase of twenty-odd steps; in this chamber is seen a bed beneath which lie the bodies of a
man and a child wrapped in leather. On the bed is placed a bull of marble, in the interior of
which is a glass jar into which penetrates a copper tube fitted with a wick of flax. When this
wick is lit, there escapes from the tube an oil that flows into the jar and that does not cease
to flow until the jar is filled and the oil spreads into the bull. This oil serves for the
upkeep of the church and its lighting. El-Gahan recounts that a trustworthy man, having gone to
visit this place, withdrew the jar from the bull, emptied the oil the jar and the bull
contained, extinguished the light, and put everything back in place with the exception of the
oil, which he replaced with oil he had brought; he likewise changed the wick and lit it; the oil
began to flow and did not cease until the jar was full and began to overflow into the bull; yet
he had done nothing other (than what we have said) and had added no substance. The same author
claims that if one removes the dead body from beneath the bed, the light goes out and the oil
flows no more. The people of the village (where this church is) assert that if a woman has
doubts about her pregnancy, to make sure of it she takes the child (lying dead beneath the bed)
in her arms; if she is really pregnant, her child stirs in her womb; if she feels no movement,
she must renounce her idea.

The author adds: Daoud ben Razaq Allah ben Abdallah, who had traveled much in the provinces of
Egypt and knew them thoroughly, told me that, having entered one day a great grotto, situated in
the Said and named the grotto of Sheqalqil, he saw there an enormous heap of sandarac, which he
passed to penetrate further into the grotto. There he perceived an extraordinary quantity of
fish, all wrapped in cloths as if they had been buried after their death. He took one, examined
it, and found in its mouth a dinar covered with a writing he could not well read. He took all the
fish one after another, withdrew a dinar from the mouth of each of them, and gathered a
considerable quantity. Taking the dinars, then, he headed toward the entrance of the grotto to
get out again, but, arrived at the heap of sandarac, he found it so grown that it obstructed the
passage. He returned to the fish, put the dinars back

[PDF p. 138]

in their place, and came back to the heap of sandarac, which had resumed its primitive
proportions and left the passage free. He therefore went out, then re-entered, took up the
dinars again, and wished once more to carry them off, but the sandarac had swelled and closed
the passage. Returning to the fish, he put the dinars back in place and came back; the sandarac
had resumed its first proportions, the passage was free, and he departed. He renewed the
experiment several times, taking the dinars and replacing them, and it was always the same; in
the end, fearing to perish there, he left them and went away. Some time after that, having taken
a house in this place, he saw in a wall a hollow stone on which another stone was placed. He
removed the latter and found beneath it six dinars similar to those he had seen in the mouths of
the fish. He took one, left the rest, and put back over them the stone he had removed. One day,
by the will of God, he embarked on the Nile to pass from the right bank to the left bank. "When
we were in the middle of the river," he recounted, "the fish began to leap out of the water into
the boat in such great number that we were on the point of sinking. The passengers cried out for
fear of death. I then thought of the dinar I had on me and supposed it might well be the cause
of this adventure. I drew it from my pocket and threw it into the water. At once the fish leaped
from the boat into the river, and soon there remained not a single one." -- A man in whom I have
full confidence told me, the author, that he had found a similar talisman and that he had it at
his home. He wished to show me the fish leaping out of the water, but God did not permit me to
see this prodigy.

Ibn Abd el-Hakam recounts that, after God had made the family of Pharaoh perish in the waters,
there remained in Egypt no one of the aristocracy; there were there only slaves, salaried
people, and women, and the women of Egypt, having wished to choose themselves a king, their
votes united on one of them, named Dalukah, daughter of Zeba, an intelligent, instructed, wise
person, of high birth, who was then a hundred sixty years old; she was therefore named queen.
Dalukah, fearing the attacks of the neighboring kings, gathered the noble women and said to
them: "Until now our country has been coveted by no one, and no one has cast on it looks of envy.
But our nobles and our great ones have perished, the magicians have disappeared -- they who made
us strong. I have therefore resolved to raise a rampart around our country; I will place there
on all sides garrisons, and we will no longer have to fear being attacked." She therefore built
a wall surrounding all the land of Egypt with its cultivated lands, its towns, and its villages.
At the foot of this wall was dug a canal filled with running water, over which bridges were
thrown and into which other canals emptied; on this wall, every three miles, she installed
garrisons and guards. In the intervals, and from mile to mile, was placed a smaller garrison. In
each post were established men who received provisions (as pay);

[PDF p. 139]

they had orders to watch, with bells; and if they saw coming toward their side someone of whom
they were afraid, they were to ring the bells one after another; in this way, from whatever
point the first stroke of the bell set out, all would be informed at the same hour and would
thus be on their guard. By this means Egypt found itself safe from surprises. The construction
of this wall was completed in six months; it is called the "Wall of the Old Woman," and there
remain in the Said numerous traces of it. El-Masoudi claims that she had built this wall only
out of solicitude for her son, who was very fond of the chase and for whom she dreaded the
animals of the desert and the sea as well as the attacks of the kings and the wandering tribes
surrounding the country; she placed all along this wall crocodiles and other beasts. Many other
things are said that we do not report. Dalukah reigned, it is claimed, thirty years.

The author says: "There are vestiges of this Wall of the Old Woman in the Said, and a certain
very aged old man, Mohammed ben el-Mas'oudi, told me that, traveling in the Said with some
companions along the Wall of the Old Woman, one of them tore from this wall an enormous brick,
of quite other dimensions than those made today. They passed it from hand to hand to examine
it, when, falling to the ground, it broke and let escape a bean of an extraordinary size and an
unheard-of dimension, such as one does not find in our days. The skin of the bean was removed,
and it was found sound and intact, free of worms and germs of corruption, as if it had just been
picked, without any difference. The assembly divided it, and each ate a piece of it; it was no
doubt for them that this bean had been preserved for centuries, for no one can die without
having eaten what God has reserved for him.

There was then, says Abd el-Hakem, an old sorceress named Badour whom the magicians venerated
and considered as surpassing them in magical

[PDF p. 140]

science. Dalukah, daughter of Zeba, sent to her a messenger who said to her: "We have need of
your magic and we have recourse to you, for we fear the kings may attack us. Make us therefore
something that will render us superior to our neighbors. When Pharaoh was alive, he had recourse
