to you; how could we do otherwise, now that our great ones have disappeared (that is, were
drowned with the Pharaoh of Moses) and that there remains of our people only a small number?"
Badour raised in the middle of Memphis a temple of stone, fitted with four doors, each turned
toward one of the four cardinal points -- south, north, east, and west; in this temple she drew
images of horses, mules, asses, boats, and men, then she said to the Egyptians: "I have made you
a work by which will be destroyed all those who would wish to attack you, from whatever side
they come, by sea or by land; by it you will be safe from the blows of fate, and you will have
nothing to fear from whoever marches against you in any direction. If they come by land, mounted
on horses, mules, or asses, embarked in ships or on foot, these images (painted in the temple)
will stir on the side from which the enemy will come, and whatever you do to these images, your
enemies will undergo in reality." Now, the kings having learned the situation of the Egyptians,
and knowing that the direction of affairs was now in the hands of women, resolved to attack them
and marched against them. As soon as they approached Egypt, the images of the temple stirred;
the Egyptians set to work; and all they did to these images happened really to the army advancing
against them. Were they horses? all they did to the horses painted in the temple -- whether they
cut off their heads or their hocks, put out their eyes or pierced their flanks -- happened exactly
to the horses of the aggressors; for the boats, for the foot soldiers, it was the same. The
Egyptians were the men most versed in magic and the most powerful, thanks to this science; this
power was maintained, and other men respected them.

Pharaoh and his people having perished in the waters, the women of Egypt, although there
remained in this country only slaves and hired servants, could not however do without men. One
woman set the example, freed her slave, and married him; a second took her domestic for a
husband, and an agreement was made with the men that they would undertake nothing without the
[...]

[PDF p. 141]

permission of the women, which was accepted. Such was the origin of the empire of women over
men. Yezid ben Abou Habib asserts that the Coptic women still enjoy today the same privileges
and that no man sells or buys anything whatever without saying: "I will consult my wife."

Dalukah, daughter of Zeba, reigned twenty years and directed the affairs of Egypt until the son
of one of the nobles (lost with Pharaoh) had reached his majority. He was named Darkoun, son of
Beloutis, and was elected king. But Egypt did not cease to be directed by the counsels of the
old woman for nearly four hundred years. If any part of the temple of images fell into ruin, no
one could repair it but this old woman; this power passed then to her children, then to the
children of her children, who formed a family in which this science was transmitted; this family
has died out and disappeared today. As for the temple, it was destroyed in the time of Lukas,
son of Marnious, without anyone being able to repair it or to rediscover the means (of rebuilding
it); it therefore remained in ruins, and its virtue, by which the Egyptians surpassed other
peoples, vanished; the Egyptians became men like the others; they are only more numerous and
richer. Bokht-Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), after his campaign of Jerusalem, having subjugated the
Beni-Israel, ravaged their country, and taken the people to Babel, attacked Egypt, overturned
its towns and villages, carried off its inhabitants, and left it desolate, so that Egypt was
ruined and deserted for forty years. The Nile flowed and disappeared without any use for anyone.
In the end, Bokht-Nasr, at the end of forty years, sent the Egyptians back to Egypt: the country
was repeopled, but since that time it has always been subject to other peoples.

A certain philosopher said: I have seen the temples (of Egypt) and examined them carefully, and
I recognized that they had been admirably ordered according to all the celestial figures. But
what clearly emerged from it for me is that they could not have been the work of a single sage,
but that peoples after peoples worked at them and completed them in a complete sidereal
revolution -- that is, in thirty-six thousand solar years; such works, indeed, could be
accomplished only by astronomical observations which, themselves, could be gathered only in the
span of time just mentioned. Their books were cut and carved in the rocks, engraved on the
stones,

[PDF p. 142]

and inlaid in the monuments. This writing, however, was employed only for books of exceptional
importance, or to recall a great event, to fix instructions of high utility, or to record the
account of a noble life whose memory one wished to perpetuate. This way of writing was employed
by other peoples than the Egyptians; one sees examples of it on the cupola of Rhamedan, on the
gate of Cairouan and that of Samarkand, on the column of Mareb, on the pillar of El-Moustaqarr,
at Ablaq Fard, and on the gate of Er-Raha (Edessa). It was employed preferentially in elevated
places, in famous localities, and it was traced at the places judged most safe from destruction
and ruin, where passers-by saw them most easily, so that they could not be forgotten in the
succession of the centuries.

According to El-Mas'oudi, Daluka raised the temples and the statues in Egypt, perfected the
magical tools, traced the image of those who might come to attack Egypt, from whatever side,
with their mounts, camels or horses. She represented as boats those who might come from the sea
of the West or from Syria, and she gathered in these immense temples of prodigious construction
all the secrets of nature and the properties of stones, plants, and animals. All this was
executed at determined astronomical moments coinciding with the celestial movements. If an army
marched against Egypt, whether it came from the Hedjaz or from Yemen, these images engraved in
the temple -- camels or others -- were subjected to treatments that really reached those of the
enemy army, and in this way the Egyptians were guaranteed against the attacks of the aggressors,
men and beasts. If the latter came from Syria, the same treatments were inflicted on the images
placed on the side from which the army of Syria came, and this army, men and animals, really
underwent the treatments inflicted on the images. It was the same for the armies coming from the
Maghreb, or from the sea of Roum, or from Syria, or from the other states. Thus kings and
peoples feared the Egyptians and protected them against their enemies. By the counsels and
artifices of this old woman, their kingdom formed a homogeneous whole and reached political
perfection. The ancients and those who followed them have spoken constantly of the properties
and secrets of nature known to the Egyptians; the account of the acts of this old woman was
transmitted by tradition and so widely spread that one cannot keep any doubt about

[PDF p. 143]

their authenticity. The temples of Egypt, in the Said and elsewhere, are still standing, and one
sees there all sorts of images which, drawn on any object whatever, still enjoy the property of
making executed that for which they were imagined and fabricated according to their doctrine of
the natural virtues; and God knows better than anyone how it is.

Several people of Akhmim, in the Said of Egypt, reported to me a saying of Abou-l-Faïd
Dhou'n-Noun ben Ibrahim el-Masri el-Akhmimi, the solitary philosopher who conducted himself by a
fixed rule and a method from which he never departed; he is one of those who most studied the
accounts relating to these temples and best examined the greater part of what is drawn in them,
and the writings and representations reproduced there: "I saw in a temple," he said, "a writing
that I examined attentively and that said: Beware of freed slaves, of young men, of armies become
slaves, and of the Nabataeans who call themselves Arabs. In another temple I saw another text
that said: Man, sustained by destiny, makes plans at which fate laughs. Finally in a third I saw
a text that, after a deep study, I read thus: You take counsel from the stars and you know
nothing, and the master of the stars does what he wishes."

This people, builders of the temples, studied with ardor the movements of the stars and scrutinized
the secrets of nature. The celestial movements taught them, among other things, that a cataclysm
was to occur on the earth, but it was ignorant whether it would be a deluge of fire that would
destroy all that was on the surface of the earth, or a deluge of water that would submerge it, or
finally a sword that would come to mow down the inhabitants. But, fearing that the annihilation of
men would entail the disappearance of the sciences, it built these temples where its sciences were
explained by writing, engraving, and drawing; these constructions were of two sorts: some of
stone, others of earth, this distinction being explained thus: "If," it said, "the cataclysm
occurs by fire, the constructions of earth will harden; if it occurs by water, the constructions
of earth will be destroyed, but those of stone will subsist; if it is a destructive sword, all
these monuments will remain, whether they be of stone or of earth." According to what is
recounted -- but God knows! -- these monuments existed well before the flood; but, according to
others, they were built well after this flood, and that cataclysm they had foreseen without
knowing precisely

[PDF p. 144]

whether it would occur by water, fire, or a sword, was perhaps indeed the sword, represented by a
people that hurled itself upon the Egyptians and by an invading king who made them perish.
According to others, this cataclysm would have been a plague that made most of the inhabitants
die; as proof one gives the hills of Tanis, made of human corpses heaped up, small and great, men
and women, and high as mountains; this place is known in Egypt under the name of the City of the
Hills; one also finds in the Said corpses piled one upon another in the underground chambers, the
grottoes, the catacombs, and a quantity of places in the ground, without its being possible to
know what this people was. The Christians do not recognize them as their ancestors, nor the Jews
as their forefathers, and the Muslims are ignorant of who they are. No history speaks to us of
them. They are still clothed in their garments, and many things found in the temples and the
hypogea served as ornaments to these bodies.

The temples of Egypt are marvelous constructions still standing, such as the temple of Akhmim,
that of Samanoud, and many others.

[PDF p. 145]

CHAPTER XI
OF THE HIDDEN CACHES AND TREASURES THAT THE EGYPTIANS CALL MOUTALEB (THINGS SOUGHT)

Here is how Abou Amr ben Abd el-Barr and el-Baihaqi, in their book of the Indications, in the
chapter of the traditions reported by Ibn Abbas, recount the origin of the legitimacy of the
search for treasures: "On leaving Et-Taif, the Prophet of God passed near the tomb of Abou
Raghal and said: Here is the tomb of Abou Raghal, father of the tribe of Tsaqif. When his people
perished, he cried out in the sanctuary and God preserved him, but when he went out of the
temple, God made misfortune fall upon him. As proof of what I advance, he had buried with him a
column of gold." The believers (who were with the Prophet) rushed toward the tomb, cleared it,
and brought out the column.

According to the traditions of Abd Allah ben Omar, it is said: "Going to Et-Taif, we passed near
a tomb, and I heard the Prophet say: Here is the tomb of Abou Raghal who, as long as he remained
in the sanctuary, was preserved (from death), but as soon as he went out, was struck by the same
death as his people; he was buried here, and the proof of it is that there was buried with him a
staff of gold. If you clear the tomb, you will find this staff there." The people rushed and drew
out the staff, which was indeed near the dead man.

There are in Egypt the treasures of Joseph, as well as those of the kings who preceded and
followed him. Joseph indeed hoarded all the riches that remained after having provided for the
expenses and the purchases of provisions in view of the years of dearth; and it is of these
treasures that God meant to speak when he said: "We tore them from their gardens, their springs,
their treasures (Koran, XXVI, 57)." (The book of) the science of treasures is found, it is said,
in the church of Constantinople, where it was brought from Toledo. It is recounted also that the
Greeks, on leaving Syria and Egypt, had buried most of their riches in special places [...]

[PDF p. 146]

specially intended for this use, and had written books in which these places were designated, as
well as the means of finding them. These books are said to have been deposited at Constantinople,
and it is there that one would find all that relates to the treasures. The Greeks, it is said on
the other hand, wrote nothing, but discovered books on the science of treasures left by the kings
who had preceded them -- Greeks, Chaldeans, or Egyptians; on their departure from Egypt and Syria,
they carried these books with them and deposited them in the church (in question). They are
entrusted, it is asserted, to no one except the old servants of the Church, and even then only a
single sheet is given to each, which is for him his chance of good fortune. According to
El-Maçoudi, there circulate in Egypt marvelous accounts of the treasures, the monuments, and the
riches buried in the hypogea -- objects deposited there by the kings and other personages who
inhabited this country. These treasures are still called today moutaleb (things sought), and we
have spoken of all this in our previous works.

Among other accounts, here is what Yahia ben Baqir recounts: "Abd el-Aziz ben Merwan was governor
of Egypt on behalf of his brother Abd el-Malik ben Merwan, when a man, who called himself a giver
of good counsel, came to him. 'And what is the counsel you have to give me?' asked Abd el-Aziz.
'It is that in such a cupola is found a considerable treasure.' 'And who proves it?' asked the
governor. 'The proof of it,' said the man, 'is that after digging very little one will discover
plaques of marble and alabaster; continuing the clearing, one will reach a door of bronze, beneath
which is placed a column of gold surmounted by a cock whose eyes are made of two rubies worth the
empire of the world, and whose wings are inlaid with rubies and emeralds; its feet rest on leaves
of gold placed at the summit of the column.'" Abd el-Aziz had money delivered to the man for the
wages of the diggers and of those who would have to work at the treasure. It was a considerable
hill; a great hole was made in the ground, and the objects of marble and alabaster indicated by
the man were discovered. This first discovery filled Abd el-Aziz with enthusiasm; he had a greater
number of workers brought and increased the sum necessary for their wages. The digging continued,
and the head of the cock was brought to light; as soon as it appeared, there

[PDF p. 147]

spread an extraordinary brilliance and light caused by the rubies that served it as eyes. Then
appeared its wings; then its feet; then the summit of the column; then, around the column, a
colonnade made of all sorts of stones and marbles; then vaulted corridors, with rounded niches
above the doors; in these niches were seen statues and images of gold representing personages in
all forms, and coffers of stone with their lids sealed. Abd el-Aziz mounted his horse and hurried
to the place of the excavations to see what was already discovered. A worker rushed forward and
set his foot on the step of a bronze staircase that led to the bottom of the excavation. But
scarcely were his two feet set on the steps when a sword of Ad appeared to the left of the stairs
and another to the right; the two swords joined on the man, who could not be saved and whose body,
cut in two, rolled down the steps; when the body was stretched on the steps, the column stirred,
the cock uttered a terrible whistle that was heard far away; it beat its wings, and marvelous
voices came out of its pedestal; for the whole had been made by means of springs and mechanisms;
thus, as soon as something falls on these steps or merely brushes them, the staircase shifts and
the man is dragged to the bottom of the hole. At this excavation were present, between diggers,
overseers, earth-carriers, and curious onlookers, givers of advice or cumbersome persons, nearly
a thousand men who all perished. Abd el-Aziz went away, saying: "The treasure buried there is truly
marvelous and impossible to reach; God preserve us from it!" Then, on his orders, the crowd threw
the earth that had been extracted back over the bodies of the victims, and this place was their
tomb.

"There had been formed," adds Maçoudi, "an association of seekers of treasures and caches, who
worked ceaselessly and were always making soundings in the ground, in search of the treasures and
objects that the kings and peoples of old had confided to the land of Egypt. They had found a book
written in characters of the past time and giving the description of a place situated in Egypt a
few cubits from one of the pyramids, where there was a marvelous treasure. They informed of it
Akhshid Mohammed ben Tafag, who gave them the order to dig at this place and to make themselves
masters of the treasure by all possible means. They therefore dug an enormous hole and reached an
ensemble of corridors and cupolas adorned with stones cut in the rock, on which were

[PDF p. 148]

erected wooden statues standing and coated with an unguent, to preserve them from too rapid a
corruption and prevent the disaggregation of their parts. These statues differed among themselves
and represented old men, young men, women, children; the eyes were made of all sorts of stones
such as rubies, emeralds, topazes, turquoises; some had a face of gold or silver. One of these
statues was broken, and there was found in the interior a decomposed and destroyed corpse; near
each of them were placed vases, lerani and others, of marble or alabaster; these vases still
contained the unguent with which the body placed in the wooden statue had been anointed. This
unguent is a drug ground, kneaded, and worked, without odor. A little of it was put on the fire,
and there was exhaled from it a very sweet odor, different from all the perfumes known. Each
wooden statue had been made in the likeness of the man it enclosed, taking account of the
differences of age, of years, and of bodily features. Facing each of these statues was erected
another of marble or green alabaster representing the idol the proprietor of the statue had
worshiped. On each image were traced writings that no one among those who have a (revealed)
religion has been able to decipher. Certain scholars have claimed that this writing had ceased to
be in use in Egypt four thousand years ago, and what we have just said is a proof that they are
neither Jews nor Christians. The excavation produced only the statues of which we have spoken.
This happened in 328 [18 October 939 to 5 October 940], and to all those who, before or after
this period, have governed Egypt from Ahmed ben Touloun and his successors to this year -- that
is, in the year 332 [4 September 943 to 23 August 944] -- are attributed marvelous accounts of the
discoveries made in their time, in the way of treasures, riches, gems, and the finds of tombs made
in these searches for treasures. But we have spoken of all this in the preceding parts of our work.

One day, Ahmed ibn Touloun went on horseback to the pyramids. There his chamberlain came to him
with a troop of people covered with woolen garments, armed with axes and levers. Ibn Touloun asked
them what they were doing. "We are seekers of treasures," they said. "Extract none in the future
without my order," said Ibn Touloun, "or without the order of a man of mine."

[PDF p. 149]

These people informed him that, in the direction of the pyramids, was a treasure they could not
reach. He then gave them Er-Rafaqi and wrote for the governor of Ghizeh the order to furnish them
men and money. Then he departed. The others worked a long time; in the end the treasure appeared;
Ahmed ibn Touloun went to the excavation; the diggers were still digging and had uncovered a vat
filled with dinars, on which was placed a lid covered with berbeti characters. A man knowing this
writing was brought, and here is the sense of the text: "I am so-and-so, son of so-and-so, the
king who freed the gold of its impurities and its dross; and he who wishes to know by how much my
government surpassed his has only to examine by how much the standard of my dinars surpasses the
standard of his. He who knew how to purify the gold was, himself too, pure during his life and is
so still after his death." "Glory to God!" cried Ibn Touloun; "what I have gained by this single
inscription is worth more to me than the wealth." Then he had two hundred dinars distributed to
each of the seekers of treasures. Each workman received five of them, besides the integral payment
of his wages; Er-Rafaqi had for his share three hundred dinars and his servant Nessim a thousand.
Ibn Touloun carried off what remained of the dinars and found their standard far superior to that
of all the others. From this period he became very strict about the standard of the gold in
Egypt, so much so that the standard of his dinars is now universally known under the name of
Ahmedi, which is the most perfect standard; it was his dinars alone that were used for gilding.

[PDF p. 150]

CHAPTER XII
OF THE DESTRUCTION OF THE RICHES OF THE EGYPTIANS

God reports: "Moses said: O my Lord, you have given Pharaoh and his great ones glory and riches in
the life of this world; is it, O my God, so that they may turn away from your path? O my God,
overturn their riches, and harden their hearts; let them not believe until after having undergone
the terrible punishment." And God said: "Your prayer is granted" (Koran, X, 88). Such is the prayer
of Moses against Pharaoh and his people, the Egyptians, because of their impiety, that God might
destroy their riches. Ez-Zaggag says that "to disfigure a thing" is used to say that one makes it
lose its first form.

According to Abd Allah ben Abbas and Mohammed ben Ka'b El-Qorazi, the riches and the dirhems of the
Egyptians were changed into engraved stones that preserved their primitive forms, whether they were
whole dinars, thirds, or halves of dinars. God left subsisting no mine of which one of their
descendants could make use. "We were told," says Qatadat, "that their riches and their harvests were
changed into stones." Mogahed and Atiah say that God destroyed them so thoroughly that they
disappeared. One says "a destroyed spring," to signify that a spring is dried up, and "to destroy a
place" when a place has been overturned and ruined.

According to Ibn Zeid, the dinars of the Egyptians, their dirhems, their furnishings, with all they
possessed, were changed into stones. Mohammed ben Ka'b recounts that a man and his wife lying
together on their bed were both changed into stones, and he adds: Omar ben Abd el-Aziz questioned me
one day, and I recounted this fact to him. He then had brought a sack found in Egypt and drew from
it fruits, dirhems, and dinars, and all this was of stone. "One day," [...]

[PDF p. 151]

recounts Mohammed ben Shehab ez-Zaheri, "I went to see Omar ben Abd el-Aziz; he called: 'Hey,
slave, bring the sack!' The sack was brought and emptied; there were in it dirhems, dinars, dates,
nuts, lentils, beans. 'Eat, Ben Shehab,' Omar said to me; I stretched out my hand, but all this
was of stone. And I said: 'What is this, O Commander of the Faithful?' 'This,' he answered me, 'is
a part of what Abd el-Aziz ben Merwan found, when he was governor of Egypt, and comes from the
riches of the Egyptians that God destroyed.'" El-Modareb ben Abd Allah esh-Shami says: "Someone
told me he had seen in Egypt a palm tree lying on the ground that was of stone; and indeed," he
added, "I have seen a number of people, standing or seated, occupied with their work; to see them,
one would have taken them without hesitation for real men, but on examining them more closely, one
recognized that they were men of stone. I saw an Egyptian slave occupied in plowing with two
bulls, and the man and the bulls were of stone." Ousama ben Mousa, in his History of the Prophets,
recounts that after the disaster of Pharaoh and his people, and when the Beni Israel, struck by
this prodigy, had converted to the true faith, Moses chose from among the twelve tribal chiefs two
chiefs, Kaleb ben Mouqiah and Yousha' ben Noun (Joshua son of Nun), and sent them to Egypt, each
with twelve thousand men. Egypt no longer had anyone on whom to lean since Pharaoh and his people
had perished in the waves. They therefore seized the objects and treasures of Pharaoh and returned
to Moses. This explains the verse: "I made them heirs of the land of Egypt," and the passage of
the Koran where it is a question of the people of Pharaoh: "And we tore them from their gardens,
their springs, their treasures, their places of delight (Koran, XXVI, 57-58)," adding: "And I will
make it the heritage of another people"; and this other passage: "And we will give as a heritage
to the people of the weak the east and the west of the land in which is placed our blessing
(Koran, VII, 133)" -- that is: of the land of Egypt we will make the heritage of the Beni Israel,
for these are the weak who were there; this comes in witness to this other verse: "We wish to be
benevolent toward the weak of the earth, we will make of them imams and heirs (of the soil) and we
will make them powerful on the earth" (Koran, XXVIII, 4-5).

The compiler and author of the book adds: Daoud ben Rizq ben Abd Allah, who had long traveled
through Egypt, told me that, passing through a valley near Qlimoun in the southern region, he saw
considerable fields planted

[PDF p. 152]

with watermelons, cucumbers, and fruits, which were all of stone. Formerly a great personage told
me that, in one of his journeys in Egypt, he had seen a great number of watermelons that were all
of stone. Such are the summer watermelons called Abdali.

[PDF p. 153]

CHAPTER XIII
OF THE CHARACTER OF THE EGYPTIANS, OF THEIR MANNERS, AND OF THEIR TEMPERAMENT

Abou-l-Hassan Ali ben Radouan the physician says: "According to what is recounted, Masr was the
name of one of the children of the prophet Noah. It is reported that this Masr, having stopped in
this country, took root here, peopled it, and gave it his name. The region that bears this name
today is the one where the Nile flows and which is entirely enclosed within these four limits: the
sun, rising at the eastern extremity of the earth, eight hours and a third before reaching Egypt,
sets at the western extremity of the inhabited world, three hours and two thirds after having left
Egypt. From this it results that this region is situated in the western half of the inhabited
quarter of the earth, and this western half, according to Hippocrates and Ptolemy, is endowed with
a lesser heat and a greater humidity than the eastern half; for it forms part of the division
subject to the influence of the moon, while the eastern half is subject to the influence of the
sun; this is explained by the fact that the sun rises in the eastern part and appears only
afterward in the western part, and that the moon, on the contrary, rises in the western part and
appears only afterward in the eastern part. Ancient authors have claimed that Egypt occupied
exactly the middle of the inhabited quarter of the earth, but, as we have explained, it is
situated in reality in the western half. The third limit is represented by the shortest distance
separating this country from the equator; it is from Assouan that this distance must be counted.
From this point to the equator there are 22 deg 30'. The sun passes to the zenith of the people of
this locality twice in the year, when it arrives at the end of the Twins or the beginning of the
Crab. At these two moments, an inhabitant of Assouan standing upright would cast no shadow at
noon. Heat, dryness, and torridity are the dominant states there, for the sun there makes

[PDF p. 154]

the humidity evaporate; thus the complexion of the inhabitants is black and their hair curly,
because of the burning ardor of the climate. The fourth limit is represented by the longest
distance from the north of Egypt to the equator; this distance is counted from the shore of the
sea of Roum, on which are situated a number of towns of Egypt, such as Alexandria, Rosetta,
Damietta, Tanis, Farama: the distance from Damietta to the equator is 31 deg 20', the terminal
point of the third clime and the initial point of the fourth; the sun there maintains itself at a
medium distance, neither too near nor too far. The temperature there is temperate, with a slight
propensity to heat; the temperate zone, in the inhabited part of the earth, is in reality at the
beginning of the fourth clime. The situation of Damietta on the sea, which moreover surrounds it,
makes it enjoy a climate holding the middle between the hot and the cold, but approaching above all
the mean for humidity. The dominant state there is therefore humidity, but humidity without
complication of cold or heat. For this reason the complexion of its inhabitants is brown, their
character gentle, and their hair smooth. Now, the extreme southern point of Egypt having for its
dominant state heat, and its extreme northern point a medium temperature with a slight inclination
toward heat, it follows that Egypt, being situated between these two points, has for its
characteristic heat; this heat diminishes as one moves away from Assouan and approaches the sea of
Roum. This is why Hippocrates and Galen said that the dominant state in Egypt is heat. The mountain
Luka, which extends to the east of this country, shelters it against the east wind; indeed, this
wind never makes itself felt at Fostat-Masr, where it arrives only obliquely from the northeast or
southeast; the east wind is a dry wind that preserves from corruption, but the Egyptians are
deprived of its advantages. Thus the localities of Egypt where this wind blows are in a better
state than the others; Alexandria and Tanis are in this case. This mountain prevents the sun from
shining on Egypt although it is already above the horizon; thereby the duration of its radiation on
the soil is less than it should be; this same phenomenon is the cause of the stagnation and the
thickening of the air.

The land of Egypt abounds in animals and plants, to such a point that it is almost impossible to
find a place devoid of animals or plants. It is a weak land which, when the Nile has just
withdrawn, appears like a mud. But, as soon as the heat has absorbed the humidity found there,

[PDF p. 155]

the soil splits into wide crevices. There where the animals and plants abound, corruption also
abounds. Egypt therefore unites the ardor of the temperature with the abundance of plants and
animals. This explains the calcination and the black color of its soil, for truly the earth there
is black. In the vicinity of the mountains the earth is mixed with sebakh, borax, and salt. In the
evening there rises from the soil of Egypt a black vapor or dust; this phenomenon takes place
chiefly during the summer. Egypt divides into numerous regions that each produce a thing not found
in the others; the cause of this is that this country is very narrow and extends in length over the
second and third climes. The Said is remarkable for its palms, its acacias, its thickets of reeds
and papyrus, its charcoal-works, and many other things; in the Fayoum are found a quantity of
ponds, thickets of reeds, lakes for retting flax; Lower Egypt abounds in plants of multiple
species -- colocasia, banana trees, etc. In sum, each part of Egypt has a product peculiar to it
that distinguishes it from the others. The Nile makes humid the dryness of summer and autumn, and
we have explained that what dominates in Egypt is heat and accidental humidity, that this country
is divided into numerous regions, and that its air and its water are bad. The ancients have
demonstrated that the places where corruption abounds give off numerous exhalations into the
atmosphere, which the varieties of miasmas prevent from remaining immutable. It has been
demonstrated that the atmosphere of Egypt changes very rapidly because the sun does not heat the
soil for a normal duration. Hence frequent changes in the state of the air of Egypt, changes that
sometimes occur in the course of a single day: at one moment it is hot, at another it is cold; now
it is dry, now humid; now the air is agitated, now it is calm; now the sun shines, now it is veiled
by clouds. In sum, the atmosphere of Egypt is very variable and never remains in the same state. It
is for this reason that the humors circulating in the arteries and the veins are never either in
the same state. The continual changes of the air, and the slight altitude of the mountains, remedy
the inconvenience caused by the evaporation that occurs each day at the surface of the soil and
that the heat of the soil itself prevents from condensing in the atmosphere. If, during the cold
hours of the night, the air freshens, the [...]

[PDF p. 156]

fog lowers toward the surface of the soil and forms clouds that produce rain and dew. Sometimes
these clouds are reabsorbed by an unknown phenomenon. Thus each day the fogs condensed the day
before dissolve, and that is why the rain-clouds rarely accumulate in Egypt. It is clear also that
the soil of Egypt is each day moistened by the air that has become impregnated with fogs that
resolve into rain or disperse. Certain authors have claimed that the clouds were formed by the
transformation of air into water; and if we add this fact to what we have already said, one will
realize much more clearly the variations of the air in Egypt and the corruption found there in
abundance. It is therefore well established that the climate of Egypt undergoes numerous
variations and that accidental humidity is frequent there -- humidity that accelerates corruption
in this country. The reason for this is that the seasons that are ordinarily the driest in other
regions are the most humid in Egypt; here, indeed, summer and autumn become humid, owing to the
swelling of the Nile and the inundation, contrary to what happens in other countries.

Hippocrates teaches us that the humidity of summer and autumn is accidental -- that is, that it is
produced by abnormal causes, such as the humidity of rain that falls in summer; this is what led
us to say that the humidity of Egypt is accidental, for heat and dryness constitute in reality the
normal state of Egypt, but it happens that this state changes into accidental humidity as a
consequence of the rise of the Nile during summer and autumn, a circumstance that determines a
considerable corruption. This is what explains the present bad state of Egypt, whose land is
puny, the abundance of corruption that reigns there, and the bad quality of the water and the air.
These inconveniences have no perceptible influence on the body of the Egyptians, accustomed to
this state, and their body is appropriate to it. All that Egypt produces, animals and plants, is
similar to Egypt itself: exiguous bodies, insignificant strength, frequent variability, extreme
ease in falling ill, very brief duration; the wheat of Egypt is an example of this: it corrupts
easily and rapidly and ripens in a short time; animate bodies, as is known, do not differ from
wheat in the rapidity of development. And how could it be otherwise, since bodies are a compound
of all this ensemble? The condition of the plants and animals that

[PDF p. 157]

Egypt produces, from the point of view of the weakness caused by the innumerable variabilities,
the intense corruption, the rapidity in falling ill, is similar to that of the soil itself, which
is weak too, corrupts, varies, and transforms rapidly; the situations are indeed identical. And
this is what allows the animals to live there and the plants to grow there, for, being issued from
this ensemble of circumstances, they do not differ from their milieu and can prosper. As for the
foreign objects imported into Egypt, they alter as soon as they are in contact with this
atmosphere, but if their stay is prolonged and they bend to the ambient air and accustom themselves
to it, they come to resemble the objects produced by the Egyptian soil.

As for the foods and drinks used in Egypt: the cereals alter very quickly, being weak by nature
and rapidly corrupted, like wheat, barley, lentils, chickpeas, purslane, and chickling vetch, for
all these grains spoil in a very short time, and none of the dishes prepared with these seeds has
the taste of the same dishes prepared in other countries. After a day and a night, the bread made
of Egyptian wheat is no longer edible and, if one tastes it, one no longer finds any savor in it;
it disaggregates, having no more cohesion, and spoils rapidly; likewise for the flour; this is
what explains the difference one observes (between the bread of Egypt) and that of other countries.
All the grains of Egypt are in the same case, as are its fruits and the foods drawn from them. None
of this lasts long; everything, on the contrary, decomposes rapidly and in a very short time. What
is imported into Egypt evidently alters under the influence of the frequently variable air of the
country, and loses little by little its first nature to approach the state of Egypt; it is not so
when the importation is new and the journey still recent, for the imported object then still keeps
something of its primitive qualities. The animals on which the inhabitants feed have, if they are
of the country, a nature in keeping with that of the people of the country themselves; like them
they are weak, change rapidly, and consequently suit the nature of these people. The imported
animals -- the large sheep of Barca, for example -- acquire, as a consequence of the journey, a
dryness, an aridity, and humors not in keeping with those of the Egyptians; thus, on their arrival
in Egypt, most of these beasts are ill, but, if they stay a suitable time, their nature transforms
and puts itself

[PDF p. 158]

in keeping with that of the Egyptians. Most of the Egyptians use as drink the water of the Nile; we
have spoken sufficiently of the virtues of this water. Some drink the water of wells, more in
keeping with their nature. As for the water of cisterns, few people use it in Egypt. Their best
drink is the shamsi, for the honey introduced into it preserves its virtue and retards its
corruption. The time when this drink is made is the hottest of the year; the heat makes the
beverage ferment, and the raisins that are its base come from countries where the air is better.
Wine is very little used unless honey is added to it: it is pressed from the grapes of the country,
so it is of the same nature as the people; but the shamsi is preferred to it. Apart from the shamsi
and wine, all the drinks used in Egypt are bad and without virtue, because of the rapidity of
transformation caused by the elements composing them. Such is the case of date wine, cooked wine,
and wheat beer. The food of the Egyptians differs (according to the region). The people of the Said
feed chiefly on dates and confections prepared with sugarcane; this plant is also sent to Fostat
and to other towns where it is sold as a comestible. In the Delta, colocasia and chickpeas are
eaten most often -- products that are likewise transported to Fostat and elsewhere, where they are
sold and eaten. Most of the Egyptians make great use as food of fresh or salted fish; others feed
on milk or milk products. The peasants prepare a kind of bread named ka'k, made with pounded and
dried wheat; it is the basis of their food throughout the year. As a general rule, each class of
the people maintains its body by means of things that suit it and to which it is habituated and
appropriated. But among the Egyptians the food is rather bad, which has no influence on their
temperament, long since made to it. It is nevertheless one of the causes of the weakness and
debility of their constitution and of the ease with which they become ill. The people of the
countryside move and walk more than the people of the towns; thus their bodies are more solid, for
walking straightens and fortifies the limbs. The Saïdians are more slender, darker in color,
thinner, and weaker because of the much stronger heat among them than in the Delta. The people of
the Delta have abundant stools and urine because the heat

[PDF p. 159]

is less in their country and they make use of cold and compact foods, such as colocasia.

As for the humors of the Egyptians, they resemble one another; the vigor of the soul, indeed, is a
consequence of the state of the body, and their body is weak, quick to change, not very robust, and
not very hardy against ills. Their character is exactly the same; what dominates in them is
fickleness, indecision, indolence, cowardice, despair, avarice, impatience, disdain for study,
quickness to take fright, jealousy, slander, lying, the facility to calumniate others before the
king and to accuse them; in short, the foundation of their character is composed of the vilest
defects produced by the baseness of the soul. Not all are thus; but these defects are met with in
most of them. There are however some to whom God has apportioned virtue and beauty of character and
whom he has preserved from vices. This property of the land of Egypt of infiltrating into souls
cowardice and baseness is the cause that lions do not live there, or, if there is one in the
country, it degenerates and loses its virtue of reproduction. The dogs of Egypt are less bold than
those of other countries. Exception must be made for the animals whose nature is everywhere the
same, like the ass and the hare.

Galen, it is said, held that the season of spring was naturally temperate; he was far from
believing it hot and humid. Among other virtues, this season enjoys the property of fortifying the
bodies, facilitating digestion, bringing back the heat, purifying the animal spirits by the
equality and limpidity of the air and the equilibrium of the days and nights, and developing the
blood. One calls "equal air" that in which is met neither excess of cold or heat, nor excess of
humidity or dryness; in these conditions it is pure and limpid, a circumstance that fortifies the
animal spirits; the bodies are put back into the normal state, the vivacity of the animals
increases, beings grow, enlarge, and are pushed to reproduction. Now, if we seek in Egypt some air
such as we have just described, we find it only during the months of Amchir, Barmahat, Barmoudah,
and Bachans -- the time when the Sun occupies the second half of the Water-Carrier, the Whale, the
Ram, and the Bull. We meet then in Egypt days equal to the nights, a pure and limpid air without
excess of heat or cold, of humidity or dryness. The sun there is free of clouds, the air is calm
and without agitation, except in the months of Barmoudah and

[PDF p. 160]

Bachans, during which it is necessary that the north wind come to temper by its freshness the heat
of the sun. Then too the animals take more movement, give themselves over to coitus, their voice
becomes more beautiful; the trees cover themselves with leaves, the flowers half-open, the
reproductive force increases, the chyme predominates in the blood. In Egypt, this season advances
by a number of days equal to that of the days by which it is diminished at the end, because of the
heat proper to this period. At the beginning of this season are met very cold days, in the month of
Amchir, when the north wind blows and the sun is veiled by clouds. This is due to the fact that the
season of spring penetrates into the season of winter, and if the north wind blows at this moment,
the freshness cools the air, which from temperate becomes cold; moreover, the abundance of humid
vapors rising from the soil renders the air humid and brings it back to its winter state.
Sometimes, however, the air is freshened by other winds than the north wind; if, for example, the
south wind -- which is the hottest of all the winds -- blows in this season, it borrows cold from
the earth and the water previously cooled by the air of winter, and, passing over a cold thing,
takes from it a part of its freshness. But if this wind continues to blow for many consecutive
days, it becomes burning again and heats the air and dries it. A proof that the freshness of the
south wind, called by the Egyptians marisi, comes indeed from the cold of the water and the earth
of Egypt and not from a cause inherent in this wind, is that, as long as this wind blows, one does
not see accumulate in the atmosphere those clouds which, by the effect of the heat, give off humid
vapors and condense by the effect of the cold of the night. The heat of the south wind prevents
the cold from concentrating and disperses it. If this wind persists, it warms the water and the
earth and returns to its natural state, which is heat. When the season of spring is in advance of
its normal time, these changes occur, and the wind, on its arrival in Egypt, is subject to the
variations caused by this multiplicity of states and by the quantity of fogs it absorbs. Think
what it must be during the other seasons. Thus in spring the winds are frequent, and the physicians
delay the administration of purgatives until the season is well established -- that is, until the
time when the sun traverses the signs of the Ram and the Bull.

Then one enters the season of summer, which comprises the end of Bachans, Boo- [...]

[PDF p. 161]

nah, Abib, and a part of Mesori -- the time when the sun traverses the Twins, the Crab, the Lion,
and a part of the Ear (Virgo). The heat then becomes stronger, as does the dryness; the grains dry
out, the fruits swell, and those who eat them fill their bodies with bad chyme. When the sun has
entered the Crab, the Nile begins to grow and to spread over the land of Egypt. The natural
condition of summer is changed by the enormous accumulation of vapors that rise from the water
into the atmosphere. At the beginning of this season, when the sun is in the sign of the Twins,
certain days are met that enjoy an air similar to that of certain days of spring, when the sun is
veiled by clouds and the north wind blows. A great number of physicians are deceived by this and
then administer purgatives, believing themselves to be in spring; the skillful physician will not
be deceived and will wait until the heat is well established; but most care very little about it.
At the end of summer the Nile is at its full; and it is clear that this season was in advance of
its normal time by as many days as it will be diminished at the end; the end of summer is marked
by great disturbances brought on by the considerable quantity of vapors that rise from the soil
and mix with the air. If the bodies of the Egyptians did not have the habit of these variations
and were not fashioned to this temperature, they would be subject to the diseases that Hippocrates
affirms must occur when the summer is humid.

Next comes the season of autumn, which, by its nature, is humid. This season embraces the second
half of Mesori, the months of Thot and Baba, and some days of the month of Hathor. During this
time the sun occupies successively the second half of the Ear (Virgo), the Balance, and the
Scorpion. At the beginning of this season, the Nile finishes growing and spreads over the lands,
covers the soil of Egypt, and from its waters give off considerable vapors which, mixing with the
air, change the nature of autumn and make it pass from dryness to the humid state, to such a point
that sometimes in this season rain falls and clouds accumulate in the atmosphere. In this season
are met days when the heat is very strong, although in reality it ought to be rather weak there;
but if the air is rid of all humid vapor, autumn returns to its normal state -- that is, to heat.
There are also met days similar to certain spring days: this happens when the nights become

[PDF p. 162]

equal to the days and the water vapor renders the air humid. The variations of the atmosphere are
more accentuated in this season because of the abundance of humid vapors; now it is hot and now
cold, now dry and most often humid, and this lasts until the humidity of the water prevails. In
autumn, the Egyptians catch a great number of fish which, absorbed, produce in the body a viscous
humor that transforms for the most part into bile, if it comes into contact with some bilious
humor. Thus the animal spirits inherent in the body alter, the humors set themselves in movement,
digestion operates painfully in the belly, the intestines, and the veins, and there is produced
an unhealthy chyme abundant in bilious or melancholic humors, in viscous phlegms, in raw humor or
cooked humor; most often the humor produced is a compound of all this, and it is this that
determines the appearance of diseases. At the end of autumn, the Nile withdraws, the land is
uncovered, and the air cools; the fish teem (on the ground), the vapors no longer rise, and the
corruption becomes greater. By means of it, diseases propagate, and, without the long habit they
have of it, the Egyptians would be overwhelmed with far more numerous diseases.

Finally one enters the season of winter, a season by its nature cold and dry. It lasts during the
second half of Hathor, Khiak, and Tobe, when the Sun traverses the Archer, the Capricorn, and a
part of the Water-Carrier, which makes less than three months. The cause of this is in the heat of
the soil of Egypt and the variability of the bodies. At the beginning of this season, the land is
uncovered, plowing is done; corruption then spreads because of the great quantity of seeds, animal
excrement, and detritus put to use, and because the land is weak; it is indeed, at this moment,
like mud and produces in abundance rats, worms, plants, and herbs. There also give off from the
land abundant vapors which, condensing in the atmosphere, end by forming a curtain so thick that
it becomes impossible in the morning to distinguish the colors of the nearest objects. [Footnote:
an allusion to the religious prescription that fixes the moment of the morning prayer at the
precise instant when one can distinguish a white thread from a black thread.] One catches
innumerable quantities of fish enclosed in the pools of water; these fish, incapable of moving,
corrupt and once absorbed produce

[PDF p. 163]

in the body abundant viscous matters that predispose to corruption. At the beginning of this
season, the diseases are more intense; this intensity ceases when the cold is well established,
when the digestion has become regular, when the air has taken on a perfect fixity, when the
natural heat has returned to the interior of the bodies, when the land covers itself with plants
and the corruption stops; the bodies then become more vigorous; this happens at the end of Khiak
and during the month of Tobe. It has been demonstrated that the seasons in Egypt are very variable
and that the worst weather of the year -- in other words the months of Hathor and Khiak, that is,
the end of autumn and the beginning of winter -- is the most fecund in diseases. The seasons vary
and put themselves in relation with what is unhealthy in Egypt; but these variations have less
influence on the Egyptians than they would have in other countries, if similar variations were to
occur there. It has been recognized that the first cause of this state of things is the swelling
of the Nile during the summer and its spreading over the lands during the autumn, contrary to what
happens for the other rivers of the inhabited earth, which swell only at the particularly humid
periods -- that is, during winter and spring.

From all that precedes one may conclude that the accidental humidity is considerable in Egypt, and
that the local diseases are due specially to this humidity. From the little I have seen of it, I
have been able to recognize that the diseases special to the region have no other cause and are
not determined by the presence, at the outset, of phlegm or raw humor. All diseases occur among
them at all times, as Hippocrates remarked; most of the diseases of the Egyptians are accidental
-- that is, they come from bilious or phlegmatic humors, according to the climatic state of the
country.

What we have said above demonstrates that if the morbid accidents are frequent, they have at least
among themselves an intimate relationship, and their appearance in a single year attenuates their
debilitating effects, thanks to the habit the inhabitants have acquired of them; a change in the
habitual conditions brings on diseases; to these changes from the normal conditions are inherent,
in my opinion, a multitude of morbid germs, foreign to the habitual variations of the climate. The
Nile does not make the bodies ill every year, but if its flood exceeds the mean and the inundation
prolongs itself beyond the normal time,

[PDF p. 164]

an epidemic breaks out. It has been asked whether the body of the Egyptians, being as weak as has
been said, is not always ill. To this we will answer that such is not our opinion, for disease
carries in itself its noxious action and does not act by an intermediary; the body of the Egyptian
is therefore not continually ill, but it becomes so with great ease. As for the local diseases of
Egypt, we have spoken sufficiently of them, and it is established that most of them are simple
morbid accidents that determine the mixture of bile and raw humor; the other diseases are due to
rapid and proximate causes and are particular to the end of autumn and the beginning of winter.

Of epidemic diseases. -- One gives the name of epidemic disease to that which spreads over the
generality of people in a single place and at the same time. One of them, named maouatan, is the
one that makes the most persons die. The origin of these diseases is due to multiple causes that
may be reduced to four categories: change in the state of the air; change in the state of the
water; change in the food; change in the state of the functions of the soul. The changes in the
state of the air are of two sorts: (1) normal change: this change brings no epidemic and is not
harmful; (2) abnormal change: that one produces the epidemic. It is the same for the three other
categories. There is an abnormal change in the state of the air when it is either too hot, or too
cold, or too humid, or too dry, or finally when there mix with it deleterious emanations that
corrupt it in turn. The cause of this change may be either near or distant, for Hippocrates and
Galen are of the opinion that nothing prevents an epidemic from breaking out in Greece resulting
from an agglomeration of miasmas formed in Abyssinia which, mixed with the air, arrives in Greece
and propagates the epidemic there. The air undergoes still further changes independent of its
normal variations at the arrival of considerable caravans; the people who compose them have the
body fatigued by the length of the journey, and the humors in bad state; there exhales from them
a quantity of emanations which, mixed with the air, communicate themselves to persons, and the
epidemic breaks out.

The water can equally be a cause of epidemic, if its quantity is too small or too great; there
mixes with it then a certain corruption, despite which

[PDF p. 165]

the people are obliged to drink it. The ambient air corrupts itself too. The cause of the
corruption of the water may be likewise either distant or near; the water, for example, may
traverse and bathe unhealthy places where numerous corpses are piled, or flow through hearths of
corruption. This corruption, carried by the water, mixes with it.

The food can be a cause of epidemic if the provisions, having become rare, are of too high a
price; in this case the generality of the people must feed on spoiled foods; or else, if the
people eat too much at a single time, as happens during festivals, the indigestion is then general
and everyone is stricken with the same disease; or else, again, the pastures where the animals
graze are corrupted, or the water they drink is altered.

The emotions of the soul can produce the epidemic when, for example, a whole people is subjected to
terror -- terror inspired by some invading king; one is agitated, the brain works to find some
means of escaping the tyrant, and thinks ceaselessly of the calamities that threaten. Digestion
alters, the natural heat undergoes repeated variations, and, despite this state, one is often
obliged to violent movements; or else, preoccupied with a dearth that is to occur some years
later, the people redouble their activity and movement, storing up provisions, and think
continually of the probable misfortune. All this determines in the bodies epidemic diseases that
extend to a great number of persons in the same country and at the same time. It is clear that if,
at the same time and in the same place, the diseases multiply, there escape from the bodies
abundant vapors that change the nature of the air, and if this air meets a well-disposed body, it
makes it ill in turn, even though this body had not been exposed to the same hardships as the
others.

The epidemics of Egypt always come from an abnormal corruption propagated by the air; this
corruption may be born in Egypt itself or come from neighboring countries, such as the Soudan, the
Hedjaz, Syria, or Barca; it may take its origin in the waters of the Nile which, too strong,
redouble the humidity and activate the corruption, and, too weak, leave the air drier than it
should be; in any case, the inhabitants are obliged to drink bad water bearing in it germs of
corruption gathered in hearths of contagion situated in Egypt [...]

[PDF p. 166]

or in the regions of the Soudan and elsewhere. Many people then die, and from the decomposed
corpses escape abundant vapors that alter the atmosphere, which, in turn, carries corruption to
others. The price of provisions rises, the grains are spoiled, the sheep or other beasts have some
disease. The deleterious miasmas carried by the water in its course, the rise in the price of
provisions, the alteration of cereals, the diseases that strike the sheep or other animals, a
terror or a general calamity -- these are so many causes that, in Egypt, can determine an epidemic
whose intensity is the stronger according as the determining cause is more or less grave. If the
causes are multiple, the scourge is more violent, makes more ravages, and kills more rapidly.

The climate of Egypt is hot and humid, but this latter state is only accidental; the most southerly
regions of Egypt are the hottest, and the water of the Nile is less unhealthy there than in the
northern region, especially in the part situated north of Fostat, such as the district of the
people of Bachmour; these are the coarsest people (of Egypt), and the stupefaction that predominates
among them is due to a very coarse diet and the use of unhealthy water.

As for Alexandria, Tanis, and other analogous towns, their situation near the sea, the attenuation
of the heat and the cold, the presence of the east wind -- all this renders them healthier; the
character of the inhabitants is gentler and, delivered from all care, they are far from being coarse
and heavy like the people of Bachmour. The town of Tanis, enveloped by the sea, has for its dominant
characteristic humidity, which softens the character of those who reside there.

The land of Egypt and all that is found there being weak of complexion and quick to alter and
corrupt, the physician must administer only newly prepared remedies, which still have all their
strength and are not affected by corruption; it is fitting also to prescribe remedies appropriate to
the state of the Egyptians' body (whose effect to be produced) should be slightly opposed to the
state of the patient; he will abstain from too-violent purgatives and from all energetic remedies in
general, because the bodies of the Egyptians are very weak and ready to fall ill; he will therefore
employ the purgatives and remedies whose force is most attenuated, so that they are not too much in
opposition with the nature of the Egyptians' body and that the latter are not too

[PDF p. 167]

affected by them. Let the physician beware of the remedies indicated in the books of the Greek or
Persian physicians, for most of their medicaments are prescribed for bodies of vigorous complexion
and magnificent constitution -- bodies that are met with only very rarely in Egypt. Thus the
physician would do well to abstain from these remedies; let him choose the gentlest of them, reduce
the dose, and replace some of their parts with another equivalent but gentler. Instead of honey, he
will employ syrup of vinegar, and jalap instead of honeyed water. Retain this well too: the air of
Egypt influences the electuaries and all the remedies and alters them. The medicaments, simple or
compound, electuaries or others, keep much less long in Egypt than in other countries. The
physician in Egypt must pay close attention to the dose and the kind of medicament he employs to
avoid any accident: if a purgative administered once does not suffice, it is better to begin again
after a few days than to apply at a single time a too-violent remedy. The climate of Egypt
debilitating the bodies and rendering them very apt to receive diseases, it follows that perfectly
healthy bodies are few there, the majority being composed of the rest, and among them real health
is never quite good health. The first precaution to take in Egypt to restore the bodies to a state
of health is to purify the air, the food, and the water, and to bring them back to absolute purity,
for in Egypt the first functions affected are those of digestion and the animal spirits; one must
therefore apply oneself to regularizing the functioning of the heart, the brain, the liver, the
stomach, the veins, and all the internal organs, to render the digestion normal, strengthen the
animal spirits, and rid the cavities of the impurities found there.

In the commentary on the fourth book of Ptolemy it is said: "As for all the regions that approach
the center of the inhabited quarter of the earth -- that is, the land of Barca, the shore of the
sea from Mariout to Alexandria, Rosetta, Tanis, Damietta, and Farama, the Delta of Egypt, the
environs of Memphis and Fostat, the part of the Said situated east of the Nile, the Fayoum, and all
the region west of the Nile to the most southerly point of the Said, the oases, Nubia, the land of
the Bedjas, the maritime region east of Nubia, Abyssinia -- all these countries occupy an angle that
extends its influence over all

[PDF p. 168]

the portion of the inhabited quarter of the earth situated between the north wind and the south wind
-- that is, the western half of this inhabited quarter, which the five planets together govern. The
inhabitants of this region worship God, venerate the genies, take pleasure in lamentations, bury and
hide their dead in the earth according to different rites; they have a great inclination for the
mysteries; each tribe occupies itself with some occult practice that everyone in this tribe
cultivates and puts to work; to these mysterious practices is due the invention, in the first times
of Egypt, of exact sciences such as geometry, astronomy, and others still, which from Egypt spread
into the world. Subject to foreigners, they are wretched and have for their dominant character
cowardice and astuteness. If foreigners are subject to them, they show themselves toward them full
of kindness and generosity. The men there take a great number of women, and the women on their side
take several husbands; very much given to coitus, the men have many children, and the women are
frequently pregnant. Many men, however, are weak and effeminate."

The inhabitants of Egypt, says Abou's-Salt, form a mixture of races and kinds, such as Copts,
Greeks, Arabs, Kurds, Dilemites, Abyssinians, etc., but the majority is Coptic. The reason for this
mixture is, it is said, the succession of (foreign) kings and conquerors who have possessed this
country -- Amalekites, Greeks, Romans, and others. This is why their genealogies are very mixed, and
the Egyptians distinguish themselves among one another only by the designation of their place of
origin and by the addition (to their name) of the name of their native country. In time past, it is
asserted, they worshiped the idols and frequented the (pagan) temples; Christianity appeared and
became the dominant religion of Egypt, whose inhabitants remained Christian until the conquest of
the country by the Muslims; a certain number of Egyptians then embraced Islam, the others remained
Christian.

What dominates in the character of the Egyptians is the love of pleasure, the propensity to
enjoyments, the love of futility, the belief in impossible things, weakness in resolution and
decision. They are extremely inclined to astuteness and cunning; from their birth they excel in it
and are very skillful in employing it, for there is in their character a foundation of flattery and
adulation

[PDF p. 169]

that has made them masters of it, more than all the peoples who have lived before or who will live
after them. Thus they reach a degree in it that is not found elsewhere; and their reputation in this
is so widely spread that proverbs have been made about their malice and their cunning. Abou Nouas
said:

    O Egyptians, I have given you my counsel sincerely,
        listen then a little to the counselor:
    The Commander of the Faithful has thrown you a serpent
        that will eat and drink the serpents of the country.
    For if there are still found among you the lies of Pharaoh,
        the rod of Moses is in the hand of Khasib.

The author resumes: I have already said that the sign of the Twins being at the zenith of the
inhabitants of Egypt, the Egyptians, for this reason, announce events before they have occurred,
know the future and things to come. There are on this subject among the Egyptians very well-known
legends. Ibn Et-Touaïer, speaking of the campaign of the Franks against the town of Tyre, recounts
that the guard and the garrison of this town returned to Ascalon, which did not cease to be
succored in warriors and vessels until the empire was little by little weakened by dissensions; the
defense of the town then became a painful charge for the army, and, the danger growing, they ceased
to occupy themselves with it; the Franks pressed the town so closely that they took it in the year
548, and I can certify that, many years before, I heard a man predict this event in these terms:
"In the year 8, Ascalon will surrender."

In the same order of ideas one may recall the affair of the destruction of the Christian churches.
It was executed on Friday, the 9th day of Rabi' el-akher of the year 721, when all were attending
the Friday prayer. One might believe that proclamations had been made in all the provinces of
Egypt, from Qous to Alexandria, for in all this extent of country a great quantity of churches were
destroyed at the same instant. This fact will be reported in its place in this book, when we speak
of the churches of the Christians.

To be cited again, in this connection, is the affair of Aldemer, which is this: the emir Aldemer,
commander of the guards, set out from Cairo in 730 to go on the pilgrimage. At Mecca a sedition
broke out in which Aldemer was killed on Friday, the 14th of the month of Dhu'l-Hijja; the same
day, the news was known at Cairo, at Masr, at the

[PDF p. 170]

Castle of the mountain, that a sedition had taken place at Mecca, in which Aldemer had met his
death. The news spread in the countryside of Egypt and became public the same day. En-Nacer
Mohammed ben Qalaoun paid no attention to it. But when the couriers arrived, after the normal time,
they recounted the affair and reported that the emir Seif ed-din Aldemer had been killed precisely
on the day when the news of it had been known at Cairo.

The author of the history of En-Nacer says: I was with the emir Elm ed-din El-Khazen in the
Gharbieh, where he had been sent as governor. After both having said the Friday prayer, we were
returning to his house, when one of his slaves, arriving from Cairo, announced to us that he had
learned that a sedition had taken place at Mecca, during which a great number of soldiers and the
emir Aldemer, commander of the guards, had been killed. "Has someone," asked the emir Elm ed-din,
"come from the Hedjaz bringing this news?" "No," said the slave. "Imbecile," resumed Elm ed-din,
"one cannot arrive from Mecca until three days after the festival of the immolation. How could you
have believed news that not even a sensible man would listen to?" "This rumor," said the slave,
"has been spread about." And the fact was indeed such as had been announced.

Here now is what happened to me, the author: In the month of Ramadan 791 [26 July to 23 August
1389], I was passing on the boulevard separating the two palaces, after nightfall. The crowd was
announcing that king Ez-Zaher Barqouq had come out of his prison at El-Karak and that the people
were coming to join him. I took note of this rumor; and it had circulated the very day Barqouq had
come out of prison. Many other affairs of this kind are recounted.

A point to note in the character of the Egyptians is that they are little jealous. To convince
oneself of this, it suffices to reread the passage of the Koran where it is a question of Joseph
and the attempts at corruption exercised on him by the wife of El-Aziz. A relative of this woman
deposed against her, which gave her husband the certainty that the crime came from her. He
nevertheless punished her no otherwise than by saying to her: "Ask pardon for your sin, for you
are guilty."

Ibn Abd el-Hakam recounts that after the Egyptians had perished in the waves with Pharaoh, there
remained in Egypt only slaves and servants [...]

[PDF p. 171]

for hire; but the women, not being able to do without men, set about -- some to free and marry
their slave, some to take their domestic for a husband -- imposing on the men the condition of
doing nothing without their permission; the men consented to it. The condition of the woman was
therefore superior to that of the man.

Ibn Lahiat told me he had it from Yezid ben Abou Habib that, even now, the Coptic women have the
same privilege as those who preceded them. No man can sell or buy without saying beforehand: "I
will ask my wife's permission."

It is recounted that after the disappearance of Pharaoh and the great ones of Egypt (in the Red
Sea), there was found in Egypt no one capable of being king. The ranks were therefore
distributed: the king's daughter was named queen, that of the vizier vizieress, the daughter of
the vali or governor occupied these same functions; likewise the daughters of the generals and
the warriors. These women governed the kingdom for several years and married their slaves,
agreeing with them that the government and the direction of affairs would remain with the women.
This is what took place for a long time. This is why the Egyptians are brown, for they descend
from the black slaves who, after the disaster of the Red Sea, united with the women of Egypt and
made them mothers.

The virtuous emir, in whom one can trust, Nasr ed-din Mohammed ben Mohammed ben El-Gharabili
El-Karaki, told me that since he has inhabited Egypt he has found the Egyptians of an amiable
character, tolerant toward their women, gentle and tender -- qualities they owe to their slight
jealousy. And we have always heard the proverb go around: "He who drinks the water of the Nile
forgets his homeland, if he is a foreigner."

One of the sides of the Egyptian character is never to concern himself with the future. He makes
no provisions of food like the inhabitants of other countries; everyone goes to fetch the
provisions each day at the market, morning and evening. Another of their traits is the love of
pleasure, the propensity to enjoyments, the search for frivolous amusements, and the absence of
reflection. Our sheikh, master Abou Zeïd Abd er-Rahman ibn Khaldoun, said this to me: "The
Egyptians act as if they were never to render accounts."

[PDF p. 172]

Omar ben El-Khattab, it is said, questioned Ka'b el-Ahbar about the customs of the various
countries and the character of their inhabitants. "When God," he answered, "created things, he
joined a second to each of them. 'I am going to Syria,' said Reason. 'I am going with you,' said
Rebellion. Abundance said: 'I am going to Egypt.' 'I accompany you,' said Resignation. 'I am
going to the desert,' said Misery. 'I am going with you,' said Health."

When God created the world, he also created, it is said, ten types of character: faith, honor,
courage, rebellion, pride, hypocrisy, wealth, poverty, humility, and misery. Faith said: "I will
go to Yemen." "I will accompany you," said Honor. Courage said: "I will go to Syria." "I will go
with you," said Rebellion. "I will go to Iraq," said Pride. "I will accompany you," said
Hypocrisy. Wealth said: "I will go to Egypt." "I will accompany you," said Humility. Poverty
said: "I will go to the desert." "I will go with you," said Misery.

According to Ibn Abbas, cunning comprises ten parts, of which nine for the Copts and one for the
rest of the world. It is said also that there are four things unknown respectively to four
peoples: generosity to the Greeks, frankness to the Turks, courage to the Egyptians, and duration
to the Zing.

Ibn El-Arabia, speaking of the Egyptians, says: They are slaves for whoever wishes to subdue
them; the most intelligent of men when they are small, they become the most ignorant of them as
soon as they are grown.

When Omar ben El-Khattab, says Maçoudi, subjected to the Muslims Iraq, Syria, Egypt, and other
countries still, he wrote this to a sage of his time: "We are the Arabs to whom God has subjected
the regions; we wish to make a halt on the earth and reside in the countries and the cities.
Describe to me, then, the countries, their climate, their inhabitants, and the influence of the
soil and the climate on the inhabitants." And the sage answered: "As for Egypt, it is a vast and
flat country, abode of the Pharaohs and dwelling of the valiant, to which one can address more
criticisms than praises. Its air is heavy and its heat intense; the harm there is such that it
darkens the complexion and the intelligence and pushes to crime. It is a mine of gold and gems, a
field of grains, but, if it fattens the bodies, it blackens the (hearts of) men; life there is
long; the inhabitants are full of cunning, malice, astuteness, finesse, and deceit. It is a
country where one can

[PDF p. 173]

enrich oneself, but not dwell, because of the rebellions that are continual there and the
calamities that frequently overwhelm it."

Omar ben Shebbah says: Ibn Obeïdah, in his History of El-Basra, asserts, on the authority of Ka'b
el-Ahbar, that the best women on the surface of the earth are the women of Basra (excepting, of
course, what the Prophet says of the women of the Qoreïchites), and that the worst women of the
earth are the women of Egypt.

Abd Allah ben Omar says: When Eblis was driven (from heaven), he set his foot on Basra and bred
young in Egypt. Egypt, says Ka'b el-Ahbar, is an impure land like the woman at the time of
menstruation, and each year it is purified by the Nile.

I have found, reports Moawiah ben Abou Safian, that the Egyptians divide into three categories:
one third are men, one third resemble men, and one third are not men. The first third, the men,
comprises the Arabs; the second third, those who resemble men, comprises the (former) masters;
and the third third, those who are not men, is composed of those who delivered up (Egypt) -- that
is, the Copts.

[PDF p. 174]

CHAPTER XIV
A FEW WORDS ON THE PARTICULARITIES OF THE NILE

Mouslim drew from the book of the Traditions of Anas, in the chapter concerning the ascension of
the Prophet, the following passage: "Then," said the Prophet, "there rose toward me the lotus of
the limit (cf. Koran, LIII, 14). Its fruits were like the hills of Hagar and its leaves like
elephants' ears. 'What is that, O Gabriel?' I asked. And the angel answered me: It is the lotus of
the limit, and here are the four rivers, of which two interior and two exterior. 'What is that, O
Gabriel?' I asked. The two interior rivers are the Nile and the Euphrates." It is written in the
Torah: And God created a Paradise in Eden and placed man there. And he made come out of Paradise
two rivers that he divided into four parts: Gihon, which surrounds the land of Havilah; Sihon,
which surrounds the land of Egypt, the same as the Nile of Egypt; the Tigris, which waters Iraq;
and the Euphrates.

Ibn Abd el-Hakam reports, on the authority of Abd Allah ben Omar, that the Nile is the lord of
rivers, to which God has subjected all the rivers, from the west to the east. If he wishes the
Nile of Egypt to flow, God orders all the rivers to feed it, and the rivers bring it their
waters. God has made come out of the earth springs that make the Nile flow where God wishes, and
when its course is finished, God orders the waters to return to their point of departure.

According to the account of Yezid ben Abou Habib, Moawiah ben Abou Sofian asked Ka'b el-Ahbar one
day: "Do you find mention of this Nile in the Book of God?" "Yes, certainly," answered Ka'b
el-Ahbar; "by him who opened the sea before Moses, I find in the Book that God, twice a year,
gives it orders and regulates its course, saying to it: God orders you to flow, and it flows as
much as God permits it, then he orders it next: O Nile, return in peace!"

There are, says Ka'b el-Ahbar, four rivers that come out of Paradise and that God has [...]

[PDF p. 175]

distributed throughout the world: the Nile, which is a river of honey in Paradise; the Euphrates,
which is of wine in Paradise; the Sihon, which is of water in Paradise; and the Gihon, which in
Paradise is of milk.

The Nile, says Maçaoudi, is one of the princes of rivers and one of the noblest among the rivers,
for it takes its source in Paradise, as the sacred Book teaches us. The same author says also:
When the Nile grows, the rivers, the springs, and the wells fall, and they increase when the Nile
falls. Its flood occurs by diminishing the other watercourses, and its fall corresponds with
their increase. The Nile of Egypt is the only river in the world to which one gives the name of
sea, because of its length and the depth of its waters.

Ibn Qoteïbah, in his Little-Known Traditions, relating the traditions concerning the Prophet,
expresses himself thus: "There are two believing rivers and two infidel rivers. The two believing
rivers are the Nile and the Euphrates, the two infidels are the Tigris and the river of Balkh."
The title of believers was given to the Nile and the Euphrates only figuratively, because both
inundate the soil and water the fields and the trees without fatigue and without effort; the
Tigris and the river of Balkh are two infidels, because they do not spread over the soil, and,
despite great fatigues and considerable efforts, they water only very little. The first two are
