good and useful like the true believers; the other two, like the infidels, are neither useful
nor good.

[PDF p. 176]

CHAPTER XV
OF THE SOURCE OF THE NILE AND OF ITS COURSE

As we have said above, the Ocean that surrounds the inhabited earth, after having formed the sea
of India, divides into two parts: one of these parts takes the name of sea of the Zing, in the
vicinity of Yemen, and of sea of the Berbers. In this portion of sea are found a great number of
islands, among others the island of Qomr -- with a damma on the qof, a soukoun on the mim, and an
unpointed re; this island is also called the island of Mala-y; its length is four months' march
and its breadth twenty days and sometimes less; it faces the island of Serendib (Ceylon). One
meets there numerous villages, among others that of Qomryeh, which gave its name to the qomri bird
(the turtledove). One also finds, it is said, on this island a tree in which one can cut planks
sixty cubits long and that can shelter a hundred sixty men. This country having become too narrow
for its inhabitants, they built themselves dwellings on the continent, at the foot of the mountain
to which they gave their name and which was called the "mountain of Qomr."

All the mountains are branches of the mountain that surrounds the inhabited earth and that bears
the name of mountain of Qâf; this mountain is the mother of all the other mountains, which are
only branches detached from it. Continuous in places, in places interrupted, it resembles the
circle of which one does not know the point of departure, or a ring whose extremities one cannot
distinguish; it does not form a perfect circle, but it is named circular because it surrounds
(the world).

Some authors claim that the mountains are derived from two mother mountains: one, taking its
origin at the western Ocean, heads toward the south; the other, beginning at the sea of Roum,
heads toward the north; and both meet at the point named the Barrier; the southern mountain

[PDF p. 177]

bears the name of Qaf, and the northern mountain that of Qaqouna. But it is clear that a single
mountain surrounds the inhabited earth, and that it is the mountain of Qaf, known under this name
in the south and bearing in the north that of Qaqouna. This mountain starts from one of the sides
of the Barrier, passes beyond the statue of the cleft line, and prolongs itself to the point where
there detaches from it the branch in which is made the gate of China proper; it thus makes a point
toward the east of China, then, bending toward the south, it bars the East, along the Ocean sea,
leaving between it and the sea of India a vast territory; at the point of origin of the sea of
India, it cuts the equator under the 170th meridian, and reaches the branch of the Indian sea that
heads toward the sea of Darkness, to the southeast and well beyond the point of origin of the
southern Indian sea. These two branches -- the branch of the Ocean which, in the southwest of the
sea of Darkness, extends in the east-west direction, and the arm that forms the Indian sea heading
toward the sea of Darkness -- meet at the point of origin of the mountain like the two parts of a
pair of drawers. At the junction point of the two seas, the waters are divided into two parts
between which rises the mountain that seems to come out of the waters. [Footnote: this whole
passage is much corrupted in the Boulaq edition.]

The beginning of this mountain is then beyond and 15 degrees east of the Cupola of Arin. It bears
at its origin the name of El-Mogarrad (the bare one); it heads toward the west and ends at 65
degrees from the extreme west; it is there that from the principal massif detaches the branch of
Qomr, in which is the source of the Nile and where one meets those stones dazzling like polished
silver, to which has been given the name of "laughter of the astonished," for all those who look
at them are seized with such laughter that they cannot move away and die. This stone has also been
called the "magnet of men."

From the mountain of Qomr detaches a branch named Asiqi, whose inhabitants are like wild beasts;
then the mountain throws toward the west a second branch that prolongs itself to the Ocean sea and
is named the mountain of the Beasts, for it is peopled with lions furnished with long, formidable
horns. Beyond this branch, other chains detach from the mountain of Qomr; two of them head toward
the equator, hugging the bed [Footnote: the text erroneously reads "from the mountain of Qaf."]

[PDF p. 178]

of the Nile to the east and the west. The eastern chain, known under the name of mountain of
Qaqoul, breaks off at the equator; the western branch, named Admariah, is bathed by the Nile of
the blacks, also called the river of the Damadem; this mountain stops at the point where it meets
the plains of Abyssinia, between the towns of Safrah and Himi.

Beyond the point of birth of the mountain (of Qomr) reappears the mother branch, which sets out
again from the place already cited, whence detaches the mountain of Asiqi, and heads toward the
equator, which it reaches under the 20th meridian. There it takes the name of mountain of
Karasqabah and is peopled with ferocious beasts; from there it takes the direction of the Ocean
sea, but, before reaching it, throws a branch whose point of origin is beyond the Takrour, near
the town of Qalamtaboura. Behind this mountain dwell the negroes named Nemnem, who eat men. Then
the mother mountain approaches the sides of the sea of Roum, having Rome the Great to its
northeast, and runs parallel to the branch named Adamdamah, interrupted between Sama'rah and Himi,
but without passing it, as far as the 35th degree of longitude. This branch (Adamdamah?) rejoins
the mother branch at the 50th degree of latitude; likewise the branch that detaches from it in the
direction of the south cuts at its extremity the 50th meridian between Sardinia and Valencia. The
mother mountain reaches the Ocean, in the region of the north, facing the island of Britain,
Soussia (?), remaining on the near side of the mountain. Then, after slight breaks of continuity,
this mountain bends in curves that leave the Ocean sea to the west, approaches the land of the
Slavs, where the sea takes the name of sea of the Anfalash, and extends to the extreme east where
it is called mountain of Qaqouna, leaving behind it the sea that is always frozen because of the
extreme rigor of the cold. Then, making a bend from the north to the southeast, it approaches the
northern edge of the Barrier. It is between the two extremities of these mountains that
Dulqorneïn (Alexander) established his barrier.

In the region of Qomr there are three rivers: one flows to the east of the mountain on the side of
Qantourah and of Ma'la; the other, which heads to the west, comes out of the mountain

[PDF p. 179]

named Adam's Foot, reaches the town of Saba, waters that of Fardara, and, in the vicinity of this
last, forms a lake to the south of which is the town of Kima, peopled with black anthropophages
(cannibals); the third river, which also flows to the west, comes out of the mountain and,
following numerous detours, surrounds the town of Dahma and makes of Dahma a peninsula; this town
is indeed in a loop of the river that envelops it to the east, the south, and the west, which
renders it similar to a peninsula; (continuing its route) to the north, the river empties into the
sea of India; near its mouth and to the west of the river is situated the town of Qouarah.

From the mountain of Qomr comes out the Nile, whose waters formerly lost themselves at the surface
of the soil; but when Naqraouch the valiant, son of the first Misraïm, son of Markabil, son of
Douabil, son of Arbab, son of Adam, arrived in Egypt, followed by a great number of the Beni
Arbab, these peopled the region, built there the towns of Amsous and others, and dug the Nile,
whose water they directed toward the towns. The river previously had no regularity in its course;
it spread in pools over the soil, and its waters lost themselves. This state of things lasted until
the time when Naqraouch sent into Nubia an expedition that embanked the river and derived from it
numerous canals intended to water the new towns; among others, a canal that brought the water of
the Nile to the town of Amsous. Egypt having been overturned by the flood, Budchir, son of Qoft,
son of Masr, son of Bensar, son of Cham, son of Noah, put back into condition the banks of the
Nile destroyed by the cataclysm.

"Then," says master Ibrahim ben Ouacif Shah, "reigned Budchir, a valiant king, who was the first
to occupy himself with enchantments and magic, and made himself invisible to the eyes. His uncles,
Ashmoun, Atrib, and Sa, reigned each in his province, but Budchir subjugated them by his bravery
and his courage, and his renown surpassed, like that of his father, that of the kings who had
preceded him; he was therefore more powerful than his uncles, and these had to submit. It is
reported that he sent the Egyptian priest Hermes to the mountain of Qomr, from the foot of which
the Nile comes out. Hermes had as his mission to raise (at the sources of the river) statues of
bronze and to put into condition the lake into which the waters of the river pour. It was, it is
said, this priest who restored the two banks of the Nile, whose waters then lost themselves on the
soil and whose course was sometimes interrupted."

[PDF p. 180]

The palace where the statues were raised contained eighty-five figures set up by Hermes to gather
the water of the Nile by means of conduits and tubes through which the water flowed. On its exit
from the mountain of Qomr, the water entered the statue and came out by the mouth; Hermes then
established a scale carefully graduated in known cubits. All the water was thus brought back to the
different beds of the river, which led it to two lakes from which it came out again to empty into
another lake where all the waters issued from the foot of the mountain gathered. By means of these
statues, Hermes regularized the course of the river that was to bring to Egypt fertility and
well-being, and which thus became useful, from harmful as it was.

"The level of the waters had to reach, for them to be beneficial, eighteen of those cubits, each of
which contains thirty-two fingers. All the surplus was directed, by means of small channels, to the
right and left of the statues, and spread into the sands and across the countryside, beyond the
equator, where they were not used. Without this precaution, the waters of the Nile would have
submerged the country they water."

The same author adds: "El-Oualid, son of Darma, the Amalekite, set out with a numerous army, going
from country to country, subjugating their kings and seeking a dwelling to his liking. Arrived in
Syria, he heard of Egypt and the extent of its riches; he learned that the government had fallen
into the hands of women, its kings having perished. He therefore sent into Egypt one of his
servants named 'Oun, entered after him, treating the inhabitants according to his caprice, seizing
the riches and massacring a great number of priests. Then the idea came to him to visit the sources
of the Nile and to know the peoples who inhabited its banks. The preparations for the expedition
lasted three years, at the end of which he set out at the head of a considerable army, annihilating
the peoples through whom he passed. He thus crossed the land of the Blacks and, having passed it,
arrived at the region of Gold, where one sees stalks of gold coming out of the soil. Continuing his
march, he reached the lake into which empties the Nile formed by the waters that come out of the
foot of the mountain of Qomr. This is a very high mountain to which has been given the name of
Qomr-Gô because the Moon never rises there, the mountain rising beyond the equator. Budchir saw the
Nile coming out of the mountain and flowing by streams and small channels

[PDF p. 181]

to the two lakes from which it comes out again in two rivers that go to reunite in another lake.
After having passed the equator, the Nile receives as a tributary a river that comes from the
region of the river Mehran, in India, a river issued, too, from the mountain of Qomr, and which,
from the first, heads toward this side (toward the Nile). The river Mehran is, it is said, similar
to the Nile; it grows and decreases like it; like it, it is peopled with crocodiles, and the fish
one meets in it are similar to those of the Nile. El-Oualid, son of Dauma, found the palace of the
bronze statues built by the first Hermes in the time of Budchir, son of Qantarim, son of Qobtim,
son of Misraïm.

Some historians report that the four (primordial) rivers come out of a single source sheltered
under a cupola in the land of Gold, beyond the Tenebrous (Dark) sea. These four rivers are the
Sihon, the Gihon, the Euphrates, and the Nile. The land of Gold, according to these writers, would
be a portion of Paradise; the cupola would be of topaz (or emerald), and the four rivers, before
arriving at the Tenebrous sea, would be sweeter than honey and more fragrant than camphor. This
opinion is also that of one of the children of El-Aïs, son of Isaac, son of Abraham, who reached
this cupola and crossed the Tenebrous sea. This man was named Gaber. Others say that these rivers
divide into seventy-two parts that determine seventy-two different languages employed by the
peoples. According to others still, these rivers would be formed by ice that the heat makes melt;
the melted snow then flows into these rivers, whose ice waters the country they cross, according as
God judges it fitting for the good of his creatures.

Arrived at the mountain of Qomr, adds the historian, El-Oualid saw that it was a very high mountain
and used cunning to reach its summit and see what was behind it. He discovered a sea black as pitch
and stinking, and the Nile flowing toward the mountain in narrow streams. From this sea exhaled
miasmas that made a great number of El-Oualid's companions perish, and he, having nearly
succumbed, hastened to descend again. Some authors assert that down there one sees neither sun nor
moon, but only a reddish glow like that of the setting sun.

[PDF p. 182]

As for what is reported of Gaber, who crossed the Tenebrous sea without even wetting his feet, it
is explained by declaring that he was a prophet and that God had granted him wisdom. He had asked
God to see the sources of the Nile, and the necessary strength had been granted him. He marched, it
is said, for thirty years across inhabited countries, and twenty years across desert regions.

As for El-Oualid, his absence was, it is recounted, of forty years, after which, retracing his
steps, he returned to Memphis and remained in Egypt, treating the inhabitants as slaves, carrying
off the women, plundering the treasures. His reign lasted a hundred twenty years, during which he
was execrated and hated; but one day, having gone hunting, his horse threw him into a precipice;
El-Oualid was killed and the people were delivered of him.

Qodamah ben Ga'far, in his book Of the Taxes, says: "The Nile takes its origin at the mountain of
Qomr beyond the equator; there is a spring from which escape ten rivers; each group of five rivers
empties into a lake; from each lake come out two watercourses that pour into a single great lake
situated in the first clime. From this last lake, finally, comes out the Nile." The author of the
book entitled Charm of Those Who Love to Traverse the Horizons (Edrisi) says that this lake is
called lake Kouri, from the name of a tribe of negroes who inhabit its shores; these negroes are
savage and eat the men who fall into their hands. From this lake come out the river Ghana and the
river of Abyssinia. On its exit from the lake, the Nile crosses the land of the Kouris and that of
the Yanahs, negro tribes who live between Katem and Nubia. Arrived at Dongola, a town of Nubia, the
river makes a bend in the second clime; it is there that, on its two banks, extend the cultivated
lands of Nubia; one meets there great islands covered with towns and villages; then the river
resumes its course toward the east and heads toward the cataracts.

I have seen in the Geography (of Ptolemy), says Maçaoudi, a map showing the Nile coming out of the
foot of the mountain of Qomr; it is formed, at its origin, by twelve springs flowing toward two
lakes like the Ponds, then, coming out of these two lakes, the waters reunite, cross sands and
mountainous regions, and water the territory of the blacks beyond the land of the Zing, giving
birth to an arm that goes to empty into the sea of the Zing. The Nile flows at the surface

[PDF p. 183]

of the soil over a length of nine hundred parasangs, or a thousand parasangs according to another
opinion; it crosses fertile countries and sterile regions, inhabited countries and others that are
deserts, and finally arrives at Assouan in the Said.

In the book of Orosius, it is said that the Nile takes its origin in the regions of the sea of
Qolzoum and flows in the direction of the west; in the middle of its bed is an island, beyond which
it bends toward the north and comes to water the land of Egypt. It is said also that it draws its
origin from a spring situated beyond the mountain (of Qomr), that it loses itself in the sands to
reappear shortly after and form an immense reservoir; then that it skirts the Ocean sea across the
deserts of Abyssinia and, turning to the left, goes to water the land of Egypt. If its course is
such as is said, one must recognize that it is immense.

The river Nile is the one called (also) Baoun, whose source is hidden; but its presence in Abyssinia
is certain, and it there forms an immense reservoir into which it empties after a course of two
hundred miles. The author speaks (next) of the course of the Nile from its source to its mouths, and
he adds: One frequently meets crocodiles in the waters of the Nile; no one disputes that this river
comes from Abyssinia, and the evaluation of its length from its known point of origin to its arrival
at the sea is one hundred ninety thousand nine hundred thirty miles. The waters of this river are
turbid, sandy, sweet, and beneficent.

The cataracts where the Nile precipitates itself form the limit of the descending navigation of
Nubia and of the ascending navigation of the Said. They are strewn with sharp rocks that allow the
boats to pass only during the flood of the Nile; from this place, the river heads toward the north,
leaving to the east Assouan, right at the extremity of the Said, and flows between the two mountains
that bound the provinces of Egypt, situated one to the east and the other to the west; the course of
the river continues thus to the town of Fostat, situated on the eastern bank; but, a day's march
beyond Fostat, the Nile divides into two branches. One, which continues its course to the sea of
Roum, into which it empties near Damietta, bears the name of River of the East; the other, the
principal branch of the Nile, named River of the West, goes to empty likewise into the sea of Roum
near Rosetta, a town formerly considerable.

[PDF p. 184]

The length of the Nile, from its source to its mouth near Rosetta, is, it is said, seven hundred
forty-eight parasangs; in its course it crosses for four months desert regions, for two months the
land of the Blacks, and flows for one month in Muslim country.

Some authors claim that the flood of the Nile is due to the flux of the sea which, driving back the
waters of the river, forces them to spread over the soil. A book has been written on this subject,
which may be summarized thus: The movement of the sea called flux and reflux reproduces itself each
day twice, twice per lunar month, and twice per year. The daily tide is subordinate to the action
of the lunar disk, whose rays project onto the two banks of the mass of waters. When the moon is in
the middle of the sky, the tide reaches its maximum; it is the same when the moon is at the pivot of
the earth; a similar tide occurs again when the moon rises in the east and sets in the west. The
monthly tide occurs when the sun and the moon are in opposition in the middle of the month; this
tide takes the name of fullness; it occurs also at the moment of the conjunction (of these two
bodies) and then bears the name of joyous; this tide occurs again at the two periods when the sun
and the moon are in the same quarter of the sky, the 7th and the 22nd of each month.

The annual flux arrives equally at two periods: (1) when the sun is at the end of the constellation
of the Ear (Virgo), and (2) when it is at the end of the Whale; if these two periods coincide with
the moment of its opposition or its conjunction, there is a combination of the monthly fullness with
the annual fullness; it is then that the tide reaches its highest point, especially if the
conjunction occurs in the middle of the sky and if one of the planets is in the vicinity of the two
luminous bodies or of one of them, a circumstance that renders the tide stronger still. If one or
several planets are in conjunction with one of the two great bodies, the tide increases still in a
surprising way and, that year, the flood of the Nile is altogether extraordinary, and the river
Mehran increases too. But if the conjunction or the gathering occurs at a point far from the center
of the sky, and no planet is in the vicinity of one of the two bodies, neither the Nile nor the
river Mehran reaches the maximum of its flood, as a consequence of the diminution of the luminous
rays to which the swelling of the waters is due, and it is then for Egypt a year of [...]

[PDF p. 185]

dearth. The annual reflux takes place when the sun is at the beginning of the Capricorn and the
Cancer.

As for the daily flux produced by the Ocean sea, it exercises no influence on the seas issued from
it beyond the distance of one celestial degree, which represents about sixty terrestrial miles; it
is the same for the valleys whose soil is very low. The monthly flux makes itself felt to the
extremity of the seas (issued from the Ocean sea) and prevents them from flowing into the Ocean;
there where the influence of the flux ceases, there is the terminal point of that sea. The annual
flux, too, makes the seas issued from the Ocean sea swell by a notable quantity, and it is to this
increase (of the sea) that is due the flood of the Nile and its fullness, as well as that of the
river Mehran and of the delta of the land of the Sind.

When he came to Egypt with Alexander, Aristotle, after having examined the mouth of the Nile,
recognized as inadmissible the hypothesis that the bed of the river was, at Assouan, similar to the
rest of its bed; on the contrary, he was of the opinion that this bed went widening as it
approached the Delta, where finally, at the moment of the inundation, the river reached a width of
a hundred miles, and by numerous mouths threw back to the sea the unused excess of the waters; but,
recognizing also that the bed of the river could not be shaped in such a way that its lower part
was too narrow to contain what came to it from the top -- the base being always wider than the top
-- Aristotle emitted the opinion that the winds, blowing against the current of the river, drove
back its waters and thus caused the inundation. Alexander held it impossible that the winds drove
back the waters in the valley to the point of making them spread over an extent of more than a
hundred miles. And even if it were so (he said), the water would still escape below (the surface)
and flow to the sea, for the sea retains only the upper part of the water; but the winds accumulate
the sands at the mouth of the rivers at the point where they pour into the sea, and these sands
establish a kind of dam that makes the waters overflow. But Alexander forgot that sand is a friable
body through which the water can pass and continue its route toward the sea; moreover, the sand
could not accumulate so as to form a very perceptible obstacle, the waters of the river flowing
constantly through the mouths of Tanis and Damietta and those of Rosetta and Alexandria. These two
personages could not recognize that the inundation came from a

[PDF p. 186]

current that swelled of itself, and they attributed this overflow to the winds and the sands,
preoccupying themselves with the air and the earth but neglecting the third element, water, for
they were ignorant of the annual movement of the Nile and had been unable to realize that its daily
rise was almost imperceptible -- a circumstance that led the emir of Egypt to install in this
country meqias (nilometers).

All the tides are due to a single cause: the moon behaves with respect to water as the sun with
respect to the earth; the light of the moon falling on the terrestrial globe warms it, just as the
sun warms the atmosphere; the air, in contact with the water, receives a certain quantity of heat
that makes the water dilate, and it swells and overflows by its particular virtue; it is the same
effect as that produced by those burning mirrors that heat the atmosphere to the point of consuming
a wick of cotton placed between the mirror and the sun; it is the phenomenon of refraction, a
phenomenon found again in the conclusive (?) experiment of the bottle filled with water which,
struck by the solar rays, likewise inflames a wick of cotton. The moon is a transparent body that
the luminous rays traverse, as they traverse the bottle; if one (of these bodies) is struck by the
luminous rays, it heats the air surrounding the bottle or the earth, and the water stores up a
certain sum of heat that dilates it and makes it overflow. Such is the effect of the refraction of
the disk; and refraction is the projection of the rays that the moon sends back to a body situated
opposite it (?). Such is the constant cause of the tide; this phenomenon occurs conformably to the
circle traced by the firmament, a circle modeled on the one described by the firmament of the moon,
which in turn is traced according to the moon itself (?). The annual tide occurs when the moon
masks the sun or is occulted by it, for it occurs only in the cases of meeting of the sun and the
moon; it is weaker when the moon is in opposition and stronger when this planet is in conjunction;
it is the same if the moon approaches the middle of the terrestrial globe (zenith); the movement
(of the sea) is then more violent, and the limits of the waters and the lands merge. This is what
is called the annual tide.

[PDF p. 187]

CHAPTER XVI
REFUTATION OF THOSE WHO THINK THAT THE FLOOD OF THE NILE IS NOT DUE TO A TORRENT

The common people do not admit that the water that spreads over the soil comes from a torrent; but
looking only at the size of the river, the development of its mouths, the narrowness of its source,
taking account neither of the water, nor the earth, nor the air, they attribute the increase of the
waters to imaginary causes. This is what the author of the book Of the Roads and the Regions did,
who claims that the water comes to the Nile from all the points of the earth and all the countries
by underground roads, which brings on the flood of the river, and he explains it thus: The Nile
grows only at the time of autumn, when the water of the springs and wells diminishes, and the Nile
then increases. Considering the increase of the one and the diminution of the others, the second
has been made the cause of the first, relying on imaginary reasons. Among other reasons given to
prove that the flood of the Nile is not due to a torrent, it is claimed that the torrents form at
another period than that of the flux of the sea, when the Nile is not itself swollen, and, the sea
being in decrease, the torrents flow and discharge into the sea without meeting any obstacle.

Another reason: The Nile grows gradually during the three months that the sun employs to go from
the initial point of the Cancer to the terminal point of the Ear (Virgo). Thus it is possible to
calculate the intensity of its flood two months before it is complete, and (for this purpose) the
governor of Egypt has at his disposal, in the middle of the river, a nilometer consisting of a
column graduated in cubits, which allows him to know the daily elevation of the waters.

Another reason: The flood of the Nile always occurs at the same period; now, if it were due to a
torrent, there would be some variation.

[PDF p. 188]

Another reason: The torrents appear at another period without the Nile growing.

Another reason: The instructed Egyptians, seeing the heat become excessive, are sure that the Nile
will increase, for the great heats make the air dilate, which in turn makes the water dilate; and
this occurs only because of the meeting of the planets and the increase of the light.

Another reason: The bed of the river at Assouan is only a narrow channel that widens as it
approaches the sea and ends by reaching nearly a hundred miles in extent. Assouan being the extreme
point where the driving-back (of the waters by the tide) makes itself felt, what should one think
of a river fifteen days (of march) long that would present no relationship between its upper course
and its extreme lower course? What should it be at its upper part if it presents such a mass of
water at its lower part?

Another reason: The inhabitants of Assouan make constant observations at the extreme point of the
driving-back, watching the river continually during the day; during the night they put a light in a
vessel of earth that they place on a stone for this use, and observe it. If the light is
extinguished by the rising water, they are certain that the driving-back has reached its extreme
point, which they know in advance; and they begin to take the water necessary for irrigation. Then
the emir has the barriers established at the intakes of the canals broken, and the water spreads
over the land of Egypt all at once.

Another reason: All these canals are obstructed, at their intake on the Nile, by heaps of wood and
earth that retain in the bed of the river the sweet water found there; thus the water of the river
increases in volume, rendering possible the irrigation of all the lands of Egypt, and preventing by
its mass the invasion of the salt water. If the flood were due to a torrent, these precautions would
be useless, and the barriers of the canals would be opened from the appearance of the torrent.

Another reason: If the canals were closed, supposing there were no driving-back caused by the sea,
the torrent, following the bed of the river, would flow toward the sea, since the delta of the Nile
is wider and lower than the upper course of the river.

Another reason: The water of the sea advances more than twenty miles into the passes of Rosetta,
Tanis, and Damietta, as it does moreover in all the valleys

[PDF p. 189]

where the influence of the flux and reflux makes itself felt. If the bed of the Nile were empty of
sweet water, the sea would rise to Assouan, the extreme point of the driving-back, for water
naturally seeks the lowest places of the earth, which is similar in its form to a perfect sphere all
of whose radii, drawn from the center to the envelope, are equal.

Another reason: When the barriers are broken and, the canals being open, the water spreads over all
the low parts of Egypt, the inhabitants of Assouan perceive it at that very instant, and at that
moment they say: "The canals have been opened and the water has spread over the land of Egypt"; they
recognize this by the level of the water, which falls all at once. If it were a question of a
torrent, those who are on the upper course of the river would say: "The rain has ceased on the land,
the rain that gave birth to the torrent."

Another reason: The arm of the river that crosses Abyssinia and which, like the Nile, comes out of
the mountain of Qomr, does not have a flood that lasts three months like that of the Nile, and its
waters do not stay on the soil as long as those of the Nile. If it happens that a torrent empties
into it, this river waters its banks as far as they extend in plain, and, if the (liquid) matter
comes to fail, the waters regain their bed. Now, if the Nile were swollen by a torrent, the two
rivers, having the same origin, would be in identical conditions, and we would not have to say that
the flood of the Nile is due solely to the driving-back produced by the flux of the sea -- since, if
it were really a question of a torrent, the driving-back caused by the sea would be like that which
one can observe in the other neighboring countries, (that is to say) that, as soon as there were no
more torrent, the coast would be invaded by the sea, which ordinarily gains on the shores.

The Egyptians are in ignorance on the subject of the flood of the Nile because they have not seen
its sources and have been unable to observe its origin at the mountain of Qomr, the latter being
situated in uninhabited country. It has not been possible for them either to realize the annual tide,
cause of the driving-back of the waters, nor to determine anything whatever of what concerns this
river, for it is beyond the reach of the common people to understand that the sea swells during the
days of summer, since habitually they see this swelling occur during the winter. This winter tide is
due simply to the winds that blow from one of the banks of the sea, make the waters swell, which
overflow on the opposite bank [...]

[PDF p. 190]

opposite. It is not the same for the Ocean sea, which is perpetually agitated from the center toward
the shore, for the Ocean, by its nature, tends to invade the surface of the earth, but the latter,
of uneven form, opposes by its very form this invasion of the Ocean, which ceaselessly seeks to rise
on the surface of the earth and spread over its shores. The strong tides are due to the abundance of
the luminous rays: indeed, if the sun and the moon are in conjunction with planets, the flux of the
sea becomes stronger, and, if this flux becomes stronger, the rivers overflow in their turn;
likewise, when the moon is in the vicinity of a planet, the vapors rise, mount into the circle of
cold, and resolve into rains. If, on the contrary, the moon is far from the planets, the rain ceases
as a consequence of the abundance of evaporation, as happens in the middle of the day, when the sun
is at the zenith and the great planets hold themselves in the middle of the line of Arin. And God
knows best how it is!

From all that has just been said it emerges clearly and as an incontestable fact that the Nile takes
its source at the mountain of Qomr; but it is quite otherwise for the opinion that would have the
flood of the Nile be due to the driving-back produced by the flux of the sea penetrating into the
bed of the river. Certainly, the continual blowing of the north wind on the enormous mass of the sea
at the moment of the tide, as well as the driving-back this mass produces, contribute to making the
flood of the Nile stronger, but if one examines the Nile attentively, one realizes easily that a
torrent has passed into its bed; during all the winter, indeed, and the first part of spring, its
waters remain always clear and limpid; but, as soon as the time of the flood is past and when the
river reaches its lowest level, the taste of the water alters, its color becomes greenish, and if one
puts a small quantity of it in a vessel, there is deposited at the bottom of this vessel a kind of
scum; here is the cause of this phenomenon: the marshes situated in the extreme south receive the
visits of elephants and other animals that corrupt their waters; during the summer, at the moment
when the rains of the south become abundant, the torrent rushes toward these marshes and makes them
overflow; the corrupted parts rise at the same time as the level of the water and are carried toward
Egypt. It is said at this moment that the Nile has its cravings; this state of the river lasts until
the moment when these waters are replaced by waters made turbid

[PDF p. 191]

which by their abundance render the river turbid. If, at the time of the flood, one puts this water
in a vessel, there forms in it a deposit of silt that one could not find outside the time of the
inundation. This silt is carried by the torrent that rolls toward the Nile and produces the
inundation; it is this silt which, after the fall of the waters, receives the sowing; where it is
not deposited, the land of Egypt remains salty and sterile, and there are no possible harvests except
in the terrains that have been covered by the water of the Nile and on which this silt has been
deposited.

The objection drawn from the fact that if the torrent occurs at another period than that of the tide,
the Nile does not grow -- precisely as a consequence of this low level of the sea, which allows the
torrent to empty into it without meeting any obstacle -- this objection is unacceptable; indeed, the
torrents to which the flood of the Nile is due are habitually produced by the abundant rains that fall
in the south; now these rains fall only during the summer season, so the Nile has never been seen to
grow during the winter. The best proof that this flood is indeed due to a torrent emptying into the
Nile is that this river increases gradually by a quantity equal to that which the torrent brings it.

The argument based on the nature of the Nile's course at Assouan, and the widening of its basin at the
frontier of the Delta, is easily eliminated if one observes that the Nile flows vertically through a
gorge narrowed between two mountains named Genadel (the cataracts), and then over the soil to the sea,
and, if it widens, it is because it meets no obstacle that prevents it from spreading.

The opinion that would have it that as soon as the barriers (of the canals) are broken the water
spreads over the lands all at once is false too: indeed, at the rupture of one of the barriers, the
water enters a canal; the channels are then opened that go from one canal to another across the
terrains that border them and that they water; of these terrains, some are rapidly irrigated, others
are so after a certain number of days; others, finally, cannot be, because of their elevation. It is
claimed that the canals are closed, at the moment when the Nile begins to rise, in order to gather
into a single mass the water of the Nile, make it increase and spread over all the lands, and prevent,
by the resistance of this mass, the invasion of the river's bed by the water of the sea. This is not
admissible, and the dikes are not such as is said: the terrains of Egypt divide, indeed, into numerous
categories: some, very elevated, are watered only

[PDF p. 192]

in exceptional floods; others, very low, are covered during the weakest floods, and, between the too-
elevated terrains and the too-low terrains, there exist some of intermediate altitudes; thus one is
obliged to dig canals in the Said and raise dikes in the Delta, in order to direct the waters and
render possible for the inhabitants of each region the suitable irrigation of their crops; without
this, certain lands would be too watered and others not at all. This is what makes one draw from the
Nile the water necessary for the irrigation of the lands before the moment of sowing. It is habitually
in Mesori that the Khalig (canal) is opened; the water penetrates it and rises to a sluice, where it
stops until the lands situated below the level of the water held in this canal have been watered; then
the sluice is opened on the day of the Nourouz, and the water extends to another sluice where it is
again stopped to permit the watering of the terrains situated below its level. This second sluice is
opened in its turn on the day of the festival of Salib, seventeen days after the Nourouz; the water
gains a third barrier where it is again stopped to permit the irrigation of the lands situated below
its level; finally, this last barrier being opened, the water goes farther to water other lands and
finally empties into the sea. Such is the functioning of the barriers of the land of Egypt.

As for saying that the water of the sea rises more than twenty miles into the passes of Rosetta,
Tanis, and Damietta, and that, if it did not find sweet water in the Nile, the water of the sea would
reach Assouan, the extreme point of the driving-back -- this assertion is that of a man who would not
know Egypt. The course of the river, indeed, is more elevated at Assouan, where the altitude reaches
several heights of men above the level of the river's mouth. If the water of the sea swells, it puts
an obstacle to the flowing of the river; the two masses of water drive each other back reciprocally,
and sometimes the sea prevails over the Nile when this river is at its lowest ebb, so much so that it
salts the water of the Nile from Damietta to Faraskour. But, at the moment of the flood, I, for my
part, was witness to the flowing of the river's waters into the sea at Damietta, and yet the two
masses of water opposed each other and mutually obstructed each other; there is a proof for whoever
seeks one.

To suppose that at the moment when the dikes are broken, the inhabitants of Assouan perceive it on the
instant, is an inadmissible hypothesis. During long

[PDF p. 193]

years, indeed, we have seen the Khalig cut and some channel opened; now the water submerges
considerable terrains without one being able to perceive that the river diminishes, anywhere but at
the very place of the canal's intake, and the crier of Qous continues to cry that the Nile is at its
full; at that moment at Qous the water reaches a height of sixteen cubits, a height that is reached by
the waters, at the meqias of Cairo, only three days after, or thereabouts.

What is said of the branch of the Nile that crosses Abyssinia and of the difference of its regime with
the regime of the other Nile is not exact either. On the contrary, the period of the flood of the Nile
of Egypt coincides with that of the flood of Nubia and the more southerly countries; there are between
these two rivers only two points by which they differ: (1) in Egypt, the Nile flows in a sunken bed,
while down there it spreads over (level) lands; (2) the flood is determined in Egypt by means of
meqias, down there it is impossible to calculate it, because of the dispersion of the waters.

He who has studied the history of Egypt knows that the flood of the waters of the Nile is produced by
the southern rains.

The Nile, it is said, is formed of ten rivers that come out of the mountain of Qomr of which we have
spoken above; these ten watercourses form two groups of five rivers each and go to empty into two
lakes, each bundle of five rivers pouring into a lake. From the eastern river detaches a thin river
that heads toward the east, skirting the mountain of Qaqouli and, after having bathed the towns
situated in this region, empties into the sea of India. (Moreover), from the two lakes come out six
rivers, three from each lake, and the six rivers reunite in an immense lake named El-Batihat (the
marsh), from which rises a mountain that divides the waters into two branches; one of these branches,
which sets out from the west of the lake of El-Batihat, is the Nile of the Soudan, which becomes the
river known under the name of river of the Damadem; it takes the direction of the west, passes between
Samghrat to the north and Ghanat to the south, throws at this point a branch that heads to the south
on the side of Ghanat, then, passing near Barnessah, it skirts the foot of the mountain situated south
of this town, crosses the equator at the height of Zafilah, and empties into a lake found in the
vicinity; the branch (of Ghanat) heads likewise toward the west, passes to the land of Malaï and
Takrour, and ends at the Ocean, north of the town of Qalbafou. The other half (of the waters

[PDF p. 194]

of El-Batihat), escaping from the north of the lake, takes the direction of the north and passes to
the east of the town of Himi. At this place, from this branch detaches a branch that flows toward the
east and, arrived at the town of Sahrat, returns toward the south to straighten toward the southeast,
heading toward the town of Sahrata, then toward the town of Markah; this branch terminates at the
equator in a lake. Beyond the birth of this last branch, to the east of the town of Himi, the
principal branch, under the name of "column of the Nile," takes the direction of the north, skirts
the frontiers of Abyssinia, then, running straight to the north, crosses the land of the blacks,
reaches the town of Dongolah, precipitates itself into the cataracts at Assouan, and from the foot of
these cataracts waters the land of the Said as far as the town of Fostat-Masr; finally, continuing its
course, it goes to empty into the sea of Syria. It is commonly believed in the Soudan that the Nile
descends from black mountains which, from afar, seem crowned with clouds, then that it divides into two
rivers, one of which empties into the Ocean, in the southern part of the sea of Darkness, while the
other bathes Egypt and empties into the sea of Syria. It is said that, in the extreme south, it
divides into seven rivers that penetrate into the uninhabited desert, then, reuniting, form no more
than a single one in the Soudan.

[PDF p. 195]

CHAPTER XVII
OF THE MEASURING OF THE NILE AND OF ITS FLOOD

Ibn Abd el-Hakam says that Joseph was the first to measure the height of the Nile, by establishing a
nilometer at Memphis. Then the old Dalouka, daughter of Zeba -- the same who built the Wall of the
Old Woman -- had raised at Antinoe a nilometer graduated in small cubits, and another at Akhmim. Abd
el-Aziz ben Merwan established one at Helouan, graduated in small cubits. Under the caliphate of
El-Oualid, Osama ben Zeïd el-Tannoukhi had a nilometer raised in Gezireh; it is the largest of all.

"I saw," says Yahia ben Bakir, "the man charged with this service take the height of the river at the
nilometer of Memphis and bring to Fostat the figure of the cubits."

According to El-Qoda'i, the first to measure the height of the Nile in Egypt was Joseph; to this
effect he built the nilometer of Memphis, the first nilometer raised by Joseph; in Egypt, it is said,
the Nile was measured in the land of Alaouat until the time when the nilometer of Memphis was built,
which was employed by the Copts until the moment of its destruction. After Joseph, the old Dalouka
raised two nilometers, one graduated in small cubits at Antinoe and the other at Akhmim. The wall
that goes around Egypt is also her work. Before the establishment of the nilometers, the height of
the waters was measured with the sounding line. Until the moment of the conquest, the nilometers
continued to serve for the measuring of the waters, and traces of them subsisted as long as the
Muslims had not executed the constructions that rise between the fortress and the river. The Greeks
likewise made use of the nilometer established in the palace, behind the gate and to the right in the
corridor. There are still vestiges of it, but they are covered and surrounded by constructions.

At the moment of the conquest of Egypt, Amr ben el-As raised a nilometer at Assouan, then another in
a locality named Denderah, and finally, under

[PDF p. 196]

the caliphate of Moawiah, a third at Antinoe; this last remained in use until Abd el-Aziz ben Merwan
had built a nilometer at Helouan, where he resided; this nilometer was graduated in small cubits. As
for the nilometer of Gezireh, Ousama ben Zeïd, who had built it, spent on it, it is said, two thousand
ounces. [Footnote: the ounce is worth 12 dirhems.] It was he too who raised the House of the Treasury
at Cairo. Later Ousama ben Zeïd el-Tennoukhi, intendant of the revenue of Egypt, informed Soliman ben
Abd el-Melek of the bad state of this nilometer, and Soliman answered him to build a new one on the
island, which was done in the year 97 [5 September 715 to 24 August 716]. At the beginning of the year
247 [17 March 861 to 6 March 862], when Yezid ben Abd Allah el-Turki was governor of Egypt,
El-Motawaqqel had the great nilometer built that is called the new nilometer, and prescribed to take
from the Christians the charge of measurer of the river. Yezid ben Abd Allah el-Turki therefore
established as the one in charge of the nilometer Abou-l-Raddad, who was surnamed El-Mo'allem, but
whose true name was Abd Allah ben Abd el-Salam ben Abd Allah ben Abou-l-Raddad el-Muezzin. He was,
according to El-Qomi, originally from Basra, and came to Egypt where he explained the traditions.
Named director of the nilometer, he was allotted a monthly salary of seven dinars by Soliman ben
Ouahb, then intendant of the revenues of Egypt. From this period and until the present, the direction
of the nilometer has remained in the hands of Abou-l-Raddad and his descendants. Abou-l-Raddad died
in the year 266 [23 August 879 to 11 August 880]. In the year 259 [7 November 872 to 26 October 873],
Ahmed ben Touloun, accompanied by the intendant of the treasury Abou Ayoub and the cadi Bekar ben
Qoteiba, went to examine the nilometer and ordered it repaired, fixing for this repair the sum of a
thousand dinars.

El-Harets also built in Sana'at a nilometer of which there remain now only insignificant traces.

"After the conquest of Egypt by Amr ben el-As, the inhabitants, according to what Ibn Abd el-Hakam
reports, came at the beginning of their month of Boona to Amr and said to him: O emir, our Nile is
accustomed to a certain custom; if one departs from it, its flood will not take place. And what is
this custom? asked

[PDF p. 197]

Amr. It is necessary, they said, that on the twelfth night of this month we take a young girl from
her parents, whom we will then indemnify, and, after having covered her with jewels and the richest
garments, we will throw her into the river. That, said Amr, is not possible under Islam, for Islam
has annihilated all that existed before it." And the Egyptians passed the months of Boona, Abib, and
Mesori without the Nile growing in any way; finally, they were thinking of emigrating when Amr,
informed of their project, wrote about it to Omar ben El-Khattab, who answered him: "You did well to
say that Islam has annihilated all that existed before it. On receipt of my letter, throw into the
river the note I send you." And having received the letter, Amr opened the note, which was conceived
thus: "From the servant of God, Commander of the Faithful, to the Nile of Egypt. If it is by your own
will that you produce the inundation, cease to produce it. But if it is the one and all-powerful God
who makes you grow, we ask God, the one and all-powerful, that he make you swell." This note was
thrown into the Nile, on the eve of the festival of the Cross, when the Egyptians were preparing to
leave and quit the country, for their only reason to stay was the Nile. And the next day, the day of
the festival of the Cross, on their waking, God had made the Nile grow sixteen cubits during the
night. It is thus that this barbarous custom disappeared from Egypt. It was, it is said, Gahel
el-Sadfi who carried Omar's note to the Nile, then stationary, and which swelled by God's order.
According to Yezid ben Abou Habib, Moses having implored God against the family of Pharaoh, Moses
stopped the Nile, to such a point that the Egyptians thought of leaving the country and begged Moses
to address prayers to God. Moses prayed, hoping the Egyptians would believe; it was the eve of the
festival of the Cross. And the next morning, when the Egyptians woke, God had made the Nile grow, at
that moment, sixteen cubits. In his goodness, God granted the prayer of Omar ben El-Khattab as he had
granted that of his prophet Moses.

"I," says El-Qodaï, "found what follows in a small writing attributed to El-Hassan ben Mohammed ben
Abd el-Mona'm: After the conquest of Egypt by the Arabs, Omar ben El-Khattab realized the
consequences that drought could entail for the country, when the Nile does not reach in the nilometer
a determined level and remains below this level. Through excess of foresight, the inhabitants hoard
the provisions, and this hoarding brings on a

[PDF p. 198]

general rise in prices that maintains itself even if the dearth does not take place. Omar therefore
wrote to Amr and asked him for some information on the situation. Here is what Amr answered: "I have
ascertained that, for an irrigation sufficient and capable of keeping dearth away from Egypt, the
Nile must reach fourteen cubits; but for all the lands to be watered, the harvests to give the maximum
and suffice even for the following year, the Nile must reach sixteen cubits; above and below these two
points, there is danger of drought or inundation; drought if the Nile does not exceed twelve cubits,
for it is too low, and inundation if it reaches eighteen, for then it is too high. When it was
delivered up by the Copts, the country was furrowed with canals and furnished with dikes, and the
leaven of prosperity was in it." The Commander of the Faithful, having taken counsel of Ali on this
subject, the latter engaged him to write to Amr to observe the following prescriptions in building his
nilometer: to make two supplementary cubits with the first twelve of which it was a question, to leave
the (two) following cubits as they were, and to remove two fingers from each of the cubits above the
sixteenth. Amr conformed to these prescriptions and thus obtained a most reassuring nilometer by
making fourteen cubits of the first twelve. Each cubit is composed indeed of twenty-eight fingers; Amr
gave the first twelve cubits twenty-four fingers, which left an excess of forty-eight fingers -- that
is, of two cubits. The fourteenth took the number 16 and the sixteenth the number 20. "One must," says
El-Qodaï, "take good account of this today, now that the river has changed and its state has been
profoundly altered. Thus the old nilometers of the Said, from the first to the last, are graduated in
cubits of twenty-four fingers (twenty-eight) and the nilometer established under Islam is such as has
just been described. As for the one erected by Ousama ben Zeid el-Tennoukhi in Gezireh, it has been
carried away by the waters. El-Mamoun built another in the Delta at a place named Barouzat, and one
last was raised in Gezireh by El-Moutawaqqel; it is the nilometer still in use today and of which we
have spoken above.

According to Ibn Afir, the old Egyptians claim that if, on the 12th of Mesori, the water of the Nile
reaches twelve cubits, the year will be good; if not, the waters will remain low. If, before the
Nourouz, the water reaches sixteen cubits, the Nile will be at its maximum; know this well.

[PDF p. 199]

Abou-l-Salt, concerning the origin of the Nile, says: This river takes its origin beyond the equator
and comes out of a mountain situated in those regions and known under the name of mountain of Qomr.
The waters begin to grow during the month of Abib, and the Egyptians commonly say: "When Abib begins,
the water makes noise." At the beginning of the flood, the nature of the river alters and corrupts;
the reason for this is that it crosses pools of stagnant water with which it mixes and which it carries
with it toward other similar marshes whose waters mix again with its own in part. As soon as the water
exceeds fifteen cubits -- even if it enters only by a finger into the sixteenth -- the Khalig is cut;
it is the occasion of a solemn ceremony and a public festival; the common people as well as the great
ones attend it, gathered in a determined place. As soon as the Khalig is cut, the dikes that close the
entrance of the canals are knocked down; the water spreads, extends, and covers the plains and the
low-lying grounds. The people of the villages gather at the tops of their houses and in dwellings the
water cannot reach and out of the torrent's range. In this way the whole land of Egypt resembles a
sea, and the waters, as long as the will of God maintains them at the necessary level, cover all the
space between the two mountains. The highest waters reach about eighteen cubits; then they begin to
fall and regain the bed of the Nile, abandoning first the highest lands and last the lowest, and
leaving each village like a dirhem and the plain like a variegated mantle.

In his book Of the Royal Maxims, El-Qoda'i Abou'l-Hassan Ali ben Mohammed El-Mawardi informs us that
the black cubit is a finger and two thirds longer than the building cubit. It was instituted by the
Commander of the Faithful Haroun al-Rachid, who made it equal to the length of the arm of a black
slave who stood near him. It is this cubit that is used for the measuring of silk, merchandise,
edifices, and for the measure of the height of the Nile.

The highest measure recorded at the nilometer, below the line of the mean level, was in the year 197,
the period when the Nile reached only nine cubits and twenty-one fingers, and the lowest in the year
165, when it did not exceed one cubit ten fingers. The greatest height reached by the river above the
mean level was eighteen cubits and nineteen fingers in 199, and the [...]

[PDF p. 200]

lowest, above this same level, twelve cubits and nineteen fingers in the lunar year 356, in the time
of Kafour El-Akhshidi.

The nilometer is a column of white marble of octagonal form, erected in a place where the water
penetrates and from which it freely exits. This column is divided into twenty-two cubits, each
subdividing into twenty-four fingers, with the exception of the first twelve, which are each of
twenty-eight fingers. [Footnote: it is evidently the opposite that must be read, if one refers to
what was said above. Each of the cubits of the nilometer is of twenty-eight fingers, with the
exception of the first twelve, which have each only twenty-four fingers.]

According to El-Maçoudi, the Indians claim that the flood of the Nile and the retreat of its waters
are caused by torrents, but we know that they are due to the continuity of clouds and the abundance
of rains.

The Greeks are of the opinion that the Nile never increases nor diminishes, but that its flood and
its fall come from its sources increasing or drying up.

The Copts assert that the flood and the fall of the waters are due to springs that gush on one or the
other bank, whose presence the travelers who have visited the upper river have been able to
ascertain.

Others claim that the Nile does not increase, and attribute its flood to the violence of the north
winds that prevent the river from emptying into the sea and consequently force it to spread over the
surface of the soil. Others, finally, estimate that this flood is due to the persistence of certain
winds named the winds of Moltan, which carry the rain-clouds to the other side of the equator; the
rain then falling in the Soudan, in Abyssinia, and in Nubia, the mass of these waters arrives in the
land of Egypt and the Nile increases. Moreover, the sea stops the water of the Nile and retains it
until it has watered the country. And on this subject it has been said:

    Listen (for he who listens to me is a benefactor
        to me, and greater than he who showers me with presents):
    The Nile is full of qualities, but
        one must thank the Moltan for them.

The Nile begins to grow at the end of the month of Boona, which corresponds to Haziran; its rise
continues during the month of Abib, corresponding to Tammouz, and of Mesori, corresponding to Ab;
and even, if the Nile is in good

[PDF p. 201]

growth, it continues to rise during the whole month of Thot, which corresponds to Eilul. If the level
of the waters reaches eighteen cubits, all the taxes must be collected, for the land will be fertile.
But this state of the soil is harmful to the livestock because of the absence of meadows and grasses.

To be profitable to the generality of the country, the inundation should reach a height of seventeen
cubits; in this case, all the lands would be watered. If this height is exceeded and the flood reaches
eighteen full cubits, a quarter of Egypt is submerged; certain villages may be destroyed, as we have
said above, because of the abundance of the waters. If the eighteen cubits are exceeded, the
consequence is that on the retreat of the Nile's waters, epidemics break out, and most floods reach
eighteen cubits.

Under the caliphate of Omar ben Abd el-Aziz, the Nile reached only twelve cubits. The length of the
first twelve cubits is twenty-eight fingers each, the cubits above the twelfth being each of
twenty-four fingers. The lowest height of the water that remains in the nilometer at low ebb is three
cubits; in the year when this fact occurs, the inundation will be very weak. The cubits for which
public prayers are made are named Mounkir and Nakir; they are the thirteenth and fourteenth cubits: if
the Nile, exceeding these two cubits, reaches the half of the fifteenth, the Egyptians make public
prayers, for the whole country is threatened with calamities; but if, the fifteenth cubit being
complete, the Nile penetrates into the sixteenth, it is a benefit for a part of the inhabitants and
public prayers are no longer made; this fact nevertheless brings a diminution in the revenues of the
sultan.

The wine that is drunk in Egypt is prepared with the water of the month of Tobe, which corresponds to
Kanoun II; it is the time when the water of the Nile is in the greatest state of purity, and the time
too when the Egyptians boast of the limpidity of the waters of their river. At this moment, the
inhabitants of Tennis, of Damietta, of Tounah, and of all the maritime villages lay in a provision of
water.

Formerly a flood of sixteen cubits sufficed to water the uncultivated and cultivated parts of all
Egypt, thanks to the good upkeep of the dikes and sluices and the dredging of the canals. The water,
in a flood of only nine cubits, entered the canals of El-Manha, of Fayoum, of Sardous, and of Sakha.
The usage

[PDF p. 202]

at present -- that is, in the year 345 [15 April 956 to 3 April 957] -- is that, if the Nile maintains
itself immediately above sixteen cubits or reaches a level below this point, the revenue of the sultan
is diminished; but at present all the reasons we have just stated have been overturned: the dikes, the
sluices, the canals are in bad state.

The rule now is that the river rises during the great heats, when the sun traverses the signs of the
Crab, the Lion, the Ear (Virgo); at this period most of the rivers of the inhabited earth diminish;
this is what made it said that the rivers, at the period of their fall, brought their waters to the
Nile to make it grow. The flood of the Nile begins on the 5th of Boona, becomes apparent on the 12th,
accentuates on the 2nd of the month of Abib, and reaches its maximum on the 8th of Baba; from the
20th of this month, the river begins to descend again. The duration of the flood, from the beginning
to the day when it begins to decrease, is three months and twenty-five days, comprising the months of
Abib, Mesari, and Thot, and twenty days of the month of Baba. [Footnote: this passage is corrupted,
as the editor of the Arabic text remarked. He says: "What the author says, 'and the duration of its
flood...,' has no relation to what precedes; but if one holds to what he said above, one sees that the
duration of the flood of the Nile, from its beginning to the day when the river begins to decrease, is
four months and fifteen days." This duration comprises indeed twenty-five days of the month of Boona,
the ninety days of the months of Abib, Mesori, and Thot, and twenty days of the month of Baba; which
makes a total of one hundred thirty-five days -- that is, four months (of thirty days each) and
fifteen days.] The duration of its fullness, after having reached its maximum, is twelve days, after
which the river begins to descend again.

In our days still, on the 27th of Baba the level of the Nile is publicly cried; this level is obtained
by deducting from the height of the waters at this moment the height of the water that remained in the
nilometer on the 13th of Baba. The great Khalig is cut when the river reaches sixteen cubits. I have
heard people cry: "May God preserve us from a finger of the twentieth cubit!" Indeed, we have been
witness to it: when the Nile reaches the first finger of the twentieth cubit, the river spreads and
submerges the villages and the gardens, and the waters come back up out of the sewers. But, since the
events of the year 806 [21 July 1403 to 11 July 1404], were the Nile today to reach the first finger
of the twentieth cubit, the inundation would be insufficient, as a consequence of the bad state of the
dikes. Until after the year 500 of the hijra [2 September 1106 to 21 August 1107], the normal level of
the Nile was, at the nilometer of Gezireh, sixteen cubits -- that

[PDF p. 203]

is, eighteen cubits in reality; and one said then: "If the river rises one cubit more, the revenue of
Egypt will increase by a hundred thousand dinars, because the highest lands will be watered." If it
reached eighteen cubits, that was the maximum height; for eighteen cubits, at the nilometer of
Gezireh, represented twenty-two cubits of the Said. If the Nile exceeded the eighteenth cubit by one
cubit, the revenue of Egypt fell by a hundred thousand dinars, because the low lands were submerged.

Ibn Moyassar, in his Chronicles of the year 544 [22 May 1148 to 10 May 1149], says that that year the
flood of the Nile reached nineteen cubits and four fingers and that the water arrived as far as the
New Gate, at the end of the outer boulevard of Cairo; everyone took refuge in Cairo, coming from Masr
and from the side of the cemetery. When the caliph El-Hafiz li din Allah Abou-l-Mamoun learned that the
water had arrived at the New Gate, he became sad and shut himself in. One of his intimates penetrated
to him and questioned him on the cause of his grief: the caliph then showed him a book in which was
written this: "When the water arrives at the New Gate, the imam Abd el-Megid will die." "This book," he
said, "makes known to us our destiny and that of our reign, as well as what will happen after it." At
the end of this year, El-Hafiz fell ill and he died at the beginning of the year 544. [Footnote: 11 May
1149 to 29 April 1150.]

The cadi El-Fadel, in his Events of the year 576 [28 May 1180 to 16 May 1181], says: On Monday, the
26th of Rabi' I, corresponding to the 16th of Mesori, the Nile reached sixteen cubits, the normal
height of the flood, which had never before been observed at such a period. This is again a condition
of the Nile that is altered in our time. Formerly it reached its fullness at the beginning of Mesori,
and, in the year 812 [16 May 1409 to 5 May 1410], this fullness was reached on the 29th of Abib, a day
before the month of Mesori. It is a rare fact and worthy of being consigned to the annals of the floods
of the Nile. In 709 [11 June 1309 to 30 May 1310], the Nile was at its fullness on the 11th of Gemadi
I, or the 19th of Baba, forty-nine days after the Nourouz; in 592 [6 December 1195 to 23 November
1196], the canal of Abou-l-Menga was opened on the 19th of Chawwal -- it was El-Melek el-Aziz Othman who
proceeded with the ceremony -- and the Nile rose in the canal by one finger, the

[PDF p. 204]

eighteenth of the eighteenth cubit, a level named by the Egyptians the great sheet. Note that if what
the cadi El-Fadel calls the great sheet were reached some year in our time, it would be famine for the
country and death for the inhabitants; such a change is due only to the negligence brought to the
upkeep of the dikes. Today, when the river reaches sixteen cubits, the Egyptians are in jubilation,
for this level was formerly the normal level of irrigation and is so still today. It is then a day of
festival, and the sultan mounts his horse, then, followed by his escort, descends into a boat to
perfume the nilometer. The solicitude of the dynasty of the Fatimids for the cutting of the Khalig is
treated in the chapter dealing with the Halls of the Pearl.

According to some commentators, the day of the fullness (of the Nile) is precisely the one that was
fixed for Pharaoh by Moses as a rendezvous; it is said in the Koran (XX, 61): "The rendezvous will
take place on the day of the festival, when this people will be gathered in broad daylight." And until
the present the custom has been preserved of gathering to perfume the nilometer on that day.

The best policy followed regarding the public proclamation of the level of the Nile is that reported
by the fiqih Ibn Zoulaq in his History of Maezz li-din Allah: "That month (that is, in Chawwal 362)
[Footnote: the month of Chawwal 362 runs from 5 July to 2 August 973], El-Maezz li-din Allah forbade
proclaiming the flood of the Nile and writing about it to anyone but himself or the general Gauher. He
permitted this proclamation only when the Nile was at its fullness -- that is, when it had reached
sixteen cubits and the Khalig was cut. Note well the utility of this way of acting: if, at a given
moment, the Nile stops in its rise, or if this rise slows, everyone is anxious and apprehends the lack
of water; the grains are held back, their sale is opposed in the hope that prices will rise; the rich
hoard the cereals, whether they expect a rise in price or are anxious to make provisions for their
family. These circumstances bring on dearth and, if it happens that the Nile rises, the price of the
provisions no longer has stability, and if it does not rise, there is at once famine and drought. By
keeping the level of the Nile secret, the greatest and most useful service was rendered to Egypt.

El-Messih, in his History of Egypt, says: "The master of the palace prescribed to

[PDF p. 205]

Ibn Hiram to take a copy of the words the criers of the Nile pronounced as preliminaries of their
proclamation of the level. Here is what they said: 'Innumerable benefits are in the inexhaustible
treasures of God! God has made the blessed Nile rise so much.'" Ordinarily, at the beginning of the
flood, the waters of the Nile become green, and the Egyptians say then that the Nile has its cravings;
thus they think that to drink of it at that moment is harmful. Here is to what they attribute the
cause of this green coloration of the waters. The wild beasts, the elephants especially, come, pushed
by the extreme heat, to wallow in the marshes the upper Nile crosses. The waters of these marshes are
thereby altered, and when, at the period of the rainy season of those regions, the rains come to fall
in the south, the torrents pour into these marshes, whose corrupted waters escape and flow toward
Egypt. Shortly after the green water appears the new water that constitutes the flood of the Nile in
Egypt. This water is reddish, for it is charged with the silt the mass of the water carries with it.
At the maximum of the flood, the land of Egypt is covered by the waters; in the provinces, the
villages and the hills are surrounded by the liquid sheet, and one can reach them only by boat or by
following the crest of long dikes whose upkeep, to be sufficient, requires a quarter of the revenue (of
Egypt); they serve to maintain the waters until all the terrains have been suitably watered. When the
watering of a province is finished, the inhabitants of this province cut the dikes at places designated
by the engineer and the sheikhs; this cutting is done at a determined moment, neither after nor before,
as is attested by the regulations of each province. Each district is therefore watered by the water
that comes to it from the neighboring district and by the water it possesses of its own. If one
neglected to repair the dikes, redo the sluices, and dredge the canals, it would hardly be possible to
use the water of the Nile. This is what has happened in our time.

Formerly a third of the revenues was devoted to the repair of the dikes, so much care was taken of
them then. By acting thus, the irrigation of the whole country was regularized in a way useful for all.
Moreover, God willing, you will be able to see soon what the ancients and those who followed them
practiced on this subject.

Under the reign of the Fatimids, there were expenses assigned to the upkeep of the nilometer; the
costs, which amounted to fifty dinars per year, were paid to Ibn Abou-l-Raddad.

[PDF p. 206]

CHAPTER XVIII
OF THE BRIDGE ON WHICH THE NILE WAS CROSSED

There was on the Nile a bridge of boats thrown between Fostat and the island known today under the
name of Rodah. Another bridge joined this island to Ghizeh. These two bridges were composed,
together, of thirty boats.

[PDF p. 207]

CHAPTER XIX
OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID ON THE SUBJECT OF THE WATER OF THE NILE, IN PRAISE OR IN BLAME

Master Abou Ali Ibn Sina (Avicenne) says: "The water of the Nile has been given singularly
exaggerated praise. Its qualities are fourfold: the remoteness of its source, the excellence of its
course, its depth, its direction from south to north. This last condition renders the water of the
Nile sweeter; as for the depth, there are other rivers that are just as deep as the Nile. The best
water is that which comes from springs -- not all springs indistinctly, but those that well up in a
warm terrain and whose nature is not dominated by foreign elements or substances, or in a stony
terrain which, all the more, is corrupted by none of the decompositions the earth can undergo; but
the springs that come out of a warm terrain are preferable to those that gush from a stony soil;
however, the springs born in warm lands are not all good, but only those which, besides this
condition, are running -- and not all running waters, but those that flow in the open air and whose
waters are exposed to the sun and the wind: this condition adds a great quality to running water. As
for stagnant water, its exposure in the open air sometimes gives it a quality it would not have had if
it had remained hidden and concealed.

The water that flows over a bed of earth is preferable to that which flows over a stony bed, for the
earth filters the water, removes the foreign matters that have mixed with it, and renders it limpid,
which the stone cannot do; but it is necessary that the earth forming the bed of the river be a warm
earth and not mud, niter, or other things of the same kind; otherwise, and if the water were deep and
of a rapid course, it would be altered by the quantity of matter that would mix

[PDF p. 208]

with it. The waters whose course is directed toward the sun -- that is, toward the east, and
especially toward the summer point (?) -- are the best, and all the more so as they are farther from
their point of origin; after these waters, the best are those that head toward the north. As for
those that flow toward the west or the south, they are detestable, and their bad quality increases
when the south wind blows. The waters that to the preceding conditions join that of descending from
high summits are better still; they are so sweet that one would believe them sugared, and one can mix
them with wine only in small quantity. They are of a light weight, cool easily and heat likewise,
thanks to their slight density; cold in winter, they are warm in summer, having neither dominant taste
nor odor. They descend the cataracts rapidly, easily dissolve what one puts in them to dissolve, and
easily cook what one puts in them to cook."

Master Ala el-Din Ali ben Abou-l-Harim ben Nafis, in his Commentary on the Canons (of Avicenne),
says: The qualities in question are not properly speaking qualities but simple conditions that
contribute to rendering the water better. One of these conditions, the remoteness of the source,
necessarily renders, as we have demonstrated, the water more subtle, because of the perdurance of its
movement. The Nile comes out, indeed, of a mountain situated beyond the equator, at [no.] 30' of the
measures of the greatest terrestrial circle divided into three hundred sixty degrees. This mountain
extends from 46 deg 30' to 61 deg 50' of longitude, counted from the extreme west, over a length of 15
deg 20', of the three hundred sixty degrees comprised in the greatest terrestrial circle. From this
mountain come out ten rivers produced by springs situated in the interior of the mountain. Each bundle
of five of these rivers empties into a great circular lake. The center of one of these lakes is
situated at 50 deg of longitude (from the extreme west) and 7 deg 31' of south latitude. The center of
the second lake is at the intersection of the 57th degree of longitude and the 7 deg 31' of south
latitude. They are equal (in surface), and the diameter of each of them is five degrees. From each of
these lakes come out four rivers that empty into a small circular lake situated in the first clime,
whose center is distant from the west by 53 deg 30' and from the equator by 2 deg, the lake being in
the first clime south of the equator. The diameter of this lake is two degrees. All these eight
rivers therefore flow into a single lake, from which comes out a single river, which is the Nile of
Egypt. The land of Nubia

[PDF p. 209]

is crossed by another river that comes out of a lake situated under the equator; this lake is great
and circular, and the length of its diameter is three degrees; the longitude of its central point is
43 deg. This river meets the Nile at 43' (sic) of longitude. After having passed the town of Masr,
the Nile, arrived at a village named Chatnouf, divides into two branches that go to empty into the
sea. One bears the name of the branch of Rosetta; it is from it that the canal of Alexandria
detaches. The second, known under the name of the branch of Damietta, detaches, on arriving at
Mansourah, a branch that takes the name of bahr Ashmoun, a branch that goes to empty into a lake
situated in those parts. The principal part, continuing its course, empties into the sea near
Damietta. The flood of the Nile comes from abundant rains that fall in Abyssinia. And God is the
most knowing!

The most scrupulous researches on the weight of water have demonstrated that very often, the lighter
it is, the better it is. This is the opinion that Ibn Sina emits in his chapter Of the Qualities of
Water. If you examine what he says of it, you will see that they are all found united in the water of
the Nile. First, the Nile comes from a spring and flows over a warm terrain; consequently, no element
of bad nature dominates in the soil that forms its bed -- a condition not presented by the springs
that flow over a soil impregnated with naphtha, alum, sulfur salts, etc.; on the contrary, the soil
over which the Nile flows produces gold, which the flakes one meets on its banks clearly prove;
certain people even occupy themselves with sorting the gold gathered on the shore and, by this means,
enrich themselves. Now one cannot deny the virtue attached to the presence of gold in the water.
Secondly, the Nile always flows uncovered, exposed to the sun and the wind. (3) The silt of the Nile
is a silt carried by the torrents the rains form and that cross warm lands; one can ascertain this by
breathing the agreeable odor that gives off from this silt when it is still humid. (4) The Nile is
very deep and its current so violent that it overturns, or nearly so, the columns that oppose its
course and carries with it the heaviest objects that obstruct it. (5) The distance separating the
source of the Nile from its mouth is considerable. Its extent, to which the extent of no other river
of the inhabited earth is comparable, was spoken of above. (6) It descends from elevated places; the
south is indeed higher than the north; and moreover it passes cataracts,

[PDF p. 210]
