a high mountain from which the river precipitates itself toward the valley of Egypt. On this subject,
Ibn Qoteïba, in his work entitled Terms Little Used in the Traditions, reports the following account
of Garir ben Abd Allah el-Bagli. One day the Prophet questioned him on his stay at Valencia, and
Garir, among other things, told him that in this country the water did not flow from the heights.
"The best water," said the Prophet, "is sanam water -- that is, that which is found at the surface of
the earth." By sanam must be understood the water that is on the surface of the earth. Every thing
superposed on another thing is sanam in relation to the latter; this expression comes from the term
sanam el-ba'ir (the humps of camels), because of their elevation. Some commentators explain the verse
of the Koran (LXXXIII, 27) where it is said: "And it will be mixed with tasnim," in this manner: "It
will be mixed with what descends from on high." (7) The Nile heads from south to north and remains
consequently always opposed to the excellent north winds. (8) The water of the Nile is light, as has
been ascertained several times by comparing it to the waters of other rivers that it leaves far
behind it in this respect. (9) Its savor is sweet, its influence excellent on the digestion of foods
and their passage into the stomach, to such a point that the ingestion of this water brings on
eructation at once.

Such are the qualities that will make the water of the Nile judged excellent by all those who have
occupied themselves with physics and medicine and who are truly in a position to recognize how useful
and beneficent this water is.

Dhu-l-Qorneïn (Alexander), it is said, wrote a book in which he enumerated the marvels he had seen,
and this book embraced all the marvels of the world. As a conclusion he said: "All this has nothing
marvelous beside that marvel called the Nile of Egypt." If God, a philosopher said, had not subjected
the Nile to a law that makes it grow little by little in summer to bring to a good end the irrigation
of the soil, and makes it decrease at the time when the cultivations are going to begin, the land of
Egypt would be annihilated and uninhabitable. For the rains there are insufficient, and one meets
there no streams that can provide for the needs of all the lands, except in the province of the
Fayoum.

An ingenious poet said:

    Oh! what marvels this Nile presents!
        It is like an incomparable virgin.

[PDF p. 211]

    In the course of the year, it meets the earth and greets it,
        and if one has had enough of it, it takes leave and withdraws.
    When it appears, it is like the new moon; and when it is there,
        at its pleasure it increases and decreases.

Another expressed himself thus:

    The Nile seems to me endowed with heart and intelligence,
        from what human eyes see of it:
    it comes when one has need of it
        and withdraws when this need has ceased.

Tamim ben El-Mo'tamer said:

    The day we spend with the Nile is short,
        and ordinarily the days of joy are short.
    Beneath our feet the boats run swift as horses;
        they go up while the army of the waves goes down.
    Their waves are like the folds of the belly
        and their whirlpools like a navel.

The same said again:

    Do you not see the thunder weep and groan,
        and the swift lightning that laughs,
    drink from the cloud dark as night:
        when it weeps, the face of the earth smiles.
    See the water of the Nile when it increases:
        it is like sandalwood and mastic.

Another:

    God makes the Nile run when the east wind blows
        and shows us on its banks the soldiers of the marine,
    ranged on its two banks and brandishing their flexible lances,
        while the waves of the river wield Indian swords.
    If its water is bitter, it has the taste of roses;
        is it limpid, it has the color of rose-water that leaves after it a taste of bitterness.

Abou-l-Hassan Mohammed ben El-Ouazir says, on the subject of the gradation of the flood of the Nile
and its immense services:

    I always see great things come from small,
        and the full moon form from the crescent.
    Be not surprised, then, if the least channel of water,

[PDF p. 212]

    in Egypt, is esteemed as a source of wealth.
    An increase of one finger per day
        brings on a cubit of well-being.

El-Shahab Ahmed ben Fadl Allah el-Amari said:

    Egypt has a surprising quality:
        life there is marvelous and splendid.
    At the foot of a garden meet
        the vivifying water and the greenery.

Ibn Qalaqs said:

    Watch the sun set over the Nile
        and see what it leaves behind it of red twilight.
    It has disappeared, sending behind it its rays,
        as if it had burned itself in plunging beneath the waters,
    and the new moon soon comes to its aid
        like a canoe made of silver.

Bichr el-Moulk ben el-Mounagem said:

    How beautiful was the boat I rode in the air;
        from the height of the horizon I cast my eyes on the earth;
    it was evening, and one would have said a battle;
        if a coward had seen it he would have died of fear.
    The setting sun headed toward the West,
        pale over the Nile and fearing the attack of night;
    the moon leaned like the point of a lance
        thrown into the fury of combat, amid the blood of the twilight.

The cadi El-Fadel said: "The water of the Nile covers the plains and converts the fingers into
cubits; like a jealous man it covers the earth and, more jealous still, it spreads over it without
exceeding its limits (?). In Egypt it is the only cutter of roads (highwayman) one meets, and yet it
is the only one that is sought and feared."

The Nile of Egypt differs in its course from most rivers; it flows indeed from south to north, and
there are only two rivers that follow the same direction: the Mokran in the land of Sind, and the
Orontes -- today the Asi -- which passes by Hamat, a town of Syria.

Certain people have disparaged the water of the Nile. Abou Bekr ben Ouahshia, in his treatise on
Nabataean Agriculture, says: The waters of the Nile take their origin in a mountain situated beyond
the land of the Blacks and named the mountain of Qomr;

[PDF p. 213]

the sweetness of these waters and their flood demonstrate that they are exposed to the sun, and the
sun, if it does not burn them completely, procures for them at least a gentle and prolonged heating
which, without removing from them, by an exaggerated violence and ardor, their humid part so as to
leave them only their heavy parts, acts moderately on its waters and renders them so sweet that they
alter the constitution of those who drink of them in great quantity and determine eruptions, pimples,
and sores. The Egyptians, who drink much of it, have become sanguine and need to bleed themselves at
very close intervals; those who know physiology indeed subject themselves to a regimen apt to
extirpate from their body the pernicious germs that the water of the Nile introduces there; if it
were not so, they would fall into the infectious diseases we have just named and would be no more
than pimples and sores; this fact is due to the water of the Nile being less cold than the others,
and to the coction it has undergone rendering its viscosity greater than the viscosity of water
should be. Mixed with the foods in the intestine, it produces in great quantity bad and corrupted
excrements that determine the diseases recalled above. To evacuate the morbid germs they ingest with
the water of the Nile, the Egyptians constantly drink a syrup made of an acid and astringent fruit
juice and take remedies that rid them of the excrements. If the heat of the sun is stronger and
activates the coction of the water of the Nile, this water becomes salty like that of those marine
pools that have no other movement than that determined by the tide and the blowing of the winds; it
is then better for plants and cultivations than for animals.

Here is what Ibn Radouan says: The Nile crosses the territories of numerous peoples who inhabit the
Soudan, and arrives in the land of Egypt after having gathered in those regions all the filth and
corrupted matters found there. It crosses the land of Egypt, flowing from south to north, and goes to
empty into the sea of Roum. Its flood begins in summer and ends in autumn, and, during the period of
the high waters, there rises into the atmosphere an abundant humidity produced by an imperceptible
evaporation; consequently summer and autumn, dry by their nature, become humid. Moreover, when the
river begins to swell, the waters spread over the soil and deposit there all they contain of filth --
carcasses of animals, refuse, detritus of wood and plants, stagnant waters of the marshes

[PDF p. 214]

that they have carried with them -- all this mixes with the soil itself and with the silt, for the
earth here is very loose, not to mention the fish of the Nile and of the marshes that deposit their
eggs there. At the beginning of the flood one sees the Nile become completely green, owing to the
quantity of stagnant water that mixes with the waters of the river, and which is saturated with
corrupted matters, mosses, and water-lentils that render the water greenish. Then the river becomes
turbid and seems until the end of the flood to carry mud; if, as soon as it has become transparent
again, you take a little of this water in a vessel, you will see form in it an abundant deposit of
silt, while the liquid part will remain viscous and of a fetid and insupportable odor; it is one of
the most evident indications of the malignity of this water and of its corruption. Hippocrates and
Galen have demonstrated that the waters that corrupt most rapidly are the rainwaters subtilized by
the sun, and one of the characteristics of the water of the Nile is that it arrives in Egypt when it
is rendered to its maximum of subtlety, thanks to the violent heats of the Soudan. If to this
condition comes to be added the state of corruption of the land of Egypt, the decomposition of the
water aggravates still more; thus there are born in this river numerous species of fish; the
excrements of the animals, indeed, the residues of plants, the very corruption of the water and of
the fish eggs, determine the production of these fish, as Aristotle said in his Treatise of Animals;
this is quite evident moreover, for every matter that decomposes engenders, by its very decomposition,
animals, and it is for this that there are produced in abundance in Egypt worms, rats, serpents,
scorpions, wasps, flies, etc. This shows clearly that what predominates in Egypt is heat and
accidental humidity, that its temperature is subject to numerous variations, that its air and its
water are of bad quality. Sometimes, at the end of spring and the beginning of summer, the Nile is
dry on the side of Fostat; the water, corrupted by the quantity of things thrown into it, becomes
there of a repugnant stench. It is quite clear that the water, arrived at this degree of corruption,
sensibly alters the health of the people (who use it); thus it is necessary to draw the water at the
places where the current of the river is most rapid and where, consequently, the corruption is less.
Everyone purifies this water according to the temperature. In summer, when it is very hot, one uses
chalk, earth of Armenia, red earth, nabq, and pounded medlars, and vinegar.

[PDF p. 215]

During winter, when it is very cold, one employs the bitter almond, the interior of the apricot pit,
pennyroyal, and alum; and even so it is necessary to filter what has been purified before drinking
it. To purify the water of the Nile, put it in a vessel of potter's clay, terracotta, or leather and
use only what transudes through the porosities of the vessel. If you prefer, boil it and let it
purify in the night air; then filter the water thus purified and use it.

If the water seems contaminated by some harmful matter, boil it then let it cool in the open air, in
the coolness of the night, then purify it by means of the ingredients we have indicated. The best is
to use this water only after having purified it several times; here is how one proceeds: one first
heats and boils it, then lets it cool in the coolness of the night, then the water thus purified will
be filtered. One purifies it again by means of some ingredient, and puts the purified part in a
vessel; one will use only what oozes through the porosities of the vessel. The vessel intended to
receive this water will be, in summer, of potter's clay or terracotta worked in the month of Tobe;
one may equally use filters of stone or leather or any other matter that cools. In winter one will
make use of vessels of glass or porcelain. The vessels fabricated in summer, of potter's clay or
terracotta, will be placed during the summer in a cellar exposed to the north wind; they will be
exposed to the heat during winter. One cools the water in summer by mixing into it rose-water or by
depositing in it a clean cloth in which one will have wrapped a piece of chalk, or seeds of purslane
or white poppy, or earth of Armenia or red earth, but in such a way that the water cools without
mixing with the ingredient. The vessels are cleaned in summer with pounded potter's clay, barley
flour, purslane, or sandalwood, and during winter with alkali or galingale; they are perfumed with
mastic or aloes. The beginning of the flood and the moment when the rise of the waters stops are the
two periods when the water of the Nile is the worst. One must then boil it and exaggerate its
purification, employing the interior of the apricot pit and all that can make the viscosity
disappear. The best water of the Nile is that of the month of Tobe, when the cold is at its maximum;
the Egyptians know well, by experience, that the water of Tobe is the best; thus many of them store
it in vessels of glass and porcelain and make use of it [...]

[PDF p. 216]

throughout the year; they claim that it does not alter, and they do not even take the trouble to
purify it, persuaded as they are that it is altogether pure. But do not trust this, and purify it
all the same, for stored water certainly alters.

This is what I have found in the way of criticism of the water of the Nile. It emerges from it that
the water alters according to the terrain over which it flows, and not because it is bad in itself.
Be not frightened, then, by what you hear said; the matter is no otherwise than I have set it forth.
And as the malignity of the water is in proportion, not to the quantity, but to the alteration, you
know the means of eliminating the pernicious substances that have mixed with it. And God is the best
guide, by his goodness and his beneficence.

[PDF p. 217]

CHAPTER XX
OF THE MARVELS OF THE NILE

Among the marvels of the Nile there is the hippopotamus. Abd Allah ben Ahmed ben Selim el-Assouani,
in his History of Nubia, says: "The distance separating Dongola from the beginning of the land of
Aloua is greater than that separating Dongola from Assouan, and one meets there many more villages,
farms, islands, livestock, palms, trees, doums, cultivations, and vines than on the side touching
the land of Islam. In these regions are islands that take days to cross, and that are all peopled
with serpents, wild beasts, and carnivores; one finds there also deserts where thirst is dreaded. At
this point (Aloua) the Nile makes a bend and heads first toward the east, then toward the west for
days (of march), and finally reaches the Said, whose terrain is much more sloping. It is the region
where the bend of the Nile touches the mines known under the name of Shatka; the country itself
bears the name of Shanqir. It is from there that the qomri (turtledove) comes, and the hippopotamus
abounds in this place.

"Simoun, hereditary prince of Aloua, affirmed to me that he had counted in one island seventy of
these animals. They are beasts that live on the banks of the river, similar to horses and large as
buffaloes; their short legs end in hooves; they have the color of horses and are also furnished with
manes; their ears are as small as those of horses, and their throat is like that of that animal;
their tail is similar to that of buffaloes; they have a very wide muzzle, such that at first sight
one would take it for a sack; their cry resembles a neighing, and their teeth are such that the
crocodile cannot resist them. If they are irritated, they attack the boats and make them sink; they
feed on the grass of the shore; their skin is of a surprising solidity -- shields are made of it."

[PDF p. 218]

This animal resembles the terrestrial horse, only its mane and its tail are longer and its color is
more beautiful; its hoof is cleft like that of the ox, and its size is a little greater than that of
the ass. It eats the crocodile with much voracity and is visibly stronger than it. Sometimes it
comes out of the water and covers the mares, and from this coupling are born the most beautiful
horses in the world. A man, one day, went down to the bank of the Nile having with him a superb
mare. A black hippopotamus spotted with white came out of the river and covered the mare, who became
pregnant and gave birth to a colt of marvelous forms. The man, wishing to have another colt,
returned to the same place with the mare and the first colt. The hippopotamus appeared, sniffed the
colt for a moment, and returned quickly toward the river, where the colt followed it. The man came
back to this place, but he never again saw the hippopotamus or the colt.

In the Nile and in the land of Egypt, recounts El-Maçoudi, there are a great number of marvelous
animals; among others, the fish named torpedo (electric ray), which measures nearly a cubit. If it
falls into the net of a fisherman, the latter feels in the hand and the forearm a shock that
announces to him that a torpedo is caught; he then hastens to take it and make it come out of the
net. If the fisherman touches it with a piece of wood or a reed stalk, he feels the same commotion.
Galen speaks of this fish and says that if one places it alive on the head of a patient affected
with cephalalgia or violent migraine, he is relieved at once. Ibn el-Beithar says, on the authority
of Galen, that it is a marine animal that causes torpor, and, he adds, it is claimed that, put in
contact with the head of a person affected with migraine, it appeases the ill, and that applied to
the rectum of a patient whose anus comes out of its place, it puts the anus back in order. I made
this double experiment and obtained no result in either of these two cases; I thought that no doubt
the beast was already dead when I had brought it near the patient's head, believing that even dead
it must still be a remedy as efficacious against migraines as the other remedies, but I ascertained
that it had effect only as long as it was living. According to Dioscorides, it is a marine fish that
numbs; if one places it on the head of a person suffering for a long time from a violent headache,
it appeases the violence of the ill, and if one applies it to a hemorrhoid sufferer whose anus comes
out, the patient is cured. Younis asserts

[PDF p. 219]

that if one rubs oneself with oil in which this fish has cooked, one appeases the most violent
rheumatisms. Ibn Beithar says: I saw on the coast of Malaga, in Spain, a flat fish of the same color
as the torpedo of Egypt; its belly is white, and it has, to numb those who touch it, the same virtue
as the fish of Egypt -- this virtue is even greater in the fish of Spain; it is never eaten. It is
said that if a woman carries on her a fragment of this fish, her husband cannot stay away from her;
and reciprocally, if the husband carries a fragment of the fish, his wife cannot separate from him.

The soqonqor (skink) is the product of the fish and the crocodile; it is not a fish, since it has
two hands and two feet; it is not a crocodile either, for its tail is flat and smooth, wide and
without spines, while that of the crocodile is thick and bristling with spines. The fat of the
soqonqor incites to coitus, and one meets it nowhere else but in the Nile and in the river Mohran,
in India. I have been told that certain people, having roasted one of these animals and eaten it,
all died on the spot. The soqonqor, says Avicenne, is a lizard fished in the Nile, and which is, it
is said, engendered by the crocodile. The best are fished in spring. According to another
(physician), the soqonqor is a young crocodile; on coming out of the egg, if the young one heads
toward the water, it is a crocodile; if it heads toward the desert, it is a soqonqor. According to
Ibn Beithar, it would be a species of locust that one dries in autumn; to drink, mixed with any
beverage whatever, the value of two drachms of the part that touches the kidneys incites to coitus.
This animal much resembles the lizard and is met in the sands of the Said that border the Nile. It
is one of the animals that live on land and stay in the water -- that is, in the Nile; thus it is
called water-lizard because it resembles the lizard and stays in the water. The soqonqor is of both
sexes: the male is furnished with two testicles similar, in form and placement, to the testicles of
the cock, and the female lays more than twenty eggs that she buries in the sand; the male has two
penises and the female two vulvas. This animal, after having bitten a man, runs to the water; if it
finds some, it throws itself in; if it does not find any, it urinates and rolls in this urine; as
soon as that is done, the bitten man dies and the soqonqor remains safe. But if the bitten man gets
ahead of the soqonqor and enters the water before the latter

[PDF p. 220]

has rolled in its urine, the soqonqor dies on the instant and the bitten man escapes. The male is
the best and most efficacious for rendering coupling fecund; it is even the only one that enjoys
this virtue, the female not being endowed with it. One chooses, among all the parts of the (male)
soqonqor, the one closest to the origin of the tail in the axis of the navel. The season when it is
fished is spring, for it is the one when it is most excited to coitus and when its virtue is
greatest. As soon as it is caught, it must be slaughtered the same day; if it is left alive, its fat
melts, its flesh softens, and its virtue weakens; then one cuts the head and the extremity of the
tail without detaching them entirely, and one splits the belly lengthwise; one throws away all it
contains except the kidneys and the scrotum, and after having cleaned it well, one fills it with
salt, sews up the opening, and hangs it head down, in the shade, at a moderate temperature, and
leaves it thus until it is dried; then, if one is quite certain it is not corrupted, one puts it in
a vessel pierced with holes -- for example a basket made of willow or palm branches or some other
analogous object -- in which one leaves it until the moment one wishes to make use of it. Fresh, its
flesh is hot and humid; dried, it is hotter still but less humid. The use of the soqonqor does not
succeed for those who have a hot and dry temperament, but succeeds very well for those whose
temperament is cold and humid. The property of the flesh and fat of this animal is to push to
coitus, excite passion, give vigor in copulation, and calm the diseases of the cold nerves; one may
employ, either simple or in composition, the part that touches the navel and is in a straight line
with the tail; but use in the simple state is preferable. When this flesh is dry, one employs it in
the dose of one to three mithqals according to the age and temperament of the individual and
according to the country and the weather. One grinds it and mixes it with a beverage -- honeyed
water or juice of raisins -- or else one sprinkles it on soft-boiled egg yolks and swallows. One
also employs the flesh by taking one to two drachms that one simply beats with egg yolks or
something analogous, such as pounded rocket seeds. One finds the soqonqor only in the Fayoum; the
period when one fishes the most of it is Lent, when, the cold being very sharp, the animal comes out
of the water and comes onto the shore; it is at this moment that one catches it.

[PDF p. 221]

One reads in Maçoudi: If the horse of the Nile (hippopotamus), coming out of the river, stops at some
point of the countryside, the Egyptians know that the Nile will rise to that very place, without
reaching higher or stopping lower. It is for them an incontestable truth based on experience and
habit. When it leaves the river, this animal grazes the cultivations and causes great damage to the
proprietors of lands and harvests; it comes out of the water during the night and goes directly to a
certain point in the fields, then, retracing its steps, it eats what is on its path from the place
where it had stopped; on the way out it does not eat. After having eaten, it re-enters the water,
begins to drink, and then gives back in different places all it had absorbed. This being repeated
several times, the damage caused to the proprietors of the farms multiplies; lupins are then brought
to the animal, deposited in numerous heaps, thick and spaced apart, at the place from which it is
known it must come out; the animal eats them and returns to the water; as soon as it has drunk, the
lupins swell in its belly, which swells in turn and ends by bursting; the dead animal floats on the
water, which throws it onto the shore. At the place where it has been seen, one never meets
crocodiles. It has the form of the horse, but its hooves and its tail are different, and its forehead
is wider.

El-Messihi says: What is designated under the name of boulli is a species of fish whose first
specimen was seen in the Nile under the caliphate of El-Aziz billah Nazar ben el-Moezz lidin Allah;
before, it had never been seen in the Nile; under the same caliph appeared also a fish named labis;
it was given this name because it resembles the bouri found in the sea, whose body has the same
exterior appearance. It is quite probable that it is a sea fish that enters the sweet water.

Among the animals of the river, there is also the crocodile. It is, says Ibn Beithar, a well-known
animal met with in the great rivers and very abundant in the Nile. One finds it also in the river
Mohran, and sometimes in the Soudan. It is the lizard of the Nile. All animals, in eating, asserts
Ben Zahran, move the lower jaw; the crocodile alone moves the upper jaw and not the lower jaw. The
fat of the crocodile, mixed with butter and furnished with a wick, placed lit on the river or in a
wood, prevents the frogs of that river or that wood from croaking. If one goes around

[PDF p. 222]

a village with a crocodile skin and hangs it from the ceiling of a corridor, neither cold nor hail
will ever enter that village. If a crocodile bites a man and one spreads crocodile fat on the bite,
the man will be cured at once. If one coats with this fat the forehead of a fighting ram, all the
rams presented to it as adversaries will flee at its approach. The gall of the crocodile is used as
kohl for eyes that have too much white, and the white that is in excess disappears. Fumigations of
crocodile liver cure madness. The excrements of this animal are sovereign against the white films of
the eye, recent or old. If, when the animal is alive, one tears out its eye and hangs this eye above
a patient afflicted with leprosy, the ill stops and makes no more progress. If one hangs a part of
its right side above a man, this man becomes vigorous for coitus. The right eye of the crocodile
cures the diseases of the right eye, its left eye the diseases of the left eye. Its fat, melted and
mixed with oil of roses, is efficacious in the diseases of the vertebral column and the kidneys and
incites to coitus. Its blood, mixed with myrobalan and emblic, and employed in unctions against
nascent leprosy (leuce), restores its color to the skin; if one rubs the forehead with it, it cures
migraine. Its flesh rubbed with ceruse (?) fattens thin people. If one lets fall drop by drop into a
diseased ear melted crocodile fat, it is of excellent effect, and, if the treatment is continued,
one cures deafness; if one rubs with this fat a man afflicted with quartan fever, the ill is
appeased. The flesh of the crocodile is bad for the chyme.

El-Maçoudi says: The crocodile is brought to grief by a little reptile met with on the banks of the
Nile and in the islands; here is how: The crocodile has no anus, and all it eats becomes worm in its
stomach. When that bothers it, it goes onto the shore, stretches out on its back, and opens its
mouth. At once a bird whose habitual function this is approaches and eats the worms that come out of
the crocodile's belly. It is then that this little reptile of which we have spoken comes out of the
sand where it is hidden and, jumping into the mouth of the monster, penetrates to its belly and
strives to pierce it; the crocodile rolls on the ground, gains the bottom of the water, but the
reptile continues its work and ends by piercing the crocodile, which sometimes kills itself before
its enemy has come out; the latter escapes after the death of the animal. This enemy of the
crocodile measures about a cubit in length;

[PDF p. 223]

it has the form of a centipede (?) and is furnished with a great number of feet and legs.

Formerly, it is said, in the mountains of Fostat, was a talisman such that the crocodiles could not
approach the neighboring countries; arrived at the limit of the talisman's action, they turned over
on their backs and the children amused themselves with them; this lasted until they had passed the
limits of the city; then only did they resume their normal position and return to their natural
state. Subsequently this talisman was broken and lost its virtue. It is said that the crocodile lays
eggs similar to goose eggs, in which sometimes form little rats that grow and reach a length of ten
cubits, and which, in aging, become longer still. The crocodile makes sixty movements at once and in
the same place. Its left tooth is efficacious against fever.

[PDF p. 224]

CHAPTER XXI
A FEW WORDS ON THE MEANS OF FORESEEING THE STATE OF THE NILE EACH YEAR

Ibn Radouan, in his Commentaries on the four books (of Avicenne), says: The state of the Nile is
subordinate to certain conditions; first, it is necessary that prolonged rains fall in the south
before and during the flood: consequently, at the beginning of summer, when Venus and Mercury are in
conjunction, the Nile is very high, because of the coolness of the air, while at the beginning of
spring or summer, at the moment of the conjunction of Mars and another planet, it must be very low
because of the rarity of the southern rains. It is also necessary that the north winds stop the
course of the river; the south wind indeed accelerates its course and prevents it from remaining
stationary. If, then, one knows that the rains are abundant or rare in the south, and what wind blows
in Egypt during the summer season, one can foresee what the state of the Nile will be and,
consequently, the degree of abundance or dearth that this state presages for Egypt.

Abou Samer ibn Younis, the astronomer, says, on the authority of Ptolemy: To know the level the flood
of the Nile will reach, it suffices to observe Venus, Mercury, and the Moon at the moment when the Sun
is in the sign of the Crab. If the state of these planets is satisfactory, and nothing bad is visible
in them, one can affirm that the Nile will grow and reach the necessary height; but if the state of
these planets is weak, one can affirm the contrary; is one of these planets brilliant and the other
weak, the Nile will reach a medium height. In sum, the good state of the three planets announces a
perfect Nile; their doubtful state a medium Nile; the weakness of their scintillation, their position,
or their point of greatest distance from the earth presages the fall of the waters and announces that
the Nile will maintain itself very low. On the contrary, the scintillation of Venus in the sign of the
Lion makes the waters of the south descend. Let one examine, says Abou Ma'cher, the three planets
Venus, Mercury, and the Moon, at the moment when the Sun traverses [...]

[PDF p. 225]

the sign of the Crab; if their march is at its maximum of rapidity, the Nile will be very high; if
their march is medium, calculate the maximum and minimum of the march of these bodies and base
yourself on the result of this calculation; if their march is slow, the flood of the Nile will be
very weak. If the three planets have different marches -- some moving very rapidly, others very
slowly -- base yourself on the fastest (and the slowest), take the mean, and establish your forecast
according to it.

The Copts say that one must see to what day of the Arabic month the 1st of the month of Barmoudah
corresponds, add to the figure of that day the number 85, and take the sixth of the sum; the result
will give the number of cubits the flood of the Nile will reach that year. Among other experiments
relating to the Nile, there is also this one: On the day when the Jacobite Christians of Egypt break
the fast, see how many days remain to run to finish the Arabic month, add 34 to the number thus
obtained, and divide the sum by 12. If after this division a number remains, it will indicate by how
many cubits that year the Nile will exceed twelve cubits; but if the number divides by 12 without
remainder, the year will be bad. Here is what the Copts say further: If the 10th of the Arabic month
corresponds to the (1st of) Abib and the Moon is in the sign of the Scorpion, in conjunction with the
heart of the Scorpion, the Nile will be low; otherwise, the Nile will be good. Another experiment:
If, on the first day of Boona, the north wind blows in the morning, the Nile will be high; if it
blows at noon, the Nile will be medium; if it blows in the evening, the Nile will be low; if this
wind does not blow at all, the Nile will not rise that year. One may, it is said, make the same
observation on the first Thursday of Boona.

Here is an experiment that I have myself verified during several years, and that the sheikh who had
indicated it to me had also verified, as did the one who had transmitted it to him, and which is
consequently exact: observe on the 1st of Mesori the height of the Nile, add to it eight cubits; the
sum will represent the number of cubits the flood of the Nile will reach that year. Another
experiment, current in Egypt and which I have myself verified and recognized exact, is the following:
on the eve of Saint Michael's, at noon, take a little silt over which the Nile will have passed; this
fragment of earth must weigh exactly sixteen drachms; put it in a closed vessel until the morning of
the festival of Saint

[PDF p. 226]

Michael, then weigh it, and by as many kharrubas as it weighs more than the weight of the eve, by so
many cubits will the Nile rise that year, each kharruba representing one cubit. Another means: Take a
little wheat flour, knead it with water of the Nile in a vessel made of the silt of the river, and
leave this vessel closed during all the night preceding the festival of Saint Michael. On the morning
of the festival, if the dough has risen of itself, the Nile will be altogether complete; if, on the
contrary, the dough has not risen, it is a sign that the Nile will be very low.

One may also examine what wind blows on the morning of the festival; if it is a moderate wind, the
Nile will be high; if not, the Nile will be low, especially if the wind that blows is the merisi
(south wind). The Nile then will be insufficient. For the Copts, it is necessary to make the three
tests simultaneously; if they do not agree, the prognosis may not be exact.

Abou-l-Rihan Mohammed ben Ahmed el-Birouni, in his book entitled Traces That Subsist of the Past
Centuries, says: When the flood of the Nile approaches, the prudent people take a plank and sow on it
seeds of all sorts of plants and vegetables, and the whole is left thus until the night of the 25th of
the month of Tammouz, one of the Greek months, the night that is the last of the period of the great
heats; then the plank is exposed directly to the rising and setting of the planets, without any object
interposed between the plank and the sky. All that is not to be a good harvest that year has become
yellow by morning on the plank, while what is to come up well remains green. This is what the Copts
did. I have myself experimented, after having been instructed in it by a writer, that if rain falls,
however little, in the month of Baba, one must observe on what day of the Coptic month this fact
occurs, to know how many drachms the wheat will reach that year; the number of drachms will be equal to
the number of days already elapsed of the month of Baba. And the first time I made this experiment, the
rain fell on Thursday, the 15th of Baba, and the oueïba of wheat was sold that year at fifteen drachms.

[PDF p. 227]

CHAPTER XXII
OF THE FESTIVAL OF THE MARTYRS

Among other things that were formerly done in Egypt, there was the celebration of the Festival of the
Martyrs, one of the greatest rejoicings of the Egyptians; this festival fell on the 8th of the Coptic
month of Bachons. The Copts believe that never, in any year, does the Nile rise if one does not throw
into it the finger of one of their dead ancestors, enclosed in a casket. This day is a day of festival
when the Christians gather from all the villages; one mounts on horseback and plays; most of the
inhabitants of Cairo and of Masr gather by castes and go to pitch tents on the banks of the Nile and in
the islands of the river. Singers (male and female), proprietors of games or places of amusement,
prostitutes, debauchees, chasers of girls, brawlers, and people of pleasure -- all without exception go
to this festival. God alone knows the number of people who gather there; incalculable sums are spent
there, and all the vices and corruptions are displayed there without shame; at these festivals occur
riots in which there is often loss of life. There is sold there, in wine alone, more than a hundred
thousand dirhems of silver, which makes five thousand dinars of gold; in a single day, a Christian sold
more than twelve thousand dirhems of silver of wine.

For this great festival, one always gathered at Choubra, in the suburb of Cairo, and the peasants of
Choubra counted only on what they sold of wine at the Festival of the Martyrs to pay their taxes. This
lasted thus until the year 702 [28 August 1302 to 14 August 1303]; at this period the sultan of Egypt
was El-Melek el-Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun, and the direction of public affairs was entrusted to the
emir Rokn ed-din Bibars El-Gashenkir, who then had the charge of intendant of the sultan, the lieutenant
of the sultanate of Egypt being the emir Seif ed-Din Salar. The emir Bibars energetically opposed the
celebration of the festival; the affairs of Egypt were then in his hands and in those of the emir Salar;
the two held El-Naser in tutelage, and the latter could not eat according to his tastes except with
their permission. The emir Bibars therefore gave the order not to throw a finger into the Nile and not to
celebrate the festival that took place on this occasion. He gave instructions to the chamberlains and
the valis of Cairo to prevent the people from gathering at Choubra, as they were accustomed. Messengers
set out into all the provinces of Egypt, carrying letters enjoining the valis to proclaim publicly
Bibars's instructions in the provinces; according to these instructions, no Christian was to leave (his
village) to attend the Festival of the Martyrs. This measure displeased all the Copts of Egypt -- as much
those who professed Islam and declared themselves Muslims as those who had remained Christian -- and all
concerted among themselves. One of these Copts, named El-Tag ben Saïd el-Doulat, occupied the functions
of writer and was then in the service of the emir Bibars; he had taken possession of his mind and
occupied himself with all his affairs, according to the usage of the sultans of Egypt and their Turkish
emirs, who abandoned their affairs to the care of their Coptic secretaries -- as much to those who hid
their infidelity as to those who let it appear.

[PDF p. 228]

The Copts therefore did not cease to circumvent El-Tag until he had, on the subject of the festival, a
conversation with his master the emir Bibars; in this conversation, El-Tag insinuated to the emir that
the yield of the taxes would be diminished if the festival were forbidden, and that most of the taxes of
Choubra were paid only thanks to it, then he said to him: "If this festival is not celebrated, the Nile
will not rise, and the lack of inundation will destroy the countryside of Egypt," and many other
persuasive words and artful discourses. But God strengthened the heart of Bibars and gave him the
necessary force to resist all the fine words that could be said to him; he persisted in forbidding the
celebration of the festival and said to El-Tag: "If the Nile is to rise only if this finger is thrown
into it, let it not rise! but if it is God who directs it, we will inflict a refutation on the
Christians." And the festival was forbidden that year; the prohibition lasted until the year 738 [30
July 1337 to 20 July 1338]. At this period, El-Melek El-Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun had the dike repaired
that was intended to keep the waters of the river away from Fostat and throw them back on Ghizeh, as will
be seen in a special chapter of this book. The emir Yelbagha El-Yahgahoui and the emir El-Tanbagha
El-Maradini asked the sultan

[PDF p. 229]

permission to go hunting and to absent themselves for some time. But the sultan, who felt for them a
violent affection and an extraordinary passion, could not resolve to let them leave and, to divert them
from their expedition, said to them: "We will reestablish the Festival of the Martyrs, and you will find
there amusements far more agreeable than your hunting party." The time of the festival approached; the
two emirs having consented, the sultan had published in the provinces the reestablishment of the
Festival of the Martyrs; the day of the festival having come, the two emirs mounted in great boats and
not in light canoes, and everyone came from all sides; there appeared also the singers, the proprietors
of games, the prostitutes; all mounted on the Nile and, according to their custom, displayed in broad
daylight their habitual turpitudes and all sorts of vilenesses. The emirs made, in victuals, pastries,
etc., unheard-of expenses of an extraordinary exaggeration, lavishing on all incalculable largesses.
This lasted thus three days.

The time of interruption of the festival, from its prohibition by the emir Bibars to its reestablishment
by El-Melek El-Naser, was thirty-six years. It was then celebrated each year until the year 755 [26
January 1354 to 15 January 1355], the year when a movement of Muslims against the Christians occurred and
when the inventory was drawn up of the mortmain property belonging to the Christian churches and the
convents. The secretary of the emirs was constrained to draw up this list and carry it to the divan of
the wakfs. It comprised twenty-five thousand feddans all belonging to the convents and the churches. This
list was handed to the emirs of the kingdom, regents of the State in the time of El-Melek El-Saleh Saleh
ben Mohammed ben Qalaoun, who were the emir Scheikhou El-Amri, the emir Sarghetmesch, and the emir Taz.
Immediately it was decided to make a gift (of these lands) to the emirs, in addition to their fiefs, and
there was left to the Christians only what they merit -- contempt. A great number of churches were
destroyed: the account of this destruction will be found in the chapter that concerns it in this book,
the chapter of the Churches.

In the last decade of the month of Ragheb of the aforesaid year (755), the chamberlain and the emir Ala
ed-din Ali ben El-Kourani, vali of Cairo, went toward Choubra el-Khiam, in the suburb of Cairo, destroyed
the church of the Christians there, and having removed the finger enclosed in its box, carried it to
El-Melek [...]

[PDF p. 230]

El-Saleh, who had it burned before him in a public place and had the ashes thrown into the Nile, so
that the Christians could not gather them; and from then until the present the Festival of the Martyrs
has no longer been celebrated. To God be glory and munificence!

[PDF p. 231]

CHAPTER XXIII
OF THE CANALS DERIVED FROM THE NILE

When the Nile has reached the normal height of its flood, the canals and the channels are opened that
carry the water to the right and the left as far as the countries most distant from the bed of the
river. The greater part of the canals, channels, dikes, and low-lying terrains is in the region of the
north; there are very few in the region of the south -- that is, in the Said; in this part of Egypt the
traces and debris of these works are effaced and have disappeared. The most known of all these canals is
the canal of El-Mengah; the others are the canal of Memphis, that of El-Menha, those of Ashmoun Tanah,
of Sardous, of Alexandria, of Damietta, of Cairo, the Bahr Abou-l-Menagga, and the canal of Naser
outside Cairo.

Ibn Abd el-Hakem reports, on the authority of Abou Rahm El-Samaï, that Egypt was formerly furnished with
sluices and dikes skillfully arranged and managed, by means of which the Egyptians brought the water to
the foot of their houses and their courtyards, imprisoning it at their will and directing it according
to their caprice. This is what God speaks of when he recalls these words of Pharaoh: "Does not the
kingdom of Egypt belong to me? And do not these rivers flow under my domination? Do you not know it?"
(Koran, XLIII, 50.) There was not then on the earth a kingdom more beautiful than the kingdom of Egypt.
On the two banks of the Nile, from the beginning to the end, extended gardens that covered on each bank
the space between Assouan and Rosetta.

What are called the seven canals are formed by the ensemble of the canals of Alexandria, of Sakha, of
Damietta, of Memphis, of the Fayoum, of El-Menha, of Sardous; all along these canals are gardens that
touch one another without any interval; the cultivations cover all that extends from one mountain to
the other and that is reached by the water, from one end of Egypt to the other. All Egypt is watered by
a flood of sixteen cubits, thanks to the management of the canals, the sluices, and the dikes. And this
is what the Koran alludes to:

[PDF p. 232]

"How many gardens, springs, fields, and places of delight they have left!" (XLIV, 25-26.) The places of
delight are, it is said, the pulpits, for there were a thousand pulpits in Egypt.

CANAL OF SAKHA. -- The canal of Sakha was dug by Nadares ben Sa ben Qobtim ben Misraïm ben Beïsar ben Ham
ben Noah; he was one of the kings of the ancient Egyptians who reigned in the first ages. Ibn Ouasif
Shah says: Nadares was the first king to govern all the provinces: he reigned after his father Sa, and,
under him, the land of Egypt was tranquil. Nadares was wise and experienced, and moreover energetic,
powerful, and skilled in affairs. He practiced justice, established the temples and their priests in the
best possible state, and extended his empire over all the provinces. It was he, it is said, who dug the
canal of Sakha, and, under his reign, the revenue of the country rose to a hundred fifty million dinars.
An Amalekite of Syria dared to attack him and marched against him, believing all permitted to him in his
regard; Nadares entered Palestine, killed many people there, and reduced to captivity some sages whom he
established in Egypt. The kings dreaded him. Toward the thirtieth year of his reign, the blacks of the
lands of Zing and Nubia made an irruption into his kingdom and gave themselves over to pillage there.
Nadares gathered the army of the provinces of Egypt and prepared ships; he sent a general named
Philotheos with three hundred thousand men and another general with an equal army, and on the Nile he
dispatched three hundred boats each mounted by a magician who knew how to accomplish marvelous things.
Then he himself set out with a considerable army, met the army of the Blacks, more than a million men
strong, beat them, killed a great number in admirable combats, and made a considerable quantity
prisoners; his army pursued the Blacks to the land of the Elephants, in the country of Zing. He took a
great number of these animals as well as tigers and other wild beasts and sent them to Egypt, where he
tamed them. He had erected on the frontier of his country a monument on which he had inscribed the
account of his expedition and his victory, and the date of his campaign. He then died in Egypt and was
buried in a naos to which were transported a quantity of images of the planets, gold, gems, jewels, and
statues; on the naos was engraved his name and the date of his death. Talismans were put on it to keep
away (the destroyers), and he left the kingdom to his son Maliq ben Nadares.

[PDF p. 233]

CANAL OF SARDOUS. -- It was dug by Haman, or, according to others, by Talma ben Qoumes. This king,
having mounted the throne, seized all that was in the treasures of the Egyptians. It is he who,
according to the Copts, would be the Pharaoh of Moses; this Pharaoh, according to the historians, would
be El-Oualid ben Mosa'b, who was an Amalekite (Shepherd). The Pharaohs, according to them, would number
seven. Talma, according to what is recounted, was small, had a long beard and blue eyes; his left eye was
smaller than the other; he had a mole on his forehead and he was lame. He was, it is said, Egyptian, and
the Egyptians know his genealogy. Others say that he had come to Memphis with an ass laden with natron
that he wished to sell; that day, the Egyptians, not knowing whom to name king, had decided to give the
power to the first man who would come. And having seen Talma arrive, they chose him for king. The latter,
after his installation on the throne, squandered the money, surrounded himself with devoted people, and
made perish those who did not obey him. Then, having put order to his affairs, he designated for his
successor Haman, one of his relatives; the latter drew from the treasury and employed it to build towns
and monuments and to dig a great number of canals. It is he, it is said, who dug the canal of Sardous.
Each time he directed it toward one of the villages of the Houf, the inhabitants of that village brought
him money, so much so that he gathered considerable sums that were subsequently restored to their
proprietors. Ibn Abd el-Hakam recounts, on the authority of Abd Allah ben Amr ben El-As, that the Pharaoh
employed Haman to direct the works of the canal of Sardous. When the latter began the works, the people
of all the villages came to beg him to make the canal pass near their village and gave him money. And
Haman, it is said, directed his canal toward the agreed village, to the east, then brought it back toward
another village to the south, then made it return toward the west, then toward another village of the
south. And the sums he received from the people of all these villages amounted to a hundred thousand
dinars that he carried to the Pharaoh. The latter asked what this money meant, and Haman recounted to him
how he had dug his canal. "Woe to you!" said Pharaoh to him; "the master must be gentle to his subjects
and show himself generous toward them, and not take from them what they possess. Give back to the people
of each village what you took from them." Haman gave back the money to those who had handed it to him.
One knows in Egypt no canal more tortuous than the canal of Sardous; this is due

[PDF p. 234]

to the way in which Haman dug his canal. Haman was Nabataean.

CANAL OF ALEXANDRIA. -- Ibn Abd el-Hakam says: The tower of Alexandria was built by queen Cleopatra, who
prolonged the canal of Alexandria and brought it into the interior of the town. Before, it did not enter
it and stopped at a village named Kosa, opposite Karioun; the queen brought it into the town and paved
its bottom. According to El-Kandi, it was El-Harets ben Meskin, emir of Egypt, who dug the canal of
Alexandria. El-Assad ben Mammati, in his book entitled Rules of the Ministries, says: The canal of
Alexandria gives birth to a great number of secondary canals. Its length from its intake is thirty
thousand six hundred qassabahs. Its width varies from two and a half to three and a half qassabahs; the
quantity of water that stations varies with the state of the Nile. If the Nile is low, the water stays
very little in this canal; if it is high, it stays there more than two months. I have heard said by a
great number of chroniclers and scholars that if an inclined plane had been established between
Miniet-Natig and Natig, the water would maintain itself in this canal during winter and summer. I have
visited the whole Behera, the Houf, Damsis, and all the villages of this distant region; sugarcane,
colocasia, indigo, and the various summer cultivations were cultivated there absolutely as on the banks
of the Bahr El-Sharq, which is the canal of Mehallah. The towns multiplied and prospered on these banks.
The establishment of this inclined plane would be easy, for one finds stone at Rabouah and brick in the
Behera. The people of whom I have spoken had drawn up an estimate of the expense this work would require;
it amounted to about ten thousand dinars. Formerly, it is said, the water circulated all year in this
canal, and the fish were so abundant there that the children took them in cloths. One of the valis of the
province monopolized it for himself and forbade fishing there, but the fish has disappeared, and one no
longer meets there any but what is taken from time to time in nets.

CANAL OF THE FAYOUM AND OF EL-MENHA. -- It is one of the canals that the prophet of God Joseph the
veracious dug, when he put the Fayoum under cultivation, as will be seen in the chapter of this book that
treats of the Fayoum. It is derived from the Nile and its course is never interrupted. Near the Nile, in
the vicinity of Derout-Siriam -- a town that is called today Derout-El-Sherif, according to Ibn Yaghlan,
who was governor in the time of Zaher Beibars -- there detaches from the river a branch named El-Menha
that forms a canal heading toward the Fayoum.

[PDF p. 235]

This canal bears today the name of Bahr Youssef; its course is never interrupted at any moment of the
year, and it constantly waters the Fayoum; the surplus of its waters flows into a lake situated in this
region. A marvelous thing! at its beginning, the bed of this canal is without water; a little farther,
it becomes humid like a field wet with dew, then the course of the water establishes itself and becomes
such that one can no longer cross it except by boat; there forms thus a principal artery from which
depart several ramifications that spread everywhere in the Fayoum, watering the villages, the fields,
the gardens, and all the inhabited parts, and God knows it!

CANAL OF CAIRO. -- This canal is situated outside Cairo, on the west side, between this town and the
Meqs. At the beginning of Islam, it was named the Canal of the Commander of the Faithful, and today it
is generally known under the name of Canal of Haliem or Canal of the Pearl. It is an old canal that was
begun by Toutis, son of Malia, one of the kings of Egypt who resided in the town of Memphis. It was in
his time that Ibrahim (Abraham), the beloved of God, came to Egypt, and it was this Toutis who carried
off Sarah, wife of the patriarch, to whom he gave as servant Hagar, the mother of Ismaïl; and when
Ibrahim had sent Hagar and his son Ismaïl back to Mecca, the latter sent a message to Toutis to inform
him of her abandonment in a sterile place and to implore his help. Toutis then had this canal dug, thanks
to which he was able to send as far as Djedda wheat and other things to Hagar; he thus gave life to the
land of the Hedjaz. Subsequently, Andromanos, surnamed Élia, one of the Greek kings who reigned after
Alexander, son of Philip the Macedonian, took up again the work of this canal, and the boats circulated
on it; this took place four hundred and some years before the hijra of the Prophet. Later, Amr ben
El-As, having conquered Egypt, put the canal back into condition; after six months of work, the boats
were able to float on it and carry provisions into the Hedjaz: it is then that it took the name of Canal
of the Commander of the Faithful -- that is, of Omar ben El-Khattab, who had advised the enterprise.
From then on, the boats did not cease to circulate on it, from Fostat-Masr to Qolzoum, a town situated
on the eastern sea at the place named today Suez, and the water of the Nile did not cease to empty into
the sea near Qolzoum until the year 150 [6 February 767 to 25 January 768], the period when the caliph
Abou Giafar El-Mansour had this canal filled in, and

[PDF p. 236]

there has remained of it only what one still sees today. God willing, you will see what I say of it in a
more detailed way in the chapter of this book entitled Of the Exterior of Cairo.

BAHR ABOU-L-MENAGGA. -- This name of Abou-l-Menagga is given to this canal by the common people; it was
dug by El-Afdal, son of the Emir el-Giouch, in the year 506 [28 June 1112 to 17 June 1113]. The director
of the works was the Jew Abou-l-Menagga Shaïa; it is he who gave it his name. I have spoken of this canal
in the chapter of this book that treats of the belvederes and the promenades of the caliphs.

CANAL OF EL-NASER. -- This canal is outside the Meqs and was dug by El-Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun, in
the year 725 [18 December 1324 to 7 December 1325]; it is spoken of in the chapter of this book that
relates to it.

[PDF p. 237]

CHAPTER XXIV
OF THE STATE OF EGYPT IN THE FIRST TIMES

El-Maçoudi says: The land of Egypt, according to what those who have occupied themselves with the
history of the world claim, was covered by the water of the Nile, which extended over all the country,
from the Said to the point of the Delta, at the place where Fostat is today. This sheet of water began
at the point named today the Cataracts, between Assouan and Nubia. It was thus until there had formed
obstacles that opposed the displacement and the current of the water, as well as what it carried from
Nubia, and which stopped thus from place to place. The water, consequently, withdrew from some points of
Egypt, and the country could be inhabited by men; the water continuing to withdraw little by little from
the lands, Egypt ended by covering itself with towns and constructions; a bed was traced for the river,
canals were dug, and the Nile was imprisoned in dikes. In the long run, the inhabitants of Egypt forgot
the first state of their country, the accumulation of years having made them lose the memory of the
condition of the first inhabitants. Such is my opinion; and Aristotle, in his treatise of Metaphysics,
says, among other things, that the land of Egypt was covered primitively by the Nile, which extended
like a sea. The water withdrawing ceaselessly, left little by little uncovered the elevated places; the
country began to be peopled and finally filled with towns, villages, and men. Before inhabiting the town
of Memphis, the men, it is said, lived at the foot of the Moqattam in numerous grottoes they had dug.
These grottoes are still seen in the mountain facing Memphis, south of the Moqattam, in that part of the
mountain that skirts the Deir El-Qoseïr, known today under the name of Deir el-Baghl, and which gives
onto the side of Tourah. If one stands near the pyramids of Nahia, one perceives these grottoes to the
east on the other side of the Nile. If, setting out from Tourah, one climbs the mountain, one meets
these grottoes and can penetrate them easily. They are vast caverns into which open other

[PDF p. 238]

underground passages that lead to Qolzoum; a single one of these grottoes can contain the inhabitants of
a whole town. If one penetrates them without taking the necessary precautions to guide oneself on the
return, one loses one's way there and dies. Egypt was, it is said, sterile and produced not the least
plant when Mathuselah ben Akhnoukh ben Yared ben Mahalaël ben Photian ben Enos ben Seth ben Adam gave it
in fief to a tribe of his children. When the latter arrived there, they found all the space comprised
between the two mountains covered by the waters of the Nile. Then, the water having withdrawn, they
cultivated the land thus uncovered, and the land showed itself full of blessings. Some time after, the
first 'Enqam ben Ariab ben Adam seized it by violence and peopled it with a multitude of men; he fought
the Beni Yared at the head of seventy thousand combatants, dug, from the river to the mountain, a canal
forty qassabahs wide, to prevent the enemies from reaching him. The Beni Yared came, but not finding a
path to arrive at 'Enqam, they addressed prayers to God, who made a fire descend on the land of Egypt.

[PDF p. 239]

CHAPTER XXV
OF THE PROVINCES OF EGYPT AND OF ITS NOMES

Formerly Egypt was divided into 153 nomes, each of which comprised one town and 365 villages. After the
repeopling of Egypt, in the time of Bokht-Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar), it was divided into 85 circles; then
this figure diminished progressively until Islam; at the moment of the conquest, it counted only 40
nomes, which comprised all the villages without exception. Finally, the whole of the country was divided
into two great parts: the Qibli, which comprises all that is south of the town of Masr, and the Bahari,
which comprises all that is north of this same town.

All Egypt, south and north, was divided into 26 provinces, which are: the Sharqieh, the Martahieh, the
Dakahlieh, the Aïouanieh, and the port of Damietta -- all this in the region of the north -- (as well
as) the island of Qouisna, the Gharbieh, the Samanoudieh, the Dangaouïeh, the Menoufieh, the Sitraouïeh
and Fouah, the two Mouzahmiehs, the island of the Beni Naser, the Beherat, Alexandria and its territory,
and the Houf-Damsis; in the region of the south, Ghizeh, the Atfihieh, the Bousirieh, the Fayoumieh, the
Behnesaouïeh, Ashmounein, the Manfaloutieh, the Assioutieh, the Akhmimieh, the Qousieh.

One also divides it into 30 circles, which are: the Fayoum, comprising 156 villages, or, according to
others, 360; Memphis and Ousim, with 55 villages; the Sharqieh, also named Atfihieh, with 17 villages;
the villages dependent on Ahnas, and among them Qimn, together 8 villages; the circles of Dallas and
Bousir, 6 villages; the circle of Ahnas, 95 villages, without counting the hamlets; the circle of
Behnesa, 120 villages; the circle of Feshn, 37 villages; the circle of Taba, 37 villages; the district
of Senoudat, 8 villages; the circle of Achmounein, 133 villages; the circle of lower Antinoe, 11
villages; the circle of Siout, 37 villages; the circle of Shotb, 8 villages; the circle of upper
Antinoe, 12 villages; the circle of Qahqouat, 37 villages; the circle of Akhmim and El-Doueïr, 63
villages; the [...]

[PDF p. 240]

circle of Sebabat and of the Oases, 63 villages, without counting the hamlets; the circle of Hou, 20
villages; the circle of Faou, 8 villages; the circle of Qena, 7 villages; the circle of Denderah, 10
villages; the circle of Qoft, 22 villages; the circle of El-Aqsar (Luxor), 5 villages; the circle of
Esna, 5 villages; the circle of Erment, 7 villages; the circle of Assouan, 7 villages; the ensemble of
the villages of the Said forms a total of 1,043, in which are not comprised the landing-stages and the
hamlets, which depend on thirty of these villages.

Circles of the Delta: the eastern Houf, 65 villages; the circle of Athribis, 108 villages, without
counting the ports and the hamlets; the circle of Benou, 87 villages, without counting the ports and
the hamlets; the circle of Nama, 150 villages, without counting the ports and the hamlets; the circle
of Basta, 39 villages; the circle of Tarabiah, 28 villages, among which El-Sadir, El-Hama, and Faqous;
the circle of Horbeit, 18 villages, without counting the ports and the hamlets; the circle of Sa and of
Ablil, 46 villages, among which Senhour, Farama, and El-Arich; in all, in the eastern Houf, 529
villages, without counting the ports, distributed in seven circles.

Belly of the countryside [Footnote: designation of the central part of the Delta comprised between the
mouth of Rosetta and that of Tanis]: the two circles of Damsis and of Menouf, 104 villages, without
counting the ports and the hamlets; the circle of Tatourat Menouf, 92 villages, without counting the
ports and the hamlets; the circle of Sakha, 115 villages; the circle of Beïdat and of El-Afrahoun, 23
villages, without counting the ports and the hamlets; the circle of Bachroud, 24 villages; the circle
of Nafar, 12 villages without counting the ports; the circle of Beba and of Bousir, 88 villages,
without counting the ports and the hamlets; the circle of Samanoud, 128 villages, without counting the
ports and the hamlets; the circle of Nousa, 21 villages, without counting the ports; the circle of
El-Osiah, 40 villages, without counting the ports; the circle of Negoum, 40 villages, without counting
the ports; Tennis and Damietta, 13 villages, without counting the ports, which abound; Alexandria.

Western Houf: circle of Sa, 73 villages, without counting the ports and the hamlets; circle of Shabas,
22 villages, without counting the ports and the hamlets; circle of Yadkoun, 43 villages without
counting the ports and the hamlets; district of Yadkoun, 29 villages, without counting the ports and
the hamlets; the Sherak,

[PDF p. 241]

9 villages; the circle of Ternout, 8 villages; the circle of Kharbata, 62 villages, without counting the
ports and the hamlets; the circle of Qortesa, 22 villages, without counting the ports and the hamlets;
the two circles of Masil and of El-Malidis, 49 villages, without counting the ports; the two circles of
Ahnour and of Rosetta, 17 villages; the Behera, the district of Alexandria, with its plantations of
vines and palms, Mariout, the town of Alexandria, Libya, the Maraqieh, 124 villages, without counting
the ports; that is, for the western Houf, 449 villages without counting the ports, the whole distributed
in 13 circles. El-Mesihi, in his History, says that Lower Egypt contains 1,439 villages. The total of
the villages of the Said and the Delta would therefore be 2,395.

The cadi Abou Abd Allah Mohammed ben Salamat El-Qoda'i says: The land of Egypt divides into two parts:
the Said, on the side from which comes the south wind, and the Delta, on the side from which the north
wind blows. The Said is divided into twenty-eight circles, which are: a circle comprising the whole
Fayoum; the two circles of Memphis and of Ousim; the circle of Sharqieh; the two circles of Dallas and
of Abousir; the circle of Ahnas; the two circles of Feshn and of Behnesa; the circle of Taha; the
district of Senoudah; the circle of Bouit; the circles of Achmounein and of Antinoe, lower and upper, of
Shotb, of Qous-Qam; the circle of Siout; the circle of Qahqouah; the circles of Akhmim, of El-Deir, and
of Abchaïa; the circle of Hou, of Qena, of Faou, of Denderah; the circle of Qoft and of Luxor; the
circle of Esna and of Erment, and the circle of Assouan. Such are the circles of the Said.

As for those of the Delta, they number twenty-five, or, according to other copies, thirty-three or even
thirty-eight. These circles are: in the eastern Houf, the circles of Athribis and of Heliopolis; those
of Bena and of Nama; the circles of Basta and of Tarabiah; the circle of Horbeit; the circles of Sa and
of Ablil; the circle of Farama, of El-Arich, and of El-Gofar; in the Belly of the countryside, which is
also part of the Delta: the circle of Beba and of Bousir; the circles of Samanoud and of Bousa; the
circles of El-Osiah and of Negoum; the circle of Dakahlah; the circles of Tennis and of Damietta; one
must join to it also the circle of the islands in front of the Delta; the circle of Mesis and of Menouf;
the circle of Touah and of Menouf; the circle of Sakha, of Beidah, and of El-Afrahoun; the circle of
Moqin and of Disa and the circle of Bachroud; in the western Houf: the circle of Sa; the circle

[PDF p. 242]

of Shabas; the circle of Yadkoun and its district; the circle of El-Kheïs and of El-Sherak; the circle
of Kharbata; the circle of Qortesa, of Mesil, and of Melidis; the circles of Akhna, of Behera, and of
Rosetta; the circle of Alexandria; the circle of Mariout; the circle of Libya and of Maraqieh.

Among the circles of the south, one comprises also the circle of the Hedjaz, which bears the name of the
circle of Tor, and that of Faran; the circle of Raïat and of Qolzoum; the circle of Aïlat and its
district; that of Madian and its district; that of El-Ounid; that of El-Hour and its district; finally
the circles of Bada and of Shaghb.

Whoever occupies himself with the affairs of the tax and the divans knows an old list, written in the
hand of Ibn Aïssa Boqtor ben Shegha, the Coptic writer known under the name of Bolos, who was at the
head of the taxes of Egypt in the time of the dynasty of El-Akhshidi. This list embraces the nomes of
Egypt and the villages up to the year 345 [15 April 956 to 3 April 957]; these villages, as much for the
Said as for the Delta, number two thousand three hundred ninety-five, of which nine hundred fifty-six
for the Said and one thousand four hundred thirty-nine for the Delta. Such was the number of villages at
the period when the list in question was drawn up. But this number has been modified as a consequence of
the annihilation of the ruined parts of Egypt.

Ibn Abd El-Hakam reports, on the authority of El-Leitz ben Sa'd, that El-Oualid ben Refaat, being
governor of Egypt, made the census of the inhabitants of Egypt, in order to distribute the tax
equitably. Accompanied by a multitude of writers and aides charged with seconding him by their vigor and
energy, he took six months to count Upper Egypt, which he traversed as far as Assouan, and three months
to count Lower Egypt. More than ten thousand villages were counted, without comprising in this figure the
hamlets peopled with fewer than five hundred heads of men liable to pay the capitation tax. The latter
amounted to five million men.

Under the reign of El-Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun, the division of the southern part of Egypt into six
provinces was rigorously maintained; these six provinces were: Qous, the largest of all, with Assouan and
the western part of Qamoulah; the province of Akhmim, comprising those of

[PDF p. 243]

Siout, of Manfalout, and of Achmounein, the latter enclosing the Tahaouïeh; the province of the western
Behnesaouïeh, with the villages situated on the western bank of the Menha, the canal that heads toward
the Fayoum; the province of the Fayoum; that of Atfih and that of Ghizeh; in the northern part of Egypt
six other provinces: the Behera, which skirts the sea, encompassing Alexandria and Barca; the Gharbieh,
formed of a single island enclosed between the two arms of the river -- the one that empties into the sea
at Damietta and called the "eastern branch," and the one that empties into the sea at Rosetta and is
called the "western branch"; the Menoufieh, comprising the wells and the island of the Beni Naser; the
province of Qalioub; that of Sharqieh; that of Asmoum Tenah, embracing the Dakahlieh and the Mourtahieh.
In this region are the ports of Bourlos and of Rosetta, Mansourah, Alexandria, Damietta, and their
provinces.

As for the oases, they form a territory apart, to the southwest; one does not count them among the
provinces and the vilayets; and it is not a vali of the sultan who administers them: they are left under
the direction of the one to whom they are attributed in fief. And God is the most knowing!

[PDF p. 244]

CHAPTER XXVI
OF THE WAY IN WHICH ONE WENT ABOUT IT IN EGYPT TO DIG THE CANALS AND RAISE THE DIKES, ETC., INTENDED TO
RETAIN THE WATER OF THE NILE AND DISTRIBUTE IT AT THE OPPORTUNE TIME

Ibn Abd El-Hakam reports, on the authority of Yezid ben Abou Habib, that the Egyptians assigned to the
cleaning of the canals and the upkeep of the dikes one hundred twenty thousand men who, furnished with
axes, hoes, and the necessary tools, remained constantly occupied with this work without interrupting
it, winter or summer.

Some old Egyptians, says Abou Qabil, claim that in the time of the kings, the villages were left under
the direct authority of their inhabitants, each village paying a determined due that was changed only
every four years, as a consequence of the reverses and the displacements of fortune that might have
occurred. When four years had elapsed, the old distribution of the taxes was annulled and a new one was
established, diminishing the due of those who really ought to be exonerated and increasing that of the
individuals who could bear an increase, without however overwhelming the latter with too-heavy charges.
Once the tax was collected and centralized, a quarter of the total sum was attributed to the king; the
king was the master in full property of this quarter and disposed of it as he saw fit; a second quarter
was assigned to the army and served for the pay of those who aided the king in his wars, and for the
salary of the individuals charged with collecting the tax and repulsing the enemy; the third quarter was
intended for the improvement of the lands -- the tracing of canals, the construction of dikes and
bridges, aid to the agriculturists for the cultivations and the good upkeep of their lands; finally the
fourth quarter was distributed among all the villages, in proportion to the tax each of them had paid,
and the sums thus distributed were buried to serve later in case of reverses or calamities that might
have struck the inhabitants of that village; this is what the ancient Egyptians did, and the sums buried
in each village constitute what is [...]

[PDF p. 245]

called the treasures of Pharaoh, treasures that, according to popular belief, must reappear one day or
another. This is why certain people make a profession of discovering them and apply themselves to
searching for them.

A certain Pharaoh, it is said, took in as taxes seventy-two million dinars; it is this same Pharaoh
who, to assure himself of the good cultivation of the lands, sent an oueïba of wheat into Upper and
Lower Egypt, at the moment of the weeding of the fields and the repair of the canals, without one
finding a space of empty land where it could be sown. Toward the end of the cultivations, it is said
again, this Pharaoh sent four oueïbas of bersim (clover) seed into Upper and Lower Egypt, and into all
the provinces; and if one found an empty terrain where this quantity of seed could be sown, the head of
the governor of the province was cut off. The cultivated part of Egypt was then forty square parasangs.
The parasang is worth three miles and the barid four parasangs; that made therefore a total of ten
square barids. The Pharaohs continued to act in this manner until the time of the Pharaoh of Moses, who
filled Egypt with justice and equity. Under his reign there was a dearth that lasted three years, and,
during these three years, the people were exempted from taxes, and the Pharaoh provided himself, from
his own purse, for his own maintenance and that of the troops. But the fourth year, he doubled the tax
and maintained this increase until he had recovered his expenses.

Omar ben El-Khattab wrote to Amr ben El-As: "Ask El-Maqoqos whence come the prosperity and the ruin of
Egypt." Amr therefore questioned El-Maqoqos on this subject, and the latter answered him: "The
prosperity of Egypt and its ruin may be attributed to five causes: the tax must be collected from the
moment when the agriculturists have finished the cultivations until the one when the harvest of the
vine is finished; one must each year dredge the canals, close the water-intakes, and repair the dikes;
finally one must not accept the delays of people who give only mendacious excuses; if one acts thus,
Egypt is prosperous; if not, it is ruined."

Zeïd ben Aslam reports this, on the authority of his father: "Omar ben El-Khattab, finding that Amr ben
El-As was slow to send him the tax, wrote to him to dispatch him an Egyptian. Amr sent him an old Copt
of whom Omar asked information on Egypt and its revenues before Islam. The old man said to him:

[PDF p. 246]

'O Commander of the Faithful, no tax was levied in Egypt as long as the cultivations were not in good
state, but your lieutenant occupies himself in no way with the cultivations and collects the tax at his
pleasure as if he wished to collect revenues only for one year.' Omar understood what the old man meant
and accepted the excuses that Amr gave him."

Amr ben El-As said to El-Maqoqos: "You who have governed Egypt, tell me what renders it prosperous." "Its
prosperity," answered El-Maqoqos, "depends on many causes; one must dredge the canals, consolidate the
dikes and the water-intakes, levy tax only on the harvests, not accept the delays that individuals
propose, respect the established conventions, shower the governors with favors -- for fear that they
accept gifts and draw from the inhabitants presents or aids, which would weaken the latter accordingly;
in this way Egypt will be prosperous and one will be able to count on the taxes."

It is recounted that the indigenous sovereigns had divided the revenues of the country into four parts:
one was the property of the king; the second served to defray the army; the third was intended for the
putting into condition of the lands; finally, the fourth was reserved to meet the unfortunate events
that might occur.

'Obeïd Allah ben El-Haggab, being intendant of the finances of Egypt for the account of Hescham ben Abd
El-Melek, went himself to measure all the lands of Egypt, cultivated or not cultivated, that the flood
of the Nile reached, and he found that these terrains represented a surface of a hundred million
feddans. On the other hand, it is said that Ahmed ben Moudabber, having measured the terrain proper for
cultivation in Egypt, found that it represented a surface of twenty-four million feddans; the rest was
submerged and impossible to cultivate. He also evaluated the time necessary for the cultivation and he
found that this time comprised sixty days; each agriculturist cultivating fifty feddans, it required, to
cultivate Egypt, four hundred eighty thousand cultivators.

[PDF p. 247]

CHAPTER XXVII
OF THE SUM OF THE REVENUES OF EGYPT IN ANCIENT TIMES

Ibn Ouacif Shah says: Monqaous divided the revenues of the country into four parts: one quarter for the
king, who did with it what he wished; another quarter assigned to the expenses necessitated by the
improvement of the lands, the repair of the dikes, the dredging of the canals, and the aid to be given to
the inhabitants for the cultivation; one quarter was buried in anticipation of unfortunate events that
might occur; the last quarter was assigned to the army. At this period, the revenues of the country rose
to a hundred three million dinars, coming from a hundred three districts, a million per district. Each
of these dinars was worth, it is said, ten of our Muslim mithqals. Today, Egypt is divided into
eighty-five nomes, forty-five for Lower Egypt and forty for the Said; each of these nomes is administered
by a priest and a military chief. Under the reign of Nadares ben Sa, the revenues of the country reached
