a hundred fifty million dinars, and in the time of Kalkun ben Kharbata ben Maliq ben Nadares, they were
still a hundred and some tens of millions of dinars. When the government of the first Egyptians had
ceased and the country was governed by the Amalekites, the state of Egypt was less flourishing, and the
first Pharaoh (Shepherd) took in ninety million dinars, on which were levied ten million dinars for the
improvement of the country, ten million dinars for the maintenance of the personnel of the king's
children and of persons of (good) condition but poor, ten million dinars for the personnel charged with
affairs, for the army and the employees, and ten million dinars for the maintenance of the Pharaoh; the
rest, fifty million dinars, was put in reserve for the Pharaoh.

In the time of El-Raïan ben El-Oualid, the Pharaoh of Joseph, the revenue reached ninety-seven million
dinars, but this prince, wishing to reach the full hundred million dinars, prescribed putting into use
all the kinds

[PDF p. 248]

of cultivation possible, repairing the dikes, and extending the cultivated terrains, so well that this
sum was reached and even exceeded.

Ibn Lahiat says: The sum collected in Egypt during the period of the Pharaohs (Shepherds) reached ninety
million dinars, in pharaonic dinars each equivalent to three of the mithqals known today in Egypt and
which divide each into twenty-four qirats, each qirat weighing three grains of wheat. According to this
reckoning, the aforesaid sum would represent two hundred seventy million Egyptian dinars.

El-Sherif El-Gouani declares that he found in one of the temples of Upper Egypt a text written in the
Sahidic language and which had been translated into Arabic; this text gave the detail of the sums
collected by the Pharaoh of Joseph, El-Raïan ben El-Oualid, as taxes levied in Egypt on objects really
struck with tax or under any title whatever during one year, according to equity, justice, and
established usage, without malevolence, false interpretation, or discussion regarding the difference that
might exist between the sum collected and the quantity of taxable matters found in the possession of the
taxed; this sum, without speaking of the one that one was accustomed to set apart in anticipation of
calamities to come, or to aid the workers and improve their lot, amounted in gold to twenty-four million
six hundred thousand dinars. And what El-Sherif reports agrees with what El-Hassan ben Ali El-Asdi says.

El-Hassan ben Ali El-Asdi reports this: "My father recounted to me having found in a Coptic book, written
in the Sahidic language and translated into Arabic, the sum of the revenues collected by the Pharaoh of
Egypt in real taxes levied on the taxed matters or under any title whatever for an entire year, according
to justice and equity, without malevolence or discussion regarding the difference that might exist
between the sums collected and the quantity of taxable matters found in the possession of the taxed; this
sum, after having set aside the funds necessary to meet eventualities, to succor and aid the workers,
amounted in gold to twenty-four million four hundred thousand dinars, representing the revenues of all
Egypt; of this sum one employed for the cultivation of the country, the dredging of the canals, the
repair of the dikes and the water-intakes, the upkeep of the roads, the functioning of the
administration, indispensable aid to the agriculturists, the establishment of works, the enlargement of

[PDF p. 249]

the cultivations, etc., the purchase of tools, the salary of mercenaries, the transport of materials --
in a word for all the expenses the cultivation of the country required -- eight hundred thousand dinars
of gold; for the costs entailed by the salary of the employees charged with affairs and of the army, for
the army itself, for the slaves and the families (of the soldiers), as well as for a thousand writers
assigned to the ministries, without counting their servants, such as cashiers and other similar
employees, whose number rises to eleven thousand men, eight million dinars in gold; for the widows and
the orphans inscribed at the treasury -- even though they might not be in need, and so that they might
always be able to count on the generosity of the king -- four hundred thousand dinars in gold; for the
priests, the temples and their personnel, the houses of prayer, one hundred thousand dinars in gold; for
the alms (one cried among the people: "Let those who are poor not be ashamed to uncover themselves!" and
none of those who presented themselves was repulsed; the employees charged with the distribution sat
down, and as soon as they perceived a man they were not accustomed to see, they had him set apart, after
having given him what was due to him; the money exhausted, these poor were gathered in great number, and
one of the intimates of Pharaoh went to him, congratulated him on having distributed all the money, and
one prayed God for the salvation and the life of the king; one gave him details on the position of these
people, and the Pharaoh gave orders that their miserable state be attenuated by giving them baths and
garments; tables were set where the poor ate and drank, then one asked each of them the cause of his
misery; if this misery was due to the misfortune of the times, one gave back to the unfortunate the
equivalent of what he had had and even more; if, on the contrary, his misery was only the result of bad
management or too weak a character, one entrusted the incapable man to a person who was to serve as his
guardian and occupy himself with his affairs until he had put them back in order) -- two hundred thousand
dinars in gold. And here is the total of the sums detailed above for the different uses of which we have
spoken: nine million eight hundred thousand dinars. One must take account, in addition, of what Pharaoh
kept in his treasury, to face calamities and eventual misfortunes: fourteen million six hundred thousand
dinars in gold.

[PDF p. 250]

One asked someone: "At what period did Egypt produce ninety million dinars?" "At the period," he
answered, "when Pharaoh sent an oueïba of wheat into the Delta and the Said, without finding sufficient
place to sow it, because all the country was put under cultivation."

[PDF p. 251]

CHAPTER XXVIII
HOW THE MUSLIMS ORGANIZED THE TAXES, AT THE MOMENT OF THE CONQUEST OF EGYPT, AND OF THE SITUATION IN
WHICH EGYPT AND THE COPTS FOUND THEMSELVES IN THIS REGARD

Zoheir ben Moawiah says: Souahil reported to me this, which he had from his father, to whom Abou
Houraïrat had recounted it: The Prophet of God said: "Iraq has kept its dirhem and its qafiz; Syria has
kept its medd and its dinar; Egypt has kept its ardeb, and you have returned to your first state."
According to Abou Obeïd, the Prophet wished to speak of things not yet accomplished but already existing
in the decrees of God; and he expressed himself in the past, for these things had already passed into
the decrees of God; in speaking of them before their accomplishment, he proved the authenticity of his
prophetic mission and gave his approval to the taxes established by Omar on the tributary Christians
inhabiting the conquered provinces.

These words are explained in two ways: either the Prophet would have known in advance that the cited
countries would convert to Islam, that they would be freed from taxes, and that, having become Muslims,
they would no longer have to pay tribute, which explains the words: "You will return to your first
state"; or else these countries would free themselves from obedience. But the first explanation is the
best.

Ibn Abd El-Hakam reports, on the authority of Abd Allah ben Lahiat, that after the conquest of Egypt by
Amr ben El-As, it was agreed that all the inhabitants of the country having reached their majority --
without counting the women, the children, and the old men -- would pay two dinars per head; the count
was made and the sum reached eight million dinars.

Hecham ben Abou Raqiat El-Lakhmi recounts that after the conquest of Egypt, Amr ben El-As said to the
Copts: "If anyone among you hides treasures in his house and I come to discover it, I will put him to
death." Now, a Copt of the Said,

[PDF p. 252]

named Botros, was denounced to Amr as having a treasure in his house. The man, summoned and questioned,
denied and protested. He was put in prison, and Amr asked whether he had not been heard to speak of
someone. "No," it was answered; "we have heard him speak only of a monk who dwells at Tor." Amr then
sent to Botros a man who took his seal from him, then he wrote to this monk: "Send me what you have in
your keeping," and he signed the letter with the seal of Botros. The messenger returned with a Syrian
flask sealed with lead. Amr opened it and found in it a sheet of paper bearing these words: "Your money
is under the great basin." One went to this basin, whose water was emptied; the slab of the bottom was
removed and, under this slab, was found fifty-two ardebs of minted Egyptian gold. Amr had the head of
Botros cut off at the door of the mosque. The Copts then brought their treasures, for fear of being
denounced by one among them and being put to death as Botros had been.

According to Yezid ben Abou Habib, Amr ben El-As acted thus with the treasures of this Copt only because
he was persuaded that he denounced to the Greeks the weak points of the Muslims and wrote to them on
this subject, and he drew from him more than fifty ardebs of dinars.

Ibn Abd El-Hakam says that Amr ben El-As sent to Omar ben El-Khattab the tribute after having retained
what was necessary to him; and the regulation of Egypt comprised, for the dredging of the canals, the
repair of the dikes, the construction of the bridges, and the upkeep of the islands, one hundred twenty
thousand men furnished with shovels, hoes, and tools, relaying one another at this work without
interruption, winter and summer.

Omar ben El-Khattab wrote to Amr: "You will mark with a lead seal at the neck the people of the
protection; they must wear this insignia in an apparent manner; their hair must be cut on the forehead,
and they will ride seated on asses. The tax will be established only on those who have already undergone
the razor; it will not be on the women or the children, and you will not permit them to wear a costume
similar to that of the Muslims."

Yezid ben Aslam, speaking of Omar ben El-Khattab, says: "It was written to the emirs of the armies to
strike with tax only the people who had already undergone the razor; to exact forty dirhems from those
who would pay in silver and four dinars from those who would pay in gold; moreover, those who were to
furnish the wheat and the oil to the Muslims were held to bring two medd of wheat and three qosat of oil
per month and

[PDF p. 253]

per head; this clause concerns the Syrians and the people of Mesopotamia who, in addition, were obliged
to furnish I no longer know what quantity of fat and honey; as for the Egyptians, they were to give per
month and per head one ardeb and I know not how much fat and honey; it was they too who were to furnish
the garment of silk intended to clothe the Commander of the Faithful; they owed in addition a
hospitality of three days to every Muslim who would lodge with them; the inhabitants of Iraq were to
furnish per head fifteen sa' and I know not how much fat. The women and the children were exempt from
taxes; and all the people subject to the tax wore a seal at the neck. The oueïba of Omar, during the
government of Amr ben El-As, was six medd.

When his authority was well affirmed, Amr ben El-As charged Copts with collecting the tax owed by the
Greeks; the tax in Egypt was subject to certain modifications: if a village was prosperous and the
number of inhabitants had increased, the tax was raised; if, on the contrary, the number of inhabitants
had diminished and the country was in ruin, the taxes were diminished. The principal men of each
village, the emirs and the chiefs of the inhabitants gathered and discussed, examining whether there
was prosperity or decadence, and if they had fixed some increase of the tax, they withdrew into their
districts, and there, gathered with the chiefs of the district, this increase was distributed according
to the importance of each village and the extent of its cultivations. Then each village gathered its
inhabitants, and in this assembly, the sum of the increase being known, a proportion was established
between this increase added to the ordinary tax and the ensemble of the cultivated terrains. One then
set to work, withdrawing first from the ensemble of the cultivated lands the feddans belonging to the
churches and those assigned to the upkeep of the baths and the ferries, then a certain number of feddans
to compensate for the hospitality to be given to the Muslims and to the king, if by chance he came. That
done, one counted the number of artisans and mercenaries in each village and attributed to them a part
of the increase, according to what they could bear, and it was very rare that this increase fell on
others than young men or married men; one then verified what remained to be paid of the tax and
distributed it according to the quantity of lands cultivated by each; these lands themselves were
divided among those who desired to cultivate them and who had the strength for it. If anyone among them

[PDF p. 254]

complained of his powerlessness to cultivate his lands, the lands he could not cultivate were divided
among those who could do it; to the latter were given the lands that the too-weak people had been unable
to cultivate. If some disagreement arose, one divided according to the number. Their dinars were divided
into qirats, each dinar containing twenty-four; the land was divided likewise. This is why it is
reported that the Prophet said: "You will conquer a land where one counts by qirats; treat its
inhabitants well." And each feddan was imposed with a due of half an ardeb of wheat and two oueïba of
barley; only the qorz (fruit of the sont/acacia) was not struck with tax; the oueïba contains six medd.
Omar ben El-Khattab took from those with whom he had made a treaty what they themselves had proposed to
give, without ever increasing or diminishing it; for those who, subject to the tax, had fixed nothing
themselves, Omar examined their situation: if they were poor, they were struck with a light tax; if they
were rich, they were taxed according to their wealth.

Hecham ben Abou Raqiat El-Lakhmi says: The governor of Akhna came to Amr ben El-As and said to him:
"Tell us what each of us must pay as tax and we will conform to it." Amr, pointing to the corner of a
church, answered: "If you bring me a heap (of money reaching) from the floor to the ceiling, I have
nothing to say to you, but for us you are a storehouse; if much is demanded of us, we will demand much
of you; if little is demanded of us, we will demand little of you." Whoever believes in the veracity of
this tradition believes also that Egypt was conquered by force.

According to Yezid ben Abou Habib, Omar ben Abd el-Aziz said: Whoever embraces Islam saves, by his
conversion, both his soul and his wealth; as for the land, it is part of what God has given to the
Muslims. Whoever has made a treaty, by means of tribute, will pay it, and all those who, among the
people having made this treaty, will have embraced Islam, will see their land and their house pass into
other hands.

El-Leitz says: Yahia ben Saïd wrote me this: If, to pay the tax justly levied on him, someone sells his
male or female slaves, his camels, his cows, or his mounts, that is permitted to him and the buyer is
not held to restitution, even though the former possessor were rich; but for the land, the renting of it
is permitted only insofar as this renting will not be prejudicial [...]

[PDF p. 255]

to the tax with which the proprietor is struck; if the contract harms the tax, the land will be restored
to its proprietor; if, on the contrary, the price of the renting exceeds the sum of the tax, one may
consider this renting as permitted to the one who consents to it.

Yahia adds: We say that the tax is of two sorts: capitation tax and general tax, the latter established
on the ensemble of the inhabitants of a village, who all participate in it. If in a village a particular
person comes to die of those whom the general tax reaches -- any tax other than the personal one -- and
this person has died without children or heirs, his lands, with all the taxes they comprise, revert to
the village. As for the one who dies without leaving heirs and who was subject to the capitation, his
land reverts to the Muslims. El-Leitz says, on the authority of Omar ben Abd el-Aziz, that the tax is
personal and has nothing in common with the land; he means there the people subject to the protection.

Omar ben Abd el-Aziz wrote to Heïan ben Sharaïh to transfer the tax payable by a deceased Copt onto the
head of his brother; this proves that Omar was of the opinion that Egypt had been conquered by force and
that, the tax striking only the villages, if one of the inhabitants of that village came to die, the tax
was maintained integrally on the others, the death of one of them entailing in no way a diminution of
the tax. It is probable, however, that Egypt was conquered by treaty and that this treaty was maintained
intact for the Egyptians who came later, so that the death of one of them could not harm the sum
stipulated in the convention.

El-Leitz says: Omar ben Abd el-Aziz exempted from taxes those of the Egyptians subject to the protection
who had embraced Islam, and attributed to them the same privileges as to those who had converted to
Islam from the first day and to those who had converted at his own hands. Before him the tax of the
converts was collected. The first to levy the tax on those of the people having embraced Islam was
El-Haggag ben Youssef. Abd el-Melek ben Merwan having written to Abd el-Aziz ben Merwan to tax the people
of the protection who had become Muslim, Ibn Hageïrat spoke to him on this subject and said to him: "May
God preserve you, O emir, from being the first to establish such a tax in Egypt, for, by God! if any
people of the protection owe the tax, it is those among them who are monks. How

[PDF p. 256]

could we establish the tax on those who have become Muslim!" And the emir abandoned this project.

Omar ben Abd el-Aziz wrote to Heïan ben Shoraïh: Discharge from the tax those of the protected who will
have embraced Islam, for God has said: "If they convert, if they practice prayer and almsgiving, let them
follow their life in peace, for God is indulgent and merciful" (Koran, IX, 5). He said also: "Fight those
who believe neither in God nor in the last day and do not consider as forbidden what God and his apostle
have forbidden, and for those among the sectaries of the Book (the Gospels) who do not practice justice,
fight them until they all pay the tribute and are humiliated" (Koran, IX, 29).

Heïan ben Shoraïh wrote to Omar ben Abd el-Aziz: "The conversions to Islam have done such harm to the
tax that I have had to borrow from El-Haretz ben Tabeta twenty thousand dinars with which I will complete
the pay of the employees of the divans, and if the Commander of the Faithful is of the opinion that I
take them (from the new converts) and wishes to give me the order, let him give it to me!" Omar answered
him: "Your letter has reached me. I had established you vali of the army of Egypt, but I recognize your
incapacity, and I have given the order to my messenger to strike you twenty blows on the head. Discharge
from the tax those who have converted to Islam. By God! your opinion is very bad, for God sent Mohammed
as a guide and not as a cashier. By my life! Omar is far too unhappy to have the joy of seeing all men
embrace Islam under his government!"

Omar ben El-Khattab, finding that Amr ben El-As was slow to send him the tribute, wrote to him: "In the
name of the clement and merciful God! From the servant of God, Commander of the Faithful, to Amr ben
El-As; may God save you! I glorify God for you; there is no God but he! I have reflected on your affair
and your situation. Your land is a vast, spacious, and fertile land, and God has made its inhabitants
numerous, patient, and strong on the land and on the sea. Certainly the Pharaohs took great care of it
and executed there magnificent works, despite their extreme violence and impiety; I have been marveled
at it, but what surprises me most is that this land no longer renders today the half of what the tax
formerly produced, and yet there is neither drought nor dearth. In your letter, you speak to me at
length of the state of the tax in your region, and I hoped that the tribute would arrive to me without
delay, thinking that you would wake up and

[PDF p. 257]

send it to me. And here you send me only excuses that are far from agreeing with what I myself think. I
will accept from you nothing other than what you had collected of tax before. Moreover, I do not see what
my letter has that is frightening and capable of making you anxious. If you were an experienced, capable,
and wise man, you would know that innocence is indispensable, but if you are only ill-advised and
clumsy, I conclude from it that the matter must be quite other than you report it. I did not wish to
renew the reproaches I addressed to you last year, hoping that you would wake up and send me the tribute,
for I know that this dispatch is delayed by a single cause: your governors are bad governors who
circumvent and deceive you by taking you for a refuge. But, thanks to God, I have for this a good remedy
that I beg you to employ, and you will not be displeased with it, O Abou Abd Allah: it is to pay what you
owe and take what is due to you; for the sea produces the pearls and the truth is limpid; leave me, then,
and tell me no more foolishness, for what was hidden has been brought to light. Farewell!"

Amr ben El-As answered: "In the name of the clement and merciful God! To the servant of God, Omar,
Commander of the Faithful, from Amr ben El-As, the salvation of God be upon you! I pray God for you;
there is no God but he! I have received, O Commander of the Faithful, the letter in which you complain
of my slowness to send you the tribute, recall to me what the Pharaohs did before me, and are astonished
at the revenues Egypt produced in their hands and at the diminution of these revenues since Islam. By my
life, it is true that then the revenues were greater and higher, the land being better cultivated, for
these Pharaohs, despite their impiety and their violence, showed more ardor for the cultivation of their
soil than we have shown since Islam. The sea produces the pearls, you say; for my part I have milked
this country so much and so much that its udders are dried up. You exaggerate in your letter, you
reprimand me at length and cover me with dust, warning me that this delay is due to causes that an
unskilled man cannot discover. Your letter is full of contained allusions, but you would have done
better to employ words cutting as the sword, brilliant as the truth. I have served as lieutenant of the
Prophet and of his successors, and always, I render thanks to God for it, I have faithfully rendered the
deposits entrusted to me, always I have safeguarded the right sacred in the eyes

[PDF p. 258]

of God, esteeming that to act otherwise was infamous and disastrous. Recognize that in me and have
confidence in my heart. God preserve me from eating such a dish, may he keep my character from this
perversity and from any audacity against all that has been accomplished. Do, then, what pleases you, but
God preserve me from this vile nourishment and from such an inclination, especially after your letter in
which you have not spared my honor and have treated so little generously a brother! By my life, O Ibn
el-Khattab, if anyone had made me such propositions, my soul would have been swollen with anger, for it
is worthy and generous, and I have never committed actions that could dishonor it. But I know things you
are ignorant of, and were I a Jew of Yatreb (Medina) I would say no more of it. I pray God to pardon you
and to pardon me also; I have kept silent things I knew, and my tongue, on this occasion, has been
docile. But may God make grow what he knows of your justice!"

Omar ben El-Khattab answered: "From Omar ben El-Khattab to Amr ben El-As; salvation be upon you! I pray
God for you; there is no God but he! I am surprised at the quantity of letters I must write you on the
subject of your delay in sending me the tribute; your answer is ambiguous. You know that I exact of you
only what is manifestly just, and that I did not place you at the head of Egypt so that this country
might become your prey and that of your people; I called you to this post counting that you would send
me the tribute and trusting in your wise policy. On receipt of my letter, send the tribute; it is the
property of the Muslims, and in my entourage, you know it, there are unfortunate people. Farewell!"

Amr ben El-As answered: "In the name of the powerful and merciful God! To Omar ben El-Khattab from Amr
ben El-As, salvation be upon you! I pray God for you, there is no God but he! The letter of the Commander
of the Faithful has reached me, in which he complains of my slowness to send the tribute and accuses me
of disguising the truth and employing subterfuges. By God, I do not depart from the conventions you
know; but the people of the country have begged me to wait until the grains are ripe. I referred the
matter to the Muslims, who are of the opinion that it is better to show oneself gentle to the
inhabitants than to tear them apart, for they would be obliged to sell what is indispensable to them.
Farewell!"

El-Leitz ben Sa'd said: The amount of the tax collected by Amr ben El-As was twelve million dinars;
before him El-Maqoqos collected per year twenty million

[PDF p. 259]

dinars. This is why Omar ben El-Khattab wrote to Amr the letters (reported above). The revenue collected
by Abd Allah ben Sa'd ben Sarah, after Othman had installed him as governor of Egypt, rose to fourteen
million dinars, and Othman said to Amr ben El-As, already deposed: "O Abou Abd Allah, the she-camel has
given more milk than before." "But you have harmed the young one," answered Amr. "The young one is not
dead," added Othman. Moawiah ben Abou Safian wrote to Ouardan, intendant of the treasury of Egypt:
"Increase the tax of each Copt by one qirat." Ouardan answered: "How increase them, since it is agreed
that they will be increased in nothing?" Ouardan was deposed by Moawiah, but it is said that the reasons
for his deposition were quite different.

Ibn Lahiat says: In the time of Moawiah, the ministries counted forty thousand employees, of whom four
thousand received each two hundred dinars. Moslema ben Meglid paid the employees of the ministries their
appointments, as well as those of their families and their food expenses; he paid also the expenses
entailed by the needs of the country, such as repairs of dikes, salary of the writers, transport of the
wheat to the Hedjaz, and he sent Moawiah the rest -- that is, six hundred thousand dinars.

Ibn Afir says: As the camels were on the road, Barah ben Kachal El-Mohri met them and said to the
camel-drivers: "What is that, and why does our wealth leave our country? Return!" They returned,
therefore, and stopped at the door of the mosque. There he said to them: "Have you received your salary
and your food and the salary of your families?" "Yes," it was answered. "In that case," said Barah, "may
the blessing not be with them. Take them away!" And the camel-drivers set out with the tribute.

Someone has said: The revenues collected by Amr ben El-As reached ten thousand [thousands] of dinars,
and Omar ben El-Khattab wrote to him, reproaching him for having harvested so little and saying: "The
Greeks collected twenty million dinars." The following year Amr ben El-As collected twelve million
dinars.

Ibn Lahiat says: "Amr ben El-As collected at Alexandria alone six hundred thousand dinars, for there
were there three hundred thousand persons subject to the protection and paying each two dinars. And God
is the most knowing!"

[PDF p. 260]

CHAPTER XXIX
OF THE UPRISINGS OF THE COPTS AND WHAT CAME OF THEM

The imam Abou Abdallah Mohammed ben Ismaïl El-Bokhari extracted from the traditions relating to Abou
Houraïrat this: The latter said: "What will become of you when you no longer collect either dinars or
dirhems?" "How will we see that?" Abou Houraïrat was asked. "Certainly," he answered, "by him in whose
hands is the soul of Abou Houraïrat, according to the veracious words of a just man." "On what
account?" he was asked. "The engagement toward God and toward his Prophet will be disdained, the people
subject to the protection will see their heart hardened by God and will refuse to give what they
possess."

Abou Amr Mohammed ben Youssef El-Kandi, in his book on the Emirs of Egypt, says: Under the government of
El-Hourr ben Youssef, emir of Egypt, Abd Allah ben El-Habhab, intendant of the treasuries, wrote to
Hecham ben Abd el-Melek: "The land of Egypt can bear an increase (of taxes)," and each dinar of tax was
increased by a qirat. Then the provinces of Tenoudimi, of Horbeit, of Tarabiat, as well as the greater
part of the eastern Houf, revolted. El-Hourr sent against them the soldiers of the divan, who beat them
and killed a great number. It is the first revolt of the Copts of Egypt; it took place in the year 107
[19 May 725 to 7 May 726]. El-Hourr occupied Damietta militarily for three months.

Later, in the year 121 [18 December 738 to 6 December 739], the people of the Said rose and took up arms
against their governors; Hamzalah ben Safouan, emir of Egypt, dispatched against them the army of the
divan, which killed a great number of Copts and beat them.

Another time, a Copt of Samanoud, named Bagish, rose; Abd el-Melek ben Merwan sent against him Mousa ben
Nasir, emir of Egypt, and Ba-

[PDF p. 261]

gish was killed with a great number of his companions. This happened in the year 132 [20 August 749 to 8
August 750].

The Copts of Rosetta revolted, and Merwan ben Mohammed El-Ga'di, who was then entering Egypt fleeing the
Abbasids, sent against them Othman ben Abou Qossa'at, who beat them.

In the year 150 [6 February 767 to 25 January 768], the Copts of the province of Sakha rose against
Yezid ben Hatem ben Qebisat ben El-Mohleb ben Aben Safrat, emir of Egypt, attacked the governors, and
chased them out. Arrived at Choubra-Sounbat, they were joined by the people of Yeshroud, of El-Arisia't,
and of Negoum. Yezid ben Hatem, informed of their approach, designated Naser ben Habib El-Mohallabi as
chief of the army of the divan and of the principal men of Egypt. This army marched against the
insurgents, but the latter were victorious and made a great carnage among the Muslims; the latter, after
having burned the Coptic encampment, fell back in rout on Masr.

Under the valiyat of Mousa ben Ali ben Rebah, in the year 156 [2 December 772 to 20 November 773], the
Copts of Belbeïs revolted; an army marched against them and beat them.

Then, in the year 216 [18 February 831 to 6 February 832], took place the great revolt of the Copts;
El-Afshin defeated them in the vicinity of Yashroud and constrained them to make submission to the
Commander of the Faithful, Abd Allah El-Mamoun, who condemned the men to death and the women and
children to be sold; and most of them were sold.

Since then God has maintained the Copts of Egypt in obedience, the grievances have been smoothed over,
and today it is no longer permitted to any Copt of Egypt to revolt or hold his head up against the
sultan. The Muslims became masters of the villages, and subsequently the Copts resumed their habits of
cunning, perfidy, and duplicity against Islam and took their revenge by laying hands on the registers of
the tax. There have moreover passed between them and the Muslims events of which, God willing, one will
find the account at the proper place in this book.

[PDF p. 262]

CHAPTER XXX
OF THE ARRIVAL OF THE ARABS IN THE COUNTRYSIDE OF EGYPT, HOW THEY SEIZED THE CULTIVATIONS TO LIVE, AND
WHAT EVENTS ACCOMPANIED THEIR ARRIVAL

While El-Oualid ben Rafe'at El-Fahmi was vali of Egypt, the tribe of Qeïs transported itself to Egypt in
the year 109 [28 April 727 to 15 April 728]. Before, no individual of this tribe was in Egypt, with the
exception of some representatives of the families of Fahm and of 'Adouan. Ibn El-Habhab went to Hecham
ben Abd el-Melek and asked him to permit some of their families to transport themselves to Egypt. Hecham
authorized three thousand of them to come settle in this country and install their divans there, on the
condition that they would not reside at Fostat. Ibn El-Habhab therefore returned to the people of Qeïs
and, having brought them with him, installed them in the eastern Houf, where they dispersed. It is
reported that Obeïd Allah ben El-Habhab, after having been named vali of Egypt by Hecham ben Abd
el-Melek, said: "I have not seen in this country any share for Qeïs, except however for the people of
Gadelat, who are of the tribe of Fahm and of 'Adouan." And he wrote: "The Commander of the Faithful --
may God prolong his days -- has illustrated and glorified the tribe of Qeïs and raised its renown.
However, I have come to Egypt and have not found that it had any share there, with the exception of the
families of Fahm. There are however here regions where there is no one, and to whose inhabitants the
introduction of Qeïssites could neither cause harm nor bring an increase in the taxes -- I mean Belbeïs,
and if the Commander of the Faithful is of the opinion that the tribe of Qeïs settle there, it will do
so." Hecham answered: "Do what you will." Obeïd Allah sent a messenger to the desert and brought back a
hundred families of the Beni Nadr and a hundred families of the Beni Selim; the vali established them at
Belbeïs, gave them lands to cultivate, then, having examined the revenue of the tithe, abandoned it to
them. The newcomers bought

[PDF p. 263]

camels and undertook the transport of provisions to Qolzoum; each man earned per month ten dinars and
more. Obeïd Allah then had them buy horses; they procured colts that they kept only a month before
riding them, and they fed camels and horses without great difficulty, so fertile were their meadows. The
rest of the tribe, having learned the prosperous state of its brothers, the greater part wished to join
them, and five hundred new families came in their turn to settle in Egypt and gave themselves over to
the same occupations as the others. At the end of a year, five hundred other families having come, there
were at Belbeïs one thousand five hundred families of Qeïs, so much so that in the time of Merwan ben
Mohammed, El-Housra ben Souhaid El-Baheli being governor of Egypt, Qeïs declared for him. At the death of
Merwan, there were in Egypt three thousand families of Qeïs that did not cease to multiply and increase
by all those who came to them from the desert.

In the year 178 [7 April 794 to 26 March 795], Ishaq ben Soliman Ali ben Abd Allah ben Abbas, emir of
Egypt, after examination of the finances, struck the cultivators with an increase of tax they could not
bear. The people of the Houf took up arms against him and assembled in troops; the army of the emir sent
against them was repulsed and lost a great number of men. Ishaq then wrote to the Commander of the
Faithful Haroun el-Rashid to inform him of what was happening. The latter sent into Egypt Hartama ben
A'eïn with a considerable army. Hartama arrived in the Houf, whose inhabitants hastened to meet him,
protesting their obedience and consenting to pay the tax. Hartama consented to it and collected the
totality of the tax.

Later, the people of the Houf rose against El-Leitz ben El-Fadel el-Bioudi, emir of Egypt, because the
surveyors sent by the emir to measure the extent of the cultivated lands had diminished the qasaba by a
few fingers. They addressed a complaint to El-Leitz, who took no account of it. They organized themselves
in troops and marched on Fostat; El-Leitz went to meet them with four thousand men of the army of Egypt,
in the month of Shaban of the year 186 [5 August to 2 September 802]; he joined the rebel troops in the
month of Ramadan [3 September to 2 October 802], but on the 12th of the month [14 September 802] the army
abandoned

[PDF p. 264]

him, and there remained to him hardly more than two hundred men with whom he marched against the people
of the Houf, whom he beat and put to rout, and he arrived at the same time as they at Rheifat; the two
armies came to blows on the territory of Geb-Amirat, and El-Leitz sent to Fostat eighty heads of
Qeïssite chiefs, after which he returned to Fostat, and the people of the Houf returned home, but again
refused to pay the tax. In consequence, El-Leitz went to the Commander of the Faithful, Haroun el-Rachid,
in the month of Moharrem of the year 187 [30 December 802 to 28 January 803], and asked him to entrust to
him an army because, he said, without an army it was impossible for him to make the people of the Houf
pay the tax. Mahfouz ben Salim, who stood at the door of El-Rachid, engaged himself toward him to bring
in the tax to the last qirat, without whip or stick. El-Rachid named him on the spot intendant of the
finances of Egypt, and El-Leitz ben Fadel was deposed from the charges he occupied in Egypt.

Under the valiyat of El-Hossein ben Gamil, the people of the Houf again refused to pay the tax, and the
Commander of the Faithful, Haroun el-Rachid, sent to bring them to reason Yahia ben Moaz. The latter
arrived at Belbeïs in the month of Shawal of the year 191 [10 August to 7 September 807], deposed
El-Hossein ben Gamil from the emirate of Egypt in the month of Rabi' el-Akher of the year 193 [22 January
to 19 February 809], and installed as vali Malek ben Dalham. Yahia ben Moaz brought the Houf back into
duty and arrived at Fostat in the month of Gamadi el-Akher [22 March to 19 April 809]. There he received
a letter from El-Rachid recalling him to him. He therefore wrote to the people of the Houf a note
conceived thus: "Come, that I may recommend you to Malik ben Delham and arrange between you and him the
affair of your taxes." All the chiefs of the Houf, originally from Yemen and from Qeïssiat, answered his
call, but Yahia, who had had chains prepared, ordered the gates closed; the chains were brought, and the
chiefs were chained, whom Yahia took away with him; this took place toward the middle of the month of
Rageb of the same year (193) [20 April to 19 May 809].

When 'Eïsi ben Yezid El-Galoudi was emir of Egypt, Salah ben Sheirzad, intendant of the treasury, showed
himself unjust toward the population and increased the [...]

[PDF p. 265]

taxes. The people of the Delta revolted and took up arms. 'Eïsi sent to fight them an army commanded by
his own son Mohammed. The latter arrived at Belbeïs and engaged in combat, but he had great difficulty
escaping the slaughter, from which none of his companions returned. This happened in the month of Safer
of the year 214 [10 April to 8 May 829]. 'Eïsi was deposed and replaced by Oumaïr ben El-Oualid
el-Tamimi, who prepared to fight the people of the Houf and set out with his army in the month of Rabi'
el-Akher [8 June to 6 July 829]. The people of the Houf marched to meet him, combat was engaged, and a
great number of rebels were killed; the rest took flight, pursued by Oumaïr and a handful of his
companions. But Oumaïr, having fallen into an ambush, was killed by the rebels on the 16th of Rabi'
el-Akher [23 June 829]. 'Eïsi el-Galoudi, named vali for the second time, marched against the
insurgents; a combat was engaged whose result was that 'Eïsi, in rout, regained Fostat, burning the
baggage and all that could hinder his march. He entrenched himself in Fostat, which he surrounded with a
ditch. It was the month of Rageb [4 September to 3 October 829]. Abou Ishaq ben El-Rachid then arrived
from Iraq, entered the Houf, and sent messengers to the inhabitants, who refused obedience. Abou Ishaq
fought them in the month of Shaban [4 October to 1 November 829] and, after having seized a great number
of their chiefs, entered Fostat in the month of Shawal [2 to 30 December 829]. Then he set out again for
Iraq in the month of Moharrem of the year 215 [28 February to 29 March 830], taking with him all these
prisoners.

In the month of Gamadi el-Awal of the year 216 [16 June to 15 July 831], all of Lower Egypt, Arabs and
Copts, revolted, chased out the governor, and refused obedience, exasperated by the wickedness the
lieutenants of the sultan showed toward them. There were between them and the army of Fostat struggles
that prolonged themselves until the arrival in Egypt of the caliph, servant of God, Commander of the
Faithful, Al-Mamoun, on the 10th of the month of Moharrem 217 [16 February 832]. Discontented with 'Eïsi
ben Mansour El-Rafeqi, emir of Egypt, the caliph ordered his pavilion detached, made him, by punishment,
put on white garments, and said: "This frightful event is only the consequence of your acts and those of
your lieutenants. You have overwhelmed the people with burdens too heavy for them, and you have kept the
events hidden from us until the circumstances had become grave and the country was in revolt." Then,
having levied an army, he sent it into the Said; for himself, he transported himself to Sakha and sent
El-Afshin against the Copts who had refused obedience. El-Afshin met them near Yashroud and kept them
surrounded until they had returned to the obedience due to the Commander of the Faithful. The latter
decided that the men would be put to death and that the women and children would be sold, and, indeed,
the greater part of the Houf was devastated. El-Mamoun pursued all those who only seemed to disobey him,
and he had a great number of people killed. Returned to Fostat in the month of Safer [8 March to 7 April
832], he went to Helouan, then returned on the 18th of Safer [25 March 832]. His stay at Fostat, Sakha,
and Helouan was forty-nine days. In the time of El-Mamoun, the revenues of Egypt, collected with the
strictest equity, reached 4,257,000 dinars.

It is recounted that, during the visit El-Mamoun made to the villages of Egypt, there was prepared for
him, at each halt, an esplanade on which his tent was pitched and which his soldiers surrounded. He
stayed in each village a day and a night. Now, passing in the vicinity of a small town named Ta-el-Naml,
he did not stop there, for it was a wretched village; he had already passed it when an old woman, named
Maria the Copt, proprietor of the place, approached him crying. The emir, believing she came to complain
of some injustice, suspended his march, and as he never traveled without interpreters of all sorts of
languages, these questioned the woman and came to translate her words to El-Mamoun: "O Commander of the
Faithful," she said, "you have stayed in all the villages and you have crossed mine without stopping
there; the Copts will mock me. I ask the Commander of the Faithful that he do me the favor of stopping
in my village, it will be an honor for me and my descendants, and thus he will not give arms against me
to my enemies." And the old woman wept so abundantly that El-Mamoun had pity on her, turned the bridle
of his mount, and made halt. The son of the old woman then came to inquire of the chief of the cooks
what he needed of sheep,

[PDF p. 266 — note: text from p.267]

chickens, hens, fish, spices, honey-sugar, perfumes, wax, fruits, fodder, and other provisions he
habitually needed. And the indicated quantity was brought, and even more. The emir was accompanied by
his brother El-Mo'tasem El-Abbas, by his nephews El-Ouatheq and El-Moutawaqel, by Yahia ben Aktam, and
the cadi Ahmed ben Daoud. To each of them the old woman presented a special service, so much so that
none of them nor any of the chiefs of the escort had need of his neighbor. As for El-Mamoun, the feast
she served him was so beautiful, so exquisite, and so abundant that he was marveled at it. The next
morning, at the moment of departure, the old woman presented herself before the caliph, accompanied by
ten young girls each carrying a tray. El-Mamoun, seeing her come from afar, said to those around him:
"Here is the Copt who brings you her rustic gift -- preserves in vinegar, fish, or myrrh." But when she
was nearer him, he saw that each tray contained a purse of gold. The caliph, quite astonished, ordered
her to take back these purses. "No, by God!" said the old woman, "I will do nothing of the kind." The
caliph examined the pieces of gold, which were all struck with the same date, and he said: "This, by
God! is even more extraordinary. Our treasury itself would perhaps not be rich enough to present as
much." "Commander of the Faithful," said the old woman, "do not break our hearts and do not mock us." "A
part of what you have done suffices us," said the caliph; "we do not wish to be a charge on you, take
back your gold, and may the blessing of God be upon you!" The old woman then, seizing a handful of
earth, cried: "This (and she showed the gold) comes to us from that (and she showed the handful of earth
she had gathered) thanks to your justice, and I possess great quantities of it." The caliph then ordered
his companions to accept the gold she offered and gave the old woman in fief numerous villages and, from
the village of Ta-el-Naml that belonged to her, he exempted two hundred feddans from the tax. After
which, he withdrew, marveled at the liberality of the old woman and the extent of her riches.

[PDF p. 268]

CHAPTER XXXI
OF THE FARMING (LEASE) OF THE LANDS OF EGYPT, AFTER THE DIFFUSION OF ISLAM AMONG THE COPTS AND THE
ESTABLISHMENT OF THE ARABS, AND OF WHAT BECAME OF IT UNTIL THE SECOND CADASTRE OF EL-NASER

After the Arabs had settled in the countryside of Egypt, had disseminated themselves there with their
families, and had laid hands on the cultivations to make of them an object of food or of trade; after
the generality of the Copts had, at least in appearance, embraced Islam, and their race had mixed with
that of the Arabs as a consequence of their marriage with Muslim women, the lands of Egypt were governed
by new institutions, among which we will recall the following:

The functionary in charge of the revenues of Egypt held his sessions in the mosque of Amr ben El-As, at
Fostat, at the period when the farming of the lands was settled. One came from the towns and the
villages to these sessions; and there a man cried for each village: "Sale! Sale!" The accountants of the
tax, who stood before the one in charge of the treasury, inscribed the sum to which the adjudication of
the village amounted and the name of the adjudicatees. This lease was made for four years, which allowed
account to be taken of the inundations, the droughts, etc. The adjudication finished, each of those who
had leased a terrain and answered for it went to this terrain and had henceforth the charge of
cultivating it, repairing the dikes that depended on it, and executing all the works its cultivation
required; he was responsible for the upkeep of his farm, and with him the members of his family and
those he had associated with himself for this purpose, under condition of paying the tax pertaining to
the leased terrain; this tax was paid by fractions at determined periods, and there was deducted from
the total of the rent and the security deposit paid the expenses effected for the repair of the dikes,
the closing of the water-intakes and the canals, all according to the estimate fixed by the divan of the
tax. The sum that, each year, remained to be paid by

[PDF p. 269]

the guarantors and the lessees was called the remainder (reliquat). The valis charged with the recovery
of these sums were sometimes very hard, sometimes also very indulgent. Every thirty years, at the end of
the year, the whole country was cadastred anew and a new distribution of the tax was made, increasing
the lands that could bear the increase, without taking account of the price of the lease, and
diminishing what should be diminished. These adjudications were always made in the mosque of Amr ben
El-As until Ahmed ben Touloun had built his mosque. El-'Asker having become the residence of the emir of
Egypt, the divan was transferred to the mosque of Ahmed ben Touloun. In the time of El-Aziz billah Nazar,
the divan was installed in the dwelling of the vizier Ya'qoub ben Koullous, and at the death of this
vizier, in the palace of Cairo, where it remained during the domination of the Fatimids. After the fall
of the Fatimids, the divan was withdrawn from the palace of Cairo, and I will, on this subject, give the
most satisfying details.

Ibn Zoulaq, in the book entitled Accounts of the Mardaniin (the Mardaniin were the writers of Egypt),
says: Abou-l-Hassan Ouahb ben Ismaïl was attending one day the council of Abou Bekr ben Ali El-Mardani in
the mosque El-Gama'; the villages were being put up for auction. Abou Bekr said to him: "Presently an
adjudication is going to be proceeded with. Let us associate to obtain it." The adjudication being
proclaimed, Abou Bekr said: "Inscribe it in the name of Abou-l-Hassan." It was therefore inscribed thus;
Abou-l-Hassan was declared adjudicatee and immediately gained 40,000 dinars, of which he received for his
own account 20,000. He did not know what to do with this sum, when one day, being in conversation with
Abou Ya'qoub, secretary of Abou Bekr, the latter said to him: "I saw the vizier today (he was speaking of
Abou Bekr El-Mardani); he was very preoccupied and was seeking to gather money without being able to
succeed." "I have at my house," answered Abou-l-Hassan, "nearly 20,000 dinars." "Bring them to me," said
Abou Ya'qoub. Abou-l-Hassan sent them to him and withdrew a receipt for the sum. Now, one day when
Abou-l-Hassan had returned to Abou Bakr el-Mardani, he said to him: "The adjudication has paid what I
owed and procured me a profit of 40,000 dinars; of this sum I had already received 20,000 dinars, I have
sent to collect the rest and will bring it." "What is this joke?" said El-Mardani. "I told you that we
would be associated together, because I distrusted your carelessness, but I fully intended to leave you
the money." And he gave Abou [...]

[PDF p. 270]

Ya'qoub the order to restore to Abou-l-Hassan the money the latter had paid, and he asked Abou-l-Hassan
to return the receipt he had taken from Abou Ya'qoub. Abou-l-Hassan therefore took back the money he had
given to Abou Ya'qoub.

In the year when the general Gouher came to Egypt, the tax rose to 3,400,000 and some dinars. In the
history of Mo'ezz lidin Allah Mo'add, it is said: On the 16th of Moharrem of the year 363 [17 October
973], El-Mo'ezz lidin Allah established at the head of the revenues, the collection, etc., Yaqoub ben
Kels and Asloug ben El-Hassan. Therefore, on the habitual day, these two personages sat in the hall of
the emir, in the mosque of Ibn Touloun, and proceeded to the adjudication of the villages and the other
means of procuring money; the people had come for the adjudication, and an effort was made to bring in
what was owed on the rents by the adjudicatees, the lessees, and their agents.

El-Hassan ben Ali El-Bazouri, the author of the history of the vizier El-Nas liddin, reports that this
vizier, wishing to know the sum of the receipts of the empire and those of the expenses, in order to
establish a balance between the two, ordered the chiefs of the divans each to establish the sum of the
receipts and expenses of his department. This was done and the statements were handed to the chief of
the divan of the council, who was the intendant of the divans; the latter made of all these statements an
overall report that he handed to the vizier. The latter ascertained that the receipts of the empire were
2,000,000 dinars, of which 1,000,000 for Syria; the statement carried opposite the statement of the
expenses of this province; Egypt and the rest of the empire produced equally 1,000,000 dinars. From this
total, it was necessary to withdraw for the uncultivated terrains or those unproductive of tax as a
consequence of the death, flight, or disappearance of their tenants, 200,000 dinars; there remained
therefore 800,000 dinars on which it was necessary to levy the appointments and costume-costs of the
collectors -- that is, 300,000 dinars; for the price of the grains necessary to the palaces, 100,000
dinars; for the expenses of the palace, 200,000 dinars; for repairs, costs of hospitality toward
travelers, kings, or private persons, 100,000 dinars. There remained therefore, all this paid, 100,000
net dinars that were sent each year to the treasury (of the caliph) and remained deposited there. This
work of the vizier rendered his person agreeable to the king, who showered him with his affection. After
the death of El-Bazouri, this total yield was 600,000 dinars, payable

[PDF p. 271]

in two terms, 300,000 dinars at the beginning of Rageb and 300,000 dinars at the beginning of Moharrem;
subsequently, the receipts fell while the expenses increased.

Ibn Misrat says: El-Afdal ben Émir el-Gouïouch had a statement drawn up of the receipts of Egypt; these
receipts amounted to 5,000,000 dinars in money and 1,000,000 ardebs in kind. The emir Gamal el-Moulk
Mousa ben El-Mamoun El-Bataïhi, in his history, speaking of the events of the year 501 [22 August 1107 to
10 August 1108], says: Then the general Abou Abd Allah Mohammed ben Fatek El-Bataïhi, seeing that the
wealth of the soldiers and the farmers was declining, that the latter complained of the diminution of
their harvest and the bad state into which this diminution plunged their affairs, while the domains of
the emirs had more than doubled their revenues -- revenues that went always increasing, contrary to
those of the others -- seeing moreover that everywhere arrears were owed to the divan, arrears whose
totality could not be recovered by the divan except by violence and by sending messenger upon messenger
on the part of the noble divan, he proposed to El-Afdal ben Émir el-Gouïouch to rescind the lease of all
the domains and reestablish them anew, demonstrating to him that in this the divan and the farmers had an
equal interest, for by this means the divan would recover the arrears in suffering and could put back
into condition a number of abandoned villages. El-Afdal having consented to it, the lease contracts of
all the domains were rescinded, and a new cadastre was established. The great ones and the lords
protested and complained, saying that they possessed only gardens, personal properties, and presses. The
vizier declared to them that those who possessed personal properties would keep them, that these
properties would not be comprised in the résiliations, and that every proprietor would be free to sell or
rent his good. The résiliation being made, the vizier engaged the poor people of the army to push the
bids, so that the increase fell on the terrains of the great lords and reached a sum fixed in advance.
Then it was established on the registers that the terrain remained in the hands of its proprietor and
that for thirty years it would undergo no increase. Then, having summoned the great ones, El-Afdal said
to them: "What displeases you in the terrains that were in the hands of the soldiers?" "It is," they said,
"that their price is too high and their revenue insignificant; they are relatively

[PDF p. 272]

sterile and one meets there very few inhabitants." "Give," he answered, "for each terrain the price it
seems to you to be worth; apply yourselves to acquiring it and do not occupy yourselves with the former
state of things." Then the hostility of the great ones was appeased, and they pushed the bids until each
of them had reached the sum he desired to pay. At this price the lease was consented and inscribed on the
registers with the stipulated conventions. The two parties found their advantage in it, and the divan
gained by it lands formerly distributed in the fiefs and of a value of 50,000 dinars.

In the account of the events of the year 515 [26 May 1116 to 4 May 1117], the same author says: The
venerable El-Mamoun had the accounts of the empire, until then established according to the lunar years,
drawn up, and prescribed transforming them into accounts of budgetary years and disposing the whole into
two sums, one going up to the lunar year 510 [22 March 1121 to 11 March 1122], with the corresponding
budgetary year, and the other up to the end of the year 515 and the corresponding budgetary year. This
statement drawn up, one found oneself in the presence of a considerable sum of arrears in gold and in
kind; opposite each sum were inscribed the name and the country of the debtor. This statement finished,
El-Mamoun published a rescript remitting all the debts up to the end of the year 510, of which here is the
copy: "Informed of the wretched state of the workers, the farmers, and the lessees, as well as of the
sums they remain owing on their taxes, we condescend that the sums inscribed as arrears in the registers
be remitted, desiring to deliver the lessees -- long asleep and whose conscience is annihilated -- from
the continual reclamations with which the ministry harasses them through the intermediary of its agents,
and wishing that they resume for cultivation the ardor they showed formerly. And as this remission is an
excellent act that has never been done by any king and that no prince does currently, I have wished that
this document be drawn up and that this rescript be joined to it, for I have seen the painful situation
of the lessees and the workers of the kingdom whom adversity pursues; I see also that the arrears of
money accumulate, and this is why, filled for them with clemency and mercy, and having in our noble and
prophetic dignity taken cognizance of all this in detail and as a whole, we have published this rescript

[PDF p. 273]

so that all may be put back into condition; and we have had a great number of copies made, intended to
spread this act of goodness and propagate it through all the countries where it will be read publicly in
all the squares." The sum of the arrears thus remitted amounted, at the moment of the signing of the
decree, to 2,720,767 dinars 20 qirats and 11/12 of a qirat, in gold; to 4 dirhems of pure silver, 67,005
dirhems 16 qirats of minted silver; 3,810,239 ardebs 5 qirats and 2/3 of a qirat of grains, 1/4 of an
ardeb of jujubes, 2,403 and 1/2 ardebs of sabagh leaves, 10 and 1/4 ardebs of myrtle seeds, 1,480
qantars 1 and 1/2 rotoli of sabagh, 913 and 1/2 qantars of alum, 531 rotolis of iron, 1,303 rotolis 18
qirats of pitch, 19 and 1/3 rotolis of cedar resin, 3 garments of Aleppo, 100 cloaks of wool, 170 sieves,
235,305 sheep, 313 qantars and 382 rotolis of green dates, 375,550 fathoms of white cloth, 438,753 palm
branches, 1,423 well-ropes, 1,703 horses, 2,793 and 1/3 ardebs of salt, 11 ardebs of alkali, 2,000
pomegranates, 541 qantars 1/6 of bee-honey, 32 jars and 1 qadous of dry honey, 440 rotolis of wax, 3,042
hives, 138 qantars of cane molasses, 22,164 oxen, 74 mounts, 2,996 matr 7 qirats of melted butter, 820
rotolis of cheese, 4,123 fleeces of wool, 6,050 and 1/4 rotolis of (goat or camel) hair; 2 tents of
(camel) hair; and all these dues were inscribed with the name and the country of the debtor.

When the decision of the divan relative to the outbidding and the résiliation of the leases in course was
handed to El-Mamoun (a decision that withdrew the lands from the hands of those who had received them and
who conformed, at the price of the most painful fatigues, to the adopted conventions, to make them pass
into the hands of those who offered an outbid without any trouble or fatigue), El-Mamoun opposed this
decision and prevented the résiliation of the lands, not wishing to commit so bad an action; he had an
order drawn up in which he took the defense of the farmers and the workers against the outbidding
decision proposed regarding the lands they occupied, and of which, according to him, they should remain
the masters as long as they faithfully executed their contracts and paid their installments; he therefore
drew up a rescript that was read in the mosque of El-Azhar at Cairo and in the old mosque of Masr, as
well as in the divan of the council and the particular divan, which then formed the superior councils;
here is the faithful copy of it: "We have been informed of the way in which act the numerous employees
and administrators of the divans who, after having given in lease to people of good faith and faithful
executors of engagements -- posts, cities, gardens, baths, magazines, or houses, etc. -- hasten to
withdraw them from them as soon as an outbidder presents himself; so that the latter is put in possession
of the leased thing, from which the original lessee is expelled, in contempt of all justice, without
taking account of the contract passed with him and without considering that he is despoiled -- a thing
forbidden by religion and illegal.

[PDF p. 274]

We have held the conduct of these employees to be bad and have blamed their way of acting, for they
depart from the truth and stray from the right path. We have submitted the case to the holy and pure
Threshold (may God multiply its lights and ever raise its insignia!), asking for sublime orders that
would permit us to dispatch this rescript to all the provinces, namely: Whoever has contracted a lease
of a post, city, garden, domain, or village and pays the installments of his lease, respecting the
clauses of his contract in all justice, let his lease be maintained and, during all the duration of his
lease, let no outbid be accepted! To act thus is to conform to justice and sublime equity, and to follow
the orders given by God himself, who in his sacred book says (and it is the most glorious of all those
who speak): 'O you who believe, be faithful to your engagements' (Koran, V, 1). Their lease will
therefore be maintained until the duration stipulated in the contract has elapsed, the contract has
reached its term, and its clauses and conditions are extinguished, according to the customs in force and
the prescriptions of the religion that renders venerable the one who does not stray from its precepts and
its laws. As for the lessees who do not fulfill their obligations and attempt to evade the conditions and
clauses of their contract, using cunning and deceit -- which is the property of a perverse mind -- those
have themselves broken their contract by the non-execution of the stipulated clauses and will be
considered as if, at the moment of the bidding, some other had outbid them; their contract will be
annulled, the terrains will be withdrawn from them, for it is they who will have first broken the
contract and opened a way against themselves. Let it therefore be prescribed to all the chiefs of the
divans, to all the administrators, to all the employees to conform to the orders given in this rescript,
to obey them, to act toward the lessees and the workers according to what is [...]

[PDF p. 275]

contained, and to take care not to infringe it; for it has been registered at the divan of the council
and at the private divan -- august councils -- in the register where similar acts are registered, when
it pleases God!"

The same El-Mamoun received from the valis, inspectors, and verifiers charged with controlling and
surveying the lands and the saqiehs (waterwheels) a report containing the result of the inspection and
the measure of the terrains occupied by the proprietors of saqiehs. These saqiehs were very numerous,
and on one of them, situated on the territory of Esneh, depended a terrain of a surface of three hundred
sixty feddans, covered with palms, vines, and sugarcane, which paid only ten dinars of tax per year;
many similar facts occurred in the provinces. The inspectors had, in the name of the divan, put the
seizure on all these lands and asked the holders for their proof of possession; but the latter declared
that they held them from their fathers and had no other titles. The inspectors therefore sent under
escort the proprietors to the Porte, so that a decision be made about them: "On their arrival," they
wrote, "hold them under good guard until they have paid what they owe of tax for these saqiehs, for it
happens too often that the proprietors do not pay what they owe." These people were therefore brought
before El-Mamoun on the day he sat to render justice. El-Mamoun had them come into his presence and
designated, to decide about them, the cadi Gelal el-Moulk Abou-l-Haggaz Youssef ben Abou Ayoub
El-Magrebi, who was then cadi of cadis. The latter, after having subjected them to an interrogation,
estimated that they were in the wrong and condemned them to pay a sum capable of absorbing their fortune
and their properties. But they pushed such complaints that they were pitied and a more just decision was
taken regarding them: they were condemned to pay the tax in the future and to leave aside what they owed
until then. On this occasion a rescript was drawn up, of which here is the tenor: "Everyone knows how
magnanimous and just the caliph is toward his subjects, how generous and attentive to the well-being of
those who are far as of those who are near him. We never learn that a harm reaches one of our subjects
without our making it cease, and we know no improvement that may be useful to him without our putting it
into effect, conforming in this to the duties of the shepherds of peoples and to our obligations toward
those who are far from us or who are

[PDF p. 276]

near our person, and following in this way the path traced by the Fatimid dynasty (may God strengthen its
empire and render it durable!) and continuing its generous decisions. Persuaded that it is our duty to
concern ourselves with the well-being of our subjects, and that to arrive at it an energetic firmness and
a wise decision are needed, we have wished to examine the affairs of the divans and make the latter
execute their duty, which is to protect the honor of religion, to make war on the infidels and the
impious, so that all our decisions, all our views, conform to what justice requires and are exempt from
all evil, with the permission of God. And we ask his aid that he grant us his support to execute what he
permits and forbid what he interdicts. We pray him to guide us in the best and most equitable path. On
him we lean, he suffices us, and what a good guide!"

The cadi El-Rachid ben El-Zobeïr, being governor of the Upper Said, addressed to the council of El-Afdal a
report on the situation of the tenants of the domains of the region, in which it was said that these
tenants had joined to their domains other terrains belonging to the divan; these terrains over which they
had extended were neighboring their properties and they had unduly installed themselves on them. The cadi
therefore drew up a table intended for the divan, and this table clearly brought out these usurpations;
all the necessary explanations were joined to it. El-Rachid asked that these lands revert to the divan and
begged the latter to decide on this subject according to the laws in use in each region and each locality.
At the end of the report he said: "I have sent into the jurisdiction of my government several inspectors
charged with verifying the situation and addressing me a faithful report. My orders have been executed
relative to the domains of which I speak to you, and I have received from the inspectors a report in which
they declare having asked the tenants of domains and saqiehs for the authentic proof of their possession,
with the enumeration of the quantity of feddans these terrains occupy and the mention of their limits;
but none was able to produce a writing or furnish explanations. In consequence, the inspectors have sent
to the divan the detail of the frauds discovered and have ascertained the flagrant usurpation and the
manifest iniquity of the occupation of these lands. The holy law required that one practice the seizure
of the terrains thus usurped and that one reclaim from the proprietors the revenues and the harvests owed
since their fraudulent installation,

[PDF p. 277]

since they had in their hands no paper establishing their right of occupation and they relied on no title
of property -- a title that by prudence they should have kept to avoid all discussion on the authenticity
of their possession; but, always guided by what we believe to be useful to the inhabitants and by the
justice whose insignia we raise high and whose traces and vestiges we restore, drawn by the desire to
restore to the country its prosperity, by rendering its situation happy and extending the cultivation of
the terrains left unproductive by the installation of the plantations and the putting into condition of
the saqiehs, we have had this rescript drawn up, which will be read in the provinces of the Upper Said,
so that all the domains, lands, and saqiehs be left in the hands of those who currently hold them,
without anything being able to be taken back or withdrawn from them, on the condition that they will be,
for the future, struck with the tax it is just to establish. I desire that the divan approve this
gracious abandonment toward the tenants; this generosity, we reclaim it with insistence and we will not
cease to ask this favor. What is past, we have pardoned and set aside, but we have forbidden beginning
again in the future; thus we have shown ourselves good toward those who have passed from the bad to the
good path, and in this we have conformed to our habits of pardon and benevolence, presenting this
transaction as a penance offered to all the guilty. As for the one among them who begins again, may God
take vengeance on him! He will be reclaimed at once the present debts and the past debts, and our
conscience will have no remorse in taking their wealth and their soul; their fine and their punishment
will be doubled, and they will see the door of mercy and salvation closed to them. For those who desire
to sow the sterile lands producing only alfa, and to put back into condition the abandoned and unused
cultivations, we have permitted that they be abandoned to them after having taken the measure of them,
and decided that tax would be levied on them only four years after their taking possession of these
terrains, each feddan being imposed according to its kind of cultivation per the tariff in force and the
customs in use. The order to execute this rescript is given to the lieutenants, to the governors of
districts, and to all those who habitually receive communication of the decisions of the council; let
them make appear all the

[PDF p. 278]

tenants of domains and saqiehs and inform them of this act of benevolence that surpasses what they could
have hoped and on which they could have counted; let the tax be established on these tenants as we have
prescribed above; the divan, I hope, will ratify this transaction and give in farm the uncultivated
lands and the unused fields to those who desire to rent them; let the necessary titles be drawn up for
this and addressed to the divan to be there, like the other titles, preserved in perpetuity. I have the
hope that this rescript will be copied into the register intended for the registration of similar acts."
And these improvements having been spread into all the provinces, one applied oneself to bringing in the
tax and putting the country under cultivation.

Under the government of the Fatimids, no more than before them during the administration of the emirs,
there were in Egypt no fiefs for the army, as is established today for the army of the Turkish government.
The country, divided into parcels, was leased to those who desired it -- emirs, soldiers, nobles,
peasants, Arabs, Copts, or others. There was not known then this kind of farming called felahat
(agriculture) whose workers attached to the land are named pure fallahs and are in the position of
slaves, sons of slaves, with respect to the one to whom the domain is conceded -- with this exception,
however, that he can be neither sold nor freed and that he is, he and his children, a slave during all
his life. Therefore those who chose lands received them on the conditions we have set forth above, and
the taxes on them were paid into the treasury. As soon as the money of the tax had reached the divan, it
was employed to pay the regiments of soldiers at the expense of the Treasury. Here is how one proceeded:
as soon as the Nile had withdrawn and the countryside of Egypt had covered itself with all sorts of
cultivations, some intelligent man of the court was designated, to whom were joined some persons known
for their equity, their good faith, and their science of the tax -- most of whom were Coptic Christians;
this commission went into each of the districts of which we have spoken, took there the measure of the
cultivated lands and the terrains left uncultivated for lack of irrigation; a list was drawn up
presenting the number of feddans, the designation of the parcels, and the kind of cultivation, and the
whole was reported to the divan of the Porte. And, after having let four months of the Coptic year pass,
officers of notorious energy and unshakeable resolution were chosen, to whom were given as auxiliaries
employees of integrity and

[PDF p. 279]

of incontestable fidelity, and a Coptic Christian writer chosen from among those who had not taken part
in the survey. And in their turn they went into all the districts and brought in a third of the tax
established according to the tables annexed to the lists. This third once collected, one proceeded to
the pay of the army, and one acted likewise at each installment during the whole course of the year; but
always some sum remained unpaid by the lessees and the farmers and formed the remainder of the tax. The
lands of Egypt then paid the tax in money, in grains, and in all sorts of products; this is rendered
manifest by the act of remission of the arrears drawn up under the caliphate of El-Amr bihakem Allah by
the vizier El-Mamoun El-Bataïhi. I have read in an opuscule of El-As'ad ben Mohazzab ben Zakaria ben
Mamati, the Egyptian writer, the following passage: "I asked one day the cadi El-Fadl Abd el-Rahim how
many was the figure of the soldiers inscribed at the divan when our master was in charge of it in the
time of Rozaïq ben El-Saleh, and he answered me: 'Forty thousand cavalry and thirty and some thousand
negro infantry.'" Abou Amr Othman El-Naboulsi, in his book entitled Beauty of the Events of the Taking
of the Castle of the Island, says: Dargham having revolted against Shaour, the latter, frightened, fled
to the sultan Nour el-Din Mahmoud ben Zengi at Damascus and asked him for help against Dargham, promising
to be in the future his lieutenant in Egypt and to remit to him the tribute, thus giving birth in the
mind of Nour el-Din to thoughts he had not yet had. The latter therefore had a corps of a thousand
cavalry prepared and put at their head Asd el-Din Sheirkaouah, to whom he gave the order to march with
Shaour. Sheirkaouah refused: "I will not go," he said, "for my loss and that of my companions would be
certain, and it is known here how perverse is the counsel the sultan has listened to. How could I march
with a thousand cavalry against a country defended by ten thousand cavalry, a hundred saphabed
(regiments) of ten thousand combatants, and forty thousand negroes, without counting the natives who
will rise to defend their homeland? I know their manner of fighting, and we could not, fatigued by the
journey, oppose to them so small a number of men." Despite this, he ended by accepting! And this -- may
God be agreeable to you! -- happened at the time when the army of Ahmed ben Touloun was composed as you
will see, God willing, in the chapter of the Fiefs.

As for the army of the emir Abou Bekr Mohammed ben Tofaz El-Akhshidi, [...]

[PDF p. 280]

many people have spoken of it, among others Ibn Khallican, who evaluates it at four hundred thousand
men. And, at the fall of the Fatimid dynasty, at the time of the invasion of the Ghozz arriving from
Syria, and the taking of possession of the government of Egypt by Salah el-Din Youssef ben Ayoub, the
situation of the army underwent some modifications, but not a complete change.

The cadi El-Fadl, in his Chronicles of the year 567 [4 September 1171 to 22 August 1172], says: On the
8th of Moharrem [11 September 1171], Salah el-Din gave the order to mount on horseback the old and the
new army; this took place when everyone had been forewarned -- as much those who were near the capital
as those who were far from it -- when all had arrived and the arms and mounts of each had been put in
condition. And that day, there was such a gathering of troops that, in the opinion of all the old men
and all the competent people, never had any prince of Islam assembled such an army; the ambassadors of
the Greeks and the Franks were present, and these infidels were struck (by such power). The parade of the
army, regiment after regiment, talab after talab (the talab in the Ghez language is the title given to
the commanding emir who possesses a special banner, a trumpet at his orders, and a number of cavalry
varying from 200 or 100 to 70), was still going on when the day ceased and night began to spread; the
order was then given to bring the troops back in, and the parade was not finished. The number of men
present constituted 147 talabs; the absent, 20 other talabs; the evaluation of this ensemble exceeds
14,000 cavalry, most of whom were touachis (the touachi is a personage who receives a salary varying from
700 to 1,000 and even 1,200 dinars; he has a troop of 10 head or more of horses, mules, or camels, and a
squire to carry his arms; his service is completed by a qara ghalamia, a troop of adolescents). In this
number are comprised the Bedouin servants whose total is 7,000 cavalry. They were reduced later to 1,300,
no more, receiving the tenth of the pay that was originally 1,000,000 dinars; it was at least what was
inscribed, but this sum was not effectively paid; thus the tribe of Taghalba, having been designated for
this service, showed itself very discontented and threatened to pass to the Franks.

[PDF p. 281]

In his Chronicle of the year 577 [17 May 1181 to 6 May 1182], the same author says: The sultan examined
attentively the affair of the fiefs that year, and, having learned their extent, he diminished some and
increased others, giving something to those who had nothing and increasing the domains of the personages
in favor, so that the number of people holding fiefs rose to 8,740 cavalry, 111 emirs, 6,976 touachis,
and 1,553 qara ghalamia, and there was attributed to them on the Treasury 3,670,500 dinars; in this
figure do not appear the retirees of the army who received as pension the tenth of the pay, nor the
Bedouins to whom were attributed the Sharqieh and the Behera, nor the Egyptian writers, nor the
jurisconsults, nor the cadis, nor the sufis, nor the ordinary employees of the divan, who all together
received at least 1,000,000 dinars.

In the Chronicle of the year 585 [19 February 1189 to 7 February 1190], by the same author, it is said:
Order was given to make the survey of the lands from Alexandria to Eizab; this work, which was to be
finished on the 24th of Shaban 585 [7 October 1189], did not comprise the frontier towns, nor the
