terrains assigned by the divan to certain tax regimes, nor the terrains of heqr (emphyteutic leases), nor
the mortmain properties, nor Manfalout, nor Manqabat, nor many other localities whose names are mentioned
in the cited work and whose measures are not given. The surveyed terrains produced 4,653,019 net dinars,
deduction made of the expenses effected in the divan of El-Afdal El-Saïd and others; of this sum, the
revenues of the Sharqieh, the Martahieh, the Daqhalieh, Bouch, and other places counted for 1,170,923
dinars, of which here is the detail: divan of El-Adel, 728,248 dinars; fiefs of the emirs and the army,
including the remainder of their taxes in the aforesaid provinces, 158,203 dinars; divans of the blessed
wall (Cairo) and of El-Ashraf, 13,804 dinars; for the Bedouins, 234,296 dinars; for the Kenanites,
25,412 dinars; for the cadis and the sheikhs, 7,403 dinars; for the Qimarites, the Salehites, and the
Egyptian army, 12,504 dinars; for the people of Gaza and Ascalon quartered at Damietta, Tanis, and other
towns, 10,725 dinars; the rest, that is 3,462,074 dinars, was distributed thus: northern region:
1,151,653 dinars, of which here is the detail: suburb of the port of Alexandria, 8,138 dinars;

[PDF p. 282]

port of Rosetta, 2,000 dinars; the Behera, 115,576 dinars; the Houf Ramsis, 92,403 dinars; the two
Mezahmiat, 15,305 dinars; the island of Beni Naser, 112,646 dinars; the island of Qousseina, 130,592
dinars; the Gharbieh, 74,605 dinars; the Samanoudieh, 245,419 dinars; the Dengaouieh, 46,264 dinars; the
Menoufieh, 148,347 dinars; for the southern region, 1,610,441 dinars, distributed thus: Ghizeh, 153,204
dinars; the Atfieh, 59,728 dinars; the Bousirieh, 60,466 dinars; the Fayoum, 152,734 dinars; the
Behnesaieh, 352,634 dinars; the interior Oasis, the two exterior Oases, and the oasis of Behnesa, 25,000
dinars; Ashmouneïn, 147,732 dinars; the Sioutieh, not including Manfalout and Manqabat, 72,504 dinars;
the Akhmimich, 108,812 dinars; the province of Qous, 362,500 dinars; the frontier nome of Assouan, 25,000
dinars; the frontier district of Eïzab belongs to another divan.

In the Chronicle of the year 588 [18 January 1192 to 6 January 1193], the author says: The sum collected
by the divan of the sultan amounted, that year, to 354,044 dinars, while the receipt for the year 587 [29
January 1191 to 17 January 1192] had been superior to that of 586 [8 February 1190 to 28 January 1191] by
22,445 dinars, and moreover the arrears of that year rose to 31,622 dinars, which makes in money received
at the particular divan of El-Naser, for the year 587, 354,454 dinars and 23 qirats. [Footnote: At the
end of this chapter, the numbers given by Maqrizi have been much corrupted, and there is no longer any
concordance between the figures of the totals and those of the detail.]

[PDF p. 283]

CHAPTER XXXII
OF THE LAST CADASTRE, OF EL-NASER

Each warrior, besides the servant he possessed, received a special salary varying from 20 to 30,000
dirhems; some of them received 15,000 dirhems, and the lowest salary was still 10,000 dirhems,
independently of the inn-right that could reach up to 5,000 dirhems for the best-paid personages. Each
soldier could go to the inn with a certain number of horses; a chief of troop was considered as emir of
ten, and when he lodged somewhere, his troop lodged there with him; most of his companions ate at his
table, and an emir could eat only in the company of his troop. The pages of his army went each day to
fetch the dishes from his kitchen; and if the emir saw some other fire and, after inquiry, had learned
that someone of his troop desired to eat something special, he showed himself very discontented with
whoever disdained to eat as he did. But, despite all, their cooking was detestable and their garments
very badly made. El-Mamoun Lazeïn, having become sultan, proceeded to the survey of the lands; Egypt was
then divided into twenty-four qirats, of which four belonged in property to the sultan, ten to the army,
and ten to the emirs; but the emirs monopolized the greater part of the terrains reverting to the army,
and the latter could draw no revenue from them, these terrains being inscribed at the divan as domains of
emirs; these circumstances favored brigandage, and seditions and revolts were fomented, so much so that
one refused to pay one's debts or the taxes owed to the divans; all these sums became the prey of the
henchmen of the emirs and their employees, to the great prejudice of the peasants of the region. The
sultan made this state of things cease, restored the lands to their proprietors, and withdrew them from
the divan of the emirs; the first terrain thus withdrawn was that of Seïf el-din Mankou Tamer, lieutenant
of the sultanate, who was stripped of all the lands he occupied and from which he drew per year a hundred
thousand ardebs of grain.

[PDF p. 284]

All the emirs, treated likewise, were held to restore all the terrains they had usurped; favoritism was
abolished, and the sultan attributed to the emirs and the army eleven qirats, of which nine destined for
the troops, among whom they were indeed distributed. Then the sultan published a decree establishing that
the emirs and the army would have to content themselves with ten qirats only, the remaining qirat being
distributed to whoever had cause to complain of the smallness of the revenues of his domain. As the
particular domain of the sultan, certain fertile provinces were reserved, and the lieutenant Mankou Tamer
was charged with the distribution of the titles of property for the service of the sultan. The heart of
the emirs was filled with discontent to such a point that they drew upon themselves the treatment that
El-Mansour and his lieutenant Mankou Tamer inflicted on them.

In the time of El-Naser, El-Naser Mohammed cadastred the country. The author of the Life of El-Naser
says: In the year 715, the sultan El-Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun resolved to establish the cadastre of
Egypt, in order to make a multitude of taxes cease and to enrich the royal treasury with a great part of
the lands. Here is why: having made the reckoning of the rations served to the mamelukes and servants of
El-Melek El-Mouzaffar Rokn-el-din Beibars El-Gashankir and the emir Salar, as well as those attributed to
all the Bordjite mamelukes, he ascertained that the salaries were between 1,000 and 800 dinars; but, not
daring to touch the pay of the servants of the two personages in question, he held council with the cadi
Fakhr el-din Mohammed ben Fadl Allah, intendant of the army; it was decided that the cadastre of the
lands of Egypt would be established, that domains would be distributed according to the will of the
sultan, and that the royal titles would be drawn up for each domain. Fakhr el-din, intendant of the army,
was charged with this work, and he drew up acts bearing the surface area and the delimitation of the
domains; after which the sultan dispatched emissaries into each province. The emir Badr el-din Geïkalcheh
El-Baba received the order to go to the province of Gharbieh with the chamberlain Azei and the accountant
El-Makin ben Farouitah; the emir Az el-din Eïdmer El-Khatiri was sent into the district of Sharkieh with
the emir Atmesh El-Magdi and the accountant Emin el-daoulat ben Qarmout; the emir Belban El-Sarakhdi,
El-Qaligi, and Ibn Taranta El-Beïbars El-Gamdar were sent into the provinces of Menoufieh and Behera;
El-Belili and El-Mourtini, into the region of the south. Each of these emissaries was accompanied by
writers, inspectors,

[PDF p. 285]

and surveyors; all went into the provinces assigned to them. Each of them, on setting foot in his
province, summoned the sheikhs of the country, the witnesses, the sages, the cadi, and the registers that
were in the hands of the feudatories; he examined the state of the revenues, in gold, in grains, and in
all sorts of things, verified the surface of the lands in feddans, making the count of the cultivated
parts and the uncultivated parts, noting the light terrains and the resistant terrains, the nature of the
plantations, the quantity of submerged lands, the extent of the region, and its dues in grains, chickens,
sheep, bersim, kischk, cakes, and other objects forming part of the diffah (hospitality due). All this
once noted, one proceeded to the survey of the domain in the presence and under the signature of the
witnesses, the surveyors, and the cadi specially charged with this operation, and one inscribed the exact
content. Then one had the list (of the inhabitants) of the villages and the land register brought, and
one set apart the particular goods of the sultan, the domains of the emirs, the military fiefs, and the
alienated terrains; and each acted thus for the totality of his province. This work was finished in
seventy-five days; special statements were drawn up for each village of Egypt, statements giving the
situation of that village, its extent, its limits, what it possessed of cultivated terrains, and what it
rendered in gold or in kind. The sultan then summoned El-Fakhr, intendant of the army, the pious El-As'ad
ben Amin El-Melek, known under the name of Kateb (secretary) of Sarlagh, and all the inspectors of the
kingdom, and constrained them to draw up statements where would be inscribed as royal properties the
terrains he designated to them, as well as the domains of the emirs. To the yield of each village was
joined the amount of what the peasants owed the feudatories as diffah-right; and to the content of this
same village, what it paid in the way of taxes. And he established for the army titles of fiefs according
to this system, and at the same time were suppressed the right of transport of the grains, from the
province in question to the port of Cairo, and the right of octroi (entry-toll) with which these grains
were struck.

The sultan likewise abolished a great number of taxes, among others: the right of disembarkation of the
grains, the principal resource of the divan and which was employed for the salary of the emirs and the
army; this right, which, amounting per year to 4,600,000 dirhems, was divided among 400 persons who
received from 10,000

[PDF p. 286]

to 3,000 dirhems, each of the emirs receiving between 40,000 and 10,000 dirhems. It was a frightful right
that brought in enormous sums; the Copts drew considerable benefits from it, but the poor people
experienced great damages from it and underwent, because of this very right, all sorts of injustices and
prejudices; the damage indeed went multiplying: the sailors stole (the grain during transport), the
measurers falsified the measures, the chiefs of the octroi, the employees too, all stole something. The
right was fixed at two dirhems per ardeb for the sultan, but a half-dirhem more was exacted, without
speaking of what had been subtracted and stolen. There existed, for the collection of this right, a local
known under the name of Hut of the Measuring, on the bank of the river, at Boulaq; there stood a chief,
sixty superior employees -- writers, inspectors, and overseers -- and thirty soldiers to watch, and no
one could sell a qodah of grain in any place in Egypt; all the grains to be sold had to be transported to
the Hut of the Measuring at Boulaq.

Among other rights, the sultan also abolished the half of brokerage. Here is in what this right
consisted: if someone sells something, he pays the broker, according to an anciently established usage,
two dirhems for a hundred dirhems; but when Naser el-din El-Kerkhi was named vizier, he imposed each
broker with one dirhem on his brokerage of two dirhems. The broker then did all his possible to recover
his benefit, and it was again the seller who had to bear the damage; one complained, but far from
listening to them, the complainants were beaten, and this lasted until this right was suppressed by the
sultan.

Another right abolished by him is the right of valiyat. It was a right conceded to the valis and the
chiefs, and that these two categories of personages collected from the directors of markets and brothels.
This right was abandoned to a farmer who had under his orders a great number of agents and employees,
emirs and others. This right gave birth to hideous injustices and infamous procedures; many respectable
people were wronged, and a number of private houses were violated.

Among other rights, he also abolished the right of belt and mule, established on the town and on all the
southern and northern provinces of Egypt. Each of the valis and the chiefs was held to bring, at the
period when the payments were effected,

[PDF p. 287]

to the Beit el-Mal (treasury), 1,000 dirhems for the price of the belt and 500 dirhems for the price of
the mule. Many people lived from this right, whose amount was set apart; the people suffered on this
subject indescribable miseries, and what the couriers (of the divan) made them endure was worse than
death.

Among the rights abolished was the right of prison, a right collected from each prisoner; every jailer
had the right to levy from a prisoner six dirhems, without prejudice to the rest (what he had been
condemned to). Many persons lived from this right, the farmers sought it and put up high bids to obtain
the concession of it, for it produced a rich revenue. Indeed, if a man quarreled with his wife or his
son, the vali had him put in prison and, as soon as he had entered, even were he to stay there only an
instant, the right in question was levied on him; it was the same for the prison of the cadi.

Among the rights abolished was the right of tax of chickens; this right was conceded to numerous farmers,
spread through all the provinces of Egypt, who forced the people to take their chickens; thus the weak
people experienced great damages on this account, the widows especially had to bear considerable
vexations and prejudices. Many people lived from this right, and no one, in any province, could buy one
or several chickens unless they came from the farmer, and if by chance someone bought or sold a chicken
other than those coming from the farmer, death came to him from all sides, and yet he did not die (Koran,
XIV, 20).

Of these rights is also the right of the cavaliers; the valis of each province were charged with the
collection in all the villages, and there was no one who, paying one dirhem (of tax), did not have to pay
two others; this right caused the taxpayers frightful terrors.

Of these rights is also the right of the canes and the presses; it is a right collected from the
cultivators of sugarcane and the proprietors and people of the press.

Of these rights is the right called right of weddings; it was collected in all the provinces; it counted
numerous farmers and had absolutely nothing fixed: one struck the people with a right that one collected;
and this right caused them unjust damages.

[PDF p. 288]

Of these rights is the protection of the boats, consisting in what was collected from each boat; it is a
fixed right known under the name of protection of the boats; it is one of the most vexatious rights for
the people, for it is collected from all those who travel on the river, even from the beggars and the
poor.

Of these rights is the right of the singing-women, which consists in what is gathered from the
prostitutes and the courtesans, and which is collected from the vilest people by the chief of the royal
office.

Of these rights is the right of guarantee; it is a right struck specially on the blacks at the inspection
of the boats; it is established on the black men or women discovered there at the moment they go down
into the inns to give themselves over to prostitution; it is collected from all, male or female; it is a
fixed right.

The right of harrowing, which is collected in all the provinces by the engineers of the country and paid
into the treasury by the aides of the vali who gather it. From this right live many people of the army.

The right of emptying, which consists in what is collected for the cleaning of the cesspits; all the
filth drawn from them is carried to the hills. If the pit of a mosque, a school, a scalding-house, a
tomb, or any house belonging to anyone whatever is full, even were the mass of filth considerable, it is
not permitted to the proprietor to remove it as long as he has not received the visit of the farmer of
the emptyings, who for the dredging asks the price that pleases him; the farmer gives himself importance
and asks double what the work is worth. If the master of the house does not accept the price asked by the
farmer, the latter leaves him and goes away; but as it is not possible to leave the filth, the proprietor
makes the farmer come back; the latter increases his pretensions and becomes harder and harder, until at
the end one consents to what he exacts for the cleaning of the pit; then he removes the filth it
contains.

Among the vexations suppressed by the sultan, one must count the inspectors of the provinces. All Egypt,
south and north, small and great villages, swarmed with writers and tormentors of every kind; the sultan
suppressed the inspectors and abolished the inspections in all the provinces, except the districts where
there were royal properties. And God, by the suppression of these taxes, relieved [...]

[PDF p. 289]

his creatures of miseries whose extent one cannot imagine and which one could not describe.

The sultan, having abolished these rights and finished the distribution of the fiefs to the emirs and
the army, set apart for the royal treasury, in the way of Egyptian lands, a good part of the lands
constituting the fiefs of the Bordjites, such as Ghizeh and its province, Hou, Korn el-Ahmar,
Manfalout, El-Marg, Khoussous, and others, which formed the ten qirats of the country. The fiefs of the
emirs and the army, etc., represented fourteen qirats. The Copts, wherever they could, used cunning;
they set about weakening the army of Egypt, distributing a single fief over several points -- part in
the Said, part in the Sharqieh, part in the Gharbieh -- to fatigue the soldier and increase his
trouble. The right of protection (on the non-Muslims) was taken by them from the royal treasury and
distributed among the districts where there were fiefs of emirs and army; for the Christians depended on
only a single divan, as you will see later, God willing! The Christians of each village paid their due
to the feudatory of that country, and the situation became favorable to the Christians, who moved from
one village to another and paid of the tax only what they wished; thus this chapter of receipts
diminished after having been most productive. As for the other chapters of taxes -- for example the food
right intended to defray the (sultan's) table -- they appropriated them and paid only what they wished.
Then they monopolized the expense of what is employed for the upkeep of the table; and the emirs as well
as the chiefs of the divans had to occupy themselves with the affairs of octroi rights.

Then the sultan examined what the two emirs Baïbars El-Gashanqir and Salar, lieutenant of the sultanate,
held in the way of lands, and he took all that was inscribed in the name of these two emirs and in the
name of their servants, without excepting what they had placed in wakf, which he unbound; and of the
whole he formed fiefs, adding to each fief what was paid as due by the peasant; he made the count of
these dues, eliminated them from the ensemble of the revenue of the fiefs, and abolished the presents;
he finished this work only at the end of the year. And when the moon of Moharrem of the year 716 rose
and the accounts had been established according to the third of the yield of the harvests of the year
715, the sultan sat in the Iouan he had had built in the Citadel of the Mountain; he had transmitted to
all the lieutenants of

[PDF p. 290]

the army, by verbal instruction transmitted by the general-in-chief, the order to present himself with
his warriors. And each day he reviewed two emirs and their troops; each emir commanding a thousand men
stood there with his troop, and the intendant of the army made, in the presence of this emir, the roll
call of his men according to their grade. And the intendant of the army, as each of the men was brought
by his general, presented them one after another to the sultan. The latter, as soon as the man was in
his presence, interrogated him himself and without intermediary on his name, his origin, his race,
inquiring about the duration of his stay in Egypt, those with whom he had come, the emir to whom he
belonged, and other things -- the combats he had attended during the war, what he knew of the military
trade, etc. When the interrogation was finished, he put into his hands a title without examining it and
such as God had designated; and no one, during the duration of the review, passed without his knowing
him and without his speaking of him afterward to the emirs to recall something concerning him. The order
had been given to the emirs to gather at the Iouan, and none of them dared disobey the sultan for fear of
some punishment. They were therefore there silent, no one daring to speak, for fear of displeasing the
sultan by his words, for he took pleasure in contradicting the emirs, and if the latter praised someone
during the review, the sultan gave that one the title of a bad fief. Having perceived this, the emirs
abstained from saying the least word, and the sultan did his affairs without them, and one knows no
soldier who presented himself before him without his having interrogated him, inquiring whether he was a
mameluke, from what merchant he had been bought, and all that we have said above. If it was an old man,
he asked him his age, his origin, how many combats he had attended, until he knew everything. He had the
infirm set apart and gave them no lands but handed to each of them a pension sufficient to make him live.
The review lasted all the month of Moharrem, and on the titles of the army he economized two hundred of
them. Then he reviewed the different categories of the sultan's mamelukes, made great economies on their
pay, and suppressed many pensions that he replaced with fiefs. Finally he assigned certain tax revenues
to the invalids of the army, whose pay he diminished, and fixed for each of them an annual pension of
3,000 dirhems.

[PDF p. 291]

Beibars and Salar El-Goukandar had frequent dealings with the treasury and the provinces -- such as
Ghizeh and Alexandria -- whether for commercial affairs or as a consequence of protections they accorded
to certain persons; the sultan took all this for himself and made this state of things cease. What he
did not distribute in fief was joined to the particular divan. Among other orders he gave at the review,
he prescribed that no one sell a title he had received from the sultan, even were the fief designated by
this title too mean, nor that any emir speak in favor of a man of the army. If anyone contravened these
orders, he was beaten, imprisoned, exiled, and his pay was diminished. Thus the king was much dreaded
and his prohibitions strictly respected, and no one ever dared sell a title given by the sultan, and no
emir ventured to speak in favor of anyone. Many people had fiefs of a thousand dinars that were reduced
to two hundred dinars, but many others who had had very poor fiefs obtained considerable fiefs, for the
sultan gave the title without examining it and such as it fell under his hand.

It happened, with the permission of God, that the sultan, among the people of his kitchen, had a buffoon
who joked in his presence; the sultan laughed at him, amused himself with him, and was not angered by the
jokes he might say. One day, the sultan was attending the review in the garden of the Citadel of the
Mountain, surrounded by the cortege of the intimate emirs, when this buffoon arrived and set about joking
according to his custom to make the king laugh. "I found," he said, "a warrior of the repartition of
El-Naser mounted on a nag, his sack on his back and his lance on his shoulder," thus mixing joke and
satire. The sultan entered into a violent anger and cried: "Seize him, and remove his garments!" The
guards ran and seized the man, whom they stripped of his garments, attached to the saqieh with the
buckets, and beat the oxen with all their might, which imprinted on the saqieh a rapid movement of
rotation. And the poor devil followed the movement of the pots, now plunging into the water, now coming
out of it to fall back again, passing and repassing in the water for nearly an hour, in such a way that
his voice died out and he thought he would die. Great was the terror of the emirs in seeing the violence
of the sultan's anger. Then the emir Taghaï El-Douadar advanced with the group of particular emirs, and
all together asked the pardon of the unfortunate man,

[PDF p. 292]

saying that he had wished to joke and make the sultan laugh by his words, without wounding intention for
the army and other similar reasons, so that the sultan gave the order to detach him; he was without
movement, and he had to be dragged before the sultan, who decided that, if he were still alive, he must
not pass the night in Egypt; and he was made to leave immediately into exile. And God was glorified by
each of the emirs that they had dared to break the silence at the moment of the review.

The state of Egypt remained such as El-Naser had established it in this cadastre until the power of the
Beni Qalaoun passed into the hands of El-Melek El-Zaher Barqouq, in the month of Ramadan of the year 784
[8 November to 7 December 1382]. The ensemble was maintained in the same state, but certain parts
disappeared progressively until the year of the events and disasters of 806 [21 July 1403 to 9 July
1404], the period when all sorts of changes took place and when injustice reached proportions no one can
imagine and which will be fully explained to you in the book of the Causes of the Ruin of the Provinces
of Egypt, God willing.

There were for the lands of Egypt determined quantities of seed that remained in the provinces; they were
divided into two categories: the royal seed and the local seed. The royal seed had been deposited in the
country by the kings. The emir or the soldier, as long as he was in possession of his fief, took what was
necessary to him of the royal seed, but, if he left the fief, these seeds were reclaimed from him. After
the institution of the cadastre of El-Naser, the seed of each province was determined by the sultan and
inscribed at the royal divan. Their total amounted to 160,000 ardebs, without counting the local seed.

[PDF p. 293]

CHAPTER XXXIII
OF THE DIVAN

The greatest among the cadis, Abou-l-Hassan El-Mawardi, writes this: "The divan is maintained as long as
are maintained the things that pertain to the rights of the sultan, whether as works or as revenues, and
those charged with them are the troop and the governors." On the origin of the word divan there are two
versions: (1) Cosroes (Khosrow), looking one day at the writers of his divan, saw them occupied in
counting mentally and cried: "Dyouaneh!" (the madmen), and this name was given to the place where these
employees gathered. Then the [letter] disappeared by usage and the word was softened to divan. (2)
Dyouan is the Persian name of the demons; and this qualification was given to the accountants because
they resolve affairs, because they know those that are visible and those that are hidden, because they
can gather scattered and distant things, and because they know equally those that are near and those
that are far. Then this name was given to the place of their gatherings, and one said divan.

The writings of the divan are of three sorts: writings of the army, writings of the tax, and writings of
redaction and correspondence. It is beyond doubt that all the powers have employed these three categories
of writings. The scholars have published numerous works on the writings of the tax and those of
correspondence, but I know no one who has composed anything whatever on the writing of the army and the
troops.

At the beginning of Islam, the writing was traced on rolled sheets, but toward the end of the time of the
Ommiades, when Abd Allah ben Mohammed Abou-l-Abbas El-Safah mounted the throne, he took as vizier Khaled
ben Barmak, who succeeded Abou Selama Hafs ben Soliman El-Khalal, and he introduced into the ministries
registers of parchment, whose use prevailed; the rolls were abandoned, and this lasted until the time
when Gafar ben Yahia ben Barmak took the direction of affairs under the caliphate of El-Rachid. This
vizier had [...]

[PDF p. 294]

put into use the paper everyone has used since, until the present.

Abou-l-Nimr the paper-maker said: Abou Hazem El-Qadi recounted to me that Abou-l-Hassan ben El-Modabber
had told him that if Egypt were completely cultivated, it would produce a revenue equal to the revenue of
the whole world; according to him, the cultivable lands of Egypt amount to 28,000,000 feddans, but there
is only one million feddans cultivated. And Ibn Modabber told me that he had been employed at the divan
of the East and at that of the West and that he had never passed a night having finished all his work
without anything remaining of it; that he had served also in Egypt, that he stayed up very late there,
but that there always remained work to him that he finished the next day.

[PDF p. 295]

CHAPTER XXXIV
OF THE DIVAN OF THE TROOPS AND OF THE ARMY

The first to establish a divan for the army and the horses was, it is said, Kiharasp, one of the kings of
the second Persian dynasty; before him, Kiqbad levied the tenth of the grains for the food of the army.
As for the times of Islam, here is what one reads in the extracts made by El-Bokhari and Moslim in the
traditions reported by Hozaïfat: The Prophet said: Write me the name of all those who believe in Islam,
and a list of 2,500 names was written for him, which are cited by El-Bokhari in the chapter that bears
this title: How the imams inscribed the people. Bokhari cites again a tradition of Abd Allah ben Abbas: A
man came to the Prophet and said to him: "O prophet of God, I am inscribed for war and my wife wants to
make the pilgrimage." "Go," said the Prophet, "and make the pilgrimage with your wife." 'Amr ben Monabbat
reports the following trait on the authority of Moamer, who had it from Qoutadat: The last thing the
Prophet received was the sending of 800,000 dirhems dispatched from El-Bahreïn, and he did not leave the
council until after having entirely distributed them. The Prophet had no treasury, no more than Abou
Bekr; the first to have one was Omar ben El-Khattab. Ibn Sha'b says that Omar was the first to organize a
divan. According to Ibn Sa'd, Aïchat would have said: My father divided the booty, and the first year he
gave to the free men 10, to the slaves 10, to the free women 10, to the slaves 10; the second year, he
divided it again, and to each he gave 20. Here, according to what is recounted, is the cause that brought
on the creation of a divan: Abou Harirat having come to Omar with the money of El-Bahreïn, Omar asked
him: "What do you bring me?" "500,000 dirhems," said Abou Harirat. Omar found the sum enormous and said:
"Do you know what that is (500,000 dirhems)?" "Yes, certainly," said the other, "it is five times a
hundred thousand." "Is all this of legitimate provenance?" asked Omar. "I know nothing of it," answered
Abou Harirat. Then Omar mounted the pulpit, glorified and praised God, and said: "O men,

[PDF p. 296]

much money has come to us. If you wish, we will measure it by the keïleh; if you wish, we will count it."
A man approached him and said to him: "O Commander of the Faithful, I have seen the Persians make use of
divans; install a divan, you too." And Omar installed it.

On the other hand, the reason given for the installation of the divan would be that while Omar was
preparing an expedition, he had near him Hormezan, who said to him: "You have paid the salary of the men
composing this army corps, but if one of them deserts, how will his lieutenant know it? Create then for
them a divan." Omar asked what a divan was, and Hormezan explained it to him. Omar at once took counsel of
the Muslims on the subject of the installation of this divan. Aly ben Abou Taleb said to him: "Each year
you will divide all the money you will have gathered without conserving anything for yourself." Othman
said: "I see that much money is distributed to the people without it being possible to distinguish those
who have received some from those to whom nothing has been given, and I fear the harm will only
progress." Khaled ben El-Oualid said: "I have been in Syria and I saw that the kings had created divans
there and gathered armies. Create then, you too, a divan, and you will gather armies." Omar held to this
opinion and summoned Aqil ben Abou Taleb, Mokhrama ben Noufal, and Gebir ben Mota'am, writers of the
tribe of Qoreïch, and said to them: "Inscribe the name of the people by tribe." These writers began with
the Beni Hachem and inscribed them; they continued with the Aoulad Abou Bekr and their tribe, then with
'Amr and his tribe, and so on, inscribing all the tribes according to the order of succession of the
caliphs. They brought the result of their work to Omar, who, having examined it, said to them: "No, begin
with the close relatives of the Envoy of God, the closest being inscribed first, and you will put Omar in
the rank where it has pleased God to put him." Abbas thanked him for this act and said: "You show yourself
generous toward your relatives." There is no agreement on the subject of the year in which Omar
established the attributions of the divan and the divan itself. It was, according to El-Kebbi, in the
year 15 [14 February 636 to 1 February 637]; according to Ibn Sa'd, who reports the opinion of Omar
El-Ouaqedi, it was in the year 20 [21 December 640 to 9 December 641]. El-Zaheri says it was in the month
of Moharrem of the year 20 of the hijra [21 December 640 to 19 January 641].

[PDF p. 297]

It is reported that when God had given the Muslims Qadisiat and Omar had finished the conquest of Syria,
the latter gathered the Muslims and said to them: "What is the vali permitted to levy on the money?" And
all answered: "For himself personally, enough to feed himself and his family neither too luxuriously nor
too poorly, enough to clothe his family and himself during the winter and during the summer, and finally
enough to maintain two mounts that will serve him in war and for his affairs and that can lead him to the
pilgrimage and the visit of the holy places; as for the rest, it will be divided equitably. Let the
inhabitants of each country receive a share proportioned to the importance of their country; let one
occupy oneself next with putting back in order the affairs of private persons, let one come to their aid
in misfortune and keep calamities away from them, beginning with the people who pay the tribute, and let
the benefits extend to the vanquished as much as the amount of the revenue will permit." El-Dahak, on the
authority of Ibn Abbas, says: "After the conquest of Qadisiat and the conclusion of the treaty with the
people of the Suad, after the submission of Damascus, and when peace was signed with Syria, Omar said to
his men: 'Gather and inform me of what you know on what God has attributed as share of the revenue to the
people of Qadisiat and to the Syrians.'" The opinion of Aly was conformable to that of Omar, and both
drew their answer from the Koran: "What God," they said, "has attributed to his envoy on the share of the
people of the villages (that is, the fifth), that is to God and to his prophet (that is, to God the order
and to the Prophet the distribution), to his relatives, to the orphans, to the poor" (Koran, LIX, 7), and
they explained this verse by the following verse, which is its continuation: "to the poor among the
Mohagerins," to the end (Koran, LIX, 8), and they took four fifths according to the agreed division that
attributed a fifth to those composing the first, second, and third categories and four fifths to those to
whom God had devolved the booty. And as proof, they cited what God says: "Know that when you have made a
booty, the fifth part reverts to God" (Koran, VIII, 42), etc., to the end of the verse of these three
categories and the four fifths to those to whom God has attributed them. And the fifths were divided
according to this principle. Omar and Aly were of this opinion, and subsequently the Muslims conformed to
it. The distribution began with the Mohagerins, then one passed to the Ansari, then to the Tabeïn who had
fought with them and assisted them, then pensions were established,

[PDF p. 298]

levied on the revenue, in favor of those who had negotiated the peace or who had aided the peace by war,
but this gratification was a simple complaisance. In the division into fifths, nothing was provided for
the people who refuse the protection, but their share was instituted by the one who had imposed it on
them, and in this share was comprised that of the people who had brought them to it, unless of their own
will they renounced it; thus there were found among them some who did not receive what was due to them.

According to Abou Salamah ben Abd el-Rahman ben 'Ouf, Omar would have said: "I intend to institute
pensions for the army of the Muslims and to organize for it a divan in order to establish justice." Abd
el-Rahman ben 'Ouf, Othman, and Aly said: "Begin with yourself." "No," said Omar, "I will begin only with
the uncle of the Prophet, and I will continue with his closest relatives and so on." He therefore set
aside a share for Abbas and began with him; then he assigned to the warriors who had attended the affair
of Bedr 5,000 (dirhems?) per person; to those who had taken part in the combats subsequent to that of
Bedr until the affair of El-Hadibiah, 4,000 (dirhems) per head; to those who had taken part in the
combats engaged after El-Hadibiah until the victory of Abou Bekr over the apostates, 3,000 (dirhems)
each, and in this category he included those who had attended the conquest and the combats fought by Abou
Bekr as well as those who attended the days prior to the conquest of Qadisiah, fixing for each of them a
share of 3,000 (dirhems). To the conquerors of Qadisiah and Syria and the combatants of El-Yarmouk, each
2,000 dirhems; those come from the distant countries had each 2,500 dirhems. And on this subject one said
to him: "You should treat on the same footing the conquerors of Qadisiah and the combatants of the prior
days." "No," he said, "I cannot treat on the same footing those who do not have an equal merit; God does
not permit it." "But," it was objected, "you treat equally those who fought far from their dwelling and
those who fought near their houses and for the defense of their hearths." "These," said Omar, "deserved
rather to be increased, for they upheld the right and had to bear the shock of the enemies. No, certainly,
far from treating them equally, I have treated each according to his merits; moreover," he added, "has it
not been the same for the Mohagerins, when we treated on the same footing the two categories so different
[...]

[PDF p. 299]

of the Mohagerins and the Ansaris? The Ansaris, too, did only defend their houses, while the Mohagerins
hastened from afar to their aid." Then he assigned to the Rouadefs (auxiliaries) who had come after the
conquest of Qadisiah and the battle of El-Yarmouk 3,000 dirhems each, treating equally all the men of
each category without making any difference among them: whether they were strong or weak, Arab or
foreign, all were treated equally in their categories, to such a point that every man of the towns who
had aided in gathering the booty and had followed the army of the Rouadefs received for his share 250
dirhems, and whoever had followed the Rouadefs was gratified with the fifth in addition to 200 dirhems
(240 dirhems?). The last to whom Omar assigned anything were the people of Hagar, who received each 200
dirhems.

When Omar died, things were still in the same state. Among the people of the category of Bedr, he
included four persons who had not attended Bedr: El-Hassan, El-Husseïn, Abou Zar, and Salman.

Abou Salamah says that Omar assigned to El-Abbas 25,000 (dirhems); El-Zaheri says he assigned him only
12,000; to the women of the people of Bedr he attributed 400 dirhems, to the women of those who had
attended the combats subsequent to Bedr until El-Aïam, before El-Qadisiah, 300 dirhems, to the women of
the conquerors of El-Qadisiah 200 dirhems; then all the women of those who had fought after Qadisiah were
treated equally, and the children of the combatants of Bedr and the others had each 100 dirhems. Finally
he had sixty poor people brought and had served them to eat, salted bread; the calculation was made of
what they had eaten, and it was found that this exceeded two shares of tax; and to every poor person,
whether he was Muslim or infidel, were attributed, to feed him and his family, two shares of tax payable
by monthly fractions. To the wives of the Prophet he gave 10,000 dirhems, except to those who had been
bought. And the mothers of the Muslims said: "The prophet of God made no difference between us and them
in the division, but treated us all equally; treat us equally, you too." And all received 10,000 dirhems.
He wished to give 2,000 dirhems more to Aïchat, but she refused. "It is," he said to her, "because your
situation with the Prophet was quite different; take this then and do with it what you will."

The army was classified by tens, and there were 3,000 chiefs commanding each

[PDF p. 300]

10 men. The horses received their provisions by sections. This continued thus until the founding of Koufah
and Basrah. Then the organization was changed: the chiefs of ten transformed into chiefs of seven, and
there were 100 chiefs, each having to supervise the distribution of 100,000 dirhems. Each group --
especially for the category of Qadisiah -- comprised 43 men, 43 women, and 50 persons of their families;
this group received 100,000 dirhems; each section of the category of El-Aïam counted 20 men, 3,020 (23?)
women, 100 persons of the family, the ensemble receiving 100,000 dirhems. Each section of the first
Rouadefs was composed of 60 men, 60 women, and 40 persons of their families, of those who received per
head 1,500 dirhems, together 100,000 dirhems. The pension was paid to the chiefs of seven and the
guardians of the flags; the flags were in the hands of the Arabs; these paid the sum to the chiefs of
squads, the lieutenants, and the intendants, who paid each of the men placed under their orders. Omar died
leaving things in this state, but he had before his death the intention of making the shares 4,000
dirhems, and said: "Certainly my intention was to make the shares 4,000 dirhems: 1,000 that the man would
spend for his family, 1,000 that he would carry on a journey, 1,000 for his upkeep, and 1,000 to give
alms." But he died without having been able to put his project into execution. He received the messengers
according to the length of the journey traveled: if they came from very far, he treated them for a year;
if they came from less far, he treated them for six months. If some man had committed a bad action in a
frontier post, he had his turban torn off; he was exposed in the mosque of his tribe and one cried: "Here
is so-and-so who has acted badly." Seif ben Omar says that the first distribution took place in the year
15 [14 February 636 to 1 February 637]. Subsequently Amr ben El-As sent to Omar ben El-Khattab the
tribute of Egypt after having retained what was necessary to him. When Othman became caliph, on the 3rd of
Moharrem of the year 24 [9 November 644], he increased the share of each person by 100 dirhems. He was
the first to make this increase and to succor the inhabitants of the towns. He was also

[PDF p. 301]

the first to come to their aid and do something for them. The caliphs took from him the custom of making
increases of shares. Omar had attributed to all the children born in the month of Ramadan 2 dirhems per
day and to each mother of a believer 2 dirhems; one said to him: "Would it not be better with this money
to give them to eat and gather them in common for that?" "One must," he answered, "satiate the people in
their houses." Othman persisted in this custom and added to it still the food for the month of Ramadan,
saying: "This is for those who pray and stay in the mosques and for the poor in the month of Ramadan." The
caliphs his successors followed his example.

Under the caliphate of Moawiah ben Abou Safian, there were in Egypt 40,000 men, of whom 4,000 received a
salary of 200 (dirhems), and one sent Moawiah only 600,000 dirhems that remained after the payment of the
army and the deduction of what was paid to the employees. Moawiah had designated for each of the Arab
tribes a man who, each morning, went around the tribe saying: "Has a child been born this night? Has a
traveler come down among you?" And one answered him: "A son has been born to so-and-so, or a daughter to
such a woman." And the man inscribed their name. Or else one informed him that a man of such a tribe had
come down among them with his family, and he inscribed the name of the traveler and the people of his
family. When he had finished his inquiry, he went to the divan to have the thing registered. Moslema ben
Moklad El-Ansari, emir of Egypt, after having paid the people of the divan their salary and that of their
family, their rations, the things they needed, the expenses required by the villages for the dikes, the
rations of the writers, the transport of the wheat to the Hedjaz, sent Moawiah 600,000 dinars that
remained. The first installation of a divan in Egypt was made by Amr ben El-As; the divan was reinstalled
anew by Abd el-Aziz ben Merwan, a third time again by Qorrat ben Sherik, and a fourth by Bichr ben
Safouan. After the reorganization of Bichr there were no more notable changes, with the exception however
of the attachment to the divan of the tribe of Qeïs, under the caliphate of Hesham ben Abd el-Melek ben
Merwan. When the domination of the Ommiades ceased and the black banner of the Abbasids prevailed, there
were some changes that continued until the death of Abd Allah El-Mamoun,

[PDF p. 302]

son of Haroun El-Rachid -- which occurred on the 7th of Rageb of the year 218 [29 July 833] -- and the
accession of his brother El-Mo'tasem Abou Ishaq Mohammed ben Haroun, who wrote to Kander ben Naser
El-Safadi, emir of Egypt, a letter ordering him to eliminate from the divan of Egypt all the Arabs there
and to suppress their pay; which was done. Merwan ben Mohammed El-Ga'di, the last of the Ommiade caliphs,
had suppressed the pay of the troops of Egypt for one year, after which he wrote them the following letter
to excuse himself: "Last year, I suppressed your pay, for an enemy threatened me and I needed money. But I
have the salary of the past year sent to you with that of the current year, eat it then and may it profit
you! God keep me from being the one by whose hands the suppression of the pay will be made!" When Kander
suppressed the salary of the Egyptians, Yahia, son of the vizier El-Geraoui, revolted with a troop of
people of the tribes of Lakhm and Gozam and said to Kander: "Nothing more grave could be done against us,
for right and justice have been refused us." And he gathered around him 500 men. Kander died in the month
of Rabi' el-Akher of the year 219 [15 April to 13 May 834], and his son El-Mazfar was named vali of Egypt
in his place. He marched against Yahia, beat him in the marshes of Tannis, and took him prisoner. The
power of the Arabs weakened in Egypt, and the armies were no longer composed there but of foreigners and
slaves, from El-Motasem until the emirate of Abou-l-Abbas Ahmed ben Touloun in Egypt. The latter increased
the number of slaves, which rose to more than 24,000 young Turks, 40,000 negroes, and 7,000 free men for
hire. His son, the emir Abou-l-Geich Khamarouyah, increased the number still after him by recruiting the
able-bodied men of the Houf of Egypt. When the emir Abou Bekr Mohammed ben Tafag El-Akhshid became emir of
Egypt, the effective of his army, in Egypt and in Syria, reached 400,000 men of very diverse races. Later,
master Abou-l-Mesk Kafour El-Akhchidi recruited new negroes during his government of Egypt, and when the
imam El-Moez lidin Allah Abou Tamim Mo'ad El-Fatimi seized Egypt, his army was composed of people of the
tribes of Qoutama, Zouïla, and other Berber peoples, with whom were mixed Greeks and Sla-

[PDF p. 303]

vonians (Slavs), who numbered as has been said. With them advanced Mo'add, whose army was innumerable;
there was no limit in what God had accorded him, and he was happy in all that could make happy; to such a
point that it has been said that since Alexander, son of Philip, the Macedonian, no army more numerous
than that of El-Moezz had trodden the earth. At his death his son El-Aziz billah Abou Mansour Nazar,
having become caliph of Egypt, took into his pay Dilemites and Turks of whom he formed his particular
escort. The emir El-Mokhtar Abd el-Melek El-Mesihi recounts in his history that when El-Aziz set out for
Syria, the particular treasury was carried by two thousand camels, without counting the treasures of the
generals and the great ones of the kingdom.

Ibn Miser reports in his history that the particular slaves of the lady mother of El-Mostanser billah
Abou Tamim Moadd ben El-Zaher li-azz din Allah Abou-l-Hossan Aly ben El-Hakem biamr Allah Abou Aly Mansour
ben El-Aziz billah numbered 5,000, without counting the corps of troops. And I have seen a writing in the
hand of El-As'ad ben Mamati saying that the effective of the army of Egypt, in the time of Rouzaïq ben
El-Saleh Talaï ben Rouzaïq, was 40,000 cavalry and 36,000 infantry. Another author adds to it 10 sea
vessels carrying 10,000 combatants, and this at the moment of the decline of the Fatimid domination. And
when the empire passed from the Fatimids into the hands of El-Melek El-Naser Salah el-din Youssef ben
Ayoub, this prince suppressed in the army of Egypt the black slaves, the Egyptian emirs, the Bedouins, the
Armenians, and others still, and composed the army above all of Kurds and Turks, and the effective of his
troops in Egypt did not exceed 120,000 cavalry. After the death of Salah el-din, this army dispersed, and
there remained to his son El-Melek El-Aziz Othman only 8,500 cavalry; only, some of these cavalry had ten
servants, others twenty, others more still, some possessed up to a hundred attached to their single
person; in such a way that when they mounted on horseback to leave Cairo, their total number exceeded
200,000 men. But continually they quarreled and mutinied, and the power ended by passing into the hands of
their slaves, the Turkish mamelukes, who followed the example of their Ayoubite masters and took for
soldiers Turks and a certain number of Kurds, reinforced by slaves sent in great number from the Turkish
countries, so that one was able to say that the number of the mamelukes of El-Melek [...]

[PDF p. 304]

El-Mansour Qalaoun amounted to 7,000 according to some, to 12,000 according to others. Those of his son
El-Achraf Khalil ben Qalaoun numbered 12,000. But subsequently their number was far from reaching this
figure, and it went declining until the fall of the dynasty of the Beni Qalaoun in the month of Ramadan
784 [8 November to 7 December 1382], the period when the power passed into the hands of El-Melek El-Zaher
Barqouq, who eliminated little by little the mamelukes of El-Achraf and chose for his particular guard
Circassian mamelukes whose number reached, both in bought slaves and in mercenaries, the figure of 4,000
men and even a little more. At his death, his son El-Naser Farrag having mounted the throne, these
mamelukes divided and mutinied, and when Naser died, a great number of them had perished, slaughtered or
in any other manner. The Egyptian army was, under the Turkish domination, divided into two classes: the
troops of the guard and the royal mamelukes. The period when the effective of the troops of the guard was
the highest is that of El-Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun; at that moment, according to what I have been able
to see by the archives of the divan of the army and in the papers of the cadastre of El-Naser, it counted
24,000 cavalry; from that time until today their number has always been declining; now this effective is
very weak and moreover a thousand men of these troops are not even worth a single one, for they serve no
purpose and are incapable of repulsing the enemy. As for the mamelukes, their number today is reduced to
very little, so that in gathering the troops of the guard and the royal mamelukes one would scarcely
reach the figure of 5,000 cavalry, of whom a thousand and perhaps fewer are fit for combat. They are
today also divided into two classes: the troops of the guard and the royal mamelukes. The latter are
divided into three corps: the Zaheris, the Naseris, and the Mayadis, the latter subdividing in their turn
into Hakemis, Nourouzis, and Moayadis proper. I greatly fear that after El-Melek El-Moayad Abou-l-Naser
Sheikh (may God maintain his reign!) there may be some troubles until the moment when God has strengthened
his son the emir Sarem el-Din Ibrahim (may God multiply his protection over him!), who has conquered in
the Greek country what no king of Egypt had ever conquered before him, since Islam: the

[PDF p. 305]

[verses:] The lion-cub by its form is similar to the lion; the son of the noble, if he is of a noble
character, is nobler than his father; it is not surprising that the son follows the example of his
father; Adi imitated his father in generosity; he who resembles his father never does ill; it is from
the root that the tree rises.

Under the reign of El-Achraf Barsebai, the mamelukes formed seven corps: the Zaheris, the Naseris, the
Moayadis, the Nourouzis, the Hakemis, the Tatars, and the Achrafis; each of these corps was differentiated
from the others, thus their force was diminished and their violence subdued, and the sultan could confide
in their guard without having to dread revolt, thanks to the division that existed among them although in
appearance they were united, and to the enmity that existed among them although they seemed all in accord.

The Ommiade, Abbaside, and Fatimid caliphs had the habit, since the reign of Omar ben El-Khattab, of
receiving personally the money of the tax. Later the divan distributed it among the divans, the
governors, or the army according to the importance and the rank of each; at the beginning of Islam this
distribution took the name of present. This custom persisted until the time of the foreign domination,
the period when the order of things was changed and the land was distributed in fiefs to the army.
According to what is known, the first to distribute fiefs to the army was Nozam El-Mulk Abou Aly
El-Hassan ben Aly ben Ishaq ben Abbas El-Tousi, vizier of El-Barchelan ben Daoud ben Mikal ben Seldjouq.
Then the caliph named as vizier his own son Melek Shah ben El-Barchelan because of the extent of the
empire. The latter was of the opinion of giving to each employee a village, or more or less, according to
the importance of the salary of that employee; for he thought that in confiding the lands directly to the
employees, they would be improved under the surveillance of the latter, which would not happen if all the
lands depended on a single divan, for the hole would only enlarge and ruin would introduce itself into
the country. Nozam el-Mulk did thus, and by this rendered the lands prosperous and increased the yield of
the harvests. The kings his successors followed this example from the year 480 [8 April 1087 to 26 March
1088] until our days. The caliph was paid by the treasury, and 'Ata ben El-Saïb reports, in his
Chronicles, that when Abou Bekr became caliph, there was assigned to him the

[PDF p. 306]

half of a sheep per day and a garment to cover his head and his belly; he reports also, on the authority
of Hamid ben Halal, that there was accorded to the caliph also two cloaks; when these cloaks were worn
out, he had to deposit them at the divan and take two others; but, if he set out on a journey, he was
given a mount. For the expense of his house, it remained the same as in the time that had preceded his
accession to the caliphate. Ibn El-Athir, in his Chronicles, says that it is to this caliph that 6,000
dinars per year were attributed, and that there was assigned to Omar ben El-Khattab, when he became
caliph, a sum sufficient to permit him to live at ease, he and his family. Aly said to him on this
subject: "You will have nothing else." And the people cried: "Aly is right; let Omar have enough to feed
himself." Omar accorded to Moawiah ben Abou Safian, when he named him governor of Syria, an annual salary
of 10,000 dinars; according to certain authors, he would have given him only 1,000 dinars, which is more
probable.

[PDF p. 307]

CHAPTER XXXV
OF THE PARCELING-OUT AND OF THE FIEFS

One says "to withdraw a portion of a thing" for "to take it"; one names "portions" what one withdraws from
a thing; the expression [Arabic] means "permit me to take a part"; the words [Arabic] mean "he asked
permission to take a share of it"; and the phrase [Arabic] is translated by "he accorded him a share of
it -- land and water." The prophet of God made distributions and showed himself generous toward the
people of Islam, and after him the caliphs made distributions among those they judged worthy to receive
shares.

Ibn Abou Nagih reports, on the authority of Abou ben Chaïb, who had it from his father, that the Prophet
having given a land in share to the people of Mouzaïnah or of Gouhaïnah, these did not cultivate it. There
came people who cultivated it. The Gouhaïnins or the Mouzaïnins lodged a complaint before Omar ben
El-Khattab, who said to them: "If this terrain came to you from me or from Abou Bekr, I could return it to
you, but it comes to you from the prophet of God. And," he added, "if someone possesses a land and leaves
it three years without cultivating it and other people cultivate it, the latter are more worthy to possess
it than that one."

Hecham ben Arouah reports, on the authority of his father, that the prophet of God gave in share to
El-Zobeïr a land in which were palms belonging to the Beni Nachir; and he adds that this land was named
El-Garf. The same author recounts that Omar ben El-Khattab divided the whole 'Aqiq among the people, in
such a way that one encroached on the share of Arouah. Ibn Zobeïr then said: "Let those who ask for fiefs
present themselves today. For if there is in this some good, it is under my foot." Khouat ben Gebir said
to him: "Give it to me as a share," and he gave it to him. Safian ben 'Eïnah reports, on the authority of
Amr ben Dinar, that when the Prophet

[PDF p. 308]

arrived at Medina, he gave a fief to Abou Bekr and another to Omar ben El-Khattab. Ach'ath ben Souar
recounts, on the authority of Habib ben Abou Thabet, who had it from Soit El-Makki, who had it from Abou
Rafeh, that the prophet of God had given a land to people powerless to cultivate it and who sold it, in
the time of Omar ben El-Khattab, for 1,000 dinars and 80,000 dirhems, a sum they deposited in the hands of
Aly ben Abou Taleb. When they wished to withdraw their money, they perceived that the sum had diminished.
"Some is missing," they said to Aly. "Make the count of the alms," said the latter. And having made the
count of the alms, they found the sum exact. "Do you think," Aly said to them, "that I receive money
without levying the alms?" Tamim El-Dari had asked the Prophet as a fief the fiefs of his native country
situated in Syria, before the conquest of that country; the Prophet accorded it to him. Abou Thalebat
El-Khashni asked as a share a land still in the power of the Greeks; the Prophet, surprised, said: "Do you
hear what he says?" But Abou Thalebat answered: "He who sent you to spread justice will make you conquer
it." And the Prophet wrote him on this subject a letter (of donation). Thabet ben Sa'd reports, on the
authority of his father, who had it from his grandfather, that El-Abiad ben Gemal asked the Prophet as a
fief the salt-marshes of Mareb; the Prophet having accorded it to him, El-Aqra' ben Habas El-Tamimi cried:
"O prophet of God, I visited these salt-marshes in the time of ignorance; they are situated in a land that
contains nothing other than this salt; whoever goes there takes it; it is like sweet water on the earth."
And El-Abiad having renounced, the Prophet said to him: "I accept it from you." "Accept it then as alms,"
said El-Abiad. "That is," said the Prophet, "indeed, an alms on your part; for this salt is like sweet
water, whoever goes there can take it."

Kethir ben Abd Allah ben 'Ouf el-Mazni reports, on the authority of his father, who had it from his
grandfather, that the Prophet gave in fief to Bilal ben El-Hareth the mines of the south, in surface and
in depth; and Malek reports on the authority of Rabiat, who had it from several scholars of the tribe,
that the prophet of God gave in fief to Bilal ben Hareth El-Mazni mines situated in the vicinity of
El-Fara'. According to this same Rabiat, who had it from El-Hareth ben Bilal, who had it from his father
Bilal ben Hareth, the Prophet would have given him the whole 'Aqiq, and according to Hamad ben Salamat,
who had it from Abou Makin, who had it [...]

[PDF p. 309]

from Abou 'Akrama, servant of Bilal ben El-Hareth, that the Prophet had given in fief to Bilal a land
where there was a mountain enclosing mines. The Beni Bilal sold a part of it to Omar ben Abd El-Aziz, who
discovered there the mine -- the two mines, according to others. The Beni Bilal then said to him: "We sold
you only a cultivable land and not the mine," and they brought the letter of the Prophet that they kept in
a roll. Omar took the roll, kissed it, placed it on his eyes, and said to his secretary: "Examine what the
mine has brought in and the expenses that have been made; make the difference and give them the surplus."

Omar ben El-Khattab chose, among the terrains of El-Souad, the properties of Kesra (Chosroes) and his
family, as well as what had been abandoned by the proprietors or whose proprietors were dead. The total of
the revenues amounted to 9,000,000 dirhems, which were employed for the well-being of the Muslims, and
nothing of it was given in fief. Later Othman made the distribution of it, persuaded that the parceling-out
would increase the harvests, which would not happen by acting otherwise. He agreed with those among whom
he divided it that he would levy on them the tax-right, and the sum of the harvest amounted to 50,000,000
dirhems, which he employed in alms and presents. The caliphs who succeeded him made various modifications,
and when came the year of the skulls in 82 [15 February 701 to 3 February 702], at the time of the revolt
of Abd El-Rahman ben El-Ach'ath, the divan was burned, and each took in land what was within his reach.

Omar ben El-Khattab gave in fief to Ibn Sander Miniet-El-Asbagh; Sander reserved for himself 1,000
feddans. Ouaki', on the authority of Safian, who had it from Gaber El-Ga'fi, who had it from 'Amer, says:
Neither Abou Bekr, nor Omar, nor Aly gave fiefs; the first to give some was Othman, and under the
caliphate of Othman the lands were sold. El-Leitz ben Sa'd says: We have never known that Omar gave any
fief to anyone in Egypt, except the one conceded to Ibn Sander, who obtained the land of Miniet El-Asbagh
and kept it until his death. It was then bought by El-Asbagh ben Abd El-Aziz Merwan from the heirs of
El-Asbagh, and there is in Egypt no fief more ancient or better. El-'Amech reports on the authority of
Ibrahim ben El-Mohager, who had it from Mousa ben Talahat,

[PDF p. 310]

that Othman gave to Abd Allah ben Mesaoud the fief of El-Nahreïn, to Omar ben Yaser the fief of Astinia,
to Khabab the fief of Sana', to Sad ben Abou Oukas the village of Harmezam; Abd Allah ben Mesaoud and Sa'd
drew from their land the third and the quarter (the seven twelfths).

Seif ben Omar reports, on the authority of Amr ben Mohammed, who had it from 'Amer, that El-Zobeïr,
Khabab, Abd Allah ben Mesaoud, Omar ben Yaser, and Ibn Habasa received fiefs in the time of Othman, and
those who have accepted this fault are more guilty than the one who committed it: and yet it is from those
that we hold our religion. Omar ben El-Khattab gave fiefs to Talahat, Garir ben Abd Allah, and El-Rabil
ben Amr; he gave to Abou Mofraz the land of the Nile, and that too is one from whom we hold our religion.
The distribution in fief is only supererogatory and forms part of the fifth belonging to God.

Omar wrote to Othman ben Hanif this letter, which was carried by Garir ben Abd Allah El-Bagali: "Give
Garir ben Abd Allah a fief sufficient to feed him, neither too great nor too small." Othman, on receipt of
the letter, referred to Omar: "Garir has arrived to me with a letter from you prescribing me to give him a
fief for his upkeep, but I did not wish to do it before taking your orders anew." And Omar answered:
"Garir spoke true; execute then this order; but you did well to consult me a second time." He also gave a
fief to Abou Mousa El-Achari, the land of Kardous ben Hani to Aly ben Abou Taleb, and a fief to Souïd ben
Rhafiat El-Ga'fi. Here is what Seïf reports on the authority of Thabet ben Harima, who had it from Souïd
ben Rhafiat: I asked Aly for a fief, and he said to me: Write this: "Aly has given Souïd in fief a land for
his mount from such to such a period, as long as it will please God." Abou'l-Qasem El-Rahman ben Abd Allah
ben Abd El-Hakem has given the list of what was accorded in fief by Moawiah ben Abou Safian and the
caliphs who succeeded him, concerning the domains of Egypt, and he cites a great number of them.

The Ommiade and Abbaside caliphs made distributions of the lands of Egypt among the people of their
entourage, but not as is done today; the revenue of the lands of Egypt was employed by him to pay the
salary of the army as well as all the necessary works, and the surplus was carried to the treasury; what
was given in fief remained in the hands of the feudatories. But since the time of the sultan Salah el-din
Youssef ben Aioub until the present,

[PDF p. 311]

all the lands of Egypt were given in fief to the sultan, the emirs, and the army.

The land of Egypt is today divided into seven parts: (1) one part pertains to the royal divan and
subdivides itself into three sections comprising all that depends on the particular divan and what
depends on the ordinary divan; (2) another part is given in fief to the emirs and the army; the detail of
it has been reproduced in the chapter of the Cadastre of El-Naser; (3) the third part comprises the wakf
or mortmain goods, reserved for the mosques, the schools, the convents of dervishes, the establishments
of beneficence, the descendants and freedmen of those who have put their goods in mortmain; (4) the fourth
part takes the name of goods of religious reserve and comprises the lands left in the hands of people who
enjoy them either because they are employed in the upkeep of the places of prayer and the mosques, or
because they have no occupation; (5) the fifth part is composed of properties one can sell or buy or that
are transmitted by inheritance or donation, because they have been bought from the treasury; (6) the
sixth part remains unproductive because it is impossible to cultivate it; the livestock graze there and
one grows wood or other similar things there; (7) the seventh part, finally, is that which the water of
the Nile does not reach and which remains sterile; this part comprises lands that have always and at all
times been thus, and others which, cultivated primitively, have become uncultivated. All that concerns
these seven parts is related in this book, and you will find it in going through it, God willing!

Abou Abd Allah El-Qasem ben Salam, in his book Of the Taxes, in the passage where he cites the traditions
reported by Ma'mer, who had it from Abd Allah ben Taous, who had it from Taous, his father, says this: The
prophet of God said: The uncultivated land is to God and to his apostle and will revert to you one day.
"What does that mean?" I asked. "It will be," he said, "divided into fiefs." That is the origin of the
distribution of the lands. One called "abandoned, uncultivated" a land all of whose inhabitants were
extinct and which, having become uncultivated, fell back under the management of the imam; it is of this
that it is said: As for the land that the Prophet has devolved to some persons and that is still
cultivated by its inhabitants, if the imam gives it, he makes a conditional act; and to this category
belongs what was given to Tamim El-Dari, who had obtained in share

[PDF p. 312]

a land of Syria before Syria was conquered and occupied by the Muslims. The Prophet therefore gave it only
conditionally, for it was still the property of belligerents and only for the case in which the Muslims
would have been victorious; likewise for the daughter of Nafilat that the Prophet accorded to Chibani
before the conquest of Herat. The promise was kept by Khaled ben El-Oualid; as Omar ben El-Khattab fulfilled
the promise made to Tamim El-Dari when Palestine was conquered, a promise made conditionally by the
Prophet. Abou Abd Allah calls conditional fiefs those that the imam promises in advance to some combatant.

Abou-l-Hassan Aly ben Mohammed ben Habib El-Mawardi, in his Royal Politics, says that the fiefs are of two
sorts: the fiefs in usufruct and the fiefs in full property. The latter divide into dead lands and
cultivated lands. The cultivated lands comprise in their turn two categories: some depend absolutely on
their proprietor, and the sultan has not to interfere in their management, except for what concerns the
tax when they are in a country subject to Islam; if the land is situated in a country in a state of war
that the Muslims have not yet conquered, the imam, if he desires, can accord it in fief so that the
concessionary takes possession of it at the moment of the conquest; this donation is licit. It is thus
that Tamim El-Dari asked the Prophet to accord him as a fief the springs of the country of which he was a
native, and this before the conquest of Syria -- a request that was granted; likewise Abou Thalebat
El-Khasni asked him for the concession of a land still in the hands of the Greeks, and the Prophet cried:
"Do you hear what he says?" "By him who sent you to spread justice," replied Thalebat, "he will make you
conquer it." And the Prophet handed him a letter of donation. "If someone," says El-Mawardi, "asks the
imam for the cession of a domain situated in a country in a state of war and possessed by its inhabitants,
or of a part of the booty or of some slave, in order to have more rights when the country is conquered,
the gift can be validly made even though the result would be uncertain and of the domain of vague things.

El-Cha'bi recounted that Khazima ben Aous El-Taii said to the Prophet: "If God makes you conquer Herat,
accord me the daughter of Nafilat." And when Khaled wished to sign the treaty with the people of Herat,
Khazima said to him: "The prophet

[PDF p. 313]

of God has given me the daughter of Nafilat, do not include her then in the treaty." He presented as
witnesses Bichr ben Sa'd and Mohammed ben Moslimah. Khaled therefore put her outside the treaty, and she
was given to Khazima, who resold her for a thousand dinars, for she had become old and had changed much.
"You sold her cheap," one said to him; "her relatives would certainly have paid you more than double what
you asked them." "I did not think," he answered, "that there was a number superior to a thousand."
El-Mawardi sets forth that for the donations and the shares thus accorded to be valid, one must examine
the state of the conquest. If it is made by treaty, the land remains the possession of the one to whom it
was accorded and is put outside the treaty as a share priming all the others. If the conquest is made by
force, the one who asked and obtained the fief has more right over the share he asked and over the gift he
solicited than the other warriors. The warriors will be questioned, and if they had knowledge of the
promise of land or share made before the conquest, they have nothing to claim; if they were ignorant of it
until the moment of the conquest, the imam, to satisfy them, must give them something equivalent on the
booty. Abou Hanifa said: The imam is not held to satisfy them either by a fief or by a share of the booty,
if he finds it preferable to act thus.

[PDF p. 314]

CHAPTER XXXVI
OF THE DIVAN OF THE REVENUE AND OF THE TAX

The writings of the taxes are called the bureau of dispatches. The first of these divans installed under
Islam was at Damascus and in Iraq, on the model of what existed before Islam. The divan of Syria employed
the Greek language, that of Iraq Persian, and that of Egypt Coptic. The divans of these different
countries then employed Arabic. The one who changed the language employed in the divan of Egypt from
Coptic to Arabic was Abd Allah ben Abd El-Melek ben Merwan, emir of Egypt, under the caliphate of
El-Oualid ben Abd El-Melek, in the year 87 [23 December 705 to 11 December 706]; this emir had all the
writings drawn up in Arabic, dismissed Antanach from the divan, and replaced him with Ibn Yarbou'
El-Fazari of the town of Homs. The one who first changed the language of the divan (of Iraq) from Persian
to Arabic was El-Oualid ben Hecham ben Makhzoum ben Soliman ben Zakouan, who died in 122 [text
erroneously reads 222]. The most widespread opinion is that this change was made by Salah ben Abd
El-Rahman, secretary of El-Haggag; he was a freedman of the Beni S'ad who was then at the head of the
divans of Iraq after the year 80 [9 March 699 to 25 February 700]. Here is, it is said, the cause of this
change: Saleh ben Abd El-Rahman had for father a slave carried off in the Sagestan; he was very skillful
in writing, and being an employee of Zadan Farrouch, secretary of El-Haggag ben Youssef El-Thafqi, he
traced for the latter specimens of Arabic and Persian writing, which was very agreeable to the heart of
El-Haggag. But Saleh, who feared Zadan, said to him: "It is you who have made me rise in grade and made me
approach the emir. I see that I am agreeable to him, and I fear he may make me rise above you and that
your rank may be lowered." "Believe nothing of it," answered Zadan; "he has more need of

[PDF p. 315]

me than I have need of him, for he will find no other than me to satisfy him for the reckoning." "By
God!" said Saleh, "if I wished to put the accounts in Arabic, I would do it easily." "Make some lines of
it, then, and show them to me," said Zadan. And Saleh having done it: "Feign to be ill," said Zadan to
him. Saleh pretended to be ill, and El-Haggag sent him his physician, which was very painful to Zadan, who
prescribed Saleh to appear no more before El-Haggag. But, a short time after, broke out the revolt of Abd
El-Rahman ben Mohammed ben El-Ach'ath, during which Zadan was killed at the moment he was leaving a house
to return home. El-Haggag then took for secretary Saleh, who taught him all that had passed between him
and Zadan on the subject of the divan. El-Haggag, marveled, ordered him to put that into practice and
replaced the Persian language with Arabic. This appeared very hard to the Persians, who offered Saleh a
hundred thousand dirhems not to effect the change. He refused, and Merwan Chah ben Zadan Farrouch said to
him: "May God make your trace disappear from the world as you have made the trace of the Persian language
disappear!" Abd El-Hamid ben Yahia said: "What a man is this Saleh, and what a service he rendered to the
accountants!"

As for the divan of Syria, the one who replaced the Greek with Arabic there was Abou Thabet Soliman ben
Sa'd, the secretary of correspondence. There is no agreement on the period when this change took place.
According to some, it would be under the caliphate of Abd El-Melek ben Merwan, but according to others, it
would be in the time of the caliph Hecham ben Abd El-Melek. The author who occupied himself with the divan
of Syria is the Christian Sargoun ben Mansour, in the time of Moawiah ben Abou Safian; after him, his son
Mansour ben Sargoun occupied himself with it equally.

[PDF p. 316]

CHAPTER XXXVII
OF THE REVENUES OF EGYPT UNDER ISLAM

The first who, in the time of Islam, collected taxes in Egypt was Amr ben El-As, who took in 12,000,000
dinars constituted by the tax of 2 dinars with which each man was struck. After him, Abd Allah ben Sa'd
ben Abou Sarh collected for one year of taxes in Egypt 14,000,000 dinars; it is on this subject that
Othman ben 'Afan said to Amr ben El-As: "O Abou Abd Allah, the she-camel has the udders more swollen than
before." "But you will harm its young one," answered Amr. The sums collected by Amr ben El-As comprised
only the capitation and not the tax properly speaking. After these two emirs, the revenue of Egypt went
diminishing as a consequence of the corruption brought on by time, the increasing devastation that
invaded the greater part of the lands, and the appearance of wars. The Ommiades and the Abbaside caliphs
did not even manage to collect 3,000,000 dinars; one must except the time of Hecham ben Abd El-Melek, who
had recommended to Obeïd Allah ben El-Habhab, governor of Egypt, to apply himself to rendering this
country prosperous. Since the lowering of the revenue of Egypt, one cites scarcely more than two fine
receipts: the first under the caliphate of Hecham ben Abd El-Melek; Obeïd Allah ben El-Habhab, who was in
charge of the finances, went himself to attend the survey of the cultivated terrains of Egypt and the
lands which, being able to be watered by the Nile, nevertheless remain uncultivated; he found that the
ensemble gave thirty million feddans without counting the high lands and the terrains in bad state; the
whole was cadastred and organized as best as possible. Under the administration of Obeïd Allah, Egypt
yielded 4,000,000 dinars, despite the low price of provisions and although the country had neither octroi
nor impositions. In the year 107 [19 May 725 to 7 May 726], in the first days of the reign of Hecham ben
Abd El-Melek, Ibn El-Habhab

[PDF p. 317]

divided Egypt into well-defined categories that were inscribed at the divans, which was maintained until
the disappearance of the Ommiades. The sum collected reached 1,700,837 dinars, of which 1,000,420 and a
half dinars for the Said, and the rest for the nomes of Lower Egypt. It is said that Ousamah ben Zeïd
collected, under the caliphate of Soliman ben Abd El-Melek, the sum of 12,000,000 dinars.

The second fine receipt was made under the emirate of Ahmed ben Touloun, who received Egypt from the hands
of Ahmed ben Modabber; at that period Egypt had fallen into such a state of ruin that the revenues
scarcely reached 800,000 dinars. Ahmed ben Touloun applied himself as best he could to cultivation, and
Egypt yielded, thanks to him, 4,300,000 dinars. His son, the emir Abou-l-Geich Khamarouyah ben Ahmed,
collected 4,000,000 dinars, despite the low price of provisions; one sold sometimes, in the time of the
Toulounides, ten ardebs of wheat for one dinar.

Ibn Khordadabah reports that the revenue of Egypt, in the time of Pharaoh, amounted to 96,000,000 dinars,
and that Ibn Habhab collected 2,723,839 dinars; in which he is mistaken, for this last sum represents only
