what was paid into the treasury of Damascus after the payment of the salaries and the necessary expenses
in Egypt. Mousa ben Eïsa El-Hachemi paid 2,180,000 dinars, after payment of the expenses and all the
costs.

When the Nile reaches seventeen cubits and ten fingers, the revenue of Egypt is 4,257,000 dinars. The
imposition was 2 dinars per feddan under the caliphate of Al-Mamoun and his successors. In the time of the
emir Abou Bekr Mohammed ben Tafag El-Akhchid, the revenue of Egypt was 2,000,000 dinars, without speaking
of the hamlets that were property of the emir. El-Akhchid was the first to remodel the salaries in Egypt;
his secretary Ibn Kala had drawn up a statement in which the expenses exceeded the receipts by 200,000
dinars. "How will we do?" asked El-Akhchid. "Take from the salaries and the wages," said Ibn Kala; "those
people are no more interesting than necessary." "Tomorrow," said El-Akhchid, "come to me and we will
arrange that." And Ibn Kala having arrived the next day, El-Akhchid said to him: "I have reflected on what
you told me, but the salaried people are either poor devils, or people of small fortune, or rich people. I
can take this diminution only from

[PDF p. 318]

you." "God be glorified," said Ibn Kala. "Glorify him," said El-Akhchid, and he gave him no respite until
he had obtained from him a paper by which he recognized himself debtor of the sum. And as one reproached
him this action, he said: Listen to what this man did: Ahmed ben Mohammed ben El-Mardani went to him one
day and said to him: "There is nothing between me and El-Akhchid, and he can do nothing against me. Here
are ten thousand dinars for El-Akhchid and a thousand dinars for you." Ibn Kala then came to me and said:
"Here are a thousand dinars that come to you carried on the water." And he gave me a thousand dinars,
keeping for himself the ten thousand. Another time Mohammed ben Aly El-Mardani sent me twenty thousand
dinars through Ibn Kala, and as I found the sum a little small, one day when I met El-Mardani, I addressed
reproaches to him, and he said to me: "I sent you a hundred thousand dinars and handed twenty thousand of
them to Ibn Kala." The latter had kept the hundred thousand dinars and brought me the twenty thousand. I
repeated to him what Mohammed ben Aly had told me. "What foolishness," he cried; "I kept the hundred
thousand dinars for you for the moment when you would need them. Take them, if you wish, but I know you
will squander them."

The sum of the salaries, in the time of Kafour El-Akhchidi, reached per year 500,000 dinars that were
paid to rich people, to people of medium fortune, and to all sorts of people among whom was no one of the
army, nor of the servants of the court, nor of the employees of the provinces. Aly ben Saleh
El-Rouzabadi, secretary of Kafour, adroitly made him understand that it would be good to make economies on
the sum of the salaries, by diminishing the salary of the people. At that very moment (he was seated and
working), his forehead itched; he scratched it with his pen; but the itching increased to such a point
that he had to abandon his work and withdraw. He was treated by the (hot) iron, and he died in the month
of Ramadan of the year 387 [7 September to 6 October 997]. Here is an example given by God to those who
intervene maliciously in the affairs of the people. For God has said: "The ruses of the wicked always
fall back on their author."

At the death of Kafour, numerous and terrible calamities fell upon [...]

[PDF p. 319]

Egypt: dearth, plague, seditions. And the revenues of the country went always decreasing until the
arrival of Gouher, come from the Maghreb at the head of the army of his master El-Moezz li-din Allah Abou
Tamim Moadd. Gouher took in as revenues of the year 358 [25 November 968 to 13 November 969] 3,400,000 and
some dinars. The vizier El-Naser li'l-din Abou-l-Hossein Abd El-Rahman El-Yazouri, vizier of Egypt under
the caliphate of El-Mostanser billah ben El-Zaheïr, received the order to draw up a statement of the
receipts and expenses of the empire. The chiefs of each divan made the count of their receipts and
expenses and handed the whole to the director of the divan of the council, which is the supreme divan.
The latter made of the whole an overall work that he carried to the vizier. The vizier ascertained that
the receipts rose to 2,000,000 dinars, of which a million for Syria, with the expenses opposite the
receipts, and 1,000,000 dinars for Egypt and the rest of the empire.

The cadi Abou-l-Hassan, in his book entitled Instructions for the Science of the Tax, says: I have
examined the tables drawn up for the general Badr El-Gemali, at the time of his arrival in Egypt in the
time of Mostanser, when he seized the country and triumphed over the corrupt who were there; these tables
present the state of the receipts of the year 483 [text: lunar and budgetary]; these receipts were
composed, according to the custom established by the divan and current in the provinces of Egypt, of the
tax and what pertains to it, of the lease-farms, concessions, and other chapters, including the free
domains of Cairo, of Masr and their suburbs, the two eastern and western provinces of the Delta and their
districts, Tannis, Damietta with their territory, Alexandria, the Behera, the provinces of the Upper and
Lower Said, the Oases, and Eïdab for the budgetary year, according to the Egyptian custom, as well as the
provinces of Syria that begin at the limit of the two trees, where begins the province of Palestine and
of Tripoli; and for this year 478 budgetary, including what had been fixed, in gold the receipt was
3,100,000 dinars; now, what had been fixed represented the total of the revenue collected in the year 466
[6 September 1073 to 26 August 1074] lunar before the arrival of Emir El-Giouch, a year corresponding to
the year 463 budgetary; the sum of it was 2,800,000 dinars; which shows for the year of El-Giouch an
excess of 300,000 dinars,

[PDF p. 320]

a fact that proves that the cultivation was flourishing and the justice general. This table was drawn up
in 483.

Ibn Miser reports that El-Afdal Ibn Émir El-Giouch ordered a statement to be made of the receipts of the
provinces of Egypt and that the sum rose to 5,000,000 dinars.

The cadi El-Fadl, in his Journal, says that the revenue of Egypt, from Alexandria to Eïdab, without taking
account of the frontier posts and the various chapters of revenue of the divan, no more than a great
number of provinces, rose for the year 585 [19 February 1189 to 7 February 1190] to 4,653,029 dinars.
Subsequently, the yield fell, and whereas the cadi El-Mouafeq Abou-l-Karam ben Ma'soum El-Asemi El-Tabisi
had collected, in gold only, for the treasury, expenses and costs paid, 1,200,000 dinars at the end of the
year 540 [24 June 1145 to 12 June 1146], after him and until the fall of the Fatimids, no one collected
such a sum any more.

The cause of the lowering of the revenues of Egypt -- which, in the last year of the Greek occupation,
before the conquest of the country by the Muslims, had reached 20,000,000 dinars -- is that the kings
scarcely worried about making expenses for the cultivation of the country, cultivation that requires a
quarter and even a third of what it yields. To finish with all that relates to the state of the land of
Egypt, let us say that it has been ascertained that the duration of cultivation is sixty days and that
the surface of the lands is 180,000,000 feddans, of which, according to Ibn Modabber, 24,000,000 are
cultivated; that, to produce the tax, 480,000 plowmen are needed, held to work ceaselessly. If this number
of workers is maintained, the prosperity of the country is complete and the revenue reaches its maximum.
But, in the final analysis, there are found there only 120,000 cultivators, of whom 70,000 for the Said
and 50,000 for the Delta. Today all that was practiced formerly has been changed, and the situation of the
country has become altogether precarious.

[PDF p. 321]

CHAPTER XXXVIII
OF THE DIFFERENT LANDS OF EGYPT AND OF THE DISTRIBUTION OF THE CULTIVATIONS

The lands of Egypt are classified into numerous categories. Those whose value is the highest, whose price
is the most elevated, and whose importance is the most considerable are the baq lands. One thus calls the
lands cultivated the previous year in leeks and cucurbits (gourds), which renders them altogether
favorable to the cultivation of wheat.

After the baq terrains come the charaqi lands: these lands have been left for a year without cultivation
and are put back into production only after the inundation of the second year; the harvests from them are
excellent.

The baraïb lands are those that, the previous year, bore wheat or barley. They are of lesser value than
the baq terrains because of the weakening of the land that results from these cultivations. Thus the
harvests produced by the lands that previously bore these two sorts of cereals are less good than those of
the baq terrains. The baraïb terrains are proper for the cultivation of leeks, cotton, and cucurbits, a
cultivation that rests the land and permits it to become in its turn a baq terrain.

The saqmahiah lands are those where, the previous year, flax was cultivated; the wheat produced by these
lands is of bad quality.

The chetouniah lands are those that have been irrigated and left fallow; they are inferior to the charaqi
lands.

The salaïh lands are those that have been irrigated and left fallow, then plowed and left again without
cultivation; they are similar to the charaqi lands and give excellent harvests.

The naqa lands are the lands absolutely free of all cultivation and where nothing opposes the sowing of
anything whatever.

One calls ouasekh (dirty, impure) a land whose impurity is such

[PDF p. 322]

that it is impossible for the cultivators to remove the filth from it; if one plows this land and sows it,
the harvests come up there mixed with alfa and other similar herbs.

One calls ghaleb every land where the grass is so abundant that one can cultivate nothing there; one makes
pastures of them.

One calls khers the lands bastardized by the abundance of matters that oppose cultivation; one makes
pastures of them likewise, but these lands are inferior to the ouasekh and ghaleb terrains. However, if
one tears out all that is contrary to cultivation, these lands become good.

One calls charaqi the terrains where the water does not arrive, either because the Nile is too low, or
because the land is too elevated, or because the water-conduits are obstructed, etc.

One calls moustabhar every low land where the water arrives and, not finding an outlet, stays on the soil
until the moment of cultivation is past.

One calls sabakh every land where salt dominates. The salty land cannot be used for the cultivation of
grains. In parts where the salt is less abundant, one can sometimes cultivate something other than
cereals -- asparagus, for example, or eggplants; one also cultivates the Persian reed there.

A condition of the most important for the cultivation of the lands of Egypt is the good state of the
dikes. The dikes are of two sorts: the royal dikes and the local dikes. The royal dikes are of general
utility, conserving the water of the Nile for the whole country until the moment when it is used. There
are on their subject special regulations in force in the provinces of the east and the west; they were
formerly maintained at the expense of the provinces, and the tenants were charged with this care, and the
expenses effected by them on this account were deducted from their dues as land tax. Later, money was
levied for this purpose in each province. The money was confided to the employees of the divan, who made
the necessary expenses and paid the surplus of the money into the treasury. They were subsequently
charged to the principal emirs of the kingdom, a state of things that lasted until the time of El-Naser
Farag. The latter levied considerable sums without spending anything of them on the upkeep of the dikes;
he kept the money for himself and made largesses of it to the lords. The upkeep of the dikes fell to the
inhabitants, and the situation only worsened and reached the point that you will be able to see, God
willing,

[PDF p. 323]

in the part of this book that treats of the causes of the ruin of Egypt. The local dikes are of a
particular utility, restricted to one province and not to another. The tenants and the cultivators are
held to maintain them with the money gathered in each province. The royal dikes are therefore like the
walls of a town to whose upkeep the sultan must attend, a care that is spared his subjects; the local
dikes are like the houses built inside the walls -- the master of each house must repair it and keep it in
good state. The custom is that, if a tenant is displaced after having made some expense for the upkeep or
repair of a dike in the year when his domain is withdrawn from him, he has the right to exact from the
tenant who succeeds him the reimbursement of a sum equal to that he spent while he was in exercise, to
assure the prosperous yield of a year when another than he will harvest.

The best WHEAT is cultivated in the baq and charaqi terrains; in the Said one cultivates wheat after wheat
because of the prodigious fertility of the soil; one also cultivates it there sometimes after flax and
barley. One sows the wheat, from the middle of Babah to the end of Hathor, in the elevated terrains that
uncover early. For the low-lying terrains that keep the water very late, one prolongs the time of sowing
until the end of Khiak. The quantity of seed necessary for a feddan varies according to the strength or
weakness of the soil, according to the greater or lesser thickness of the layer of humus, and according
to whether one cultivates by light plowing or deep. This quantity may go up to an ardeb or reach only 5 or
even 4 oueïbas. One even finds in the Said lands still less demanding, and in the Houf Ramsis terrains
where no more than 2 oueïbas of seed per feddan are needed. The wheat is ripe in Egypt in the month of
Bachons, which corresponds to Nisan. The harvest per feddan varies, according to the lands, from 2 to 20
ardebs. Abou Bekr ben Ouahchiat says, in his book Of Agriculture: "It is asserted that the harvest of
Egypt yields 300 meds for one med (there are 22 or 24 meds in the oueïba); this is due to the heat of the
air of this country, to the unctuous and fatty state of the soil, and to the quantity of silt [...]

[PDF p. 324]

held in suspension in the water of the Nile." In 806 [21 July 1403 to 11 July 1404], the water withdrew
from a part of the lake of the Fayoum, named today Bahr Youssef; this terrain was put under cultivation
and marvelous harvests were obtained, reaching per feddan 91 ardebs of barley, according to the measure of
the Fayoum where the ardeb contains 9 oueïbas. In the time of the Fatimids, some domains of the Said
produced 3 ardebs per feddan. And at the cadastre of 572 [10 July 1176 to 29 June 1177], the tax was fixed
at 2 and a half ardebs per feddan, then no more than 2 ardebs were levied. As for the terrains of the
Delta, the tax was collected in money and not in grain.

One cultivates BARLEY in a terrain previously sown in wheat or something similar; this cultivation is done
in a low terrain still humid. One sows the barley a few days before the wheat and harvests it likewise a
few days before it. The quantity of seed necessary varies with the terrain, but it is greater than that
required by wheat. Barley ripens in Barmoudah, which corresponds to Adar.

The cultivation of the BEAN is done, after plowing, in the baraïb terrains, from the beginning of Babah.
One eats the green beans in the month of Khiak; 3 oueïbas or thereabouts of seed are needed per feddan.
The bean is ripe in Barmoudah and yields per feddan at least 20 ardebs.

One sows LENTILS and CHICKPEAS from Hathor to Khiak; as for the CHICKLING-VETCH (gesse), one sows it only
in the lightest terrains, after plowing, choosing preferably the elevated lands; one cultivates it by
light plowing in the free lands. Each feddan requires, as seed, from an ardeb to 8 oueïbas of chickpeas,
from an ardeb to 4 oueïbas of vetch, and at least one oueïba of lentils; these grains ripen in Barmoudah
and yield per feddan: the chickpeas from 4 to 10 ardebs, the vetch at least 10 ardebs, and the lentils at
most 20 ardebs.

The best FLAX is cultivated in terrains lightly plowed and fertilized with sebakh. When the flax, having
become tall, has lodged (fallen over), one pulls it up by stalks. It is then named aslaf (that which is
advanced); one spreads it on the spot to dry it, and as soon as it is dry, one carries it off, retts it,
and empties the pods, from which

[PDF p. 325]

is drawn the flaxseed that produces the oil of har; one sows the flax in the month of Hathor; and each
feddan requires at least an ardeb and a half of seed. It ripens in Barmoudah and yields per feddan at
least 30 bales of textile matter and at most 6 ardebs of seeds. The tax of the flax lands amounted
formerly to 3 and even 5 dinars in the Said, to 13 dinars at Dallas, and to 3 dinars in the other regions.

One cultivates LEEKS when the water of the Nile begins to fall; this cultivation must be finished before
the appearance of the south wind named merisi; the first leeks are cultivated in the month of Babah,
sometimes after the Nourouz; for the cultivations in plowed land, one delays the sowing until Khiak and
Tobe, sometimes even until Hathor. The quantity of seed necessary is 2 and a half oueïbas per feddan. The
green leek is good to harvest at the end of Khiak; those sown in plowed land come to maturity in Tobe and
Amchir; the yield in plowed land is from 4 oueïbas to 2 ardebs per feddan.

One sows the ONION and the GARLIC from the month of Hathor until the middle of Khiak; one needs per feddan
half a quarter of an oueïba of onion seed and from 100 to 150 cloves of garlic; the garlic is ripe in
Barmoudah, and the onion set apart for the next sowing is cultivated from the beginning of Khiak to the
10th of Tobe; it yields per feddan 10 ardebs and ripens in Bachons.

One sows the LUPIN in Tobe; each feddan requires an ardeb of seed; it ripens in Barmoudah and yields per
feddan at most 20 ardebs.

Such are the winter cultivations.

As for the summer cultivations:

The WATERMELON and the BEAN (haricot) are sown from the middle of Barmahat to the middle of Barmoudah. 2
qadahs of seeds are needed per feddan; they ripen in Bachons.

One sows SESAME in Barmoudah; a quarter of an oueïba of seed is needed per feddan; it ripens in Abib and
Mesori and yields per feddan from 1 to 6 ardebs.

One sows COTTON in Barmoudah; each feddan requires for the seed 4 oueïbas of seeds; it ripens in Thot and
yields per feddan at most 8 geraoui qantars.

One plants SUGARCANE from the middle of Barmahat in the baq and berch terrains; the land is plowed seven
times, and it is recommended to have executed the first three plowings before the end of Bachons; the
quantity of terrain

[PDF p. 326]

occupied by the plantation is one eighth of a feddan (per feddan) or thereabouts. The cane requires a land
of good quality, well manured, of easy irrigation, and over which the Nile can spread at the moment of the
inundation. One tears out from the terrain all the alfa found there, one cleans it, then one passes the
berch (which is a sort of great plow) over it six times, one levels the soil by means of the harrow, after
which one plows six other times with the berch, one passes the harrow again, and one passes the plow over
it six more times, then the harrow (the word berch means "to plow"). The land being well prepared and in
good conditions, after the harrow has well spread and pulverized it, one pricks it with the spade and
introduces into each hole two pieces of cane, one simple and one double; one must have previously divided
the terrain into small squares and dug channels that are to bring the water to these squares. The length
of each piece of cane is three complete stalks with a piece of the upper stalk and the lower stalk
[footnote: that is, each planted piece comprises three entire articulations, the section being made above
the upper node and below the lower node; in other words each piece comprises four entire nodes]; for this
one chooses the canes whose stalks are short and the nodes very tight; one calls this operation the
"planting." When the planting is finished, one spreads earth over it; it is clear that in this operation
one must lay the pieces horizontally and not stick them vertically. From this moment until the beginning
of spring one waters once every seven days. The cane having grown, when the leaves begin to appear, there
also comes out of the earth alfa and purslane which, among the Egyptians, is named reglat. One then weeds
the land where the canes are planted (the word means "cleaning of the terrains planted in canes," an
operation that consists in ridding it of all that has grown at the same time as the cane), and one
continues ceaselessly to weed until the cane has become vigorous, resistant, and thick. One says at that
moment that the cane has driven out the weeding-tool; for it is then no longer possible to weed it, which
was not the case as long as the stalk had not come out. The total of the waterings one can give the canes
amounts to twenty-eight; these waterings are done by means of noriahs (waterwheels); habitually,
[footnote about node count] supposing the canes planted in terrains low enough to be covered by the
inundation and not far from the river, a noriah set in movement by vigorous oxen, although the waters are
near the surface of the soil, can irrigate (in a day?) eight feddans of

[PDF p. 327]

land; in this case eight oxen are needed. But if the wells are at a certain distance from the Nile, it is
no longer possible to irrigate more than six feddans, and sometimes only four. When the Nile swells and
rises, the canes are then fit to receive the full water. Here is how one proceeds: one makes an opening in
one of the sides of the dike that surrounds the plantation to guard it from the invasion of the waters at
the moment of the flood; by this breach one lets penetrate the water that spreads over the canes; when
this water has reached the height of a span, one stops up the opening made in the dike, in order to
prevent the water from penetrating further; and one lets the water spread over the canes stay there for
two or three hours, so that the land is well impregnated; at the end of this time one makes the water flow
off by another opening, and when it is altogether withdrawn, one brings new water in the same way. The
operation we have just indicated is repeated several times, on days spaced by a determined quantity. Then
one weans the land. If one puts into practice all that we have just indicated, the cane has all it can
require; but if one departs from it, the result is disastrous. One must also, before the cane becomes
sweet, sprinkle it (?) with tar, so that it is not eaten by the worms. The cane is cut in Khiak; one burns
the part still adhering to the soil, one waters it, one weeds it as we said above, and new canes grow that
one calls the successors (khalifes), the first being named chiefs. The sugar of the second canes is much
better than that of the first. The latter are ripe in Tobe; the others in the middle of Hathor. The
extreme period when one can put the cane to the press is the Nourouz. It yields per feddan from forty to
eighty ablouga of sugar. The ablouga is a sort of vessel containing nine qantars or thereabouts.

One sows the COLOCASIA at the same time as the cane; each feddan yields ten geraoui qantars of colocasia;
it ripens in Hathor.

One sows the EGGPLANT in Barmahat, Barmoudah, Bachons, and Baouna; it ripens from Baouna to Mesori.

[PDF p. 328]

One sows INDIGO from Bachons; one oueïba of seed is needed per feddan; it ripens in Abib.

One sows RADISHES all year long; from one to two qadah of seed are needed per feddan.

One sows TURNIPS in Abib; one qadah of seed is needed per feddan; they ripen after forty days.

One transplants LETTUCE by rootlets in Tobe and eats it two months after.

One transplants CABBAGES by rootlets in Tout; they ripen in Hathor.

One plants the VINE in Amchir (that is) one moves it and transplants it.

One plants the FIG TREE and the APPLE TREE in Amchir.

One prunes the MULBERRY TREES in Amchir.

One plants and moistens the ALMOND TREES, the PEACH TREES, and the APRICOT TREES with the water of Tobe
for three days while they are stalks, then one plants them and transplants them when they are shrubs in
the month of Tobe.

One sows the DATE stone, then one moves it when the shrub is still very small and transplants it.

One buries the bulb of the NARCISSUS in Mesori.

One sows the JASMINE during the Nasi (intercalary days) and the month of Amchir.

One plants the MYRTLE by cuttings in Tobe and Amchir.

One sows the BASIL in Barmoudah.

One sows the seed of the GILLYFLOWER (wallflower) when the Nile rises.

One plants the winter BANANA in Tobe and the summer one in Amchir.

One transplants the CASSIA TREE in Barmahat.

One prunes the VINE at the time of the north wind until the first days of Barmahat to make the buds come
out.

One prunes the trees in Tobe and Amchir, with the exception of the sedr (jujube), which is the tree that
produces the nabq and which is pruned in Barmoudah.

One waters the trees once in Tobe (the water of Tobe is called "water of life"), once in Amchir when the
flowers appear, twice in Barmahat when the fruit forms, and three times in Bachons; one waters them once a
week during the months of Baouna, Abib, and Mesori; and only once during the months of Toub and Baba,
saturating them with water of the Nile; one [...]
waters again with the water of the Nile in Hathor, flooding the low stalks. In Hathor one waters only once
with great water the vines not yet irrigated.

All the lands of Egypt are measured by the feddan (about 4,000 square meters); the feddan is equivalent to
a surface measuring 400 hakemi qassabats in length by 1 qassabat in width; the qassabat is worth ten and
two-thirds cubits of those used to measure cloth, and about five of the cubits of the carpenter. The cadi
Abou-l-Hassan, in his book The Instructions, says that the tax of Egypt was established by the qassabat,
the usual measure. It is according to this measure that the agriculturists estimate the lands. The surface
value of the feddan is 400 qassabats, for it represents a square of 20 qassabats on a side. The qassabat
of surveying bears the name hakemi and is worth about 5 cubits of the carpenter.

[PDF p. 330]

CHAPTER XXXIX
CLASSIFICATION OF THE REVENUES OF EGYPT

The revenues of Egypt form at present two categories: one named kharagi, and the other hilali. The kharagi
tax comprises all that is levied annually on the lands cultivated in grains, palms, vines, fruits, and
what is collected from the cultivators, as dues -- sheep, chickens, cakes, and other products of the
countryside. The hilali tax consists in a multitude of rights established one after another by unjust
governors. Here is the origin of these impositions under Islam: the Commander of the Faithful, Omar ben
El-Khattab, having learned that Muslim merchants, on their passage over terrains belonging to the army,
had been imposed by the latter with the tithe, wrote to Abou Mousa El-Ach'ari, governor of Basra: "From
every Muslim merchant who passes through the province take 5 dirhems for 200 dirhems; from every merchant
having treated with Islam -- that is, submitted to our protection -- take 1 dirhem per 20 dirhems, and
from every merchant belonging to a country at war with us, take 1 dirhem for 10 dirhems." One said one day
to the son of Omar: "Omar levied the tenth on the Muslims." He answered: "No!" Omar ben Abd El-Aziz
abolished this right and wrote: "Discharge the people of these rights; for these are not rights but
exactions."

It is recounted that Omar ben El-Khattab received one day the visit of Syrians who said to him: "We have
found mounts and money; levy on this the alms so that we may be purified." "How," said Omar, "would I do
what our predecessors have not done?" and he asked counsel. Aly ben Abou Taleb said to him: "There is no
harm in this if your successors do not do it," and Omar took per head of slave 10 dirhems and as much per
horse; as for the dromedaries, he collected per head 8 dirhems, and 5 dirhems per mule.

The first who, in the time of Islam, struck the shops with a tax

[PDF p. 331]

was the Commander of the Faithful Abou Abd Allah Mohammed ben Abou Ga'far El-Mansour, in the year 167 [5
August 783 to 23 July 784], and the one charged with the collection was Saïd El-Garati.

The first who, in Egypt, collected money outside the kharagi tax was Ahmed ben Mohammed ben Moudabber,
intendant of the revenues of Egypt after the year 250 [13 February 864 to 1 February 865]; he was the most
wicked of men and the most diabolical accountant. He invented all sorts of vexations that only increased
after him, far from diminishing. He had the natron guarded and appropriated the revenue of it, although
formerly the natron remained at the disposal of all. He put on the pastures where the livestock grazed a
tax named "right of pasturage." On the products of the waters that God gives as nourishment to everyone he
established the "right of fishing," and many others still. It was then that the revenues of Egypt were
classified into kharagi and hilali. Under Ahmed and his successors, the hilali tax was given the names of
"assistance" and "aid." When the emir Abou-l-Abbas Ahmed ben Touloun became governor of Egypt, the
Commander of the Faithful El-Mo'tamed 'ala Allah having attributed to him in addition the direction of the
tax and the shares of Syria, he abandoned and suppressed the rights of aid and assistance and proclaimed
the abolition of them throughout the extent of his government. The sum produced by these taxes rose each
year to 100,000 dinars. There are on this subject many accounts, of which the most important specimens are
related in the chapter of this book that treats of "the mosque of Touloun." The hilali were reestablished
in the time of the Fatimid dynasty, then in its decline, under the name of "customs duties." When the
sultan El-Naser Salah el-Din Abou-l-Mazfar Youssef ben Ayoub seized the kingdom of Egypt, he had the
customs duties of Masr and Cairo abolished, and the cadi El-Fadel wrote for him a regulation on this
subject. The annual sum (produced by these taxes) rose to 100,000 dinars, of which here is the detail:

Ibn Abou Taï reports that the total amount of the sums owed for the taxes and that were remitted by the
sultan Salah el-Din rose, including the arrears, up to and including the year 564 [5 October 1168 to 24
September 1169], to more than a million dirhems and two million ardebs of provisions, a sum he graciously
remitted, having them struck (from the registers) of the divan and discharging the taxpayers. But when the
sultan El-Malek El-Aziz Othman ben Salah el-Din Youssef took the government, he reestablished these rights
and increased their iniquity still. The cadi El-Fadel, in his Chronicle of the year 590, says: In the
month of Chaban [21 July to 19 August 1194], the inhabitants of Masr and Cairo displayed in broad
daylight their turpitudes, mocking the reprobation they might raise. The people of the government and the
representatives of authority let it happen, and everything became so corrupt that the grapes reached
considerable prices, so great was the quantity of people who put them to the press; a mill in the
Mahmoudieh street was specially constructed for the milling of the grain used to make beer, with no other
destination than that. The houses where this beer was sold were favored while being struck with a heavy
due; some of them yielded per day up to 16 dinars. It was forbidden to make beer in private houses in
order to favor the sale done in the protected houses. Vessels of wine were brought publicly into the
markets and without the least dissimulation. But the vengeance of God manifested itself by the unexpected
stopping of the flood of the Nile and the increase of the price of provisions at the period when ordinarily
they were the most abundant." The same author adds, in his Chronicle of the year 592 [6 December 1195 to 23
November 1196]: The situation became so grave that, in the palace of Abd El-Aziz, the provisions of bread
and meat ran short and one was reduced sometimes to contenting oneself with a meager piece of bread. The
lamentations were

[PDF p. 336]

great: one cried but one was not heard. This state of things had for cause the expense made at the palace
of the sultan, for the food of his family and the nourishment of his children; and the proprietors of
magazines, from whom provisions were taken by force, indemnified themselves on others; all this had as
consequence a stronger rise in the price of provisions. The merchants of provisions increasing the price
of foods to cover themselves for the losses caused them by the depredations committed at their place by
the palace of the sultan, each sought to earn his bread in a shameful way; the product of the tax on beer
and wine reached 12,000 dinars. One could licitly display the turpitude caused by these drinks, and the
sale of them was done in the squares and the shops, although one was near the moon of Rageb, and no one,
among the people, dared make a reproach either by gesture or by voice, for all this formed part of the
illicit rights the sultan used for his expenses and the upkeep of his table. The revenues of the ports
and the tax of the capitation, legal revenues, were conceded to people who no longer had any notion of
permitted or forbidden things. In the month of Ramadan, the price of grapes became exorbitant because of
the great quantity that passed to the press, and the farmers prided themselves on the privilege the sultan
had given them and on their exactness in paying the collector their farm to the last para; this farm
reached up to 17,000,000 dinars, and in addition the farmer gave the sultan a part of the beer and wine he
made. I have been told that the sultan had had made for these drinks cups of gold and silver and that many
women and men gathered in these orgies in the month of Ramadan, principally at the Khalig at the moment of
the opening of the dike, or on the Nile at the moment of the flood, and the Nile there meets debauchery.
We pray God that he not call us to account for all this and that he not hold us responsible for the
temerity of these people.

The author of the History of the Turks says: When the emir El-Melek El-Maezz 'Az el-Din Aïbek
El-Turkomani El-Salehi took the government of Egypt, in the year 680 [22 April 1281 to 10 April 1282;
text inconsistency in source] after the fall of the Ayoubite dynasty, he chose for vizier one of the
chiefs of divans named Charf el-Din Habbat ben Sa'd El-Faïzi, an accountant of Coptic nationality who had
feigned to embrace Islam in the time of El-Kamel and who

[PDF p. 337]

had attained high charges in the service of the bureaus. The latter, during his vizierate, established
taxes on the merchants, the rich people, and the proprietors, and instituted taxes and farms to which he
gave the name of "rights and dues." But when El-Melek El-Mazfar Seïf el-Din Qotouz, after the deposition
of El-Malek El-Mansour Aly ben El-Maezz Aïbek, had seized the government of Egypt, he established, at the
moment of undertaking the journey in which he was killed, a great number of taxes in order to gather the
money necessitated by his expedition against the Tartar hordes: among other exactions one must recall
this one; the properties were measured, and, on the value fixed for them, the right of alms was exacted;
moreover, each man was imposed with a dinar he had to pay, and the emir attributed to himself the third in
each succession. The whole constituted a sum of 600,000 dinars per year. Qotouz having been killed,
El-Melek El-Zaher Rokn el-Din Beibars sat after him on the throne, in the Citadel of the Mountain,
abolished all the taxes created by his predecessor, and wrote on this subject circular letters of
renunciation that were read from the pulpit. Then he suppressed the farm of the beer and all that
pertained to it, in the year 662 [4 November 1263 to 23 October 1264], and he wrote from Syria to the emir
Azz el-Din El-Halli, royal lieutenant of Egypt, to destroy the beer outlets, to make the trace of them
disappear, by demolishing the houses and breaking the vessels that served for these liquids, and to strike
this tax from the registers of the divan. "A pious man," he says in his letter, "spoke to me on this
subject and said to me: Is it possible that the wheat, of which God has made a nourishment for man, be
trodden underfoot? And I have drawn near to God by making this abuse cease. Whoever abandons something to
God, God gives him in exchange something better; and whoever abandons what came to him from an impure
source, God restores it to him by permitted ways." El-Halli therefore abolished this tax, giving some
indemnity to those who lived from it. In the year 662 he abolished the right of day-guarding at Cairo and
at Masr, a right that yielded considerable sums, and he wrote on this subject a circular. He likewise
suppressed in the provinces of Daqhalieh and of Moustahieh the right of the vali, which yielded 24,000
dinars. And on the 25th of Ramadan of the year 662 [21 July 1264],

[PDF p. 338]

there was read, at the mosque of Masr, a rescript carrying the abolition of the rights fixed as rights of
the vali of Egypt and amounting to 100,000 Egyptian dirhems; this right was therefore abolished, and with
it the farm of the hashish, which was suppressed throughout the extent of Egypt in the year 665 [2 October
1266 to 21 September 1267]; orders were given for the wine to be poured out (into the streams); the
turpitudes consequently ceased, the destruction of the houses of debauchery was decided, the cafes and the
brothels were forbidden throughout the territory of Egypt and Syria, and each locality was purged of them.
When these orders reached the cadi Nasr el-Din Ahmed ben Amir, he said:

[verses:] Eblis (the Devil) has no more to do among us; his domains are elsewhere than among the people
of the emir; his means of existence are wine and hashish, two forbidden things that were his water and
his pasture.

And the virtuous man of letters Abou-l-Hassan El-Gazzar said:

[verses:] The cup no longer has its little bubbles, and the lips are deprived of their moisture; and in
the morning the old man weeps over what is past of his youth.

On the 9th of Gamadi El-Akher of the year 666 [25 February 1268], El-Melek El-Zaher Beibars had the wine
poured out into the streets; debauchery was hunted down, and the women of the public houses were forbidden
to give themselves over to prostitution at Cairo, at Masr, and in all Egypt; the country was purged of
these turpitudes, the establishments that served for these shameful things were pillaged and their
proprietors stripped of all they possessed; some even were exiled; as for the women, they were kept in
prison until they were married. The emir prescribed all the provinces to act likewise; he withdrew from
the divan the money collected on prostitution and gave to the personages who lived from it equivalent
revenues but coming from licit sources. On the 17th of Zu-l-Hagga of the year 667 [27 July 1271], the emir
again had the wine poured out and suppressed the farm of it, which yielded 1,000 dinars per day. On this
subject, he wrote a circular that was read from the pulpit. At the beginning of the year 704 [...]

[PDF p. 339]

the wine was again poured out and rigorous measures were taken against debauchery; this day is celebrated
at Cairo. In the year 674 [27 June 1275 to 12 June 1276], the emir learned that the eunuch Chouga el-Din
'Anbar, known under the name of Sadr el-Baz (eagle's breast) and who had over the prince a considerable
influence, drank wine; he had him hanged at the foot of the Citadel of the Mountain.

When El-Melek El-Mansour Seïf el-Din Qalaoun took the direction of the affairs of Egypt, he abolished the
alms of the empire, a right collected from each individual; this right of alms, calculated according to
the fortune of each, was maintained even though the taxpayer ceased to possess anything whatever; at the
death of a person, this right was collected from his heirs. The sultan also abolished the due paid by all
the inhabitants of Egypt at the news of the taking of a fortress or any other similar fact. It was levied
on the people of Cairo and Masr in proportion to the rank they occupied, and considerable sums were
gathered by this means. He also suppressed the tax collected from the people of the protection (infidels
submitted to Islam), fixed at 1 dinar, apart from the right of capitation; this tax was attributed to the
annual upkeep of the army; he likewise suppressed the tax of the dinar levied on the merchants at the
moment of the departure of the troops and the warriors; this right was paid by all the merchants of Cairo
and Masr, each merchant being taxed at 1 dinar. He also abolished the tax collected at the moment of the
full flood of the Nile; with the money this tax yielded, feasts of preserves and fruits were made at the
Meqias; the expense of it was henceforth borne by the Treasury. He abolished finally quantities of taxes
of the same sort.

El-Melek El-Nacer Mohammed ben Qalaoun suppressed a great number of the dues of which we spoke in the
chapter of the Cadastre of El-Naser, and the last measure, of which we have been contemporary, was the
abolition of the farm of the singing-women and the farm of the qirats in the year 778 [27 May 1376 to 9
May 1377], a suppression that was executed by El-Melek El-Achraf Cha'ban ben Hasseïn ben Mohammed ben
Qalaoun. The farm of the singing-women was an abominable institution that consisted in drawing money from
the prostitutes; if one of the most considerable women went out in Masr to give herself over to debauchery
and have her name inscribed with the procuress, the latter furnished her with all she needed, and it was
impossible for the greatest man of Egypt to prevent her from giving herself over to debauchery.

[PDF p. 340]

If this woman gave birth, or became engaged, or rubbed her hands with henna, or if someone asked her in
marriage, she had to pay the fixed right to the procuress. Whoever hired, for a marriage or the
childbirth of his wife, a singing-woman without the permission of the procuress was the target of unheard-
of vexations. The right of qirat consisted in what was levied on all those who sold a property; it was
fixed at 20 dirhems for 1,000 dirhems. These two rights yielded a most considerable sum.

El-Melek El-Zaher Barqouq abolished the right collected from the people of Bourlos, of Chaoura, and of
Beltin and that had some relation with the capitation; this right produced per year 6,000 dirhems. He
suppressed the right of octroi on the wheat; this tax was paid above all by the poor people of the port of
Damietta -- that is, by those who bought two ardebs or less; he also suppressed the right with which were
struck the chicken-ovens of Nahririah and the provinces of the west; the right of present exacted from
whoever led horses, camels, or sheep to graze at El-Abassat; the tax on the dry fodder and the alfa, a tax
collected at Bab El-Nasr, outside Cairo; the farm of the singing-women at Miniet Ibn Khasib, in the
province of Achmouneïn, and at Zefta in the province of Gharbieh; the obligation to throw oxen into the
Nile, in the Delta, at the moment of the completion of the dikes, was also annulled. The emir Balbagha
El-Salemi, on his entry into the charge of equerry of the sultan El-Melek El-Nacer Farrag ben Barqouq, in
the year 801 [13 September 1398 to 2 September 1399], abolished the tax of grains at Miniet Ibn Khasib, the
right of warehousing, and that fixed on the huts of the washerwomen, taxes of a revolting injustice. He
likewise suppressed at Cairo the farm of the lake of the ox, which the Copts reestablished subsequently.

Some of these taxes have persisted until our days. And the vizier-counselor, the emir-equerry Balbagha
El-Salemi, recounted to me, in the time of his vizierate, that the sum produced by these taxes in all
Egypt reached per day some 70 and some thousand dirhems; that after examination, he had recognized that
nothing of it was spent for the well-being of the kingdom, but that this money was useful only

[PDF p. 341]

to the Copts and their friends; he had intended to abolish these taxes but had not been able to manage it.

The hilali tax comprises what is collected monthly -- for example the price of rent of covered buildings,
such as houses, shops, baths, ovens, mills, sheep-stables, and of the open-air properties, rented or not
rented. An accountant has gathered the rights collected for the hekr houses (rented according to
emphyteutic lease), the terrains planted in gardens whose price was paid each month, the fishing of fish,
the presses of flax-oil or olive-oil, under the title of hilali tax.

Ancient accountants of Egypt were of the opinion of placing the tax fixed on the people of the protection,
Jews and Christians, in a special place, after the hilali tax and before the kharagi tax, for although
this tax was collected annually, one was nevertheless of the opinion that it be paid monthly; there is,
indeed, in this manner of proceeding, some utility for those who convert to Islam or who die in the course
of the year, because they are held to pay only according to the time elapsed before their conversion or
before their death; this is why this tax has been placed between the hilali tax and the kharagi tax.

The fiefs of the army were also considered as hilali goods at the moment when a holder of a fief was
dispossessed to make place for a second feudatory, for they were taxed by lunar month and not by solar
month, in such a way that, according to the custom, if the first proprietor disappeared in the course of
the year, whether by death or by transfer of this fief to another, the first had the right to reclaim a
sum equal to the amount due for the number of months elapsed at the moment when the fief had been
withdrawn from him, and not based on the estimate of the harvest to come (the second feudatory had right
only from the date of his investiture, according to the financial custom, and the interval comprised
between the departure of the first feudatory and his replacement by the second reverted by right to the
divan and entered into the category of fief-goods without concessionary). Among the hilali taxes there
were found some that were called "dues," such as the rights of alms, of inheritance, of the ports, of
commerce, of alum, of natron, of giouchi plaster, of the mint, of the house of the title of alloys, of
buffaloes, of plaster-mills, of sheep, of plantations, of gardens, of heqr lands, of cities, of boats, the
right collected from the people of

[PDF p. 342]

the protection in addition to the capitation, the tax on the disembarkation of the sont (acacia), on the
fruits of the sont, on the vines, the guarding of the straw, the tax on the canes, the right levied on the
coursers, the tax of the carpets, the tithe of the brandies (?), and other dues. As for the individual tax
named in our time "capitation," it was collected in advance and entirely at the beginning of the year and
yielded formerly considerable sums.

The cadi El-Fadel, in his Chronicles, says: The receipt of the tax of the capitation for the year 587 [29
January 1191 to 17 January 1192] rose to 130,000 dinars. In our time, this tax has diminished much because
of the great number of Christians who pretended to be Muslims following events that took place among them.
When the sultan El-Melek El-Moayyad Cheikh took the government of Egypt after the caliphate of the
Commander of the Faithful El-Abbas ben Mohammed (surnamed) El-Mosta'ïn billah, he chose a man who was
charged with the collection of the tax of capitation; then the pursuits against the protected ones of
Islam became more ardent, and great zeal was deployed to draw money from them. This tax produced, in 816
[3 April 1413 to 22 March 1414], 114,000 dinars, without counting the gifts made to the great ones, which
were considerable.

The name of pasturage is given to all simple and pure grass that God makes grow to feed the livestock of
men. The first who had the pastures inscribed at the divan (of the tax) in Egypt was Ahmed ben Modabber,
then intendant of the revenues; to this effect, he created a bureau at the head of which he put an
energetic man charged with preventing the people from selling or buying a pasture from another person than
the divan; we have seen that, in the Said, the pastures were attached to the domains and that the emir
collected, from every person leading his herds to graze on his territory, the annual tax of grazing, a tax
he levied per head of livestock and that he received from the master of the herd in proportion to the
number of animals. When, as a consequence of the events that succeeded one another from the year 806 [21
July 1403 to 9 July 1404], the state of the Said had been completely upset, this custom fell into disuse.
The habit formerly was to name, for the pastures, a director, witnesses, and

[PDF p. 343]

accountants who made the enumeration of the herds and who collected from their master so much per head.
This collection took place only after the recession of the Nile, the germination of the pastures, and
their utilization for the livestock.

As for the right on fishing, it is established on what God makes produce as food by the fishing of the
rivers. The first who had it inserted in a divan was again Ibn Modabber, who created a special bureau but
who, ashamed to mention it under the title of right of fishing and finding the word iniquitous, had it
given the denomination of right of planting of lines and installation of nets. This right was maintained,
and for its collection there were instituted a director, witnesses, and accountants who went to different
points, such as the canal or the lake of Alexandria, the lake of Nasterou, the port of Damietta, the
cataracts of the frontier post of Assouan, and everywhere there were ponds or lakes. They set out at the
moment of the recession of the Nile, when the water withdraws from the cultivations to regain the bed of
the river and the mouths of the canals are barred and the sluices closed, which is done toward the end of
the flood of the Nile, the period when the water coming from the cultivated terrains is restored to the
river. It is then that the nets are fixed; one lets the water flow off, the fish arrive carried by the
current of the water, but the nets prevent them from fleeing with it, they gather there, one pulls them
onto the shore, one spreads them on mats, one salts them, and one encloses them in vessels. When this fish
is ready, one sells it under the name of salted fish or brine. One makes this preparation only with fish
at most a finger long. This sort of fish, when it is fresh, is called basaria (from the Greek); one eats
it grilled or roasted. One fishes in the lakes of Nesterou, of Tannis, and of Alexandria fish that one
names bouri -- named thus because they are fished near one of the villages of the district of Tannis
called Bourat, a village today destroyed and whose ethnic name is bouri. Many people bore this name, among
others the Beni Bouri; this fish also draws its name from that of this village. In our time this right of
fishing is abolished, except for the lakes of Nasterou in Bourlos and of Tannis in Damietta only; these
two lakes pertain to the particular divan, and special employees are attributed to them; all that is
fished there, bouri or other fish, belongs to the sultan, and no one has the right to take anything there
unless he is among the number of the fishermen depending on the [...]

[PDF p. 344]

ones assigned to these lakes. All the bodies of water other than these two lakes -- ponds, marshes, or
canals -- do not belong to the sultan. The lake of Alexandria, for its part, is dry, and the frontier post
of Assouan is out of the hands of the sultan and in the possession of the infidels. There are also ponds
belonging to private persons, such as Berket el-Fil (pond of the elephant), which is the property of the
descendants of El-Melek El-Zaher Beibars, and the Berket el-Ratli, belonging to the heirs of the emir
Boktamer El-Hagab, etc. The fish of these lakes are their property, they sell them, but despite this no
one is forbidden to fish there.

As for the fish of the Nile, they are carried to the fish market of Cairo where, at the moment of the sale,
the right of the sultan is collected. But the emir-equerry Gemal el-Din Youssef having increased the
tariff collected on the fisheries, the fish became rarer on the market of Cairo and their price became
higher. Abou Saïd Abd El-Rahman ben Ahmed ben Younas, in his History of Egypt, says that there was at
Alexandria an idol named Sharahil placed on one of the rocks of the sea and pointing with its finger
toward Constantinople; one did not know whether it was the work of the prophet Soliman or of Alexander.
The big fish made the circuit of (the port of) Alexandria and, it is claimed, had themselves fished near
the statue. Zeïd ben Abd El-Rahman ben Zeïd ben Aslam says: My father, who had it from his father,
recounted to me that, lying on his belly with hands and feet extended, his length was that of the foot of
the statue. A man named Ousama ben Zeïd, lieutenant of Egypt for El-Oualid ben Abd el-Melek, Commander of
the Faithful, wrote this: "We have, at Alexandria, a statue named Sharahil; it is of copper, and as silver
is rare among us, if the Commander of the Faithful desires that I overturn it and make money of it, it
will be done; if he is of another opinion, let him write me on this subject." And the emir answered: "Do
not overturn it before I have sent delegates who will attend the operation." He therefore sent faithful
people; the statue was overturned from its rock and one discovered that its eyes were two red rubies of an
inestimable price; of the copper money was made, and the fish withdrew and no longer returned to the place
where they had gathered before.

As for the right of alms, the sultan Salah el-Din Youssef ben Ayoub was the

[PDF p. 345]

first who collected it in Egypt. The cadi El-Fadel, in his Chronicles of the year 567, says that on the
13th of Rabi' El-Akher [14 November 1171], the alms, having been gathered, was distributed among the poor,
the indigent, the travelers, and those who had aided in its collection, after the four parts that revert
to the governors and the converts to Islam had been paid into the Treasury, or which are used for the way
of God and the ransoming of slaves; for these a determined right was fixed that was levied on the money and
the merchandise and on the sum produced by the collection of the tax on the herds, the palms, and the
vegetables. The total of the capitation for the year 587 amounted to 30,000 dinars, and the highest sum
that was employed for the alms and the coinage rose, in the two years 586 and 587, to 21,861 dinars. In
the year 588, says the same author, Ibn Hamdan, employee at the divan of the alms, inscribed in his hand,
for that year, a sum of 52,000 dinars as the amount of the collection of this right; he named the eunuch
Qaraghach as depository of this money, which he was not to spend, but on the contrary to keep in a chest
to employ it according to the orders that would be given to him. When Ibn 'Oneïn the poet, leaving El-Melek
El-Aziz Seïf el-Aslam Taftakin ben Negm el-din Ayoub ben Chadi, king of the Yemen, came to Egypt, he
brought with him all that this prince had given him, which was considerable; the officials of the divan of
the alms, in Egypt, seized all the merchandise he brought and reclaimed from him the right of alms on what
he brought. This happened in the time of El-Melek El-Aziz Othman ben Salah el-Din Youssef ben Ayoub ben
Chadi, and Ibn 'Oneïn made the following verses:

[verses:] Not all those who are called 'Aziz deserve this name, just as not all the clouds with lightning
produce rain. What a difference between the acts of the two 'Aziz! One gives the alms, the other takes it.

El-Aziz occupied himself, subsequently, with the collection of the right of alms and, on this subject, he
committed infamous acts, among others these: from a poor man

[PDF p. 346]

selling salt that he carried in a basket on his head, the right of alms had been reclaimed for the content
of his basket; for a camel sold for five dinars, five dirhems had been collected as right of alms. This
right, by order of the sultan, was exacted from the rich people and from all those who could bear it.
El-Melek El-Kamel Nasr el-Din Mohammed ben El-'Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub, on his arrival to power, withdrew
from the sum collected from everyone as right of alms the two parts of the poor and the indigent and
prescribed employing them entirely for these two classes of needy, according to (the precepts of) religion;
he also determined the part reverting to the jurisconsults, the pious people, and the people of good; this
was found very equitable; those who carried the right of alms to the divan were welcome, and those who
carried nothing were not troubled; but it happened that the rich showed themselves avaricious and did not
give the alms levied on their wealth, so much so that the poor and the indigent complained and that
denouncers proposed taking this right to farm in order to bring its revenue back to the point it reached
before. The sultan named as inspector of the divan of the alms the cadi El-As'ad Cherf el-Din
Abou-l-Mokarem ben Mohageb ben Mammati, who collected this right from all those who could pay it.
Subsequently, it was ceded to farm, for a strong due, and the injustices and exactions began again as
before. The aides of the vali of the alms went to Minieh Ibn Khasib, to Akhmim, to Qous to inspect the
objects belonging to the travelers, the pilgrims, etc. They inspected all that these people possessed and
went even so far as to search themselves under their garments to verify whether they did not carry money
on them. They obliged them to terrible oaths, to affirm that they had on them and with them nothing other
than what had been found. Some of these diabolical agents carried long iron needles with which, when they
had boarded the boats, they pierced all the bales and sacks there, fearing they might contain some
merchandise or some money. And they pushed the spying and their investigations so far that it was horrible
and shameful, and the pilgrims found themselves in a humiliating and ignominious situation before these
aides who did not fear to search under their garments and in their provision-sacks; thus the injustice was
crying and the damages

[PDF p. 347]

considerable. It is thus that one acted throughout Egypt since the time of the sultan Salah el-Din ben
Ayoub.

As for the ports (and frontier posts), one designates under this name the towns of Damietta, Tannis,
Rosetta, Eizab, Assouan, and Alexandria, the last by far the most important. In these localities, the
charges were very numerous, and among them the right of the fifth and the tax of the merchandise. The
right of the fifth was collected on the merchants who arrived by sea, on the objects of commerce they
brought, according to a tariff established by treaty. This right rose sometimes from 100 to 235 dinars
(for a single merchant); sometimes it did not even reach 20 dinars. This right bore the name of right of
the fifth; among the Greek merchants some paid the "tenth," but for this it was necessary to have a special
convention. The cadi El-Fadel says: The amount of the right of the fifth collected at Alexandria in the
year 587 rose to 28,618 dinars. The tax of the merchandise comprised the objects the divan levied (in
kind) according to what it judged necessary.

The author of the History of the vizier El-Bazouri says: In 444 [3 May 1052 to 22 April 1053], the Nile
was very low, and one possessed in magazine only a very weak quantity of grains, thus the famine was
terrible in Egypt. There was for this small abundance of grains a determining cause: it is that the vizier
Naser el-Din, having joined to his charge of vizier the functions of cadi, in the time of Abou-l-Barakah
El-Ouazir, had bought each year, on the account of the sultan, a thousand dirhems of grains in which he
traded. The former cadi then presented himself before the caliph El-Mosta'ïn billah and declared to him
that the commerce of grains was very prejudicial to the Muslims; that sometimes the value fell below the
purchase price, and as it was not possible to sell them in these conditions one kept them in the magazines
where they molded and spoiled; that there was no lack of other kinds of traffic that could cause no
prejudice to the people, yielding twice as much as the commerce of grains, without having to dread that
the objects would deteriorate in magazine, and whose price could not fall -- such as wood, soap, iron,
lead, honey, or other things of the same nature. The sultan followed this counsel, and the state of things
having thus continued, the low price of cereals

[PDF p. 348]

was maintained; it was thus for years; then the kings established a divan for commerce, and the last who
occupied himself with it was El-Zaher Barqouq.

The alum came from mines situated in the Said; on average, the divan spent for a leïtzi qantar thirty
dirhems; the Bedouins brought it from the mine to the river, at Akhmim, Siout, or Behnesa, whence it was
transported to Alexandria by the canals during the inundation. One bought it by the leïtzi qantar and sold
it by the geraoui qantar. One sold to the Greek merchants about twelve thousand geraoui qantars at the rate
of four to six dinars the qantar. In Egypt, one sold to the felt-makers and the dyers about eighty geraoui
qantars at the price of six and a half dinars the qantar. No one could buy any from the Bedouins or other
persons, and if it was discovered that someone had sold or bought any from another than the divan, he was
molested and all that was found at his place was destroyed. This right was abolished.

One finds natron to the west of Egypt in the province of Terranat; it is red or green. One also finds it
in the Faqousiyeh, but much less than in the Terranat. It is again one of those things that, after having
been the property of all, was reserved by Ibn Modabber, who had it incorporated into the divan of the
sultan. It has been thus after him until this day. The rule established by the divan was to put on sale
each year ten thousand qantars, of which thirty qantars were given annually to the official of the natron.
This quantity came from Terranat. One sold the natron at Cairo by masri qantar, on the Bahr el-Charqi and
in the Said by geraoui qantar, and at Damietta by leïtzi qantar. The cadi El-Fadel says: "The revenue of
the natron was farmed until the end of the year 585 [19 February 1189 to 7 February 1190] for the sum of
15,500 dinars, and one drew from it, in the year 586 [8 February 1190 to 28 January 1191], the sum of 7,500
dinars." We have seen that the natron had been ceded in fief to some men of the army. And when the emir
Mahmoud ben Aly became equerry and chargé d'affaires of the kingdom, in the time of El-Zaher Barqouq, he
laid hands on the natron, for which he built a place of sale, and it was not permitted to sell it
elsewhere. It is still thus.

As for the plasters of El-Giouchi, the terrains that produced them [...]

[PDF p. 349]

were situated in the eastern and western parts of Egypt; in the east at Bahteïn, Amiriat, and Miniat,
lands that were inscribed at the finances as lands subject to dues; in the west at Saft, Nahiat, Ousim;
all these domains had been sequestered by the Emir el-Giouch Badr El-Gemali for his descendants, with the
gardens situated outside Bab el-Foutouh. At his death and long after, the viziers seeking to procure money
rented them for weak sums, then they were incorporated into the divan. Ibn El-Mamoun, in his History, says:
All the gardens that belonged in property to the heirs of the Emir El-Giouch, as well as the terrains that
depended on them, did not cease to remain in their hands during all the vizierate of El-Mamoun El-Bataïhi,
without anything being reclaimed from them either as farm or for any other cause. The caliph El-'Amr bi
ahkam Allah being dead, Abou Aly ben El-Afdal ben Emir El-Giouch, having become vizier, had the domains
restored to the rightful claimants because the greatest part of it reverted to him. When he was killed and
the caliph El-Hafiz li din Allah took power, the latter ordered all the properties freed and had the
sequestered goods belonging in property to the Emir El-Giouch unbound; but Yanis, servant of El-Afdal and
vizier at that period, as well as 'Az El-Moulk, servant of El-Aouhad ben Emir El-Giouch, did not cease to
circumvent and insinuate themselves with the sultan, presenting him the books found by the heirs and
bearing the signature of the caliphs, so much so that the sultan left them the goods (they held) and these
goods no longer left their hands. Subsequently, the divan of El-Hafiz consented to a release on these
goods, in the year 527 [12 November 1132 to 31 October 1133]. In the year 531 [29 September 1136 to 18
September 1137], when El-Khatir and El-Murtadi were employees of the vizier Redouan ben Oualakhchi, the
gardens only and not the other lands returned to the heirs, in the state in which they were -- that is, in
very bad condition and yielding little. The heirs of El-Giouch having died out, and as there remained only
an old woman, the fiqihs of that time rendered a decree that made the sequestration cease, and the
terrains were seized and incorporated into the properties of the sultan. Of these goods, some are still
today the property of the sultan, others have become wakfs, sequestered properties, etc.

[PDF p. 350]

There was a mint at Cairo, a second at Alexandria, and a third at Qous; only the cadi of cadis, or his
agent, had the right to verify the title (purity) of the mint. In our time this custom is much fallen;
this privilege has become the appanage of corrupt Jews who simulate Islam but who, despite their apparent
conversion, remain plunged in turpitude. Formerly one put the greatest zeal into controlling the purity of
the gold and the maintenance of its title, but the corruption arrived with El-Nazer Farrag, who had struck
the naseri dinars, money of very bad alloy. The transactions were done from then on at Cairo in silver,
but this was rendered impossible by El-Malek El-Kamel Mohammed ben Abou Bekr ben Ayoub in the year 20-some;
this prince struck the round dinars named kameli, which were composed of a third of copper and two thirds
of silver. One continued to coin money at Cairo until the emir Mahmoud El-Astadar multiplied the striking
of copper at Cairo and Alexandria; the dirhems then disappeared from Egypt, and from that period until the
present the transactions are done among the inhabitants in copper money, which replaces gold and all
merchandise. I will give an account of all this, God willing, when I come to speak of the causes of the
ruin of Egypt. The mint yielded the sultan strong sums, but this revenue has much diminished in our time
because of the lack of riches. Today the mint depends on the particular divan.

The house of verification had been instituted for the greatest good of the subjects and to verify their
weights and their measures. The sultan also drew money from it, and the sultan Salah el-Din put it in wakf
for the upkeep of the wall of Cairo; it will be spoken of when there is question of the quarters of Cairo
in this book.

One calls hekr the price fixed for (the rental of) vacant terrains at Cairo and at Masr: of these goods
some serve as lodging for the inhabitants, others are cultivated in gardens; this revenue formed part of
the royal goods formerly, since then it has been withdrawn from the royal divan. The hekr goods were
situated at Masr, at Cairo, and in the interval comprised between these two towns; they were put in wakfs
and assigned to very diverse chapters.

The plantations were found only in the Gharbieh and comprised certain terrains on which a right similar to
the hekr right and fixed per feddan was levied. This has been withdrawn from the divan.

[PDF p. 351]

The right of the dikes was common to all the provinces, proportionally for each to a determined number of
parcels; each parcel being taxed at 10 dinars; this money was employed for the repair of the dikes; the
surplus, a strong sum moreover, was paid into the Treasury. This right was abolished too, and Naser Farrag
established for the dikes new rights of which there will be question in the book of the Causes of the ruin.

The right of the straw. -- All the straw of the land of Egypt was divided into three parts: that of the
divan, that of the feudatories, and that of the cultivators. Such was the rule for the collection of the
straw throughout the extent of Egypt; for a hundred loads of straw, one received four dinars and a sixth,
and by this means much money was gathered. This right was also struck from the divan.

Of the land tax. -- There were in the province of Behnesa, of Saft Richeïn, of Achmounein, of Siout, of
Akhmim, and of Qous, innumerable acacias that people were charged to guard and destined for the
construction of the vessels of the fleet. One cut them only as needs arose, and certain trees had a value
of a hundred dinars. One drew from these provinces certain revenues called tax of impost, which were
collected supposedly as reimbursement of what the inhabitants of these provinces cut and employed -- the
sont wood in their constructions. One collected from them again another right named right of sont, and the
money thus obtained served to pay the felling of the wood; per hundred loads one collected one dinar. The
employees of this service had to watch that what could be used for the buildings of the fleet was
respected and that only the extremities of the branches were cut -- parts that could be used only to make
fire. The wood thus cut was called heating wood and was sold to the merchants at the rate of four dinars
the hundred loads. One inscribed in their presence the weight of what was sold to them, and when the boat,
with its cargo of wood, arrived at the quay of Masr, one verified by comparing the content of the boat with
the statement that had been sent; the tax was collected according to what was carried on the statement.
Ordinarily, for the woods of Behnesa, one sold only what was useless to the needs of the sultan. All this
was abolished and these trees fell into the public domain; there remained no more trace of this right,
which was forgotten by the divan.

As for the qarz -- that is, the fruit of the sont tree -- nothing of it could

[PDF p. 352]

be traded except by the divan, and if any was discovered at someone's place of another provenance than the
divan, the individual was maltreated and all that was found at his place was destroyed. When the harvest of
the qarz was finished, boats were loaded with it and, when it was sold, one collected a quarter of the
price at the moment of the arrival of the qarz at the quay of Masr, whether it was bought at a debated
price or whether the sale took place at auction. That was a crying injustice and was abolished.

Tax on the people of the protection. -- This right was collected at Masr, Alexandria, and Akhmim only, and
not in the other countries; it was established on the merchandise the protected ones imported or exported,
according to a tax established by the divan. It was likewise abolished.

Tax on the buffaloes, the field-oxen, and the sheep. -- The sultan drew from this tax considerable money.
The divan collected indeed, per head of buffalo, from five to three dinars per year for those employed in
the works (of the fields), the small ones paying the half of what the big ones paid; the least one drew
from it was about fifty percent (of the value of the animal); similar to the tax that struck the buffaloes
was that which applied to the field-oxen, the white sheep, the goats, the bees. These rights were
abolished, which had been established only because of the lack of money of the sultan, who cared less for
the prosperity (of the country) and the means of attaining it than for multiplying the causes of the ruin.

In the time of the Fatimids, the inheritances were not regulated as today; one had then the habit of
making all the relatives inherit, and if a daughter found herself alone, she had right to the totality of
the inheritance. But after the domination of the Fatimids, the Ayoubites, and the Turks, the sultan made
the successions in escheat enter into his revenues -- that is, those which, for lack of heirs, were to
revert to the Treasury. The viziers, regarding these successions, acted sometimes with justice, but
sometimes also very unjustly.

For the customs duties, we have set forth above when and by which kings they were instituted; some have
remained until the present under the direction of the vizier, but in reality they are useful only to the
Copts, who use them without any right. In our days, at the moment when we live, these rights have doubled
since the time when the emir Gemal el-Din Youssef El-Astadar occupied himself with the royal finances, as
will be explained in the book of the Causes of the ruin.

[PDF p. 353]

As for the gifts, one thus calls the money one receives from the vali, the functionaries, the cadi, the
governor of a country; the first who collected money in this way was El-Saleh ben Raziq, who took it from
the valis of the provinces only; then this due was abolished in the time of El-Aziz ben Salah el-Din, but
for some time only, for it was reestablished by El-Zaher Barqouq, as one will see in the Causes of the
ruin.

As for the protections and the right of surety, these taxes were established in the time of El-Nacer
Farrag, who created for them a bureau and employees; the emirs did likewise, and it was one of the
principal causes of the ruin, as one will see in its place, God willing!

[PDF p. 354]

CHAPTER XL
OF THE PYRAMIDS

The pyramids were formerly very numerous in Egypt; there were a great number of them in the district of
Aboukir: some great, others small; some of silt and bricks, but most of stone; some stepped, others with
a smooth surface. At Gizeh, facing the town of Masr, there were a great quantity of them, all small, which
were destroyed, in the time of the sultan Saleh el-Din Youssef ben Ayoub, by Qaraqouch, who used the
materials thus obtained to build the Citadel of the Mountain, the enclosing wall of Cairo and Masr, and
the bridges of Gizeh. The three greatest are those that still subsist facing Masr. There is agreement
neither on the period of their construction, nor on the name of those who raised them, nor on the cause of
their erection. Many contradictory legends have been recounted on this subject, most of which are without
foundation; for me, I will tell you of their history things that will satisfy and content you, God
willing.

The writer master Ibrahim Waçif Shah, in his History of Egypt and its Marvels, in speaking of Sourid ben
Sahluq ben Seriaq ben Tumidoun ben Badresan ben Housal, one of the kings who governed Egypt before the
flood and who resided in the town of Amsous -- of which there will be question in the chapter of this book
that treats of the towns of Egypt -- says: It is he who raised in Egypt the two great pyramids that are
attributed to Sheddad ben 'Ad: the Copts claim that, thanks to the power of their magic, the Adites could
not penetrate into their country. Here is the cause of the erection of the two pyramids: Three hundred
years before the flood, Sourid had a dream in which it seemed to him that the earth turned over; the men
fled straight before them, the stars fell and collided with one another with a terrible din; Sourid,
frightened, spoke to no one of this dream, but he was convinced that a grave event was going to occur in
the world. Some days after he had

[PDF p. 355]

another dream in which it seemed to him that the fixed stars fell upon the earth in the form of white
birds and, seizing the men in flight, hurled them between two high mountains that closed over them, and
these brilliant stars became somber and dark. Full of terror on his waking, he went to the temple of the
Sun, prostrated himself, rolled his face in the dust, and wept. As soon as the day appeared, he assembled
the chiefs of the priests of all the provinces of Egypt, to the number of 130. He shut himself up with
them and set forth to them what he had seen in his first and his second dream. The priests explained to
the king that an extraordinary event was to occur in the world, and the greatest among them, named
Aqlimoun, said to him: The dreams of kings are not produced without reason, because of the importance of
princes. I will recount to Pharaoh a dream that I too have had and of which I have spoken to no one. It
seemed to me that I was seated with the king in the tower of Amsous; the sky, leaving its place, descended
and drew near our heads, forming above us a sort of dome that enveloped us. The king raised his hands
toward the sky, whose stars intermingled in multiple images and diverse forms; the people ran, seeking a
refuge toward the palace of the king and asking help. The king carried his hands to his head, ordering me
to do likewise, and we were both in a terrible anxiety. And behold, from the tower where we were, we saw a
part of the sky open up; a dazzling light escaped from this breach, the sun appeared there, and we set
about imploring it. And the Sun told us that the sky would return to its first place. I awoke full of
terror, then I fell asleep again and I saw the town of Amsous overturned with its inhabitants, the idols
falling on their heads; men descended from the sky holding in their hands whips of iron with which they
struck the mortals: "Why," I asked them, "do you treat the men thus?" "It is," they answered, "that they
have shown themselves impious toward their God." "Have they not," I said, "some means of redeeming
themselves?" And they answered: "Yes, let him who wishes to be saved go to join the master of the ark."
Thereupon I awoke full of fright. The king then said: "Take the elevations of the stars and see what is to
come." After a minute examination, it was recognized that a flood was to take place, after which would
appear a fire come out of the constellation of the Lion that would burn the world. "See again," said the
king, "if this disaster will reach

[PDF p. 356]

our country." "Yes," they said, "the flood will reach the greatest part of it and it will remain ruined
for long years." "See," said the king, "if this country will become prosperous again as before or if it
will remain always covered by the waters." "The countries," answered the priests, "will return to their
ancient state and will become prosperous again." "And after?" asked the king. "Our country will be
attacked by a king who will exterminate the inhabitants and seize their riches." "And after?" "A barbarous
people, come from the mountains of the Nile, will attack it and make itself master of the greatest part of
the territory." "And after?" "The Nile will be cut off and the country abandoned by its inhabitants." Then
