the king ordered the pyramids to be constructed and corridors to be made in them through which the Nile
would penetrate up to a determined point, then flow off toward certain regions of the west and the Said;
he had the pyramids filled with talismans, marvels, riches, and idols; he had the bodies of the kings
deposited there and, according to his orders, the priests traced on these monuments all the maxims of the
sages; one therefore wrote, on all the possible points of the pyramids -- ceilings, bases, walls -- all
the sciences familiar to the Egyptians, and one drew there the figures of the stars, one wrote there the
names of the drugs and their useful and harmful properties, the science of talismans, of mathematics, of
architecture, all the sciences in a word, and all this was set forth very clearly for those who know their
writing and understand their language.

Having taken this resolution, the king had blocks cut, enormous slabs polished, lead extracted from the
land of the West, and the rocks from the region of Assouan, and the foundations of the three pyramids --
Eastern, Western, and Colored -- were laid. The workers had with them sheets (of papyrus) covered with
writing, and as soon as a stone was cut and dressed, one placed one of these sheets on the stone, to which
one gave a blow, and this blow sufficed to make it traverse a distance of 100 sahmes (200 bow-shots); and
one began again until the stone arrived on the plateau of the pyramids. There, one put in place the slab
in the middle of which one pierced a hole; in this hole, one planted vertically a rod of iron, then one
placed on the first slab a second pierced likewise with a hole into which the iron rod penetrated; then
one made molten lead flow into the hole around the rod in order to fasten the two slabs and render them
immovable; one continued thus until the completion of

[PDF p. 357]

the pyramid. These monuments finished, the king had doors dug in them 40 cubits below the level of the
soil. The door of the Eastern pyramid is turned toward the east and opens 100 cubits from the face of the
pyramid; the door of the Western pyramid is to the west and 100 cubits from the face of the pyramid; the
door of the Colored pyramid is turned toward the south and 100 cubits likewise from the face of the
pyramid. If at this distance one digs (vertically), one finds (at 40 cubits of depth) the door that
permits, by a vaulted and masoned corridor, entering the pyramid. The king calculated, for each of the
pyramids, a height above the soil of 100 cubits, which makes 500 of our present cubits; the length of each
of the faces was also 100 cubits, and the faces were calculated in such a way that the summit was stopped
at 8 of our cubits (from the geometric apex). The construction of these pyramids was begun at a favorable
rising of constellations, chosen by all by common accord. When they were finished, they were covered from
top to bottom with colored brocade, and a feast was instituted for them at which all the inhabitants of
Egypt attended. In the Western pyramid were arranged thirty magazines of colored granite filled with all
sorts of riches and diverse objects: statues of precious stones, magnificent iron tools, rustless arms,
malleable glass, extraordinary talismans, simple and composed drugs, mortal poisons. In the Eastern
pyramid were executed chambers where the sky and the stars were represented, where were heaped what the
ancestors of Sourid had done in the way of statues, the perfumes one burned to the planets, the books that
concerned them, the table of the fixed stars and the table of their revolution in the succession of time,
the list of the events of past epochs subject to their influence, and the moment when one must examine
them to know the future, finally all that concerned Egypt until the end of time; moreover, one deposited
there the basins containing the magic water and other similar things. In the Painted pyramid, one
deposited the bodies of the priests enclosed in coffins of black granite; with each priest was a book
where were retraced the marvels of the art he had exercised, his acts and his life, what had been done in
his time, and what had been and will be from the beginning until the end of time; on each face of the
pyramids were represented personages executing all sorts of works and ranged according to their importance
and their dignity; these

[PDF p. 358]

representations were accompanied by the description of the trades, the tools necessary to them, and all
that concerns them; no science was neglected: all were there described and drawn; one deposited again in
the pyramid the treasures of the planets, what had been given to the stars, and the treasures of the
priests; all this forming enormous and incalculable sums.

To each of the pyramids a guardian was assigned: the Western pyramid was placed under the guard of a
statue in granite mosaic; this statue was standing, holding in its hand something like a javelin, and
coiffed with a viper folded upon itself. As soon as someone approached the statue, the viper darted upon
him, wound itself around his neck, killed him, and returned to its place. The guardian of the Eastern
pyramid was a statue of black stone spotted with black and white, with open and shining eyes; it was
seated on a throne and held a javelin. If someone looked at it, he heard from the side of the statue a
frightful voice that made him fall on his face, and he died there without being able to get up. Over the
Painted pyramid watched a statue in eagle-stone (aetite) placed on a pedestal of similar stone. Whoever
looked at it was drawn toward it, stuck to it, and could not detach himself from it until he was dead. All
this being finished, the pyramids were surrounded with immaterial spirits; victims were slaughtered for
them, a ceremony that was to protect them against whoever would wish to approach them, with the exception
of the initiated who would have accomplished the necessary rites.

The Copts recount in their books that on the flanks of the pyramids is engraved a text that in their
language signifies: "It is I, Sourid, the king who raised these pyramids at such and such a period; I
finished their construction in six years; if anyone of those who come after me claims to be my equal, let
him destroy them in six hundred years; one knows however that it is easier to destroy than to construct. I
have, after their completion, covered them with brocade; let another cover them only with mats." And after
examination it was recognized that the most prolonged times could destroy nothing of them.

The Copts recount again that the spirit attached to the pyramid of the north is a yellow and naked devil
whose mouth is furnished with long teeth; that of the pyramid of the south is a naked woman who shows her
natural parts; she is beautiful, but her mouth is garnished with long teeth; she charms the [...]

[PDF p. 359]

men who look at her, smiles at them, draws them, and makes them lose their reason. The spirit of the
painted pyramid is an old man who holds a church censer in which perfumes burn. Many people have seen on
repeated occasions these spirits making the circuit of the pyramid toward the middle of the day and at
sunset.

After his death, Sourid was buried in the pyramid, and with him his riches and his treasures. It is Sourid
who, according to the Copts, would have built the temples, deposited treasures in them, engraved on their
walls the sciences, and given them as guardians spirits charged with protecting them against whoever might
wish to destroy them. As for the pyramids of Dachour, they were, it is said, raised by Shaddat ben 'Adim
with stones cut formerly by his father. According to some authors, this Shaddat would be the same as
Haddah ben 'Ad; but those who refuse to admit that the Adites entered Egypt fail to recognize the name of
Shaddat ben 'Adim and say Shaddat ben 'Ad, a name they have much more often occasion to pronounce than the
other, which is not of frequent use; according to those, a single (foreign) king would have penetrated
into Egypt and subdued its inhabitants: this king is Bokht Nasr (Nebuchadnezzar). But God is the most
learned!

In his book entitled News of the Times and of Those Whom Misfortunes Have Annihilated, Abou-l-Hassan
El-Maç'oudi recounts that the caliph Abdallah Al-Mamoun, ben Haroun El-Rachid, during his journey in
Egypt, having gone to visit the pyramids, had the desire to demolish one to know what it enclosed. "It is
impossible," he was told. "It is absolutely necessary to open one," he answered. And the breach that is
still gaping today was made for him; one employed for this fire, vinegar, levers; smiths worked at it and
spent considerable sums on it. The thickness of the wall was about 20 cubits; having reached the end of
this wall, they found at the bottom of the hole a green basin filled with minted gold; there were 1,000
dinars in it, each dinar weighing an ounce. Al-Mamoun admired the purity of this gold and, having had the
sum of the expenses caused by the breach made in the pyramid established, it was found that the gold thus
discovered was the absolute equivalent of this sum. The caliph was filled with astonishment in seeing that
the ancients had been able to know precisely the sum that would be spent and the precise place where the
basin of dinars would be found. This basin was, it is said, of emerald; Al-Mamoun had it carried to his
treasury, and it was one of the most astonishing marvels fabricated in Egypt.

[PDF p. 360]

For long years, use was made of the breach of Al-Mamoun, and a number of people penetrated there and
followed the slope thus arranged; some returned safe and sound, others perished. One day, a score of young
men gathered to penetrate there and prepared for this effect all that was necessary -- foods, drinks,
ropes, candles, etc. They engaged in the corridor and saw there bats as big as vultures that struck their
faces. Then one of them was lowered by means of ropes, but the opening of the well closed over him; they
made all their efforts to pull him out and ceased only when at the end of their strength. They then heard
a frightful voice that made them faint. When they came to themselves, they left the pyramid, and while they
were seated, astonished at what had happened to them, behold, their companion came out of the earth before
them, set about pronouncing words they could not understand, then fell dead. They took him and carried him
off, but the police seized them and led them to the vali, to whom they recounted their adventure. Then
they asked the explanation of the words their companion had pronounced before dying, and they were
translated thus: "Thus will be punished whoever seeks what he must not know." This explanation was given
to them by a man of the Said.

"I have reflected," says Aly ben Radouan the physician, "on the construction of the pyramids, and I have
concluded that profound theoretical and practical knowledge in architecture and mechanics had been needed
by those who had traced the square of their base, cut the male and female stones, and coated the whole
with marine plaster, so as to make the construction rise to the point where it was possible to raise heavy
weights. The more the construction rose, the more it went narrowing, in such a way that the surface of the
square (of the second course), parallel to the square of the base, formed a square smaller than that of
the base itself. Then on this second course was traced another square narrower still by the quantity
necessary for the heavy weights to be raised there, and at each course a stone perfectly fitted,
alternately male and female, was deposited, forming a course equal to the preceding; one continued thus
until the point where it was no longer possible to continue; then the height was truncated and the
projecting edges, used for the elevation of the heavy materials, were beaten down, and in doing this
operation from the top to the bottom, they obtained a (smooth) block forming the pyramid."

[PDF p. 361]

The first pyramid, measured according to the cubit still in use today in Egypt for construction, counts
for the length of each face (side of the base) 400 cubits, which makes in black cubits -- whose length is
24 fingers -- 500 cubits, and the base being square, the sides are equal as well as the angles. Two of
these sides are parallel to the meridian line, the two others are parallel to the east-west line, and each
side is 500 black cubits. The apothem descending from the summit of the pyramid to the middle of the side
of the base is 470 cubits and would be, if the pyramid were complete, also 500 cubits. The faces of the
pyramid form four triangles; these four triangles are isosceles, and each of their sides would measure, if
the pyramid were complete, 560 cubits, and the four triangles would be joined by their summit at a single
point that would be the summit of the pyramid. These diverse dimensions entail for the height a value of
430 cubits; it is on this line that the centers of gravity are found. Each of the triangles forming the
faces of the pyramid measures a total surface of 125,000 square cubits, and in making the total of their
surface, one obtains, for the total surface of the pyramid, 500,000 black cubits. And I have never heard
it said that there was in the world a more colossal construction, nor more beautiful, nor more grandiose.
And God knows better!

Al-Mamoun, having opened a breach in this pyramid, discovered there a corridor that led, by a sloping path,
to a chamber of cubic form; on the floor was a coffin of marble, still in place today, for no one has been
able to draw it out. It is according to this that Galen recounts that the pyramids were tombs. Here is what
he says on this subject toward the end of the fifth book of his treatise on Hygiene: "They give the name
of haram to whoever has reached that age (old age); this name is derived from that of the pyramids (al-ahram)
in which they will soon have to be placed." El-Hauqali, in his Description of Egypt, says: "One sees in
this country the two pyramids that have not their likes on the surface of the earth, neither in Muslim
country nor in infidel country; one has never made and one will never make any like them. One of the
Abbasids read the following phrase on one of them: 'I have built them both; let him who claims the title
of powerful king demolish them! to demolish is however easier than to construct.' And the Abbasid attempted
it (I believe it is a question here of Al-Mamoun or El-Mo'tassem),

[PDF p. 362]

but the revenues of Egypt could not have sufficed for the task, and yet in his time, these revenues,
collected with equity, justice, benevolence toward the subjects, the Nile reaching 17 cubits and 6
fingers, amounted to 4,257,000 dinars, the tax being 2 dinars per feddan. He therefore abandoned his
project and occupied himself with it no more.

At the limit of the territory of Fostat, to the west of the Nile, one meets colossal constructions, in
considerable number, and which are spread even into the Said; they are called pyramids; but they could not
be compared to the two pyramids situated facing Fostat and at two parasangs from this locality. The height
of each of these two pyramids is 400 cubits, their width is equal to the height; they are constructed in
stone of El-Kaddan; each stone has a length and a thickness of 10 to 8 cubits according to the place it
was to occupy per the exigencies of the technique; for these two pyramids become narrower as they rise, so
as to leave at the summit a surface equal to that which would be necessary to permit a camel to kneel; the
faces of these pyramids are covered with Greek writings. It has been claimed that these monuments were
tombs, but that is not exact; their constructor had them raised only because he had foreseen the flood and
knew that this cataclysm would destroy all that was found on the surface of the earth, with the exception
of what could be conserved in edifices such as these two pyramids; thus he stored in them all he could of
precious objects and treasures, and the flood having occurred, then having withdrawn, all the content of
the pyramids became the property of Bensar ben Mesraïm ben Ham ben Nouh (Noah). The later kings converted
these monuments into magazines and established deposits in them. And God knows it better than anyone.

Abou Ya'koub Mohammed ben Ishaq El-Nadim, the paper-maker, in his book entitled The Index, says regarding
Hermes El-Baheli: "There is no agreement on his account; he was, it is said, one of the seven guardians
charged with the surveillance of the seven temples (of the planets), and to whom was assigned the guard of
the temple of Atared (Mercury) whose name he took, for Atared in the Chaldean language signifies Hermes.
It is recounted that for certain motives he transported himself to Egypt where he reigned and had children,
among whom Ta, Sa, Ashmoun, Atrib, and

[PDF p. 363]

Qouft; that he was the wisest of his time, and that after his death he was buried in the monument known at
Masr under the name of Abou-Hermes, but to which most of the Greeks give the name of El-Harameïn (the two
pyramids), for one of them is his tomb and the other the tomb of his wife. According to others, the latter
would be the tomb of the son of Hermes, a son who would have succeeded him after his death.

These monuments -- I mean the pyramids -- have a length of 480 hachemite cubits by a width of also 480
cubits. From the base, the construction goes narrowing and, at the summit, the dimensions (of the plateau)
are no more than 40 cubits (on each face), and this is done intentionally and by calculation. In the
middle of the plateau is constructed a pretty chamber, in the interior of which rises a sort of mausoleum.
At the summit of the tomb are two blocks perfectly polished and magnificent, surmounted by two stone
statues representing a man and a woman who face each other. The man holds in his hand a stone tablet
covered with writing, and the woman a mirror and a tablet of gold ornamented with admirable sculptures.
Between the two pedestals is a stone vase closed with a lid of gold; if one lifts the lid, one perceives a
sort of odorless and dried pitch, in which is placed a box of gold enclosing a mass of blood that takes,
on contact with air, the coagulation particular to blood, then dries up. The tombs are closed with stone
lids which, once withdrawn, let one see in one of them a man lying on his back, perfectly conserved and
dried and whose flesh is still apparent as well as the hair; in the neighboring sarcophagus is the body of
a woman in the same position and in the same state as that of the man. In this terrace is pierced a
corridor of a man's height, sinking like an underground passage; the vault of it is made of stones, and
one sees there portraits and statues lying or standing, and quantities of other things whose signification
is not known.

The ulema Mouafeq el-Din Abd el-Latif ben Abou-l-'Az Youssef ben Abou-l-Barakat Mohammed ben 'Aly ben Sa'd
El-Baghdadi, better known under the name of Ibn El-Moutahan, recounts, in his History, that one day a
foreign infidel came to the king El-Aziz Othman ben Salah el-Din ben Youssef and persuaded him that under
the small pyramid was a treasure. One sent stonecutters [...]

[PDF p. 364]

of stones and a multitude of soldiers who set about demolishing it and spent at this work months and
months; but, unable to come to the end of it, they abandoned it; the sums spent and the technical
researches employed in this enterprise were considerable. And today, whoever might see the mass of stones
removed from the pyramid would believe that it is completely destroyed, but in looking at the pyramid
itself, one discovers there only insignificant breaches. I had the occasion to see the stonecutters, and I
asked their chief if he could put these stones back in their place. "Even though," he answered me, "the
sultan gave us a thousand dinars per stone, it would be impossible for us."

Abou-l-Hassan El-Maçaoudi, in his Prairies of Gold, expresses himself thus: "As for the pyramids, their
height is astonishing and their construction marvelous. They are covered with several sorts of
inscriptions in the diverse languages of peoples past and disappeared. People versed in the science of
measures assure that the vertical height of the great pyramid is at least 400 cubits, and that as the
construction rises, it narrows progressively. The width is approximately equal to the height; its faces
are covered with texts and tables relative to the sciences, to the magical recipes, to the secrets of
nature; one of these inscriptions says: We have built them (the pyramids), and if some king claims to
equal us and attain our power, let him destroy them and efface their trace! To destroy is however easier
than to construct, and to disaggregate easier than to unite."

It is recounted that a Muslim king had the idea of destroying one, but the revenues of Egypt could not
have sufficed for it, for it was of stone and marble. These pyramids were tombs of kings. Formerly, when a
king died, his body was placed in a stone vat, named by the Egyptians and the Syrians geroun, which was
closed; then one constructed the base of a pyramid according to the dimensions established per the chosen
height, and one deposited the sarcophagus in the middle of the pyramid, and over it one built a vault,
then one raised the construction according to the determined dimensions, reserving the entrance of the
pyramid below the pyramid itself; from the door started a corridor vaulted in stone whose underground
length was 100 cubits at most. Each of these pyramids has a door that leads there, as we have just said.
One constructed some of these pyramids

[PDF p. 365]

with edged steps like staircases; when the construction was finished, one smoothed the faces from top to
bottom. Such was their method of construction, and for this they needed strength, patience, and obedience.

In the book of the Constructions and Marvels, it is said that the two pyramids situated to the west of
Fostat Masr are monuments that can count among the marvels of the world. Each of them is 400 cubits in
height by as much in width; they are constructed in enormous stones and exposed to the four winds, each of
the edges of their angles facing one of the winds; the wind that has the most influence on them is that of
the south named merisi. One of these pyramids is the tomb of A'adimoun and the other that of Hermes;
between these two personages there is nearly a thousand years, A'adimoun being the elder of the two. The
inhabitants of Egypt -- that is, the Copts -- claim that these two personages were two prophets appeared
before the coming of Christianity; this opinion is conformable to that the Sabeans profess on the subject
of the prophets, but not with that one must have regarding the high prophecy; but for the Copts, the two
prophets in question were pure souls, holy, exempt from terrestrial corruptions and provided with the
celestial inspiration. Thus they knew the events before they had occurred and were ignorant of nothing of
the secrets of the world and the rest. Among the Arabs of the Yemen, some consider the two pyramids as the
tombs of Sheddad ben 'Ad and another of their kings who conquered Egypt formerly; those are pure Arabs of
the tribe of Amalek and others. But, according to what we have just said of the doctrine of the Sabeans,
they are the tombs of pure bodies.

Abou Zeid El-Balkhi found, in the midst of the inscriptions traced on the pyramid, a certain line that was
translated into Arabic and that signified: "These two pyramids were raised when the falling Eagle was in
the Crab (Cancer)." The calculation has been made of the time elapsed since that moment until the hijra of
the Prophet, and it was found 2 times 36,000 solar years -- that is, 72,000 solar years.

El-Hamadani, in his book Of the Crowns, says: Of all that was submerged by the flood, nothing has
subsisted but the village of Nehaouend, found such as it had been before the cataclysm, and the pyramids
of the Said.

[PDF p. 366]

Abou Mohammed Abd Allah ben Abd El-Rahim El-Qisi, in his book Present of the Hearts, reports that the
pyramids are square by the base and triangular by their faces and that they are eighteen in number. Facing
Fostat there are three, of which the principal has a perimeter of 2,000 cubits, each side being 500
cubits; its height is 500 cubits also. Each of the stones that composes it has 30 cubits of thickness by a
width of 10 cubits; the disposition and the cut of these stones are perfect. Near the town of the Pharaoh
of Joseph is another pyramid still greater and more imposing, its perimeter being 3,000 cubits and its
height 750; the stones of which it is built measure each 50 cubits. In the vicinity of the town of the
Pharaoh of Moses is a pyramid still greater and more extraordinary; finally another pyramid known under
the name of pyramid of Madoum (Meïdoum) is similar to a mountain and is composed of five stages. Al-Mamoun
opened the greatest of the pyramids situated facing Fostat, entered the corridor of this edifice, and
penetrated into a chamber square at the base and vaulted at the summit, very great and in the middle of
which was dug a well of 10 cubits of depth. This well was square, and the men who descended there met on
each face a door leading to a vast hall filled with dead bodies each of which was wrapped in a shroud
longer than would be a hundred robes (sewn end to end). Time has altered these cadavers, which have become
black; these bodies, which are not bigger than ours, have lost nothing of their tissue nor of their hair;
one finds there no body of old men or men with white hair; these bodies were still solid, and no one could
detach a single limb from them, but they were extremely light, time having rendered them as little heavy
as dry straw. In this well were thus four chambers filled with cadavers and enormous bats. The ancients
buried likewise all the animals in the sand, and, for me, I found a roll of cloth forming a big volume of
more than a cubit of thickness. The cloth had been worn by time; but, having unrolled it, I found a piece
of linen intact and white like a turban, with some traces of red silk, and finally, in the interior, a
dead hoopoe to which was missing neither a feather nor any part of its body and such as if it had died
recently. In the chamber reserved in the interior of the pyramid is a door that leads to the

[PDF p. 367]

summit of the monument; the corridor has no stairs and measures nearly five spans in width. It is
recounted that in the time of El-Mamoun a man having penetrated there arrived at a small chamber where was
a statue of a man in green stone like the dahang. This statue was brought to El-Mamoun. It had a lid that
was withdrawn, and one found the body of a man clad in a cuirass of gold incrusted with all sorts of
precious stones; on the chest was placed a sword of an inestimable price, and near the head was a red ruby
the size of a hen's egg that lit up like a flame and that Al-Mamoun took for himself. The statue from
which this dead man had been drawn was thrown near the door of the king's palace at Cairo, where I saw it
in the year 511 [5 May 1117 to 23 April 1118].

The cadi El-Galil Abou Abd Allah Mohammed ben Salamat El-Qoda'ï says: Aly ben El-Hassan ben Khalaf ben
Qadid reports the following fact on the authority of Yahia ben Othman ben Salèh, who had it from Mohammed
ben Aly ben Sakhr El-Tamimi: An inhabitant of the village of Qoft, very versed in the affairs and the
history of Egypt, and who occupied himself with its ancient books and its ruins, recounted to me having
found in an antique volume a text that said, regarding the pyramids: Some people, having cleared a tomb in
the convent of Abou-Hermes, found there a dead man wrapped in his shroud and bearing on his chest a paper
rolled in a cloth. Having drawn it out, they looked at the writing but could understand nothing of it, the
paper being written in the ancient language of the Egyptians. They sought someone who could read it to
them but in vain. They were then told that at the convent of Qlimoun in the Fayoum was a monk who knew
this kind of writing. They went in search of this monk, doubting much that he could explain it to them,
but he read it, and here is what the text signified: This book was written in the first year of the
emperor Diocletian, and we have copied it from a book itself copied in the first year of the emperor
Philip. This emperor had had it copied from sheets of gold on which the writing was separated letter by
letter. A translation was made of the original book for Philip by the two Coptic brothers Eïlou and
Yertsa. The emperor having asked them how they knew how to read things the others were ignorant of, they
recounted that they were the descendants of one of the ancient Egyptians who alone

[PDF p. 368]

had not been drowned by the flood; that he owed his salvation to this circumstance, that, alone among the
Egyptians, he went to Noah and believed in him, and that Noah took him with him in the ark; that, the
water of the flood having withdrawn, he came to Egypt with some of the descendants of Cham (Ham), son of
Noah, and that he remained there until his death; that his son inherited his knowledge of the Egyptian
language and that they had inherited it likewise, this science transmitting itself in the family from
eldest to eldest. The duration of the time elapsed until the copy of Philip was 2,372 years. As for the
one who had the copy made on sheets of gold in writing separated letter by letter such as Philip found it,
his epoch was separated from that of the original manuscript (?) by 1,785 years. The copied book said this:
We have examined what the stars prognosticated and we have seen that a scourge would descend from the sky
or come out of the earth; when this event was certain for us, we sought what it would be and we discovered
that the water would cover the earth, destroying its animals and its plants. Being altogether certain of
the event, we said to our king Sourid ben Sahlouq: Have lodgings constructed for us, a tomb for you and
another for the members of your family. Then the king raised for the others the Eastern pyramid, for his
father Houheït the Western pyramid, and for the son of Houheït the Painted pyramid. One raised the lodgings
(?) in the Delta and in the Said, and we represented on their walls the profound sciences, astronomy and
prognostication, the stars, alchemy, the arts, medicine, and all the useful or harmful things, succinctly
explained and easy to understand for those who know our writing and our language. The arrival of the
misfortune that threatened the earth was to take place at the moment when the heart of the Lion would be
in the first minute of the head of the Crab, while the planets would be at the following points of the
sky: the Sun and the Moon, at the first minute of the head of the Ram; Qouris at 1° 28' of the Ram; Raouis
at 29° 28' of the Whale; Aouis at 29° 3' of the Whale; Afrad and Batn at 28° and some minutes of the
Whale; Hermès at 27° and some minutes of the Whale, and El-Gouzher in the Balance, the apogee of the Moon
being at 5° and some minutes of the Lion. Then we studied what would happen after this catastrophe and
what the world would have to bear of calamities, and we discovered that the planets presaged a [...]

[PDF p. 369]

new scourge descending from the sky and that would be the very contrary of the first. This scourge would
be the fire that would set ablaze the four corners of the earth. In seeking the period at which this
catastrophe would occur, we saw that it would be at the moment when the heart of the Lion would be at the
last minute of the 15th degree of the Lion, and that Eilis would be, in the same minute, followed by
Qouris of the triangle of the Sagittarius, that Raouis-Jupiter would be at the beginning of the Lion at
the end of its evolution and with it Aouis, in the same minute that Salis would be in the Aquarius facing
Eilis-Sun and with it the tail in 22° (?). Then would occur a long eclipse of the Sun, the Moon walking
parallel to it; Hermès-Atared would be at its aphelion, having facing it the Moqabalin, Afrad and Batn
following the direct route, while Hermès would be on the return. The king asked: "Have you other
misfortunes to announce to us?" They said: "If the heart of the Lion is stopped at the ninth of its
revolution, there will remain on the earth no living being; all will be burned and will perish. If the
course of this star is achieved, the bonds that hold the sky will be broken and it will fall on the earth."
"And on what day will the displacement of the sky take place?" asked the king. "Two days after the
beginning of the movement of the firmament," they answered. Such was what was on the paper.

And when Sourid died, he was buried in the Eastern pyramid, Houheït in the Western pyramid, and Krours in
the pyramid whose base is in stone of Assouan and the summit in stone of Kaddan. These pyramids have
entrances made in underground vaults; the length of each corridor is 150 cubits. The door of the Eastern
pyramid opens to the north, that of the vault of the Western pyramid opens to the south. And in the
pyramids are heaped gold and emeralds in innumerable quantity.

The one who translated the Coptic book into Arabic made the calculation of the dates until the Sunday
first day of Thot (or first day of the rising of the sun) of the year 225 of the Arab years, and the
figure reached 4,321 solar years; then he calculated how many years had elapsed from the flood until that
day, and he found 1,741 years, 59 days, 13 hours, 56 minutes, 51 seconds, and subtracting this last number
from the first, he obtained as remainder 399 years, 205 days, [footnote: All this passage is incorrect in
the text of Boulaq and cannot lend itself to an exact interpretation.]

[PDF p. 370]

10 hours and 2 minutes and 1 second, by which he knew that the book in question had been written before
the flood, precisely the same number of years, days, hours, minutes, and seconds. [footnote: There is, in
the text of Boulaq, error in the data.]

As for the pyramid of the convent of Abou-Hermès, it is the tomb of Qarias, an Egyptian cavalier who was
worth by himself a thousand cavaliers. If he met a like number of cavaliers, these could not resist him
and took flight. At his death, the king made a great mourning and all the people were plunged in grief; he
was buried at the convent of Abou-Hermès, and over his tomb the stepped pyramid was built. The earth and
the stones that served for the construction come from the Fayoum, as it is easy to ascertain on
examination; one meets this earth indeed only in the Fayoum, and one finds no similar earth, neither at
Memphis nor at Ousim.

The tomb of the king under whom this Qarias lived is the great pyramid situated to the north of the
Deïr-Abou-Hermès. It has at its entrance a stele in stone of Kaddan, bearing an inscription in blue
letters; this stele has two cubits of height and one cubit of width, and is all covered with a writing
similar to that of the temples. One accedes to the door of the pyramid by steps of which some are still
completely intact. In this pyramid are accumulated the precious objects of its master, gold and emeralds;
but the door of it is obstructed by stones fallen from the summit, and if one climbs on these stones, one
sees on the other side a sort of chamber.

Ibn Afir reports, on the authority of his masters, that Giad ben Miad ben Shamr ben Sheddad ben 'Ad ben
Ous ben Arem ben Sam ben Nouh reigned at Alexandria, which was then called Aram Zat El-'Amad. His reign
was very long and lasted 300 years; it was he who, after his arrival in Egypt, constructed the pyramids
and wrote upon them: "I am Giad ben Miad ben Shamr ben Sheddad, the skillful sower of the valleys, inspired
by God in his way; it is I who gathered the rocks in the region, I the assembler of armies, the raiser of
columns, the destroyer of the ungrateful. (My tomb) will be discovered by a people who will have a prophet
of the name of Hamad, and that will happen when the country of countries (Egypt) is attacked by seven
chiefs of black tribes. The date of this inscription is 1,400 years."

[PDF p. 371]

Ibn Afir and Ibn Abd El-Hakem say: In the time of Sheddad ben 'Ad were built the pyramids, according to
what the historians recount, and we have found among none of the scholars of Egypt the profound knowledge
of the pyramids, nor certain notions.

Mohammed ben Abd Allah ben Abd El-Hakem says: I cannot believe that the pyramids were not constructed
before the flood; if they had been after, some people would know it.

Mohammed ben Shabremat El-Garhami says: The Amalekites, chased from Mecca by Garham, took refuge in Egypt
where they raised the pyramids, constructed fortresses, and edified all sorts of marvels; they remained in
Egypt until the moment when they were expelled from it by Malek ben Darr El-Khaza'i.

Mohammed ben Abd El-Hakem says: To the west of the pyramids were four hundred towns, without counting the
villages, from the frontier of Egypt to the Maghreb.

Ibn Afir says: Our old men of Egypt have always recognized that the pyramids had been built by Sheddad ben
'Ad; it is also this king who dug grottoes where treasures were buried (?). The people of that epoch
believed in the resurrection, and when an individual died, one buried with him all he possessed; if the
dead man was a worker, one buried with him the tools of his trade; the Sabeans made the pilgrimage of the
pyramids.

Abou-l-Rihan El-Birouni, in the book entitled Traces That Subsist of the Elapsed Centuries, says: The
Persians and the magi deny the flood; some Persians however admit it, but they claim that this cataclysm,
which occurred in the epoch of Timhurts, had effect only in Syria and in the West, and did not extend to
all the inhabited earth; according to them, it would not have passed (to the east) the wadi of Helouan and
would have left intact the empires of the East; as for the Westerners, forewarned of the disaster by their
sages, they would have raised constructions in the manner of the pyramids of Egypt, to take refuge there
at the moment of the cataclysm. The traces of the flood and the height attained by its waters are still
seen at mid-height of the pyramids, limits they could not pass. It is claimed that, when the waters of the
flood had withdrawn, one found, after the recession of the waters, only the village of Nehaouend, which
had remained absolutely similar to what

[PDF p. 372]

it was before, and the pyramids and the temples of Egypt; these had been built by the first Hermes, the
one the Arabs name Idris, to whom God had inspired the science of the stars, and who, in consulting them,
had foreseen the catastrophe that threatened the earth and would leave subsisting only some persons to
whom the knowledge of the sciences would be necessary. This is why, aided by the people of Egypt, he
raised the pyramids and the temples where he retraced the description of the sciences.

Abou-l-Solt El-Andalousi, in his opuscule, says in speaking of the character of the Egyptians: According
to the state of this people, it seems that there was among it a caste of scholars, and in particular of
architects and astronomers. This is proved by all they have left of marvelous constructions, such as the
pyramids and the temples, whose ruins overturn the most perspicacious mind and stupefy the most
clear-sighted imagination. One sees there the debris of a work that astonishes and confounds. Thus Abou-l-Ala
Ahmed ben Soliman El-Ma'ri was able to say in the poetry he composed on the death of his father:

[verses:] The firmest mind loses of its firmness, and the most upright judgment loses of its rectitude,
and the eloquent people, each time that they see a beautiful thing, regard it as the work of the genies.

And what more astonishing and more marvelous, after the power of God and the works of the Most High, than
the power that raised these gigantic constructions composed of colossal stones whose base is square, the
form conical, the height 319 cubits, and limited by four triangular faces whose bases are equal, each of
them being 460 cubits! And despite this enormous mass, thanks to the perfection of the work, to the
technical precision, to the beauty of the ensemble, they have nothing to fear from the breath of the winds
nor from the rain of the clouds, nor from the earthquakes. This description applies equally to each of the
two pyramids that rise facing Fostat on the western bank of the Nile, such as we have seen them, and which
are counted among the marvels of Egypt. And there exists in the world no monument for which the effects of
the days and the nights are not to be feared, except the pyramids which, according to me, are formidable
for the day and for the night. The

[PDF p. 373]

pyramids rise above the soil of Egypt, dominate its marshes, and sink into its atmosphere. It is of them
that Abou-l-Taïb El-Moutanabbi wished to speak in these verses:

[verses:] Where is the one who built the two pyramids? What is his people? When did he live? When did he
die? The monuments survive some time those who inhabited them, then, struck by annihilation, like them they
disappear.

One day we had gone to the pyramids, and after having made the circuit of them and examined them well, our
admiration redoubled, and one of us said:

[verses:] By your life! What have you seen more marvelous in all that you have seen than the pyramids of
Egypt? Raised toward the sky and plunging into the atmosphere higher than the phoenix and the eagle, they
stand upright, dominating the earth like two breasts raised on a chest.

It is claimed that the pyramids are the tombs of illustrious kings who wished to distinguish themselves
thus after their death, as they had distinguished themselves during their life, and to render their memory
imperishable during the duration of the centuries and the length of the ages.

When the caliph Al-Mamoun came to Egypt, he gave the order to open one of the pyramids; one attacked one
of those that face Fostat; after unheard-of pains and a considerable fatigue, one arrived in the interior
of the pyramid, which one found all sown with wells and arduous ramps; the passage was perilous; finally,
at the end was a cubic chamber of about 8 cubits on a side. In the middle of the chamber was a vat of
marble closed with a lid that was removed; and one found in the vat only a cadaver corrupted as a
consequence of the length of the centuries. Al-Mamoun then prescribed opening no other pyramid, the
expense made for the opening of this breach having been, it is asserted, extraordinarily considerable.

Some think that the first Hermes, the one surnamed the Triple, because of the three gifts he possessed --
prophecy, royalty, and wisdom -- is the same as the one the Hebrews name Khanoukh (Enoch) ben Bared ben
Mahlaïl ben Fatian ben [...]

[PDF p. 374]

Anouch ben Seth ben Adam; it is the same as Idris. He foresaw, according to the position of the planets,
the arrival of a flood that would submerge the entire earth; he therefore had constructed a great number
of pyramids where treasures were deposited, books of science, and all that he feared to see annihilated
and disappear and that he wished to guarantee from destruction. It is also said that their constructor was
a king named Sourid ben Sahlouq ben Siriaq. According to others, the personage who raised the pyramids
situated facing Fostat would have been Sheddad ben 'Ad, who would have constructed them following a dream.
The Copts, who contest the invasion of the Amalekites in Egypt, attribute the construction of these
monuments to Sourid, also following a dream announcing to him that a calamity would descend from the sky;
it is a question there of the flood. Sourid, say the Copts, raised the two pyramids in the space of six
months, covered them with multicolored brocade, and engraved this inscription: "I have built them in six
months: tell those who come after me to destroy them in 600 years; yet it is easier to demolish than to
construct. I have covered them with brocade of color; let my successors cover them with mats; yet mats are
more common than brocade." We have examined the faces of these pyramids, they are cut with longitudinal
lines forming narrow and parallel bands all filled with a writing very visible but that one no longer
knows how to read and whose signification one no longer understands. In sum, it is a work so marvelous that
to wish to describe it in detail and with precision would be the contrary of what Aly ben Abbas El-Roumi
recommends, although there is no point of resemblance between the two objects, which are on the contrary
very different:

[verses:] If you wish to describe something, do not exaggerate, diminish rather; if you exaggerate, it
gives one to think that you stray much from the truth; and one will diminish in proportion to how much you
have exaggerated, to bring back what one has not seen to what one knows.

It is reported that El-Mamoun had a man mount on the great pyramid provided with a rope 1,000 royal cubits
long, each of which is worth 1 cubit and two fifths. The perimeter of the base, each face being equal, was
400 cubits for each face. It took to mount on the pyramid three hours

[PDF p. 375]

of day, and the man on reaching the summit found that it terminated in a plateau of a surface equal to the
place eight kneeling camels would occupy.

The bodies buried in the pyramid were, it is said, wrapped in cloths gnawed by time and of which there
remained only the threads of gold; the drugs with which they were impregnated formed a mass of myrrh and
aloes of the thickness of a span.

It is recounted that one discovered, in a certain place of these pyramids, a vaulted portico pierced with
three doors giving into three chambers. Each door had 10 cubits of height by 5 of width; it was of marble
cut and perfectly fitted, and on the lintel was traced an inscription of blue color, indecipherable. One
spent three days trying to open these doors; at the end one noticed, about 10 cubits facing them, three
columns of marble in each of which was a hole dug toward the summit; each hole contained the statue of a
different bird: in the first column the image of a dove in green stone; in that of the center the image of
a vulture in yellow stone; in the third the image of a cock in red stone. One displaced the vulture and
the door facing it displaced itself; one lifted the vulture and the door lifted itself likewise, and it
was so heavy that a hundred men would not have succeeded in carrying it. One removed the two other statues
and the two other doors lifted themselves. One penetrated into the central chamber in which were three
beds of transparent and luminous stone and on these three beds three bodies covered with three robes, and
near the head of each of them a book in unknown characters. In the second chamber were arranged quantities
of stone shelves supporting stone baskets containing vases of gold of a marvelous work and incrusted with
precious stones. In the third chamber were also found shelves and stone baskets in which were deposited
instruments of war and a great number of arms. One of the swords was measured, it had no less than seven
spans; one of the cuirasses measured eighteen spans. Al-Mamoun had all that had been found in these
chambers carried off, then the birds having been put back in their place, the three doors closed again and
resumed their former position.

The number of the pyramids amounted, it is said, to eighteen, of which three facing

[PDF p. 376]

Ghizeh; the greatest of these has a perimeter of 2,000 cubits; it is square and each of its sides is 500
cubits. Al-Mamoun, having opened it, found there, it is said, a vat of stone closed with a slab and filled
with gold; on the lid was an inscription that was translated into Arabic and signified: "We have made this
pyramid in a thousand days; we give another a thousand years to destroy it, and one knows that it is
easier to demolish than to construct. We have hung it entirely with brocade, let another try to hang it
with mats; it is however easier to procure mats than brocade. And on each side we have deposited a sum
equal to that which will be spent to arrive this far." Al-Mamoun having had the count established of what
had been spent to penetrate this far, one found in the vat an equivalent sum, neither more nor less.

It is recounted again that he found there a statue of a man in green stone similar to the daheng, closed
with a lid in stone similar to the adouat; when the lid was withdrawn, one found in the statue the body of
a man clad in a cuirass of gold ornamented with precious stones, and on his chest was extended a long
sword of an inestimable price; near his head was a red ruby as big as a hen's egg. Al-Mamoun took it,
saying: "This is worth more than gold." Some Egyptian chroniclers affirm that the green statue where this
body was found remained standing near the palace of the king in the town of Masr until the year 611 [13
May 1214 to 1 May 1215] of the hijra.

Near the town of Far'oun (Pharaoh) were two pyramids, and near Meïdoum was another, the last.

In the year 579 [26 April 1183 to 13 April 1184] of the hijra one discovered on the territory of Busir,
province of Ghizeh, the house of Hermes. The qadi Ibn El-Shahrzouri opened it and drew from it all sorts
of things: rams, monkeys, frogs in bezoar, vases in daheng, and statues of bronze.

Ibn Khordadabah says regarding the Marvels of the Constructions: The two pyramids of Egypt each have a
thickness of 400 cubits, and the more they rise, the more they narrow. Both are of alabaster and marble;
their height is 400 cubits by 400 cubits of width, and on their faces

[PDF p. 377]

have been retraced by hand all the art of magic and all the marvelous secrets of medicine; there is in
addition this inscription: "I, I built them; let the king who proclaims himself powerful destroy them; and
to destroy is easier than to construct!" One has established the estimate of the expenses necessary for
this work and one has recognized that the revenues of the whole world could not have sufficed for it.

In the book entitled Marvels of the Constructions, it is said, regarding the pyramids: This kind of
construction is particular to Egypt, and one finds nowhere else anything similar. One would imagine, in
seeing them, that they are the two breasts of Egypt, and the stranger who penetrates into this country
could imagine that they were put there by the generosity of the inhabitants as a sign of hospitality. If
one sees them only from afar and one is told some facts that concern them, one imagines that they are
fables. The accounts that relate to the pyramids, to their description, to their measures abound. They are
very numerous; all on the territory of Ghizeh and on a line passing through Masr el-Qadima and long three
days of march. At Abou-Sir there are many. Some are great, others small; some are of earth, others of
bricks, but the greatest number is of stone; some are stepped, others with smooth faces.

There were still at Ghizeh a great number of very small pyramids; but, in the time of the sultan Salah
el-Din Youssef ben Ayoub, they were destroyed by the eunuch Baha el-Din Qarâqoûsh, who employed the
materials of them for the construction of the bridges of Ghizeh. Of these pyramids there remain no more
than hills of rubble.

As for the pyramids of which one always speaks, they are the three pyramids that are situated at Ghizeh,
directly facing Fostat; there is between them a certain distance, and each of them presents one of its
angles to the east. Two are very great and of the same dimension, they are near one another and built in
white stones; the third is smaller than the two others by about a quarter, but it is built in spotted rose
granite, of an extraordinary force and solidity and on which the iron itself leaves a trace only with
great difficulty. In comparison with the two others it seems small; but, if one looks at it in isolation
and abstracting from the two others, the sight is frightened and the gaze is troubled to examine it.

[PDF p. 378]

In the construction of the pyramids a truly admirable method was followed, both for the form given to the
monument and for the perfection of the execution; thus they have borne with impunity the passage of time,
while time has had difficulty bearing their duration. In examining them closely, one sees that superior
minds exhausted themselves, that subtle intelligences surpassed themselves, that luminous souls spent for
them all the genius they possessed, and that masters in art edified them as proof of their power, to such a
point that they seem to speak of the superiority of the people who built them, that they recount its
history, set forth its science and its intelligence, and deliver to us something of its life and its
chronicles; and this because they gave the pyramids the form of a cone with a square base and terminated
in a point. One of the particularities of the cone is that the center of gravity is found in the middle,
that the faces lean one on the other, penetrating and supporting one another, for there exists no other
side on which they can lean. The square form has this remarkable, that the breath of the four winds comes
to strike against an angle; now the wind breaks on an angle, which does not happen if it meets a plane
surface.

The geometers claim that the base of each of the two great pyramids has 400 cubits, in black cubits, and
that the platform of the summit presents a surface of 10 cubits on a side. It is recounted that an archer
having launched an arrow toward the summit of one of these pyramids, his arrow did not even reach the
middle of the monument. It is also said that the platform of the summit forms a square of 11 cubits on a
side, in natural cubits, and that one of these pyramids possesses a door by which one can penetrate and
which leads the visitors to narrow paths, to abrupt underground passages, to wells, precipices, etc.; it
is at least what some of those who have visited it report. Many people, pushed by curiosity, do not cease
to enter and descend into the depths, but, without any doubt, they would end by arriving at some place
without exit. As for the cleared and beaten path, it is a ramp that leads to the summit where one meets a
square chamber enclosing a naos of stone; this path was not traced by the constructors, it was pierced by
chance, and it is said that it was Al-Mamoun who had it opened.

People who have followed this route and mounted to the summit have [...]

[PDF p. 379]

recounted, on their return, having seen extraordinary things: the chamber is filled with bats and
encumbered with their filth; these animals attain the size of a pigeon; near the summit are also seen
windows and dormers intended to let pass the air and the light; these openings are cut in enormous stones
measuring each from 10 to 20 cubits of length by 2 to 3 cubits of width and as much of thickness.

What is most marvelous is the admirable arrangement of the superposed stones; it is impossible to do
better, to such a point that between two stones we could not succeed in introducing either a needle or
even a hair. Between the stones is spread an earth of blue color whose nature and composition one is
ignorant of, and on the surface of the stones are traced inscriptions in unknown antique characters; no
one in Egypt has heard it said that anyone understood them. These inscriptions are so numerous and so
extensive that if one transported them onto paper, they would cover ten thousand sheets. I have read, in
certain old Sabean books, that one of these pyramids was the tomb of Adamoun and the other the tomb of
Hermès; according to them, these two personages would have been great prophets, and Adamoun would have
been the greatest; one made the pilgrimage of the pyramids and came there from the depths of all
countries.

The king El-Aziz Othman ben Salah El-Din Youssef ben Ayoub, who reigned after his father, was pushed by
ignorant people of his court to destroy the pyramids. He began with the small red pyramid and sent there
quarriers, stonecutters, under the conduct of some emirs of the kingdom and great ones of the empire,
intimating to them the order to destroy it. These planted their tents near the pyramid, gathered laborers
and workers, and did not spare the expense; they stayed there nearly eight months with their people and
their horses, destroying each day one or two stones with infinite pains and after unheard-of efforts. Men
posted at the top lifted with levers the stone that others pulled from below by means of ropes and cables.
The stone in falling made a frightful noise that was heard from very far, the mountains started at it and
the earth trembled from it; the stone sank into the sand, and new efforts were needed to lift it by means
of levers in order to dig beneath it a path on which it was made to roll; then it was broken into heaps,
and each piece was carried on carts and thrown at the foot of

[PDF p. 380]

the neighboring mountain. And after very long efforts and enormous expenses, exhausted with fatigue and at
the end of their strength, they saw themselves obliged to abandon the work without having been able to
accomplish it; all they obtained was to disfigure the pyramid and give a proof of their impotence and the
inanity of their efforts. This happened in 593 [24 November 1196 to 12 November 1197]. Today, if one looks
at the heap of stones torn from the pyramid, one might believe that it is completely destroyed; but if one
examines the pyramid itself, one remains convinced that nothing has been removed from it and that only a
part of the flanks has crumbled. A personage who had been witness to the trouble experienced in demolishing
each stone asked the chief of the workers: "If the sultan gave you a thousand dinars to put one of these
stones back in its place and such as it was, could you do it?" "No, by God," answered the other, "it would
be impossible for us, even if the sum were doubled."

Facing the pyramids are numerous grottoes, so great and so deep that a cavalier could enter there with
lance in hand and ride for an entire day without reaching the bottom, so high, spacious, and deep are
they; according to their situation, it seems that these are the quarries from which the stones of the
pyramids were extracted.

As for the quarries that furnished the stones of the red pyramid, they are situated, it is said, at Qolzoum
and at Assouan. Near these pyramids one still sees the vestiges of superb constructions and of numerous
grottoes cut in the rock; it is very rare that there are not found in these grottoes inscriptions in this
unknown language (of which we have spoken); and the jurist Amarat El-Yenini drank at the same breast as
God when he said:

[verses:] O my friends! there is not, under the sky, a construction that equals in perfection the two
pyramids of Egypt; it is an edifice that time dreads, and yet all that is on the surface of the earth
dreads time. The eye is ravished by the beauty of their arrangement, and the mind could not seize the aim
of their construction.

This thought is drawn from the words of a sage: Every thing fears time, except the pyramids, for time, on
the contrary, fears them.

[PDF p. 381]

Abd El-Ouaheb ben Hassan ben Gafar ben El-Hageb, who died in 387 [14 January 997 to 2 January 998], said:

[verses:] Contemplate the two pyramids when they point, before the eyes, their summit in the height and
the extent; as if the vast earth had had thirst because of the long heat of its liver, it has uncovered
its two prominent breasts, invoking God because it is separated from its child. And God heard it and gave
it the Nile to console it by watering it, and to make it forget its pain, thanks to the generosity of the
lord who directs it, who leads the people toward improvement, and organizes the affairs.

Seïf El-Din ben Gobarat said:

[verses:] By God! What marvels, what admirable things the two pyramids say to the hearts! The history of
their people is mute to the ears, but they lift the veil and show us innumerable beauties; they are like
tents raised without pole or ropes.

Another said:

[verses:] Look at the two pyramids and learn from them what they recount of the times past; contemplate
the shadowy mystery they enclose, contemplating it with the eye of the heart, not with the gaze. If they
spoke, they would recount to us what was done at the beginning and at the end of time. When they begin to
point before the eye that looks at them, they seem the two ears of a buried horse.

The imam Abou-l-Abbas Ahmed ben Youssef El-Tifachi said:

[verses:] Have you not seen the pyramids whose construction persists while the law of the world makes men
and genies disappear? Like a mill, of which the upper millstone would be the sky, the lower millstone the
pyramids, and the world the grinding.

[PDF p. 382]

He said again:

[verses:] The people of old who inhabited Egypt were strong. Virtue is a remnant of them, and science for
them was a banner; but their banners have fallen, and their science and they are extinguished; look, you
will see it visible, old age upon it is sensible.

One has said:

[verses:] O my friends, nothing resists the two accidents (the day and the night); if a first thing had
subsisted, a second would subsist; the two pyramids of Egypt are the supreme point attained by the force
of man, and the two pyramids have aged with their time. Do not be astonished to see me age, for time has
thrown me into the loss of my youth. Go to Carthage and contemplate there the monuments of the Adites and
you will weep; and the portico of Cosroes (Chosroes), contemplate it, it will speak of all the times, as
with sincerity. And do not believe that death is particular to me, far from it! all that is on the globe is
perishable.

I found this written in the hand of the cheikh Shehab el-Din Ahmed ben Yahia ben Abou Heglat El-Tlemsani:
The cadi Fakhr El-Din Abd el-Ouahab El-Masri recited to me verses he had composed in 655 on the pyramids
and that are excellent:

[verses:] The construction of the pyramids is like a preacher who would touch the hearts without using
speech. Behold there comes to my mind a very ancient word: "Where is the one who raised the pyramids?"
They are elevated mountains and that are almost more elevated above the earth than Saturn. If Cosroes had
had their flank for a throne, he would have preferred it to the throne of his portico. They have passed
through the heat and the cold of time for very long, and have felt nothing of these two things,

[PDF p. 383]

[verses, continued:] neither of the burning sun, nor of the wind that blows, nor of the torrent that
flows. Did a pious man raise them in testimony of his piety, and did he build the pyramids for some one of
his idols? Or is it the work of a man believing in the return of the soul toward the body after having
left it? And did he build them for his treasures and for his cadaver, like a tomb that was to preserve them
from the flood? Or are they observatories for the planets chosen by the observers because of the excellence
of the place? Or are they the description of planetary calculations, such as the Persians and the Greeks
made formerly? Or has there been engraved on their faces a science that the mind strives to understand? In
the heart of whoever sees them, to know their writing, there surges a desire that makes one bite the tip
of the fingers.

[PDF p. 384]

CHAPTER XLI
OF THE STATUE NAMED "THE TERRIBLE"

This statue is situated between the two pyramids and was formerly called Belheïb; today the Egyptians name
it Abou-l-hôl (the father of terror).

El-Qoda'ï says: The statue of the pyramids, named Belhoubah, is a colossal statue in stone, situated
between the two pyramids, and of which one sees only the head. The common people give it the name of
Abou-l-hôl; it is also called Belheïb. It is, it is said, a talisman against the sands and that prevents
them from invading the cultivated terrains of Gizeh.

In the book Marvels of the Constructions, it is said: Near the pyramids, one sees, emerging from the soil,
a head and a neck of colossal grandeur; the people give to this figure the name of Abou-l-hôl and claim
that the rest of the body is buried under the sand. Proportionally to the dimensions of the head, the total
length of the body must be 70 cubits and even more. The face is painted in red and covered with a brilliant
varnish perfectly conserved. The figure is beautiful, the features agreeable and imprinted with charm and
beauty; the face seems to smile.

One questioned an eminent man on what he had seen most marvelous: "The proportion of the face of
Abou-l-hôl," he answered. Indeed, the different parts of the face, the nose, the eyes, the ears, are as
well proportioned as the features one meets in nature. The nose of the child, for example, is in proportion
to his size, and this nose, which renders him beautiful, would render hideous a man who had it in the
middle of his face; likewise, a child would be hideous if he had the nose of a man. It would be the same
for any one whatever of the parts of the body. It is therefore necessary that all the members be
proportioned to the rest of the body and to its size. What is admirable in the artist who executed the
statue of Abou-l-hôl is that he was able, despite the enormity

[PDF p. 385]

of the monument, to conserve the proportions of the members, although nature has never created a body of
this dimension.

Facing this statue, on the territory of Masr near the royal palace, was found a second, of colossal size
likewise and perfectly proportioned like the first. In its lap it holds a child and on its head is placed
a basin; the whole is of a single block of granite. It is claimed that it is a woman, the spouse of
Abou-l-hôl of whom we have spoken. She is found in a street to which she has given her name. It is asserted
that if one put on the head of Abou-l-hôl the extremity of a thread and that, the thread stretched, the
other extremity rested on the head of the woman, one would obtain a line exactly horizontal. Abou-l-hôl is,
it is said, a talisman destined to prevent the sands from joining the Nile, and the woman is another
talisman whose virtue is to prevent the waters of the Nile from inundating the town of Masr.

Ibn el-Moutaouag says: The lane of the Statue is a lane that begins at the extremity of the Great Market,
in the vicinity of the street of 'Amar. The idol is known under the name of woman of Pharaoh and is
regarded as a talisman destined to preserve the countryside from the invasion of the waters of the Nile.
It is said that the Belheïb of the pyramids faces her, the back of Belheïb being turned toward the desert,
while the back of the woman is turned toward the river, the two statues facing the east. In 711 [20 May
1311 to 8 May 1312] an emir, of the name of Balât, arrived with workers, stonecutters and quarriers; they
broke the statue known under the name of statue of the Woman and cut it into large and small pieces,
thinking that beneath must be hidden a treasure, but one found there only a pedestal of enormous stone
under which one dug until one met the water, but one discovered nothing. With these stones one constructed
the base of the granite column that one can see in the new mosque built outside Masr and that one calls
the New Mosque of El-Naser; it is thus that this statue disappeared, and God is the most learned!

In our time, a personage, the cheikh Mohammed Saïm El-Daher, one of the Sons of the convent of dervishes
founded by Saïd El-Sa'ada, set out

[PDF p. 386]

toward 780 [30 April 1378 to 18 April 1379] in order to combat and destroy the superstitions; he went to
the pyramids and mutilated the face of Abou-l-hôl, which has remained in this state until the present.
Since then, the sand has invaded in great part the territory of Gizeh, and the inhabitants of this
province attribute this encroachment of the sands on their lands to the mutilation of the statue. To God is
the consequence of things, and what more beautiful than what Zâfer El-Haddad said:

[verses:] Examine the form of the two pyramids and admire; between the two is Abou-l-hôl the marvelous.
Like travelers who, the night having passed, are going to depart, beloved with beloved, between the two of
them stands the jealous one. And the water of the Nile, at their feet, is like tears; and the voice of the
wind, which blows near them, is like a lament. And the prison of Joseph appears like a lover abandoned, and
who sadly laments.

It is recounted that Atrib ben Qobt ben Masr ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh, at the moment of dying, recommended
to his brother Sa to put his body in a boat and bury it in an island in the middle of the river. When he
was dead, Sa executed the order of his brother, without any Egyptian having knowledge of it. Sa was accused
of the murder of Atrib, and there formed against him an uprising that lasted nine years. At the end of the
fifth year, Sa proposed to the rebels to lead them to the tomb of Atrib; they went there, but, after having
dug his tomb, found no more the body, which the demons had transported to the place where Abou-l-hôl is, to
bury it near the tomb of his father and his grandfather Beïsar. The suspicions from then on only increased
against Sa, and the rebels, returned to Memphis, continued the war. Eblis (the Devil) went to them and
showed them the body of Atrib where he had transported it. One drew Atrib from his tomb and placed him on a
bed; and the demon spoke to them by his tongue (Atrib's), subjected them to his ideas, so much so that one
prostrated oneself before him and adored him as one had adored the idols. Sa was killed and his body buried
on the bank of the Nile; but the Nile, in rising, did not submerge his tomb. Seeing which, a part of the
rebels rallied to him, declaring that he had been killed unjustly, and went to prostrate themselves on his
tomb as the others did for

[PDF p. 387]

Atrib; some cut a stone and gave it the form of Achmoum. This stone, called later Abou-l-hôl, was placed
between the two pyramids and became an object of veneration: there were thus three sects in Egypt. And the
Sabeans never ceased to venerate Abou-l-hôl, to sacrifice to him white cocks and to burn for him
sandarac.

[PDF p. 388]

CHAPTER XLII
OF THE MOUNTAINS

The whole land of Egypt is embraced by two mountains that run from south to north; very little elevated,
they are of unequal height, that of the east being the highest; it bears the name of mount Louqa; the
mountain of the west, rather low, is not continuous. The space that separates these two mountains is very
narrow in certain places and widens in certain others. The widest part is found in the Delta. These two
mountains are sterile and produce no plant, contrary to the mountains of other countries. The cause of it
is that they are saturated with niter and salt, for the force of the silt of Egypt attracts to itself the
humidity of these mountains, a humidity necessary to germination, and the excessive heat eliminates from
it the sweet and subtle substance; thus the water of the wells of these mountains is salty. These two
mountains dry up what one buries in them, because the rains are naturally rare in Egypt.

Mount Louqa, situated to the east of Egypt, protects it against the east wind; thus this wind is
absolutely lacking in Egypt. Moreover, it intercepts for this country the rays of the rising sun when it is
still near the horizon. The names of these two mountains are very numerous and vary according to the
provinces they traverse. The one that dominates Fostat and El-Qahira is the mount Moqattam.

[PDF p. 389]

CHAPTER XLIII
OF MOUNT MOQATTAM

Mount Moqattam begins at the east of China, at the Enveloping Ocean, traverses the country of the Tatars,
reaches Farganah and the mounts Yetam where the river Soghd takes its source, and extends to the Gihoun
(Oxus); this river cuts the mountain in two and flows between its two sections; the mountain, which seems
there cut in its middle, resumes beyond the Gihoun the direction of Gourgan and, passing by Talkhan,
traverses the provinces of Merv and of Roud until Tous. All the towns of the district of Tous are situated
in this mountain, to which are attached the mountains of Ispahan and of Shiraz before it reaches the
Indian Ocean. There, the mountain makes a bend in the direction of Sharzour, passes the Tigris, and reaches
mount Goudi where the ark of Noah stopped at the time of the flood. Then, traversing the provinces of Amad
and of Miafaraqeïn, it reaches the frontier post of Aleppo and there takes the name of mount Lakam. After
having passed Aleppo, it takes until Homs the name of Nahra; beyond Homs, one designates it by the name of
mount Liban (Lebanon). From there, traversing Syria, it reaches the (eastern) shore of the sea of Qolzoum.
On the other side (on the western shore), it takes the name of Moqattam. At this point, it divides into
several branches whose last ones go to die at the extremity of the west. It is claimed that its name comes
to it from Moqtam ben Masr ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh.

Mount Moqattam lodges the two banks of the Nile in the direction of Nubia, passes above the Fayoum, and
reaches to the west the territory of Mouqraouat and farther west still Sagalmasat, whence it directs itself
toward the Enveloping Ocean, which it reaches after five months of march.

Ibrahim ben Ouacif Shah, speaking of the arrival of Misraïm ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh in the country of
Egypt, says: The companions of the priest Aqlimoun

[PDF p. 390]

brought to light the treasures of the Egyptians and their manuscripts, enclosing the sciences set forth in
berabi writing; they cleared their monuments and found again the mines of gold, emeralds, and turquoises,
etc. They reestablished the description of the arts -- that is, of alchemy. And Misraïm instituted as chief
of alchemy a man of the sacerdotal caste named Moqaïtâm the sage, who exercised his art on the eastern
mountain, which took from him the name of Moqattam, because Moqaïtâm the sage practiced alchemy there. The
name of the sage was abbreviated, and this abbreviation served to designate the mountain, which was called
mount Moqattam -- that is, mountain of Moqaïtâm the sage.

El-Bakri says: The Moqattam is a mountain that borders Masr and where one buries the dead.

El-Qoda'ï says: The Moqattam, according to Abou Abd Allah El-Yemani, is this mountain attributed to
Moqattam ben Masr ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh, who was a pious servant of God and who withdrew to this
mountain to give himself over to his devotions; whence the mountain would have taken its name. But that is
not exact, for one knows at Masr no son of the name of Moqattam.

Here now is what the scholars recount: The name of Moqattam is derived from the word equivalent to "to
cut"; indeed, it would seem that one had cut all the trees and all the plants of this mountain, whence the
name of Moqattam. It is at least what Ali ben El-Hassan El-Henaï El-Doussi surnamed Kara' and others still
claim.

Abd El-Rahman ben Abd Allah ben Abd El-Hakem recounts, on the authority of El-Leïtz ben Sa'd, that
El-Maqoqos asked Amr ben El-As to sell him the foot of the Moqattam for 70,000 dinars according to some,
20,000 dinars only according to others. Amr, astonished, said to him: "I will refer it to the Commander of
the Faithful." And he wrote indeed on this subject to Omar ben El-Khattab, who answered him: "Ask him why
he made you such a proposition for a mountain that cannot be cultivated and where one cannot procure
water." Amr questioned Maqoqos, and the latter said to him: "We have found in the books the description of
this mountain, and we have seen that it would enclose the plants of Paradise." Amr transmitted this
explanation to Omar, who answered: "As for plants of Paradise, I know only the Muslims. Bury then in this
mountain

[PDF p. 391]

the Muslims who die in the country where you are, and sell it at no price." And the first Muslim buried
there was a man of the tribe of Mo'afar named 'Amer, and from then on the mountain was peopled (cultivated)
[footnote: play on words on the word that signifies "to people, to cultivate"]. And El-Maqoqos cried:
"What! that is not conformable to our treaty!" And one traced the limit that separates the property of the
Copts from the cemetery (of the Muslims).

Omar ben Abou Omar El-Kandi, speaking of the merits of Egypt, recounts that Amr ben El-As, having gone to
the foot of the Moqattam, asked El-Maqoqos who accompanied him: "What is the matter with your mountain to
be thus sterile; no plants grow there as in the mountains of Syria. What if we had a canal dug that would
bring there the water of the Nile and if we planted palms there?" "We have found in the books," answered
El-Maqoqos, "that this mountain was, more than any other, fertile in trees, in plants, and in fruits. It
was the abode of Moqattam son of Masr son of Beïsar son of Cham son of Noah. And when came the night when
God spoke to Moses, God said to the mountains: I am going to speak with one of my prophets on one of you.
All the mountains stood up and raised themselves, except the mountain of Jerusalem, which lowered itself
and made itself quite small. God asked it: Why have you acted thus? and he knew it better than anyone. The
mountain answered: By veneration and respect for you, O my Lord. And God then prescribed the other
mountains to give it all the plants they possessed. And the Moqattam gave all the plants that covered it,
and since that epoch it has remained stripped as you see it at present. God then said to the Moqattam: In
recompense for what you have done, I will give you the trees of Paradise, or, according to another version,
the plants of Paradise." Amr wrote all this to Omar ben El-Khattab, who answered him: "I know, as for plants
of Paradise, only the Muslims. Make them then a cemetery of this mountain." El-Maqoqos, irritated, said to
Amr: "That is not in our conventions." And Amr reserved for him a terrain on the side of El-Habech, where
the Christians were buried. It is recounted that Moses having prostrated himself, all the trees of the
Moqattam as far as Tourah prostrated themselves with him.

It is written: "When the holy country will be conquered"; by that is understood the valley of

[PDF p. 392]

the Adoration of Moses in the Moqattam, near the quarry of stones. For Moses spoke to his Master in this
valley.

Abd ben Mousa says: I was attending a burial with Mousa ben Lahi'at; we were near the dead man when Mousa,
raising the head, looked at the mountain saying: "Jesus, son of Mary, passed at the foot of this mountain
clad in a caftan of wool and girded with a ribbon; his mother was near him, and Jesus, turning toward her,
said to her: O my mother, here is the cemetery of the people of Mohammed."

Abd Allah ben Lahi'at reports, on the authority of 'Yach ben Abbas, that Ka'b el-Ahbar asked a man who was
going to Egypt to bring him back some dust taken from the foot of the Moqattam. The latter brought it back
to him in a sack, and when Ka'b died one placed, according to his orders, this dust in his coffin, under
his body.

It is reported that Ka'b, questioned on the mountain of Egypt, answered: "It is sacred from Qoseïr to
El-Yahmoum."

Ibn Lahi'at says: The Moqattam is the mountain comprised between Qoseïr and the quarry of stones (Tourah);
from this point, it takes the name of Yahmim; one finds there precious stones and steel (?), and it
