extends to the extremities of the country of the Blacks.

[PDF p. 393]

CHAPTER XLIV
OF THE RED MOUNTAIN

This mountain, which dominates Cairo to the northeast, is known under the name of Yahmoum.

El-Qoda'ï says: The Yahamim are diverse mountains that dominate Cairo and its countryside on the side of
the east; they terminate at a certain road of the Cistern. One gives them the name of Yahamim because of
the variety of their colors. El-Yahmoum in Arabic signifies black, dark.

Ibn Abd El-Hakem reports, on the authority of Sa'ï ben Obeïd, that, at the time of his journey to Masr, the
inhabitants had established their place of prayer in a place situated facing the saqieh of Abou 'Oun in the
quarter of El-Asker, and he asked: Why have they established their place of prayer on the cursed mountain
and abandoned the holy mountain -- that is, the Moqattam?

Ibn Abd El-Zaher says: The red mountain, according to El-Qoda'ï, is the Yahmoum that dominates Cairo, and I
see indeed no mountain dominating Cairo other than that one.

El-Bakri says: El-Yahmoum, with a fatha on the first letter, a soukoun on the second. El-Harbi says:
El-Yahmoum, mountain of Egypt.

Abou Qabil reports that Abdallah ben Amr, questioning Ka'b on the subject of the Moqattam, asked him if it
was cursed. "Far from being cursed," answered Ka'b, "it is sacred from Qoseïr to El-Yahmoum."

El-Bakri reports again that Abed is a mountain of Egypt facing the Moqattam.

[PDF p. 394]

CHAPTER XLV
OF THE MOUNTAIN OF YACHKOUR

This mountain is found between Cairo and Masr, and it is on it that the mosque of Touloun is built.

El-Qoda'ï says: Mountain of Yachkour; this Yachkour was son of Gadelat of the tribe of Lakhm. It is on
this mountain that rises the mosque of Ibn Touloun. The Yachkar ben Gadelat are a small Arab tribe that,
at the moment of the conquest, settled on this mountain, which took from them the name of Yachkour.

Ibn Abd El-Zaher says: The mosque of Ibn Touloun is built on the mountain of Yachkour; it is a place
celebrated for its miracles and a blessed place. It is said that it is on this mountain that Moses opened
his mouth to speak to his Lord. It dominates the Nile, from which nothing separates it. It dominates also
the two ponds, the Birket el-Fil (pond of the Elephant) and the pond of Qaroun. It is also on this mountain
that the machines of war were tested before their dispatch to the frontier posts.

El-Kabch is a mountain situated in the vicinity of the Yachkour and that dominated formerly the course of
the Nile, to the west. Then when, after the conquest, the Muslims had founded Fostat, this mountain was
included in the quarter of El-Hamra el-Qousoua, which took the name of Kabch.

El-Sharf is the name of three places: two are found between Cairo and Masr and the third between the Birket
el-Habech and Fostat Masr. For those situated outside Cairo, one of them, on which rises today the Citadel
of the Mountain, forms part of the Moqattam; the second is situated between Masr and the mosque of Touloun;
this one dominates to the west the great canal that separates Kom el-Gareh and the quarter of the mosque of
Touloun;

[PDF p. 395]

it formed part of the quarter of Tagib, but was later attached to the quarter of El-Asker.

As for the third Sharf, it bears today the name of El-Rased (the observatory) and dominates the quarter of
Rashidat. This Sharf bore the name of Sanad, and sanad is the name one gives to the part of a mountain that
one has before oneself and that is above the soil. One says [Arabic] to say "leaning."

[PDF p. 396]

CHAPTER XLVI
OF THE OBSERVATORY (EL-RASED)

El-Rased is an elevation that dominates to the west the quarter of Rashidat and to the south the Birket
el-Habech; for whoever looks at it from the side of Rashidat it is a veritable mountain, but for whoever
comes from the side of the east it seems a plateau, and one can indeed reach it without climbing, by
passing through the cemetery. This hill faces the Sharf of the quarter of El-Askar and the Sharf that
bears today the name of Kabch. It was formerly called the Garf, but it took subsequently the name of Rased
(observatory) after El-Afdal Abou-l-Qasem Shanshah, son of the general Badr el-Gemali, had installed at its
summit a sphere to observe the planets. From then on it bore the name of Rased.

In the book Of Observation, it is said: There were brought from Syria to El-Afdal Shanshah, son of the
general Bedr, a hundred tables on which were inscribed the (astronomical) events that were to occur in the
years subsequent to the year 500 [2 September 1106 to 21 August 1107] of the hijra. The astronomers of His
Excellence were then Ibn El-Halebi, Ibn El-Heitzmi, Sahloun, and others to whom were accorded a monthly
salary, plus an (annual) pension and garments, and who were charged with establishing also tables each
year. Each of them gave himself over to his personal calculations and to the operations for which he had
the most aptitude. At the beginning of the year each brought his tables. In comparing them with those
brought from Syria, one found between them notable divergences, which displeased the sultan. Thus at the
beginning of the year 513 [14 April 1119 to 1 April 1120], when the tables were gathered, according to
custom, El-Afdal convoked the astronomers, the calculators, and the scholars and asked them the reason for
the discrepancies the tables presented. "The Syrians," it was answered, "observe and calculate according to
the

[PDF p. 397]

method today abandoned of El-Mamoun; we others follow the method of the tables of El-Hakem, for it is more
recent, and between the old and the new system there are discrepancies and divergences. The sages of
antiquity recognized that recent things are preferable to old ones, because of the displacement of the
stars and the change that occurs in the calculations." And on this subject, they conversed with the sultan
of things that are reported in the special works and ended by advising him to build a new observatory that
would permit verifying the calculations and making the errors and faults disappear, which, besides the
real and considerable utility one would draw from it, would procure the sultan a brilliant glory and an
imperishable renown. "Whom to charge with this?" asked El-Afdal. One of his friends and counselors, the
venerable cheikh Abou-l-Hassan Ibn Abou Osamat, took the word and said: "The cadi Ibn Abou-l-'Eich
El-Taraboulsi, the virtuous and learned engineer." Ibn Abou-l-'Eïch was his son-in-law, for he had married
his daughter; he was a personage very old and very powerful and moreover very rich, who was supported again
in this affair by the general Abou Abd Allah, who had taken the vizierate after El-Afdal and who was
designated under the name of El-Mamoun Ibn El-Bataïhi. El-Afdal found the counsel judicious and said: "Let
him be given the order to occupy himself with this affair and let him ask for what will be necessary to
him!" All this being thus arranged, the cadi began by boasting very loudly; now what El-Afdal detested
above all things was to hear people boast or to see them adorn themselves with brilliant robes. "These
instruments," said the cheikh, "are enormous and their manipulation hazardous; not everyone knows how to
use them as is fitting." And he spoke, spoke at length, not ceasing to boast and saying: "It is necessary
that the one who is charged with this work be supported generously and magnificently, so that his heart
remains calm to supervise closely the operation, that his chest be at ease and his mind free and reassured
by the justice that will have been rendered to him." El-Afdal, very discontented, cried: "By God, he boasts
too much! he exalts too much his science; I no longer wish to hear of it nor have anything to do with
him!" And the general Ibn El-Bataïhi made a sign and said: "There is here someone capable of accomplishing
this work easily, in very little time and in the best manner; it is Abou Saïd Ibn Qaraqat the physician,
who is currently charged with the magazine of arms, saddles, tools, etc." He was made

[PDF p. 398]

to come on the spot; and he set about speaking well and simply, explaining for what purpose the instruments
had been made and who had invented them. He spoke of the scholars of antiquity and of all those who, until
the latest times, had made astronomical observations, and all this clearly and calmly as if he had recited
by heart or had read in a book. El-Afdal and the assistants were marveled; and El-Afdal having asked him
what he needed, he answered: "I need very little, and I can even procure it easily since all that is
necessary to me is found in the magazines of the sultan, may God strengthen his reign! I need copper, lead,
tools; but, all that I need, I will ask for it one after another, except the money for the expenses and the
salary of the workers, with which another than I will be charged." El-Afdal, surprised, cried: "Let a
salary be allotted to him for himself." But the old man resumed: "I form part of the employees, and what is
allotted to me suffices me; I am a servant of the kingdom and have no need of another salary. If I reach my
goal, and if I lead things to a good end, that will be my recompense." It had been said to El-Afdal that
the installation of this observatory would cost much money; thus he asked: "How much do you need, in sum?"
"That," answered Abou Saïd, "will not demand more expenses than a mosque or a belvedere." And as El-Afdal
insisted, he said: "Bring me paper," and he wrote on it this: "The servant kisses the earth and says: I
have made the list of the things I need; let a sublime decree prescribe to the Dar el-Ouakalat to remit to
me 200 qantars of copper in blocks, 80 qantars of copper of Spain in rods, 40 qantars of red copper, 1,000
qantars of lead; to furnish me from the arsenal the wood to burn, the iron, the steel, and the construction
wood; finally, for the expenses, 100 dinars that will remain in the hands of a writer charged with the
accounts and of which I will ask the renewal when they are exhausted. I will choose a place favorable to
the establishment of an observatory and, during the work, the sultan will supervise the operations and
watch over the execution of his orders." El-Afdal approved all and wished in addition to accord him a robe
of honor. "That," said the general, "must be given later, when we will have seen his work." And from the
beginning until the end, Abou Saïd did not claim a single dirhem for himself; he would have been ashamed to
beg, he who was an employee of the sultan. Each of those who were [...]

[PDF p. 399]

there hoped indeed to live long, but El-Afdal was killed the following year and the situation found itself
at that moment modified.

One had therefore first chosen, to install the observatory, the mosque of the Oven on the Moqattam; but it
is found too far from all that was necessary, and, by common accord, the choice fell on the plateau of
El-Garf in the great mosque of El-Filat. For this mosque alone one had spent 6,000 dinars. One dug there a
hole in the mountain, at the place where the cisterns are found today, and one constructed there a mold for
the great circle whose diameter was 10 cubits and the circumference 30 cubits. One took long days to arrange
and install it; then one built around it ten furnaces each provided with two bellows; in each furnace one
threw 11 qantars of copper, more or less, the whole making 100 qantars and a fraction distributed in the
ten furnaces. One lit the fire in the afternoon and one blew until the second hour of the following day. In
the morning El-Afdal came and sat on a throne; and when the furnaces were ready and in full work, El-Afdal
gave the order to open the furnaces; on each of them stood a worker, and, when the order was given to open
the doors, all were opened at the same time and the copper rushed like water into the mold; but there had
remained there a little humidity, and, when the copper had penetrated it, its heat made the humid place
burst and the circle was not perfect. When it was cooled and one had uncovered it, it was found perfect in
all points, except at the place where the humidity had stayed. El-Afdal was very discontented and his chest
narrowed; he threw the workers a purse of 1,000 dinars and, filled with anger, he mounted on horseback. Ibn
Qaraqat managed to appease him by explaining that an instrument of this dimension, and such as one had never
spoken of a similar instrument, had great chances of not succeeding at the first try and that one should
esteem oneself happy if one obtained it after ten trials. "Prepare yourselves then to begin again," said
El-Afdal. It was therefore recast, and this time it was perfect. This time, El-Afdal was absent but he was
very happy at the completion of the work. The finished circle was raised on the terrace of the mosque of
El-Filat: at this work were present all the people who work copper. One made for this circle a gigantic
compass in oak wood. Then one built in the middle of the circle a bench of stone, in which one arranged a
hole to lodge the foot of the compass, which had

[PDF p. 400]

there the aspect of a mill-tree (axle). In this tree was fixed an arm, similar to the arm of a mill, and
provided with an armature of iron. The rest was in very solid oak wood. The point of the arm was destined
for multiple uses, now flattening the surface of the circle, now polishing the sides, now tracing grooves.
One employed a very long time in the cleaning of the circle and the polishing with the file. The workers,
the engineers, the scholars, everyone was there, and Ibn Qaraqat had a tent asked of the sultan to cover
the whole; and below the circle one constructed a solid vault. One would have wished to leave this circle
on the terrace of the mosque of El-Filat, but it was not possible, for one recognized that the first rays
of the rising sun were masked. One was therefore of the opinion of transporting it to the mosque of
El-Giouch, which one also calls mosque of the Observatory. El-Afdal had begun its construction, more
magnificent than that of El-Filat, but he had not finished it. As soon as he knew that one was to make of
it the observatory, he finished it. He attended the transport of the circle from the mosque of El-Filat to
the mosque of El-Giouch. One brought masts, cables, and hooks from Alexandria and the other ports; and one
gathered sailors and negroes, cavalry and infantry to lower the circle and conduct it on carts to the
mosque of El-Rased el-Giouchi. And the next day all set to work to raise it on the terrace; this operation
finished, the circle was installed, and at the two extremities of the diameter one raised two columns of
marble that were fastened by means of molten lead poured at the base and at the summit, so that the weight
of the bronze did not make them lower. At the center was raised another column of marble, at the summit of
which was the pivot of the alidade; the latter had first been cast in copper, but as one could not use it
nor make it turn, one remade it in sag wood with the points and the pivot in copper to facilitate the
revolution of the alidade. Then by means of this circle one observed the sun; one had much trouble, for at
every instant the circle inclined by a degree and some minutes because of the weight, so one made a column
of copper in addition to the column of marble, in order to check the sinking; then one tried again; but one
ascertained always discrepancies, despite the supports that propped the instrument and although the alidade
was made only of wood. And El-Afdal, despite his age and his weakening, came often. The general carried him
to the top, and often on the way the fatigue

[PDF p. 401]

constrained him to sit without being able to speak and with hands all trembling. One made several
observations in his presence. It is toward this moment that he was killed during the night of the breaking
of the fast of the year 515 [the night of 12 to 13 December 1121]. One had said to El-Afdal that Ibn
Qaraqat had exaggerated the grandeur of his circle and given too much length to its diameter; thus the
sultan had said to Ibn Qaraqat: "If you had made your circle smaller, the work would have been easier." "By
your generosity!" answered Ibn Qaraqat, "if I had been able to make it in such a way that one of its
extremities was at the pyramids and the other on the Tannour, certainly I would have made it. The greater
the instruments, the more exact the operations. What are indeed these instruments in comparison with the
celestial world?" But as one insisted on this subject, Ibn Qaraqat constructed a smaller circle that was
installed in an edifice of red brick, at the foot of the mosque of El-Giouch; the diameter of this small
circle was only 7 cubits and the circumference 21 cubits. It had just been finished when El-Afdal was
killed. One had spent in money, for all the costs and the salary of the workers, only about 160 dinars.

El-Mamoun El-Bataïhi, having become vizier, wished to finish this work and give it the name of Rectified
Observatory of El-Mamoun, just as one had given the old observatory the name of Essay of El-Mamoun. For
this, he published a decree prescribing the transport of the observatory to Bab el-Nasr, at Cairo; this
transport was effected in the same conditions as previously, and one employed the same engines as well as
sailors and troops of workers. For the lunch of these men one spent each day a quantity of dirhems. When
the circle was mounted on the carts, one made it pass along the ditch behind the mosque of El-Fatah, of the
quarter of El-Meshahed, and one conducted it thus until the mosque of El-Dakhirat, outside Cairo; one had
much trouble to bring it under the gate (Bab el-Nasr), for one feared to strike it and warp it. Once there,
masts were raised under the vault of Bab el-Nasr, under the gate itself, and a great number of laborers
were harnessed to the cables, some hoisting from below, others pulling from above, and the instrument
arrived finally at the great terrace whence one transported it to the upper terrace; there it was installed
on columns, as we

[PDF p. 402]

have explained above. By means of the great circle one made observations as one had made on the plateau of
El-Gorf; one observed with exactitude all that concerned the sun, but the sun only. One then resolved to
make a circle whose diameter would be only 5 cubits, one cast it in a hostelry of the quarter of
El-'Atoufiah at Cairo, a work truly easy for people who had succeeded with the first two circles. El-Mamoun
came frequently to the foundry and was keenly interested in the operation. Ibn Qaraqat came there twice a
day, and one met there also Abou Giafar ben Hasandaï and Abou-l-Barakât ben Abou-l-Leitz, chief of the
divan and charged with the direction of affairs. Al-Mamoun had said to him: "Go up to them each day and,
all that they ask, give it to them without asking me for orders." The aim of the vizier was to finish the
work rapidly and give the observatory the name of Rectified Observatory of El-Mamoun. If God had permitted
that El-Mamoun remain still a little, all the observatory of the planets would have been finished, but he
took him in the night of Saturday the 3rd day of Ramadan of the year 519 [3 October 1125]; and,
subsequently, one made a crime of this vizier for the construction of this observatory and the interest he
took in it, affirming that his ambition had been to give the observatory the name of El-Mamoun and not that
of the caliph El-Amr bihakam Allah. As for the crowd, it claimed that this construction had no other aim
than to converse with Saturn and to know by it the hidden things. Others accused them of magic and other
futilities.

After the death of El-Mamoun, the work was abandoned, and, as the caliph refused to pursue it, no one dared
speak to him of it; one even demolished it by his order and the materials were carried to the magazines.
All those who had been employed there, near or far, fled. Among those were the engineers who had been
charged with the service and the daily upkeep of the observatory and who were never to absent themselves:
the cheikh Abou Giafar Ibn Hasandaï; the cadi Ibn Abou-l-Yach; the orator Abou-l-Hassan Aly ben Soliman ben
Ayoub; the cheikh Abou-l-Nagga Ibn Sanad, clockmaker of Alexandria and engineer; Abou Mohammed Abd El-Kerim
El-Saqli, the engineer, and others still, mathematicians or

[PDF p. 403]

astronomers, like Ibn El-Halebi, Ibn El-Heïtsmi, Abou Naser, disciple of Sahloun, Ibn Diab, El-Qala'ï, who
all were present each day from dawn, as well as the chief of the divan Ibn Abou-l-Leitz. Ibn Hasandaï
absented himself sometimes for several days, for he was a great personage, very proud and very powerful.
Each day, El-Mamoun sent an emissary to supervise the personnel and note the absent ones, for he liked to
occupy himself with everything and employed spies and reporters who always had the eye open, so that the
smallest thing could not be done, whether among the great or among the people, at Cairo or at Masr, without
his knowing it. He had even organized in the provinces a service of espionage that informed him of all that
happened there.

For me, I have seen this place, still called today the Observatory, where is found the mosque of El-Filat;
it was still a place very peopled and covered with houses and mosques; but all that has disappeared and
there are no more inhabitants. The king El-Nacer Mohammed ben Qalaoun had saqiehs dug there to bring to the
foot of the hill of the Observatory and from there to the Citadel, the water of a canal starting from the
Nile, in the vicinity of the station of El-Atsar el-Nabouïat. But this sultan being dead, the work remained
unfinished; this moreover will be recounted to you in the chapter of this book that treats of the Citadel
of the Mountain. The site of the observatory still serves as a goal of promenade for the inhabitants of
Masr.

It is reported that El-Moezz lidin Allah Moadd, arriving from the Maghreb at Cairo, was discontented with
the site chosen for the town and said to the general Gouher: "Since you neglected to build Cairo on the
Nile, why did you not construct it on the Garf?" (that is, at the place of which we speak).

The meat, it is asserted, spoils at Cairo after a day and a night; it conserves itself two days and two
nights at the Citadel of the Mountain, but it remains intact for three days and as many nights at the
Observatory; this fact is due to the purity of the air.

And this poet drank at the same breast as God, who said:

[The verses themselves are not preserved in the source text at this point.]

SECOND PART

[PDF p. 404]

CHAPTER I
OF THE TOWNS OF THE LAND OF EGYPT

The verb madana, says Ibn Saïdat, signifies "to reside in a place"; the word medinat (town) has the sense
of "shelter raised above the soil"; it derives from the first and makes in the plural [Arabic forms].
Starting from there, Abou-l-Hassan, cited by El-Faresi, has very justly declared that [the word] is of the
[given] form. The ulema Athir el-din Abou Hiân says likewise that it is a common noun derived [as
indicated]. Some claim however that this term is of [another] form and derived from [another root], in
which they are mistaken; for the Arabs agree to hamza it in the plural and write it with the hamza and not
with the [other letter]. [Grammatical discussion of the word's derivation.]

The towns of Egypt are very numerous: some of them have disappeared without leaving traces and without even
their name having been conserved; others are better known to us and vestiges of them subsist; others
finally are still inhabited.

The most ancient town of Egypt whose name has been retained is the town of Amsous; the flood effaced the
trace of it, but there remain to us about it numerous accounts; it is there that the kings of Egypt resided
before the flood. The capital of Egypt after the flood was the town of Memphis, where resided the kings of
the Copts and the Pharaohs until its destruction by Bokhta-Nas'ar (Nebuchadnezzar); and when the Macedonian
Alexander, son of Philip, come from Greece, his empire, arrived in Egypt, he founded at Alexandria a new
town, in its turn capital of Egypt until the conquest of Amr ben El-As, who, at the head of the Muslim
army, subjugated the land of Egypt. The new conqueror founded Fostat-Masr, which remained the seat of the
government of Egypt until

[PDF p. 405]

the time when the general Gouher, come from the West with the troops of El-Mo'ezz li din Allah Abou Tamim
Mo'add, seized Egypt and raised Cairo there. This last town remained the capital of the kingdom until the
fall of the Fatimid dynasty, chased out by the sultan Salah el din Yousef ben Ayoub, who built the citadel
of the mountain; but Cairo has not ceased to be the capital until the present epoch.

In Egypt, multitudes of important towns are met that have not been capitals: El Fayoum, Dallas, Ahnas,
Behnesa, El Qeis, Talkha, Achmouneïn, Ansena (Antinoë), Qous, Siout, Faou, Akhmim, Beliana, Hou, Qena,
Denderah, Qoft, El Aqsar (Luxor), Esna, Erment, Edfou, and the frontier post of Assouan that we assimilate
to a town. These localities are found in the southern region. The Egyptians give to the Copts who inhabit
the Said the name of Maris and to the inhabitants of the Delta that of Bima.

In the northern region one meets the town of Noub of the eastern Houf, which forms part of the Delta, and
the towns of: Aïn Shams (Heliopolis), Atrib, Tanoua with the district of Zankaloun, the town of Nemy,
Basta whose site is designated today under the name of Tell-Basta, Qarbeit, El Batnoun, Menouf, Tarah,
another Menouf, Sakha, El Ausah which is the same as Demirah, Tidah, El Afrahoun, which comprises Nisha
among its dependencies, Baqîrah, Bena, Shoubrasàt, Samanoud, Noussa, Sabta, El Negoum; the town of El
Negoum has been completely invaded by the sands and the sebakh, and one no longer knows of it but the
borough of Edkou on the shore of the sea between Alexandria and Rosetta; then come the towns of Tennis,
Damietta, Farma, El Arish, Sa, Bornout, Qortassa, Akhnou, Rashid (Rosetta), Mariout, Loubiah-Maraqiah;
beyond Loubiah-Maraqiah, one enters on the territory of the Cyrenaica (Pentapolis), which is the desert.

In the region of the East (the direction of the qibla, the orient for Egypt) are the towns of Farân,
Qolzoum, Râïah, Aïlah, and Madian.

Most of these towns have been ruined, but on many of them run very widespread accounts; some date only from
Islam; God willing, I will give of all these accounts enough to satisfy the reader.

The land of Egypt forms today two regions, southern and northern, whose ensemble is divided into fifteen
provinces. The region of the South is the largest and comprises nine provinces: (1) that of Qous, the most

[PDF p. 406]

considerable, extending to Assouan and to the west of Qamoulah; Assouan is situated at the extreme limit of
the Empire on the side of the South; (2) the province of Akhmim; (3) that of Siout; (4) that of Manfalout;
(5) that of Achmouneïn where is found El Tahaouyah; (6) the province of Behnesa; (7) that of the Fayoum;
(8) that of Atfîh, and (9) that of Gizeh. The northern region encloses six provinces: (1) the province of
Beheïrah which runs along the sea toward Alexandria and Barqah; (2) the province of Gharbieh (western)
formed by a single island occupying all the space comprised between the two arms of the Nile named branch
of Damietta and branch of Rosetta; (3) the province of Menoufieh of which form part the wells designated
under the name of "island of the Beni Naser"; (4) the province of Qalioub; (5) that of Sharqieh (eastern);
(6) that of Ashmoum Tanah comprising the Daqhalieh and the Mourtahieh; it is in this province that are
found the frontier posts of Bourlos and of Rosetta and Mansourah. In this region also are Alexandria and
Damietta, towns that form part of no province.

Abou-l-Hassan El Masa'oudi, in his book "Chronicle of the Time," reports that the Koukas, a tribe belonging
to the people of Aïlah, seized the country of Egypt and divided the Said into eighty districts distributed
in four provinces; in these districts were comprised thirty Egyptian towns of the interior where one met
all sorts of marvelous objects; it is there that were found districts like those of Akhmim, of Qouft, of
Qous, and of the Fayoum.

It is claimed that Masr, son of Beïsar, divided the country among his children, giving to his son Ashmoun
the territory that extends from the town that bears his name (Ashmouneïn) to Ras el Bahr on the side of
Damietta; to his son Ansena the region comprised between Ansena and the Cataracts; to his son Sa the
country that goes from Sa in the Delta to Alexandria; to his son Menouf the interior of Lower Egypt,
Memphis, and the surrounding territory; to his son Qoft the west of the Said to the Cataracts; to his son
Atrib the east of the kingdom to the desert of Farân, and finally to his three daughters Farma, Siriâm, and
Badourah portions of Egyptian lands enclaved in the shares of their brothers.

[PDF p. 407]

CHAPTER II
OF THE TOWN OF AMSOUS, OF ITS MARVELS AND OF ITS KINGS

Master Ibrahim ben Ouacif Shah the writer, in his book entitled Accounts and Marvels of Egypt, reports that
the town of Masr bore in ancient times the name of Amsous, and that the first king of Egypt was Naqrâoush
the powerful, son of Misraïm. Naqrâoush signifies "king of his people." This Naqrâoush, son of Misraïm the
Ancient, son of Mourqaïïl, son of Douaïïl, son of 'Ariab, son of Adam, set out with seventy and some valiant
cavaliers of the Benou-'Ariab seeking a country where to flee the sons of their father, for, in that time,
they were jealous of and oppressed one another, and the Benou 'Ariab were molested by the Benou Qabîl. The
Benou 'Ariab stopped their course only at the Nile and, marveled at the beauty and the extent of the
country, they settled there and constructed admirable edifices there. Naqrâoush raised the town of Masr to
which he gave the name of his father Misraïm, then he abandoned it and had a second built for himself that
he called Amsous. This prince, according to what Ibn Ouacif Shah says, knew a part of the sciences that
Douaïïl had learned from Adam; he constructed towers, raised stelae, edified palaces, had the metals
extracted from the earth, raised talismans, dug canals, and founded towns; all the elevated sciences the
Egyptians possessed came to them from Naqrâoush and his companions. These sciences were represented on
stone, and it is they that the priest Qlimoun, who accompanied Noah in the ark, explained later.

Naqrâoush, having founded Amsous, peopled it with marvels among which must be cited: a bird that each day
whistled twice at sunrise and twice at sunset; by this whistling one was informed of the events that were
accomplishing themselves, so much so that one could take the dispositions these events necessitated; a
statue of black stone placed at the center of the town and to which faced another similar statue; if some
thief penetrated into the town, he could not do otherwise than pass between these two statues, and as soon
as he found himself there, they joined together upon him and one arrested him; another statue of bronze
placed on an elevated tower and above which one saw ceaselessly clouds heaped up: whoever addressed himself
to

[PDF p. 408]

this statue and asked it for rain obtained from it what he desired. He had also raised on the frontiers of
the country statues of copper, hollow and filled with sulfur, over which watched spirits of fire; as soon
as someone approached them, these statues launched from the mouth flames that burned him. On the mountain
of Botros, he raised a tower from which escaped a watercourse that watered all the cultivations of the
vicinity. These monuments remained standing until the moment when the flood overturned them. It was
Naqrâoush, it is said, who improved the course of the Nile; before, the river spread between the two
mountains; to remedy it, this prince sent into Nubia a troop charged with diking it and deriving from it a
great canal on which were built towns and traced plantations. Naqrâoush wished next to know the source of
the Nile, and having set out, he reached the country situated beyond the Equator; there, he found himself
on the shore of the shadowy sea of Pitch and saw the Nile flowing on the surface of this sea, similar to a
network of threads, and penetrating finally under the mountain of Qomr to come out of it and throw itself
into lakes. It is by him also that were raised the statues that are found in this region. Returned to
Amsous, he divided the country among his children, giving to his eldest son Naqâoush the western region and
to his son Shourab the eastern region. Finally he built for his youngest son Misraïm the town of Borsân
where he resided. He reigned 180 years over Egypt, and at his death his body was embalmed with aromatic
drugs, then enclosed in a coffin of gold; one constructed for him a naos plated with gold where the body
was deposited with an innumerable quantity of treasures, essences, vases of gold. On the naos was engraved
the date of his death, and talismans were raised to keep away from it the destructive insects.

After him reigned his son Naqâoush who was, like his father, versed in the science of magic and talismans;
he is the first to have raised a temple in Egypt: he placed there the image of the seven planets and on
each of their chapels he wrote their good or their bad influence; he clothed each statue with splendid
garments and assigned to it servants and slaves. Then he set out from Amsous, directing himself toward the
West, reached the Enveloping Ocean and raised on its banks columns surmounted by statues whose eyes
sparkled in the night; from there he returned toward the country of the Blacks in the direction of the
Nile; along the river, he had built a wall provided with doors through which the water of the river flowed
off. Beyond the oases, in the desert of the West, [...]

[PDF p. 409]

he built three towns on high columns of colored and transparent stones; in each of these towns he
established a great number of houses of sciences, and in one of them he raised the statue of the Sun,
represented under the features of a man with the body of a bird, the whole of gold, except the eyes which
were of yellow precious stones; the statue was placed on a pedestal of magnet (lodestone) and held in its
claw a volume of science. In another of these towns, he erected a statue with a human head and the body of
a bird near which was the image of a seated woman; the latter was of solidified mercury, she was coiffed
with two tresses and held in her hand a mirror; on her head was the emblem of a planet, and she raised the
mirror to the height of her face. In the third town, one put a basin into which flowed seven waters of
different colors and that did not mix at all. In one of these towns was the image of an old man made of
turquoises, having before him young children seated, all made of rubies; in one town rose the image of
Hermes -- that is, of Mercury -- bent over a table placed before him, made of sal ammoniac and mounted on
feet of red sulfur; in the middle of the table was placed a page written in (incrusted) precious stones.
There was found also the image of an eagle in green emerald, with eyes of yellow topaz, holding in its
talon a blue serpent in silver whose tail wound around the eagle's legs and whose head reared up as if to
hiss against it. There was found still a representation of Mars mounted on a horse and holding in its hand
a naked sword, the whole in green iron. One saw there a column of red precious stones surmounted by a
cupola of gold in which rose the statue of Jupiter; one saw there still a cupola of zinc placed on four
columns of blue glass; at the summit rose the statue of the Sun and the Moon represented under the features
of a man and a woman in the act of conversing. There was found also another cupola of red sulfur enclosing
the image of Venus under the features of a woman occupied in braiding her hair; at her feet a man, in green
emerald, held in his hand a book enclosing some one of their sciences and that he seemed to read to his
companion. In the rest of the magazines, he deposited treasures in silver, in precious stones and in
jewels, precious elixirs, specimens of remedies and mortal poisons, the whole in innumerable quantity. At
the door of each of these towns was applied a talisman to defend access to it. Then he had executed long
underground corridors by which these towns communicated with one another, each

[PDF p. 410]

underground passage being three miles long. He constructed still in Egypt another town named Halgama, in
which he traced a garden whose walls were ornamented with precious stones incrusted in gold; he planted
there all sorts of trees under which he made canals run; there were planted likewise trees producing all
species of edible fruits; then he built a cupola of red marble surmounted by a statue that turned at the
same time as the sun, and he set to its guard demons charged with killing whoever went out of his house
during the night. One raised there also stelae on which were engraved all the sciences, the recipe of the
drugs, their utility and their harmfulness. For this town also, he made an underground passage that joined
the underground passages of the three other towns; between the latter and the other underground passage
there were twenty miles. These towns lasted until the flood. And when Naqâoush died, after having reigned
109 years over Egypt, one buried his body and deposited it in a naos provided with talismans.

After him reigned his brother Misrâm, son of Naqrâoush the powerful, son of Misraïm; it is from him, it is
said, that Egypt took its name of Masr. This prince was a sage, and he raised to the Sun a temple of marble
plated with red gold in the middle of which was a horse of blue stone bearing the statue of the Sun in red
gold; on the head of the statue was a vase of glass enclosing a special stone endowed with a brightness
more vivid than that of a lamp. He tamed the lions and used them as mounts. He went as far as the Enveloping
Ocean and raised in the middle of this sea a white citadel on which rose the statue of the Sun, and on this
monument he engraved his name and his portrait. He made still another statue of copper on which he engraved
these words: "I am Misrâm the powerful, the revealer of mysteries, the victorious, the strong; I have
executed true talismans; I have raised statues endowed with speech, I have raised formidable monuments on
the shore of the undulating sea. Let posterity learn that no one has the vigor of my arm!" Then he returned
to Amsous and withdrew himself from the eyes of the world during thirty years, having established to
replace him a man of the lineage of 'Ariab, son of Adam, named 'Eïqâm, priest and magician at once. Time
continuing to pass, the people of Egypt had the desire to see their king; 'Eïqâm, having taken the
instructions of Misrâm, gathered the people, and the king appeared on a throne enriched with all sorts of
ornaments and in a frightful array that filled the hearts with terror; his subjects fell prostrate before
him and adored him; Misrâm had

[PDF p. 411]

a feast prepared for them where all ate and drank, after which Misrâm ordered them to regain their
dwellings, and since then he was no longer seen.

After him reigned 'Eïqâm, the one who had held his place. On his subject, there are among the Egyptians
legends that reason refuses to believe. It is in his time, it is reported, that appeared Idris, thanks to
whom 'Eïqâm could foresee the flood and have constructed, beyond the Equator, on the plateau of the mountain
of Qomr, a palace of copper where were raised eighty-five statues of copper by whose mouths flowed the
water of the Nile, falling first into a lake to direct itself next toward Egypt. 'Eïqâm himself left Amsous
to go to this palace and see with his own eyes the ordinance of the constructions and the ornaments of the
walls, such as the engravings representing the celestial images, etc. The interior of the palace was lit by
lamps, and tables were set there on which were served all sorts of delicious dishes in magnificent vases,
and these dishes, however much the soldiers of his escort ate of them, diminished in nothing, and one could
know neither who had prepared them nor who had served them. In the middle of the palace was a basin filled
with water solidified at the surface, but mobile beneath, and whose movement one saw through the solid part.
Charmed by what he had seen, 'Eïqâm returned to Amsous, chose to replace him his son 'Ariâq, confided to him
the power and gave him his instructions; for himself, he returned to this palace and remained there until
his death. It is to this 'Eïqâm that are attributed the Coptic books that enclose the history of this people
and of all that is to happen until the end of time.

After him, the power passed to 'Ariâq who is also called 'Ariâq ben 'Eïqâm surnamed El Athîm (the guilty).
He fabricated also diverse marvelous objects, among others: (1) a yellow tree whose iron branches were
armed with claws; if some malefactor approached this tree, he was seized by these claws and could deliver
himself from them only by confessing his crime and restoring his theft to the injured person; (2) a statue
in black pumice stone to which he gave the name of 'Abd Zahal (servant of Saturn). It is before it that one
was cited in justice, and the one who was in the wrong remained fixed to his place and could not move away
except by confessing his crime himself, even were he to remain there a year. Every person who lacked some
object had only to rise during the night and look at the planets, praying and pronouncing the name of
'Ariâq; in the morning on his waking, the desired object was at his door. He had fabricated also an

[PDF p. 412]

iron tree whose branches had been coated with a prepared drug that attracted all sorts of animals, lions
and wild beasts, so much so that the hunters could easily seize them. If he was irritated against the
inhabitants of a province, he loosed upon them the wild beasts and the lions, and sometimes he changed
their (beneficent) rains into furious downpours. It is claimed that Harout and Marout appeared under his
reign. He had constructed a splendid garden and had gathered there the most beautiful women, whom he had
had carried off; one of them, using cunning, managed to poison him.

At his death, he was replaced by Lugim ben Naqâoush, who is claimed to be a descendant of Naqrâoush the
powerful and who is called Lugim the Young; it is he who took back the empire from 'Ariâq, son of 'Eïqâm
the priest, and who returned it to the Benou Naqrâoush from whose hands it had gone out, and this without
war or combat. He was learned in magic and the art of talismans and executed several marvelous things. In
his time, the vultures and the crows had multiplied and devastated the harvests; he raised four towers at
the four corners of the town of Amsous and placed on each of them the image of a crow holding in its beak
a serpent that wound around it; the harmful birds, terrified by these images, disappeared at once never to
return as long as the towers remained standing, but they were overturned by the flood. The conduct of
Lugim was admirable; he showed himself full of equity for his subjects, just and generous toward the
priests. At his death, he was buried in a naos and his treasures with him, and one attached to this naos a
preservative talisman.

After him reigned his son Khaslim, a virtuous prince and instructed in magic, who executed also marvelous
objects. It is to him that is due the first meqias (Nilometer) destined to measure the flood of the Nile;
having gathered the princes of science and the engineers, these raised on the bank of the river a
construction of marble in the middle of which was placed a small basin of copper containing a determined
quantity of water; above this basin were placed two eagles of copper, one male, the other female; on the
first day of the month in which the flood began, one opened the house, the priests gathered there in the
presence of the king and mumbled their prayers there until one of the eagles whistled. If the male eagle
whistled, it presaged an excellent Nile; if on the contrary it was the female, the Nile would be
insufficient. According to this, one could take one's precautions against the rise of the price of grains
and make one's provisions in advance. It is this prince also who established in Nubia the bridge over

[PDF p. 413]

the Nile. At his death, one enclosed him with his treasures in a naos to which was attached a talisman.

After him reigned his son Housâl or Yousâl, a word that signifies "servant of Venus"; some name him Soumâl
ben Lugim El Naqrâoushi, for he was of the family of Naqrâoush the powerful. It is in his time, it is said,
that Noah was born. He was a virtuous prince, very versed in magic and the art of talismans, and who made,
he too, marvelous things, among others a town in the middle of which he raised to the Sun a statue that
turned at the same time as this star, setting in the west and rising, in the morning, in the east. He dug
also a corridor under the Nile, followed an underground path, and arrived unexpectedly at Babel to visit
there the monuments raised by the king. Noah lived in his time. He had twenty sons to each of whom he
assigned a region; he was the great chief of magic and remained on the throne 117 years, after which he
occupied himself no more than with the temples, leaving to each of his sons the care of regulating the
affairs of the territory that had been attributed to him by his father. And for seven years it was thus.

Then their suffrages gathered on one of them whom they elected king; he was called Todareshan or
Todaresar. As soon as the latter was king, he exiled all his brothers into the towns of the interior, to
the west of Egypt, and keeping with him only a woman, his cousin, who was a magician, he built himself a
pavilion of wood where were engraved the images of the planets; he stretched the richest carpets and,
having had it transported onto the water, he promenaded there reclining (on cushions). Now, one day when he
was promenading thus, a violent wind began to blow that raised the waves, overturned and broke the
pavilion; the king was drowned as well as all those who were with him in the floating palace.

After him reigned his brother Nimroud the powerful, who is also called Shimroud ben Housâl. This prince had
an admirable conduct, he was just toward his subjects and full of equity; he gathered his brothers and
divided with them the treasures of their dead brother; thanks to him, the people were happy. He had the
wife of his brother, the magician, sought, but the latter took flight with her son and took refuge in a
town of Upper Egypt where she put herself out of reach of the pursuits of her brother-in-law, thanks to
her magic. At the end of a certain time, the magicians she had gathered around her son Toumidoûn suggested
to him the idea of seizing the power. Nimroud and his brothers marched against him; a terrible combat was
engaged in which Toumidoûn was victorious and where perished Nimroud.

[PDF p. 414]

After him reigned Toumidoûn ben Todareshan, who established his capital in Amsous. He was a skillful and
wise prince whom the magic of his mother rendered formidable. The latter executed for him marvelous works:
a cupola of glass, made in the image of the celestial sphere, and that turned at the same time as the
firmament; in this cupola were represented the images of the planets: by it one knew the secrets of nature
and all the sciences of the world. Toumidoûn had reigned for 60 years when his mother, the magician, died.
One coated her body with aromatics destined to preserve it from corruption and from insects, then one
buried her under the statue of the Moon. It is recounted that after her death one heard, coming from her
tomb, the voice of a spirit that predicted marvelous things and answered the questions that were posed to
it. When Toumidoûn died, after a reign of 100 years, one made for him a statue of glass that opened in two
parts and into which one introduced his body impregnated with all the aromatics preservative of
putrefaction; then the statue was closed again and soldered, and finally deposited in the temple of the
idols; near him were buried his treasures, and one instituted for him an annual feast.

After him reigned his son Shariâq, also called Sariâq ben Toumidoûn ben Todaresân ben Housâl; like his
father, he was very versed in magic, sorcery, and the art of talismans, and he made marvelous works. Above
the gate of the town of Amsous, he placed the image of a duck of copper perched on a column; if a stranger,
coming from any country whatever, entered the town, this duck beat its wings and uttered a cry; at once one
seized the stranger and one clarified his affair, in order to know the reason for his arrival. He dug a
canal that, starting from the Nile, directed itself toward the towns of the West, and, along this canal, he
built monuments, towns, and places of pleasure. A king of the lineage of Fouracha ben Adam or, according to
others, of the lineage of Souaniti ben Adam, arose in his time on the side of Iraq, subjugated the
provinces of Syria, and marched against Egypt, in order to seize its king. He had been told: "You will be
able to do nothing against this country because of the magical power of its inhabitants," but he would
believe nothing of it and, accompanied by an escort, he came himself to make himself account of the
situation of the Egyptians; from his appearance at the frontier, he was taken, with all those who
accompanied him, by the people charged with supervising this region, who sent a report and awaited the
instructions

[PDF p. 415]

of the king regarding the prisoners. Now, the king had had a dream in which he saw himself on an elevated
tower where an enormous bird precipitated itself upon him uttering cries; in wishing to avoid it, he had
nearly fallen from the tower, but the bird had passed beyond the king who in this way had been saved. On
his waking, frightened by his dream, he recounted it to the chief of the magicians, who said to him: "A
king will attack you, but he will be able to do nothing against you." And having consulted the stars of the
king, he saw that the prince who was to attack him had already entered Egypt; at this precise moment
presented itself the messenger bringing the report on the prisoners of the frontier. The king gave the
order to bring them to him, but to have them first examine all the marvels of the country. Solidly bound,
they were promenaded among the marvels of the land of Egypt, and one showed them all the talismans that
were there. They arrived first at Alexandria, then at Assouan, and finally at the garden constructed by
Misrâm and where the king Shariâq went. At the moment when the cortege presented itself, the magicians made
marvelous statues appear. The prisoners entered into the presence of the king surrounded by the priests and
before whom burned a fire that whoever wished to approach the king had to cross. This fire spared the
innocent, but seized any man who wished to do some harm to the king or who felt for him the slightest
aversion. The whole troop, man after man, passed through the fire without it doing them any harm; finally
came the turn of the king of Iraq, but at the moment when he approached the fire, the heat seized him and
he sought to take flight. One set about pursuing him and, having reached him, one brought him back to
Shariâq, who interrogated him at length and ended by knowing all that concerned him. The order was given to
hang him, and he was hanged on the citadel where he had been taken, and at the moment of his torture, one
proclaimed that such would be the chastisement of whoever coveted what would be out of his reach. As for
the other prisoners, they were pardoned; they left Egypt, recounting everywhere the marvels they had seen
there, and these accounts took from the kings of the earth all desire to conquer Egypt. Shariâq died after
a reign of 130 years. One buried him in a naos at the same time as his riches, and one executed talismans
to protect him against whoever would attempt to destroy his body.

After him reigned his son Shahlouq, very versed in magic and the art of talismans. He distributed the water
of the Nile in well-measured portions that he distributed exactly in all directions; he put in order the
affairs of the Empire and erected a temple to the Fire, for he was the first who adored this element. In

[PDF p. 416]

Amsous he executed marvelous monuments. He placed on the highest of the mountains a tree that divided the
winds and that repelled whoever wished to harm Egypt or diminish it, whether they were genies, men,
quadrupeds, or birds; he constructed also in the town a cupola with a heptagonal base and that had seven
doors, one at each face. In the middle of the cupola was found a second of yellow copper, at the summit of
which was the image of the seven planets, and below another cupola placed on seven pillars. Above the first
door of the cupola, a lion and a lioness of yellow copper, both crouched, to which one immolated a small
lion-cub, burning, in the way of perfumes, the hairs of this animal; on the second door a bull and a cow,
to which one sacrificed a calf whose hairs were burned; on the third door a boar and a sow, to which one
immolated a small piglet whose bristles were burned; on the fourth door a ram and a ewe, to which one
sacrificed a lamb whose fleece was burned; on the fifth door a male fox and a female fox to which one
sacrificed a fox-cub whose hairs were burned; on the sixth door a vulture and its female, to which one
sacrificed a young vulture whose feathers were burned; on the seventh door an eagle and its female, to
which one sacrificed an eaglet whose feathers were burned likewise; and one anointed each couple of beasts
with the blood of the animal one sacrificed to it; one burned the victims entirely and one buried the ashes
of them under the threshold of the doors of the cupola; he assigned to this cupola servants charged with
maintaining lamps day and night. He divided the people of Egypt into seven castes, to each of which was
attributed one of the doors of the cupola. If some plaintiff approached one of these images and the wrongs
were on his side, he found himself stuck to this image and could detach himself from it only by confessing
the truth; the man found himself thus fixed to the male animal and the woman to the female animal, and in
this way one recognized the oppressor and the oppressed. This cupola remained standing in Amsous until the
flood destroyed it. Shariâq, it is said, saw in a dream his father who ordered him to go to one of the
mountains of Egypt that he designated to him; on this mountain he would find an opening of such and such a
fashion; above the door he would see a viper with two heads that showed its teeth to whoever approached it.
"Take with you," added the apparition, "two small birds, one male, the other female; offer them to this
viper that it may swallow them; the viper will seize them by the head and carry them off into an underground
passage. As soon as it has disappeared, enter there in your turn.

[PDF p. 417]

There you will find an admirable woman made of hot and dry light (?); she will touch you and her heat will
make itself felt to you, do not approach her, you would be burned, but hold yourself seated facing her and
salute her; she will speak to you. It is up to you to understand well what she will tell you and to execute
it, you will derive from it much honor; she will indicate to you the treasure of your ancestor Misrâm of
which she is there the guardian." On his waking, Shariâq did what his father had prescribed to him, and when
he was seated near the woman and had saluted her, the latter said to him: "Do you know me?" "No," he
answered. "I am," she resumed, "the image of the Fire, adored by the past peoples. I wish that you make my
name live again and that you raise to me anew a temple in which you will maintain for me a perpetual fire in
a brazier, and that you institute in my honor an annual feast at which you will attend with your people. In
exchange, you will find near me a help that will render you illustrious more than you are illustrious and
powerful more than you are powerful. I will keep away from you whoever will wish to harm you, and I will
show you the treasures of your ancestor Misrâm." Shariâq having promised to execute what she asked, the lady
led him to the treasures buried under the suspended towns and taught him the manner of making himself master
of them and of guarding himself from the spirits set to their guard, giving him to this effect all the
necessary instructions. "How," asked Shariâq, "will I be able to see you again?" "Do not return any more,"
she said, "for the viper would no longer spare you, but perfume your house in such and such a manner, and I
will come to you." Thereupon, she left Shariâq all joyous; he set out and accomplished all she had ordered:
he raised a temple to the Fire, removed the treasures of Misrâm, and, at his death, one buried him in a naos
and with him all his riches and all his treasures, and a preservative talisman was placed on his tomb.

After him reigned his son Sourid, a wise and virtuous prince; it is he who, the first, collected taxes in
Egypt, had distributed, from his treasury, money to the sick and the incurable, and instituted the morning
genuflexion; he executed marvelous things: a mirror made of mixed substances, in which one saw the
different climates and by which one knew the events accomplished, and one could in consequence foresee the
abundance or the dearth; one placed this mirror, which was of copper, in the middle of the town of Amsous.
He raised also in Amsous the image of a woman seated, holding in her lap a child that she suckled; this
woman was such that if an Egyptian woman, suffering from some ill in a part of her body, came to rub the
sick part of her body against the corresponding part of the body of the statue, the ill at once disappeared;

[PDF p. 418]

if it was a question of an exhaustion of the milk, the woman had only to rub her breasts against the breasts
of the statue, and the milk returned; if it was a question of a suppression of the menses, the woman had to
rub her natural parts against those of the statue, and the menses returned; if on the contrary the blood
came in too great abundance, the woman rubbed the lower part of her pubis against the corresponding part of
the statue. In the case of a laborious childbirth, one rubbed the head of the child placed in the lap of the
statue, and the delivery accomplished itself. Did a woman wish to be loved by her husband, she rubbed her
face against that of the statue saying: "Do this or that." But if some sinful woman placed her hands on the
statue, she was seized by a trembling that calmed itself only when the criminal woman manifested her
repentance. This statue remained standing until the moment when the flood overturned it; according to the
books of the Copts, it was found again after the flood and many people adored it. Sourid raised also another
statue composed of a great number of mixed substances, and if someone suffered in some part of his body, he
had only to wash the corresponding part of the statue and to drink the water that had served for the
washing, the ill ceased at once. It is this Sourid who raised in Egypt the two great pyramids attributed to
Sheddad ben 'Ad; but the Copts refuse to admit that the Adites ever entered their country, from which their
magic would have repelled them. When Sourid died, one buried him in the pyramid with his treasures. He
lived, it is claimed, 300 years before the flood and reigned 190 years.

After him reigned his son Hargib, instructed and versed like his father in magic and the art of talismans;
thus he executed marvelous objects; he had quantities of metals extracted, brought to light the art of
chemistry, and constructed the pyramids of Dahchour, where he transported considerable riches -- precious
stones, drugs, poisons -- and confided the guard of them to spirits. A man having wounded another, he had
his fingers cut off; another having stolen money, he made of the thief the slave of the robbed. At his
death, he was buried in the pyramid, and with him his riches and his treasures.

After him reigned his son Minaous, who is also called Minqaous; he was, like his father, very learned, but
violent, vicious, sanguinary, tearing the women from their husbands, which his intimates did likewise as a
thing [...]

[PDF p. 419]

licit, following his example. He executed marvelous things and discovered treasures. He built palaces of
gold and silver that canals watered; the sand there was replaced by precious stones. He chose, to govern
his subjects, a violent man named Qornâs and set out to make war against the peoples of the West, of whom
he massacred a great number, and at his death he was buried in one of his palaces and his treasures with
him. On his tomb one put a talisman to protect him and defend him against whoever would approach.

After him reigned his son Afrous, versed like his father in knowledge and science. From his accession, he
made show of justice and equity and returned to their husbands the women his father had carried off. He
built a cupola 50 cubits long and 100 wide, and placed on its flanks birds of copper that whistled in
different fashions during an hour without stopping. In the middle of the town of Amsous, he raised a tower
at the summit of which was a human head of copper that uttered a cry each time one of the hours of the day
or the night had elapsed, and whoever heard this cry knew that an hour had just elapsed. He raised another
tower surmounted by a cupola of gilded copper and coated with unguents; and each night, as soon as the sun
was set, a light radiated from the cupola, illuminating the town of Amsous all night, so much so that one
would have believed oneself in full day; and neither the wind nor the rain could extinguish this light,
which disappeared at the moment when the day rose. He sent as a present to a king of Babel a flask of
emerald whose diameter was five spans; this flask was found again, it is said, after the flood. He had
raised also in the mountain of the East a colossal statue standing on a pedestal; this statue was painted
and the yellow parts were reproduced with gold; its face was constantly directed toward the sun and turned
at the same time as it until the moment of its setting; during the night the statue continued its evolution
and at dawn found itself facing the East, the face turned toward the rising sun. He constructed in the
desert of the West numerous towns that he provided with magnificent treasures. He lay with three hundred
women without having a child, for God had rendered the matrices sterile, having decided to annihilate the
world by the flood and to make destruction fall on men and animals. At his death, he was placed in a naos,
in the mountain of the East, and, with him, his riches and a talisman to protect him.

After him reigned Armalinous, who executed marvelous works, built

[PDF p. 420]

towns and palaces and multiplied talismans. He had a cousin named Far'an who was audacious. He removed him
by putting him at the head of an army with which he set out, subjugating the kings, massacring numerous
peoples, and pillaging their riches; on his return, one of the wives of the king became enamored of him and
left him no rest until he united himself with her; they bound themselves therefore and remained thus a long
time, then they feared that the king might discover them, and the woman prepared for Armalinous a poisoned
beverage of which he died.

After him reigned his cousin Far'ân ben Meshour; no one dared hold his head up to him because of his
violence and his skill, and he had reigned a little time when the priest Qlimoun had a dream in which white
birds seemed to descend from the sky and say: "Whoever wishes salvation, let him go to the master of the
ark." One already knew, among the Egyptians, the future arrival of the flood since the time of Sourid, and
it is for this reason that one had built the pyramids and that the people had made themselves underground
habitations plated with glass where the winds had been carefully imprisoned. Far'ân had made a certain
number of them for himself and his own. Qlimoun did not hesitate, and gathering his relatives, his children,
and his disciples, he went to Noah and embraced his faith. He remained with him and mounted with him into
the ark. The flood therefore arrived under the reign of Far'ân; Egypt was entirely submerged, its
constructions destroyed and its sciences annihilated. The water stayed on the soil for six months and rose
to the half of the great pyramids, and God willing, we will give some account of this event in the chapter
of this book that treats of the calamities of Egypt. It is said that Far'ân was arrogant and cruel, that he
seized the riches and carried off the women, and that he wrote to El Darshil ben Lahouïl of Babel, advising
him to kill Noah, for he despised the priests and the temples. In his time, the land of Egypt altered, the
cultivations were reduced to almost nothing, the two regions annihilated, for both, espousing his errors
and his crimes, associated themselves with his diversions and his games; the people followed the same path
as he and the vice propagated from one to the other. When the flood arrived and the rain began to fall,
Far'ân, drunk, rose to flee to the pyramid; but the earth opened up before him at the moment when he reached
the door: his feet failed him and he fell without strength and crying, and all those who had taken refuge
in the underground passages died of consumption. And God is the most learned.

[PDF p. 421]

CHAPTER III
OF THE TOWN OF MEMPHIS AND OF ITS KINGS

This town was situated to the west of the Nile, twelve miles from Fostat Masr; it was the first town built
in Egypt after the flood, and it became the capital of the kingdom after the town of Amsous of which we have
just spoken. Its role of capital lasted until its destruction by Bokhta-Nasar (Nebuchadnezzar). God has
spoken of it in his sublime book: "And he entered the town without the knowledge of its inhabitants" (Koran,
XXVIII, 14). The imam Abou Ga'far Mohammed ben Garir El Tabari, in his book entitled Collection of
Clarifications serving as commentary to the Koran, reports this remark of El Saddi: Moses, having become
grown, used mounts similar to those of Pharaoh and wore garments like those of the king; he was even called
"son of Pharaoh." Now, one day Pharaoh mounted on his chariot, while Moses was not near him, and, when the
latter arrived, he was informed that Pharaoh had departed. Moses mounted in a chariot and ran on the traces
of the king whom he rejoined in a place called Menf where he entered toward the hour of noon, the hour when
the markets were closed and the streets deserted. It is of this town that God speaks when he says: "And he
entered the town without the knowledge of its inhabitants." Ibn Abd el Hakem reports, on the authority of
Abd Allah ben Lahiah, that the one who first inhabited Egypt, after the destruction by the waters inflicted
by God on the people (contemporary) of Noah, was Beïsar, son of Cham, son of Noah. Beïsar established
himself at Memphis, the first town built after the flood, with his descendants; together thirty persons,
of whom his four sons, already adults and married. These four sons were Masr, Fareq, Mâg, and Yâg, sons of
Beïsar: Masr was the eldest. To this circumstance, the new town owed its name of Mafah, a word that, in the
language of the Copts, signifies "thirty." Before, they lived at the foot of the Moqattam, where they had
dug themselves numerous habitations. Ibn Khordadabah, in his book of the Routes and the Empires, says:
"Memphis is the town where Pharaoh resided and that this prince had provided with seventy gates of iron and
surrounded with walls of iron and yellow copper; there flowed rivers that took their source under the
throne of the king, and these rivers were four in number." It is recounted that the town of Memphis was
provided with bridges and dikes

[PDF p. 422]

executed with an art and a precision such that the water flowed under the houses of the town and under the
courts, and that one could retain it or distribute it at will. It is to this that God alludes in this
passage where there is question of Pharaoh: "Is it not to me that belongs the kingdom of Egypt, and do not
these canals flow by my will?" (Koran, XLIII, 50). There were at Memphis numerous statues that remained
standing until the moment when they were overturned with the other statues that fell at the hour when the
Prophet pointed the finger toward the idols, the day of the conquest of Mecca; that day the Prophet, a rod
in hand, made the circuit of the town crying: "The truth has come, the falsehood has vanished, the
falsehood is destined to disappear" (Koran, XVII, 83). And all the statues whose face his rod menaced fell
on the nape, and all those whose nape he menaced fell on the face, so much so that there remained no statue
that did not fall. And at this same hour were overturned all the idols of the earth, from the Orient to the
Occident, and their adepts remained stupefied, ignorant of the cause of their fall. And since that time, the
idols of Memphis remained overturned. It is in this town that were seen the two great statues neighboring
the Green House that enclosed the statue of El 'Aziz, all of gold with the eyes made of two incomparable
rubies; later, after the year 600 [10 September 1203 to 28 August 1204], the statues and the Green House
were put to pieces.

Memphis, it is said, had thirty miles of length and twenty miles of width. In the time of Misraïm, a
descendant of Japhet, son of Noah, had made an apparatus to raise the water and transport it to the crest
of the wall of the town; this apparatus was composed of hollow rungs, and, each time the water reached one
of these rungs, the following filled itself; in this fashion, the water reached the summit of the wall
whence, by a skillful distribution, it penetrated into each house of the town and came out of it to be
conducted outside the city.

There was at Memphis a house (naos) of green granite of a single piece and very hard, on which the iron
could not bite; this naos enclosed a statue and characters were engraved on it. On the lintel of the door
were represented serpents with swollen necks. Thousands of people gathered could not have managed to shake
it, so enormous and heavy was it. The Sabeans claim that it was a temple of the Moon and that it formed part
of the seven temples

[PDF p. 423]

raised in Memphis to the seven planets. This Green House was demolished by the emir Seïf el Din Sheïkhoun El
'Amri after the year 750 [22 March 1349 to 10 March 1350]. There remain some debris of it in the convent and
in the mosque that this emir had constructed in the street of Salibah, outside Cairo. Abou 'Abd Allah
Mohammed ben 'Abd el Rahman el Qeïsi, in his book Present to the Intelligences, says: "I saw in the palace
of the Pharaoh of Moses a great house made of a single stone, green like the myrtle and in which were
represented the firmaments and the stars: we have never seen a more beautiful marvel."

Abou-l Solt Ommyah ben 'Abd el 'Aziz el Andalousi says: "In ancient times, the capital of Egypt was the
town of Memphis, to the west of the Nile and twelve miles from Fostat; but when Alexander had founded the
town of Alexandria, the people flocked there and peopled it, and it became the abode of science and the
residence of the government until its conquest by the Muslims, in the time of 'Omar ben El Khattab, when
'Amr ben el 'As founded the town known under the name of Fostat. The Egyptians and others still, Arabs and
non-Arabs, came to inhabit it in crowds, and it remained the chief-place of the provinces and the districts
of Egypt until our epoch."

Master Ibrahim ben Ouacif Shah, the writer, after having reported the history of the town of Amsous and the
destruction of its edifices by the flood of Noah, adds: "The waters having withdrawn, the first who reigned
in Egypt after the flood was Beïsar, son of Cham, son of Noah: he was accompanied by thirty persons, of the
most courageous of his family and his children; all gathered and edified the town of Memphis where they
installed themselves. With them was the priest Qlimoun, of whom there was question above regarding the town
of Amsous. This priest had married his daughter to Beïsar, and she had accompanied her husband to Egypt
where she gave him a son named Misraïm. Beïsar having died, one buried him in the convent of Abou Hermès, a
name given, it is said, to the region situated to the west of the Pyramids. It was there, it is claimed, the
first cemetery where one buried in Egypt. The death of Beïsar arrived 1806 years after the time of the
flood." Another author says: "Then Misraïm built a town to which he gave his name. A descendant of Japhet
came to him and raised for him a vertical wall and made a machine with rungs, thanks to the perfection of
which he raised the water to the summit of the wall whence this water redescended into the town to be
employed there without fatigue and without cost, and [...]

[PDF p. 424]

came out on another side. And on the wall one put the inscription: This is the work of a mortal and not the
work of the Eternal."

After Beïsar reigned his son Misraïm (also called Masr) ben Beïsar. Qlimoun discovered for him the
treasures of Egypt, taught him its writing, and instructed him in the science of the Egyptians. Misraïm
founded towns, dug canals, planted trees, and constructed a magnificent town to which he gave the name of
Darsan and which is the same as El 'Arish. From a woman of the caste of the priests he had a son named
Qoftim; then he built the town of Rakoudah, site of the future Alexandria. At his death, one made him an
underground passage 150 cubits long, all covered with white marble; in the middle was a pedestal plated
with leaves of gold and provided with four doors above each of which was a statue of gold, bearing on the
head a crown of gold and seated on a throne of gold with feet of emerald. On the chest of each of the
statues one engraved verses destined to protect the body, enclosed in a vat in the form of a human body,
made of green emerald and 40 cubits long. With him was buried all that his treasures contained -- gold,
silver, precious stones -- among others: a thousand pieces of cut emerald, a thousand statuettes of precious
stones, a thousand vases of gold filled with admirable pearls, a thousand cups of gold, a great number of
ingots of silver. One placed on the body a talisman to defend it against whoever would attempt to approach,
and one engraved on the tomb: "He is dead, Misraïm, the son of Beïsar, the son of Cham, the son of Noah,
2600 years (or according to others 2700) after the flood; never did he adore the idols, and he has departed
toward the garden where there is neither old age, nor sickness, nor chagrin, nor sadness. He has written
here the name of the very great God who will permit no one to approach him, save a king who will appear at
the end of time and who will proclaim the religion of the king of justice and will believe in the
resurrection, in the holy Book, and in the Prophet propagator of the true faith at the end of the ages."
Then one rolled above the underground passage enormous rocks on which one spread sand, forming thus a
barrier between two opposed mountains.

Masr ben Beïsar was, it is said, in the ark with the grandfather of his father, Noah, and the latter prayed
God that he might accord to Masr to inhabit the excellent and blessed land, mother of the nations and refuge
of the faithful, whose river is the purest of rivers, asking that he put in it the best of his blessings,
that he subject the world to Masr and his descendants, that

[PDF p. 425]

for them he render the earth easy, and that he give them all power over it. Masr asked his grandfather to
describe to him this land, and Noah described it to him; and Beïsar having become old and feeble, his son
took him with all his brothers to Egypt where they installed themselves, and it is from him that this
country took the name of Masr.

After him reigned his son Qobtim, also called Qoft ben Misraïm. He was the first who executed marvelous
things after the flood, extracting the metals, digging canals, raising stelae and towers, and making
talismans.

It is recounted that after the death of Misraïm, discord set in among his children, of whom Qoft was the
youngest; having gathered near the pyramids, they decided that the empire would be the share of the one who
would vanquish his brothers. Ashmoun and Atrib struggled first and Atrib was vanquished; then Sa struggled
against Ashmoun and Ashmoun was vanquished; finally Sa struggled against Qoft and Qoft carried off the
victory. It was therefore Qoft who took the government after his father, and his brothers made their
submission to him. Qoft continued to inhabit Memphis, capital of his father, and married a woman who gave
him four children: Qaftarim, Ashmoun, Atrib, and Sa, who grew, multiplied, and peopled the country. At the
moment of his death, Qoft divided the land among his four children: To Qaftarim fell the territory from
Assouan to Qouft; Ashmoun had as share the country situated between Qouft and Memphis; Atrib received the
Garf entire, and Sa all the region from the Beheirah to the Occident; Qaftarim had in addition the
suzerainty over all the others. Qoft prescribed moreover to each of his sons to construct himself a town in
the territory that was attributed to him and built for himself a vault under the great mountain; this vault
was covered with marble, dormers were arranged in it for the circulation of the air, which gave rise to a
very violent current of air; one placed there balls of copper coated with a certain unguent and that lit up
like lamps night and day. After his death, his body was deposited in this vault, in a coffin of gold, after
having been clad in a robe embroidered with pearls and coral; at the head of the coffin one raised a column
of marble surmounted by a sparkling stone; around were arranged boxes in painted stones containing his books
of science; finally one placed near him his riches, his treasures, his precious objects, and one engraved on
the tomb what had been engraved on the tomb of his father. Each of his

[PDF p. 426]

children withdrew into his province; Sa withdrew with his family and his children and went to inhabit the
town of Sa of which there will be question further on.

It is recounted that the confusion of languages took place in the time of Qoft, to whom God taught by
inspiration the Coptic language; that this king kept the empire for 480 years, then that after his death he
was buried in the country of the Oases.

After him reigned his brother Ashmoun ben Masr; it is said however that, during his life, Qoft had installed
his son Qaftarim in his province and that the latter rendered it rapidly prosperous. He was a bold man of
high stature; he had extracted a quantity of metals such that never had a similar quantity been extracted
before. He built the town of Dendérah and constructed in the mountain of Qouft an elevated tower from which
