one saw the Eastern sea; there he discovered mines of mercury and dug the pond that one calls the hunter of
birds. It was toward the last times of his reign that 'Ad was annihilated by the wind. In his time the
demons made reappear the idols that the flood had submerged, and one adored them. He kept the empire for
480 years.

Ibn Abd el Hakem reports: After Masr ben Beïsar reigned Qoft ben Masr; after Qoft reigned his brother
Ashmoun, then Atrib ben Masr, then Sa ben Masr, then his son Todras ben Sa, then Mâliq ben Todras, then
Hazaba ben Mâliq, then Kalkala ben Hazaba. It is recounted that when Ashmoun had taken the empire after his
brother, Sheddâd ben Haddad ben Sheddad ben 'Ad marched against him, seized the land of Egypt, destroyed
its edifices, built the pyramids, and directed himself toward the place where Alexandria later was, founded
a town there and remained there a certain time, then that, the Adites having gone out of the land of Egypt,
Ashmoun returned into his kingdom; after him reigned his brother Sa, then after Sa his son Todras: it is in
his time that God sent Saleh to the Thammoud.

Todras having died, his son Mâliq El Budsir succeeded him; he was one of the most audacious men and of a
high stature who executed magnificent works, among others: a tower surmounted by a quadrangular cupola; on
each face opened a dormer from which, on certain days of the year known to all, came out a thick smoke of
different colors, each color having a particular signification: the green smoke indicated fertility and
abundance for that year; the white smoke was a sign of dearth and misery; the

[PDF p. 427]

red smoke presaged wars or attacks of enemies; the yellow smoke announced fires or deaths caused by the
king; the black smoke was a sign of rains, of inundations, of upheavals of the soil; the smoke of mixed
colors presaged innumerable calamities and injustices committed by people one toward another. He made also
a tree of copper that attracted all the wild beasts; these came to attach themselves to it and remained
there until one had taken them; thus the Egyptians were able to nourish themselves on the flesh of the wild
beasts. One day, it happened that a crow burst the eye of a young boy of the caste of the priests and tore
it out. The king then fabricated a tree of copper on which was placed a crow, the wings deployed, holding
in its claws a serpent and bearing an inscription on the back. And the crows fell on this tree and detached
themselves from it only dead. In his time, the sand having increased in an alarming fashion on the side of
the Occident of Egypt, he raised a statue of black granite on a pedestal of the same material: on the
shoulder of the statue was placed a basket containing a shovel, signs were engraved on its face, its chest,
and its arms; it faced the Occident; before it the sands uncovered themselves and the winds brought them
back behind, where they formed high hills. This same king sent Hermes to the mountain of Qomr whence comes
the Nile; there, Hermes raised statues of copper and regularized the banks of the Nile, which before flowed
in places and in places interrupted its course; then he marched on the side of the Occident to see what was
beyond. He arrived at a vast land furrowed with streams and covered with trees; he built places of pleasure
there, installed himself there, and had come there a great number of people of his family who peopled this
country, to the point of covering all the land of the Occident; then, having found themselves in contact
with the Berbers, there arose between them wars where perished a great number of men, and the country became
a desert again and of the past state there remained only the oases. El Budsir withdrew himself from the
regards of men, showing himself only from time to time on his throne, and often he addressed the word to his
subjects without these seeing him.

Abou-l Hassan El Masa'oudi, in his book Accounts of the Time, recounts that the first who was really a
magician and changed the religion to adore the planets was El Budsir. The Copts affirm that the planets
conversed with him. To him are attributed numerous marvels, among others this one: Having withdrawn himself
from the regards of men and retired from the affairs of the kingdom for several years, he appeared only from
time to time, once each

[PDF p. 428]

year, at the moment when the sun enters the sign of the Ram; at that moment his subjects could approach him:
he spoke to them ostensibly, prescribing them certain things, forbidding them certain others, and putting
them on guard against disobedience to his orders. He had constructed for himself a cupola of silver plated
with gold, at the summit of which he sat and from there, the face uncovered, addressed the word to his
people.

After his death reigned his son Araqlimoun, priest and magician, who executed surprising things. He sat on
the clouds, where one saw him under the features of a man of high stature, and he remained thus a long time.
Later, he abandoned the Egyptians who remained without a king, then, a certain day, they saw him under the
fiery image of the disk of the sun at the moment when it enters the sign of the Ram; he ordered them to
confer the power on 'Adim ben Qoftim, warning them that he would no longer return among them.

They therefore took for king 'Adim ben Qoftim, an audacious man of high stature. It was he who introduced
the torture of the cross into Egypt. Here is how: a man and a woman having committed the crime of adultery,
he crucified them, placing the back of one against the back of the other. He built four towns that he
provided with considerable treasures and in which he put talismans and a number of marvelous objects. He
raised also, on the shore of the Eastern sea, a tower surmounted by a statue turned toward the Orient, to
prevent the sea from invading the land of Egypt. In Nubia, he threw a bridge over the Nile. He kept the
empire for 140 years and died aged 730 years.

After him reigned his son Shaddat ben 'Adim, who is generally named Sheddad ben 'Ad; he was a priest learned
in magic, and it is he, it is said, who constructed the pyramids of Dahchour. He executed magnificent works
and marvelous talismans and constructed towns on the eastern bank (of the Nile). It is in his time that Qous
was built; he made an expedition among the Ethiopians and ravaged the country. His reign lasted 90 years;
it is he who, the first, captured birds of prey and trained them for the hunt and produced (by crossings)
the race of greyhounds. He put in the lake of Siout tamed crocodiles that attracted the crocodiles of the
Nile; one killed the latter and with their skin one covered the boats. One day, being at the hunt, his
horse overturned him, he fell into a precipice and killed himself: previously, irritated against one of his
servants, he had hurled him from the top of a high mountain and the man had been put to pieces; the same
fate reached him in his turn. At his death, one [...]

[PDF p. 429]

placed him in a naos and one buried with him his riches; one placed a talisman to defend him against whoever
would wish to do him harm, and one wrote on his tomb: "It does not befit the powerful to stray from the good
path nor to do what is forbidden; for they will be requited according to their acts. This is the naos of the
son of Shaddat son of 'Adim; he did what he ought not to have done and the same fate struck him."

After him reigned his son Minqâoush, a wise, virtuous prince and magician who did marvelous things, raised
astonishing constructions, among others, 8 parasangs from Memphis, a temple that he dedicated to the
planets, and gathered incalculable treasures; in his time, more mines were opened than under all the other
reigns. Once, having set out, he marched for a day in the direction of the South, then for a day and a day
again in the direction of the West, and arrived, on the third day, at a black mountain under which he dug
underground passages and grottoes where he buried his riches, and on the door of the underground passage he
engraved an inscription. His riches were, it is said, so considerable that he buried thus the load of twelve
hundred chariots of gold and precious stones, and for four years he sent again once a year numerous chariots
whose load was buried in this hiding place. For a very long time, one could see the trace of the wheels of
these chariots between Memphis and the Maghreb. He raised a temple to the Moon, and it is also he, it is
said, who built the town of Memphis for his daughters, who were thirty in number. He encouraged the study
of chemistry and everyone occupied himself with it night and day; by this means he gathered considerable
riches and innumerable precious stones. It is again this king who built the town of 'Aïn Shams and divided
into four parts the revenues of Egypt; a quarter for the king, a quarter for the army, a quarter for the
putting in order of the soil, and the other quarter destined to be buried to provide for events to come; he
divided also Egypt into 130 districts. He died after a reign of 91 years.

After him reigned his son 'Adim ben Menqaoush. He was powerful and no one could resist him. It is in his
time that appeared the two angels, who taught magic to men. The Copts claim that these two angels descended
first in Egypt and went next to Babel.

After him reigned his brother Menaoush ben Menqaoush, a learned and wise magician. He edified numerous
constructions in the mountain and the desert, buried considerable treasures there and raised stelae there.
He built in the

[PDF p. 430]

desert of the Occident a town where he raised a tower near which he buried incalculable riches; he planted
in this town a tree that produced all sorts of fruits. He was the first in Egypt to adore the ox; he loved
science and sought the books that treat of it. And thus all these kings strove to accomplish things more
extraordinary than those executed by their predecessors, studying with perseverance and engraving on the
stone.

After him reigned his son Hermès, a prince little learned and who did none of the things his fathers had
done; he died after a reign of 11 years.

After him reigned Ashmoun ben Qobtim ben Masr ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh (Noah), whose territory extended
from Ashmoun to Memphis, to the Occident, and to the Orient as far as the sea on the side of Barqah, extreme
limit of Egypt; in the Said, it reached the frontier of Akhmim. He had established his residence in the town
of Ashmouneïn which measured twelve miles of length by an equal width. This prince built to the east of the
Nile the town of Antinoë, where he raised a magnificent palace and which he provided with edifices, circuses,
and numerous marvels. He built also the town of Tahratis and was the first who played at ball and at mallet.
It is said that he built numerous towns, in which he executed marvelous objects, among others a town raised
on the flank of the mountain, with four doors opening on the four cardinal points; on the eastern door was
the image of an eagle; on the western door that of a bull; on the northern door the image of a lion and on
the southern door that of a dog; to these images were attached spirits, and if some stranger presented
himself, he could not penetrate into the town without the permission of its guardians; under each of these
four statues were buried all sorts of treasures, and in the town one planted a tree that produced fruits of
every species; a tower was raised, of 80 cubits of height and surmounted by a cupola that, each day, colored
itself with a particular color, and this for seven days, to begin again the eighth with the initial color;
and each day the town was lit with a color similar to that emitted that day by the cupola. At the foot of
the tower circulated a canal derived from the Nile and filled with fish of all sorts; one placed around the
town talismanic statues with a human body and the head of a monkey. Ashmoun made of this town the abode of
the magicians, and it took the name of Town of the Magicians, and there one gave oneself over to all the
practices of magic. In the vicinity of this town, he built a second known under the

[PDF p. 431]

name of Town of the Marvels. He constructed also, in the middle of the Nile, pavilions plated with colored
glass, and dug an underground passage connecting Ashmouneïn to Antinoë. To him is attributed also the
foundation of the town of 'Aïn Shams, and it is asserted that he reigned 800 years, but that toward the
600th year of his reign, the Adites ravished the power from him and remained in Egypt for 90 years after
which, chased out by the plague, they withdrew on Medina, by the road of the Hedjaz to the Ouadi-l Qora.
Ashmoun recovered the kingdom after the departure of the Adites. It is to him that is due the institution of
the Nourouz in Egypt, and it is in his time that was constructed the town of Bahnesa. At his death, one dug
him a naos at the extreme frontier of Ashmouneïn, one buried him there with his magnificent treasures and
numerous marvels, such as a thousand vases containing drugs composed according to precise formulas: on the
naos one engraved his name and his genealogy and a talisman was placed there to protect him.

After him reigned his son Sa, to whom succeeded his son Todras or, according to others, Menaqioush, a bold
and virtuous prince, who actively pushed the cultivations and the construction, building villages, raising
stelae, and executing astonishing marvels. He founded towns, among others the town of Akhmim, to which he
assigned priests. He reigned forty and some years, and at his death one buried him in the eastern pyramid
and his treasures with him.

After him reigned his son, on whose name there is no agreement. He was a wise prince, resolute and venerated
by the Egyptians. He founded the first hospital, and the first established special places for the exercises
of the body. It is in his time that was built the town of Santaryah in the desert of the Oases. But his
wives having become jealous on his account, one of them killed him with a knife-blow; one buried him in a
naos with his riches, and one made him a preservative talisman.

After him reigned his son Merqourah, a learned magician, who first tamed the lions and used them as mounts;
he built towns, founded temples, raised statues. At his death, one buried him in a naos in the desert of the
Occident and one buried his riches with him.

After him reigned his son Bilâtes; as he was still very young, it was his mother who took charge of the
direction of the affairs of the kingdom; of an energetic character, she administered the Empire with skill
and behaved according to equity, lightening the tax of her subjects who adored her. Her son, having become

[PDF p. 432]

grown, gave himself over to the hunt and his mother executed for him marvelous things. Bilâtes reigned 13
years after which he died of smallpox, and the power passed to his uncles.

After him reigned Atrib ben Qobtim ben Misraïm, thirteenth king after the flood. He built the town of Atrib
and lived 500 years of which he reigned 360. Under his reign, it is said, the Nile remained without floods
for 140 years and the animals disappeared from the land of Egypt; one no longer met a single one. Atrib went
pensive, stretching and clenching his hands, torn by hunger; the greatest part of the Egyptians succumbed to
the famine. Subsequently, the abundance returned, the ease only increased for 200 years; to such a point
that the ardeb (of wheat) sold for a dâneq (1/6 of the drachma) and less. At his death, his brother Sa was
accused of having assassinated him; he had to sustain against the Egyptians wars that lasted nine years,
after which he was killed.

After Atrib reigned his daughter Tadrourah, a skillful magician, who directed the kingdom in a superior
fashion and regulated the affairs admirably. She made marvelous talismans, one among others that prevented
the wild beasts and the birds from drinking at the Nile, so much so that almost all died of thirst. In her
time, a great cry made itself heard, the earth trembled at it, opened, and engulfed the queen.

After her reigned her brother Qlimoun ben Atrib, a learned and wise prince, who raised edifices and executed
talismans. In his time, was constructed the town of Tennis the ancient, as well as the town of Damietta; he
reigned 90 years and, after his death, was buried in a naos.

After him reigned his son Farsoun, a wise magician, who built towns and multiplied the temples. While he was
still a young man, a Himyarite king attacked him at the head of a considerable army. Farsoun marched to meet
him and rejoined him at the town of Aïlia; a fierce combat was engaged in which perished the major part of
the two armies and where the Egyptians employed a little of their magic. The Himyarite took flight with the
few men who remained to him, and Farsoun, having killed the greatest part of the enemies and having seized
all they had brought with them, returned triumphant to Memphis. He raised, on the shore of the sea of
Qolzoum, a tower surmounted by a mirror that attracted the ships to the shore and did not permit them to
take the sea again except after having acquitted the duty with which the king struck them. He reigned 260
years and, at his death, was buried in a naos, behind the black mountain

[PDF p. 433]

of the Orient. There one had made a cupola surrounded by twelve houses each enclosing a marvelous object.
With him one buried his treasures, and on the tomb was placed a preservative talisman.

After him succeeded four kings, then the kingdom fell to Sa, son of Qobtim, the youngest of the sons of this
prince and his favorite.

Sa having died, Nourriat the magician succeeded him. This magician sat on a throne of fire. If someone came
to bring a complaint before her and he was in his right, the fire drew aside without doing him harm; if on
the contrary he was in the wrong, the fire seized him. Each day, Nourriat took a great number of different
forms. She built herself a palace where she withdrew, and in the wall of this palace she installed hollow
tubes of copper and wrote, above the mouth of these tubes, one of the formulas to which could have recourse
the persons who would come to bring a complaint before her. Whoever came for a matter stopped before the
tube relative to his case, setting forth his request and questioning in a low voice. When he had finished,
he applied the ear to the tube and received the answer to his question. This palace and these tubes remained
until the time when they were destroyed by Bokhta-Nasar (Nebuchadnezzar).

After her reigned Marqounos, a wise and learned prince. He had for mother the daughter of the king of Nubia;
this princess executed marvelous things. In his time, all sorts of prodigious objects were fabricated. He
reigned 73 years and died at the age of 240 years.

After him reigned his son Aïsad, aged 45 years, a bold prince with an insolent gaze. He lay with the wife of
his father and displayed his liaison with her. The greatest of his passions was diversion and play. He gave
free access to all the religions in his Empire, abandoned the sciences, neglected the temples and the
priests, and ceased to occupy himself with the affairs of his subjects. He raised on the shore of the Nile
palaces to divert himself there and spent in pleasures considerable sums. He was hated by his subjects whom
he abhorred and who ended by poisoning him; he died aged less than 120 years.

After him reigned his son Sa. One gives to this prince the name of Sa ben Marqounos; if that is exact, he
was the brother of Aïsad. He established his residence in Memphis and his subjects founded on him great
hopes. Having made himself master of all the provinces, he executed there marvelous things and talismans,
put the priests back in their rank, chased out the criminals and the perverse, [...]

[PDF p. 434]

and abolished the penalties established by his father, honored his temple and prayed for him. He built a
town inside the Oases, raised near the sea numerous stelae, and established at all the points of the kingdom
couriers charged with informing him of what happened at the frontiers. On the two banks of the Nile he
raised towers, at the summit of which one lit fires when something unforeseen occurred or an enemy advanced
to attack the country. He constructed on the shore of the sea a tower, thanks to which one knew all that
happened on the sea. He built also, it is said, the greatest part of the town of Memphis and all the superb
edifices of Alexandria. When he had gathered in his hand the country entire, he assembled the scholars,
examined the stars, a science in which he was very versed, and recognized that Egypt would inevitably be
submerged by the Nile, then ravaged by a man come from the side of Syria; he therefore gathered all the
workers of Egypt and constructed a town in the extreme Oasis. A Frankish king came to attack him and seized
the town of Memphis; with him advanced a thousand ships, and Alexandria having been in great part destroyed,
the fleet entered the Nile at Rosetta and the Frankish king made himself master of Memphis, whence Sa had
fled to take refuge in the towns of the interior where he had fortified himself against his enemy. Sa
protected the town that served him as asylum by means of talismans and maintained himself there a long time;
then his turn came, the enemy was put to rout, and Sa returned to Memphis, pursued the priests, killed a
great number of them, and after a reign of 67 years died aged 170 years.

After him reigned his son Todras who extended his power over all the provinces and whose reign over Egypt
was tranquil. He was energetic, adroit, vigorous, tenacious, and versed in affairs. He gave proof of equity,
put in excellent state the temples and their personnel, raised a chapel to Venus, dug the canal of Sakha,
made war on an Amalecite of Syria, entered Palestine, killed there a number of people, and brought back a
part of the inhabitants captive to Egypt. Wishing to make an expedition to the country of the Blacks against
the Zing and the Ethiopians, he launched on the Nile 300 boats, met the Blacks, to the number of a million
men, put them to rout, killed the greatest number, and led away a considerable crowd of prisoners; he
brought back also to Egypt elephants and tigers and raised, on the frontiers of his country, towers on which
he wrote his name, his campaigns, and his triumph. It is in his time that God sent his prophet Saleh to the
Thammoud, and it is he also,

[PDF p. 435]

it is said, who made the Nubians inhabit where they are today; here is why: during the campaign of Ethiopia
and his march against the Blacks, he met a people who read the books of Adam, of Seth, and of Idris; he
rallied to their faith and made them descend into a country situated a month's march from the land of Egypt;
these were the Nubians. He died at Memphis.

After him reigned his son Mâliq, an intelligent, generous prince, beautiful of face, experienced, who walked
on the traces of his father. The Egyptians adored the planets and the ox, while he adored a single God like
his ancestors Qobtim and Misraïm, for which the Copts blamed him. One day, the order was given to prepare
the best war-horses, to procure arms and gather travel-provisions, then 200 boats having been launched on
the Western sea, the king set out followed by a considerable army that followed him both by land and by sea;
he reached thus the country of the Berbers, put them to flight and massacred the greatest part of them, then
arrived at Ifriqiah, passed into Spain wishing to reach the country of the Franks. He passed among no people
without subjugating it. The king of the Franks went to meet him; they fought for a month; at the end, the
king of the Franks asked for peace and made presents to Mâliq who left him and went to subjugate the peoples
of the littoral of the Green sea. The Copts recount that this king saw seventy marvels, that he raised stelae
on the shore of the sea, that he engraved there his name and his campaigns, that he destroyed the towns of
the Berbers; on his return, the people of Egypt went before him with all sorts of perfumes and all the
apparatus of feasts; one covered the roads with carpets on his passage; the kings dreaded him and sent him
presents; and he believed in the unity of God until his death.

After him reigned his son Hazaba. He was of a soft and even character; his father had taught him the religion
of the single God and had turned him away from the cult of the idols, but after the death of his father, he
returned to the religious practices of his people. Wishing to undertake an expedition into India and against
the country of the Blacks, he had fabricated a hundred boats similar to the Indian boats and set out taking
with him his wives and the principal personages of his court and leaving on the throne of Egypt his son
Kalkala, still a child, near whom he put a priest as vizier. This done, he disembarked on the shore of the
Yemen, pillaged the towns of the region, and reached Serendib (Ceylon) whose inhabitants he treated cruelly;
from there he went to the islands situated between India and China,

[PDF p. 436]

reduced the inhabitants of them to obedience, and remained long years in these islands. The expedition
lasted, it is said, 17 years, after which he returned laden with booty. Dreaded by the kings, he built a
number of temples and raised statues to the planets; then he ravaged the coast of Syria, subjugated the
inhabitants of it, and returned to Egypt; he ravaged equally Nubia and the country of the Blacks, and struck
the inhabitants with tributes that they had to bring him. He restored the prestige of the priests and their
books. He had seen that these victories would be accorded to him with the help of the planets. He died after
having reigned 75 years.

He was replaced by his son Kalkala, who was proclaimed king at Alexandria, where he stayed for a month
before going to Memphis. He was an adorer of the idols and the people of Egypt were with him. He loved the
sciences and created marvelous things. He honored the scholars and heaped privileges on them. He occupied
himself with chemistry and amassed considerable treasures in the deserts of the West. He was the first to
spread in Egypt the science of chemistry that, until then, one practiced only in secret, certain kings of
his predecessors having forbidden the practice of it. Kalkala gave himself over to it and filled the houses
of science with it, to the point that never was gold more abundant in Egypt than in his time, and never was
the revenue of Egypt as considerable, for under his reign it reached more than 110,000,000 metsqals. The
Egyptians had become rich thanks to the products of the mines. He fabricated also a great quantity of colored
and transparent stones as well as turquoises and other jewels; he created things that surpass reason, so much
so that one surnamed him the Sage of the Kings; he surpassed in science all the priests, teaching them things
that were hidden from them. The Nemrod (Nimrod) of Abraham lived in his time; this prince, having heard
speak of the magical science of Kalkala, invited him to come to him. He was an audacious man of fierce
aspect who dwelt in the countryside of Iraq; God had accorded him vigor, strength, power, and he commanded
numerous peoples. According to the Copts, Nemrod, after having sent his invitation to Kalkala, made known to
him that he would meet him at a determined place. Kalkala therefore went to this place on a chariot carried
by four winged horses, surrounded by a light brilliant as fire, and escorted by terrible images in the midst
of which he flew at the gallop of his horses. He bore, in the way of a belt, a serpent coiled on itself and
the mouth open, and he struck it with a wand of myrtle. At his sight, Nemrod, seized with terror, recognized
his superiority

[PDF p. 437]

in science and asked him for his protection. It is recounted that Kalkala went up to sit on the western
pyramid, under a cupola raised above his head. And the people of the country, when a calamity fell upon them,
gathered around the pyramid, where the king remained days without eating or drinking. Once, he disappeared
for a certain time, so much so that one believed him dead; the kings then became audacious and one of them, a
king of the Occident, advanced with a considerable army and arrived at the Ouadi Habib. But Kalkala arrived
in his turn and having, thanks to his magic, gathered clouds laden with a stifling heat, he covered with them
the enemy army that for days and days could not free itself from this heat. Then Kalkala flew toward Egypt and
gave the order to his people to march to meet the enemies; and the Egyptians found them all dead, them and
their mounts. Thus the priests dreaded Kalkala more than they had feared any of his predecessors. This prince
lived a long time still, then disappeared and never again did one hear speak of him. According to Ibn Abd el
Hakem, Kalkala was son of Hazaba; he reigned in Egypt about a hundred years and died without leaving
children.

Then reigned his brother Malia ben Hazaba. Ibn Ouacif Shah says: "Then reigned his brother Malia; he was a
gluttonous man who ate and drank to excess, giving himself over solitarily to his pleasures and neglecting
absolutely the sciences. He confided the affairs to his vizier and abandoned himself to the women; he
possessed eighty of them. His son Toutis threw himself upon him, one day when he was drunk, and killed him as
well as the woman who was then with him."

After him reigned his son Toutis. It is said that this prince is the same as A'mr ben 'Amrou-l Qeis ben
Babilioun ben Himyar ben Sala ben Yashgab ben Ya'reb ben Qohtan; others name him El Oualid ben El Rian. He is
one of the Pharaohs (Shepherds) of Egypt, who descend from Dan ben Fahloug ben Amraz ben Ashoud ben Sam ben
Nouh; it is said also that the Pharaohs of Egypt were of the race of the first Amalec ben Laoud ben Sam ben
Nouh. Toutis was a man enemy of disorder, bold, hard, haughty, and dreaded. The Copts claim that he was the
first Pharaoh of Egypt; it is the Pharaoh of Abraham. The Pharaohs were, it is said, seven in number, and
Toutis was the first of them. He dug a canal to the east of Egypt, at the foot of the mountain, in order to
be able to go by boats to the sea. He sent to Hagar, mother of Ismaïl, of whom he himself had made present to
Abraham, wheat and all sorts of grains that he brought as far as Djeddah; he could thus make the Hedjaz live
for a certain time, and it is recounted that all that was then beautiful at the Caaba had been given by the
king of Egypt. And what Toutis had sent to the Hedjaz was so considerable that the Arabs of the tribe of
Gorham surnamed him the Generous.

[PDF p. 438]

One reads in the book of Orosius that in the time of Abraham the government of Egypt was in the hands of a
people named the Benou Faliq ben Darech and that their reign lasted in Egypt 120 years. Ibn Ishaq, speaking
of one of them, says: "The Pharaohs of Egypt were descendants of Dan ben Fahloug ben Amraz ben Ashoud ben Sam
ben Nouh. The most widespread opinion makes them Amalecites. Among them one counts El Rian ben El Oualid; it
is asserted that El Oualid ben El Rian was the Pharaoh of Joseph, and El Oualid ben Mo'sab the Pharaoh of
Moses; among them one counts also Senan ben 'Alouan." Ibn Ouacif Shah says that one gave to the latter the
name of Pharaoh only because he committed many murders, sparing only a very intelligent girl, who, terrified
by the number of his crimes, poisoned him in his 170th year.

After him reigned Gouriaq; this princess treated her subjects with kindness, amassed riches, honored the
priests, the scholars, and the magicians, extended their power, and multiplied the temples. Those who did
not wish to submit to her authority went to the town of Atrib and chose for king a man of the lineage of
Atrib. The account of what concerns him is found in the chapter of Alexandria. Gouriaq is the first woman of
the family of Noah who was queen of Egypt.

After her death, her cousin Zalfa bent Mamoun succeeded her. She was a wise and intelligent virgin who
treated her subjects with gentleness. Aïmen the Atribite revolted against her and called to his aid the king
of the Amalecites who dispatched to him a general. Zalfa sent to meet him an army; the two troops joined at
El Arich and, after a combat where a great number of men perished, the partisans of Zalfa fled to Memphis,
pursued by the enemies. Zalfa withdrew into the Said and stopped at Ashmouneïn, and the war continued
between her and the Amalecites, a war in which the latter were put to rout, abandoned Memphis after having
devastated it, and withdrew into the Gorf where they fortified themselves. Egypt was then divided into two
parts; Zalfa recommenced the war, but, after three months of struggle, had to retrograde as far as Qous,
pursued by Aïmen; seeing herself on the point of being taken, she poisoned herself. Ibn Abd el Hakem says:
[...]

[PDF p. 439]

"Toutis ben Malia having died, his daughter Gouriaq, his only child, succeeded him. At the death of Gouriaq,
the government passed into the hands of her cousin Zalfa bent Mamoun ben Malia who lived a long time... Then
they grew and multiplied and filled the land of Egypt entire. And the Amalecites bore them envy, and the
country was ravaged by El Oualid ben Douma' who delivered them terrible combats. The Egyptians consented to
recognize him for king, and he reigned over them for nearly a hundred years. Then, filled with pride and
injustice, he abandoned himself to all the turpitudes, and God unleashed against him a ferocious beast that
put him to pieces and devoured his flesh."

There were five Pharaohs who reigned in Egypt.

Then reigned the fierce Aïman who put to death a great number of those who had borne arms against him. The
Amalecite El Oualid ben Douma having gone on an expedition with a considerable army, sent one of his
servants, named Fara'oun, into Egypt; the latter conquered it, and El Oualid came in his turn, subjugated
the Egyptians and, having seized their treasures, continued his march to stop only at the sources of the
Nile; he visited the mountain of Qomr and remained there, in retreat, for forty years, after which he
returned to Egypt where Fara'oun, who had taken his place, fled at his approach. El Oualid reduced the
Egyptians and reigned over them until his death -- that is, for 120 years.

After him reigned his son El Rian ben Oualid ben Douma', one of the Amalecites. He was the strongest man of
his time and the greatest king.

The Amalecites descend from Amalek ben Laoud ben Sam ben Nouh. This El Rian is the pharaoh of Joseph and
bears among the Copts the name of Nahraoush. It is said that the pharaoh of Joseph was called El Rian ben El
Oualid ben Leith ben Qarân ben 'Amr ben Amaleq ben Balqa' ben 'Aber ben Ashlikha ben Loud ben Sam ben Nouh;
the pharaoh of Joseph was, it is recounted, the grandfather of the pharaoh of Moses, being father of his
father, and his name was Barkhou. He was of high stature, beautiful of face, and intelligent. He behaved
admirably with his subjects, suppressed their taxes for three years, and divided his riches with them.

Then reigned a man of his house named Atfin; it is he whom one calls El Aziz, an intelligent man, lettered,
active, just, and desirous of rendering the country prosperous. He had made for himself a throne of silver
in the palace of the king; he took his place there and thus received the writers and the viziers; as for
Nahraoush,

[PDF p. 440]

he contented himself with what passes behind the curtain and, giving leave to the affairs, gave himself over
to pleasures; for a long time it was thus and the country only prospered; but an Amalecite having attacked
him and having marched with his army against Egypt, El Rian set out to meet him, gave battle, and having put
him to rout, pursued him, drew him into Syria, ravaged the region, and the kings, filled with fear, no longer
dared attack him. He pushed, it is said, as far as Mosul and struck with a tribute the people of Syria, then
set out for the conquest of the countries of the Occident with an army of 900,000 men, traversed the
territory of the Berbers of whom he subjugated the greatest number, and skirting the Green sea, directed
himself toward the South, conquered Nubia, and returned finally to Memphis. For what passed between him and
Joseph, one will find the account in the chapter of the Fayoum.

After him reigned his son Drimoush who is also called Darem ben El Rian; it is the fourth Pharaoh; but he did
not follow the traditions of his father. He still had for intendant Joseph, but sometimes he accepted his
advice, sometimes he repulsed it. In his time was discovered a mine of silver from which he drew considerable
riches. It is under his reign that Joseph died, whom he replaced, as vizier, by a man who did the greatest
harm to the Egyptians, appropriating their riches and gathering thus considerable treasures. His turpitude
became such that he carried off from their families all the pretty women of the town of Memphis, and as soon
as he learned that in such or such a place was a beautiful woman, he went there and had her brought to him;
troubled by these exactions, the people despised him and deserted the factories, the workshops, and the
markets. The vizier treated him as an enemy and killed a great number of them; finally he became so
execrated that one revolted against him. He then became gentler again, suppressed the taxes for three years,
and distributed money to the rebels, which silenced them. In his time, the Copts rose against the Israelites
and asked the vizier to expel them from Egypt, and they insisted so much that they ended by obtaining their
case. The king, then retired into the Said, learned the news and menaced the Egyptians who gathered, rose
against him, and declared war on him; a great number of them perished; the rest had to undergo the
oppression; some were killed, others hanged on the two banks of the Nile; after which the king returned to
his old habits, appropriating the riches of his subjects and carrying off their women; the principal of the
Copts and the Israelites were reduced to

[PDF p. 441]

slavery, and all had to undergo his tyranny. Having embarked on the Nile for some diversion, a violent wind
was unleashed against him; he drowned, and his body was found again only in the province of Shatnouf, it is
said, between Tara and Helouan.

Then the vizier put forward his son Ma'adious, still a child, and who is also called Mo'dân. The latter
suppressed the taxes established by his father and behaved admirably; under his reign the affairs were put
back in order and he returned to their families the women carried off under the preceding reign. It is the
fifth of the Pharaohs, and one refers to his time the flood of Egypt. The Israelites had multiplied and
hated the idols. One cantoned them in a region distant from the country so that they would not mix with the
others, and one assigned them a territory to the south of Memphis where they gathered and built an oratory.
A Canaanite having seized Syria forbade the Syrians to pay the tribute they owed to Egypt and excited the
population against Mo'dân. The subjects of the latter exhorted him to march to combat, but he refused and
took refuge in a temple. It is claimed that he shut himself up in the temple of Saturn to pray, and that
Saturn manifested itself to him and spoke to him: "I have," it said, "established you as sovereign of the
inhabitants of your country and I have accorded you the power over them and over others still; I will raise
you up to me, but do not cease to glorify me." And the king grew proud in his heart and, filled with
arrogance, had himself called lord (God), and disdained to occupy himself with the affairs of the kingdom at
the head of which he put his son Aksamès.

His son Aksamès therefore took the government of the kingdom. One gives still to this prince the name of
Kâsem ben Ma'dan. He put the people back in their rank, divided the country into districts and provinces,
occupied himself with inventions useful to the prosperity of the country and to the development of industry;
he increased the ease of his people, had the temples repaired, made new their costumes and furniture, and
augmented the offerings. It is he whom one calls Kâshem ben Mo'dân ben Darem ben El Rian ben El Oualid ben
Douma' the Amalecite; he is the sixth Pharaoh. This name of Pharaoh comes from the first Fara'oun whose name
has transmitted itself to all the arrogant monarchs. The situation of Aksamès became greater and greater, his
power extended. He raised numerous stelae around Memphis, built a great number of towns, lighthouses, and
talismans. He reigned for seven years, managing admirably the affairs and, when the vizier of his father
died, he replaced him by a man of the caste

[PDF p. 442]

of the slaves, named Zalma ben Qoumès, a violent man, but a magician, sorcerer, learned writer, and versed in
all the sciences. He took pleasure in the exercise of power, organized the affairs of the kingdom, and built
towns on the two banks of the Nile; having read in the stars that some event was to occur, he had
constructed on the side of Alexandria and in the Said circuses and edifices. The Copts gathered to ask him
for the departure of the Israelites, but he answered them: "The Israelites are your servants; lower them from
now on." Then he set out for the countries of the Berbers and ravaged, killed, pillaged. In his time was
built the tower of Alexandria, and the sea, having risen, submerged a great number of villages, gardens, and
edifices. Aksamès died after having reigned 31 years, and during eleven of these years Zalma, his vizier,
had directed the affairs. At his death, there was a great emotion among the people; one accused Zalma of
having poisoned him, but Zalma remained in power.

Then reigned Latis ben Aksamès, a bold, vain, and hard prince; he prescribed certain things, forbade others,
and obliged the people to work, saying: "I am loyal and you are not; now, if you stray from the straight
path, I will stray from you." And he lowered certain personages below their rank, removed Zalma from the
vizierate and replaced him; Zalma was exiled into the Said with all the Israelites, and the king multiplied
the construction of temples, built villages, and opened a great number of mines; he buried in the desert of
the Orient considerable treasures and devoted himself to science. Later, pride seized him and his successes
exalted him; he forbade everyone, priest or other, to sit in the reception hall; each had to hold himself
standing until the moment of withdrawing. His injustice and his hardness toward his subjects went
increasing; by his order, no one could possess more than the necessary and each was reduced to the
indispensable; he appropriated the riches, sought the women, diverted himself with them, and did worse than
his predecessors. The Israelites were reduced to slavery, a considerable quantity of priests were put to
death; thus he was detested by all in general and by each in particular. Zalma, who had taken refuge in the
Said, was recalled by the Egyptians; but Latis gave the order to dismiss him from his functions of governor;
Zalma refused to obey, fought the troops sent against him, advanced, and entered Memphis.

Zalma ben Qoumès is the pharaoh of Moses. His name was, it is said, El Oualid ben Mous'ab ben El Rahoun ben
El Helout ben Qarân ben 'Amr ben

[PDF p. 443]

Amaleq ben Balqa' ben 'Aber ben Ashlîkha ben Loud ben Sam ben Nouh; he was of the race of the Amalecites,
but of small stature, the beard long; his right eye was very large, his left eye very small; moreover, he
was lame. It is claimed that he was Copt and that the Egyptians know perfectly his genealogy and that of his
family; one says other things still. His history will be recounted in the chapter that treats of the church
of Damouah. Here is what Ibn 'Abd el Hakem says: When God had drowned Pharaoh, there remained after him no
one of the great ones of the country; only the slaves, the mercenaries, and the women remained. And the most
noble of the women of Egypt concerted to name a queen, and their choice fell on a woman named Daloukah.

Then reigned Daloukah, daughter of Zaba, who is also called Daloukah, daughter of Qarân. She was intelligent,
energetic, and instructed, moreover one of the most noble of the women of Egypt. At the moment of her
elevation to power, she was aged 160 years. She constructed, to defend Egypt against the enemies, a wall that
extended from the frontiers of the Zings to Ifriqiah, to the Oases, and to Nubia; and all along this wall
were doors where guardians watched day and night, maintaining fires that never went out; in six months, she
had finished building this wall around Egypt; it is that which one calls the "wall of the old woman." It is
in her time that the sorceress Tadourah built the temples that are in the middle of Memphis. The reign of
Daloukah lasted 20 years at the end of which reached his majority a young man of the race of the great ones
of Egypt named:

Darkoun ben Bilâtis; the latter, at his death, was replaced by his son Toudesat, to whom succeeded Adqash
who reigned only three years; at his death, he was replaced by his brother Marina ben Marinous; Marina having
died was replaced by Astades ben Marina, a proud, violent, and sanguinary prince, who made show of so many
vices that one ended by revolting against him and killing him. In his place was elected a man of the caste
of the nobles, named Baltous ben Minâkil, who reigned over them 40 years; at his death, his son Malous
succeeded him, and, Malous having died, his brother Minâkîl ben Baltous ben Minakil became king and kept the
power a long time. His son Noulah ben Minakil reigned after him for 120 years; it is he the lame king who
subjugated the king of Jerusalem and brought him back to Egypt; he was proud and arrogant, and his pride
reached a degree to which had not yet attained the pride of any of his predecessors since the Pharaohs. This
prince died from a fall from a horse; one had surnamed him "the Lame" because [...]

[PDF p. 444]

during the pillage of Jerusalem, after having annihilated the Jews and taken their king Josiah, son of
Amoun, son of Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, he wished to mount on the throne of the prophet Soliman (Solomon),
son of David; now, to this throne one acceded by a step on which one could mount only with the two feet at
the same time; Noulah wished to mount it with a single foot, the right foot, but the step fell on his other
leg which was broken; and he felt it until his death, whence his surname of "the lame."

After him reigned Marinous ben Noulah, who governed very long; he was replaced by his son Qerqourah who
reigned 60 years; at his death, his brother Niqas ben Marinous succeeded him; in his time the temples were
destroyed and no one could raise them again. Niqas having died, his son Qoumis ben Niqas succeeded him and
reigned a long time; Bokhta Nasar (Nebuchadnezzar), having made war on him, killed him and ravaged the town
of Memphis and other towns of Egypt; he led away in captivity the Egyptians and left in the country no one,
so much so that the land of Egypt remained for 40 years ruined and deserted.

In the translation of the book of the Spaniard Orosius, entitled "Description of the Dynasties and the
Wars," one reads: 107 years after the Pharaoh of Moses had drowned, there was in Egypt a king named
Noûcherdis who killed the guests and the strangers, immolating them to his idols to which he presented their
blood as offerings; 328 years after this same date there was in Egypt a king named Beroubah whose reign was
admirable and the government powerful; he conquered by arms numerous provinces on the side of the South, by
land and by water; it is he the first who had dealings with the peoples of Roum who later took the name of
Goths. He had sent them a messenger to invite them to obedience, threatening them with war. "It is unworthy
of a powerful king," they answered, "to make war on a poor people; the fate of war is hazardous, and victory
as well as defeat are always unforeseen issues. Far from bending before your insolence, we will hold our
heads up to your attack." And they prepared to keep their word. Pharaoh having set out, they went to meet
him, put him to rout, seized his camp and the riches that were there and the treasures of Pharaoh, then,
continuing their route, they sacked the country of Egypt, and they would almost have made themselves masters
of it if a great mass of mud had not barred their road. They therefore directed themselves toward Syria,
continued their wars there, enslaved the Syrians, and obliged them to pay them tribute; and they remained
thus 15 years

[PDF p. 445]

making war against whoever held his head up to them, sacking and pillaging; they would never have returned
to their country if some of their women had not come to say to them: "If you do not come to acquit
yourselves toward us of your conjugal duties, we will ask children of our neighbors." Then they returned to
their country, the hands full of riches, leading away numerous flocks and innumerable packages, and leaving
behind them a dreaded memory. Five hundred years after the death in the waters of the Pharaoh of Moses and
the reign of Dalouka, the kings of Madian seized, it is said, Egypt, from which they were chased out by the
prophet of God Soliman, son of David. The empire then returned to the hands of the Copts, and, Galout
(Goliath) ben Balout having been killed by David, his son Galout ben Galout went to Egypt where reigned the
kings of Madian who installed him in the country as king of the western region; he remained there a certain
time, but at the end he set out for the countries of the Occident. The Copts, it is said, reigned in Egypt
after Dalouka and her son for 620 years; the number of their kings is 27: Diosqoulita, 78 years or,
according to others, 88 years; Samânadous, 26 years; Soumanas, 100 years; Moufkaras, 4 years; Amânâqoûnâs,
9 years; Ashouris, 6 years; Fasinakhes, 9 years; Fasousanes, 35 years; Sesounakhousis, 21 years; Asalioun,
15 years; Tafalounis, 13 years; Matafanastalas, 25 years; Asarathoun, 9 years; Fosameres, 10 years;
Aoufaïnouas, 44 years; Sayaqour, 12 years; Sakhis the Ethiopian, 12 years; Tarahouch the Ethiopian, 20
years; Amras the Ethiopian, 12 years; Astatafinias, 7 years; Bakhfasous, 6 years; Yakhou, 8 years;
Fasamamaltiqoush, 44 years; Bahnouqa, 6 years; Fasamartas, 17 years; Ouafris, 25 years; Amaseles, 42 years.

After these kings, reigned in Egypt five kings of the kings of Babel: Amartiouch, 6 years; Mafartas, 7
years; Aukhris, 12 years; Fasamout, 2 years; Moutatous, 7 years.

Then reigned three kings of Assour (Assyria); they are the Garmakides who reigned at Mosul and in
Mesopotamia: Nafatanebouch, 13 years; Tous, 7 years; Nafataninas, 18 years.

Then from them the empire passed to Alexander, son of Philip the Greek. All these names are Roumi (Greek),
and perhaps the kings who bore these names, or at least a part, reigned after Dalouka. Between Bokhtanasar
and the Flood, there are 2356 years and some months. This figure agrees with what is said in the Jewish law.
Between the Flood and the ruin of Jerusalem by Bokhta Nasar, there are 2684 years; which differs a little
from what we have borrowed from Masa'oudi. And God knows it better than anyone.

[PDF p. 446]

CHAPTER IV
OF THE TOWN OF ALEXANDRIA

This town is one of the greatest and most ancient of the world. It was built several times; the first time,
it was after the Flood, in the time of Misraïm ben Beïsar, son of Noah; it was called then Raqoudah.
Subsequently, it was rebuilt twice, and, in the time of the Greeks, it was enlarged by Alexander the
Macedonian, son of Philip, the same who vanquished Dara (Darius) and subjugated the Empire of the Persians,
120 solar years after the destruction of Memphis by Bokhta Nasar. It then took the name of Alexander and,
after this prince had extended its importance, it substituted itself for the town of Memphis in the role of
capital of Egypt, a role it conserved until the conquest of Islam and the arrival of 'Amr ben El 'As who, at
the head of the Muslim army, made himself master of the citadel and of Alexandria. From this moment, Egypt
became a province of Islam, and the role of capital passed from Alexandria to Fostat-Masr. God willing, I
will recount to you all that I have been able to learn of the history of Alexandria.

Abou-l Hassan El Masa'oudi, in his book Accounts of the Time, says: The Koukah, conquering tribe of the
people of Aïlat, seized the land and divided it into thirty districts and four great divisions, each
division forming a province; in each of these provinces was built a town where resided a king who sat on a
throne of gold; near the king was a temple -- that is, a house of science -- and a temple dedicated to a
planet and containing idols of gold. Alexandria, which one named then Raqoudah, comprised fifteen districts;
it is there that were installed the principal of the priests, and its temples enclosed more statues of gold
than those of the other towns; one counted there two hundred statues of gold. The Said was divided into
eighty districts distributed in four provinces and comprising thirty towns, all filled with marvels.

Ptolemy, in his book Of the Climates, making the description of the islands, the seas, and the towns,
reports that the town of Alexandria belongs to the sign of the Lion and undergoes the influence of Mars;
the average duration of the day there is 14 hours, its longitude is 60° 30', which represents (as distance
from the initial point of the longitudes) 4 full hours and 1/5 of an hour.

[PDF p. 447]

Ibn Ouacif Shah, speaking of the accounts that relate to Misraïm ben Beïsar, son of Noah, adds: He taught
them also to make talismans; beasts having come out of the sea that devastated their fields, their gardens,
and their habitations, one made against them talismans, and these beasts disappeared never to return again.
One constructed, elsewhere than on the river, towns among which Raqoudah, on the site of Alexandria; in the
middle of Raqoudah was raised, on columns of gilded copper, a cupola gilded likewise and surmounted by a
mirror made of diverse mixed substances; the diameter of this mirror was five spans, and the cupola was a
hundred cubits high; and if among the peoples who surrounded Egypt and of whom some bore it envy, there was
found someone who wished to attack the Egyptians on the side of the sea, the mirror, by means of some
artifice, set about throwing flames in the direction of the assailants and set them on fire. This mirror
remained standing a long time, but was overturned by the sea. It is claimed that it is in imitation of this
mirror that Alexander constructed his tower, on which was placed also a mirror where one could see the
assailants coming from the country of Roum. But a certain king of this country, using cunning, sent an
emissary who managed to overturn this mirror, which was of composed glass. According to what a Copt recounts,
a survivor of the sacerdotal caste massacred by Eïsad, king of Egypt, took refuge with a king of the country
of the Franks, vaunted to him the numerous treasures of Egypt and its marvels, and inspired in him the
desire to make himself master of the country and to seize its treasures and its talismans, thanks to which
he could obtain all he would desire. Sa ben Marqounos, brother of Eïsad, then king of Egypt, having learned
that the king of the Franks was advancing against him, went to a mountain situated between the sea and the
east of the Nile, had brought there the greatest part of his treasures, and built magazines vaulted and
plated with lead. The king of the Franks appeared with a thousand ships; all that he had met of stelae or
Egyptian edifices, he had overturned, as well as the statues, with the help of the renegade priest. Arrived
at Alexandria, he ravaged the town and the surroundings, destroyed most of the edifices, entered the Nile by
the mouth of Rosetta, and went up as far as Memphis. The people of the different regions he traversed
resisting him, he devastated the country and massacred all that opposed his passage. He arrived thus at the
towns of the interior, desirous of seizing the treasures of the Egyptians; but he found these protected by
powerful talismans, and defended by deep waters, ditches, and barricades. He remained

[PDF p. 448]

there many days without being able to seize them and, irritated against the priest, he killed him. Almost
all his companions had perished, and the Egyptians having gathered killed a great number of those who had
remained in the ships and burned some vessels; in addition, calling on their magical art and their science
of terrors, they raised a tempest that unleashed itself and engulfed most of the ships, so much so that the
king of the Franks alone could escape and flee. The Egyptians returned to their habitations and their
villages, and the king, returned to Memphis, prepared an expedition against the country of Roum, where he
went, ravaging the islands; he became thus formidable to the kings and pursued the priests of whom he
massacred a great number. He reigned 67 years, died at the age of 170 years, and was buried in an
underground passage in the middle of the town of Memphis, and with him, his treasures, precious stones,
statues, talismans, as one had done for his ancestors; among other things, four thousand metsqals of gold
in the forms of terrestrial and marine animals, the image of an eagle in green stone, that of a dragon in
gold, and one engraved on his tomb his name, the victories carried off by him over the kings, and his
campaigns; after him the empire passed to his son Todras.

When Gouriaq, daughter of Toutis, the first Pharaoh of Egypt and Pharaoh of Abraham, mounted on the royal
throne, after having killed her father, she governed her subjects with wisdom and gathered treasures such as
the kings had not yet gathered; she heaped honors on the priests, the scholars, the great magicians, and
raised their rank. She multiplied the temples. Those who refused to obey her took refuge in the town of
Atrib and chose for themselves as king a man of the lineage of Atrib, named Eïdâkhes. One girded him with
the crown and one gathered in a crowd around him. Gouriaq sent to combat him an army that put him to rout
and killed most of his partisans. Eïdâkhes fled into Syria where were the Canaanites; he implored the help
of their king who had prepared for him a numerous army. Gouriaq then opened her magazines, distributed her
treasures, rendered powerful the magicians who did their work. Eïdâkhes advanced with the Canaanite army
commanded by a general named Giroun. As soon as the enemy had entered Egypt, Gouriaq, without the knowledge
of Eïdâkhes, sent to the general her nurse, a woman of the most intelligent, who made known to him that
Gouriaq desired to marry him, that she loved no one of the people of her house, and that if he would kill
E�dâkhes, she would become his wife and would have him proclaimed king of Egypt.

[PDF p. 449]

Giroun, all happy, poured for Eïdâkhes the poison sent by the queen and made him die. But Gouriaq, after the
murder of Eïdâkhes, had it said to Giroun that she could not marry him as long as the Canaanites were in
Egypt and he had not constructed a marvelous town. In that time, the Canaanites had the reputation of being
excellent constructors of edifices and passed for knowing how to execute marvelous things. "Leave the place
where you are," she continued, "and go to the west of my country; repair the numerous ruins that are with
us, raise the constructions, and, on them, edify new ones." Thus did Giroun, and he built, in the desert of
the Occident, a town named Qidoumah where he brought the water of the Nile by means of a canal; the town was
surrounded with numerous plantations and a very high tower was raised there, at the summit of which was
arranged a belvedere plated with gold, silver, glass, and marble. The queen heaped riches on Giroun and
wrote, without his knowledge, to the king his master. When Giroun had finished the construction of the town,
Gouriaq said to him: "Another of our strong towns, which our predecessors possessed, has been, in certain
parts, destroyed; its citadel is overturned; go and work to repair it, after which I will be able to go to
the town you have constructed. And when you have finished repairing the second town, send me your army so
that I may go to you and remove myself from my town and the people of my house; for my desire is that you
enter with me who am their close relative." And Giroun went and constructed the second Alexandria.

The historians recount that the one who had come to attack Gouriaq was Oualid ben Douma' the Amalecite and
the second Pharaoh; here is what would have been the cause of this aggression: El Oualid being ill, sent
into all countries messengers charged with bringing him back water from these regions, so that he might
recognize which could cure him; he had sent into Egypt a young man who was marveled at all the goods he met
there; having drunk of the water of the country, he found it delicious, and returned to his master, he
informed him of the situation of Egypt. El Oualid went there with a numerous army; the secretary of the
kingdom wrote to the queen to ask her for her hand; the queen answered him and agreed with him that he would
build her a town where her force and her power would be recognized, a town that would become the dower of
the queen. He accepted and, traversing the country, went to the west of Egypt; the queen sent him all sorts
of odorous flowers and fruits and furnished him mounts. He went to Alexandria, ruined since the departure of
the Adites, removed

[PDF p. 450]

all the stones, the constructions, and the columns that were there, and laid the foundations of a
magnificent town; he employed to build it a hundred thousand workers who worked a very long time, and he
spent on it all he possessed of riches. Now, each time he had constructed some part of an edifice, there
came out of the sea an animal that destroyed the work of the day before, and the next day one found no more
trace of it, which worried the constructor. Gouriaq had sent him a thousand milk-goats, whose milk he
employed for his kitchen; this flock was accompanied by a shepherd who led it to graze in this place (on the
shore of the sea); each evening, at the moment of withdrawing, the shepherd saw come out of the sea a
magnificent woman whom in his heart he desired; this woman spoke to him and agreed with him that they would
wrestle together, and that if he was victorious, she would belong to him, but that if on the contrary she
carried off the victory, she would take two of his goats. Each evening, the woman was victorious and led
away two of the beasts of the flock; this lasted until she had taken more than half of the goats; as for the
rest, they only wasted away, the shepherd being too much in love to take care of them. One day, his master
passing near him inquired of his state, and he, dreading his severity, recounted to him his adventure. The
king, then taking the garments and the functions of the shepherd for a whole day, saw, toward evening, the
woman come to him and renew the pact; he accepted, wrestled with her, carried off the victory, and treated
her roughly. "Would to God," she cried, "that my vanquisher might return me to my first companion, for he
was good to me and I made him suffer long." He therefore returned her to the shepherd to whom he said:
"Question her on the subject of these constructions which, scarcely raised, are overturned in the night. Ask
her who does this and if there is some means of remedying it." The shepherd questioned the woman who said to
him: "It is the marine animals who overturn your constructions." "What ruse is it fitting to employ?" asked
the shepherd. "Here," she resumed: "you will make coffers in thick glass with lids and will have enter there
skillful draughtsmen, provided with sheets of metal and styluses as well as all they may need for several
days; then, one will transport the boxes, by means of boats, after having attached them with ropes; and
when the boxes are descended into the midst of the waters, let the draughtsmen draw all that will pass near
them; after which, the coffers will be raised and one will execute statues conforming to the drawings,
either in copper, or in stone, or in lead, and one will raise

[PDF p. 451]

them on the side of the sea, in front of the constructions. The animals, in coming out of the water, will
see these images and will flee never to return." The shepherd instructed of all this his master who had the
orders of the woman executed, and he could thus finish his constructions and build the town.

It is claimed that the man of the constructions and the flock was Giroun who had attacked the Egyptians
before El Oualid, and that El Oualid came only after the reign of Gouriaq, vanquished the Egyptians, and
seized Egypt.

It is recounted that Giroun spent on the construction of the town all his riches without being able to
finish it and that he ordered the shepherd to speak of it to the woman. "In the ruins of the town," she
said, "is a circus surrounded by seven columns surmounted by statues of copper standing; immolate to each of
these statues a fat bull and anoint the column that supports it with the blood of this bull; perfume also
the statue by burning the hairs of the tail of the bull and some particles of its horns and its hooves,
saying: 'These offerings are for you, give me what you possess.' Then measure from each column and in the
direction of the face of the statue a distance of a hundred cubits, and at the moment when the full moon
will coincide with the rising of Saturn, make a hole. After having descended fifty cubits, you will find an
enormous slab; rub it with the gall of the bull and lift it. You will descend to an underground passage
fifty cubits long at the end of which is a magazine closed with a lock; the key of the lock is under the
threshold of the door; take it, rub the door with the rest of the gall and the blood of the bull and burn
pieces of its horn and its hoof and some hairs of the tail, then enter. You will find yourself in the
presence of a statue bearing at the neck a tablet of copper on which is written the list of what the
magazine contains. Take what you will, but touch none of the cadavers you may see nor anything of what it
will have on it. Do the same for each column and for each statue. Each of them will procure you a similar
magazine. These are seven naos (tombs) of kings and their treasures." Provided with these instructions, the
king went with the shepherd to put them into execution, and he found things that it is impossible to
describe and innumerable marvels. Thus he finished the construction of the town. The news of it reached
Gouriaq who worried and wished to frighten him and make him perish by ruse. It is reported that among the
objects thus discovered was a sealed roll enclosing a flask of emeralds that contained a green powder and a
red stick. Whoever

[PDF p. 452]

rubbed the eyelids with this powder by means of the stick -- his hair, were it white with old age, became
black again, and his gaze acquired a penetration such that he could perceive the spirits. He found also a
statue of gold that made the sky cover itself with clouds and the rain fall, and images of crows in stone
that answered when one posed them questions. In each magazine he found ten marvelous objects.

When the construction was finished, he sent to ask Gouriaq to come to him. The queen had a rich carpet
carried to him to hang the room where he sat, saying: "Divide your army into three parts; send me the first
third, and, when I will have done a third of the road, send me the second; finally when I will have
traversed half the road, send me the last third; thus your troops will find themselves behind me and no one
will see me when I enter your home. Keep with you only the pages who habitually serve you; for me, I will
come only with the women indispensable to your service, and you will not have to blush before them." Thus
was it done; Gouriaq gathered her escort and her baggage and set out. Forewarned of her departure, Giroun
sent before her the third of his army; the queen had prepared for these troops poisoned foods and drinks and
had them served by her slaves and the members of her family who presented to them the dishes and the
refreshments, perfumes, and all sorts of delicious things. None of the soldiers of Giroun awoke alive in the
morning, and the queen continued her march. The second third of the army having come to meet her, she made
it undergo the same fate and informed Giroun that she had sent his army to his palace and his capital to
keep them for him. Then she set out again and arrived at his place with her nurse and her serving-women. The
nurse blew on the face of Giroun a breath that stupefied him, and she sprinkled him with a liquid she
carried with her. The members of Giroun set about trembling and he said: "Whoever believes he can prevail
over women lies to himself, for the women prevail over him." The queen opened his veins saying: "The blood
of kings is a remedy." She cut off his head, carried it off, and planted it at the summit of his palace; she
seized all his riches, sent them to the town of Memphis, and built at Alexandria a tower on which she
engraved her own name and that of her victim, and the account and the date of her exploit. When the kings
had learned what Gouriaq had done, they dreaded her, submitted to her, and sent her presents. She did in
Egypt numerous marvels and

[PDF p. 453]

constructed on the frontier of the kingdom, on the side of Nubia, a fortress and a bridge under which flowed
the water of the Nile; then, having fallen ill, she remitted the power to her cousin Zelfa, daughter of
Mamoun, and died.

Ibn Khordadabah says: It is recounted that Alexandria was built in 300 years and that, for 70 years, its
inhabitants had, to promenade there, to use black veils in order to protect their eyes against the dazzling
whiteness of the walls of the town and of the marvelous lighthouse raised in the middle of the sea on a crab
of glass. Alexandria counted, besides its ordinary inhabitants, 600,000 Jews mixed with the population.

According to Ibn Ouacif Shah, the cultivations extended, through the desert of Rosetta and Alexandria, to
Barqah; up to there the foot trod the land of Egypt; one had no need of provisions, so abundant were the
fruits and other good things; and one walked constantly sheltered by the shade of the trees against the
ardor of the sun. The king Sa, son of Qobtim, raised in this desert palaces, made there great plantations,
and brought there from the Nile canals that, starting from the western bank of the river, went to the western
frontier of the country, across uninterrupted cultivations. And when the population had disappeared, its
traces remained in this desert; the palaces are destroyed, the inhabitants are dispersed, but one does not
cease to recount, on this region and on what one has seen there of ruins and marvels, surprising legends.

Ibn Abd el Hakem recounts that the one who built Alexandria and laid the foundations of it was Dhu'l Qorneïn
the Greek, whose name is Alexander, and who gave his name to Alexandria; it is he who first made stuffs with
threads of gold, and his father was the first Caesar; it is said that the first constructor was a man of
Egypt, named Mourzebah son of Mourzeba, the Greek, of the lineage of Younan, son of Japhet son of Noah;
according to others, he was of Libya, one of the western districts of Egypt. Ibn Lahi'at says that the
population of this country was Greek; as for (Alexander), he claims that he is Himyarite. Ibn Tobba' said:

[verses:] My grandfather Dhu'l Qorneïn was Muslim and king, before whom the kings bowed in the assemblies;
he reached the West and the East, seeking to obtain the science of a philosopher with a wise mind; he saw
the sun set at the point where it sets, there, where is a source without rain and filled with a fetid mud.

[PDF p. 454]

In another reading, it is said: "Dhu'l Qorneïn was before me a Muslim."

Othman ben Saleh told me: Abd Allah ben Ouaheb, who had it from Abd el Rahman ben Ziad ben An'am, who had it
himself from Sa'd ben Mesa'oud El Tagibi, who had it from two old men of his tribe, recounted to me what
follows: We were at Alexandria and, finding the time long, we said: "What if we went to find 'Aqabah ben
'Amer and conversed with him!" We went therefore to his home and found him seated in his house and informed
him that we had found our day too long. "I too," he said, "finding the time too long, went out (and came
back)." Then, advancing toward us, he added: "I was on duty with the apostle of God. And behold, there
arrived people who believe in the Book (Jews or Christians) bringing with them leaves or books and who said
to me: 'We ask permission to present ourselves before the apostle of God.' I went to the prophet and
informed him of what was happening. 'What is there between them and me?' he said; 'they come to question me
on what I cannot understand. I am only a servant and know only what my lord has taught me.' Then he added:
'Bring me the water of the ablutions.' And having purified himself, he went to the oratory of his house,
prostrated himself twice, and came back, joy and satisfaction painted on his face. He came back therefore
and said to me: 'Have them enter, as well as all those of my companions you will find at the door.' I
introduced them, and when they were in the presence of the apostle of God, the latter said to them: 'If you
desire it, I will set forth to you that on which you wish to question me before you speak; or, if you prefer
it, speak first and set forth yourselves your affair.' 'Certainly,' they answered, 'set it forth to us before
we speak.' 'You desire,' resumed the prophet, 'to question me on Dhu'l Qorneïn, and I am going to tell you
what is written in your books on his subject: First he was a young boy of the country of Roum who obtained
the royalty. Then he undertook an expedition, arrived at the shore of the sea of Egypt, founded there a town
that took the name of Alexandria; when its construction was finished, an angel came who took him and lifted
him little by little into the air to a very great height. Dhu'l Qorneïn, a first time, raised his eyes, and
the angel said to him: "Look below you." "I see," said Dhu'l Qorneïn, "my town and other towns with it." The
angel rose still and said: "Look." "I see my town all alone and see no other." "What you see thus," said the
angel, "is all the earth,

[PDF p. 455]

and what surrounds the earth is the sea. Your Lord has wished to show you the earth and he has given you a
power that, later, will be a teaching for the ignorant and a proof for the sages." Then Dhu'l Qorneïn went to
the place where the sun sets, then to the place where the sun rises; finally he arrived at the double barrier
formed by two very soft mountains on which everything slides, and there he constructed the barrier; then
passing beyond Yagog and Magog (Gog and Magog), he met a people whose face was similar to a face of a dog and
who made war on Yagog and Magog; passing further, he found a dwarf people who made war on the dog-faced
people, then a people of cranes who made war on the people of the dwarfs; then, continuing his route, he met
a people of serpents each of which could swallow an enormous rock. Finally he arrived at the sea that
envelops the earth.' And the visitors of the prophet said to him: 'We certify that such is his history and
that it is thus recounted in our books.'"

According to Khaled ben Ma'dan El Kala'i, the prophet of God, questioned on Dhu'l Qorneïn, answered: "He
governed the surface of the earth from the depth of the soil." The same Khaled reports that 'Omar ben El
Khattab, hearing a man cry: "O Dhu'l Qorneïn!" said: "O my God, pardon! Do the prophets no longer suffice you
that you invoke the angels?"

Qotada affirms, on the authority of El Hassan, that Dhu'l Qorneïn was a king and a pious man, to whom the
name of Dhu'l Qorneïn would have been given for this reason: Aly, questioned on the subject of this personage,
answered that it was neither an angel nor a prophet, but a pious servant loving God, loved by God, sincere
toward God and toward whom God was sincere. The Lord sent him to his people who struck him on his two horns.
He died and was surnamed Dhu'l Qorneïn (the two-horned). It is said on the other hand that this surname was
given to him because he had reached the two horns (extreme points) of the sun, the setting and the rising;
according to others, because he had two tresses of hair that he rolled up, or two little horns that he
concealed under the turban.

According to Ibn Shehab, he was called Dhu'l Qorneïn because he reached the horn of the sun in the Occident
and the horn of the sun in the Orient.

According to Abd Allah ben 'Amr ben El 'As, as soon as Alexandria was built, Pharaoh began by installing
there workshops and habitations; these were the first traces of civilization and construction that appeared
there;

[PDF p. 456]

since then, the constructions have constantly continued there and the workshops have not ceased to function
there. After this Pharaoh, the kings of Egypt changed the state of the town, and Daluka bent Zaba raised the
tower of Alexandria and the lighthouse of Bouqir. When Soliman, son of David, appeared on the earth, he built
there a habitation and a place of prayers. Then Dhu'l Qorneïn having made himself master of it destroyed all
the edifices that the kings, the Pharaohs, and the other personages had raised there, except those that
Soliman had constructed; these, he respected without changing anything in them, contenting himself with
repairing what was in bad state. It is thus that he repaired the lighthouse and raised in Alexandria
edifices that resembled one another from the first to the last. After Alexander, the kings succeeded one
another, Greeks and others, and none of them forgot to construct at Alexandria some monument known today by
the name of the king who constructed it and to whom it is attributed.

Ibn Lahi'ah says: I have been told that one found at Alexandria a stone bearing this inscription: "I am
Sheddad ben 'Ad, who raised the columns, dug the quarries, and, with my arm, barred the rivers. I did not
believe, in accomplishing these works, in either old age or death, and the stone was soft like the silt." In
another account one reads: "I have buried in the sea a treasure of more than twelve cubits and no one will be
able to bring it out, except the people of Mohammed." Ibn Lahi'ah says that the word [used] is the equivalent
of the word for grottoes, caverns. Abou 'Aly El Qali, in the Kitab El Amali, says: Ibn El A'râbi and others
have recited these verses:

[verses:] You ask me the number of my years, and I have said: "If I had lived the age of the lizard, or the
age of Noah since the Flood, if I had been able to come to understand the voiceless insects, if I had lived
all the duration of the time that followed the Flood, certainly I would have been already the lot of old age
or of death."

And in another reading:

[verses:] Soliman learned the language of the ant, in the time when the rock was like mud.

Another said: "In the time that followed the Flood, the solid was soft."
