[PDF p. 457]

For them, the time of the [jadid/post-flood era] is the period that followed the Flood, a period during
which the fertility was marvelous and the prosperity admirable. Someone said: "the time of [that era] is a
time that has not had its like. As for the words [voiceless creatures], one calls [voiceless] those of the
animals whose voice one does not hear." These verses are of Roubat ben El 'Agag ben Roubah ben Labid ben
Sakhr ben Kathif ben Heï ben Bekr ben Zabi'at ben Sa'd ben Malek ben Zeïd manah ben Tamim. Here is on what
occasion he made them: Having led camels to drink at a source belonging to the tribe of 'Aql, he saw a young
girl who pleased him; he asked her for her hand in pledge of betrothal. "I see years," she said; "do you
possess also some property?" "Yes," he answered, "a flock of beasts." "Is there also money?" asked the young
girl. "No," said Roubah. "O people of 'Aql!" she cried; "you have so much pretension and you are poor!" And
Roubah said then:

[verses:] In despising my situation and making light of my flock, she showed her discontent and humiliated,
among the people of 'Akl, my position, and made of the head a sign as if to prove it to me. You ask me the
number of my years, and I say that if I had lived the age of the lizard or that of Noah since the Flood,
when the humid stone was similar to the muddy silt.

And in another reading:

[verses:] If I had come to know the language of the voiceless animals, (as) Soliman knew the language of the
ants.

Abou Bekr ben Darid, who was questioned on the time of [that era], answered: "The Arabs claim that it is the
time when the stones were soft."

One reads in 'Abd el Hakem: It is said that the constructor of Alexandria was Sheddad ben 'Ad, and God is the
most learned.

Alexandria comprised three juxtaposed towns, namely: the lighthouse and its surroundings, Alexandria proper
-- that is, the heart of present Alexandria -- and Nafitah. Each was surrounded by a wall behind which a
second wall rose that completely surrounded each of the three towns. It is said that Alexandria was defended
by seven well-armed fortresses and seven ditches. Alexander clad with marble the walls and the soil of the
town of Alexandria, whose inhabitants wore then black and red garments. Formerly the

[PDF p. 458]

monks dressed in black, because of the dazzling whiteness of the marble, which was so brilliant that it was
not necessary to light torches during the night, and as soon as the moon appeared, one could easily sew and
thread a needle.

It is recounted that Alexandria was built in three hundred years, inhabited for three hundred years, and
for three hundred ruined. What is certain is that for seventy years, no one could penetrate there without
covering the eyes with a black veil, because of the whiteness of the plaster and the slabs, and during this
time one lit no lamps there. The town remained white and brilliant during the night as during the day, and
as soon as the sun was set, no one went out of his house any more; whoever ventured outside his home
disappeared. Among the inhabitants of the town was a shepherd who led his flock to graze on the shore of the
sea, and from the sea came out someone who carried off some beast of his flock; the shepherd having hidden
himself in this place awaited the coming of the ravisher. And he saw a woman who smoothed her hair and who
tried to repel him, but he made himself master of her and dragged her to his house where she lived intimately
with him. Seeing that the inhabitants of the town no longer went out of their homes after sunset, this woman
asked them the reason for it, and they explained to her that those of them who ventured outside were carried
off. She then prepared for them talismans, and it was she who, the first in Egypt, made talismans at
Alexandria. It is recounted that the marble was a veritable inconvenience for the inhabitants; from dawn, it
was brilliant like flour, and this brilliance became more vivid still when noon arrived.

According to El Masa'oudi, some historians recount that when the Macedonian Alexander had regulated the
administration of his States, and had set out to conquer the entire world -- air, earth, and water -- he
arrived at the place where Alexandria is and found there ruins of monuments and numerous columns of marble;
in the middle of the town rose an enormous column bearing the following inscription in musnad characters,
which is the primitive writing of the peoples of Himyar and the kings of 'Ad: "It is I, Sheddad, son of 'Ad
who, with my arm, barred the rivers, cut the gigantic columns, the hills, and the high mountains; I built
Iram Zat El 'Amad which has not its like on the earth. Here I wished to build a town like Iram and transport
there all that my family and my people count of noble and of [...]

[PDF p. 459]

generous, and this without taking account of fear, of old age, of chagrin, or of sickness. But the moment of
the reckoning has come for me and has removed me from my projects; and the arrival of this moment has been
to me the cause of long chagrins and long sorrows. Short has been my dream and my sojourn (on the earth);
yesterday, I had to leave my house, and there is no king, however powerful he be, who does not find himself
subject to this reality; there is no army, whatever its number, that is not subject to the fear from which
one cannot defend oneself either by will or by disdain; there is a term to power; the monuments disappear and
also the sublime and glorious sultan. Whoever will see the monuments I have left, whoever will know my
history, the duration of my life, and the annihilation of my genius, despite the powerful precautions I had
taken, that one will no longer be deceived by the world; for the world is deceiving and perfidious; from it
one must claim only what it gives and take only what one can receive from it. There are long discourses that
demonstrate the inanity of the world, put one on guard against its deceptions, and turn one away from seeking
repose there."

Alexander, pensive, descended musing on these words and taking them for a rule. Then he had the artisans of
all countries gathered, traced the foundations of the town to which he gave some miles of length and width;
he gathered there columns and blocks of alabaster, and had come boats laden with alabaster, marble, and
stones of all sorts, from the island of Sicily and the countries of Greece and Crete and the extremities of
the sea of Roum, there where it joins the Ocean sea. One brought some also from the island of Rhodes. Order
was given to the workers to raise around the terrain where the foundations had been traced a wall that would
enclose the town, and at each point where the earth had been dug one planted a beam, each beam being
connected to its neighbor by a cord stretched from one to the other; the whole was joined to a column of
marble placed facing his tent. To this column was suspended a big sonorous bell, and everyone -- masons,
workers, and artisans -- were warned that as soon as they heard the sound of this bell and saw the cords
agitate (the support-posts all bearing a smaller bell), they were to lay the foundations of the town at the
same time on all sides. Alexander desired that this operation be executed at a moment chosen by him and at a
favorable rising (of the stars). But Alexander inclined little by little the head and was taken by a light
sleep while he watched for the propitious instant, and a crow,

[PDF p. 460]

settling on the cord that supported the big bell suspended from the column, set this bell in movement. The
bell rang, the cords agitated, and the little bells they supported tinkled, for all this was done by
movements ingeniously combined and scientifically prepared. The workers, seeing the cords agitate and
hearing the little bells ring, laid all together the foundations uttering cries of praise and purification.
Alexander, awakened, asked what was happening; in learning it, he was marveled and said: "I wished one thing
and God wished another, and what God does not wish to accord, he refuses it. I wished that the duration of
this town be long, and God wished that its disappearance and its ruin be rapid and that the kings change its
fortune." Alexander, having therefore regulated the construction of the town and fixed its foundations, the
animals of the sea came out of the waters as soon as the night had come, and rushed on the constructions
already made. Seeing this the next day, Alexander said: "Behold, already begins the ruin of the constructions
of this town; let its end come according to the will of the Creator!" And he augured ill of the damage
accomplished by the beasts of the sea; yet the construction continued; each day one constructed, one made
plans, and overseers had been posted to repel the animals at their coming out of the sea. But when one came
back in the morning, one ascertained that the animals had come and destroyed the constructions. Alexander,
very worried, was terrified by this danger come from the sea; he reflected therefore and examined what it
was fitting to do and what ruse he should employ to set aside this calamity and remove this misfortune from
the city. And while he was alone, reflecting on all this, the sought ruse presented itself to his mind at the
same time as the means of putting it into execution. In the morning, he had the workers come and ordered
them to fabricate for him a box of wood, ten cubits long and five wide; one arranged there windows of glass,
surrounded by the wood of the box in all their circumference, and maintained by pitch, mastic, and other
resinous and impermeable matters, to prevent the water from entering the box. One reserved there also
emplacements for the cords. Into this box entered Alexander, and with him the people of his bureau who knew
how to paint, and the doors were closed again on him, after he had given the order to caulk (the joints)
with the matters of which we have spoken; then, two big ships conducted the box into the open sea, and there,
after having suspended under the box weights of lead and

[PDF p. 461]

of iron and stones, in order to draw it into the depths, the box was placed between the two boats which one
joined by beams, in order to avoid any separation; the cords that held the box were moored on the two ships,
then paid out. The box plunged and reached the bottom of the sea, and those who were inside saw demons of
human form, but some of which had heads of animals; some were armed with axes, others with saws or picks, in
imitation of the workers and artisans of the town provided with their construction tools. Alexander and his
companions examined attentively these figures and drew them on paper, interpreting them according to their
different species and reproducing the ugliness of their forms and their bodies. Then the cord was agitated,
and, warned by this signal, the men who had remained in the boats hauled on the moorings and brought the box
to the surface. Alexander came out of it and prescribed to the workers who worked the iron, the copper, and
the stone to execute the images of the animals such as they had been drawn; this done, the statues were
raised on columns on the shore of the sea, and the construction was resumed. The night having come, the
destructive animals came out, but, seeing their images placed on columns and turned toward the sea, they
left and reappeared no more. Alexandria could thus be built; one covered its walls with a coating of plaster,
and on the gate of the town Alexander had this inscription engraved: "It is here, Alexandria, that I wished
to build for salvation, success, happiness, felicity, joy, and the duration of the centuries; but the
Creator, the king of the heavens and the earth, the annihilator of peoples, did not wish that it last thus.
I founded it and regulated its construction; I covered with plaster its wall, and God gave me every thing,
science and wisdom, and he smoothed for me the difficulties. All that I desired of science, he accorded it
to me; he prevented nothing of what I wished to undertake. To God returns the complaisance, to me the work;
perfection is the lot of those of my contemporaries who served him. Glory to God, the master of men; there
is no God but he, he is the Lord of all things." Following this inscription he had represented all that was
to occur after him, in his country, of calamities, of prosperity, and of ruin, and all that was to happen to
Alexandria until the end of the world.

The construction of Alexandria reposed on vaults forming arcaded bridges on which rose the houses of the
town and under which

[PDF p. 462]

cavaliers armed with lances passed at ease and thus made the circuit of the town under the vaults placed
below. One had arranged in these underground passages openings and dormers for the light and conduits for
the air. During the night, Alexandria remained lit, without one lighting lamps, thanks to the whiteness of
the alabaster and the marble; its markets, its streets, its avenues were protected by vaulted roofs, in such
a way that the inhabitants did not have to preoccupy themselves with the rain. The town was surrounded by
seven walls constructed in stones of diverse colors and separated by ditches dug at a certain distance from
the walls. In addition, the town was hung with hangings of green silk to protect the eyes of the inhabitants
against the brilliance of the marble, whose whiteness was dazzling. The town once constructed and peopled,
there occurred calamities of which one finds the account among the writers who have occupied themselves with
the history of Egypt and Alexandria: each night, inhabitants were carried off, and the next day a good number
of them had disappeared. Having learned it, Alexander had talismans placed on columns named obelisks and
which have remained standing until the present. Each of these columns had the form of a cypress and was
eighty cubits high; it reposed on a socle of copper. Under each of them one had deposited figures, images,
and an inscription.

Of all the histories that precede, says the author (Maqrizi), those of Ibn Ouacif Shah are evidently
authentic; as for what El Maça'oudi reports, claiming that it was Alexander who made the box that served to
draw the animals of the sea, that is imaginary. For Ibn Ouacif Shah is very instructed in the Chronicles of
the Egyptians. Likewise what El Maça'oudi says, relative to the obelisks raised by Alexander, is pure
imagination. These obelisks are simply the lighthouses that lit the town and the signals raised by the
ancient kings of Egypt. They are works of the first kings of the Copts and the Pharaohs who reigned in Egypt
in the ancient times.

[PDF p. 463]

CHAPTER V
OF ALEXANDER

It is Alexander, son of Philip, son of Amintah or Amyntas, son of Heraklesh or Hercules, the formidable, who
was himself son of Alexander the Great; the king Philip governed for his father the country of Magedoniah or
Makedoniah for twenty-five years, made show there of all sorts of ruses, and imagined all the possible
wickednesses, surpassing in this by far all those who had reigned before him in the country.

At the beginning of his life, his brother Alexander had delivered him as hostage to a chief of the country
of Roum with whom he remained three years. The chief of Roum was a philosopher and the young prince learned
philosophy with him; after the murder of his brother Alexander, the people chose to succeed him Philip who
was proclaimed chief; he was a remarkable king, made war on the Greeks, vanquished them, traversed the
deserts, killed there thousands of people, and took towns. He gathered around him an innumerable crowd and an
extraordinary army, lowered the Greeks, lost an eye in a battle, invaded the country, ravaged, pillaged,
sacked, then, gathering all the inhabitants of the country of Roum, he formed of them an army of a hundred
thousand infantry and fifty thousand cavalry, without counting those who constituted his national army,
composed of Macedonians or people of other countries, and marched to the conquest of Persia.

While he gathered his troops, he occupied himself with the marriage of his daughter Cleopatra whom he wished
to unite to the father of his wife, the uncle of his son Alexander; two days before the marriage, he was
seated conversing with his generals, when one of them asked him what kind of death seemed to him preferable
for a man. "That," he said, "which is necessary for the strong, valiant, and proven man," wishing to say
that, for himself, he did not desire to die otherwise than by the sword. And, during the night, the sickness
surprised him, his strength abandoned him, subdued by the pain, and he hastened the accomplishment of the
marriage; he attended the feasts, mounted on his chariot between his son Alexander and Alexander his
relative; but, having withdrawn a moment apart, a young Greek pierced him with a lance-blow and killed him,
avenging thus his father. Alexander therefore took the government of the kingdom after his father Philip,
and

[PDF p. 464]

began by undertaking an expedition against the country of Roum which had shaken off the yoke of Macedonia to
submit to the domination of the Persians. He made the trace of it disappear, exterminated the inhabitants,
destroyed the towns, reduced to slavery or sold the population; all the country, down to the smallest
villages, had to pay him tribute. After that, he made perish all the members of his family and most of his
relatives, while preparing his expedition against Persia. His army comprised twenty-two thousand cavalry and
sixty thousand infantry, his fleet counted five hundred eighty ships. It is with forces so minimal that he
made the greatest kings of the earth tremble, that he reached Alexandria and entered Jerusalem where he
offered sacrifices to God. He left Jerusalem to make war on Dara (Darius). The army of Dara, king of Persia,
at his first encounter with Alexander, was of six hundred thousand combatants. It was vanquished by
Alexander, and this defeat was for the Persians a frightful catastrophe and an abominable misfortune; there
was killed an extraordinary number of them, and Alexander for his part killed a hundred twenty cavaliers and
ninety infantry.

Alexander continued his route, taking the towns and pillaging what they enclosed, when he learned that Dara,
after new preparations, was marching to meet him with considerable forces. Fearing to be rejoined by him in a
defile, between two mountains, where he was then, he operated a forced march of nearly a hundred miles, with
a prodigious rapidity, and reached the town of Tarsus; during the road, he had nearly died of the excess of
the cold which had contracted his nerves. Dara advanced with three hundred thousand infantry and a hundred
thousand cavalry, and, when the two armies were in presence, Alexander, terrified by the immense number of
the enemies and the insignificant force of his own army, was on the point of taking flight. But the combat
was engaged, the generals paid with their persons, the brave descended into the melee, the lance-blows and
the (sword-)blows were exchanged, and the plain became too narrow for the crowd (that filled it). The two
kings, Dara and Alexander, fought body to body. Alexander was the most accomplished cavalier, the bravest and
most vigorous of his time; and the two kings fought until they were both covered with wounds and Dara took
flight. Then the carnage of the Persians began; one killed nearly eighty thousand infantry and nearly ten
thousand cavalry; about forty thousand men were made prisoners; the army of Alexander had hardly lost more
than two

[PDF p. 465]

hundred infantry and a hundred fifty cavalry. The camp of the Persians fell to the power of Alexander who
gathered there incalculable quantities of gold, silver, and precious furniture. Among the prisoners were the
mother, the wife, the sister, and the two daughters of Dara. The latter asked Alexander to return them to him
for the half of his empire, but the Macedonian refused. Dara therefore made for the third time his
preparations and gathered the Persians to the last man, composing thus an army of all those who, among his
peoples, were in state to bear arms. Alexander sent one of his generals who, with a fleet, descended to the
country of Porus, and marched himself on Syria where the kings of the world came to make him their
submission. To some he accorded pardon, he banished others and made perish the rest, then advanced against
the fortress of Tarsus; Tarsus was an ancient and superb town and the inhabitants had known how to capture
the confidence of the Africans who, thanks to the alliance they had contracted, trafficked with them.
Alexander blocked them so closely that they ended by opening their gates; from there, the conqueror passed
to Rhodes, then into Egypt, ravaging everything on his passage. In Egypt, he founded Alexandria; Orosius
speaks of this foundation and enters, on this subject, into interminable accounts and considerations that we
renounce citing, for they would lengthen too much our book.

Dara having finished repairing (his disasters), set out with four hundred thousand infantry and a hundred
thousand cavalry, and met Alexander, returning from Egypt, in the surroundings of Tarsus. The battle was
gigantic and the Greeks, prepared and accustomed to victory and to death, fought with fury; on the part of
the Persians, the fury was no less, excited as they were to the carnage and preferring death to servitude
and slavery. All that has been able to be said of a melee is nothing in comparison with the slaughter that
signaled this one. Finally Dara, seeing his army vanquished and in rout, thought of forestalling death in
this encounter and of avoiding captivity by paying with his person and seeking to get himself killed in the
battle. One of his generals, taken with pity for him, tried to console him; Dara took flight in his turn:
the army and the power of the Persians were in full rout, and behind it fled also the king. All the regions
of the Orient were subjugated to the country of Roum and the Persian kings disappeared for 450 years.
Alexander occupied himself with examining and classing all that was found in the camp of the Persians; the
division among the Greek troops lasted thirty days, after which the conqueror

[PDF p. 466]

marched on the principal town of Persia which was also the capital of all the kingdom and where were
gathered the riches and the treasures of the world; he destroyed it and gave it over to pillage. Having
learned that Dara was captive and loaded with chains of silver at the home of one of his subjects, Alexander
made his preparations and set out with six thousand men; on his road, he met Dara, pierced with numerous
wounds of which he soon died; the Macedonian made of him great mourning, pronounced the funeral discourses,
and had him buried in the tomb of the kings of Persia. The three combats of which one has just spoken are an
example for whoever likes to regulate himself according to examples, an advice for whoever likes advice; one
saw fight, in these three encounters, nearly fifteen million men of a single empire, cavaliers and infantry
of Asia -- that is, of Iraq. Sixty years before, nearly nineteen million men of this empire had been killed,
and in addition a million representing the cavaliers and infantry of Iraq, of Syria, of Tarsus, of Egypt, of
the island of Rhodes, and of all the countries that Alexander subjugated. He reigned over the world, and the
world that he had made tremble by the extraordinary misfortunes he had brought it was divided among his
generals. And the inhabitants of the earth were either annihilated by a frightful death, or, overexcited by
the passion of murder, made themselves the accomplices of these horrible massacres. At the moment of dying,
Alexander wished that each of his generals be, after his death, surnamed Ptolemy, in order to terrify the
enemies, for the word Ptolemy signifies "the warrior." Such is the truth on the history of Alexander; as for
what strays from it, one must take no account of it.

It is said that Alexander had red hair and blue eyes; he was the first man who kept vigil during the night.
He had buffoons who made him laugh and storytellers who told him extraordinary stories, wishing by this means
to keep his empire over himself and master his soul, and not for jest. It is from him that the kings took the
habit of keeping vigil and of having buffoons and storytellers.

[PDF p. 467]

CHAPTER VI
OF THE ERA OF ALEXANDER

Abou-l Rihan Mohammed Ahmed El Birouni says: The era of the Greek Alexander, whom some confuse with Dhu'l
Qorneïn, governs the years of the Persians and it is of it also that the major part of the peoples make use.
It begins at the epoch when Alexander, at the age of twenty-six years, set out from Greece to go to combat
Dara, king of the Persians.

On arriving at Jerusalem, he prescribed to the Jews to abandon the era of David and of Moses to adopt his;
the Jews conformed to his orders, adopted his era, and made use of it for their needs, making it start from
the twenty-sixth year of the conqueror -- that is, exactly a thousand years after Moses; they have remained
faithful to this computation and still employ it. It is also according to the era of Alexander that counted
the Greeks who previously had taken, as initial date of their calculations, the epoch when Younan, son of
Nourés, left Babel for the Occident.

The Alexandrine era begins the Monday 1st of Teschrin I, corresponding to the fourth day of Baba; the day
begins at sunrise, going until the setting of this star and ending the next day at sunrise; the day completes
itself thus with the following night. The beginnings of the months return at uniform intervals, following a
series that repeats itself constantly. The number of the months of this year is twelve; they differ one from
another by the number of the days that compose them. Here are the names of the twelve months and the number
of days of each of them: Teshrin I, 31 days; Teshrin II, 30 days; Kanoun I, 31 days; Kanoun II, 31 days;
Shabbath, 28 days 1/4; Adhar, 31 days; Nisan, 30 days; Aïar, 31 days; Haziran, 30 days; Tammouz, 31 days; Ab,
31 days; Eïloul, 30 days; therefore, seven months have 31 days, four months have 30, and a single one has 28
1/4; this is why they give Shabbath 28 days for three consecutive years and, the fourth year, 29 days. Thus
the year is composed of 365 days 1/4, and each fourth year comprises 366 days; one gives it the name of
intercalary year. In adding this quarter of a day to the year, one wished to draw near the number of the days
of the solar year, in such a way that affairs execute themselves following an invariable series and that the

[PDF p. 468]

months of cold or heat, the season of sowing, of the pruning of the trees, or of the harvest of the fruits
return at a determined epoch of the year, without any change. The first intercalary year was the third year
of the era of Alexander, and between the Monday, first day of the Alexandrine era, and the Thursday first day
of the month of Moharram when our prophet Mohammed ben 'Abd Allah ben 'Abd El Motaleb, the apostle of God,
fled from Mecca to Medina, there have elapsed 933 years and 155 days. Between this same day (beginning of the
era of Alexander) and the Friday, first day after the Flood, one counts 1792 years and 193 days. From the
beginning of the reign of Bokta Nasar (Nebuchadnezzar) to the first day of the era of Alexander there have
elapsed 435 solar years and 238 days.

Abou Bekr Ahmed ben 'Aly ben Qeïs ben Ouahshiah, in his book of the Nabataean Agriculture, reports that,
according to the accounts of the Copts, who would have found this in their books, the month of Tammouz owes
its name to a man whose history is long and marvelous. This man had invited the king to adore the seven
planets and the twelve signs of the Zodiac; the king had him put to death, but Tammouz, after having been
killed, lived anew; the king made him perish again several times by means of frightful tortures, but, after
each murder, Tammouz always revived: finally he died. All these months take their name from a virtuous and
learned man who lived formerly among the Nabataeans, in the time when they inhabited the region of Babel,
before the Chaldeans; for this Tammouz is neither a Chaldean, nor a Canaanite, nor a Hebrew, nor a Djermaq;
he is one of the ancient Hazanasis; this is why they say that each of their months bears the name of a man of
the times past; that Teshrin I and Teshrin II were two brothers skilled in the sciences; likewise for Kanoun
I and Kanoun II; as for Shabbath, it is the name of a man who lay with a thousand virgin women without
procreating or engendering anything, so they have placed him at the end of the series of the months, because
of his impotence to engender, and, for this same reason, they have diminished the number of his days. Today,
all the Sabeans, or Babylonians, or Hazanasis lament and weep over Tammouz, during the month that bears this
name; they have a feast consecrated to Tammouz; and to this month they have given a greater number of days
and have consecrated it to the women. There all the women afflict themselves, lament, and weep over Tammouz
and conduct a long mourning. And they know of him nothing more than what they recount thus: "We have found
that our ancestors [...]

[PDF p. 469]

lamented over Tammouz in the feast consecrated to Tammouz." The Christians claim that they do the same thing
for a man named Georgis (George), one of the disciples of Jesus, who invited a certain king to embrace the
Christian religion, and the king punished him by these successive murders. If I am not mistaken, the history
of Tammouz reached the Christians who changed his name to that of Georgis and took, in the succession of
time, the place of the Sabeans; for the Sabeans made the commemoration of Tammouz the first day of the month
of Tammouz, and the Christians celebrate Georgis at the end of Nisan. It is said that a king of Rome added to
the months of the peoples of Roum the months of Kanoun II and of Shabbath; until then they had only ten
months, each of which counted thirty-six days.

It is recounted that Fioufious, first king of the town of Rome and who reigned forty-three years, added
Kanoun II and Shabbath to the months of the peoples of Roum who until then possessed only ten, each counting
thirty-six days. The reason for which Shabbath had two days less than the other months was that there was,
in the time of Fiten, chief of the army of Roum, an incursion following which occurred wars with Fariourious,
wars that ended with the victory of Fiten and the conquest by the latter of the Empire of Roum. Orders were
given on the subject of Fariourious and one made for him this proclamation: "Aya Mordya," which means: "Go
out, O Shabbath," and he was drowned in the sea. And Shabbath was named Feriourious (February) to recall by
that his wickedness. And as this happened in the two last days of the month, the 29th and the 30th of
Shabbath, these two days were cut from this month and transferred to Tammouz and Kanoun II which had each 31
days. Later, came another king who said: It is not fitting that Shabbath be in the middle of the year, and he
put it at the end, and, since that time, the Greeks have not ceased to hold Shabbath apart.

[PDF p. 470]

CHAPTER VII
OF THE DIFFERENCE THAT THERE IS BETWEEN ALEXANDER AND DHU'L QORNEÏN, WHO ARE TWO DISTINCT PERSONAGES

The people who know history hold for certain that Dhu'l Qorneïn is the personage of whom God makes mention in
his sacred Book when he says: "One will question you on Dhu'l Qorneïn; answer: I will tell you something of
him; we gave him for domain the earth and we provided him with all things" (Koran, XVIII, 82, 83). Thus he
has become for the Arabs a subject they have treated frequently in their poetry. His name was El Sa'b ben Dhu
Morathed ben El Hareth El Raïsh ben El Hemâl Dhu Seded ben 'Ad Dhu Menah ben 'Amer El Moultat ben Saksak ben
Ouaïl ben Himyar ben Seba ben Yashgab ben Ya'rab ben Qahtan ben Houd ben 'Aber ben Shaleh ben Arfakhshad ben
Sam ben Nouh; he was a king of the Himyarites -- that is, of the pure Arabs whom one also calls the
full-blooded Arabs. Dhu'l Qorneïn was therefore a Tobba (name of the Himyarite kings) who wore the crown.
When he was named king, he behaved at first proudly, then he humbled himself before God and joined El Khidr.
Those have been mistaken who have wished that Alexander, son of Philip, be the same as Dhu'l Qorneïn who
raised the barrier; the words Dhu 'arabiah and Dhu'l Qorneïn are indeed surnames that the Arabs give to the
kings of the Yemen; Alexander was a Roumi, a Greek. Abou Dza'far El Tabari reports that El Khidr lived in the
time of the king Afridoun, son of El Dahak; it is at least the opinion of the generality of the people who
believe in the Book; the epoch of El Khidr is therefore anterior to the time of Moses, son of Amran; he was,
it is said, a precursor of Dhu'l Qorneïn the Great, contemporary of Abraham. El Khidr traveled with Dhu'l
Qorneïn, reached with him the country where flows the river of life, and drank of its waters without the
knowledge of Dhu'l Qorneïn and his companions. This is why El Khidr lived and still lives, according to what
these historians claim. According to others, Dhu'l Qorneïn would have attended the oath of Abraham and would
be the same as Afridoun son of El Dahak, of whom El Khidr would have been the precursor.

Abou Mohammed 'Abd el Melek ben Heshâm, in his book Of the Crowns treating of the knowledge of the kings of
the times past, after having

[PDF p. 471]

recalled the genealogy of Dhu'l Qorneïn that we have cited, adds: He was a crowned Tobba' who, having
obtained the empire, showed himself at first proud and later humbled himself before God, rejoined El Khidr at
Jerusalem, and went with him to the Occident and the Orient of the earth; all was accorded to him, as God
himself recalls, and he raised the barrier that separates Yagog and Magog. He died in Iraq...

As for Alexander, he is a Greek well known under the name of Alexander the Macedonian. Ibn 'Abbas,
questioned on Dhu'l Qorneïn, answered: "He is a Himyarite, named El Sa'b ben Dhu Morathed, to whom God gave
the earth for domain and whom he heaped with all goods. He reached the two horns of the sun and the extremity
of the earth and constructed the barrier between Yagog and Magog." "And Alexander?" one asked him. "He is,"
he answered, "a pious man of the country of Roum and a skillful man who raised a lighthouse in Africa on the
shore of the sea, made himself master of the town of Rome, reached the sea of the Occident where he
accumulated monuments, palaces, and towns."

One questioned Ka'b el Ahbar on Dhu'l Qorneïn: "In the opinion of our scholars and our ancestors," he said,
"he was Himyarite and was named El Sa'b ben Dhu Morathed; while Alexander was a Greek of the race of Esau,
son of Isaac, son of Abraham; the people from which Alexander came followed the religion of the Messiah, son
of Mary; from this people came Galen and Aristotle."

Here is what El Hamadani says, in the book Of the Genealogies: Kahlan ben Sebas engendered Zeïd; Zeïd
engendered 'Ariba, Malek, Rhalba, and 'Amikareb. (According to El Heïtham, 'Amikareb ben Seba is the brother
of Himyar and of Kahlan) and 'Amikareb engendered Abou Melek Fadrah and Mahilil who are the two sons of
'Amikareb; Rhaleb engendered Genadah ben Rhaleb who reigned after Mahalil ben Amikareb ben Seba; 'Arib
engendered 'Amr; 'Amr engendered Zeïd and El Hamisa surnamed Abou-l Sa'b who is the same as Dhu'l Qorneïn the
Ancient, the traveler and the constructor, on the subject of whom El Na'man ben Bechir said:

[verses:] To whoever before us would boast of belonging to a tribe of generous men, we would answer: Dhu'l
Qorneïn and Hatem are of ours.

El Haretz speaks of him when he says:

[verses:] Name us someone of you, that we may know if he bore the title of king in the time of ignorance,
like the two Tobba' and Dhu'l Qorneïn; for these, that is admitted by the people of a good mind. And it is
what is most true that must be accepted.

[PDF p. 472]

It is also to him that allude these verses of Ibn Abou Dib El Khoza'i:

[verses:] It is from us that came the one who traveled in the two parts of the world and traversed all the
countries above and below; he touched the horn of the sun at the Orient and at the Occident, and, on the
ruins of Yagog, he edified and established a government; that one, it is Dhu'l Qorneïn; Himyar boasts that one
of its kings had an army impossible to contain and to count.

According to El Hamadani, the scholars of Hamadan name Dhu'l Qorneïn El Sa'b ben Malek ben El Harem el a'ia
ben Rabi'ah ben El Gobar ben Malek, and, on the subject of Dhu'l Qorneïn, there are numerous legends. The
Imam Fakhr el Dîn El Razi, in his commentary on the generous Koran, among other traits he lets fly against
those who claim that Alexander is the same as Dhu'l Qorneïn, says: Alexander had had for master Aristotle and
conformed to his prescriptions and abstained from what he forbade him; Aristotle was renowned for his
hardness. As for Dhu'l Qorneïn, he is a prophet. How has one been able to confuse a prophet with a pagan of
this species?

El Gahez, in the book Of the Animals, says that the mother of Dhu'l Qorneïn was a mortal and that his father
was an angel, and it is for this reason that Omar ben El Khattab, hearing a man hail another man saying: "O
Dhu'l Qorneïn!" cried: "Do the names of prophets fail you, that you invoke the angels?" El Moukhtar Ibn Abou
'Obeïd recounts that 'Aly, when he spoke of Dhu'l Qorneïn, always called him "that hairless angel." And God
is the most learned.

[PDF p. 473]

CHAPTER VIII
OF THE KINGS WHO REIGNED AT ALEXANDRIA AFTER ALEXANDER

It is said, in the book of Orosius, that Alexander reigned over the world for twelve years, and, during all
his reign, the world was in his power. At his death, he left it to his generals who marched under his orders,
acting with them like a lion that throws to its cubs the product of its hunt, on which, after the father, the
cubs rush; thus the generals of Alexander divided among themselves the regions; Egypt, all of Africa, and the
Occident fell to the general commanding his cavalry and who reigned in his place, Ptolemy, son of Laoui, or
otherwise, Ptolemy, son of the speaking hare. Orosius speaks also of the rest of the countries divided among
the other generals, from the extremity of the countries of India to the extreme point of the Occident. Then,
he added, there arose between them wars caused by a letter emanating from Alexander, ordering that all the
strangers be sent back to their countries and that they be freed from slavery and servitude. The king of
Roum was very affected by it, for he feared that the strangers and the exiles, once returned to their country
or to their fatherland, would seek to avenge themselves. And this is why they ceased to obey the king of
Macedonia.

According to another author, this Ptolemy ravaged the country of the Benou Mo'add after having seized
Palestine; later, he gave them back their liberty and made them present of vases ornamented with precious
stones that were placed in the Temple of Jerusalem. This prince reigned twenty years, or according to others,
forty years, or even thirty-eight years. One had surnamed him Philadelphus, which means who loves his father
(sic); he was Macedonian, and it is he who subjugated the Jews and led away a great number of them to Egypt.
In his time lived the philosopher Zeno, and he himself was a philosopher. Perdiccas, one of the generals of
Alexander, having advanced against Egypt with a numerous army and considerable forces, dividing thus in two
parts the Empire of Macedonia, Ptolemy marched to meet him, put him to rout, pillaged his camp, killed him,
and seized all he possessed; this Ptolemy made war also on a great number of the generals of Alexander.
Another historian says that this Ptolemy was a wise, prudent, fine, and adroit man; he was the first who,
having made [...]

[PDF p. 474]

[OF THE KINGS WHO REIGNED AT ALEXANDRIA AFTER ALEXANDER, continued]

taken falcons, tamed and trained them. Before, the kings were ignorant of this diversion.

After him, reigned at Alexandria Ptolemy II, surnamed Philodhofos, who was also called "who loves his
brother"; he reigned 38 years. It is he who gave back liberty to the Jews captive in Egypt and who restored
the sacred vases to the prophet 'Azir (Ezra); he chose also among the Jewish scholars the seventy
interpreters charged with translating the Books of the Law and the Prophets, from Hebrew into Greek and into
Latin. He was a philosopher and astronomer.

After him, reigned his son Ptolemy Aurakhitis, surnamed "who loves his father"; he reigned 20 years.

After him, reigned his brother Ptolemy Philopator; his reign lasted 7 years. It is he who had massacred
nearly sixty thousand Jews and who made his yoke heavy upon them. It is said that he was very versed in
astronomy, and that one owes him the book of the Almagest.

After him, reigned his son Ptolemy Asfamish "who loves his mother"; the duration of his reign was 24 years.

After him, reigned his son Ptolemy Philonatrah -- that is, "the artisan"; during his reign, which lasted 35
years, he vanquished the king of Syria and inflicted on the Jews a thousand miseries and a thousand
torments.

After him, reigned at Alexandria his son Ptolemy Abriatish the Alexandrian; he reigned 29 years; in his time,
the Romans seized Spain and burned the town of Carthage; the fire lasted there seventeen days; the town was
entirely destroyed and its foundations so overturned that the marble of its walls was reduced to dust; there
were about 900 years that Carthage had been founded. All the inhabitants were sold as slaves, even the most
noble and the best; the destruction of the town had been ordered by the general of Rome.

After him, reigned his son Ptolemy Soter surnamed "the Iron"; his reign lasted 17 years. He was of abominable
morals; he married his sister, then repudiated her in a fashion still more detestable than that in which he
had married her. There are legends on this. He married next his step-daughter who was daughter of his sister,
then he gave her in marriage to the son he had had from his sister. His conduct was so horrible that the
Alexandrians chased him out, and he died in exile.

[PDF p. 475]

Then reigned his brother Ptolemy Alexander "the Prudent." His reign was of 10 years.

After him, reigned his son Ptolemy Dionysos. During his reign, which was of 38 years, the general of the
Romans seized Jerusalem and obliged the Jews to pay the tax of the capitation. In his time also, manifested
themselves frightful signs: there appeared in the sky, to the southeast of the town of Rome, a fire with
gigantic flames; another time a man who was making bread, having broken one, there flowed from it blood in
torrents; for three consecutive days, there fell on the town of Rome a hail mixed with stones and shards;
the earth opened up, and there formed in it enormous crevasses from which came out flames so long that they
reached, one believed, the sky; and the Romans of then saw a column that rose from the earth to the sky; it
was of the color of gold and so colossal that the sun was almost veiled by it.

After him, Cleopatra reigned two years at Alexandria. The supremacy of Alexandria -- that is, of the
Macedonian dynasty -- had therefore lasted until the first Caesar, who is also the first Roman emperor, 281
years. Caesar sent two generals, with numerous armies, to conquer Egypt, and one of them married Cleopatra,
daughter of Ptolemy Dionysos, killed his colleague, and revolted against Caesar. The latter marched against
the rebel, and, after a battle, seized Alexandria, had himself proclaimed king of Egypt, killed Cleopatra
and her two children, as well as the general who had married the queen. It is said, on the contrary, that
Cleopatra poisoned herself at the moment when she was going to fall into the power of Caesar. According to
what is reported, this queen was endowed with resolution, science, and judgment; it is she also who dug the
canal of Alexandria to bring there the water of Egypt, and who raised in this town marvelous monuments, such
as the temple of Saturn where she erected a statue of black bronze. The Alexandrians and the Egyptians
consecrated to her as a feast the 22nd day of Hathor; the Greeks came there in pilgrimage from all sides, and
one sacrificed to her innumerable victims. When the Christian religion made its appearance at Alexandria, the
temple of Saturn was converted into a church and remained thus until the moment when it was destroyed by the
army of Mo'ezz li din Allah, at the time of his arrival from the Maghreb in Egypt in 358 [25 November 968 to
13 November 969] of the hijra of the prophet.

[PDF p. 476]

It is said that it is Cleopatra who raised in Egypt the wall of the Old Woman; but that does not seem exact.
To her is attributed also the construction of a meqias (Nilometer) in the town of Akhmim and of another at
Antinoë. It is claimed still that she reigned 30 years, but that neither is true. The death of Cleopatra put
an end to the kingdom of Egypt; this country passed under the domination of the kings of Roum who inhabit the
town of Rome, then under that of the emperors of Roum who reside at Constantinople and who continued to send
there governors of their choice, whose seat was at Alexandria, until the moment of the invasion of 'Amr ben
El 'As and the Muslims to whom God delivered the citadel, Alexandria, and all of Egypt. The name of Cleopatra
signifies, it is said, "the Weeper."

From the fall of the dynasty of the Ptolemies to the conquest of Egypt by 'Amr ben El 'As, there have elapsed
670 and some years. In this interval, the kings of Persia carried off several victories over the Caesars from
whom they took Syria; they even had themselves proclaimed kings of Egypt and Alexandria, in the time of
Cosrou Abrawiz (Khosrow Parviz), son of Hormuz, who sent into Egypt a general, who seized Alexandria, killed
the Greeks who were there, and maintained himself there for ten years. Heraclius having become emperor of
Roum, gathered all the forces of his empire and set out from Constantinople; master of Hama and of Damascus,
he went to Jerusalem which the Persians had destroyed, and gave the order to rebuild the town; then,
penetrating into Egypt, he arrived at Alexandria, massacred the Persians who were there, and installed a
patrician (patrice). After which, he returned to Constantinople, and from then on, Egypt remained under the
domination of Roum until the Muslim conquest. All the constructions of brick that one meets in Egypt are, it
is said, Persian, while all the constructions of stone are Greek. And God is the most learned.

[PDF p. 477]

CHAPTER IX
OF THE PHAROS (LIGHTHOUSE) OF ALEXANDRIA

As for the Pharos of Alexandria, says El Masa'oudi, most of those of the Egyptians and the Alexandrians who
occupy themselves with the history of their country claim that it was constructed by Alexander, son of
Philip, the Macedonian; according to others, it would be the queen Dalukah who would have raised it to watch
the enemies who might have threatened Egypt. There are however those who suppose it the work of the sixth
pharaoh of Egypt; others finally admit that the founder of Rome was also the founder of Alexandria and the
constructor of the Pharos and the Pyramids of Egypt. I incline, for my part, to attribute Alexandria to
Alexander, for he is universally celebrated by his conquests of almost all the regions of the earth and,
thanks to him, the town of Alexandria has become famous. Yet, all the writers of whom we speak have recounted
on Alexandria numerous histories to demonstrate the veracity of their sayings. But no enemy threatened
Alexander on the side of the sea, and he dreaded no king who could come to attack him in his own country nor
beat him in his Empire. It is he however who established this Pharos as a watchtower. Whoever it was who
constructed it placed it on a pedestal of glass to which he gave the form of a crab; it was situated in the
open sea, at the extremity of the cape that advances into the waters. At the summit were placed statues of
copper and other materials, among others a statue that showed with the index of the right hand the sun, at
whatever place of the sky it was; if the sun rose in the firmament, the finger of the statue stretched on its
side, and, if it lowered toward the horizon, the hand of the statue lowered equally, following it in its
course. Another statue kept the hand stretched toward the sea; if some enemy advanced from this side, even
during the night, if he threatened the town or disembarked and approached close enough to see with his own
eyes, this statue uttered a piercing cry that was heard at two or three miles; and thus the inhabitants of
the town knew that the enemy threatened them and could see him themselves; a third statue uttered, each time
an hour of the day or the night had just elapsed, a cry different from the one it had uttered at the end of
the preceding hour, and this cry was agreeable to hear.

[PDF p. 478]

[OF THE PHAROS OF ALEXANDRIA, continued]

space, which has only accentuated itself since. It is reported that in the month of Ramadan of the year 344
[19 December 955 to 17 January 956] the summit of the Pharos was decapitated over a height of nearly 30
cubits by the earthquake that made itself felt at the same time in Egypt, in several localities of Syria, and
in the Maghreb; this is at least what tradition reports to us. While we were at Fostat Masr, there took place
an earthquake enormous, terrible, frightful, which lasted nearly half an hour: this happened toward the hour
of noon, the Saturday 18th of this month, corresponding to the 5th of Kanoun II and the 9th of Toba. On the
Thursday of the lentils, one gathered at the Pharos. Everyone left his house that day and went to the Pharos,
carrying his meal which comprised an inevitable dish of lentils. The doors of the Pharos were open; everyone
penetrated there, some to invoke God, some to pray, some to divert themselves. One remained there until noon,
then withdrew; and, from that day on, one watched the sea attentively to watch for the possible unexpected
arrival of enemies.

It is said that formerly the Pharos was very far from the sea, but that in the time of Constantine, son of
Constantine, the sea drew near and submerged a number of points and a quantity of churches of the town of
Alexandria; from then on, the marine invasion continues and the sea covers one parcel after another.

An author claims to have measured the Pharos and affirms that its height was 233 cubits, comprising three
distinct courses: the first course, of square form, measured 121 cubits 1/2; the second course, of octagonal
form, measured 81 cubits 1/2, and the third, of circular form, measured 31 cubits 1/2.

In his Relation of Travel, Ibn Gabir (Ibn Jubayr) says that the Pharos of Alexandria is seen from a distance
of more than 70 miles; he asserts having measured one of its four sides in 578 [7 May 1182 to 25 April 1183]
and declares that it was nearly 50 cubits (or fathoms). The height of the Pharos was more than 150 heights of
men, and at its summit was an oratory where the people prayed to obtain the celestial benediction.

According to Ibn Abd el Hakem, it has been claimed that she who constructed this Pharos [...]

[PDF p. 479]

[OF THE PHAROS OF ALEXANDRIA, continued]

of Alexandria is covered by the sea, and one draws from it fragments of all sorts of precious stones from
which one makes the bezels of rings. It is claimed that these fragments come from the drinking-vessels that
Alexander had made for himself and that, after his death, were broken by his mother and thrown by her in this
place. Others assert that Alexander himself had gathered all these stones and thrown them into the sea around
the Pharos by the bushel to protect the approaches of the Pharos against (the rapacity of) the people, for it
is the property of precious stones to be sought after. It is said that this Pharos had been provided with a
mirror at its summit only because the kings of the country of Roum were, after the death of Alexander, to
make war on the kings of Egypt and Alexandria, and that, for this reason, the king who reigned at Alexandria
installed this mirror which permitted him to see any enemy coming from the side of the sea; one could thus go
to meet whoever wished to enter the town, unless he was recognized as one of the inhabitants, which one could
not know at first, because of the multitude of houses, places, and streets that constituted the town. When
the Maghrebis, in the time of the Caliphate of Moqtader, came with the army of the master of the Occident (El
Mo'ezz li din Allah), they all went on horseback toward the Pharos, lost their way in the town, and fell into
a path leading to a well that descended toward the glass crab. There were there fissures communicating with
the sea; the horses fell into them, a great number disappeared, and one heard no more of them. They had
fallen, it is recounted, on a pedestal where their chests were broken. In the Pharos was then an oratory
where garrisoned volunteers, Egyptian and other. In 777 [2 June 1375 to 20 May 1376] the summit of the Pharos
was overturned by an earthquake. The Pharos was, it is said, constructed of juxtaposed stones held together
by means of lead, the whole seated on a vault of glass placed on the back of the crab. This Pharos counted
three hundred superposed chambers, and the beasts of burden went up with their loads to all the lodgings of
the interior of the Pharos; each of these lodgings had a window giving on the sea. On the eastern side of the
Pharos was an inscription that has been translated into Arabic, here it is: "She who constructed this
belvedere is Qaribah, daughter of Marinous the Greek, to observe the stars."

Ibn Ouacif Shah, after having recalled the history of Misraïm ben Beïsar

[PDF p. 480]

ben Ham ben Nouh, adds: They built on the sea towns, among others Raqoudah, site of the future Alexandria,
and they placed in the middle a cupola placed on pillars of gilded copper; the cupola was equally gilded.
Above the cupola one raised a tower surmounted by a mirror formed of diverse substances and whose diameter
was five spans. The height of the cupola was a hundred cubits. If anyone of the peoples of the surroundings
wished to attack them and destroy them, or advanced from the side of the sea, one directed on the arrivals
the rays of this mirror and burned them. The mirror conserved this virtue until it was overturned and
destroyed by the sea. Alexander, it is said, only reconstructed a Pharos similar to the first, on which he
placed equally a mirror, where one saw the enemies coming from the country of Roum. But a certain king of
Roum managed, by ruse, to make cease the protective virtue of this mirror which was made of glass prepared
with art.

El Masa'oudi, in his book Of the Warning and the Illustrious Men, recounts that, when the vizier of El
Moutawaqqel, Obeïd Allah ben Yahia ben Khaqan, was exiled by Mousta'ïn to Barkat in the year 248 [7 March
862 to 23 February 863], he went to Alexandria where he saw the summit of the Pharos lit by the rays of the
sun while the sun was already set, and remained persuaded that he should not break the fast as long as the
sun was not set for all the regions of the earth. He had one of his people go up to the summit of the Pharos,
carrying with him a stone, and the order was given him to look attentively at the place where the sun set and
to throw the stone at the moment when the star would disappear. The man executed the order, and the stone
reached the ground while the last prayer of the evening was finished. The vizier therefore fixed the moment
of the breaking of his fast after the last prayer of the evening. And subsequently, when he had to fast, he
acted as he had done at Alexandria; and returned to his fatherland, the memory of what he had seen came back
to his mind, and he fasted until after the last prayer of the evening; he had made of it a law for himself,
and the two times were equivalent. This shows to what point the science of the laws was little advanced and
how little one was fixed on the march of the sun from Orient to Occident. Aristotle, in his Metaphysics,
reports that, on the side of the summer Orient, is a very high mountain and cites among other particularities
concerning it the fact that, for it, the sun sets only at three hours of the night and rises three hours
before the day.

[PDF p. 481]

The Pharos of Alexandria is one of those learned and marvelous constructions that the Greek dynasty of the
Ptolemies raised after the death of the king Alexander, son of Philip, when it found itself, on land and on
sea, at war with the kings of Rome. These kings constructed the Pharos, placing at its summit an enormous
mirror, made of all sorts of chosen stones, to watch the ships of the sea that might have approached the
shore, forestalling thus their disembarkation. They saw all that in the mirror, and the alert was given to
the inhabitants before the arrival of the enemies. The height of the Pharos is currently about 230 cubits,
but formerly it reached nearly 400 cubits; the height has sensibly diminished, time, the earthquakes, and the
rains having in part crumbled it; for it rains abundantly at Alexandria; it is not like at Fostat where,
because of the more considerable altitude, it rains only rarely. The construction of the Pharos was made
following three different types: nearly the half, or at least more than the third, is of square form and in
white stones; this construction occupies nearly 110 cubits; to this square part succeeds an octagonal part
constructed in stone and in gypsum over a height of 60 and some cubits, all around are inhabited lodgings;
finally, the summit is of circular form.

Ahmed ben Touloun repaired it in part and had placed at the summit a cupola to which one was to mount by the
interior of the Pharos; but the interior of it was smooth, constructed with art and without steps. On the
north face was a Greek inscription in characters of lead incrusted in the stone; each letter was a cubit high
and a span wide. The surface occupied by the monument was about 100 cubits, but the waters of the sea, having
undermined the foundations, made the angle that faces the sea to the west collapse. Abou-l Geïch
Khamaraouyah ben Ahmed ben Touloun repaired it. Today, between the Pharos and the town of Alexandria, there
is a distance of about a mile; the Pharos is constructed at the extremity of the tongue of land of which the
sea bathes the two sides, at the entry of the present port of Alexandria and not in the old port; the latter,
indeed, is found in the antique town, and the ships no longer enter it, for it is too far from the inhabited
quarters. The port (mina) is the place where the ships of the sea come to land.

The Alexandrians recount, on the authority of their ancestors, that between the Pharos and the sea, there was
formerly about the same distance as today between the town and the Pharos, but that the water of the sea had
in little time invaded this

[PDF p. 482]

[Note: the following passage on El Oualid belongs earlier in the chapter sequence in the source layout.]

Under the reign of El Oualid ben 'Abd el Melek ben Merwan, a king of the country of Roum sent one of his
particular servants endowed with wisdom and ruse. The latter went full of confidence to a certain town of
the frontier and, provided with sumptuous presents and accompanied by an escort, he arrived at El Oualid and
recounted to him that he was one of the particular friends of the king, but that the latter had wished to
kill him in a moment of irritation; as the attempt of which he had been the object had no reason to be, he
was very affected by it and wished to make himself a Muslim. He converted therefore to Islam between the
hands of El Oualid and knew how to gain his affection by revealing to him the existence of buried treasures,
which he brought out of the earth for him at Damascus and in other towns of Syria, thanks to certain books he
possessed and in which was read the description of these treasures. Once master of these treasures and these
precious stones, El Oualid became avid and his desire only increased. His servant said to him one day: "O
Commander of the Faithful, over there are riches, precious stones, and the treasures buried by the kings." El
Oualid asked him for details. "Under the Pharos of Alexandria," answered the servant, "are the treasures of
the kings of the earth, for Alexander gathered the riches and the precious stones of Sheddad ben 'Ad and the
kings of Egypt, and for them he constructed an underground passage and a vault with cupolas, caves, and
corridors, and deposited there these treasures -- gold, silver, and precious stones; and over it, he built
this Pharos. The height of it is a thousand cubits, and a mirror surmounts it, around which are seated
criers; and as soon as these see some enemy, thanks to the gleam projected by this mirror, they warn by cries
those who are in their vicinity and raise signals that those who are more distant can see. Thus the
inhabitants are warned, the country puts itself on its guard, and the enemies find the road barred." El
Oualid therefore sent his servant with an army and people of confidence and of his intimates. The upper half
of the Pharos was demolished and the mirror ceased to be efficacious. The inhabitants, seeing this, revolted,
understanding that there was beneath it some artifice and some ruse. At this news, the servant, knowing well
that he had lied to El Oualid, and his stratagem having succeeded, fled during the night on a boat he had
prepared on purpose. The protective virtue of the Pharos was annihilated, and this monument has remained in
this state until the present -- that is, until the year 332 [4 September 943 to 23 August 944]. The base of
the Pharos

[PDF p. 483]

[she who constructed it] was the queen Cleopatra, the same who dug the canal that she succeeded, by her
ingenuity, in bringing as far as Alexandria. This canal started from the village of Kassa, facing El Karioun;
she dug it until its entry into the town and paved its ceiling.

Ahmed Ibn Touloun, when he was governor of Alexandria, built at the summit of the Pharos a cupola of wood
that was later carried off by the winds. In the time of Zaher Beïbars, one of the angles of the construction
buckled and fell; Beibars had reestablished what had been destroyed, in 673 [7 July 1274 to 26 June 1275],
and he reinstalled at the same time the emplacement of the cupola as a mosque; this mosque was destroyed in
its turn at the time of the earthquake of 702 [26 August 1302 to 14 August 1303]; during the course of the
year 703 [15 August 1303 to 13 August 1304] he had it rebuilt under the direction of the emir Rokn el din
Beïbars El Gachenkir; from then on, it has remained until our time, and El Deraoui was very well inspired
when he said, regarding the Pharos of Alexandria:

[verses:] An elevated terrace guides the one who walks at night, by its light when the nocturnal shadows
fall. I have worn there a mantle of unmixed pleasure among my friends, and this mantle was ornamented with
the memory of my companions. From its heights, a cupola gave me its shade, and from there I saw my friends
like stars. It seemed to me there that below me the sea was like a cloud and that I had raised my tent in the
middle of the sky.

Ibn Qolaqes made the following verses:

[verses:] The house surpasses, in height, the Gemini, which seem thus to have at their summit a nest of
eagles. Its foundations are anchored in the soil, the body of the building rises: in its hand is the
communication between the whales and the light. There I gave free rein to my poetry; and it made its horses
run in a hippodrome of beautiful poetry.

The vizier Abou 'Abd Allah Mohammed ben El Hassan ben 'Abd Rabbah said:

[verses:] To God the pearl of the Pharos of Alexandria; how many pupils of eyes rise toward it? It has the
nose very high, and the bone of the nose rises as if it were in ecstasy before the horizon that surrounds
it.

[PDF p. 484]

[verses, continued:] For the swift vessels, its sight is like the sleep that falls on eyelids accustomed to
insomnia.

According to 'Omar ben Abou 'Omar El Kandi, in his Marvels of Egypt, the scholars report that the Pharos
remained in the middle of Alexandria until the sea submerged its surroundings, and thus it found itself in
the middle of the waters. Do you not see with evidence that the construction and the foundations of it are
still at present in the sea?

According to Abd Allah ben 'Amr, there were in the world four marvels: the mirror suspended at the summit of
the Pharos of Alexandria; people seated at the foot of this mirror saw there those who came from
Constantinople, from whom they were however separated by all the width of the sea. Then he speaks of the
three other marvels.

[PDF p. 485]

CHAPTER X
OF THE CIRCUS THAT WAS AT ALEXANDRIA AND OF SOME OTHER MARVELS

Among the marvelous things of Egypt, says Qoda'i, there is Alexandria and the marvels it encloses, among the
number of which are: the Pharos, the Column, and the Circus where one gathered on a determined day of the
year; there, one threw a ball, and the one in whose lap it fell back was infallibly to reign over Egypt. At
one of these feasts attended 'Amr ben El 'As who received the ball in his lap, and later, in the time of
Islam, he governed Egypt. This Circus could contain a million spectators who all saw perfectly the one who
faced them. When one made some reading there, everyone heard it, and if one gave some spectacle, each saw it
distinctly to the last one, without being in any way hindered by the multitude of tiers that rose before or
behind him.

In the year 18 of the hijra [12 January 639 to 1 January 640], says Ibn Abd El Hakem, 'Omar ben El Khattab
was marching against Damascus, when 'Amr ben El 'As secretly approached him and asked him for the
authorization to go attack Egypt. 'Amr had already come to this country in the time of the ignorance and knew
its roads; he had also seen there a great number of the things it enclosed. Here is on what occasion he had
come to Egypt: Going to Jerusalem with people of Qoreich to traffic there, they met a Greek priest of
Alexandria who came to pray at Jerusalem. This priest had gone to promenade on one of the neighboring
mountains where 'Amr was pasturing his camels and those of his companions, for the guard of the camels fell
to each of them in turn; 'Amr was therefore keeping his flock when the priest passed near him, overwhelmed by
an ardent thirst, for the heat was excessive. He stopped near 'Amr and asked him for drink. 'Amr gave him
water from his skin, and the priest, having quenched his thirst, fell asleep there. Near the sleeper was a
hole from which came out an enormous viper; 'Amr, having perceived it, launched at it an arrow and killed it.
On his waking, the priest, seeing the enormous reptile against which God had protected him, asked 'Amr what
it was. 'Amr informed him that he had killed the

[PDF p. 486]

viper with an arrow-shot. The priest then, approaching 'Amr, kissed him on the head and said to him: "God, by
your intermediary, has saved my life twice; first in appeasing my ardent thirst, then in protecting me
against this serpent. What have you come to seek in this country?" "I have come here," answered 'Amr, "with
my companions to seek the benefits that commerce gives." "And how much can this commerce bring you?" said the
priest. "I hope," resumed 'Amr, "to be able to gain enough to buy myself a camel; I possess only two, the one
I hope to gain will make the third." "Tell me what is, among you, the price of blood." "A hundred camels."
"But if one has no camels, and one possesses only dinars!" "In that case," said 'Amr, "it is a thousand
dinars." "I am a stranger in this country," said the priest, "and have come only to pray in the temple of
Jerusalem and visit this mountain; I will stay here only a month, it is a vow I have made and imposed on
myself. After that, I will return to my country. Will you come with me? There, I attest God of it and take
him as witness, I will pay you twice the price of blood, for God has saved me twice by your intermediary."
"Where is your country?" asked 'Amr. "I inhabit Egypt," said the priest, "in the town that is called
Alexandria." "I do not know it," said 'Amr, "and have never gone there." "When you will have come there,"
said the priest, "you will recognize that you have never seen a town like it." "And will you pay me what you
say?" asked 'Amr; "do you take toward me the engagement and the responsibility of it?" "Thanks to you," said
the priest; "God is my witness and I hold him guarantor that I will pay it to you and bring you back to your
companions." "And how long will my absence last?" "A month," said the priest; "ten days to go, ten days to
stay at Alexandria, and ten days to return. I promise to protect you during the going and to give you an
escort for the return." "Wait then," said 'Amr, "that I consult my companions on it." And having gone to
them, he made known to them the proposition of the priest and said to them: "Wait for my return and I
promise to give you the half of the sum, on condition that one of you accompany me." "It is agreed," they
said, and one of them was sent with him. 'Amr and his companion set out with the priest and arrived in
Egypt; 'Amr, seeing the prosperity of the country, its numerous population, its riches, and its treasures,
was marveled and said to the priest: "I have never seen a country like it." They continued their route until
Alexandria; 'Amr could admire the numerous riches that were there, the luxury of the

[PDF p. 487]

constructions and the considerable number of the inhabitants, and his astonishment was immense. The arrival
of 'Amr at Alexandria coincided with the celebration of a feast in which was assembled a crowd of kings and
princes of the country; the kings threw in the air a ball of gold enriched with precious stones and before
which they ran, lap deployed, for, according to what is recounted on the subject of this ball and of what had
already happened regarding it, if it falls in the lap of someone, that one does not die without having
reigned over the country.

'Amr having arrived at Alexandria, the priest treated him magnificently, made him present of a robe of
brocade, clad him in it, and both took their place in the middle of the assembly where one threw the ball
and where each precipitated himself to receive it in his lap. Now, the ball having been launched, stopped
only in the lap of 'Amr. All were astonished and said: "This ball has never lied to us but this time! Do you
see this Arab reigning over us! That will never happen." And the priest, mingling with the Alexandrians,
informed them that 'Amr had saved his life twice and that he had to pay him two thousand dinars, asking them
to gather this sum for him. Which they did; and 'Amr, having received his two thousand dinars, set out with
his companion. The priest furnished them a guide and a courier, and showed himself full of generosity and
benevolence for them. They arrived finally near their companions. And it is thus that 'Amr learned the road
to Egypt, that he knew its revenues, and according to what he saw there, he retained that it was the country
richest in marvels and in resources. Returned to his companions, 'Amr paid them a thousand dinars and kept
the other thousand for himself and, as he repeated himself, it was the first treasure that fell to him and
that had been gathered for him.

[PDF p. 488]

CHAPTER XI
OF THE COLUMN OF THE MASTS

This column is a block of spotted red granite. Around it were ranged nearly 400 other columns that were
broken by Qoraga, vali of Alexandria, in the time of the sultan Salah el din Yousef ben Ayoub, and thrown on
the shore of the sea to hinder the march of the enemies who approached. This column is, it is said, one of
those that supported the porticoes where Aristotle taught philosophy -- a veritable temple of science where
was deposited the treasure of the books, burned later by 'Amr ben El 'As, on the orders of 'Omar ben El
Khattab. It was high, it is said, 70 cubits; its diameter is 5 cubits. An author affirms that its length
between the base and the capital was 62 cubits 1/6 and that the capital had 28 cubits 1/2, which makes in
total 85 cubits 2/3. The length of the base was 12 cubits and that of the capital 7 cubits 1/2.

One reads in El Masa'oudi: On the western bank of the Said of Egypt, there is an enormous mountain of marble
where the ancients cut columns and other objects that they transported after having detached them. As for
the columns, bases, and capitals that the Egyptians name Assouanites and from which one has made millstones,
the ancients cut them in the quarry, two hundred years before the origin of Christianity; of those form part
the columns of Alexandria and this column which is so colossal that no one knows of one similar. I have seen,
in the mountain of Assouan, the sister of these columns which had been worked and cut without detaching it
from the quarry and without one having carried it off. The ancients wished to show us by that how one did to
detach them from the mountain, and to lead them then to the point where one wished finally to raise them.

There were at Alexandria enormous columns, in all sorts of stones and marbles, of which thousands of men had
difficulty detaching the smallest fragment and which one raised between earth and sky; their height reached
more than a hundred cubits; the pedestals, which served them as support, had a perimeter varying from 15 to
20 cubits, and the capital measured [...]

[PDF p. 489]

[OF THE COLUMN OF THE MASTS, continued]

ten cubits of width by ten cubits of height and as much of thickness, and these columns were of surprising
colors.

There was also at Alexandria, on a hill raised facing the gate of the town, a colossal palace measuring 500
cubits of length by half as much of width; the gate of it was of a marvelous art, each jamb being made of a
single piece, as well as the lintel. This palace enclosed nearly a hundred pillars, and, facing the palace,
rose a gigantic pillar such as never has one heard speak of a similar pillar. It was wide 36 spans and its
height was so great that in launching a stone one could not reach the summit of it; this pillar was crowned
with a capital of admirable work and that must have been surmounted by some object; its foot reposed on a
socle of red stone, of beautiful execution, and of which each side measured 20 spans of length by a height
of 8 spans. The rod fixed in the column was of iron and penetrated into the soil. I have seen, in great
winds, the column move, while the base remained immobile and crumbled as a consequence of the violence of
the movement of the column. This monument was considered as one of the marvels of the world, and a number of
people have imagined that it was the work of the genies who would have executed it for Solomon, son of David;
for one attributes habitually to the genies every surprising work. But this idea is false, the column in
question being the work of the ancient Egyptians. In the middle of this palace was a dome surrounded by
pillars, on the ensemble of which reposed another dome, made of a single block of white marble, as beautiful
as all you have been able to see of most beautiful in this kind of work.

It is recounted that a king of Egypt, having come to Alexandria, was marveled in seeing this palace and
wished to construct one similar; he gathered workers and engineers to raise him a magnificent palace on the
model of the first. All declared themselves powerless to execute it, except an old man who was among them and
who engaged himself to construct a similar palace. The king, all joyous, authorized him to ask for what would
be necessary to him in victuals, tools, and workers. "Let there be brought to me," said the old man, "two
vigorous bulls and a great chariot." They were brought to him on the spot, and, having gone to the old
cemetery, the old man dug there a pit, brought to light an enormous skull that was hoisted onto the chariot,
thanks to the arms of a great number of men, and the two bulls, despite all their vigor, succeeded in
dragging it only with much pains and efforts. Arrived with the skull in

[PDF p. 490]

the presence of the king, the old man said to him: "O my lord, if God permits that one furnish me men whose
head be similar to that which possessed this skull, I will make you a palace similar to the palace you have
seen." The king understood that the people of his time were incapable of raising a like palace.

It is recounted that there was at Alexandria, at the home of a butcher who used it to weigh meat, a tooth of
a man weighing 8 ratls.

The Column of the Masts (?) which is today at Alexandria outside the town, is one of the seven columns that
(were brought from the Said); this one was brought by El Batoun ben Marrât El 'Adi, who carried it under his
armpit from the red mountain of Ibrim, south of Assouan, to Alexandria. The side of it was broken because El
Batoun was one of the least strong of the men of his tribe; this was painful to Ya'mer ben Sheddad ben 'Ad:
"To whoever brings me one (intact)," he said, "I will give the half of my kingdom." El Gahed ben Senan El
Thamoudi came with another column; he was very strong and brought it under his arm from Assouan. And the
other men of the tribe came likewise, each bearing a column. El Garoud ben Qotn El Moutafeki raised these
seven columns, and the erection was finished only after one had chosen a propitious rising of the planets,
as was the custom for almost all one executed. A writer asserts that in the ancient times, the stone was soft
and that one made then the columns of Na'et, of Mâreb, of Binoun, of Mater, of the Yemen, those of Damascus,
of Egypt, of Madian, of Tadmor (Palmyra). In that time everything was endowed with speech. Ommayah ben
Abou-l Sait said:

[verses:] And they had no garments and they were naked, and for them the solid rock was soft.

The Column of the Masts, it is said, formed part of the ensemble of the columns that supported the portico
named House of the Science, and this at the epoch when the scholars of the Occident divided themselves into
five categories: (1) the disciples of this portico; (2) the disciples of the pillar, who were at Balbek; (3)
the disciples of the shade, at Antioch; (4) the disciples of the temples, in the Said of Egypt, and (5) the
seekers, in Macedonia. It seems to me that some ignorant person will blame me for having written this
chapter, treating its content

[PDF p. 490, continued]

of absurdities and fables invented at pleasure and taxing the author with lying; but let my account not
surprise you and listen to what God says on the subject of 'Ad, tribe of Houd:

[PDF p. 491]

"Remember that he has established you successors of the people of Noah and that he has enlarged your stature"
(Koran, VII, 67) -- that is, that he has rendered you greater and has increased your body. 'Abd Allah ben
'Abbas says that the greatest of the Adites had 100 cubits and the smallest 60; the increase in question
relates to the stature of their fathers, or, according to others, to the stature of the people of Noah.
