Ouaheb ben Monabbah says: "The head of one of these men was similar to an enormous cupola; in one of their
eyes the lionesses could give birth; likewise in their nose." Shahr ben Houtheb reports that Abou Harirat had
said: "Certainly, the people of the people of 'Ad would carry the two leaves (of a door) that 500 men of this
country would not manage to shake." An Adite, in striking the soil with the foot, entered into it. 'Abd Allah
ben Lahi'at reports, on the authority of Yezid ben 'Amr El Mo'aferi, that Ibn Bagrat had said: "Seventy men
of the people of Moses could put themselves in the shade under the skull of an Amalecite." "One recounted to
me," says Zeïd ben Aslam, "that a hyena and her young lived in the cavity of the eye of a man of Amalec." And
God says: "Do you not see what your Lord did with the people of 'Ad, who inhabited Iram Zat El 'Amad, town
whose like did not exist in any country?" (Koran, LXXXIX, 5, 6.) El Moubarrad says: El Khansa, by [the word],
means the height of the columns. When one says [the expression], that signifies: a man long (like a column).
The expression Iram Zat el 'Amad, employed by God, applies to the length of the columns. El Baghaoui says
that one named this town Zat El 'Amad because it belonged to a nomad tribe of the people of 'Amad; it is what
Qotadah, Mogahed, El Kelbi say, and it is the opinion of 'Ata according to Ibn Abbas. Another claimed that it
owed this name to the size of its inhabitants who, as Ibn Abbas says, were tall like columns.

Each of them, says Moqâtel, was high 12 cubits, and in the Kochaf of El Zamakhshari it is said that the
stature of the Adites has never been equaled in any country; they were of a size and a force surprising; the
size of a man reached there 400 cubits; however great a stone was, an Adite could lift it and throw it on the
serpents to kill them. Another reports that, under the caliphate of Moqtader Billah Abou-l Fadl Ga'far ben Al
Mo'tadad, one discovered in Egypt a hiding place enclosing a human rib 14 spans long and 3 wide.

The eyes of the sons of Adam are small and their soul develops itself in a

[PDF p. 492]

narrow space; thus when one comes to speak to them of things out of the reach of their intelligence or that
surpass their corporeal greatness, of those things for which they have not at their reach identical objects
that can serve them as a term of comparison, unless they have seen or fabricated themselves these objects,
quickly they hasten to set aside these things and doubt what one reports to them, unless they are endowed
with science and intelligence. In this last case, they seek to assure themselves of the truth of what one
sets forth to them and often pass the night to make themselves account of it or to set it forth in their turn
to others. But how to acquire the truth on such accounts? The truth is what the prophet of God said: "God
created Adam high 60 cubits; since, the human size has only decreased until this day." Mohammed ben 'Abd el
Rahim ben Soliman ben Rabi' El Qeisi El Gharanâti recounts what follows in the book Present of the Hearts:
"In the work entitled History of the Kings, El Sha'bi reports that El Dahak ben 'Alouan, at the moment when
Lam ben 'Amer fled from his court to reach the regions of the North, sent in pursuit of him two emirs, each
accompanied by a troop of fierce people. One of these emirs took the direction of Balghar, the other that of
Bashqerd, and their troops installed themselves in these two towns. El Aqlichi says having seen in Bashqerd
their images and their tombs. "I have seen among other things," he adds, "a tooth of one of them; it measured
4 spans of length by 2 spans of width. I have also had in my hands at Bashqerd the half of the root of
another tooth that one had extracted for me from the inferior jaw (of a skeleton); it was wide a span and
weighed 200 metsqals; I weighed it myself, and it is still today in my house at Bashqerd. The arm of one of
these skeletons was long 28 cubits, and each of its ribs, wide 3 spans and more, resembled a plaque of
marble. One exhumed for me the half of a wrist, which was so heavy that I could not move it with a single
hand and had to employ the two hands to lift it. I can assure having seen in the town of Balghar, in the year
530 [11 October 1135 to 28 September 1136], a descendant of the Adites, a man whose size surpassed 5 cubits;
one called him Danqa. This man put a horse under his arm as easily as an ordinary man would have done of a
child; and, if there arose some war in the country, he went to combat armed with an oak that he had uprooted

[PDF p. 493]

and that he carried in the hand like a stick; each time he struck an elephant with it, the animal fell dead.
He was good and humble, and every time he met me, he saluted me, invited me, and treated me generously. I
hardly reached to his belt. He had a sister as tall as he, whom I have seen many times. The cadi of Balghar,
Ya'qoub ben Na'man, recounted that this Adite woman had killed her husband, who was called Adam and was one
of the strongest men of Balghar. In pressing him against her chest, she broke his ribs, and he died on the
spot. There was in Balghar only one bath that had doors wide enough to permit them to enter."

The governor, Abou 'Abd Allah Mohammed ben Mohammed ben Ahmed El Fariabi, recounted to me that his father had
seen a tomb cleared at Carthage in Africa; one had discovered there the skeleton of a man of gigantic size;
his head was big like the heads of two powerful bulls; near him was a plaque of marble bearing an inscription
in musnad characters, which are the characters of the Adites; the letters were separated, and here is what
the inscription signified: "I, Koush ben Kana'an, son of the kings of the tribe of 'Ad, I reigned in this
country over a thousand towns; I lay with a thousand virgins and I had as mounts of race 7,000 coursers --
red, yellow, piebald, white, and black. But all that served me in nothing. A crier came toward me to utter
his cry and made me go out of the world. Let every intelligent man, who will come after me, meditate the
example I offer him and recite this:

[verses:] O you who standing contemplate the sky, on the ruins of a destroyed quarter, stop and listen; be
instructed by the example, if you are a man of mind. Yesterday we were above (the earth), today we are below.
Every thing has a goal; every thing has an end."

The sultan Abou Bekr ben Yahia El Hafasi, lord of Tunis, gave the order to close again this tomb, and the
tomb was filled in again. The author (Maqrizi) adds: I too have had knowledge of something analogous, here is
how: One day, in the year 790 [11 January to 30 December 1388], a troop of quarriers, who disputed a treasure
[...]

[PDF p. 494]

[OF THE COLUMN OF THE MASTS, continued]

found by them in the mountain of Moqattam, presented themselves before the sultan El Melek El Zaher Barqouq.
As they were occupied in cutting stones in a grotto that faces the north flank of the citadel of the
mountain, they had discovered a black stone bearing an inscription. They united their efforts to cut the
rock at the foot of this stone, hoping to discover a treasure. They came to an enormous column that rose in
the heart of the mountain and, in their haste, seizing their iron bars, struck the column and put it to
pieces. This column was hollow and contained the body of a man, raised vertically on his feet, and from
whose head escaped numerous dinars that fell on the heads of the quarriers. They set about dividing them
among themselves, but, far from being in agreement, they disputed so much that their affair became known and
they were brought before the sultan. The latter sent an emissary who found again the grotto and discovered
the stone and the column which was broken. One removed from the quarriers what they had of dinars; but one
could discover no one who could read what was engraved on the stone. The populace, having had wind of the
news, went toward the grotto where each played with the fragments of the skeleton. Someone who had seen one
of the teeth of the dead man recounted to me that it was black and of the size of an eggplant and that the
bone of the leg, between the foot and the knee, measured 5 cubits; the total size must in proportion have
reached the height of 20 cubits and even more; the root of a single one of his teeth being of the size of an
eggplant, the man must therefore have been as tall as the great cupola.

The illustrious master, the Cadi of the Cadis of Damascus, Shehab el din Ahmed ben Aly ben Ibrahim El
Hasseini, better known under the name of Ibn 'Adnân or of Ibn Abou-l Genn, recounted to me that in the year
814 [25 April 1411 to 12 April 1412], he had found in the cemetery, near the little gate of Damascus, a tomb
where the diggers who cleared it discovered a skeleton. The tomb was not adorned, and one had quickly found
the well where one had made the cadaver descend. From this well there came out a quantity of blue flies so
considerable that they almost stole from the diggers the rays of the sun. The diggers descended into this
well found a sarcophagus 22 cubits long and enclosing a body extended following the length of the vat and
fallen into dust. One of those who had seen this tomb recounted to me that there was there a

[PDF p. 495]

human tooth broken in three pieces, and that he had taken one of them. The tooth was big like a watermelon
and he had had it weighed before him; it weighed 2 ratls and 9 ounces, in ratls of Syria; the piece he had
broken from it weighed 2 ounces of Syria. According to this weight, the entire molar must have weighed nearly
12 ratls of Egypt, and God knows better.

[PDF p. 496]

CHAPTER XII
A GLANCE AT WHAT HAS BEEN SAID ON THE SUBJECT OF ALEXANDRIA

According to Abou 'Amr El Kandi, one is in agreement that there is in the world no other town than Alexandria
that can correspond to three series [of marvels]. When 'Abd El 'Aziz ben Merwan entered Alexandria, he
questioned a Greek scholar on its subject and on the number of its inhabitants: "By God," he answered, "O
emir, never was any king able to know the number of them; as for the Jews, on whom one was able to inform
you, they were 600,000 according to the enumeration executed by order of a Greek king. But what is this
figure beside the ruins one finds on all sides? It has been reported to me that a certain king of the Persian
dynasty who reigned in Egypt had imposed a dinar on each adult Alexandrian. The notables and the scholars of
the town came to find the king and said to him: O king, do not give yourself this trouble; for Alexander
took three hundred years to build the town, which remained flourishing for 300 other years, but which for 300
years has been ruined. Its inhabitants, for 70 years, could walk in the streets of the town only provided
with black veils to protect their eyes against the dazzling whiteness of the walls."

Among the divine citations that have been made of it, it is fitting to recall that a learned commentator
regards it as the town that God, in his sacred book, wished to designate when he says: "Iram Zat El 'Amad
which has not its like in the world" (Koran, LXXXIX, 6, 7). Ahmed ben Saleh reports that one day Sofian ben
'Eïïnah said to him: "O Egyptian, where do you live?" "At Fostat," he answered. "Have you been to
Alexandria?" "Yes." "It is," said Sofian, "the quiver where God has deposited the best of his arrows."

Abd Allah ben Marzouq El Sadfi says: "When one announced to me that my cousin Khaled ben Yezid had died at
Alexandria, I met one after the other Mousa ben 'Aly ben Rabah, 'Abd Allah ben Lahi'ah, and El Leith ben
Sa'd, who all said to me: 'Is he not dead at Alexandria?' 'Yes,' I answered. 'Then, he lives with God who
favors him and recompenses him for his sojourn on the earth, and he will have the recompense of the martyr,
(for) God will resurrect him for that.'" Those who occupy themselves with cosmography, with the description
of the countries, with the arrangement of the climates and the regions, affirm that in no

[PDF p. 497]

country of the world is the age of men as long as at Marbout, in the district of Alexandria, and at the Ouadi
Farghanah. According to El Hassan ben Safouan, Alexandria, Tennis, and the other similar countries enjoy,
thanks to the vicinity of the sea, a moderate temperature, without excessive heat or cold; the east wind,
which blows there more particularly, only renders them stronger and refines them, removing from them all
care and guarding them from the rudeness that the people of Yachmoun possess by nature and by temperament.
The characteristic of the Alexandrians is avarice. Gelal el din ben Mokram ben Abou-l Hassan ben Ahmed El
Khozragi, the master of those who know by heart, said:

[verses:] He who descends at Alexandria receives as a gift of hospitality only water or the description of
the column of El Souari. When one wishes to treat him well, one goes so far as to give him sweet air and the
indication of the Pharos; one paints for him also the sea and its waves, joining to it the description of the
great Greek boats. Let the guest (of the Alexandrian) not have the ambition of having bread, for there is
there for that letter no reader.

Ahmed ben Gordadiah says: From Fostat to Daouat el Sahel, there are 24 miles; from there to Marbout 30 miles,
then to Kom Sherik 30 miles, then to Karioun 24 miles, then to Alexandria 24 miles. Another said: The road to
Alexandria, in the season of low water, follows the towns and the villages; this road goes first from
Shatnouf to Sabak El Obeid, a station that encloses a pretty port; distance 12 saqs. From Sabak to Menouf, a
great town where are baths and markets and whose inhabitants count rich and notable people, there are 16
saqs. From Menouf to Mehallah Sard, where is a pulpit, a bath, hostelries, an important market, 16 saqs; from
Mehallah Sard to Sakha, a great town with numerous baths and markets, a very extensive province, a
considerable region, seat of a military administration with an important garrison, a country very productive
in flax, radish oil, and magnificent wheat, 16 saqs. From Sakha to Shoubra Kamiah, a great town enclosing a
mosque and markets, 16 saqs. From Shoubra Kamiah to Masir, a mosque and markets, 16 saqs; from Masir to
Senhour, a town of considerable extent with baths and markets, an important province, 16 saqs; from Senhour
to El Nakhoum, a province comprising baths, hostelries, markets, 16 saqs; from El Nakhoum to Nestarou, a town
formerly considerable and very beautiful, on the lake of Yachmoun,

[PDF p. 498]

20 saqs; from Nestarou to Bourlos, a town where reside the numerous fishermen of the lake and where are
baths, 10 saqs; from Bourlos to Khana, a fortress on the shore of the sea, 10 saqs; from Khana to Rosetta, a
town built on the Nile and where this river throws itself into the sea by the mouth known under the name of
mouth of Ashtoum, from the name of the village that is at the entry, 30 saqs; there were there important
markets and a bath; the palms abound there and one pays there a duty on the objects brought from Alexandria.

This road, from Shatnouf to Rosetta, unless it be cut by the high waters, is the best way to go to
Alexandria; no other equals it, and it leads to all the points of the earth. Among the stuffs woven at
Alexandria is that tissue of flax that one names El Sharb, of which each drahme is worth a dirhem of silver,
and also those sorts of embroideries that one sells for several times their weight in silver.

[PDF p. 499]

CHAPTER XIII
OF THE CONQUEST OF ALEXANDRIA

Abou 'Amr El Kandi reports that when the Muslims had made themselves masters of the citadel and what it
enclosed, 'Amr gathered his troops to march against Alexandria and set out in Rabi' I of the year 20 [18
February to 19 March 641], or, according to others, in Gamadi II of the same year [18 May to 17 June 641].

According to Seïf ben 'Omar, 'Amr ben El 'As, while he was himself at Aïn Shams, sent to Alexandria 'Ouf ben
Malek who had it said to the inhabitants that, if they wished to submit, one would accord them the aman
(safe-conduct). The Alexandrians having consented to it, 'Ouf entered into parleys with them, the troops of
'Amr being still at 'Aïn Shams, and having set out only during the negotiations.

"It is said," recounts Ibn 'Abd el Hakem, "that El Maqoqos made peace with 'Amr ben El 'As only when the
latter had seized Alexandria after a siege of three months, a siege so pressing that the inhabitants dreaded
'Amr. El Maqoqos asked for the Alexandrians a peace similar to that which had been consented to the Copts, on
condition of ratification on the part of the emperor. Yezid ben Abou Habib recounted to us that the Greek El
Maqoqos was the grand master of Egypt with whom 'Amr ben El 'As signed a treaty permitting certain Greeks who
desired it to withdraw, and certain others to remain for affairs mentioned in the treaty. When the news of it
reached Heraclius, emperor of the Greeks, he entered into a violent anger and opposed the most formal
refusal. He had set out on the spot an army; the gates of Alexandria were closed and war was declared on
'Amr. It is then that El Maqoqos came to find the latter and said to him: "I ask you three things." "What are
they?" asked 'Amr. "First you will not accord to the Greeks what you have accorded to me, for I have been
good to them and they have been wicked to me; next, you will not break with the Copts, for they are in no way
involved in the (present) rupture; finally, in what concerns me, if I come to die, you will have me buried at
Bakhans." "All that is

[PDF p. 500]

easy for us," said 'Amr. And profiting from the fact that the sortie was still possible, 'Amr withdrew with
the Muslims, accompanied by a crowd of the principal of the Copts who assured them the road and prepared for
them the ways and the encampment. Thus the Copts assisted them in all the combats that the Muslims delivered
to the Greeks; the latter, having been informed of it, made their preparations in consequence and asked for
reinforcements; one dispatched to them from the country of Roum ships laden with Greek soldiers, arms, and
provisions. (These having disembarked), 'Amr went to meet them and set out from Fostat for Alexandria; he met
no one until Marbout; there, he collided with a troop of Greeks with whom he engaged a light skirmish. God
put the Greeks to flight, and 'Amr, continuing his route, met the bulk of the Greeks at Kom Sherik; a combat
was engaged that lasted three days, at the end of which God gave the victory to the Muslims and the Greeks
showed their shoulders (fled).

According to another version, 'Amr (after the first engagement) would have sent in pursuit of the Greeks
Sherik ben Sami who reached them near the hill, which took from him the name of Kom Sherik. Sherik marched
therefore in advance of the army of 'Amr which had remained at Marbout, but the Greeks obliged him to take
refuge near the Kom (hill); Sherik having entrenched himself there, was surrounded there by the Greeks.
Seeing himself thus closely pressed, Sherik ben Sami gave an order to Abou Na'mat Mâlek ben Na'mat El Sadfi,
owner of the chestnut horse named Ashqar Sadf whose speed no mount equaled. Abou Na'mat took his run and
leaped from the Kom over the Greeks who set about pursuing him, but without reaching him. Abou Na'mat could
therefore rejoin 'Amr and warn him of what was happening. 'Amr set out immediately, and the Greeks, having
learned it, stirred themselves. The two armies met at Salatis, where a fierce combat was engaged. God put the
Greeks to rout, and the two armies having met again at Karioun, a combat was engaged that lasted more than
ten days. 'Abd Allah ben 'Amr fought in the first rank, and the standard-bearer was then Ouardan, freedman
of 'Amr. 'Abd Allah ben 'Amr, already covered with numerous wounds, cried: "O Ouardan, if you drew back a
little, we could rest." "You wish to rest?" said Ouardan. "The rest is in front and not behind." And 'Abd
Allah carried himself forward. A messenger of his father having come to question him on his wounds, he said:

[PDF p. 501]

[verses:] I say to her, that she may come out of her sadness and console herself: Calm yourselves! Either
you will gain something by it, or at least you will rest.

These verses are of 'Amr ben El Atnabah; he was a man of the tribe of the Benou Naggar and neighbor of El
Mo'az ben El Na'man. The latter (El Na'man) having been killed, Mo'az said: "He can only have been killed by
'Amr ben El 'Atnabah." This 'Amr was then the most noble of the tribe of Khazreg, and he answered:

[verses:] Oh! who will say on my part to those who believe themselves capable (of killing me) -- (sometimes
an advice can be given to a counselor) -- : You are in a state such that you cannot do me the slightest harm
by a veiled or clear word. Someone of you will promptly attempt to do it, but the trace of a tongue is not
that which a wound leaves. By my innocence, by the experience I have acquired, by the precious praises I have
been able to conquer, by the largesses I spread to set aside the ills of others, by my courage to brave the
valiant heroes, by what I say to myself each time I cannot appease and console myself: "Be at rest, you will
praise yourself for the result or at least you will rest," I will defend my good actions, I will preserve my
honor intact, with a sword having the color of limpid salt and a soul that can find no rest in face of a bad
thing.

[Philological gloss on three Arabic words follows.]

The messenger returned to 'Amr and informed him of what had been said to him: "It is truly my son," said
'Amr, and he addressed to God the prayer of danger. God therefore gave the victory to the Muslims who killed
a considerable number of Greeks and pursued the enemy until Alexandria where the Greeks entrenched
themselves. The town was surrounded by solid and uninterrupted ramparts, citadel after citadel. The Muslims
took position and installed themselves, seconded by the Coptic chiefs who procured them the necessary
victuals and fodder. This lasted two months thus. Then there occurred a change. Cavaliers, launched from the
side of the lake hidden by the citadel, charged

[PDF p. 502]

'Amr and killed twelve Muslim infantry. The Greek emperor sent on several occasions to Alexandria ships
bringing reinforcements more and more important to the besieged.

The Greek emperor said: "By God! if the Arabs seize Alexandria, it is done with the Greeks, they will perish."
For the Greeks had nowhere churches greater than the churches of Alexandria and, after the conquest of Syria
by the Arabs, the feasts of the Greeks were celebrated at Alexandria. And the emperor said: "By God! if they
take Alexandria from us, the Greeks are lost and their Empire destroyed." Then he made his preparations and
organized his departure for Alexandria, in order to see the siege of it with his own eyes. And when his
preparations were finished, God overturned him and made him die, and his provisions served the Muslims. He
died in the year 19, and by his death, God broke the sting of the Greeks and many of those who had fled
returned.

Heraclius, says El Leith, died in the year 20 [2 January to 20 December 640], that during which was conquered
Caesarea of Syria. The Arabs, made audacious by this victory, did not cease to combat the Alexandrians and
delivered them fierce combats. A handful of Greeks, come out by the gate of the citadel of Alexandria, had
thrown themselves on a troop of Muslims and had killed them a man of the tribe of Maharrah; they cut off his
head and carried it off. The Maharrah entered into a violent anger and declared that they would not bury the
cadaver of their companion without his head. "Carry yourselves," said 'Amr to them, "as you would do facing
people who care about your anger. If some Greek troop comes out, throw yourselves on it, kill it a man and
throw them his head; they will throw you that of your companion." Indeed, the Greeks having made a sortie,
the Maharrah threw themselves on them, killed one of their patricians, cut off his head, and threw it to the
Greeks who sent back that of the Maharrah. "And now," said 'Amr to them, "bury your companion."

"Of the three tribes of Egypt," said 'Amr, "the Maharrah beat and are not beaten, the 'Afeq are beaten and
do not beat, and the Bêla have been for the most part companions of the Prophet and have, as principal
quality, that of being excellent cavaliers." A man having proposed to 'Amr to dispose machines to launch
stones and demolish the walls, 'Amr answered him:

[PDF p. 503]

"Arrange yourself so that your rank may disappear?" "The enemies are already there," one said to him once,
"and we fear for the veil (they wished to speak of the wife of 'Amr)." "Many other veils will have been taken
before," he answered.

The siege dragging on in length, a Greek presented himself who challenged Mousallimah ben Mokhalled to
combat. The Greek overturned the latter and, having made him fall from his horse, rushed upon him to kill
him, when a companion of Mousallimah ran to his rescue. Mousallimah no longer struggled and seemed condemned;
the Greek, all joyous, struck on the two Muslims, which irritated 'Amr. Mousallimah was very fleshy and his
belly was heavy. "Who has given me such a man?" cried 'Amr. "Is it not this individual who resembles a woman
and wishes to meddle in what men do?" Mousallimah, furious, resumed without answering the combat; the
combatants entered into the citadel of Alexandria and the combat continued, but the Greeks, arriving in a
crowd, forced the Arabs to withdraw, with the exception of four men who, dispersed in the citadel, were shut
up in it. One of them was 'Amr ben El 'As, the second was Mousallimah; the name of the two others has not
reached us. They found themselves therefore separated from their companions, but the Greeks were ignorant of
who they were. Having perceived their abandonment, 'Amr ben El 'As and the others took refuge in the
underground passage of the baths; the Greeks penetrated there after them and, having made them come out, a
Greek interpreter questioned them in Arabic. "Here you are become our prisoners," he said; "surrender then
and do not kill yourselves." The Arabs refused. "You must have with you some of ours whom you retain
prisoners; we promise you to exchange you against our companions and not to kill you." The Arabs refused.
"Have you," said the Greek, "some acceptable means? (Here is one:) If our champion prevails over yours, you
will surrender to us, and we will be your masters. If on the contrary your champion prevails, we will let you
return to your companions." The Arabs declared themselves satisfied, and the agreement having been made
between the interpreter, 'Amr, Mousallimah, and their two companions, in the underground passage of the
baths, one brought the Arabs out into the open air. A man of Roum, whose courage and valor the Greeks prized,
presented himself, and the Greeks said: "One of you is going to wrestle with our companion." 'Amr wished to
present himself, but Mousallimah prevented him: "Why [...]

[PDF p. 504]

[OF THE CONQUEST OF ALEXANDRIA, continued]

commit this double fault?" he said. "You have already separated yourself from your companions, you their
chief; it is in you that their force resides, it is in your hands that their courage is deposited. They do
not know what you have become and will be happy only in seeing you reappear to lead them again to the
combats. If you are killed, what a loss for your companions! God willing, I will take your place and suffice
for the task." "Well, go," said 'Amr, "and may God favor you!" And Mousallimah advanced toward the Greek and
both turned for an hour, but God assisted Mousallimah who was victorious. He and his companions withdrew; the
Greeks, faithful to their word, kept their promise and opened them the gates of the citadel. They came out,
and it is only later that the Greeks learned that they had held in their hands the enemy general. They were
very irritated and gnawed their fists with rage at having let him escape. When they were outside, 'Amr
blushed at what had happened and said to Mousallimah: "Perish anger!" and he added: "Pardon me what I said to
you." Mousallimah pardoned him. "I have committed villainies," added 'Amr, "only three times; twice in the
time of ignorance and this one which is the third; each time I had to repent of it and to blush; but what I
blush at most is what I said to you. By God! I hope not to commit a fourth as long as I live." 'Amr besieged
Alexandria for months, and the news of it having reached 'Omar ben el Khattab: "They would not put so much
slowness into conquering this country," he cried, "if they were not plotting something." And he wrote to 'Amr
ben El 'As: "I am surprised at your slowness in conquering Egypt. Here are two years that you deliver battle,
and how would it be thus if you did not plot and if you did not act according to the desire of your enemies?
And God accords victory only to those whose intentions are pure. I send you four men and advise you that each
of them is worth a thousand infantry, as I have been able to see; and if there be others than they, those
will not prevail over them. As soon as my letter will have reached you, make a proclamation to your men and
exhort them to combat the enemies; let them arm themselves with patience and resolution; put at their head
the four men I send you, place them in front of the troops, and let everyone march and combat as a single
man. Let this be done at the end of Friday, at the hour when mercy descends, in the time of the granting. Let
all the army utter a cry toward God asking him for victory over the enemies." When this letter reached 'Amr,
he gathered his troops and read them the letter of

[PDF p. 505]

'Omar. Then he had the messengers come, presented them to the troops, and gave the latter the order to purify
themselves and to pray in all haste, then to invoke God and ask him for victory. They did it and God accorded
them the victory.

'Amr, it is said, asked the advice of Mousallimah, adding: "For me, my advice is to fight." "I opine,"
answered Mousallimah, "that you question a competent man and that you rely on the experience of someone of
the companions of the Prophet of God; gather the men in his presence and it is he who will proclaim the
battle; that must suffice you." "But who?" asked 'Amr. Mousallimah answered: "'Abadat ben El Samet." 'Amr had
him called and when he had arrived, mounted on his horse, he wished to descend. "Before descending," said
'Amr to him, "show me the teeth of your lance." 'Abadat having shown them to him, 'Amr removed his turban from
his head, gave it to 'Abadat to whom he remitted the command of the combat against the Greeks. 'Abadat
therefore took the command, the Greeks drew back and were beaten, and, by his intermediary, God conquered
Alexandria that very day. The siege of Alexandria had lasted 9 months, since the death of Heraclius, and had
begun 5 months before the death of this prince. The town was carried the Friday, 1st day of Moharrem of the
year 21 [10 December 641]. According to Abou 'Amr El Kandi, 'Amr would have besieged Alexandria only for 3
months, after which he would have seized it by main force; it is there, adds the author, the first conquest.
However, it is claimed that 'Amr seized the town the 1st Moharrem of the year 21.

According to El Leith, cited by El Qoda'i, 'Amr besieged Alexandria for 6 months, seized it, then marched on
Fostat which he took as capital in Dhu-l qaddeh.

When God, says Ibn 'Abd El Hakem, had put the Greeks to flight and had made Alexandria be conquered by the
Muslims, the Greeks dispersed by land and by sea. 'Amr, leaving at Alexandria a thousand of his companions,
set out with the rest of his troops in pursuit of the Greeks who fled by land; those of the Greeks who had
taken the sea then returned to Alexandria and killed all they found there of Muslims; there were spared only
those who took flight. This news having reached 'Amr, he returned in all haste, retook the town, installed
himself there, and wrote to 'Omar ben El Khattab: "God has

[PDF p. 506]

made us conquer Alexandria without convention or treaty." 'Omar answered him that he detested his advice and
that he ordered him not to pass beyond Alexandria. Here, says Ibn Lahi'at, is how he conquered Alexandria for
the second time: A man named Ibn Besamat, who was a porter, questioned 'Amr on his religion, on himself, on
his country, on his people, before opening him the gate. 'Amr answered all these questions, and it is then
that, Besamat having opened the gate, 'Amr could enter. From the beginning of the siege to the taking of the
town, there were twenty-two men killed. 'Amr ben El 'As sent Moawiah ben Khadig as messenger to 'Omar ben El
Khattab, to announce to him the victory. "Do you not give me a letter?" asked Moawiah. "Why a letter?"
answered 'Amr, "is an Arab made to carry letters? have you not seen by yourself and were you not present?"

When the messenger had arrived at 'Omar's to announce to him the taking of Alexandria, 'Omar prostrated
himself and rendered glory to God. Here is what Moawiah ben Khadig recounts: "'Amr ben El 'As having sent me
to carry to 'Omar the news of the taking of Alexandria, I arrived at Medina at noon and went in all haste to
the gate of the mosque; I entered there and held myself standing, when a slave-woman coming out of the house
of 'Omar ben El Khattab perceived me out of breath and covered with my travel-garments; she approached me and
said to me: 'Who are you?' 'I am,' I answered, 'Moawiah ben Khadig, messenger of 'Amr ben El 'As.' The slave
withdrew, then returned running, and I heard the light noise of her mantle on her leg. She approached me and
said to me: 'Stand up! the emir of the believers deigns to ask for you.' I followed her, and when I entered,
'Omar held his mantle with one hand and refastened with the other his breeches. 'What do you bring?' he asked
me. 'Good news,' I answered. 'Alexandria is taken.' 'Omar came out with me, went to the mosque, and said to
the crier: 'Call everyone to prayer.' And when the people were gathered, he said to me: 'Come, recount to
your companions what has happened.' I rose and made my account. Then 'Omar set about praying, withdrew into
his oratory, and there, turned toward the qibla, absorbed himself in prayers. Then having sat down, he asked:
'Slave, is there something to eat?' The slave advanced with bread and oil. 'Eat,' he said to me, and I ate
abundantly. He said to me again: 'Eat, for the traveler has need of nourishment, and if I had to eat, I would
eat with you.' And I threw myself on the food. Then he said: 'Slave, are there dates?' And the slave brought
dates on a tray:

[PDF p. 507]

'Eat,' he said to me, and I ate avidly. 'What did you say on arriving at the mosque?' he asked me. 'I said,'
I answered, 'that the prince of the believers was making his siesta.' 'What you said or what you thought is
bad. If I sleep indeed by day, I do prejudice to my subjects; if I sleep by night, I do prejudice to myself.
How could I sleep in this alternative, O Moawiah?'"

Later, 'Amr ben El 'As wrote to 'Omar ben El Khattab: "I have conquered the town of Alexandria and will not
make you the description of it; I will tell you only that I found there four thousand constructions with four
thousand baths, forty thousand Jews whom I have struck with the capitation, and four hundred royal places of
pleasure." According to Abou Qabil, 'Amr, after having seized Alexandria, found there twelve thousand
merchants selling vegetables. And during the night when 'Amr entered the town and that when one had dreaded
his entry, seventy thousand Jews fled from Alexandria.

One counted in Alexandria, in the way of baths, twelve thousand vaults, of which the smallest enclosed a
thousand halls each able to contain a great number of persons. The number of the Greeks of Alexandria reached
two hundred thousand, the most vigorous reached the country of Roum on boats. There were there a hundred
great boats that transported thirty thousand persons and all they could carry of riches, utensils, and
servants. Those who remained had to pay the tribute, and they were to the number of six hundred thousand;
without counting the women and the children. The troops were not in agreement with 'Amr for the division;
almost all the soldiers claimed it; but 'Amr declared that he could not accord it before having referred it
to the emir of the believers. He wrote to him therefore, announcing the conquest and enumerating to him the
riches of the town, informing him that the Muslims claimed the division of them. 'Omar answered him: "Divide
nothing, touch not these riches; the taxes will be the share of the Muslims and will be to them a force
against the forces of their enemies." And 'Amr had the town repaired, enumerated the inhabitants, and imposed
on them the tribute. And all of Egypt was subjected to the tax of two dinars per man, each paying only two
dinars per head, unless he had the means to pay more because of the extent of his lands and their
cultivations. It was not thus at Alexandria, whose inhabitants paid the tribute and the capitation according
to the good pleasure of the vali, for Alexandria had been carried by

[PDF p. 508]

main force and not ceded by treaty or convention, and for the Alexandrians, there was neither peace nor
protection.

Certain districts of Egypt were treated on a war footing; the territories of Belheib, of El Kheïs, and of
Salatis were ravaged. The product of the pillage was sent to Medina and to the other towns (of Arabia), but
'Omar ben El Khattab sent it back to the pillaged districts and had it restored to them. And the totality of
the Copts became protected ones (dhimmis) of Islam.

According to Yezid ben Abou Habib, 'Amr having pillaged the districts of Belheib, of Salatis, of Qoratia, and
of Sakha and having made the division of the booty, the first fruits of it were sent to Medina, but 'Omar ben
El Khattab wrote to 'Amr to return this booty to its proprietor, and 'Amr restored what he could find again
of it. It is said in another account that 'Omar ben El Khattab wrote specially on the subject of the people
of Salatis: "Whoever of them is in your hands, be favorable to him and demonstrate to him the truth of Islam;
if he embraces Islamism, let him be considered as a Muslim; let him have part in the common wealth; but if he
prefers to conserve his religion, leave him tranquil in his town." The people of Belheib, who were then just
men, chose Islamism.

In another account, it is reported that the people of Salatis, of Sa, of Belheib aided with all their power
the enemies of the Muslims against the latter; the Muslims having vanquished them, believed it licit to
pillage them and said: "These countries will be for us a booty like Alexandria." 'Amr wrote to 'Omar ben El
Khattab on this subject and 'Omar answered him: "Make of Alexandria and of these three districts protected
ones of Islam; impose on them a tribute, and this tribute, joined to what the Copts must pay, will be for the
Muslims a force against their enemies. Let no booty be drawn from it and let them not be made slaves." And one
did thus.

It is said, on the contrary, that 'Omar brought them back to the pact concluded previously with them. 'Amr,
says Ibn Lahi'at, collected, for the capitation at Alexandria, six hundred thousand dinars, for he found there
three hundred thousand protected ones of Islam, each imposed two dinars, which gives the aforementioned
total. It is said that the product of the capitation at Alexandria was eighteen thousand dinars. Under the
caliphate of Hecham ben 'Abd El Melek, this tax produced thirty thousand dinars; and it is asserted that
'Amr ben El 'As left their lives to the Alexandrians and that, far from massacring and pillaging, he made of
them protected ones of Islam, as he had done of the Nubians.

[PDF p. 509]

CHAPTER XIV
OF WHAT THE MUSLIMS DID AT ALEXANDRIA AND THE UPRISINGS OF THE GREEKS

As for Alexandria, says Ibn 'Abd el Hakem, there was found there no terrain belonging in property to anyone,
but whoever desired to remain somewhere with his brothers could do so. After the taking of Alexandria, 'Amr
ben El 'As and 'Abadah ben El Samet went forward and mounted the hill where today is the mosque of 'Amr ben
El 'As. "Let us descend," said Moawiah ben Khadig. And 'Amr descended and established himself in a house to
the west of the oratory of 'Amr, on the side of the sea, which has since been destroyed; Moawiah established
himself on the eminence where 'Abadah ben El Samet planted a tent in which he remained during all the time
of his sojourn at Alexandria. Abou-l Derda was, it is said, with him, but God knows it better than anyone.

After the pacification of the country, 'Amr ben El 'As divided his army thus: a quarter was left in garrison
at Alexandria; another quarter occupied the shore of the sea; the rest remained under his orders. The quarter
that held garrison at Alexandria stayed there regularly during the six months of summer and was relieved
during the six months of winter. To each chief was assigned a castle where he established himself with all
those who accompanied him; they took there gratuitously their provisional lodgings.

According to Yezid ben Abou Habib, the Muslims remained at first tranquil in their cantonments at Alexandria,
but later, become impatient, they made some expeditions outside, and the one of them who returned first
occupied the house that pleased him. Having to set out again on campaign, 'Amr said to them: "I fear that you
may put in bad state the houses that served you as lodging, if you take them from one another." And, in
approaching Karioun: "Go," he said to them, "with the benediction of God, and the one of you who plants his
lance in a house, this house will belong to him, to him and to his children." And when a man entered a house,
he planted his lance in a room, then another came who planted his lance in another room, and thus the house

[PDF p. 510]

became the property of two or three families who installed themselves in it. At their departure, the Greeks
came back to take possession of their lodging and repaired it. And Yezid ben Abou Habib claims that one had
the right neither to give these houses in rental nor to take them on lease, no more than to transmit them by
inheritance; one could only inhabit them as places of cantonment.

According to the account of Yezid ben Abou Habib, 'Amr ben El 'As, after the taking of Alexandria, seeing the
houses and the edifices deserted, had the design of installing himself there. "Here," he said, "are houses
that will not cost us much trouble." He wrote therefore to 'Omar ben El Khattab to ask him for the
authorization to install himself at Alexandria. 'Omar asked the messenger if, in this case, there would be
water between him and the Muslim army. "Yes, Emir of the Believers," answered the messenger, "at the moment
of the flood of the Nile." And 'Omar wrote to 'Amr: "I do not want you to install yourself with the Muslims
in a place where the water would separate us during the winter or during the summer." And 'Amr ben El 'As
transported himself to Fostat. 'Omar wrote in the same sense to Sa'd ben Abou Ouaqâs who occupied the towns
of Cosrou (Khosrow), to his governor of Basra, and to 'Amr ben El 'As who was at Alexandria: "Do not put
water between you and me so that, if I desire to go on horseback to you, I may ride as far as you and rejoin
you by land." And Sa'd ben Abou Ouaqâs transported himself from the towns of Cosrou to El Koufa, the governor
of Basra left the town he occupied to go to Basra, and 'Amr ben El 'As went from Alexandria to Fostat. Each
year, 'Omar ben El Khattab sent a corps of troops from Medina to Alexandria, for he did not neglect the new
conquest and always dreaded a surprise attack of the Greeks.

Othman wrote to 'Abdallah ben Sa'd ben Abou Sara': "I have learned what the Emir of the Believers had
resolved on the subject of Alexandria; the Greeks having risen up twice, he was obliged to leave the
garrisons at Alexandria and to furnish provisions to these garrisons which relieved each other every six
months." At the time of an uprising of the town, the Greeks, having at their head the eunuch Manuel, arrived
in boats and blockaded it. The Greeks of Alexandria made common cause with the besiegers; only El Maqoqos
remained tranquil and did not violate the treaty. At this epoch, 'Amr ben El 'As had been deposed by Othman
and one had named as vali 'Abd Allah ben Sa'd ben El Sara'. At the arrival of the Greeks, the Alexandrians
asked Othman for the recall of 'Amr to hold his head up to the

[PDF p. 511]

Greeks, for he had the experience of war and the enemies dreaded him. Othman consented. 'Amr returned, and,
as at this epoch Alexandria was protected by walls, he swore that, if God gave him the victory, he would raze
the enclosure of the town and render Alexandria similar to a house of debauchery into which one can penetrate
from all sides. 'Amr operated several sorties against the besiegers by sea and by land, and the Copts, who
obeyed El Maqoqos, joined him; as for the Greeks, none was of the party of El Maqoqos. Kharagah ben Hazafah
having said to 'Amr: "Combat them before the number of the rebels increases and let us not leave all of Egypt
to rise up," "No," answered 'Amr, "I will on the contrary let them come to me, and as they will do prejudice
to those near whom they pass, God will make them destroy one another." And the Greeks moved away from
Alexandria, and with them all the insurgents of the provinces. They stopped in the villages, drinking the
wine, eating the provisions, and pillaging all the places through which they passed, without 'Amr attacking
them. They arrived thus at Nafious where the two armies met at once on the land and on the water; the Greeks
pushed toward the side of the Copts and made rain into the river a hail of arrows, and an arrow reached in
the heart the mare of 'Amr who was on the shore. The animal was wounded and 'Amr leaped down from his mount;
the Greeks at this moment left the river, rejoined on land the other Greeks, and launched a cloud of arrows
on the Muslims. These having yielded slightly, the Greeks charged them with so much violence that the Muslims
turned their backs; Sherik ben Sami took flight with his cavalry. The Greeks were disposed in successive
ranks, and at this moment one of the patricians arrived from the country of Roum, mounted on his horse and
covered with a gilded armor, came out of the ranks and provoked the Muslims. A man of the tribe of Zobeïd
named Houamel and surnamed Abou Madhag presented himself; and both fought a long time charging with the
lance. Then the patrician, throwing his lance, drew his sword; Houamel threw his lance in his turn and seized
likewise his sword; his courage was known and 'Amr set about crying to him: "O Abou Madhag!" and the latter
answered: "Here I am!" The armies were ranged on the two banks of the Nile, grouped in order of battle. The
two adversaries fought with the sword for an hour. Finally the patrician precipitated himself against Houamel
who threw himself likewise on him. Houamel was slender; he drew the dagger that was at his belt, or attached
to his arm, and struck with it the throat or the clavicle of the barbarian, took him

[PDF p. 512]

bodily, overturned him under himself, and despoiled him. (Some days after, Houamel died and 'Amr had his
funeral litter carried between the two columns of his funeral couch until he was buried in the Moqattam.)
Then the Muslims, redoubling in vigor, put the Greeks to rout and pursued them as far as Alexandria which God
delivered to them. The eunuch Manuel was killed and 'Amr pursued the enemies with so much fury that he
penetrated into the heart of the town. Yielding to the supplications, he ordered to cease the carnage, and at
the very place where this order had been given, he built a mosque; it is the mosque of Alexandria that bears
the name of mosque of the Clemency, in memory of the order given there by 'Amr to cease the massacre. Then
the walls of the town were razed. The people of the provinces who had remained faithful gathered and came to
find 'Amr: "We have," they said, "remained faithful to the treaties, but these brigands have passed through
our home and have carried off our goods and our livestock which are at present in your hands." 'Amr had
restored to them what they recognized as having belonged to them and after they had furnished the proof that
these objects were indeed their property. One of them however said to 'Amr: "You have conducted yourself
unjustly toward us, for you should have defended us, we who are under your protection and have not revolted.
As for those who revolted, may God remove from them the good." And 'Amr repented and said: "Would to God that
I had been in front of them when they came out of Alexandria!" This revolt of Alexandria had had for cause
the following fact: Zalma, governor of Akhna, had come to find 'Amr and had asked him: "Make known to us what
each of us must pay for the capitation." 'Amr, showing with the finger the angle of the church, answered him:
"If you give us with what to fill this edifice from the bottom to the roof, I will have nothing to claim. You
are for us only cashiers; the more you give us, the more we will be in our turn generous toward you, the less
you give us, the less great will be our generosity." The governor of Akhna, irritated, went to the country of
Roum and came back with the Greeks. God put them to rout and rendered captive the governor of Akhna who was
brought to 'Amr. "Kill him!" one cried. "No," said 'Amr, "let him be set at liberty," he said; "go and come
back again with another army." And he adorned him, crowned him, clad him in a burnous the color of purple.
Zalma then accepted the tax of the capitation. One said to him: "If you had fallen thus into the hands of the
king of the Greeks?" "If I had fallen there," he answered, "he would have had me put to death

[PDF p. 513]

saying that I caused my companions to perish." According to Abou Qabil, 'Atabah ben Abou Safian proclaimed
'Alqamah El Qatifi governor of Alexandria, and sent him 12,000 men. And 'Alqamah wrote to Moawiah ben Abou
Safian complaining that 'Atabah deceived him as well as his companions. Mo'awiah wrote to him: "I had you
accompanied by 10,000 men of Syria and 5,000 men of Medina, and at Alexandria there were already 27,000 men."
According to another account, 'Alqamah ben Yezid commanded at Alexandria with 12,000 men; and he wrote to
Mo'awiah: "It is you who designated me as your lieutenant at Alexandria, and I have with me only 12,000 men;
it is hardly that we perceive one another, so little a thing is this number." Mo'awiah answered him: "I have
dispatched you 'Abd Allah ben Moti' with 4,000 men of Medina; I have given the order to Mo'n ben Yezid El
Salmii to go to Ramleh with 4,000 auxiliaries; when, thanks to their cavalry, they will have rejoined you and
delivered you from your frights, they will remain with you." According to Ibn Lahi'ah, 'Amr would have said:
"The valiyat (governorship) of all of Egypt is worth the rest of the caliphate."

In marching on Alexandria, 'Amr ravaged the village that today bears the name of Kharabah Ouardan. One has
reported to us diverse causes of this devastation; Sa'id ben 'Afit recounted to us that 'Amr, while he was
going to Nafious to combat the Greeks, sent in the morning Ouardan to execute an order. The Greeks of
Kharabah carried him off and hid him. 'Amr inquired of him, set about searching for him, followed his traces,
and found him in one of their houses. The order was given to destroy them; and the order was executed. It is
said that all the inhabitants of Kharabah were monks and that some soldiers of the rear-guard of 'Amr having
lingered, were killed by them, while 'Amr had already reached Karioun. He stopped the army, dispatched
against them Ouardan who massacred the inhabitants and destroyed the town which until the present has
remained a heap of ruins. It is said that the people of Kharabah were people of the rope and the sack (rogues
fit for hanging). 'Amr sent into their country to take a skin full of the dust of their soil. Then he spoke
to them, but they answered nothing, and 'Amr having made them come out, had the dust in question spread under
his prayer-rug on which he sat; he called them back and spoke to them, and they consented to what he wished.
Having made them come out again, one removed the dust, and when one had called them back and addressed the
word to them, they did not [...]

[PDF p. 514]

[OF WHAT THE MUSLIMS DID AT ALEXANDRIA, continued]

answered nothing. The experience was repeated a great number of times, and 'Amr ended by saying: "This
country does not deserve that one tread it underfoot!" And he ordered the destruction of it. When God had put
the Greeks to rout, Othman manifested the intention of leaving 'Amr ben El 'As at the head of the army and of
naming 'Abdallah ben Sa'd as superintendent of the finances. "Here I am," said 'Amr, "like the one who takes
the cow by the horns while another milks it." And he refused. This conquest of 'Amr was made by main force
under the caliphate of Othman in the year 25 [28 October 645 to 16 October 646], and between this second
conquest and the first there are 4 years. El Leith says: "The first conquest was made at the beginning of the
year 22 [30 November 642 to 18 November 643] and the second in the year 25. And the army remained [engaged in
operations] for seven years after the conquest, combating the people, for one opened against them the waters
and the marshes. Then 'Abdallah ben Sa'd ben Abou Sara' ravaged Dhu'l Souari in the year 34 [22 July 654 to
10 July 655]; and, on the subject of this expedition, it is recounted that 'Abdallah ben Sa'd on arriving at
Dhu'l Souari had the half of his troops disembark under the orders of Basr ben Artha; and when they had
disembarked, a messenger came to find 'Abdallah ben Sa'd and said to him: "What you would do if the son of
Heraclius came to you with a thousand ships, do it at once." The boats of the Muslims were to the number of
200 and some. 'Abdallah ben Sa'd placed himself standing between the two masses of the army and said: "One
announces to me that the son of Heraclius comes to us with a thousand ships. Counsel me." And as no one
answered, he resumed, after a moment of silence: "Be of some use, then." And after having kept silent an
instant, he spoke to them again, but no one answered. He sat down therefore and for the third time, after
having waited some time, he said: "Come, there is nothing to be done!" Then there rose a man of Medina who
had made the holy war with 'Abdallah ben Sa'd: "O emir," he said, "God has said: 'How many times has a

[PDF p. 515]

small troop vanquished a numerous army with the help of God; God is with those who persevere'" (Koran, II,
250). And 'Abdallah said: "Embark then!" The embarkation was done, but each boat received only the half of
its effective, the other half finding itself on land under the orders of Basr. They reached the enemy and
engaged the combat with the bolts and the arrows. The son of Heraclius had remained behind; it was night, and
at the moment of the rout the night-couriers set about searching for him to carry him news. "What is being
done?" the prince asked them. "One combats," answered the runners, "with bolts and arrows." "In that case,"
he said, "the Greeks are victorious." Later, other couriers having come, he asked them: "What is being done?"
"The bolts and arrows having run short, one has thrown stones." "Then," he said, "the Greeks will be
victorious." Other couriers came: "What is being done?" "The stones having run short, one has tied the boats
together and one has fought with the sword." "The Greeks are therefore victorious," he said. In that time the
boats were attached during the combat with chains. The boat of the emir 'Abdallah finding itself tied to an
enemy boat, the latter dragged it toward the bulk of the Greek fleet. Then 'Alqamah ben Yezed El Qatifi, who
was on the boat of 'Abdallah ben Sa'd, rose, struck the chain with his sword, and cut it. 'Abdallah, later,
questioned his wife Basisah bent Hamzah ben Yeshrah, who was then with him, for foreseeing that the combat
would be hard, one had brought the women on the boats, and Basisah answered: "'Alqamah is the master of the
chain." When 'Abdallah had asked Basisah of her father, the latter had said to him: "'Alqamah has already
asked for her and I am engaged with him. If he abandons her, I accord her to you." And 'Abdallah spoke to
'Alqamah who consented to desist, and Basisah became the wife of 'Abdallah ben Sa'd. Then 'Abdallah having
left her a widow, 'Alqamah married her and left her a widow in his turn; she then married Karib ben Abrahat
and remained his wife until his death. It is recounted that in the year 35 [11 July 655 to 29 June 656] the
Greeks went to Constantine, son of Heraclius, and said to him: "Will we leave Alexandria in the hands of the
Arabs? it is our greatest town." "What would I do with you," answered the prince, "you cannot hold an hour as
soon as the Arabs appear." "Come only," they said, "and if it is necessary, we will die." Thus agreed,
Constantine

[PDF p. 516]

set out for Alexandria with a thousand ships; for long days he remained the plaything of the winds; at the
end, God raised a hurricane that drowned them all, with the exception of Constantine who was saved with his
ship and who was pushed by the wind as far as Sicily. The inhabitants of the island questioned him; he
recounted to them his adventure, and they cried: "It is done with Christendom and the Christians if the Arabs
penetrate to our home, for we will find no one to repel them." "We had set out powerful," cried Constantine,
"and behold what we have become!" One prepared him a bath, and as one approached him: "Woe to you," he cried,
"one will carry off your men and kill your king." "Why did he not drown with the others!" they cried, and
they killed him, sparing those who were with him on his ship. The place where his expedition foundered, says
Abou 'Amr El Kandi, was called Dhu'l Souari, because of the quantity and the mass of the masts of his ships.

[PDF p. 517]

CHAPTER XV
OF THE LAKE OF ALEXANDRIA

The lake of Alexandria, says Ibn Abd El Hakem, was formerly entirely planted in vines and belonged to the
wife of El Maqoqos; she drew her revenues from the wine that was paid to her as a due. And the wine became
there so abundant that it was impossible for her to occupy herself with its placement. Then she said to her
farmers: "The wine no longer makes my affair, bring me dinars." "We have none," they answered. It is then
that she made penetrate into the lake the water that drowned the vines, and this place became a lake where
one fished enormous fish. This lasted thus until the moment when the Abbasid Caliphs, having dried up the
lake and protected it by dikes, sowed it. Later, it became again a lake long a day's march and of an equal
width. The water came there from Achtoum, on the sea of Roum, and went out of it to go into a second lake
situated beyond the first, by a canal on which are the two towns of El Hadebah and of Edkou. It is a place
abundant in plantations of cucumbers and palms, all planted in the sand. Into this lake also throws itself a
canal derived from the Nile and called El Hafer, long a half-day's march and abundant in birds, fish, and
grasses. The fish of this lake sell in great quantity at Alexandria, for they are very small and have an
infinitesimal value. The water has withdrawn from this lake since [...]

[PDF p. 518]

CHAPTER XVI
OF THE CANAL OF ALEXANDRIA

It is said that it was the queen Cleopatra who made the canal of Alexandria penetrate into the town. Before,
the water did not reach there, but the queen had the canal deepened, brought it as far as into the town, and
paved its ceiling with plaques of marble, from the beginning to the end; one still finds some of them today.
Abou-l Hassan El Makhzoumi says, in his book of the Ways: As for the canal of Alexandria, from the
water-intake of the canal to the canal of Boudarah, there is nothing, but from there on, one meets Bou
Mouharag, Mehalla Benouk, Asinat, Aourin, Mehallah Farnou, Mehallah Hassan, Minieh Terad (known under the
name of El Qa'ah), the two Mehallah of Naser and of Mesrouq. As for the canal of Loqanah, one opens it after
the seventh day of Thot; the new canal is opened the 16th of Thot; the canal of Boudarah after the 7th of
Thot; the canal of Bou Yahia and those of Bou-l Sahama and of El Qahouqia have absolutely no closure; the
canal of El Sherak is opened after the 7th of Thot; the canals of Bou Khorâshah and of El Barbit which feed
Deïssou, Somkharat, Shirnoubah, Minieh Hamad, Senadah, and a part of Mahallah Mâriah, and the canal of Fishah
Balkha are opened the 12th of Thot; the custom is to open on the day of the Nourouz the canal of Bouit; the
section of Samdissah is opened the 22nd of Thot; that of Yates the 19th of Thot; when this section is closed,
one digs a canal charged with watering the southern lands of the region and that one opens on the day of the
Nourouz, and, as soon as the canal of Aflaqah has penetrated into the lands of Yates, one has the habit, as
soon as the lands situated to the south of Aflaqah have been watered, of abandoning the canal to itself, so
that it waters freely the northern region situated beyond Yates. The canal of El Qarourah is newly made; the
canal of Bafiouha is opened the 12th of Thot; the canal of Aflaqah the 10th, and that of Askanidah the 6th.

The canal Bahr Damanhour is opened from the 20th of Mesori to the 6th of Thot; it waters a part of Tamous, of
the Church of the Garden, of Qortassa, and of Damanhour.

The canal of El Qouadis serves Shoubrah el Nakhleh and Kom el Teloul; and the canals of Shoubrah el Nakhleh
are opened at the epoch when they are the [...]

[PDF p. 519]

[OF THE CANAL OF ALEXANDRIA, continued]

higher, the 1st of Thot. The canal of Bastara is opened the 15th of Mesori; the canal of Mesid is opened the
7th of Thot; the canal of Santouyah the 18th; the Bahr Damshouva the 20th of Mesori; this last furnishes the
water to Minieh Razkoun, Saft, Kardassah, Damchouya, Mehallah El Sheikh, and Masil; the canal of Damshouya is

Mehallah Barsiq has no closure.

Mehallah El Keroum is opened the 8th of Thot; this canal feeds a great number of localities which are:
Mehallah el Keroum and the villages that depend on it, Denissah, Kom el Oualid, Kom El Sakhrah, Dirames, El
Safasef, and some countries that do not depend on it, such as: Talmessa, El Galmoun, which depend on Mehallah

Shoubra Barlis is closed; the canal of Qafelat was opened the 8th of Thot, but no longer has a closure today;

a fraction of El Kharbatah, of Balkhous, of Boulin, of Mahallah Ouafed and El Beida, and a part of Tilas.

Mo'an, Minieh Asami, a part of Seïfiah; then one cuts the dike of El Fotami, new also, and which serves a

the dike of Dessouhes and of Abou Dinar, and one opens the canal of Tabrinah to which

[PDF p. 520]

are fed Densal and Talmous; the water is left there 6 days to water Miniah Atiah and Salatis.

As for the Bahr Damanhour, it remains closed above Salatis until the 17th of Thot; it serves Salatis, Zahera,
a part of Tabous, of Qertassa, of Kenisset El Rheit, and Damanhour; then one cuts the new dike of Nadibah
where the waters had stopped; in this new portion of canal, the water sojourns for 8 days and feeds Nadibah,

Mehallah Namir; and the canal remains thus open until the lowering of the waters.

As for the new canal of Tebrinah, as soon as the territory of Tebrinah has been watered, one lets its waters
go beyond Dessounes Om Dinar; then one cuts it a little below Tamous and one lets it go, during the high
waters, over the terrains of Qerâqes; the water flows passing by Qertassa and Kenisset El Rheit. At the exit
of the canal of Tebrinah, from the beginning of the flood, the water is constantly used up to the dike of

Mesged Rhanem, El Souaf, Kom Sherik, Minieh Moghiin, Tell el Fotami, and Mahallah Ouafed. Then one cuts the
dike of Daliga, and then are watered the terrains of a part of Kharbatah, Falichan, Boulin, El Beida, Densat,
Telbana El Abrag, Tell Baqa, El Haddin, El Yehoudiah, El Nessoum, Abou Semadah, El Hasn, Qalaouah Benou
Obeid, Toukh Dekhaiah, Dersha, Saqra, Daliga, Lamhah, Tibah; then one cuts it to water Minieh, Zeraqat El
Hagar, El Mahzoum, a part of Hiares, Afrim, Abou Semar, and Om El Derou'.

For the canal of Ibn Zeloum, also named canal of Ibn Zeloum, the water-intake at El Ta'idi remains closed and
is opened only the 10th of Thot; this canal feeds Shabour, Kenisseh Moubarek, a part of Sersiqah and of
Damoushah, Minieh Yezid, the Hod El Maseli, Hasah Salmoun, a part of Sanit, of El Ta'idi, and of Falishan;
then one cuts the following dike, and then it serves Amlit, a part of Anbaï, of

[PDF p. 521]

Kenisset 'Abd el Melek, of Armeniah, Misna, a part of Mehallah 'Obeïd, Saft Khaled, Bornamah, Shoubra Noubah,
Kiman Sheras, a part of Damshouah; the guardians remain on the dike of Saft. At the canal of Alexandria and
its derivatives are fed the people of the interior and of the Behera, and the surplus of the waters pours
itself into the defiles and the valleys; these waters are altered. As for its riparians, they belong to the
tribes of Dananah, of El Ramhanah, of the Benou Yezan, and to the Berber tribes; they cultivate the banks of
the canal and draw from them with what to pay the tax. From the east of Pelusium, on the side of Gougir and
of Faqous, to the extremity of the country served by the canal of Alexandria, there is a month's march; and
all this space remained covered with cultivations more or less dense until after the year 350 [20 February
961 to 8 February 962] of the hijra; but the greatest part of it has been destroyed.

Abou Bekr El Tartoussi, citing some old sailor who had recounted it to him, says: I was witness at Alexandria
of a fishing made in the canal and abandoned to the people; the fish let themselves be seen there in such
abundance that the children took them with cloths; then the vali interdicted this fishing and prevented the
people from taking the fish; thus it has diminished there in such a way that it is hardly that, today, one
perceives one from time to time.

Abou 'Amr El Kandi, in his book of the Masters, reports, on the authority of El Hareth ben Meskin, that the
latter was named grand cadi of Egypt, by order of the emir of the believers El Watheq Billah in the year 239,
and, citing the passages of his history, he says: "The canal of Alexandria was cleaned by him and the letter
prescribing the cleaning of it was dated the month of Rabi II of the year 245 [6 July to 3 August 859]."

The chronicler of the Toulounides says: "In Rabi I of the year 59 [12 June 853 to 1 June 854] Ahmed ben
Touloun ordered the canal of Alexandria to be dug."

The Nile, says El Masa'oudi, did not arrive as far as the territory of Alexandria before the year 332 [4
September 943 to 23 August 944]. Alexander had built the town on a canal derived from the Nile, and the
greatest part of the water of the Nile arrived there; it is thus that were watered Alexandria and the country
of Marbout, which formed an uninterrupted succession of cultivations and

[PDF p. 522]

of gardens until Barqah; and the ships, following the course of the Nile, arrived at the markets of
Alexandria; and the ceiling of this canal, in its course across the town, was paved with stone and marble;
the water ceased to penetrate there as a consequence of the obstruction of its bed, and the people, no longer
able to feed themselves from it, had to drink the water of the wells, the Nile being a day's march from the
town.

El Messihi reports that El Hakem bi amrillah Abou Mansour ben El 'Aziz consecrated, in 404 [13 July 1013 to 1
July 1014], to the deepening of the canal, a sum of 1,500 dinars; one dug it over all its course. In 662 [4
November 1263 to 23 October 1264], El Mélek El Zaher Bibars sent the emir 'Ali, commander of the bodyguard,
to clean the canal of Alexandria whose mouth, filled with mud, let arrive at Alexandria only a very feeble
quantity of water. The emir began his operations from El Ta'ïdi, founded there a mosque, and named as
inspector of the works master Te'asif, inspector of the divans. Later, in the year 664 [13 October 1265 to 1
October 1266], the sultan sent to clean this canal the emir 'Elm el din Sangar El Masouri; and, escorted by
numerous emirs and an army, he came himself to inspect the work; the emirs and the troop were employed at the
works until the sand that obstructed the canal between El Taïdi and Foumm el Khalig had disappeared; and,
pushing as far as Barenbar, he sank boats there and raised over them a construction of stones; and, his goal
attained, he returned to the citadel of the mountain. Little by little the water ceased to flow in this canal
all the length of the year; one cleaned it about two months after the arrival of the waters, and the
Alexandrians had during all the year to drink the water of the cisterns, where the water was stored until the
year 710 [31 May 1310 to 19 May 1311]. The emir Badr el din Biktoub El Khaznadari, known under the name of
emir Shekar, vali of Alexandria, went to the citadel of the mountain and demonstrated to El Mélek El Naser
Mohammed ben Qalaoun how useful it would be to dig the canal; he set forth to him what commodity it would
present first for the transport of the grains and all sorts of merchandise to Alexandria by boats, which,
while diminishing the fatigue, would increase the revenues of the divan; in the second place, for the putting
into cultivation of the terrains on the two banks of the canal, where would rise villages and

[PDF p. 523]

markets, source of considerable revenues; thirdly, for the amelioration of the lot of the people who would
cultivate their gardens and drink constantly the water of this canal. This pleased the sultan who sent the
emir Badr el din Mohammed ben Kanda'di ben El Ouaziri with Biktoub to put into execution this project; he
prescribed to all the emirs of the kingdom to send messengers charged with gathering the people of the
districts of their government to have the work executed, and he wrote to the valis of provinces to advise
them of it. In the districts one gathered about 40,000 men in 20 days, and the work began in Regeb of the
above year [24 November to 23 December 1310]; the people of each province had a portion to dig, so much so
that the length of the dug part, from the mouth of the Bahr el Nil to the district of Shanbar, measured 8,000
hakemite kassabahs, and from Shanbar to Alexandria as much. In the primitive part of the canal, the water
penetrated there from the frontier of Shanbar; one directed there the mouth of the canal, to which one gave a
depth of 6 kassabahs and a width of 8. When one had arrived at the limit of the old canal, one gave it the
same proportions as to the new part, and of the whole one made a single canal furnished with locks and
bridges. In cleaning the old canal, one found a considerable quantity of lead employed in the substructures
of the cisterns. But the sultan drew nothing of it for himself and made a gift of it to the emir Biktoub. The
pain one had in cleaning this canal was enormous, for the part nearest the river had been submerged by the
waters; the workers had to dive to remove the earth from the bottom, and thus the mass of water became
stronger. The canals derived from this principal canal multiplied to the point of exhausting it, but its
importance and its utility were no less for that; for all the length of the year the boats could navigate
there and the Alexandrians were no longer obliged to drink the water of the cisterns. One hastened to put
into cultivation the two banks of the canal, and in little time more than a hundred thousand feddans were put
into cultivation there where formerly there was only sebakh (salt marsh); more than six hundred saqiehs
(waterwheels) functioned for the irrigation of the plantations of colocasia, indigo, sesame; more than forty
villages were founded, and at Alexandria more than a thousand gardens were traced. Thanks to this canal, a
crowd of localities became prosperous and a considerable number of persons went to people the villages
established on its banks.

For what concerns him, as soon as the works were finished, the emir Biktoub hastened to have raised at his
expense a dike, for the riparians [...]

[PDF p. 524]

[OF THE CANAL OF ALEXANDRIA, continued]

at the time of the flood experienced a considerable damage, because the waters covered the terrains of sebakh
(salt marsh). He took three months to build a dike whose foundations were of stones and lead and the upper
part of stone and lime. He furnished it with three locks and raised a hostelry where the travelers could
stop; he put there overseers and assigned a revenue for its functioning. He spent there nearly sixty thousand
Egyptian dinars, without counting the stones he had brought from an old palace situated outside Alexandria,
nor the lead found in a corridor of this same underground palace which extended as far as near the sea, nor
the lead found in the canal. The water filled this canal during all the year, and that lasted until after the
year 770 [16 August 1368 to 4 August 1369]. At that moment, the water no longer penetrated there except at
the time of the flood, and the canal remained dry at the epoch of the low water. Thus most of the gardens of
Alexandria withered and disappeared; a great part of the villages established on the banks of this canal were
abandoned.

The cause of the drying-up of the canal was that the Greeks had seized Achtoum, the locality where the water
of the sea passed to go into the lake of Alexandria before its desiccation, and that the sand, accumulated by
the wind, had obstructed the mouth of the canal; moreover, the ceiling had risen. On several occasions, the
sovereigns of Egypt had had the intention of cleaning the canal, but this project remained without
realization until the reign of El Mélek El Ashraf Barsebaï, who confided this work to the emir Gerbash El
Karimi, known under the name of 'Acheq. The latter went there and gathered there all he could of people of
the region, to the number of 875. The cleaning began the 11th of Gamadi I of the year 826 [22 April 1423] and
lasted until the 11th of Sha'ban [20 July 1423], in all 90 days; the work finished, the water penetrated
again into the canal and arrived as far as Alexandria; the boats circulated there and the people were quite
joyous. The sums spent for this cleaning by the provinces were recovered from the cultivators of the domains
riparian to the canal and the proprietors of the gardens of Alexandria. And during this considerable work,
there was committed none of those turpitudes that the valis generally commit on similar occasions. The glory
is to God! And when it was finished, the emir Gerbash went to the

[PDF p. 525]

citadel of the mountain; the sultan gave him a robe of honor and, to thank him, created him grand chamberlain.
But the effects of the cleaning of the canal made themselves felt only for a little time; soon it was again
filled up by the sand, and it was no longer possible for the boats to circulate there except at the moment of
the inundation.

[PDF p. 526]

CHAPTER XVII
COLLECTION OF TRADITIONS ON ALEXANDRIA

In the year 199 [22 August 814 to 10 August 815], the war became more violent in Egypt between El Motaleb ben
'Abd allah El Khoza'ï, emir of Egypt, and 'Abd el 'Aziz ben El Ouazir El Geraoui the Rebel, of Tennis. El
Motaleb confided the government of Alexandria to Mohammed ben Habirat ben Hesham ben Khadig, and Mohammed
took as lieutenant his maternal uncle 'Omar ben 'Abd el Melek ben Mohammed ben 'Abd el Rahman ben Moawiah ben
Khadig, surnamed 'Omar ben Melâk. At the end of three months, El Motaleb deposed 'Omar and replaced him by
his brother El Fadl ben 'Abd allah ben Malek. At this epoch were found at Alexandria boats of Spaniards
(Andalusians) gone out on expedition. These ships were found there, following what had happened at Cordoba
where, in the year 182 [22 February 798 to 11 February 799], the troops that accompanied El Hakem ben Hesham
had expelled a great number of inhabitants who had taken refuge at Alexandria. The Spaniards were furious
because a butcher of Alexandria had thrown in the face of one of them the tripes of animals, a thing for
which they had repugnance, and it is then that there happened what happened; this had taken place at the
moment when they had come to the place of Alexandria to buy what they had need of. For a long time it had
been thus, the emirs not permitting them to enter the town; but the Alexandrians went out and went to traffic
with them. When 'Omar ben Melâk was deposed, 'Abd el 'Aziz El Geraoui wrote to him, urging him to throw
himself on Alexandria and to call him there. 'Omar ben Melâk sent the Spaniards a messenger to invite them to
rise up with him and to chase El Fadl from the town. They joined therefore 'Omar, El Fadl was chased, and one
called El Geraoui; but the Alexandrians threw themselves on the Spaniards, chased them, and delivered El
Fadl. A certain number of the Spaniards were killed, the rest took flight toward the ships. El Motaleb
deposed his brother and installed as vali Ishaq ben Abrahat ben El Sabah, in the month of Ramadan of the year
199 [15 April to 14 May 815]; then replaced him by Abou Zakr ben Genadah el Mo'aferi. And when the war broke
out

[PDF p. 527]

between El Seri ben El Hakem and El Motaleb ben 'Abd allah and El Seri had seized Egypt, 'Omar ben Melâk threw
himself on Abou Zakr, chased him from Alexandria, and called El Geraoui. The Spaniards joined him, but as they
devastated everything, he ordered them to reintegrate their ships, which irritated them. There had appeared
in Alexandria a sect that one named the Soufis, preaching the good and braving the orders of the king. They
had at their head one of them named Abou 'Abd el Rahman El Soufi; these people went hand in hand with the
Spaniards and had asked the assistance of the Lakhm, the most powerful tribe of all the region of Alexandria.
Abou 'Abd el Rahman El Soufi was summoned before 'Omar ben Melâk, on the subject of a woman. He was condemned
and, full of anger, went to the Spaniards, formed an alliance with them and with the Lakhm, the Spaniards
hoping to draw vengeance on 'Omar ben Melâk. To the number of 10,000, they went against him and besieged him
in his palace; 'Omar, not believing himself in safety there and fearing that the enemies might penetrate by
main force as far as him and seize his women, had himself washed, rubbed with aromatics, and clothed in a
shroud, then he ordered his servants to make him descend toward the Spaniards; one made him descend, but the
enemies received him with sword-blows and killed him. The valiyat then passed to his brother Mohammed ben
'Abd Allah, surnamed Gious, who was killed, he too; in his place was named vali of Alexandria, 'Abd Allah El
Battal ben Abd el Ouahed ben Mohammed ben 'Abd El Rahman ben Mo'awiah ben Khadig; he was killed and replaced
by his brother Abou Habirah El Hareth who was killed; in his place was named Khadig ben 'Abd El Ouahed; he was
killed and the revolt ceased. This happened in Dhu'l Qa'dah [13 June to 12 July 815]. At this moment was
broken the alliance formed between the Lakhm and the Spaniards at the time of the murder of Ibn Melâk. The
