war broke out between them: the Lakhm were put to rout and the Spaniards, having made themselves masters of
Alexandria, in the month of Dhu'l Higga, named as vali Abou 'Abd el Rahman El Soufi. Then the pillage, the
rapine, and the murder reached unheard-of proportions. Then the Spaniards, having deposed Abd El Rahman,
named as vali one of them whom one called El Kenani. The Benou Modalleg made war on the Spaniards who,
victorious, chased them from the country, and the Benou Modalleg could not return to Alexandria until El Seri
had asked the Spaniards for the authorization to recall them. The authorization was accorded and they
returned.

[PDF p. 528]

"I," said Abou Qabil, "would fear much more for Alexandria than for the Greeks if I saw come some forty ships
mounted by sailors who would be Muslims only in name and who would come at the end of summer." "What could
forty boats do against such a quantity of people, even were these boats sparkling fires?" "Be silent,
wretches that you are," he cried; "from these boats and those who would mount them would come the ruin of
Alexandria and the surroundings." The news of the death of Ibn Melâk having reached El Geraoui, he set out
with fifty thousand men, established himself before the citadel of Alexandria, and made the siege of it until
its inhabitants were at the end of their forces. But, having learned that El Sari ben El Hakem had sent an
army to Tennis, he returned on his steps, in Moharrem of the year 201 [30 July to 28 August 816]. The
Spaniards called El Sari to their rescue; and, the Egyptians having dismissed El Mamoun to call on Ibrahim
ben El Mahdi, El Geraoui marched against Alexandria, blockaded the Spaniards, and ended by entering the town
without striking a blow, by treaty, and the inhabitants prayed in his name. Then, marching on Fostat, he
combated El Sari, killed his son, and withdrew. The Spaniards, in concert with the governor named by El
Geraoui, chased and deposed the latter and called on El Seri. El Geraoui marched against them in the month of
Ramadan of the year 203 [2 to 31 March 819]. At Sakha, the Copts, to the number of two hundred thousand and
supported by the Benou Modalleg, attempted to resist him; El Geraoui put them to flight and sent back his
army to Alexandria of which it made the siege. At this moment, wars broke out between El Sari and the
inhabitants of the Said. Geraoui went therefore for the fourth time to Alexandria, besieged it, and set up
machines of war. This lasted seven months, from the 1st of Sha'ban of the year 204 [21 January 820] to the
end of the month of Safar of the year 205 [14 August 820]. El Geraoui, struck by a splinter of stone launched
by a machine, died the last day of Safar of the year 205. His son Ali succeeded him. The troubles caused at
Alexandria by the Spaniards ceased only at the arrival in Egypt of Abd allah ben Taher, sent by the emir of
the believers El Mamoun. He expelled from Egypt Obeid allah ben El Sari and went to Alexandria with the
non-Muslim chiefs of the Khorassan at the beginning of Safar of the year 212 [2 May 827]; he besieged [...]

[PDF p. 529]

[COLLECTION OF TRADITIONS ON ALEXANDRIA, continued]

the town for more than ten nights; the inhabitants came to ask the aman (safe-conduct). He made peace with
the Spaniards and agreed with them that they would leave Alexandria and would withdraw where they wished, on
condition that they would not take on their ships anyone of Egypt, neither slave nor free man. If they did
it, it would be permitted him to kill them and break the pact. When they had departed, Ibn Taher sent someone
to inspect their ships and one found there a quantity of people whom the treaty forbade them to take. The
order was given to burn their ships, but they supplicated and promised to execute the conventions. One
accorded them pardon, and they departed for the island of Crete and seized it under the conduct of the emir
Abou Hafs 'Omar ben 'Eïssa. After him, his son took the government of the island which the Spaniards occupied
until the year 345 [19 April 956 to 3 April 957], epoch when the Greeks attacked it and seized it after a
long siege. Ibn Taher named as vali of Alexandria Elias ben Ased ben Saman and returned to Fostat in Gemadi
II, then left for Iraq; and when the revolt of the Delta broke out in Gemadi I of the year 216 [16 June to 15
July 831], El Afshin combated the insurgents in agreement with Eïsi ben Mansour El Rafeqi, emir of Egypt.
'Abd Allah ben Yezid ben Mezid El Shibani was sent into the Gharbieh, but he was put to rout and pursued as
far as Alexandria where the Benou Modalleg, gathered against him, besieged him in Shawal. El Afshin entered
into campaign and, by a rapid march, went on Alexandria with his army. He met a party of the Benou Modalleg,
put them twice to rout, made them prisoners, killed them people, and entered into Alexandria the
next-to-last day of Dhu'l Higga [5 February 832]. The governor of the town fled; this chief was Mo'awiah ben
'Abd el Ouahed ben Mohammed ben Abd El Rahman ben Mo'awiah ben Khadig. El Afshin arranged the affairs of
Hashem, then marched against the people of Bashroud who held their heads up to him until the arrival of Al
Mamoun in Egypt. The latter went to El Bashroud where El Afshin had attacked the Copts, as is reported above.

When Ibrahim ben Ahmed ben Mohammed ben El Aghlab was vali of Ifriqiah in the year 261 [16 October 874 to 5
October 875], his conduct was very beautiful; the caravans and the merchants

[PDF p. 530]

traveled in all confidence on the roads. He built fortresses and watchtowers on the shore of the sea, in so
great a number that Ceuta and Alexandria were connected by a line of fires and that the news was transmitted
in a single night from one town to the other.

In Moharrem of the year 302 [27 July to 25 August 914], Habassat entered Alexandria with the army of Ifriqiah
comprising 100,000 men and more; but an army of rescue having been sent from the Orient by El Tekin, emir of
Egypt, Habassat abandoned Alexandria. A military proclamation was made at Fostat the 20th of Gemadi II [10
January 915]; no one remained behind nor abstained from going to Ghizeh, except those who could not, either
by cause of sickness or for any other valid cause. Habassat having advanced against them, they went to meet
him and put him to flight; but Habassat turned them, killed nearly 10,000 men of the Egyptians, and departed
again for Ifriqiah leaving Egypt filled with troubles. In Ramadan [20 March to 18 April 915], the slave
Mounas arrived from Iraq with a numerous army, chased El Tekin in Dhu'l Qa'dah [18 May to 16 June 915], named
as vali Deka the One-Eyed, in Safar of the year 303 [16 August to 13 September 915]; then marched with his
troops on Alexandria, having pursued and imprisoned whoever, by letter, qualified him as lord of Africa; a
great number even were killed, and the people of Libya and of Maraqiah made their appearance at Alexandria in
Shawal of the year 304 [28 March to 25 April 917], fleeing for fear of the master of Barca.

In the year 307 [3 June 919 to 22 May 926], the vanguard of El Mahdi 'Obeïd Allah, commanded by his son
Abou-l Qassem, arrived from Ifriqiah into Libya, put to flight the Alexandrians, and the Libyans abandoned
the town. Mozaffar, son of Deka the One-Eyed, came out of it with his troops, and the army of Abou-l Qassem
entered there the Friday 22nd of Safar [24 July 919]. The people of the militia fled from Fostat into Syria.
Deka, emir of Egypt, went to Ghizeh, camped there, then fell ill and died on his camp bed, at Ghizeh in Rabi'
I [1 to 26 April 919]. After him, Takin was named vali for the second time by El Moqtader; he installed
himself at Ghizeh. The ships

[PDF p. 531]

of the sovereign of Ifriqiah advanced toward Alexandria, commanded by the slave Soliman; the fleet of Tarsus,
having at its head the slave Thamal, arrived in its turn, and the two fleets met near Rosetta, in the month
of Shawal, and gave each other battle. God raised a wind that pushed back the fleet of Soliman toward the
shore where the greatest part of its ships was broken and their contents removed by main force; the crews
were for the most part massacred, the rest led away in captivity to Fostat; one killed them thus nearly seven
hundred men. Abou-l Qassem ben El Mahdi went from Alexandria to the Fayoum, seized the island of Ashmounein
and the Fayoum, and repelled from it the Egyptian army. Thamal the slave arrived with his boats at
Alexandria; the soldiers of Ifriqiah who were there attempted to repel him, but they were vanquished and the
Alexandrians fell back on Rosetta. Thamal reached Fostat and, with his boats, went to Illahoun, where he was
rejoined by the army, and with it penetrated into the Fayoum, in Safar of the year 307 [3 to 31 July 919];
Abou-l Qassem ben El Mahdi, who had marched on Barca, returned to Fostat without having delivered battle.
Alexandria and its territory remained thus in continual troubles until the time when appeared the army of El
Mo'ezz li din Allah, commanded by the general Gouher (Jawhar), in the year 358 [25 November 968 to 13
November 969]; this army seized the town and maintained itself there until the time when appeared Nezar ben
El Mostanser. What the latter did is reported in the chapter that treats of the magazines of the palace.

In the year 612 [2 May 1215 to 19 April 1216], three thousand Frankish merchants gathered at Alexandria and a
warship presented itself in the port carrying two Frankish kings come with the intention of assailing and
combating the inhabitants and seizing the country. But El Malek El 'Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub marched on
Alexandria, had arrested the merchants of whom we have spoken and the people of the ship, removed what they
possessed of precious, imprisoned them, and imprisoned also the two kings; at the end of a certain time, the
sultan gave back the liberty to the captives and to their wives and returned to Cairo.

In the year 554 [23 January 1159 to 11 January 1160], El Melek El Saleh Talah' ben Rozik built, to protect
Belbeis, a citadel of bricks.

In the year 562 [21 December 1166 to 9 December 1167], took place the collision of El Babein between the
vizier Shaour and Ased

[PDF p. 532]

el din Shirkaouah (Shirkuh); the troops of Shirkaouah were put to flight and a part passed to Alexandria;
then, fate favored Shirkaouah against Shaour who took flight toward Cairo; Shirkaouah having gone to
Alexandria, the garrison commanded by Negm el din Mohammed ben Mousal, vali of the frontier, the Cadi El
Achraf ben El Khebab, his intendant the Cadi El Rashid ben El Zobeid came to meet him, saluted him, and
delivered him the town. He left it to go into the Said, leaving his nephew Salah el din Youssef ben Ayoub
(Saladin) as lieutenant charged with the frontier post with a thousand cavaliers. Shaour came to attack him,
seconded by Mori (Amaury), king of the Franks; but the entire population marched with Salah el din and
delivered to Shaour innumerable combats. The latter had managed to gather 24,000 cavaliers. Moreover, he
promised the people to lighten the taxes and the laws and to abandon to them the fifth of the booty if they
delivered him Salah el din. They refused and claimed the combat. Then Shaour rendered the siege more pressing
and the victuals became rare among the besieged. But Shirkaouah, having gathered a considerable troop of
Bedouins, arrived to their rescue. Shaour sent to him a messenger charged with offering him five thousand
dinars if he wished to return to Syria. Shirkaouah accepted, the town was opened, and Salah el din went to
Mori, the king of the Franks, and remained with him. Shaour gave no respite to the Frankish king, that he
deliver him Salah el din. But far from consenting to it, Mori sent him back to his uncle Shirkaouah; Salah el
din, as well as all those who were with him, went first by sea to Acre to rejoin his uncle, and from there to
Damascus. Shaour entered Alexandria the 17th of Shawal [29 September 1162]. Ibn Mousal hid himself, then fled
into Syria; but, Shaour having seized Ibn el Khebab, he held him prisoner until his people had bought him
back for an enormous ransom; he could do nothing against Ibn el Zobeïd, and marched against Rosetta. The
fiqih Abou-l Taher ben 'Ouf and a great number of the inhabitants had fortified themselves in the Pharos.
Shaour occupied himself with their affair and Ibn 'Ouf said to him: "Grant our prayer, O emir of the army,
and pardon us what we have done." He pardoned them. He named as intendant of the Treasury the Cadi El Ashraf
Abou-l Qassem Abd el Rahman ben Mansour ben Naga; then he left for Cairo, accompanied by Mori, the king of
the Franks who, subsequently, returned to his country.

In the year 671 [29 July 1272 to 17 July 1273], arrived the news that the Franks were preparing an expedition

[PDF p. 533]

against the littoral of Egypt. El Melek El Zaher Beibars had the galleasses prepared and planted on the walls
of Alexandria about a hundred machines.

The Thursday 5th of the month of Rageb of the year 727 [5 Rageb 727 = 27 May 1327], a Frankish merchant having
gone to the sea-gate where a popular feast was being held, took up a dispute there with a young beardless boy
whose complaisance he was claiming. A Muslim who was there took the thing badly and said: "That is not
licit." The Frank, removing his shoe, struck with it the face of the Muslim who called for help. One ran up,
the Franks took the side of their companion; the melee became general and the military commander had to mount
his horse, close the gates of the town, and set about searching for the instigators of the brawl; these
having taken flight, the commander returned to his palace and had the gates of the town kept closed. There
was thus outside the town a considerable number of persons whose affairs claimed them and who had to pass the
whole night outside their homes, howling and crying near the gates. The guardians went to the commander and
insisted that the gates be opened. One ended by opening them and all precipitated themselves to enter,
jostling and pushing one another, so much so that more than ten persons died there, that there was a crowd of
broken limbs, a number of turbans, handkerchiefs, and other objects lost, and weeping and cries during all
the night. Thus when, the morning come, the vali wished to go on horseback to make account of the situation,
he was thrown down from his horse and one launched stones at him; he attempted to escape and regained his
castle; one pursued him there and assailed him; he answered from the top of his castle and there were floods
of blood spilled. The rebels set fire to the gate of the castle and pillaged the neighboring houses. The vali
had to write to ask the assistance of the vali of Damanhour and of the Bedouins of the vicinity. These
arrived, surrounded the town, and sent by pigeons to the sultan the news that the Alexandrians had revolted.
The sultan entered into a violent anger, for he feared that the populace might set at liberty the imprisoned
emirs. He had the Cadis come and, having gathered them, asked them what should be done regarding this
struggle, and they wrote: "What is fitting." And the vizier Mogholtay El Gemali, Toughan Shah El Dawawin,
Aïdmer, commander of the bodyguards, and a great number of royal mamelukes, departed with the intendant of
the private Treasury. The vizier was bearer [...]

[PDF p. 534]

[COLLECTION OF TRADITIONS ON ALEXANDRIA, continued]

of a note ordering to put to death the corrupt people and instigators of quarrels; to seize the goods of the
people of the country, to seize the arms which served only to multiply the brawls, to make sure of the Cadi
and the clerks, and to transport the imprisoned emirs to Cairo. All departed therefore in all haste and
reached in 3 days Alexandria. The vizier stopped at El Kheis, on whose inhabitants he struck a contribution
of 500,000 Egyptian dinars; he had put in irons the Cadi of the Cadis, 'Amad el din, and his clerk; for one
found it bad that both had proclaimed the holy war in the country; but both denied having provoked these
incidents, alleging that it was not in their power to bring back to duty a crowd so considerable. The clerk
Ibn El Shibi was struck with terrible blows and constrained to pay 600,000 dirhems; the cadi had to pay
500,000. One wished to have him hanged, but in the letter he wrote to the sultan, he showed himself so humble,
asking for pardon and absolution, that the sultan pardoned him and pursued the populace. Thirty rebels were
sawed in two the Friday 13th [13 Rageb 727 = 4 June 1327]. The population, filled with terror, regained its
lodging; numerous turbans flew off and for twenty days, the terror only increased. The sultan sent an order
to punish the rebels and confiscate their goods. The vizier showed himself devoted in his response, and
having prepared the imprisoned emirs, he left in his turn the frontier post, after having asked the
surrender of the arms that were there; he gathered thus six thousand complete equipments which he put all in
a hall on which he affixed the seals. He collected also from the population more than 260,000 dinars. This
was one of the most painful trials and one of the most deplorable events. To God belongs what has preceded
and what must follow.

[PDF p. 535]

CHAPTER XVIII
OF THE TOWN OF ATRIB

This town was built by Atrib ben Qobtim ben Maiz ben Beïsar, son of Cham, son of Noah. "After the death of
his father Qobtim," says Ibn Ouacif Shah, "Atrib withdrew into his province -- that is, into the town his
father had constructed for him. It was twelve miles long and possessed twelve gates. He placed in its
principal street three cupolas raised on columns, one above the other. Of these cupolas, one was at the
center and the two others at the two extremities of the town. Each cupola was surmounted by a great
watchtower. In each quarter was a circus, places where one could sit, places of pleasure exposed to the
Orient. To the west of the town, he dug a canal on which he threw bridges bearing uninterrupted seats; round
about were habitations bathed by the canal and communicating by bridges with gardens full of vegetation,
beyond which extended orchards and flowerbeds. Each of the gates was endowed with a marvel; statues, images
that moved, talismans defending the approach of the gate. At the entrance of each of the gates, and on each
side of the gate, was raised the image of a demon made of copper; if some man of good approached it, the
statue of the right laughed aloud, while the demon of the left wept if some dishonest man approached it. In
each of the places of pleasure, he gathered what was found of most beautiful in the way of tamed animals and
singing birds. On the cupolas of the town, he placed a statue that whistled when the wind blew, and raised a
mirror in which one saw the distant countries. Facing it, to the Orient, he constructed a town where he
established circuses and, on the exterior, raised statues of different aspects; in the middle was placed a
basin such that if a bird passed near it, it fell in and could not come out, so much so that one could take
it. He furnished this town with a citadel of twelve gates, on each of which was a statue that did marvelous
things. All around were planted gardens, and in the vicinity, on the side of the East, was built a belvedere
raised on eight pillars and surmounted by a cupola on which was a bird with deployed wings that whistled
three times a day: in the morning, at noon, and at the setting of the sun. In the interior were

[PDF p. 536]

raised statues and numerous marvels. This king constructed numerous towns and installed there a man named
Borsan, who occupied himself with chemistry and struck there dinars weighing each seven metsqals and bearing
his cipher. Atrib reigned 360 years and reached the age of 500 years; one made him a naos in the eastern
mountain; one dug there an underground passage plated with glass and marble, and the body was deposited on a
bed of gold incrusted (with precious stones); near him, one deposited his treasures and one put on the door
the image of a dragon that no one could approach without perishing. One threw over it sand and one inscribed
on the tomb his name and the epoch of his life."

There are in Egypt, says Ibn El Kandi, four regions that have not their like on the surface of the earth, nor
under the sky: the region of the Fayoum, the region of Atrib, the region of Samanoud, and the region of
Antinoe. The region of Atrib forms part of the ensemble of the regions of the Delta and comprises 108
villages. The towns of the magicians were, it is said, in Egypt, to the number of seven: Erment, Beba,
Bousir, Antinoe, San, Atrib, and Sa.

[PDF p. 537]

CHAPTER XIX
OF THE TOWN OF TENNIS

Tennis is a locality of Egypt, situated in the middle of the water; it forms part of the region of the Khalig
and takes its name from Tennis, son of Cham, son of Noah. It is said that it was built by Qlimoun, of the
lineage of Atrib ben Qobtim, one of the ancient kings of the Copts.

After Atrib, says Ibn Ouacif Shah, reigned his daughter who administered and directed the kingdom wisely and
guided it with energy and vigor for 35 years, after which she died, leaving the government to the son of her
sister, Qlimoun; the latter gave back to the viziers their prerogatives, reintegrated in their ranks the
priests whose advice directed every thing. He rendered the country more prosperous and sought with ardor the
science.

In his time was built the first Tennis which the sea submerged, although it was primitively at a great
distance from it and the town was surrounded by cultivations, plantations of trees and vines, villages,
wine-presses, and a territory more prosperous than any other. In the middle of the region, the king had had
raised a belvedere surmounted by cupolas and decorated with the most beautiful ornaments and the most
beautiful engravings; he had had it hung with hangings and skillfully arranged. As soon as the Nile began to
rise, the king went to this town, installed himself there until the Nourouz, then returned. The king had had
the idea of distributing the waters and giving to each village its part. There was, in these villages, a
citadel surrounded by bridges, and each king came there and worked to render it prosperous and to improve
it; all made of it their place of pleasure.

It is said that the two gardens of which God speaks in his sublime book, when he says: "Propose to them the
example of these two men: to one, we have given two gardens planted with vines that we have surrounded with
palms, etc." (Koran, XVIII, 31); it is said that these two gardens were those of two brothers of the royal
house, between whom was divided this region and who regulated admirably its culture, its industry, and its
construction; the king

[PDF p. 538]

came to divert himself in these two gardens which produced the most beautiful fruits and vegetables, of which
one made the most delicious dishes and drinks. One of the two brothers, hospitable and charitable, marveled
at this place, gave his part by way of beneficence; the other, egoistic and avaricious, seeing his brother
give all his goods, mocked him, and each time the first wished to sell something, the second bought it from
him, so much so that the first came to possess nothing more and the garden became the property of his brother
of whom he was obliged to ask alms. But the avaricious one repelled him and chased him, reproaching him for
his prodigality. "I had," he said, "advised you to keep what you had and you did not do it; my avarice
profited from it, and I have become richer than you, my children are also more numerous." And he turned away
from his brother, happy to be the master of so much riches and of so beautiful a garden. But God gave an
order to the sea which submerged the region and drowned it entirely; and the proprietor set about lamenting
and groaning over his ruin, saying: "Would to God that I had associated no one with my Lord! For God has
said: There is no troop so small that it cannot be victorious with the help of God!"

In the time of the king Qlimoun was built the town of Damietta; Qlimoun reigned 90 years and constructed
himself a naos in the eastern mountain; he disposed all around treasures, precious stones, and all sorts of
precious things; at the entrance, he placed statues that turned by means of mechanisms, and that held in hand
swords with which they pierced whoever wished to enter. To the right and to the left, he placed two lions of
gilded copper furnished with a mechanism and that tore those who approached. On the naos one engraved these
words: "This is the tomb of Qlimoun ben Atrib ben Qobtim ben Masr, who lived long days. When death came to
find him, he could not repel it. Let whoever will come to him remove nothing of what is his, but let him take
what is near him."

It is said that Tennis was the brother of Doumiat (Damietta), and El Masa'oudi, in his book of the Prairies
of Gold, and other authors report that Tennis was a land that had not its like in Egypt; the climate there
was temperate, the soil excellent, the gardens, the palms, the vines, the trees, the fields abounded there,
canals watered there the high lands, and no one had seen a country more beautiful than this region, nor where
the gardens and the vines were as continuous; and, in Egypt, there was no canton that resembled it,

[PDF p. 539]

[OF THE TOWN OF TENNIS, continued]

except the Fayoum. The water arrived there without interruption summer and winter, and the inhabitants
watered, when it pleased them, their gardens and their cultivations. All the water then threw itself into the
sea, both by its own canals and by the place called El Ashtoum. Between the sea and this region, there was
the distance of a day's march.

Between El 'Arish and the island of Cyprus, there was formerly a road that led to Cyprus and where the beasts
walked dry-shod; and between El 'Arish and Cyprus, there was only a small space of sea, until the moment when
the water submerged the road that connected El 'Arish to Cyprus. 251 years after Diocletian, the water of the
sea covered a part of the places that today bear the name of lake of Tennis and submerged them; and the
invasion increased each year, so much so that the waters ended by entirely covering this lake. All the
villages situated in the low part of the region were submerged, while of those situated on the high terrains,
there remained Tounah, Boura, and others still that exist even at present, and are surrounded by the waters.
The inhabitants of the villages situated in this lake transport their dead to Tennis, and there one has been
able to disinter them after the others. The total inundation of the region was accomplished a hundred years
before the conquest of Egypt. A king who resided at Farma had wars to sustain with one of the governors of
Baliana and the surrounding places; to defend one against the other, they dug ditches and opened canals going
from the Nile to the sea; thus the water, forced to escape from the Nile, extended itself and covered this
region.

Masa'oudi, in his book "Chronicle of the Time," recounts that Tennis was a considerable town furnished with a
hundred gates. According to Ibn Batlan, Tennis is a small country situated in an island in the middle of the
sea, at five degrees to the south of the middle of the fourth climate; the land of it is salty and the air
very variable. The inhabitants drink water stored in cisterns that one fills each year at the moment when the
waters of the lake become sweeter, thanks to the arrival of the waters of the Nile. All the town has need of
is brought by boats: the inhabitants there feed themselves above all on fish, cheese, and cow's milk; indeed,
the farm of the sultani cheese brings 700 dinars, each thousand cheese-molds bringing a dinar and a half. The
farm of the fish produces 10,000 dinars. The character of the inhabitants is gentle and easy; their nature is
inclined to indolence and to softness. The physician Abou-l Seri reports that there were born there each year
two hundred hermaphrodite (?) children who loved cleanliness, gentleness, song, and voluptuousness, and most
of them passed the nights in drunkenness and took very little exercise, because of the smallness of the
country; thus their bodies were filled with corrupt matters. In this town appeared a malady named the hiccup
of Tennis, which raged for thirty years on the inhabitants.

[PDF p. 540]

The author of the history of Damietta recounts that Tennis was governed by Abou Thour, a Christian Arab;
after the conquest of Damietta, the Muslims marched on Tennis; an army of 20,000 men composed of Christian
Arabs, Copts, and Greeks went to meet them. The war lasted until the moment when Abou Thour fell into the
hands of the Muslims and his army was put to rout. The Muslims entered into the town, converted the church
into a mosque, divided the booty, and left for Farma. And Tennis did not cease to belong to the Muslims until
Bechr ben Safouan El Kelbi took, in the name of Yezid ben 'Abd el Melek, the government of Egypt, in the
month of Ramadan of the year 101 [16 March to 14 April 720]. At this epoch, the Greeks descended at Tennis,
killed Mozahem ben Mosallimah El Mouradi, governor of the town, and a great number of notables. It is
regarding them that the poet said:

[verses:] Were you not struck and edified when men recounted to you the misfortunes befallen the lords of
Tennis?

Tennis was a great town, in which were a great number of monuments of the Ancients; the inhabitants of it
were rich and opulent. The greatest number were weavers; and at Tennis, one wove robes of linen such as one
made nowhere else; one executed there for the caliph a robe named el badnah in which entered of thread only
two oques, for the weft and the warp, the rest of the stuff being of gold; the whole was of a perfect work
and had no need to be cut or sewn; the value of this robe reached a thousand dinars. There was nowhere in the
world a loom where was executed a robe of simple linen without gold, elsewhere than at Tennis and at
Damietta. When one let free course to the Nile, the people who inhabited to the east of Farmah, in the
regions of Gergir and of Faqous, could feed themselves there by the canal of Tennis. Tennis was one of the
towns

[PDF p. 541]

most considerable of Egypt. At Sheta, Difou, Damirah, Tounah, and in the neighboring islands, one fabricated
light tissues, but which remained well below those of Tennis and of Damietta. The exportation of these stuffs
into Iraq produced per year, until after the year 360 [4 November 970 to 23 October 971], from twenty
thousand to thirty thousand dinars. When the vizier Ya'qoub ben Keles was named intendant of the finances, he
made this industry disappear by his vexations. The inhabitants of Tennis and of Damietta were Christians
submitted to the protection. The people of the country took with nets, at the door of their houses, the
quails and other birds; the semani is a bird that comes from the sea and falls into these nets. The boats
went from Tennis to Farma, following the shore of the sea.

At the death of Haroun El Rashid, his son Mohammed El Amin succeeded him and wished to act treacherously and
perfidiously toward El Mamoun. Egypt had for governor Hatem ben Harthemah ben A'ïn who administered in the
name of El Amin. The people of the Tenou and of Nama having revolted against him, he sent against them El
Seri ben El Hâkem and 'Abd El 'Aziz ben El Ouazir El Geraouï who were victorious after the 8th of Shawal of
the year 194 [15 July 810]. Then the emir Gaber ben El Ash'ath El Tayi was named governor and Hatem ben
Harthamah was destituted. Gaber was a gentle man. In that time, the relations grew tense between Mohammed El
Amin and his brother Abdallah El Mamoun. Mohammed despoiled his brother of the Empire to which he had right,
had his name suppressed in the prayers pronounced from the pulpit, and replaced it by that of his son Mousa
to whom he gave the surname of El Shedid, name under which the prayers were recited. The troops of Egypt who
held for El Mamoun came to an understanding in order to dispossess Mohammed. Gaber sent a messenger to turn
them away from this project and to frighten them on the disastrous results their mutiny would have. But El
Seri ben El Hakem arrived inciting the people to overthrow Mohammed. El Seri was one of those who had come to
Egypt in the time of El Rashid with the army of El Leith ben El Fadl; he was an obscure man who made himself
celebrated by the ardor he put into overthrowing Mohammed El Amin.

El Mamoun wrote to the notables of Egypt to engage them to rise up in his favor; they consented to it,
proclaimed El Mamoun caliph, in Rageb

[PDF p. 542]

of the year 196 [18 March to 16 April 812], and went against Gaber, expelled him, and named as vali 'Abad ben
Mohammed. Mohammed El Amin, instructed of these facts, wrote to the principal chiefs of the Hauf to announce
to them the nomination to the post of vali of Rabi'ah ben Qeis El Garshy, chief of the Qeïssites of the Hauf.
All the inhabitants of the Hauf, Yemenites and Qeïssites, embraced his cause, united themselves openly to
Amin, and rejected El Mamoun; they went to Fostat to combat there the inhabitants; after two combats, they
departed again, then returned on several occasions to deliver battle. 'Abad ben Mohammed sent 'Abd El Aziz El
Geraouï with an army destined to combat the rebels at their home. 'Abd El 'Aziz set out, in Dhu'l Qa'dah of
the year 197 [4 July to 2 August 813], and engaged the combat at 'Aïrit. But El Geraouï, put to rout,
withdrew to Faqous with his troops of Arabs of Lakhm and of Godam. His soldiers said to him: "Why are you not
of your own party; certainly you are worth as much as those who are masters of the country." And with them he
passed to Tennis, established himself there, and sent employees to collect the tax of the Delta; but Rabi'ah
ben Qeïs sent in his turn people charged with preventing the collection. The inhabitants of the Hauf went, in
Moharrem of the year 198 [1 to 30 September 813], to Fostat where they delivered a combat in which perished a
great number of soldiers of the two armies. The news of the death of El Amin having reached the people of the
Hauf, they dispersed. El Mamoun named as emir of Egypt Motaleb ben 'Abd Allah El Khoza'i, who came to take
possession of his post in Rabi' I [30 October to 28 November 813], and confided the command of the guard to
'Abd el 'Aziz El Geraouï; later, he deposed him and charged him with a military expedition in the Delta. Then
El Motaleb having been destituted was replaced by El 'Abbas ben Mousa ben 'Eïsi, in Shawal [25 May to 22 June
814]; El 'Abbas recalled 'Abd el Aziz to the command of the guard. When the troops, again revolted, had
recalled El Motaleb, in Moharrem of the year 197 [22 August to 20 September 814], El Geraouï fled to Tennis;
El 'Abbas ben Mousa ben 'Eïsi set out from Mecca for the Hauf, camped at Balbeïs, and asked the assistance of
the Qeïssites; then he went to Tennis to El Geraouï who gave him the counsel to install himself on the
territory of the Qeïssites; he returned therefore to Balbeïs in Gemadi II [17 January to 14 February 815] and
died there,

[PDF p. 543]

poisoned in a dish that El Motaleb had prepared for him by the Qeïssites. The inhabitants of the Haufs then
submitted to El Motaleb and proclaimed him their master; they hastened to go to the well of 'Amirah and, as
soon as they had met him, made peace with him. El Motaleb sent to El Geraouï the order to go to Fostat; but
he refused to obey and navigated on his ships as far as Shatnouf. El Motaleb sent him El Seri ben El Hakem
with an army to ask him for peace; he consented to it, then sought to use ruse with them; but they were on
their guard. El Geraouï then retrograded on Bena, pursued by the enemies who harassed him. In his turn, he
asked for peace and showed himself amiable to El Seri. The latter went to meet El Geraouï on a boat. El
Geraouï did the same, and both met in the middle of the Nile, facing Sandefa. But El Geraouï had had prepared
in his boat ropes and given the order to his men who had remained at Sendefa to pull the ropes to themselves
as soon as his boat would be stuck to that of El Seri. The boat of El Geraouï therefore, having accosted that
of El Seri, El Geraouï attached it to his own boat and, the ropes being pulled, El Seri was made prisoner and
led to Tennis where El Geraouï had him imprisoned. It was in Gamadi I [18 December 814 to 16 January 815]. El
Geraouï continued the campaign, and having joined the army of El Motaleb at Saft Salit in Rageb [15 February
to 16 March 815], he defeated it. When 'Omar ben Melak had been destituted from his post of governor of
Alexandria, he revolted with the Spaniards and took the party of El Geraouï; 'Abd Allah ben Mousa ben 'Eïsi
marched on Egypt to avenge the murder of his brother El 'Abbas, in Moharrem of the year 200 [11 August to 9
September 815]; he united his troops to those of 'Abd el Aziz El Geraouï and both set out with numerous
troops, by the river and by land, and arrived at Gizeh. El Motaleb went to meet them with the Egyptians and a
battle was delivered in the month of Safar [10 September to 8 October 815]. El Geraouï returned to Sherqioun
and 'Abd Allah ben Mousa passed to the Hedjaz. El Motaleb having learned, beyond doubt, that it was Abou
Harmelah Farag El Asoued who had written to 'Abd Allah ben Mousa and had pushed him to undertake his
expedition, had him searched for, but Abou Harmelah fled to El Geraouï. El Motaleb activated his preparations
to combat El Geraouï, but the latter, having brought El Seri ben El Hakem out of prison, made with him a
treaty that obliged him [...]

[PDF p. 544]

[OF THE TOWN OF TENNIS, continued]

to revolt against El Motaleb and to depose him. El Seri having accepted this convention, was set at liberty;
he made known to the inhabitants of Egypt that letters had reached him naming him vali. The army composed of
people of the Khorassan came to meet him and recognized him as master, but the Egyptians refused to accept
him as vali. He went therefore to his house at El Hamra and, his troops having increased by a crowd of
Qeïssites who had joined him, he delivered combat to the Egyptians, put them to flight, and made of them a
great massacre. El Motaleb asked him for the aman which was accorded him, left Egypt, leaving El Seri ben El
Hakem completely master of the country, at the beginning of the month of Ramadan [3 April 816].

After the massacre of 'Omar ben Melak by the Spaniards, El Geraouï marched on Alexandria with 50,000 men. But
El Seri having sent an army to Tennis, El Geraouï returned on his steps and reentered Tennis in Moharrem of
the year 201 [30 July to 28 August 816]. The army having revolted against El Seri in the month of Rabi' I [27
September to 26 October 816], and having proclaimed Soliman ben Rhaleb, 'Abad ben Mohammed rose up against him
and deposed him. 'Ali ben Hamzah ben Ga'far ben Soliman ben Aly ben 'Abd Allah ben 'Abbas seized the power at
the beginning of Sha'ban, but Abad refused to recognize him and united himself to El Geraouï to whom soon
came to join himself also Soliman ben Rhaleb; El Seri, who was also with him, reentered possession of the
valiyat of Egypt, in Sha'ban, and fortified his authority. In Moharrem of the year 202 [20 July to 18 August
817], reached El Seri a letter of El Ma'moun prescribing to have proclaimed as heir of the caliphate Aly ben
Mousa El Radi who was, indeed, recognized in Egypt. But Ibrahim ben El Mahdi rose up against him at Baghdad;
he wrote to the chiefs of the army of Egypt, engaging them to depose El Mamoun and his adoptive heir and to
attack El Seri. In consequence, El Hareth ben Zar'ah ben Moharrem at Fostat, 'Abd el 'Aziz ben El Ouazir el
Geraouï in the Delta, and Mosallimah ben 'Abd el Melek El Tahaoui in the Said revolted against El Seri and
declared themselves for Ibrahim ben El Mahdi. They confided by common accord the direction of the affair to
'Abd el 'Aziz ben 'Abd el Rahman El Azdi. El Seri having delivered him battle made him prisoner in Safar [19
August to 16 September 817]. All those who refused to recognize Aly El Radi

[PDF p. 545]

joined El Geraouï who had entrenched himself in Tennis and who saw his authority grow. He marched on
Alexandria, seized it, had the prayer made there in his name as well as in the towns of the Said; then he set
out with a strong army to combat El Seri; each of the two adversaries had gathered the most forces possible
to crush the other. El Seri sent against El Geraouï his son Meïmoun; the two armies met at Shatnouf and
Meïmoun was killed in Gemadi I of the year 203 [4 November to 3 December 818]. El Geraouï went with his fleet
to Fostat to burn the town; the people of the mosque came to find him and by their supplications softened
him; he left therefore Fostat and went on several occasions to make war against Alexandria. He was killed
there, at the end of Safar of the year 205 [14 August 820], by a stone launched by a machine; three months
after, El Seri died in his turn, at the end of Gemadi I [11 November 820]. After El Geraouï, his son Aly ben
'Abd el 'Aziz El Geraouï took his place and made war on Abou Nasr Mohammed ben El Seri, who had been named
emir of Egypt at Shatnouf after the death of his father. The two armies met at Damanhour, and it is said that
in the combat that was then delivered 7,000 men were killed; the son of El Seri fled to Fostat, pursued by
the ships of the son of El Geraouï; but the ships turned back and Abou Harmelah Farag interposed himself
between the combatants until they had made peace.

The son of El Seri died in Sha'ban of the year 206 [30 December 821 to 27 January 822], and after him the
valiyat passed to 'Obeïd Allah ben El Seri, who provoked in nothing the son of El Geraouï. El Mamoun sent to
Egypt Mokhallad ben Yezid ben Mozid el Shibani with an army of Arabs Rabi'ah; but 'Obeïd Allah ben El Seri
refused to make him his submission and fortified himself; they delivered each other battle, and Ali ben El
Geraouï joined Khaled ben Yezid, procured him victuals and provisions, and having set out, came to camp in
advance of the entrenchments of 'Obeïd Allah ben El Seri. The two armies delivered each other battle in the
month of Rabi' I of the year 207 [15 July to 23 August 822], and other combats followed which lasted until
the moment when Khaled withdrew into the Hauf. The son of El Geraouï, worried, used ruse and made depart from
his province Khaled who passed to the west of the Nile, where he established his encampment at Nahia, and the
son of El Geraouï withdrew to Tennis leaving Khaled in

[PDF p. 546]

a very precarious situation. The son of El Seri, profiting from these circumstances, marched against him in
the month of Ramadan [18 January to 16 February 823], made him prisoner, and dispatched him from Egypt to
Mecca by sea. El Ma'moun sent to 'Obeïd Allah ben El Seri his nomination as vali of the territory he
administered -- that is, Fostat Masr, the Said, and the west of the country; at the same time he named as
vali of Tennis and of the eastern Hauf, with farming of the taxes, 'Ali ben 'Abd el 'Aziz el Geraouï. But
when the son of El Geraouï came to collect the taxes of the people of the Hauf, these resisted and wrote to
the son of El Seri, asking him to aid them against El Geraouï. The son of El Seri sent his brother to their
rescue. The two armies met in the district of Bena, at Belqina, and delivered each other battle in Safar of
the year 209 [3 June to 1 July 824]. The struggle continued between them until the 2nd of Rabi' I [3 July
824] without one prevailing over the other. El Geraouï, with those who accompanied him, withdrew to Damietta,
and the son of El Seri marched on Mehallah Sheriqoun which he ravaged. He then sent an expedition against
Tennis and Damietta of which he made himself master. The son of El Geraouï, who during this time was at El
Farma, went to El 'Arish and camped between this last town and Ghazah, then, returning on his steps, he
attacked by surprise Farma, in Gamadi II [29 September to 27 October 824]. The partisans of Ibn El Seri fled
from Tennis and Ibn El Geraouï advanced as far as Shatnouf. Ibn El Seri marched to meet him, and the combat
was engaged. At the beginning of the day fate favored Ibn El Geraouï, but, fallen into the ambushes of Ibn El
Seri, he was put to rout in Regeb [18 October to 16 November 824] and went to El 'Arish. Ibn El Seri marched
on Tennis and Damietta, but, in Moharrem of the year 210 [24 April to 23 May 825], Ibn El Geraouï arrived and
seized Tennis and Damietta without combat. Ibn El Seri sent against him several corps of armies to which El
Geraouï delivered battle. While these two enemies fought thus, 'Abd Allah ben Taher arrived in Egypt; Ibn El
Geraouï went to meet him with riches and provisions, joining himself to him, and with him camped at Balbeïs.
Ibn El Seri resisted and Ibn Taher temporized, thus softening the adversary; he had contributions levied on
the country and went to camp at Zefta. At Zefta, he established across the Nile a dike by which he sent to
Shatnouf

[PDF p. 547]

'Eïzi El Geloudi. He placed at the head of his fleet, which had come from Syria, Ibn El Geraouï whose military
science he knew. El Geraouï put to flight the ships of Ibn El Seri, in Moharrem of the year 211 [13 April to
12 May 826]. Ibn Taher made peace with 'Obeïd Allah ben El Seri in Safar [13 May to 10 June 826], gave him a
robe of honor and made him a gift of 10,000 dinars; then he had him depart and sent him to El Ma'moun; and the
mutinies of Egypt were appeased by 'Abd Allah ben Taher.

In 377 [3 May 987 to 20 April 988], at Tennis, a goat brought to light a kid that had a great number of
horns; the head, the breast, the belly, and all the anterior part of the body were covered with white wool
and the posterior part with black hairs; the tail was like a tail of a ewe. A woman brought into the world a
little kid with a round head and that had two hands, two feet, and a single head, and the antepenultimate day
of Dhu'l Heggah of the same year [19 April 988], there was, at Tennis, a thunder, lightnings, a violent wind,
and profound darkness in the atmosphere; then, when the day reappeared, one saw in the sky a column of fire
that spread a color of a violent red on the sky and on the earth; and there rose a dust and a fog that seized
the throat. And this phenomenon ceased only at the fourth hour of the day, the moment when the sun
reappeared; it renewed itself for five days.

In 332 [4 September 943 to 23 August 944], a man and a woman presented themselves before the cadi of Tennis,
Abou Mohammed 'Abd Allah ben Abou-l Reïs. The woman asked that her husband accomplish that to which he was
obliged. The husband replied: I married her five days ago and I found that she had the attributes of the man
as well as those of the woman. The cadi charged a woman to verify the thing, and the latter declared that the
plaintiff had above her sexual part a member with two testicles and that the vagina was below; the member had
still its prepuce. The woman was very beautiful, but her husband repudiated her.

Abou 'Amr El Kandi says: Abou Naser Ahmed ben Aly told me that Yes ben 'Abd El Ahed had assured him having
heard his father recount this: "When 'Abd Allah ben Taher entered Egypt, I was among those who approached him,
and he said to me: '"Abd Allah ben Lahi'ah recounted to us that Abou Qabil had it from Sabi', who had said:
"O Egyptians, how can

[PDF p. 548]

your affairs march, when the dissension is in your country and you are governed sometimes by a lame man,
sometimes by a yellow man, sometimes by a beardless man. Finally, comes a man of the lineage of El Hasseïn
whose march cannot be delayed and who, despite all the obstacles, fills with justice the Green Sea."'" I have
explained this thus: There was trouble when El Seri governed, who was lame; the yellow man was his son Abou-l
Naser; the beardless one was 'Obeïd Allah ben El Seri, and you, 'Abd Allah ben El Taher, are the descendant
of El Hasseïn.

'Abd Allah ben Taher went to Alexandria, reestablished order there, and sent back Ibn El Geraouï to Iraq;
then, El Afshin came back with him to Egypt in Dhu'l Hegga of the year 215 [19 January to 17 February 831]. El
Afshin had for instructions to ask Ibn El Geraouï for the riches he possessed and, if he refused to deliver
them, to kill him. He asked him for them indeed, but Ibn El Geraouï having delivered him nothing, he killed
him three days after the feast of the Sacrifices (Courban Baïram).

In Gamadi II of the year 219 [13 June to 11 July 834], Yahia ben El Ouazir revolted at Tennis. El Mozaffar
ben Kandar, emir of Egypt, marched against him, engaged the combat near the lake of Tennis, made him
prisoner, and his army abandoned him.

In the year 239 [12 June 853 to 1 June 854], El Moutawaqqel gave the order to raise at Tennis, on the shore
of the sea, a citadel and put at the head of the construction Anbassah ben Ishaq, emir of Egypt, who made
great expenses for this work and for the citadels of Damietta and of Farma. In 249 [24 February 863 to 12
February 864], the waters of the lake of Tennis became sweet summer and winter, then became salty again
summer and winter; previously, they remained sweet for six months and salty for the six others.

In the year 348 [14 March 959 to 2 March 960], arrived from Sicily a fleet that ravaged the town of Tennis.

In the year 378 [21 April 988 to 10 April 989], one fished at Ashtoum-Tennis an enormous fish 28 cubits 1/2
long; on this length, the head occupied by itself 9 cubits; the circuit of the belly and the back was 15
cubits. The opening of the mouth measured 29 spans, and the width of its tail 5 cubits 1/2. It had two hands
that served it as fins and that were each three cubits wide. Its skin was thick, polished, and smooth; the
belly was striped with white and black streaks; its tongue was red and armed with points in the form of
feathers, long about [...]

[PDF p. 549]

[OF THE TOWN OF TENNIS, continued]

a cubit, and of which one made combs, for they resembled shell (tortoiseshell). This fish had two eyes like
eyes of an ox. The emir of Tennis, Abou Ishaq ben Loubah, had its belly opened and the body salted; there was
needed for this a hundred ardebs of salt. The upper jaw was raised and maintained with a long beam of wood,
and a man entered standing upright into the interior of the beast with baskets of salt without bending. One
transported this fish to the palace to show it to El Aziz Billah.

During the night of the Friday 18th of Rabi I of the year 379 [26 June 989], the people of Tennis saw nine
columns of fire shine in the horizon of the sky on the side of the North. And the people came out outside the
town, praying God until the morning, the hour when these fires disappeared. That year, one fished in the lake
of Tennis a big fish a cubit long. Its anterior half, comprising the head, the eyes, the neck, and the
breast, had the form of a lion; the two front paws were fixed to the breast and armed with claws; the
posterior part had the form of a fish without scales. One transported it to Cairo.

In the year 397 [27 September 1006 to 16 September 1007], a young woman brought into the world a daughter with
two heads, one having a white round face and the other a dark and gracious face; each head had two eyes.
These two heads suckled and ate, were placed on a single neck, and had only a single body with two hands, two
feet, a vagina, and a backside. One brought her to El 'Aziz to show her to him; he had money given to the
mother; the child, brought back to Tennis, died there some months after.

In 571 [22 July 1175 to 9 July 1176], arrived at Tennis nearly forty vessels of Sicily that occupied the town
for two days and withdrew; then in the year 573 [30 June 1177 to 18 June 1178] forty ships of Sicily came
again to Tennis, attacked the inhabitants, and seized the town. Mohammed ben Ishaq, admiral of the fleet,
finding himself separated from his vessels, having taken refuge with a handful of Muslims in the place of
prayer of Tennis. When the night had come, he and his companions rushed on the town and threw themselves on
the Franks who were not on their guard; he seized 120 of them and had their heads cut off. In the morning,
the Franks attacked the mosque, struggling with what was there of Muslims and killed nearly 70 of them; the
rest fled to Damietta. The Franks having pillaged Tennis,

[PDF p. 550]

set fire to it, burned it, and withdrew, the hands filled with booty and leading away numerous captives, in
the direction of Alexandria; they had stayed at Tennis for four days. In 576 [28 May 1180 to 16 May 1181],
the Franks of Ascalon arrived with ten fire-ships at Tennis. The commander of the town, a native named El
Mo'ez, captured a part of them. Egypt was then governed by El Melek El Adel who administered for the account
of his brother El Melek El Naser Salah el din Yousef, then in Syria. El Mo'ez passed, then returned making
prisoners and ravaging; the Muslims took arms against him and combated him; God gave them the victory over
him; they seized him, cut off his two hands and his two feet, and crucified him.

In the year 577 [17 May 1181 to 6 May 1182], the sultan had the citadel of Tennis put in state and the
apparatus of defense renewed, for the inhabitants, full of terror, no longer wished to stay in the town. The
remaking of the old walls, which one raised on what remained of the primitive foundations, cost 3,000 dinars
for the price of the materials and the salary of the workers.

In the year 588 [18 January 1192 to 6 January 1193], a rescript was published ordering Tennis to be evacuated
and its inhabitants transported to Damietta. The women and the baggage left the town in Safar [17 February to
16 March 1193], and there remained only the garrison of the citadel.

In Shawal of the year 624 [14 September to 12 October 1227], El Melek El Kamel Mohammed ben El 'Adel Abou Bekr
ben Ayoub had the town of Tennis destroyed, which was one of the most considerable cities, where were woven
the stuffs of linen and the veil of the Ka'bah.

El Fakehi, in his History of Mecca, says: I saw in the part of the Kasbah that is toward the western angle, a
veil bearing this inscription: "This veil forms part of the things that El Seri ben El Hakem and 'Abd el Aziz
ben El Ouazir El Geraouï ordered and was executed by the care of El Fadl ben Sahl Dhu'l Riasateïn (of the
double function) and of Taher ben El Hassein, in the year 197 [12 September 812 to 31 August 813]." And I saw
also a carpet in qobati of Egypt, placed in the middle of the Ka'bah, on the subject of which one had only
written on the angle of the temple in tenuous and black writing: "By order of the emir of the believers El
Mamoun, in the year 206 [6 June 821 to 26 May 822]." I saw also one of the carpets of El Mahdi on which was
written: "In the name of God,

[PDF p. 551]

may the benediction be given by God to 'Abd Allah El Mahdi Mohammed, emir of the believers; may God protect
his duration! Ismail ben Ibrahim has ordered to execute this carpet in the manufactory of Tennis, and it was
made by the hand of El Hakem ben 'Obeïdah in the year 162 [28 September 778 to 16 September 779]." I saw still
a carpet of qobati of Egypt bearing the inscription: "In the name of God, may the benediction of God (love
us). Made by order of 'Abd Allah el Mahdi Mohammed, emir of the children, may God affirm him! Mohammed ben
Soliman has prescribed to have executed in the manufactory of Tennis the veil of the Ka'bah, by the hand of
El Khatab ben Mosallimah, his employee, in 159 [31 October 775 to 18 October 776]."

El Messihi, in his events of the year 384 [15 February 994 to 4 February 995], says: In Dhu'l Qa'dah [7
December 994 to 5 January 995], Yahia ben Yemân arrived from Tennis, from Damietta, and from Farma, with
presents composed of baskets, stools, boxes filled with money, horses, mules, asses, three canopies, and two
cows for the Ka'bah.

In Dhu'l Haggah of the year 402 [15 March 1024 to 3 March 1025] arrived the gift sent each year by the town
of Tennis and which was composed of five she-camels with their housings, a hundred horses with their saddles
and their bridles, armors and numerous objects, three tents in cloth of Dabik with their divans, standards,
and all that the town gave habitually in furniture, money, and stuffs of price.

When El Hakem had disappeared, his sister, the lady Sett el Moulk, asked the governor of Tennis, on behalf of
El Hakem, to bring as soon as possible the money gathered by the governors who had preceded him. The sum
amounted to about 1,000,000 dinars and 2,000,000 dirhems, representing the taxes levied in the country for
three years and that had remained with the governor by order of El Hakem. The governor brought this money to
the princess who employed it according to her caprice.

In the year 415 [24 June to 22 July 1012], the news reached the caliph El Zaher li A'zaz din allah Abou
Hashem Ali ben El Hakem bi 'Amr allah, that the black soldiers and others had risen up at Tennis and claimed
their pay, accusing the governor who had had to take flight. As for the mutineers, they ravaged the country,
putting

[PDF p. 552]

all to pillage, robbing the inhabitants, infesting the roads; they had even removed from the Treasury 2,500
dinars. El Gergeraï, furious, rose, sat down again, and said: How has one been able to commit such an attempt
against the cash-box of the sultan? This action has harmed Tennis as much as the Treasury. And he sent fifty
cavaliers to seize the culprits. Tennis did not cease to prosper, and there was in Egypt no town more
beautiful nor better defended, until the time when it was destroyed by El Melek El Kamel Mohammed ben El
'Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub, in the year 624 [22 December 1226 to 11 December 1227]. Since, it has always
remained in ruins and there remains of it only the razed foundations in the middle of the lake. Of the
district of Tennis formed part Boura, Ayouan, and Sheta. The lake where the fishing is done today is little
deep; one can cross it by ford. Two boats navigate on this lake, one going up, the other going down, by the
same wind, and each of them has its sail equally filled with wind and their speeds are equal. In the middle
of the lake are numerous islands that one calls today El 'Ozab, plural of 'Ozbah. They are inhabited by
groups of fishermen; in some are salt-works where one gathers a sweet salt of an agreeable savor. The waters
of the lake, which are generally salty, become sweet at the moment of the flood of the Nile.

Tounah. -- Among the dependencies of the province of Tennis was a village named Tounah where were fabricated
stuffs similar to those of Tennis and where sometimes one executed the veil of the Ka'bah. El Fakehi says: I
saw also a veil given by Haroun El Rashid, made of qobati of Egypt and bearing this inscription: "In the name
of God; may the benediction of God reach the caliph El Rashid 'Abd Allah Haroun, emir of the believers: may
God treat him with generosity! According to the instructions of El Fadl ben El Rabi', this veil was made in
the manufactory of Tounah in the year 190 [27 November 805 to 16 November 806]."

Semnaï. -- Village of the district of Tennis, which was invaded by the waters of the lake and has become an
island. In the month of Rabi' I of the year 837 [16 October to 14 November 1433], one discovered a stone and
in turning it over one found medallions of glass in great number, bearing the names of the imam El Mo'ez li
din allah, of the imam El A'ziz billah Nazar, of the imam El Hakem bi 'Amr Allah, of the imam El Zaher El
'Azaz din Allah, and of El Mostanser; these last were the most numerous. This was recounted to me by someone
who had seen them.

[PDF p. 553]

Boura. -- Village between Tennis and Damietta; it is from it that takes its name the bouri fish and also the
Benou-l bouri who inhabited Cairo and Alexandria.

In the year 610 [23 May 1213 to 12 May 1214] the enemies arrived there on galleys and ravaged it, but the
forces of Rosetta having directed themselves on Boura, the enemy withdrew.

El Qeïs. -- is the village that has given its name to the qeïssiah stuffs; it forms today a heap of ruins on
the shore of the sea between El Souadah and El Ouaradah. Its distance from the town of Farma is about six
barids by land. There, an enormous hill of sand advances into the sea of Syria; the Franks put themselves in
ambush there to rob the travelers. Near this hill are saline terrains, from which one draws a salt that the
Bedouins carry to Gaza and to Ramleh. In the vicinity of these salty terrains are wells near which the
Bedouins of this valley cultivate fields of cucumbers.

[PDF p. 554]

CHAPTER XX
OF THE TOWN OF SA

When, says Ibn Ouasif Shah, Qobtim ben Misraïm had divided the country between Ashmoun, Atreb, Qoft, and Sa,
each of them withdrew into the domain that had been assigned to him. Sa, with his people, his children, and
his servants, went into his province which occupied the territories of the Beheirah and of Alexandria and
extended as far as Barca; Alexandria did not yet exist, and he installed himself in the town of Sa. Sa was
the youngest of the sons of Qobtim and his dearest child. As soon as he had taken possession of the
government of his province, he watched over the prosperity of the region, founded towns and villages, raised
temples, and executed marvelous objects as his brothers had done, and sought still to surpass them.

According to Marhoun the Indian, governor of Bânah, Sa raised towers along the sea from the limit of the
country of Sa to that of Libya and of Maraqiah; on these towers were placed mirrors made of diverse
amalgamated matters; of these mirrors, one was destined to repel the marine animals and to guard against
their depredations; another, if enemies arrived from the islands of the sea to attack them, directed on their
ships the rays of the sun and set them on fire; in another, one could see the towns situated just opposite,
on the other side of the sea, and what their inhabitants did; in another, one saw the diverse provinces of
Egypt, and consequently one knew the abundance and the dearth each year. He made baths that heated by
themselves, built belvederes and places of pleasure, and each day he went to one or the other with his
particular slaves and his servants. All around extended gardens where fluttered in liberty the singing birds
and where ran freely the tamed beasts; these gardens were furrowed by canals that flowed perpetually across
admirable flowerbeds. The windows of his palace were of colored glass that sparkled when it was struck by the
sun and dispersed its rays around. He had neglected nothing of what can please and charm. And the
cultivations extended without interruption across the desert from Rosetta and Alexandria to Barca, and each
could travel on the land of Egypt without provisions, thanks to the abundance of the fruits and all sorts of
excellent things, and one walked

[PDF p. 555]

constantly in the shade and sheltered from the sun. In these deserts he built palaces, made plantations of
trees, and brought there canals from the Nile. Thus, on the side of the Occident to the western frontier, it
was only an uninterrupted succession of cultivations. And when the inhabitants of it had disappeared, there
remained vestiges of it in these deserts; their dwellings have disappeared, the men are dispersed, but all
the travelers who have penetrated into these regions do not cease to recount that they have seen there
marvelous ruins.

From the author (Maqrizi): People worthy of faith who had it from the witness himself recounted to me that a
traveler, who had penetrated into the town of Sa and walked across its ruins, had met a brick four spans
long, that he had picked it up and examined it in all directions; then having broken it, he had found in the
interior an ear of grain a span long and laden with all its grains as if it had just been gathered. He
shelled it between his hands, and he drew from it white wheat with enormous grains, each of them big like a
bean seed; he ate it and found that the taste was the same (as that of present wheat). Another traveler
entered this same town toward the year 790 [11 January to 30 December 1388], picked up there a brick a cubit
and a half long and a cubit wide; he broke it and found there an ear of wheat very heavy, each grain being of
the size of the biggest chickpea. He managed to crush it only by grinding it vigorously with a stone. One has
found at Sa a pretty statuette a finger long. This statuette having fallen into a jar of water, the water was
changed into wine. This happened at the home of a man of Tennis who made his fortune in selling this wine.
The emir El Aouhad, governor of Tennis, had this man summoned and left him no rest until he had obtained from
him the statuette.

[PDF p. 556]

CHAPTER XXI
OF THE SAND OF THE OCCIDENT (THE WESTERN SAND)

This sand extends over the surface of the earth and has been named by someone the mamelonated (hummocky)
sand. The length of this desert, which begins behind the mountain of Tay and extends to the Eastern sea,
directing itself from behind this mountain toward Egypt, Nubia, and the Enveloping sea, is five months'
march; a branch detaches itself from the Holy Land toward the Bahreïn, traverses the Bahreïn, grazes the east
of Kouristan and Persia, returns toward the Sagestan, takes the direction of the Orient as far as Merw,
crosses the Gihoun in the desert of the Khouarezm, and, traversing the countries of Hadalahiah, extends as
far as China and the Enveloping sea to the east. According to the description one gives of it, it extends
therefore from the Enveloping ocean to the East to the Enveloping ocean to the West. There are found there
gigantic and inaccessible mountains. One of them, situated in the country of Sahlat, displaces itself from
one place to another. This sand is sometimes yellow and soft to the touch, or red, blue-grey, dark black,
dark brown like indigo, or white like snow. There is some that resembles a very fine dust; there is some that
is rough and coarse to the touch. Some people claim that the sand of the Occident, or at least what is
comprised between the frontier of El 'Arish and El 'Abbassah, is recent.

The cause of its formation has given rise to an account of high interest and very instructive: Sheddad ben
Haddad ben Sheddad ben 'Ad, one of the Adite kings, having marched against Egypt with a considerable army,
vanquished Ashmoun ben Masr ben Beïsar, son of Cham, son of Noah, who was then king of the country; he
destroyed all that this prince had constructed and what his fathers had constructed; he himself raised the
pyramids and erected a tower on which he engraved talismans: he traced the quarters of Alexandria, and stayed
there a long time; but a scourge having raged against him and his people, they left Egypt for the Ouadi-l
Qora, between the town of El Nabouyah and the country of Syria. He constructed circuses and reservoirs to
capture the waters of the rains and the torrents; each reservoir was a mile wide by an equal length; palms
and other trees were planted, cultivations of all sorts extended between Raïah and Aïlah to the sea of the
Occident; the dwellings they occupied

[PDF p. 557]

covered all the space between El Dathna, El 'Arish, and El Goufar, in the land of the Shalah; one found there
gushing springs, fruit trees, and considerable cultivations. The Adites remained in this country very long
and ended by becoming quarrelsome, wicked, proud, and noisy. "We are," they said, "the most valiant, the
strongest, the most powerful." And God raised against them a hurricane that made them perish, destroyed their
reservoirs and their houses, and the sand extended over the country they had inhabited; such is the origin of
the sand one sees in the country of El Goufar -- that is, in the space comprised between El 'Abassah, there
where today are the village of El Salahieh and El 'Arish; all this sand comes from the crumbling of the
edifices of the Adites and the degradation of their materials, when God made them perish by the wind and
annihilated them definitively. Take heed! This fact has been denied because of its strangeness. But a passage
of the Koran testifies of its authenticity, it is when God says: "And among 'Ad, when we sent against them
the destructive wind, all on which this wind passed became dust" (Koran, LI, 41, 42); that is, something worn
out, worm-eaten. One says of a dried terrestrial plant trodden underfoot that it is [ramim]. One says of torn,
burned paper that it is [rufat] (like a dried and crushed plant). The term [rufat] (same signification)
applies to every thing worn out and fallen into dust.

Maraqiah. -- The town of Maraqiah forms one of the districts of western Egypt; it is the extreme frontier of
Egypt, bordering on the land of the Pentapolis or land of Barca. It is about two barids from the town of
Santariah. It was formerly an important region, abundant in palms and in cultivations, where one found living
springs; one meets there still at present admirable ruins. The culture there was so prosperous that a single
grain of wheat produced a hundred ears, or ninety ears at the least. It was the same for the rice which was
superb. One meets there still in our days numerous gardens. Formerly Maraqiah was inhabited by the Berbers
whom David had chased from the land of Palestine; a great number of them fixed themselves in this region; the
rest separated from the first; the Zenabah, the Magilah, and the Darissah went to inhabit the mountains (the
desert), while the Louata fixed themselves in the land of Barca and the Hawarah at Tripoli of the Occident.
Later, the Berbers covered the country as far as Suez. In Shawal of the year 304 [18 March to 27 April 917]
of the hijra of Mohammed, the populations of Libya and of Maraqiah

[PDF p. 558]

made their appearance at Alexandria; they fled to escape the tyranny of the despot of Barca. Maraqiah has
always been in a state of anarchy, but in our days it is completely destroyed; there have remained however
magnificent traces of monuments.

Kom Sherik. -- This locality is situated in the vicinity of Alexandria; it is spoken of in the chronicles.
Its name comes to it from Sherik ben Sami ben 'Abd Yaghouth ben Gez El Mouradi El Qatifi, one of the
companions of the Prophet. He marched in the vanguard of 'Amr ben El 'As, at the conquest of Alexandria.
Pressed by the Greek army, Sherik and his companions took refuge on this Kom (hill) where they held their
heads up to the Greeks until the arrival of 'Amr. Kom Sherik forms part of the Hauf Ramsis.

Rheïfah. -- Village in the vicinity of Belbeïs, two stages from Fostat. It was a place of halt for the
caravan of pilgrimage. It is recounted that the measure of the king (the royal measure) that one had sought
since the town of Masr, was found again at Rheïfah, among the utensils of the brothers of Joseph.

Samanoud. -- There was in this locality a temple where was represented a shield bearing an inscription. Ibn
Zaoulaq recounts that Abou-l Qassem Mamoun El 'Adel had copied the inscription on a sheet of paper to which he
had given the form of a shield, and he adds: "No one could find himself facing him without turning away and
taking flight." There were there also statues and the image of those who were to reign over Egypt, among
others a people bearing the turban and armed with the javelin above which was written: "These will seize the
town of Masr."

[PDF p. 559]

CHAPTER XXII
OF THE TOWN OF BALBAIS

This country is named, in the book of the Jews, the land of Goshen. It is there that Jacob descended when he
came to find again his son Joseph, who had him installed in the land of Goshen -- that is, of Balbaïs El
'Alaqamah -- to pasture there his flocks. According to Ibn Saïd, the vali of Balbaïs commands as far as El
Maradah, extreme limit of Egypt. Up to this point the traffic is done in silver; from there on, one uses
copper as far as El 'Arish, which is the first point of Syria, or, it is said, the last point of Egypt.

Abou 'Obeïd El Bakri says that Balbaïs is a locality very well known situated near Masr. Ibn Khordadabeh, in
his book of the "Roads and the Kingdoms," says that between Balbaïs and the town of Fostat Masr there are 24
miles.

El Ouaqedi recounts that El Maqoqos married his daughter Armanosah to Constantine, son of Heraclius, and sent
her with her treasures, her slaves, her pages, and her escort to rejoin her spouse who was to accomplish his
marriage with her in the town of Caesarea. As enemies besieged this last town, she went to Balbaïs and stayed
there; she sent her grand chamberlain with two thousand cavaliers to Farma to guard the road and prevent
whoever it might be, Greek or other, from passing into Egypt. El Maqoqos dispatched messengers toward the
frontier of his country, on the side of Syria, with order to let no one enter Egypt; he feared that if one
spread the news of the conquest of Syria by the Muslims, fear might penetrate into the heart of his soldiers.
'Omar ben El Khattab having gone to El Gabiah, 'Amr ben El 'As marched on Egypt and camped before Balbaïs
where was Armanosah, the daughter of El Maqoqos. The people of Balbaïs delivered battle, but 'Amr killed them
nearly a thousand cavaliers, made three thousand prisoners; the rest fled and went to rejoin El Maqoqos.
Armanosah was taken with all her treasures

[PDF p. 560]

and all that was at Balbaïs belonging to the Copts. 'Amr, desiring to be amiable to El Maqoqos, sent him his
daughter Armanosah whom he treated generously, and restored to her her riches. Armanosah was accompanied by
Qeis ben Abou-l 'As El Sahmi. El Maqoqos was happy to receive his daughter. Then 'Amr went to the palace.
Balbaïs did not cease to be one of the most important towns of Egypt until the arrival of Mori (Amaury), king
of the Franks, who seized it by main force after a long siege where thousands of its inhabitants were killed.
There are numerous accounts that concern it. It has been ruined since the accidents that occurred in Egypt
after the year 806 [21 July 1403 to 9 July 1404]. Previously, I had seen this town quite prosperous; one
counted there numerous gardens and its inhabitants were rich and fortunate.

[PDF p. 561]

CHAPTER XXIII
OF THE COUNTRY OF EL OUARADAH

El Ouaradah forms part of the territory of El Gofar. 'Obeïd allah ben 'Abd allah ben Khordadabeh, in his book
"of the Roads and the Kingdoms," says: The road and the territory that extend from Ramleh to Ardoud is 12
miles; from Ardoud to Gaza there are 20 miles; then, to El 'Arish, 24 miles, across the sands; from there to
El Ouaradah, 18 miles; from there to El Gharib, 20 miles; from there to Farma, 24 miles. The caliph El Mamoun
said:

[verses:] Your night has been at Meïdan shorter than at Farma. A stranger in the towns of Egypt, you
experience chagrin and sadness.

From Farma to Garir, 30 miles; from there to Qaserah, 24 miles; from there to the oratory of Qoda'ah, 18
miles; from there to Balbaïs, 21 miles; from there to Fostat Masr, 24 miles.

The author of the History of Damietta says: The Muslims, already masters of Damietta and of Tennis, having
seized Farma, went to El Baqarah whose inhabitants embraced Islamism; from there they went to El Ouaradah
whose inhabitants converted likewise, as well as the population of the surroundings as far as Ascalon.

The cadi El Fadl, in his accounts relative to the month of Moharrem of the year 567 [4 September to 3 October
1171], says: We arrived in the morning at El Ouaradah; we had passed the night in the port, after which we
entered into the town. I saw the date inscribed on the minaret of the mosque, 408 [30 May 1017 to 19 May
1018], and I read there the name of El Hakem bi 'amr allah. This town forms part of the territory of El Gofar
and takes, it is said, its name from the word [el ouroud] (the arrival). Its mosque was opened to the cult
and frequented by the faithful until after the year 700 [16 September 1300 to 5 September 1301]. The country
that El Ouaradah anciently occupied is found to the east of the present locality of El Salahieh; one meets
there some traces of constructions, but the palms there are rare.

El Salahieh. -- This country was founded by El Melek El Saleh Negm el din

[PDF p. 562]

Ayoub ben El Kamel Mohammed ben El 'Adel ben Abou Beker ben Ayoub ben Shadi in the country of the Mosâneh and
of El 'Alaqamah, at the entrance of the expanse of sand that separates Egypt from Syria. There he raised
palaces, a mosque, a market to serve as a halt for the troops, at their coming out of the sands, and this in
the year 644 [19 May 1246 to 7 May 1247].

[PDF p. 563]

CHAPTER XXIV
OF THE TOWN OF EILAH

Ibn Habib says that Othal is the valley of Eïlah, and that Eïlah is a town situated on the shore of the sea
between Egypt and Mecca; it takes its name from Aïlah, daughter of Madian, son of Abraham. Aïlah is the first
point of the land of the Hedjaz; it had been a powerful town on the shore of the sea and of a flourishing
commerce; its population was a mixture of diverse races. It was formerly the limit of the Empire of Roum. At
a mile from this town rises a triumphal arch of Caesar; there the emperor had established a post of customs.
Between Aïlah and Jerusalem there are six stages, and El Tor, where God spoke to Moses, is a day and a night
from Aïlah. In the time of Islam, it was a place where the Benou Omayah stopped, most of whom were freedmen
of Othman ben 'Afan and distributed the water to the pilgrims. It was a country where one honored science and
belles-lettres; the commerce there was prosperous, the markets flourishing, the cultivations considerable,
and the palms numerous. The hill of Aïlah was not practicable on the backs of mounts, but Faïq, freedman of
Khamaraouya ben Ahmed ben Touloun, had it arranged, leveled the road, and repaired all that could be
repaired. There were at Aïlah numerous mosques and a great quantity of Jews. These claim to possess the
mantle of the prophet that he would have sent them as a safe-conduct, and they showed it. It was a mantle of
Aden enveloped in a stuff of which one raised only a span. It is said that Aïlah is the town of which God
spoke in this passage of his book: "Question them on this country situated on the shore of the sea and whose
inhabitants transgressed the sabbath; there the fish appeared at the surface of the water on the day of the
sabbath and disappeared the other days. Thus we tried them because they were prevaricators" (Koran, VII, 163).
One is not in agreement on the identification of this town. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Akramah, and El Saddi claim that this
town is Aïlah; according to Ibn 'Abbas also it would be a locality between Aïlah and El Tor; El Zaheri
believes that it is Tabriah (Tiberias). Gobadah and Zeïd ben Aslam are of the opinion that it is a point of
the coasts of Syria, between Madian and 'Aïnounah, named Ma'nah.

[PDF p. 564]

[OF THE TOWN OF EILAH, continued]

One asked one day El Hasseïn ben El Fadl: "Does one find in the book of God this proverb: That which is
permitted is met only with great difficulty, that which is forbidden presents itself of itself?" "Yes,"
answered El Hasseïn, "one finds that in the history of Aïlah, where it is said that the fish came to the
surface of the water on the day of the sabbath and disappeared the other days."

The inhabitants of the country, according to what the legend says, were Benou Israïl to whom God had
