forbidden to work on Saturday. But Eblis (Iblis), using ruse, came to say to them: "It is forbidden you only
to take the fish on Saturday." They prepared therefore basins where they deposited the fish on Friday; the
fish remained there and could not come out because the canal of communication was too narrow. One took them
on Sunday. One of them, it is said, had thought of making a slip-knot in a cord and of throwing it to the
tail of a fish, and the fish was left thus until Sunday. The other fishermen amused themselves at first in
seeing their companion act thus, but thought of putting his invention into practice only when the fishing had
taken considerable proportions and these fish had become an object of commerce and a cause of manifest
impiety. A part of the Benou Israël protested and rose up against this practice of the forbidden things,
declaring that they would no longer dwell with the others, and, indeed, they separated the village into two
parts by a wall. Now, one morning, the just awoke in their dwellings and none of the wicked had yet crossed
the wall. "Certainly," said the just, "something must have happened to the others." And, having mounted on
the wall, they saw that the others had become apes. They descended on their side, and these apes, remembering
their human origin, came to them and sniffed their garments weeping. The sages said to the apes: "Had we not
forbidden you to do what you have done?" And the apes made sign of yes in moving the head. The young ones,
adds Qobadah, had been changed into apes and the old ones into swine; only the sages escaped. All have
disappeared since. This fact, according to what is reported, happened in the time of the prophet David. It is
said that the primitive name of Aïlah is Aïlailiah, of which it is question in the Pentateuch. The sherif
Mohamed ben As'ad el Gawarii says that the Berbers Dakalah are a branch of the Mousamedah; others say that
the Dakalah are the descendants of Aïlah. Ail is, it is said, the one who

[PDF p. 565]

gave his name to the hill of Aïlah. According to another, the Dakalah would descend from Daghfal ben Aïlah;
as for them, they claim themselves Berbers and say: "We are a branch of the Persians;" but on this subject
there are great contradictions. Masaoudi reports that Joshua, son of Nun, made war on Samida' ben Hazber ben
Malek the Amalecite, king of Syria, combated him in the country of Aïlah in the surroundings of Madian,
killed him, and seized his kingdom; it is on this subject that 'Oun ben Saïd El Garhami said:

[verses:] Have you not seen that the Amalecite, son of Hormez, had his flesh torn at Aïlah? For a great
number of Jews had hurled themselves against him, to the number of 80,000, cuirassed and not cuirassed.

This piece comprises a great number of verses. Ibn Ishaq recounts that when the prophet of God arrived at
Tabouk, the governor of Aïlah, Tahiah ben Roubah, came to ask him for peace and to bring him the tribute. The
inhabitants of Gerba and of Agrah came likewise to bring the tribute. The prophet wrote them a letter that
they have conserved. Here is what he wrote to Tahiah ben Roubah: "In the name of God the clement and
merciful; sincere letter on the part of God and of his prophet Mohammed to Tahiah ben Roubah, to the people
of Aïlah, to their bishops and to them all on land and on sea; to them protection on the part of God and
protection on the part of the prophet. Whoever is with them of the people of Syria, of the Yemen, or of the
sea: if anyone of them has committed some crime, his money cannot save his soul; their goods are the property
of who seizes them; they cannot prevent what they wish to prevent, nor pass by the road they would wish to
take by sea or by land. This letter was written by Gahim ben El Sait and Sharhabil ben Hassanah, with the
permission of the prophet of God in the year 9 of the hijra [20 April 630 to 8 April 631]." And the town of
Aïlah did not cease to be prosperous and peopled.

In the year 415 [15 March 1024 to 3 March 1025], 'Abd allah ben Edris el Ga'feri attacked by night Aïlah,
with the help of some Benou-l Gerrah, pillaged it, levied there 3,000 dinars and a great quantity of grains,
carried off the women and the children, then left the valiyah of Ouadi-l Qora. A detachment of cavaliers set
out from Cairo to combat him.

[PDF p. 566]

In the year 566 [14 September 1170 to 3 September 1171], says the cadi El Fadl, El Melek El Naser Salah el din
Youssef ben Ayoub (Saladin) thought of constructing articulated boats, loaded them on camels, and with a
numerous army set out from Cairo to attack the citadel of Aïlah of which the Franks had made themselves
masters and where they had fortified themselves. He arrived before Aïlah in Rabi' I [12 November to 11
December 1170], had the boats raised and assembled, launched them to the sea, garnished them with arms and
combatants. He put the siege before the citadel by sea and by land, and seized it the 20th of Rabi' II [31
December 1170], killed or made prisoners the Franks who were there, established as garrison a detachment of
his own troops, to which he left all of which they had need in arms and other provisions, and returned to
Cairo at the end of Gemadi I.

In the year 77 [year 677], arrived a letter of the governor of Aïlah saying that the vessels kept good guard,
but that one dreaded the coming of the Franks. Soon after, indeed, presented himself Alaïris (Edward?), may
God curse him! He surrounded the citadel of Aïlah, sent his army into the region of Tabouk to make sure of
the coasts of Syria, for he feared that an army might have been sent against him from Syria or from Egypt. In
the month of Sha'ban of this same year, the rains fell with such abundance on the mountain that faces the
citadel that the garrison of Aïlah could for two months neglect to descend to the fountain; the persistence
of the rains even damaged the constructions of the citadel which cracked, because of the little depth of
their foundations; the proprietors had to repair and consolidate them.

Abou-l Harran El Masa'oudi, in his book Accounts of the Time, at the beginning of the account relative to the
history of the Koukas, recounts that this people had four kings who governed the land of Aïlah and the
Hedjaz; each of them had built himself a town to which he had given his name. The rest of the country was
planted with tents and divided into thirty districts distributed in 4 provinces, each province having a king
seated on a throne of gold and residing in his own town. Each of these kings raised a palace for the science
and a temple for the planets, placed there statues of gold, each statue having a special rank. To Alexandria,
whose name was then Raqoudah, were attached fifteen districts; this town became the sojourn of the greatest
of the priests, and in

[PDF p. 567]

its temples were raised more statues of gold than in the temples of the other towns; there were there two
hundred statues of gold. The Said was divided into eighty districts forming four provinces, and the towns
inhabited by the Egyptians of the interior in the districts of the Said were to the number of thirty, all
filled with marvelous things. It is recounted that Himyar the Great, whose name was 'Arangah, son of Saba the
Great, whose name was 'Amer, better known under that of Abd Shams ben Yeshgab ben Ya'reb ben Qohtan, it is
recounted that this Himyar, having succeeded his father, gathered his army and set out, subjugating the
peoples and subduing the kings as his father had done. He continued his course to the Orient, repelled Yagog
and Magog toward the point where the sun rises, then he turned back toward the Occident. A tribe of the
people of the Yemen, of the lineage of Hud ben 'Aber ben Shaleh ben Arfakhshad ben Sam ben Nouh came to him
fleeing Thamoud ben 'Ather ben Aram ben Sam ben Nouh and the calamities he made them undergo. He gave
therefore the order to remove them from the land of the Yemen and to transport them to Aïlah, and they
peopled the country from Aïlah to Zat El Asal at the extremity of the mountain of Negd. There Thamoud cut the
rocks; one dug houses in the mountains and, as this people had become insolent and proud, God sent it Saleh
as prophet and as apostle; but these people did not believe him and asked him to make a she-camel come out of
a rock; when the prophet had made her appear, they cut her hocks. And God destroyed them by a cry, and the
next morning, they lay all inanimate in their houses.

It is reported that after the death of his brother Aaron, Moses went with the Israelites to the land of the
children of El 'Eïss whom one calls the mountains of El Serah, near the country of El Shoubek. And having
traversed it, he passed to the country of Aïlah, then, many days after, took the direction of the desert of
Bab, there where are the countries of the Kark, and made war on these peoples. There was near Aïlah a
considerable and very important town named 'Asaboun.

Marbout. -- It is one of the districts depending on Alexandria, a town so white that one did not perceive
there the fall of the night until a very long time after. The people, to walk there, held in the hand a black
stuff to protect their eyes; because of the dazzling whiteness of the town, the monks there were dressed in
black. The town of Marbout was situated at the extremity of the cultivations and the gardens that succeeded
one another to the land of Barca; today, it forms part of the districts depending on Alexandria; one
cultivates there the fruits

[PDF p. 568]

and other products. El Melek El Mozaffar Rokn El din Bibars El Gashankir put it in waqf as a gift of
beneficence to the mosque of El Hakem at Cairo. There, a mosque was constructed in the year 666 [22 September
1267 to 9 September 1268]; then El Melek El Moayyad Sheikh El Mahmoudi took it on lease in the year 821 [8
February 1418 to 27 January 1419], extended there the culture of the gardens which had been ruined by the
incursions of the Arabs of Lebdah and of Barca, and it was attached to the divan of the sultan.

Ouadi Habib. -- This Ouadi is situated to the west of the land of Egypt, between Marbout and the Fayoum. One
gathers there the salt and the natron. It takes its name from Habib ben Mohammed ben Mo'aqqel ben El Ouaqe'ah
ben Hozâm ben 'Afan El Ghafari, one of the companions of the apostle of God and who had attended the conquest
of Mecca. On his subject, Abou Tamin El Gishani recounts what follows: the freedman of Tagib converted to
Islamism at the same time as Saïd ben 'Abd el Rahman El Ghafari. In the time of the revolt of Othman, he had
taken refuge in this Ouadi which took his name. And he said: "There is no difference to establish between men
for the Ramadhan, and one must do the two prayers even during the voyage." This Ouadi is also called: Ouadi El
Melouk, Ouadi El Natroun, Berriah Shahab, Berriah el Asqi, Mizan el Qoloub. There were there a hundred
Christian convents, but there remain only seven of which one will speak in the chapter of this book that
treats of the convents. It is a Ouadi of an extreme utility; one finds there the natron, from which one draws
a considerable revenue; one finds there also the Andrani salt and the Soultani salt; this last has the form
and resembles tablets of marble. There also one harvests the ammoniac and the black antimony; one fabricates
there the glass. It is there also that one finds the Masekah, a sort of yellow earth enclosed in a black
stone; one dissolves it in water, and one drinks the solution which is efficacious against the maladies of
the stomach. The Ouadi produces still the Bardi reed of which one makes the mats. One meets there the spring
of the Crow, a sort of little basin about fifteen cubits long and as wide, which is found in a grotto in the
interior of the mountain. One does not know whence this water comes, nor where it goes; it is sweet and
limpid.

It is reported that from this Ouadi came out 70,000 monks holding each a staff in the hand, who went to meet
'Amr ben El 'As at El Teranah,

[PDF p. 569]

[OF THE TOWN OF EILAH, continued]

while he was returning from Alexandria. They asked him for the Aman for themselves and their convents. 'Amr
therefore wrote them an Aman that they have conserved. He made them also another letter, on the subject of
the dues to be paid by the region of the North, and remitted it to them. And their dues amounted, in a single
year, to more than fifteen thousand ardebs; today, it is hardly that they reach a hundred of them.

[PDF p. 570]

CHAPTER XXV
OF THE TOWN OF MADIAN

Madian is a town of the people of Sho'aïb, of the lineage of Madian, son of Abraham; their ancestress was
Qantourah, daughter of Yoqtan the Canaanite, who gave Abraham eight sons of whom each was the stock of a
people. Madian is situated on the sea of Qolzoum, facing Tabouk and at about six stages from this point; it
is greater than Tabouk. It is there that is found the well where Moses drew the water for the camels of
Sho'aïb and near which he had raised his tent.

According to El Farra, Madian is at once the name of a town and that of a region. It is also, it is said, the
name of a tribe that drew its denomination from its ancestor Madian, son of Abraham, a name that signifies
"the warriors," etc. Almost everyone agrees in saying that Madian is a non-Arab word, although some claim it
Arab; if it were Arab, it would be of the form [fa'lan] and would derive from [dana]; it would then have the
sense of "place where one resides"; but it is a rare construction. Others see in it a word of the form
[mif'al] or [maf'al] derived from [dana]; but in sum, the origin of it is not clear; one cannot know with
certainty if it is a name of land or of tribe, and if the word is Arab or non-Arab.

El Masa'oudi reports that the people of the Koran were in discussion with the people of Sho'aïb ben Noufal ben
Ra'ouil ben Masr ben 'Eïqa ben Madian ben Ibrahim, a people who spoke Arabic and who, according to some,
would be none other than degenerate and corrupt descendants of Arabs; one of the writers we have cited goes
so far as to say that they are the representatives of a people completely disappeared; for others, they are
of the lineage of El Mahasen ben Gendal ben Ya'seb ben Madian ben Ibrahim, and Sho'aïb would be the last of
the race. They obeyed several kings who had divided regions neighboring one another. Among them were Abgad,
Hawaz, Hataï, Klamen, Sa'fas, and Qorshat. These kings are, as we have said, the descendants of El Mahasen
ben Gendal. The ensemble of the names of these kings is none other than the union of the twenty-two letters
that form the complete alphabet. These letters

[PDF p. 571]

have been interpreted also in another fashion than that we have reported. Abgad was king of Mecca and of the
part of the Hedjaz that touches it; Hawaz and Hataï were two kings of the country of Oug -- that is, of the
Taïf and of the country of Negd that adjoins it; Kliman, Sa'fas, and Qorshat were kings of Madian or, it is
said, of the country of Egypt; Kliman dominated at Madian; certain authors claim that Kliman reigned over all
the countries we have just named; those who think thus are fairly numerous and approach our opinion. What is
certain is that the chastisement by the burning wind reached Kliman, one of these kings. Sho'aïb had engaged
them to embrace the true religion, but as they refused to believe him, he threatened them with the
chastisement by the burning wind: the sky opened on them a door of fire; Sho'aïb and all those who had
believed in him saved themselves at the place called Aïlah, a marsh situated in the vicinity of Madian; the
others, feeling the catastrophe come, for the heat became terrible and death appeared certain, sought to
rejoin Sho'aïb and his companions who were protected by a white cloud under which they breathed a cool air
and felt no harm. They chased Sho'aïb and his companions from the place where they kept themselves, imagining
that thus they would make cease the scourge descended on them; but God raised a fire that reached them. The
daughter of Kliman made an elegy for her father; she was then in the Hedjaz:

[verses:] Kliman has broken my support in dying in the midst of Mahallah; the chief of the people has
received death by the fire in the midst of a burning wind. This wind has formed a fire by which has
disappeared the house of my tribe.

El Motanasser ben El Mounzer El Madiani said:

[verses:] O Sho'aïb, you have said a thing that made 'Amr perish and made the son of 'Amr live; they were the
kings of the land of Hedjaz whose face was like the rays of the radiant sun or of the disk of the moon; they
inhabited the sacred land; they were the ornament of the countries they inhabited; they carried it off by
generosity and glory. They are the kings sons of Hâtai and Sa'fas the generous and of Hawaz, the master of
Thaniah and of Hegr.

On these kings, says El Masa'oudi, there are Muslim histories that

[PDF p. 572]

speak of wars and expeditions, of the conquest of these kingdoms, of their government, and of the fashion in
which they annihilated the peoples who were there before them. It is claimed that the forest of which God
speaks in the Koran, at this passage: "The masters of the forest treated the envoys as importunate" (Koran,
XXVI, 176), and at this other: "And the inhabitants of the forest were wicked, we drew vengeance of them"
(Koran, XV, 78-79), is Madian; according to others, it would be the region of the seashore near Madian;
according to others, a forest in the vicinity of Madian; on another side, it is claimed that the masters of
the forest are the people to whom Sho'aïb sent a message and who resided at Tabouk between El Hagar and the
frontier of Syria, and that Sho'aïb was not one of theirs, but a Madianite. According to Abou 'Obeïd el Bakri,
the forest cited in the book of God is that which served as shelter to the people of Sho'aïb. On this subject,
Ibn Abbas cites two interpretations: according to one, the forest would be at Madian itself and would have
been of the domain of Sho'aïb; according to the other, this forest would have occupied the seashore on the
side of Madian. Their trees were the doum palms, and among this people the word aïkah signifies "a bushy
tree." They possessed therefore bushy trees. According to certain commentators, El Aïkah signifies "the
forest"; as for Leïkah, it is the place-name designating the surrounding country, as one says Mekkah and
Bekkah. Abou Ga'far el Nahas says that the word Leïkah is not known as a place-name. Some, says Ibn Qoteibah,
think that Bekkah is the place of prayer and the region that surrounds it is Mekkah; one makes a similar
difference between El Aïkah and Leïkah, El Aïkah signifying "the forest," and Leïkah the region that
surrounds it.

Madian, says El Bakri, is a country of Syria in the vicinity of Gaza; it is cited in the book of God. Others
believe however that Madian forms part of the land of Egypt. The prophet of God sent a detachment of cavalry
to Madian under the conduct of Zeid ben Harethah who brought back people of Mita prisoners. According to Ibn
Ishaq, Mita is the seashore. These people were sold and the mothers were separated from their children; now,
the prophet having come out as they were in the process of weeping, asked what was happening. When one had
told it to him: "Sell them only together," he declared. Madian is one of the points inhabited by the tribe of
Gedam ben 'Adi ben El Hareth ben Massah ben Âdad ben Zeïd ben 'Amr ben 'Azeïb ben Zeïd ben Kahlan. And the
prophet Sho'aïb who was sent to the people of Madian is a descendant of Ouaïl ben Gedam.

[PDF p. 573]

It is recounted that the prophet of God said to the troop of Gedam: "Welcome to the people of Sho'aïb and to
the family of the wife of Moses; the hour will not pass that the Messiah will have chosen his wife among you
and that he will not have from her his child." According to Mohammed ben Sahl, the surroundings of Madian are
of the nature of the soil of Medina like Fadak, Fara', and Rohat.

From the author (Maqrizi): There were on the territory of Madian numerous important towns, but, the
inhabitants having abandoned them, they have become deserted, and until our days -- that is, until the year
825 [26 December 1421 to 14 December 1422] -- there have remained standing about forty towns of which one
knows some; as for the others, their name is unknown. Among those whose names are known, and in the space
comprised between the Hedjaz, Palestine, and Egypt, there are sixteen towns, of which ten on the side of
Palestine: El Khalesa, El Sanita, El Modasrah, El Meniah, El A'oug, El Khouiraq, El Birein, El Maein, El
Saba', El Mo'allaq; the most considerable of these ten towns are El Khalesa and El Sanita. One draws from
them many of the stones that one transports to Gaza where one employs them for construction. On the side of
the sea of Qolzoum and of El Tor, the towns of Madian are Faran, El Raqah, Qolzoum, Aïlah, and Madian. In the
town of Madian, there are still today marvelous ruins and gigantic columns.

One found in the citadel of the town of El A'oug, in the year 760 [6 December 1358 to 22 November 1359] and
some, a well very wide and of a depth of nearly a hundred cubits: in the bottom were a great number of books
on shelves; one carried to the surface one of these books two cubits long and more and bound between two
little planks of wood; it was written in musnad characters and the alif and the lam had nearly a span of
length. One found in the country of Kark someone who could decipher them; it was a volume of a work in ten
volumes that began with "The glory is to God!" then spoke of the going out of Moses from the land of Egypt
for the country of Madian, and of the kings of Madian successors of Sho'aïb; in this book, one gives to Moses
a quantity of names, among others his Arab name Mousa ben 'Amran, his Hebrew name Moshé, his Persian name
Daran, his Coptic name Herousis; one recounts there that he had married the daughter of Sho'aïb and that he
remained at Madian for eight years, after which he said to the son of Sho'aïb: "I have accomplished the
convention made with you, but by goodness on my part, I will accord you two years more."

[PDF p. 574]

CHAPTER XXVI
END OF THE ACCOUNTS CONCERNING THE TOWN OF MADIAN

"And Moses departed directing himself toward Egypt; the king of Madian was then Abgad whose power had become
considerable and overflowed onto the Hedjaz and the Yemen. He had five sons: Hawaz, Hataï, Klimen, Sa'fas,
and Qorshit. Abgad, after having reigned for a hundred years over the Yemen, died leaving, to succeed him in
the government of this region, his son Klimen; to his son Hawaz he had attributed in division the Hedjaz; to
his son Hataï the land of Egypt; to his son Sa'fas Mesopotamia and the countries of Mossoul and of Harran as
far as Iraq; and to his son Qorshit Iraq and the regions of the Khorassan that adjoin it. Of the five
brothers, Qorshit was the most violent; Sa'fas, Hawaz, and Klimen were, on the contrary, just and patient; as
for Hataï, he was renowned for his brutality and his insolence. At this epoch, the Israelites were in Syria, a
region that did not yet obey the sons of Abgad and had escaped their domination. Since the death of their
father Abgad, his sons reigned about a hundred fifty years; the duration of this dynasty, including in it the
reign of Abgad, was therefore three hundred years and more. After them, the Israelites were subjugated by
Rouzeït ben Hawaz and by Arzeit ben Hataï ben Abgad who reigned over them for nearly seven years, after which
the lineage of Abgad ceased to reign."

The Madianites kept this book a long time and had it at the end carried back into the cistern of the citadel
of A'oug.

I hold this account from the vigilant and energetic guardian Abou 'Abd allah Mohammed ben Ahmed Mohammed ben
'Abd El Rahman El Rhariani El Tounisi, who added: This was reported to me by Shater ben Rhanim el 'Amari who
had it from an old man he had met in Palestine and who, having seen this very old book, had retained the
passage we have cited.

It is recounted that Mâlek ben Da'r ben Hagar ben Gadilat ben Lakhm had twenty-four male children whose
descendants had become so numerous that they constructed towns, villages, and fortresses, peopled

[PDF p. 575]

all the country of Madian, and conquered Syria, Egypt, the Hedjaz, and other countries still that they
possessed for five hundred years after the death in the waters of the Pharaoh of Moses and the death of
Daloukat bent Zafân; it was the prophet of God Solomon, son of David, who expelled them, and the kingdom
remained thenceforth in the hands of the Copts.

[PDF p. 576]

CHAPTER XXVII
OF THE TOWN OF FARAN

This town, one of the towns of Amalec, is situated on the shores of the sea of Qolzoum and occupies the
summit of a hill that rises between two mountains. In these mountains are pierced innumerable grottoes filled
with cadavers. From the town to the sea of Qolzoum, there is one stage. The shore bears in this place the
name of "Banks of the sea of Farân"; it is there that God made Pharaoh perish in the waters. Between the town
of Farân and the desert of Tih, one counts two stages.

Farân is, it is said, the name of the mountains of Mecca or, according to others, of the mountains of the
Hedjaz. In the Torah and in the Explanation (the Targum), it is said that Farân and El Tor are two towns of
eastern Egypt. But the town of which we speak is not the Farân of which it is question in the Torah. It was,
according to what is said, Farân ben 'Amr ben 'Amaliq who gave his name to the mountains of the Holy Places
which are called mountains of Fârân or of Farân. The town of Farân forms still today part of the ensemble of
the towns of Madian; it abounds in palms with edible fruits and one sees there the traces of a considerable
canal; today, it is no more than a desert visited only by the caravans.

[PDF p. 577]

CHAPTER XXVIII
OF THE LAND OF GOFAR

The Gofar is the name given to an ensemble of five towns: El Farma, El Baqarah, El Ouaradah, El 'Arich, and
Rafag. The Gofar entirely is only sand, and this name was given to it because of the difficulty that men and
animals experience in walking there, so abundant is the sand there and so distant the stages one from
another. The camels become foundered (exhausted) in the Gofar; thus one named it Gofar as one called [hagar]
the cord that serves to tie the camel, [hagar] that with which one hobbles it, ['aqam] that which ties its
foot, [batan] the cord that serves as a girth, [khalam] that which holds the muzzle, [zamam] that by which
the muzzle is tightened.

El Baqarah takes its name from el baqar (the cowherds); El Ouaradah from el Ouarid (the one who descends to
the watering-place); El 'Arish from el 'Arsh (the shelters). As for Rafag, it is, it is said, the name of a
mountain.

In the ancient times, Khodam ben El 'Arian inhabited the Gofar which formed, according to what is recounted,
an uninterrupted succession of cultivated fields and renowned for their fertility; the inhabitants cultivated
there in abundance the saffron, the safflower, and the sugarcane; the waters there were abundant and sweet;
but the sand came that invaded from all sides the region, and God ended by making it disappear; since, it is
no more than an immense heap of sand that extends as far as El 'Arish and Rafag, forming a vast desert more
painful to traverse than the desert of the Occident; the water there is rare, the flocks are absent from it,
and one meets there no trace of men. Let us adore the one who transforms the state of things.

[PDF p. 578]

CHAPTER XXIX
OF THE SAID OF EGYPT

The word Saïd designates a portion of terrain raised above the soil; one says of a terrain that it is raised,
by opposition to that which forms a depression; one gives also this name to a terrain where there enters
neither sand nor sebakh. This same word designates still the "surface of the soil," "a good earth," "all good
loam." It was applied by the Arabs, in the time of Islam, to the southern part of Egypt, because this region
is raised, contrary to the other parts of Egypt; it is for this reason that one calls it "the High Land," and
because its soil contains neither sand nor sebakh, but is, in all points, excellent and blessed. The Said
bears as well the name of "Region of the South."

When Misraïm, says master Ibrahim ben Ouacif Shah, saw death arrive, he made his recommendations to his son
Qobtim; he had previously divided the land among his children and attributed to Qobtim the territory
comprised between Qouft and Assouan; to Ashmoun the region that extends from Ashmoun to Memphis; to Atrib the
Hauf entirely, and to Sa from the town of Sa of the Beheirah to the surroundings of Barqa. To his brother
Fareq, he had said: "I give you the territory that extends from Barqa to the Occident"; and Fareq became the
master of Ifriqiah and his descendants were the Afareq (the Africans). And Misraïm prescribed to each of his
sons to build himself a town in his province.

The children of Masr, reports Ibn 'Abd el Hakem, and the children of their children having multiplied, Masr
divided the territory among his sons, assigning to each of them and to his posterity a portion of the country
and a section of the Nile; Qoft received as an apanage the region of Qouft where he installed himself and
which from him took the name of Qouft; he had in addition all the region situated upstream as far as Assouan
and downstream as far as Ashmoun, to the east and to the west of the river; the share of Ashmoun comprised
the territory that extends from Ashmoun to Memphis, to the east and to the west; Ashmoun established himself
in the town of Ashmoun, to which he gave his name; to Atrib fell the region situated between Memphis and Sa;
he resided at Atrib which was named thus after him; finally to Sa was devolved the country

[PDF p. 579]

[OF THE SAID OF EGYPT, continued]

that extends from Sa to the sea; he established his residence in the town of Sa and gave it his name. All of
Egypt formed thus four divisions, two in the Said and two in the Delta.

Abou-l Fadl Ga'far ben Tha'leb ben Ga'far El Edfaoui, in his book of the Happy Risings (of the planets), says
regarding the Said: The extent of the upper Said is twelve days' march by camel and its width three hours'
march at most, taking account only of the cultivated part; to the orient, its territory borders on the sea
and the country of the Bedjas; to the occident, it extends as far as the Oases; the Said forms therefore two
divisions, one eastern and the other western, separated by the Nile. The eastern region begins at the
prairies of the Benou Hamim, whose district borders that of Girga in the province of Akhmim, and ends to the
south of El Hou, there where begins the country of the Nubians; it is in this region that are Tig, Qoûft, and
Qous. The region of the occident begins at Bardis, whose district borders, it too, that of Girga; in this
region is the town of Samhoud; it ends at Assouan. The palms abound there on the two banks of the river. The
surface of the lands of these two regions, planted with palms and with gardens, is about 20,000 feddans; the
planet that dominates over the Said is Jupiter.

There was, it is said, formerly in the Said a palm that produced six ardebs of fruit; a vali having had its
bark torn off, the tree, that year, bore not a single fruit. This palm was on the western bank; in the times
of dearth, an oueiba of its fruits sold for a dinar. It is reported that when the world was subjected to the
emir of the believers Haroun ben Mohammed el Rashid, this prince found nothing truly beautiful except the
province of Siout, in the Said of Egypt; this province comprises 30,000 feddans of flat lands, and a single
drop of water suffices, in falling on it, to make it flourish entirely.

There are in the Said traces of the magic of the ancients.

The emir Taqtaba, vali of Qous, in the time of El Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun, recounts the following fact:
"Having had a sorceress arrested, I asked her to show me a sample of her know-how. 'My best trick,' she
answered, 'is to enchant a scorpion in the name of a person, and the animal will absolutely have to sting
that person, communicate to him its venom, and make him die.' 'Make me see that,' I said to her, 'and
designate me

[PDF p. 580]

for the experiment.' She took a scorpion, made over it her grimaces, and gave the liberty back to the animal
which set about pursuing me; I sought to avoid it, but it persisted after me. Finally I went to sit on a
chair placed in the middle of a basin filled with water; the scorpion approached the water and made a
thousand efforts to reach me; it had to renounce it however and, directing itself toward the wall, it climbed
there, followed the ceiling, and, as soon as it was above my head, let itself fall quite near me; I gave it
at once a blow and killed it. Then I had the sorceress also put to death."

The Said abounds in pastures where graze sheep and other animals that reproduce there in a fashion so
extraordinary that a single ewe gives birth in ten years to one thousand twenty-four offspring, and this in
the most natural way in the world, each ewe giving birth only once a year and giving only a single ewe per
litter; if each litter were of two young and if each mother gave birth twice a year, the number in question
would find itself multiplied by itself; make the calculation and you will ascertain the truth of what I
advance. And it happens frequently that ewes of the Said give birth three times a year and give three young
per litter.

The greatest part of the Said was the property of six tribes: the Benou Helal, the Bala, the Gahinat, the
Qoraïchites, the Laouatah, and the Benou Kilab. With them had established themselves a great number of members
of other tribes, 'Ansaris, Mezinat, Benou Darag, Benou Kilab, Tha'lebat, and Gezam.

I have heard say, regarding the prosperity of the Said, that in the time of El Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun,
and even after him, a man could go from Cairo to Assouan without carrying provisions, for he found in each
village, in each hamlet, a great number of houses destined to receive the strangers; if he stopped in one of
them, one gave the fodder to his mount and for himself one prepared all he could desire as nourishment, and
one served him. Today, it is quite different: the times are so hard that between Cairo and Assouan a traveler
would find no one who would offer him hospitality. The prosperity of the Said began to decline from the year
of anguish, under the reign of El Ashraf Sha'ban ben Hosseïn ben Mohammed ben Qalaoun, in the year 776 [12
June 1374 to 1 June 1375]. The situation became still more precarious in the time of El Zaher Barqouq, thanks
to the oppression

[PDF p. 581]

of the valis, and the region became more and more miserable until the year 806 [21 July 1403 to 9 July
1404], when Egypt was reduced to extremity by the absence of the flood of the Nile; the inhabitants of the
Said were, consequently, struck with indescribable calamities and such that, in the town of Qous, 17,000
persons died; at Siout 11,000 cadavers were washed and buried; at Hou the number of the dead rose to 15,000;
and in these numbers are not comprised the people gathered up on the roads, the unknown, the travelers, or
other people who were found in analogous conditions. Finally, the Said received the last blow in the time of
El Moayyad Sheikh. There remain today only vestiges of the ancient prosperity, vestiges that the valis have
forgotten to make disappear. We ask God to ameliorate the end.

[PDF p. 582]

CHAPTER XXX
OF THE CATARACTS. -- SURVEY OF THE ACCOUNTS CONCERNING NUBIA

'Abd Allah ben Ahmed ben Selim El Assouani, in his work entitled "Accounts on Nubia, the Maqorrah, 'Alouah,
the Bedjas, and the Nile," sets forth what follows: The country of Nubia begins at the village named El Qasr,
five miles from Assouan; the extreme stronghold occupied by the Muslims is the island of Bilak (Philae)
situated only a mile from the village that forms the frontier of Nubia; this interval constitutes the
"Nubian March." From Assouan to this place, the river is sown with numerous rocks that render the navigation
of it difficult for the boats; these can indeed cross this passage only by employing all sorts of complicated
means and by taking, to direct them, the most skillful fishermen of the place; the river is indeed barred by
steep rocks from which the water precipitates itself with an enormous noise that is heard from very far. There
is in the village (of El Qasr) a garrison and a gate by which one penetrates onto the territory of Nubia. From
this point to the first cataract of the country of Nubia, there is a distance of ten stages. In this region,
the Muslims are completely free; in the lower part they possess properties and do commerce with the upper
part; thus a great number of Muslims have established themselves there, but none of them speaks Arabic
correctly. The trees abound there, although the country is narrow, rugged, covered with mountains, and the
edge of the cultivated terrain departs only very little from the Nile. The river is bordered with villages.
The trees one meets there are the palm and the moql. The upper part of the province is wider than the lower
part. One cultivates there the vine. The Nile not being able to cover the lands that are there too elevated,
the water is brought there by machines set in movement by oxen, and one can thus irrigate terrains of one, of
two, or of three feddans. One harvests there only little wheat, but the barley and the rye are more abundant
there; the cultivated band being very narrow, one forces a little the cultivations of it; one amends it
during the summer with manure and silt, and one sows there dokhn, maize, millet, sesame, and peas. It is in
this region that are Negrash, capital of the Maris, the fortress of Ibrim, and another fortress situated more
to the North; there is the port of Adoua, fatherland of the sage Loqman and of Dhu'l Noun, where is seen a

[PDF p. 583]

marvelous temple. This province is submitted to a vali who depends on the suzerain of Nubia, and whom one
calls "the Lord of the Mountain"; the territory he administers touching, to the North, the country of Islam,
the Muslims who penetrate into Nubia have dealings with him, whether they sell him their merchandise or remit
him presents for him or for his master. The vali accepts everything and gives in exchange slaves, but
authorizes no one, neither Muslim nor other, to go to the sovereign.

The cataract of Nubia begins at the village of Taqouï. It is a beach where stops the navigation of the boats
that have gone up the river from El Qasr, (northern) limit of the province. The boats cannot go further, and
no one, neither Muslim nor other, can pass beyond this place without the authorization of the Lord of the
Mountain. From the village of Taqouï to the upper Meqs one counts six stages; all the interval comprised
between these two points is only a heap of rocks; it is the most abominable region I have seen in Nubia; the
soil there is rugged, narrowed, and the roads abrupt. On the side of the river, rocks and mountains obstruct
its course, so much so that the Nile can escape only through narrow gorges, and sometimes it is so narrowed
that its width, between the two banks, hardly reaches fifty cubits; on the side of the land, there are only
strangled defiles, steep mountains, and roads so narrow that it is impossible for a cavalier to follow them,
and that even a pedestrian cannot cross them, if he is not very robust. To the East and to the West, extend
indefinitely sands that serve as ramparts to the kingdom and where take refuge the inhabitants of the region
that touches the country of Islam. In the islands, grow rare palms and some meager cereals; the inhabitants
feed themselves above all on fish whose grease serves them to rub the body. These islands form part of the
Maris and depend on the Lord of the Mountain. The upper Meqs is occupied by a garrison whose chief depends
directly on the king of Nubia and watches the region so actively that, if the king himself comes to pass by
this place, he is stopped by the chief of the garrison who makes the simulacrum of searching him in order to
be able to act likewise with the son of the king, or his vizier, or any other functionary of less elevated
rank. Beyond this point, there are no longer either dinars or dirhems; the Nubians indeed do not [...]

[PDF p. 584]

[OF THE CATARACTS. -- SURVEY OF THE ACCOUNTS CONCERNING NUBIA, continued]

use money except to the north of their cataract to trade with the Muslims; on the other side, they do not
traffic among themselves, but exchange the objects of which they have need for slaves, livestock, camels,
iron, and grain. No one can pass beyond this point without the permission of the king; whoever transgresses
this order, whoever he be, is punished with death. Thanks to this precaution, one can know nothing of what
happens at their home, and a Nubian army can attack a neighboring country or a nomad tribe without one having
been able to suspect it. It is there that one gathers in the Nile the emery, that matter which is employed to
polish the precious stones. One plunges into the river and one finds the emery which one recognizes easily,
for it is colder to the touch than the other stones. If one has some doubts, however, one has, to recognize
it, only to blow on it with the mouth. Another cataract extends from the post in question to the village of
Saï which is the last bishopric of Nubia; there, the Nubians have a bishop, and one sees there also a temple.
Beyond, begins the province of Soqlouda, whose name signifies "the seven valis." This region resembles in
all points that which touches the country of Islam; like this one, it is sometimes wide, sometimes narrow,
and produces palms, vines, cereals, moqls; one sees there even some cotton-plants of which one makes coarse
stuffs; one cultivates there also the olive tree. The vali depends on the sovereign and commands particular
valis. In this province is the fortress of Astanoun, built at the point where begins the third cataract (of
Nubia), still more painful to cross than the others, for the course of the river is barred there by a
mountain that crosses it from east to west; the Nile escapes through three openings, and through two only
when the waters are low; the fall, which produces a deafening noise, presents a magnificent spectacle, the
river precipitating itself from the top to the bottom of the mountain. To the south of this cataract, the bed
of the Nile is sown with stones over an extent of three barids to the village of Yastou, where ends the
province of Maris and where begins that of Moqarrah. From this place to the Muslim frontier, one speaks only
the marisi. It is there the last province that belongs to Nubia; beyond, begins the district of Baqoun, whose
name signifies "the marvel," and which was given to this region because of its beauty. I have indeed seen
none on the banks of the Nile that is more vast; the river itself, according to what I have been able to see,
reaches in these regions a width of

[PDF p. 585]

five stages from east to west; its course is all sown with islands between which the waters flow; the banks
are very low and covered with villages that follow one another; the lands there are admirably cultivated, and
one sees on all sides dovecotes and prairies where graze the flocks; this region produces the greatest part
of what the capital consumes; the birds one meets there are: the naqit, the nubi, the parrot, and a thousand
other magnificent fowl; it is there that the sovereign goes most often on holiday. I accompanied him there
once, and to go there, we followed narrow canals whose two banks were shaded with trees. The crocodiles, it
is said, are inoffensive in these parts, and I have often seen some that crossed the canals by swimming.
After this district comes that of Safad Bâql, a district very narrow and quite similar to the region where
Nubia begins, only the islands are very numerous and magnificent; one meets there, in less than two days,
nearly thirty villages with pretty houses, churches, convents, numerous palms, vines, gardens, fields, very
extensive prairies where pasture livestock and camels of a russet color and of an excellent species. The
king goes there very often, for the southern limit of this district extends as far as Dongola, the capital of
the country. From Dongola, chief town of the province, to Assouan, one counts fifty stages. The author then
describes Dongola and adds: One employs, to make the roofs of the dwellings, beams of sont wood and of sag
wood that the Nile carries at the moment of its flood and that it brings all squared, and of which one is
ignorant of the provenance. I have myself seen on one of them strange signs. From Dongola to the frontier of
the country of 'Alouah, the nearest, there is a distance greater than from Dongola to Assouan. One finds also
on this side more villages, hamlets, islands, flocks, palms, trees, moqls, fields, vines, than on the banks
of the river on the side of the countries of Islam. One meets in this region considerable islands measuring
several days' march in extent, where rise mountains filled with wild beasts and ferocious animals and where
extend deserts where one can suffer from thirst. From this place, the Nile makes numerous bends toward the
Orient and toward the Occident, bends that prolong themselves for days and lengthen considerably the route,
as well to go up as to go down. It is in this province that the bend of the Nile is formed which extends to
the mines of El Shelah in

[PDF p. 586]

the region of the Shanqir. It is from there that set out El Amari, who seized the region and remained master
of it until there happened to him what happened to him. In this place abound the hippopotamuses, and it is
from this point that sets out the road that leads to Souakin, Basé, Dahlak, and the islands of the sea of
Qolzoum, a road that the Ommiades followed who, escaped from the massacre, took refuge in Nubia. A tribe of
the Bedjas, the Zénafegs, emigrated formerly into Nubia, has installed itself in this region; they continue
there the pastoral life and have conserved their language without mingling with the Nubians whose villages
they have refused to inhabit. They obey a vali who depends on Nubia.

[PDF p. 587]

CHAPTER XXXI
OF THE COURSE OF THE NILE FROM THE PROVINCE OF 'ALOUAH AND OF THE DIFFERENT PEOPLES WHO LIVE ON ITS BANKS

The Nubians and the Maqorrah form two distinct peoples not speaking the same language, but both living on the
banks of the Nile. The Nubians are none other than the Maris who inhabit in the vicinity of the countries of
Islam. Between the beginning of their territory and Assouan, there are five miles. It is reported that Selha,
ancestor of the Nubians, and Maqorris, ancestor of the Maqorrah, were originally from the Yemen; others claim
that the Nubians and the Maqorrah are Himyarites; but the generality of the genealogists is of the opinion
that the ones and the others descend from Kham, son of Noah. The Nubians and the Maqorrah made war on each
other before the appearance of Christianity. The territory of the Maqorrah begins at the village of Nafah, a
stage from Assouan. Their capital, which is named Negrash, is less than ten stages from the same town. It is
recounted that Moses, before his mission, made an expedition against this people, in the time of Pharaoh, and
destroyed Nafah. The inhabitants then were Sabeans and adored the stars, to whom they raised statues. Later,
the Nubians and the Maqorrah embraced Christianity. Their capital is Dongola. The country of 'Alouah begins
at a village situated on the eastern bank of the river and named El Abouab (the Gates); it is submitted to a
vali depending on the sovereign of 'Alouah and who bears the title of rahrah. From this region, the Nile
divides into seven branches; one of them, which comes from the Orient, carries a muddy water; but it is dry
during the summer and its bed is inhabited during this season. As soon as the time of the flood of the Nile
returns, the water begins to well up in the bed of the river and the depressions that are there fill little
by little; then come the rains, torrents form on all sides, and the river begins to overflow. It is said that
the extremity of this river is a considerable spring that escapes from a mountain. The historian of Nubia
continues thus: Simioun, hereditary prince of the country of 'Alouah, recounted to me that one finds in the
bed of this river a fish without scales and of a species that is not found in the Nile. It is necessary, to
make it come out, to dig a hole of the dimension of a man's height and even more; this fish

[PDF p. 588]

is enormous. On the banks of this river lives a tribe that partakes at once of the 'Alouah and of the Bedjah
and that one calls Digioun; to this tribe succeeds another, that of the Bazah from whose home comes the bird
that one calls the bazin pigeon. This people borders the territory of Abyssinia. The second river is the
White Nile, which comes from the side of the West and whose waters are as white as milk. I questioned a
traveler, who had traversed the countries of the Blacks, on the course and the color of the river that waters
these regions; here is what he taught me: the river in question comes out of sandy mountains and pours itself
into immense lakes situated in the country of the Blacks; from there it directs itself toward unknown
regions; its waters, which up to there are not white, owe their color to the soil on which they flow or to
another river it receives. On its two banks live diverse peoples. The third river is the Green Nile, which
comes from the South-East; its waters are very green, but extremely limpid, letting one see the fish that
inhabit them. The savor of these waters differs from that of the waters of the Nile, and they soon alter
(disorder) the one who drinks of them. The fish that people these rivers are of the same sort, but have a
different taste. At the moment of the flood, this river carries woods of Sag, of Boqani, of Rhatha (a wood
that has the odor of incense), and thick woods that one works and of which one makes oars. This sort of wood
grows equally on the two banks of the river. It is said that one finds there also odorous wood. I have seen,
adds the author, one of these pieces of Sag wood brought thus by the flood and which bore strange signs.
These two rivers, the White Nile and the Green Nile, join near the capital of the country of 'Alouah, and,
for nearly a stage, the waters of each of these rivers keep their color; then they mingle. Their waters, in
colliding, form enormous waves. Someone recounted to me having taken water of the White Nile and having
spread it in the Green Nile, where it remained, keeping the milky color, for nearly an hour, before mingling
in it. Between these two rivers is an island of which one does not know the end, no more than one knows the
end of these two rivers. One knows the width of them at their confluence, but the interval that separates
them goes certainly widening and reaches a [...]

[PDF p. 589]

[OF THE COURSE OF THE NILE, continued]

distance evaluated at a month's march; further, one can no longer know exactly which are the peoples who
inhabit the banks of these two rivers; these peoples dread one another; they are of very diverse races and of
high stature. One recounted to me that one of the sovereigns of the country of 'Alouah, wishing to know the
extent of this island, penetrated into it, but, after years of march, he could not reach the end of it. Those
who inhabit the south of the island remain with their flocks in houses dug under the soil like underground
corridors, shelter themselves there during the day against the excessive heat of the sun, and come out of
them only at night; some of them are completely naked. As for the four other rivers, they come also from the
South-East and their point of departure is unknown equally. They are however not as wide as the White Nile
and the Green Nile, and form neither as many arms nor as many islands; all four, like the first river, throw
themselves into the Green Nile which in its turn throws itself into the White Nile; the banks of all these
rivers are inhabited and cultivated and their course is navigable; one of them traverses Abyssinia. I have
myself made numerous observations on these rivers, and I have had them made by other travelers, but I have
found no one who had seen with his own eyes the source of any of them; what I have managed to know, by people
who informed me and who themselves had informed themselves of other persons, is that these rivers come out of
uninhabited regions and that at the time of the flood, one sees float on their surface debris of boats,
doors, and other objects that prove that beyond the desert region is an inhabited country. As for the flood
itself, everyone knows that it is the result of rains and of another special cause. The best proof of it is
the phenomenon that occurs for one of these rivers; it remains dry during the summer, and its bed is then
inhabited, then it fills at the time of the flood. An astonishing thing is that the flood occurs at once, and
in the same time, in all the rivers thus united, and in all the regions, at Masr and in the neighboring
region, in the Said, at Assouan, in Nubia, at 'Alouah, and further still. One has however observed many times,
regarding the flood, that when, for example, it occurs at Assouan, one ascertains it at Qous only a little
later. When the rains are abundant in the regions of the upper river and the torrents multiply there, one
knows that the year will be prosperous; but if the rains are rare, it will be the drought. I hold from
certain travelers, who have visited the country of the Zing, information on the route they followed: when one
is on the sea of China, one is pushed toward the country of the Zing by the

[PDF p. 590]

wind of the North; one follows, for two days, the eastern coast of the island of Egypt, and one arrives at a
place named Ras Haferi, which is considered as the extremity of the island of Egypt; then, observing the
stars to guide oneself, one directs oneself toward the Occident, then one turns to the North and, navigating
always toward the Septentrion, one reaches the town of Qabilah, where resides the sovereign of the Zing. When
these peoples prostrate themselves for the prayer, they turn in the direction of Djeddah. One of the four
rivers comes from the country of the Zing, for it carries trees that grow in this region. Soubah, town of the
country of 'Alouah, is found to the East of the great island formed by the white river and the green river,
at the northern point of this island, at the confluence of the two rivers; to the east of the town is the
river whose bed dries up and is inhabited. One sees in this town very beautiful constructions, vast convents,
churches where gold abounds, and gardens; one of its suburbs is peopled by Muslims. The king of 'Alouah is
richer than the king of Maqorrah; he has more warriors and more horses; his country is more fertile and more
vast; the palms and the vines however are rare there; the most abundant harvest is that of the white dourrah
which resembles rice; one makes of it bread and beer. One finds there much meat, for the livestock abounds as
well as the pastures which are there so vast and extended that one needs several days' march to reach the
mountains. The country produces horses of good race and Arab camels with russet hair. These peoples are of
the Jacobite Christian religion; as among the Nubians, their bishops are sent to them by the patriarch of
Alexandria. They use the Greek books that they translate into their language. They are less intelligent than
the Nubians. Their king is absolute master and reduces to slavery whom it pleases him among his subjects,
whether they be guilty or innocent; far from protesting, the man thus treated prostrates himself before the
master, and, without complaining of the injustice that strikes him, he cries: "Long live the king! may his
will be accomplished!" The king wears a crown of gold, for the gold is very abundant in his country.

One of the astonishing things of this country is that in the great island formed by the two rivers is a
people, the Kernina, who occupy a very extended region watered by the Nile and by the rains; at the time of
the sowing, each individual comes with what he possesses of seeds and forms an enclosure in relation with the
quantity of seeds he has brought; then he sows at the four angles of the enclosure a little quantity of this
grain and deposits the rest,

[PDF p. 591]

with a little beer, in the middle of the enclosure and goes away. The next morning, all the enclosure is
sown and the beer has been drunk; at the time of the harvest, one cuts some stalks that one deposits in a
place with beer, and one withdraws; when one returns one finds the harvest done and put into sheaves. One
does the same when it is a matter of threshing the grain or of winnowing it. But if someone, wishing to weed
his field, tears out by chance the least ear, he finds the next day all the field torn out. The district
where this happens forms an immense territory two months' march long by an equal width and is sown at the
same time. The subsistences of the country and of the king of 'Alouah are drawn from this region; boats are
sent there that come back with a cargo of grains; sometimes one must fight with the inhabitants.

The account we have just made is real and well known; one speaks of it throughout all Nubia and all the
country of 'Alouah; the Muslims who have traversed these regions to traffic there are convinced of its
reality and doubt it in no way. Moreover, if this fact were not attested by a number of persons so great that
one cannot really suppose that they have agreed on it, I would certainly not have spoken of it, so improbable
is it. The people of the country attribute this to the genies; they believe that certain persons can oblige,
by means of certain stones, the genies to serve them, to obey them, and to accomplish for them marvelous
things; even the clouds would obey them.

Among other marvelous things relative to Nubia, the king of Maqorrah recounted to me that, as soon as the
rain has fallen on the mountains, one gathers fish on the soil immediately after. I asked what species of
fish were found thus, and it was answered me that they were of small size and had a red tail. I have seen by
myself numerous individuals of the different tribes of which one has spoken above. Most recognize the
Creator; they make him sacrifices under the form of the sun, of the moon, or of the stars. Certain of them do
not know the Creator and adore the sun and the fire. Others adore all that pleases them: tree or animal. The
same recounted to me having seen one day, at an assembly held by the king of Maqorrah, a man whom he asked
what was his country: "My country," said the man, "is at three leagues from the Nile." Questioned on his
religion: "My lord is the same as yours; it is that of the king and of all men." "And where is he?" "In
heaven," answered the man, and he added: "When the rain fails us, or a scourge desolates us, or the sickness
descends on our flocks,

[PDF p. 592]

we go to the summit of a mountain, and there we address to God prayers immediately granted and which are
accomplished before we have descended from the mountain." One asked him if God had sent to their home some
prophet; he answered no; and as one reported to him what touches the mission of Moses, of Jesus, and of
Mohammed and the proofs they had given of it: "If they have done all that," he said, "one should believe in
them," and he added: "I would have believed in it, if I had seen them do all that."

The author resumes: The sons of Kenz el daoulah seized Nubia and reigned there from the year [...] (blank in
the text).

One raised at Dongola a mosque in which one gave hospitality to the travelers.

On the bank of the Nile, one meets still El Kanem where governs a Muslim chief; from this locality to the
country of Mali, there is a considerable distance; the seat of the government is established in a town named
Hima. On the side of Egypt, this kingdom begins at the country of Zerla; at the other extremity is the
country of Kaka. Between these two localities, there is a distance of nearly three months' very painful
march. The king of the country remains hidden and shows himself only on the two days of feast, in the morning
and in the afternoon; the rest of the year, he gives audience only hidden behind a curtain. The inhabitants
feed themselves on rice which grows in their country without cultivation; they harvest also wheat, maize,
figs, lemons, eggplant, radish, and green vegetables. They weave stuffs that bear among them the name of
dendi and of which each piece is ten cubits long; they use them as money by fractions of a quarter of a
cubit, or more; they employ also, as money, shells, glass beads, pieces of copper or of silver, the whole
brought back to the equivalent value of these stuffs. In the south of this country extend forests and
deserts where live wild individuals, such as the Fioul, fairly similar to man; a cavalier cannot reach them;
they scratch man and, at night, one sees shine at their home something that resembles fire. If one wishes to
approach them, they take flight; and if one wishes to pursue them, it is impossible to reach them; they flee
without cease

[PDF p. 593]

before the strangers. If one throws stones at them, they use them to produce sparks in striking them one
against the other. In this region, the gourds reach a size such that one makes of them boats in which one
crosses the Nile.

These countries extend from Ifriqiah and Barqah in the South to the middle of the western ecliptic. They are
regions dried up, deserted, and detestable. The first who carried Islamism there was the missionary El Hadi
el Othmani, a descendant of Othman ben 'Afan; since, these peoples have united with the sect of the Yeznis,
descendants of Seif ben Dhu Yezn, who follow the doctrine of the imam Malek ben Anis; between the two is the
just middle. They are of austere principles and not at all conciliating; in 640 [1 July 1242 to 20 June
1243], they raised at Masr for the Malekites a school known under the name of school of Ibn Rashiq, where
descend those who come to render them visit. God willing, we will speak of it in the chapter of the Schools.

[PDF p. 594]

CHAPTER XXXII
OF THE BEDJAHS, WHO ARE, IT IS SAID, OF THE RACE OF THE BERBERS

The country of the Bedjahs begins at the village of El Hazabah, a locality of the desert of Qous, where are
the emerald mines. From El Hazabah to Qous there are nearly three stages. El Gaheg (El-Jahiz) asserts that
there is no other emerald mine in the world than that one. The gem is found in deep and dark caverns into
which one enters with lamps and by fixing cords to guide oneself on the return; without this precaution, one
could lose one's way. One digs the soil by means of picks and one finds the emerald among the stones and
surrounded by a gangue that is neither as brilliant nor as pure. At its other extremity, the country of the
Bedjahs borders Abyssinia. The Bedjahs occupy in the interior of this island -- I mean the island of Egypt --
a territory that extends to the shore of the sea, on the side of the islands of Souakin, of Bada', and of
Dahlak. It is a nomadic population that transports itself, with its tents of skins, everywhere there are
pastures. They establish their descent by the maternal line, and each of their tribes obeys a particular
chief, but they have no king; they follow no religion. Among them, the inheritance is transmitted to the son
of the daughter or to the son of the sister, and no account is taken of the sons of the deceased, for they
claim that the birth of the son of the sister and of the son of the daughter raises not the least doubt, and
that these children, whether their mother had them from her husband or from any other, are no less the sons
of their mother. Formerly, they had a chief whom all the other chiefs obeyed and who resided in the village
of Hagr, at the extremity of the island of the Bedjahs. They ride russet camels that are born in their
country. The camels of Arab race are also very numerous among them, as well as the herds of oxen, of sheep,
and of ewes; their oxen are beautiful and shining and have very long horns; likewise their rams; these last
have a spotted skin; these herds furnish much milk. The Bedjahs feed themselves on the flesh of these animals
and use their milk as a drink; they eat very little cheese; however some eat of it. Their body is vigorous
and their belly

[PDF p. 595]

is lean; their complexion is of a yellowish color. They are very rapid at running and dispute on this point
with the other men. Their camels have also an extreme speed; they run a very long time and bear admirably the
thirst. With such mounts, the Bedjahs can compete in speed against the horses and surpass them; they make them
turn as it pleases them, and traverse, thus mounted, considerable extents of country. These camels serve them
still as mount to go to war; seated on their backs, they launch their javelins; when the launched javelin has
touched the target, the camel runs at full speed and its master can take the object; if on the contrary the
dart falls to earth, the animal lowers itself to permit its master to pick it up.

There was formerly among the Bedjahs a vigorous and bold man, named Kelâz, who possessed a camel of an
incomparable speed and one-eyed like its master. Kelâz had engaged himself before his tribe to go to the
oratory of Masr for the day of the feast; the feast was then near, and it seemed impossible to arrive at
Fostat in so little time. Kelâz however executed his promise and arrived at the agreed moment on the
Moqattam. Cavaliers set about pursuing him, but could not rejoin him. It is also he who was the cause that on
the day of the feast one posted sentinels at the foot of the mountain. The Toulounides and the other princes
of Egypt placed on this occasion at the foot of the Moqattam, on the side that looks toward the quarter named
El Habash, an important post of soldiers charged with watching over the security of the inhabitants until the
return of the feast. The Bedjahs are of a remarkable honesty; if anyone among them has wronged another, the
latter attaches a piece of stuff to the end of his lance and says: "This is the shelter of so-and-so" -- that
is, of the one who has committed the fraud. And he leaves thus the stuff and the lance until he has received
satisfaction. This people is very hospitable; if some stranger stops at the home of a Bedjah, the latter
kills for his guest an animal; if he receives the visit of more than three travelers, he kills for them some
beasts of the nearest herd, whether this herd belongs to him or belongs to another. If he has nothing he can
serve to his guest, he slaughters for him the mount of the latter, and, to compensate him, makes him a
present of a greater value. They have for arms lances sebaïah of which the iron measures three cubits and the
wood four cubits, whence their name. The iron is as wide as a sword; it is very rare that this arm escapes
their hands, for at the extremity of the wood is a sort of loop that prevents the lance from leaving the
hand. These arms are

[PDF p. 596]

fabricated by women in a place where no man approaches, except those who come to them to make their
purchases. It happens however that sometimes one of them becomes mother by the fact of a traveler; if the
child she brings into the world is a girl, one leaves her to live, but if it is a boy, one kills him, for,
they say, the men are good only to stir up quarrels and war. The Bedjahs have shields of ox-skins on which
one leaves the hairs; they also make use of shields of buffalo-skin, like the people of Axum, or of the skin
of a marine animal. Their bows have the form of the Arab bows; they are large and massive and made of sidr
wood or of shouhal; with these bows they launch poisoned arrows; the poison with which they impregnate them
is drawn from the roots of the ghalâq tree that one puts on the fire and that one lets boil until the liquid
becomes gluey. To test it, one of them pricks a part of the body and lets the blood flow; he then applies the
poison, and if the blood returns backward, one is certain that the poison is perfect; one wipes then the
blood, for fear that, reentering into the body, it kill the man; for every man reached by this poison dies at
once, were the wound no greater than the prick of a lancet. This poison has action only on the blood
contaminated by a wound; one can drink it with impunity. All the territory of the Bedjahs is only mines, and,
as one goes up into the interior, the gold is purer and more abundant. One finds there also mines of silver,
of copper, of iron, of lead, of magnet, of marcasite, of amethyst, of emeralds, and of asbestos stone which,
soaked in oil, lights like a wick; one meets there still other minerals; but one applies oneself above all in
the country to the search for gold, and the Bedjahs neglect absolutely the other mines. In the valleys grow
the moql, the myrobalans, the rush, the absinthe, the senna, the colocynth, the tree that produces the ban,
etc. At the very extremity of their territory one meets palms, vines, odoriferous plants that grow there
without cultivation. In this country live all sorts of wild beasts: lions, elephants, tigers, panthers,
monkeys, badgers, civets, and an animal pretty as the gazelle and that bears two horns the color of gold;
when it is taken, this animal cannot live long; in the way of birds, one meets there the parrot, the naqit,
the noubi, the turtledove, the hen of Abyssinia, the bazin pigeon, etc. From all the men, among this people,
one removes the right testicle; as for the women, one

[PDF p. 597]

cuts them the lips of the vulva; these lips afterward are drawn near and weld so well that at the moment of
marriage the man is obliged to make there an incision to his size; but this operation has become rarer. Here
is what would be its origin: A king had formerly made war on the Bedjahs, then he had concluded peace,
exacting from them that they cut the breasts of the girls who would be born to them and the member of the
boys, wishing thus to prevent the reproduction of the race; but the Bedjahs inverted the terms of the treaty
and cut the teats of the boys and the vulva of the women. There is among them a tribe that tears out the
incisors, in order not to resemble asses. Among another tribe, that of the Bazahs, established at the
extremity of the country, all the women bear the same name; likewise for the men. One day, a Muslim, a pretty
boy passing in the country, all the inhabitants called one another, saying: "Here is a god who has descended
from the sky and who has sat under the tree," and they remained to look at him from afar.

The serpents of this country are enormous and of very different species. One saw once in a pond a serpent
whose tail was already out of the water, throw itself on a woman who was drawing water and squeeze her with so
much force that the unfortunate one rendered her grease by the fundament. One meets there also a serpent
without head, spotted and of small size. Whoever walks on its trace dies; if someone kills it with a stick or
a javelin, and he does not throw his arm at the instant, he dies equally; one of these serpents having been
killed by means of a piece of wood, this piece of wood broke. If someone looks at this serpent, alive or dead,
its venom operates and kills the curious one. The Bedjahs are turbulent and very disposed to do harm. In the
time of Islam, and even before, they have committed depredations in Upper Egypt on the right bank of the
Nile; they have destroyed there numerous villages. The Pharaohs of Egypt have made against them several
expeditions and have signed treaties with them, because they had need of their mines; the Greeks acted
likewise, in the time of their domination in Egypt. One sees still their traces in the mines, of which the
directors were still at their post at the moment of the conquest of Egypt by the Muslims.

'Abd el-Rahman ben 'Abdallah ben 'Abd el Hakem reports that 'Abd allah ben Sa'd ben Abou Serah, returning
from Nubia, met on the banks of the Nile a group of Bedjahs and questioned them on their affairs; he learned
thus that they obeyed no king; their condition appeared to him so contemptible

[PDF p. 598]

that he left them without concluding with them either arrangement or treaty. The first who made a convention
with them was 'Obeid Allah ben El Hagab El Selouli, and 'Abd el Rahman recounts having found the letter
addressed by ben El Hagab to the Bedjahs, a letter bearing that one would send each year three hundred young
camels to the place of the countryside of Egypt that this people traversed to traffic, but without stopping
there; on the condition that on their side the Bedjahs would kill no Muslim nor any other subject of Islam;
if a murder were committed, the treaty would find itself annulled; that the Bedjahs would not give asylum to
the slaves of the Muslims, and that, if anyone took refuge with them, they would return him to his masters.
Every Bedjah who would steal a ewe would pay four dinars and for a stolen cow ten dinars. They had a
representative who resided in the countryside of Egypt and who served as hostage to the Muslims. Subsequently,
the Muslims flocked to the mines, mingled with the population, and married the women of the country, and the
greatest part of the tribe of the Hadareb became thus Muslim, without being however of a very austere dogma.
The Hadareb form the advanced point of the Bedjahs and occupy the region neighboring Egypt, from the northern
frontier of their country to El 'Alaqi, 'Aïdab where one embarks for Djeddah, and further still. Another of
their tribes, the Zénafegi, is more numerous than the Hadareb; but it is submitted to these last; it furnishes
them escorts and pastures their herds. Each of the chiefs of the Hadareb has in his patrimony a group of
Zenafeg, whom he regards as slaves and whom one transmits by inheritance; formerly however the Zenafeg had
been their masters. Then the incursions of the Bedjahs on the Muslim lands multiplied; the valis of Assouan
depended then on Iraq. The news of the depredations of the Bedjahs having reached the emir of the believers
El Mamoun, the latter sent to reduce them 'Abd Allah ben El Gahm; after several combats, a treaty intervened
between the Muslim general and the great chief of the Bedjahs, Kenoun, who resided in the village of Hagr of
which we have previously spoken. Here is the copy of this treaty: "Letter written by 'Abdallah ben El Gahm,
servant of the emir of the believers, chief of the expeditionary army, delegate of the emir Abou Ishaq, son
of the emir of the believers El Rashid, in the month of Rabi' I of the year 216 [18 April to 17 May 831], to
Kenoun ben Abd el 'Aziz, great chief of the Bedjahs, in the town of Assouan: You have asked me with
insistence to grant you [...]

[PDF p. 599]

[OF THE BEDJAHS, continued]

protection, you and the people of the Bedjahs, and to accord you the aman, to you and to them, on my part and
on the part of all the Muslims. I have consented to make with you a treaty that will be observed by me and all
the Muslims, as much as you and the people of the Bedjahs will keep the promises you have made and which are
registered in this letter. The portion of your country, plains and mountains, that extends from the frontier
of Assouan of Egypt to the region comprised between Dahlak and Badè, will be domain of El Mamoun 'Abd Allah
son of Haroun, emir of the believers; you and all your subjects will be slaves of the emir of the believers;
you will remain however sovereign of your country as you are presently, on the condition that you will pay
him each year the tribute that the Bedjahs paid formerly, a hundred camels or three hundred dinars sounding
and weighing true, which will be carried to the Beit el Mal; the choice in this is reserved to the emir of the
believers and to his valis; of this tribute you should retain nothing; when anyone among you speaks of
Mohammed, the apostle of God, of the divine book, or of the religion, let him speak of it as is fitting; if
anyone of your subjects kills a Muslim, free or slave, he will cease to be protected by God, by his apostle,
by the emir of the believers, and by the ensemble of the Muslims, and his blood will be spilled as is spilled
the blood of an enemy in battle. If anyone of you comes to the aid of the enemies of Islam, whether by giving
money, or by indicating the badly defended places of the Muslims, or by spying on the army, the protection
accorded by the present treaty will cease and the blood of the traitor may be spilled. If anyone of you,
voluntarily or involuntarily, kills a Muslim free or slave, or a protected person of Islam, if he steals
whatever it may be belonging to a Muslim or to a protected person of Islam, whether it be in the country of
the Bedjahs, in a Muslim country, in Nubia, or in any country whatsoever, on land or on sea, he will pay for
the murder of a Muslim ten times (the established price); for the murder of a Muslim slave, ten times the
price of the slave; for the murder of a protected person of Islam, ten times the price fixed in the country
of the victim; in case of theft done to a Muslim or to a protected person, he must repay ten times the amount
of the theft. If a Muslim enters into the country of the Bedjahs, whether to do commerce there, or to
establish himself there, or to traverse it, or to go to the pilgrimage, he will be among you in safety, as if
he were one of yours, until the moment when he will have come out of your territory. You will receive no
fugitive slave of the Muslims, and, if one comes to you, you will return him to the Muslims; you will return
also to the Muslims who would be

[PDF p. 600]

among you what belongs to them without their having to pay you any duty for it. If you descend into the
countryside of the Said to traffic there or only to pass there, you will be without arms and you will enter
under no pretext into the towns nor into the villages; you will prevent no Muslim from penetrating into your
country and from doing commerce there, whether by land or by water; you will maintain the roads safe and will
not cut the roads to the Muslims nor to the protected persons of Islam; you will steal nothing either from
the Muslims or from the protected persons; you will destroy nothing of the mosques raised by the Muslims at
Sihat, at Hagr, and in all your territory, over whatever length and whatever width it extends. If you did it,
the treaty would become null and the protection that is accorded you would cease. Kenoun ben 'Abd el 'Aziz
will dwell in the countryside of the Said of Egypt to represent there his country and to assure to the
Muslims the payment of the agreed tribute and the payment of what would be due to the Muslims as price of
blood or as restitution of objects stolen by the Bedjahs. No Bedjah will venture into the region that extends
from El Kasr to the village of Qôban, in Nubia, limit of the territory that the nomads traverse. 'Abd Allah
ben El Gahm, servant of the emir of the believers, accords to Kenoun ben 'Abd El 'Aziz, chief of the Bedjahs,
a general pardon, under the conditions enumerated and established in the present letter, and which must be
