ratified by the emir of the believers. If Kenoun does not conform to it and commits some violence, the treaty
will become null and the protection will cease. Kenoun must authorize the representatives of the emir of the
believers to penetrate into the country of the Bedjahs to collect there the duty of alms from those of the
Bedjahs who would be Muslims. He must execute strictly all that has been agreed between him and 'Abdallah ben
El Gahm and that he has engaged himself to observe in the name of God and by the gravest oaths that men can
make. In exchange, Kenoun and all the Bedjahs can count on the faithful protection of God, on the protection
of the emir of the believers, that of the emir Abou Ishaq, son of the emir of the believers El Rashid, on
that of Abd allah ben El Gahm and that of all the Muslims; this protection consented by 'Abd allah ben El
Gahm will be of full effect as long as Kenoun ben 'Abd El 'Aziz keeps faithfully his engagements. If Kenoun
or any Bedjah whatsoever changes or alters some clause of the treaty, the protection of God will cease, and
likewise the protection of the emir of the believers, that of the emir Abou Ishaq, son of the emir of the
believers El Rashid, that of Abd allah ben El Gahm

[PDF p. 601]

and that of all the Muslims. All that is contained in this letter has been translated word for word by
Zakaria ben Saleh El Makhzoumi, inhabitant of Djeddah, and by 'Abd allah ben Ismaïl El Qoreïshi, and
registered by the assembly of the notaries of Assouan." The Bedjahs remained thus for a certain time, then
they recommenced to make incursions into the countryside of the Said of Egypt. Complaints, more and more
frequent, were carried against them to the emir of the believers Ga'far El Moutawakkel 'ala Allah, who sent
to reduce them Mohammed ben 'Abd allah El Qomi. The latter asked to make a choice among the men he preferred,
for he did not wish to lead a considerable army, because of the difficulty of the roads. He set out therefore
from Masr with a troop not numerous, but chosen, and marched against the Bedjahs, while his ships went up the
river. The Bedjahs came to meet him in an innumerable crowd and mounted on camels. This multitude frightened
the Muslims; but, to occupy the Bedjahs, Mohammed El Qomi wrote them a long letter on a rolled paper and
enveloped in a piece of stuff. The Bedjahs gathered to read it, and the Muslims rushed on them, having
attached to the necks of their horses little bells whose noise terrified the camels of the Bedjahs which took
flight carrying off their cavaliers. The Muslims threw themselves in pursuit of them and killed a considerable
number of them; the chief of the Bedjahs perished in the affair. His nephew, named chief in his place, asked
the suspension of hostilities, which was accorded him on the condition that he would himself go to make his
submission to the emir of the believers. He went therefore to Baghdad and from there went to present himself
to El Moutawakkel and at Serr-men-Raï in the year 241 [22 May 855 to 10 May 856]. One accorded him peace by
means of an annual due and the delivery of a certain number of slaves. It was decided also that the Bedjahs
would not prevent the Muslims from working at the mines. El Qomi remained some time at Assouan and left in the
magazines of the town all he had brought with him of arms and engines of war. The valis drew constantly from
these magazines, until at the end they emptied them. The Muslims having flocked to the mines and having mixed
with the Bedjahs, these became little by little less ferocious. After long researches, one discovered native
gold; the rumor of it having spread, a crowd of people arrived from all the countries. Abou 'Abd El Rahman
ben 'Abdallah

[PDF p. 602]

ben 'Abd El Hamid El 'Amari, after his expedition of Nubia, in 255 [20 December 868 to 8 December 869],
entered into the country of the Bedjahs, accompanied by the Rabi'ahs, the Gahinahs, and other Arab tribes.
The country of the Bedjahs was so peopled that the beasts of burden charged with carrying them the victuals
from Assouan were to the number of sixty thousand, without counting the boats that set out from Qolzoum and
disembarked at 'Aïdhab. The Bedjahs had an inclination for the Rebi'ahs and got along very well with them. It
is claimed that, before the introduction of Islamism among the Bedjahs, the priests of this country had
predicted to them, on the part of their divinity, that they would one day obey the Rabi'ahs, and this
prediction was indeed accomplished. After the murder of El 'Amari, the Rabi'ahs seized the islands, aided in
this by the Bedjahs; they chased from them the Arabs who were still there and married the daughters of the
chiefs of the Bedjahs. Thus was appeased the hostility of this people against the Muslims. The Bedjahs of the
interior -- that is, those who inhabit the desert of the country of Alouah, on the side of the Red Sea, to
the frontier of Abyssinia -- are nomads like the Hadareb, possess like them numerous herds, use the same
aliments, and employ the same mounts and the same arms; however the Hadareb are more courageous and less
turbulent. The Bedjahs of the interior have remained pagan, adore the demons, and regulate themselves
according to the decisions of their priests. Each group of population has a priest for whom one raises a hut
of beast-skins in which they go to make their adorations. When one has resolved to question him on something
of which one has need, the priest removes his clothes, enters into the hut backward, and comes out of it like
a madman and an epileptic, crying: "The demon sends you his salutations and tells you to withdraw from such a
place, otherwise such a people is going to rush on you. You have asked to make an expedition into such a
country; go, for you will have the victory and will carry off such or such booty. The camels that you will
carry off in such a place will belong to me, as well as such a young girl that you will find in the tent of
so-and-so and the ewes of such a species," and other similar discourses. The Bedjahs assert that most of
these predictions are accomplished. When they have carried off some booty, they withdraw from it what the
priest has mentioned and give it to him as being his property; if one of them opposes himself to it,

[PDF p. 603]

they refuse him the milk of their she-camels. If they wish to leave the place where they are established, the
priest charges the hut in question on a special camel, all covered with sweat, although the tent is empty and
contains nothing. They claim that this camel has great difficulty in rising and walking, and there has
remained among the Hadareb a tribe that still follows the same customs; some even ally these pagan practices
to those of Islamism.

All that I have just reported has been extracted from the work of the historian of Nubia. I have also seen in
a letter, addressed by certain tribes to the emir of the believers 'Ali ben Abou Taleb, that mention was made
of the Bedjahs and of the Kadjahs, who are very wicked, but little given to pillage. The Bedjahs are thus; as
for the Kadjahs, one knows of them only what 'Abdallah ben Ahmed, the historian of Nubia, says of them.

For his part, Abou-l Hassan El Masa'oudi reports what follows: The Bedjahs are established between the sea of
Qolzoum and the Nile of Egypt; they are divided into several tribes that all obey a single chief. In their
country are found mines of native gold and of emeralds. By numerous bands or by small groups, they go by
camel as far as the country of the Nubians where they commit depredations and carry off prisoners. Before it
was thus, the Nubians were more powerful than the Bedjahs; but, since the development and the triumph of
Islamism, the Muslims have come in crowds to establish themselves in the gold mines of the countries of
'Alaqi and of 'Aïdhab; into the same region have come also to inhabit a great number of Arabs of the tribe of
Rabi'ah ben Nazar ben Mo'add ben 'Adnan. Their importance has only grown by the crossings resulting from the
marriages contracted by the Arabs among the Bedjahs. These gained in power and married in their turn the
daughters of the Rabi'ahs. Thus with the aid of the Bedjahs, the Rabi'ahs became more powerful than the rival
tribes of the vicinity, the tribe of Qahtan and the other tribes established in these regions. It is thus
that the mine is found still in our epoch -- that is, in the year 332 [4 September 943 to 23 August 944] -- in
the hands of Beshir ben Merwan ben Ishaq ben Rabi'ah. This Beshir commands three million Rabi'ahs or allies
of the Rabi'ahs residing in Egypt and in the Yemen and thirty thousand Bedjahs armed with lances and
indigenous shields and mounted on camels. These warriors are of the tribe of the Hadareb, the only ones among
the Bedjahs who have made themselves Muslims; the Bedjahs of the interior are still [...]

[PDF p. 604]

[OF THE BEDJAHS, continued]

pagan and adore a special idol. The territory of the Bedjahs who possess the emerald mine extends to El
'Alaqi, where is the gold mine. From El 'Alaqi to the Nile, there are fifteen stages. The inhabited point
that is nearest to it is the town of Assouan. The island of Souakin is not quite a mile in length nor in
width. Between this island and the sea of Abyssinia extends a narrow strait that one can cross by ford; it is
inhabited by a tribe of the Bedjahs, the Khasahs, who are Muslims and have a king residing in the island.

According to El Hamadani, Kana'an ben Ham married Artib, daughter of Shawil ben Tares ben Yafeth, and had from
her Haqa, El Asaoud, Noubah, Qorân, El Zing, and El Zoghawah, ancestor of the Blacks. The Bedjahs, it is said,
descend from Cham, son of Noah, or according to others, from Qoush ben Kana'an ben Ham. Some hold the Bedjahs
to be a tribe of Abyssinians; however they live under tents of hair and have a complexion darker than the
Abyssinians. They wear the same costume as the Arabs and have neither towns, nor villages, nor cultivated
fields. Their victuals come to them from Abyssinia, from Egypt, or from Nubia. Primitively the Bedjahs adored
the idols; they converted to Islamism in the time of the emir 'Abdallah ben Sa'd ben Abou Serah. They are
large (generous) and generous, and distribute themselves into tribes and into groups of which each has its
special chief. It is a nomadic people that feeds itself only on flesh and milk.

[PDF p. 605]

CHAPTER XXXIII
OF THE TOWN OF ASSOUAN

Assouan comes from the word asa (to have need of consolation, to be sad, afflicted); one says of an afflicted
man [...]; a man who saddens himself, who afflicts himself.

Assouan is situated at the extremity of the Said and forms one of the frontier posts of the region,
separating Nubia from Egypt. One harvests there in abundance the wheat and other cereals, fruits, green
plants, and vegetables. One finds there also many camels, oxen, and sheep, whose flesh is excellent and very
fat and always sells very cheap. It is an entrepot for the merchandise and the objects that one dispatches
from this point into Nubia. To the East, Assouan touches countries that are not submitted to Islamism. To the
South rises the mountain that contains the emerald mine; this mountain is situated in a desert, far from
every inhabited place. At fifteen stages from Assouan is the gold mine. To the West, the territory of Assouan
extends to the Oases. One goes from Assouan to 'Aïdab, port where one embarks for the Hedjaz, the Yemen, and
India.

The town of Assouan, says El Masa'oudi, is inhabited by Arabs of the tribes of Qahtan, of Nezar ben Rabi'ah,
of Modar, and a great number of Qoreïshites; most of these Arabs come from the Hedjaz. The country abounds in
palms, and the soil there is so fertile that, if one plants in the earth a pit, there grows a palm that, at
the end of two years, gives fruits. The people who reside at Assouan are proprietors of numerous domains
situated in Nubia and whose taxes are paid to the king of the Nubians. These domains had been acquired from
the Nubians at the beginning of Islamism, under the reign of the Ommiades and the Abbasids. The king of Nubia
had sent to El Mamoun, at the time of his voyage in Egypt, messengers charged with asking the caliph the
restitution of these domains. The delegates, arrived at Fostat, set forth that inhabitants of Nubia and
slaves of their master had sold some of their domains to their neighbors of Assouan, that these lands
belonged to the king, for the Nubians are the slaves of the king and have no property

[PDF p. 606]

and occupied these domains only as slaves charged with putting them into cultivation. El Mamoun referred the
affair to the judge of the town of Assouan, and to the savants and the sheikhs established in this locality.
The people of Assouan, acquirers of these terrains, informed that they were going to escape them, sought the
means of deceiving the king of Nubia. For this, they went to find the Nubians who had sold them these
domains and engaged them to declare, when they would be cited before the judge, that they did not consider
themselves as the slaves of their king, and to say: "Our situation, we Nubians, is exactly yours vis-à-vis
your king; we must obey him and not infringe his orders. If you, others, are the slaves of your king and if
your goods belong to him, we are in the same situation." When the judge had them appear in the presence of
the delegate of the king, they repeated to him these words and others of the same kind that had been inspired
in them. As they refused to recognize themselves as slaves of their king, the sale has remained valid until
present, and the lands in litigation have been transmitted by inheritance; these lands are in Nubia, in the
province of Maris. Since, the Nubians submitted to the king of Nubia are divided into two categories; one, of
which we have just spoken and which does not consider itself as slave, and the other which is slave of the
king. These last inhabit the provinces of Nubia that are not neighboring Assouan; as for that which touches
this town, it is the province of Maris.

The Nubians divide into two branches: one has established itself to the east and to the west of the Nile and
occupies the two banks of it. Its territory touches the territory of the Copts of the Said of Egypt and has
developed itself in going up the river; it has arrived thus to the highest parts of its course and has built
there a capital; it is a considerable town that bears the name of Dongola. The second branch of the Nubians,
the 'Alouah, has also built a great town, Saraqtah. The part of the kingdom that touches the territory of
Assouan is called the Maris; it is from it that the marisi wind has taken its name; this province of the
kingdom borders the provinces of Egypt, on the side of the Said and of the town of Assouan. To the orient of
the Said of Egypt rises an enormous mountain of alabaster from which the ancients drew columns and other
pieces of architecture; as for the columns, bases, and capitals that the Egyptians name Assouanites and of
which one has made millstones, the ancients cut them hundreds of years before the appearance of Christianity;
of these columns formed part the column of Alexandria.

[PDF p. 607]

In Dhu'l Heggah of the year 344 [17 March to 14 April 956], the king of Nubia invaded Assouan and killed
there a great number of Muslims. Aunougaur ben El Akhshid sent against him, in Moharrem of the year 345 [15
April to 14 May 956], the Egyptian army, under the orders of Mohammed ben 'Abdallah El Khazen. The army
advanced by land and by water and sent prisoners into Egypt a great number of Nubians who had their heads cut
off. The king of Nubia beaten, El Khazen continued his march, carried the town of Ibrim, reduced its
inhabitants to slavery, and took again the road of Masr in the middle of Gamadi I of the year 345 [26 August
956], with a hundred fifty prisoners and a great number of (cut) heads.

According to the cadi El Fadl, the frontier post of Assouan brought, in 585 [19 January 1189 to 7 February
1190], 20,000 dinars; according to El Kamal Ga'far El Edfaoui, there were at Assouan eighty delegates charged
with the distribution and one gathered there in a single year 30,000 ardebs of dates. The employee of a
bureau affirmed to me that in this bureau there were forty directors, and that in another bureau there were
sixty of them, without counting the small employees. I have found myself, after the year 620 [of the hijra],
in a bureau that counted nearly forty archivists.

At the frontier post of Assouan dwelt the Benou-l Kenz, of the tribe of Rabi'ah, men admirable and worthy of
envy; El Fadl El Shedid Abou-l Hassan ben 'Arama composed their history in which he gives the relays, the
name of their towns, and of those who attacked them. And when the sultan Salah el din Youssef ben Ayoub
(Saladin) sent an army against Kenz el daoulah and his companions, this army set out from Egypt, entered into
the enemy houses, and found there qasidahs recalling their praises; among others the qasidah of Abou Mohammed
El Hassan ben El Zebir, where was this passage:

[verses:] He whom fortune abandons finds a support in these people whose support has nothing humiliating;
when they accord it, all that is under the stars is afraid; if they accord it, all that is on the earth is
miserable.

There was given him for these verses a thousand dinars and one constituted for him as

[PDF p. 608]

property a saqièh (water-wheel land) of the value of a thousand dinars. There were, in garrison at Assouan,
soldiers well provided with arms and charged with guarding the frontier post against the attacks of the
Nubians and the Blacks. At the fall of the Fatimites, this usage fell into desuetude and the king of Nubia,
at the head of 10,000 warriors, came to establish himself in the island that faces Assouan and made prisoners
the Muslims who were there. Since then, the situation of the frontier post went declining and the Benou-l
Kenz made themselves masters of it after the year 790 [11 January to 30 December 1388]; they committed
depredations and had with the valis of Assouan wars without number, until the appearance of the scourge that
followed the year 806 [11 July 1403 to 9 July 1404] and desolated all the province of the Said. The sultan
had no longer any authority over the frontier post of Assouan and was no longer represented there by a vali.
The situation remained thus long precarious. In Moharrem of the year 815 [13 August to 12 May 1412 -- error
for 1412], an expedition was sent against Assouan; the army delivered battle to the Benou-l Kenz, put them to
rout, destroyed the ramparts of Assouan, pillaging the town and leaving there only a heap of deserted ruins
without inhabitants. The army withdrew, abandoning the country in the state in which Abd allah ben Ahmed ben
Selim el Assouani described it, in his book entitled Chronicle of Nubia, where he says: When Abou 'Abd el
Rahman 'Abd allah ben 'Abd el Hamid el 'Amari had made himself master of the mines, he wrote to Assouan to
invite the merchants to go to him with the tools proper to the miners; and a man, named Othman ben Heïkhalah
el Tamimi, came to rejoin him with a thousand beasts of burden charged with tools and with wheat.

It is reported that after El Amari had returned from his campaign of Nubia to the country of the Bedjahs, the
prosperity increased to such a point that the camels that carried them the provisions from Assouan were to
the number of sixty thousand, without counting the boats that made the transit between Qolzoum and 'Aïdab. A
man worthy of faith among the Sheikhs of Assouan and who resided in the village of Asashi recounted to me
that one had seen, to the east of the Nile, a village with walls; a sycamore was planted before the gate and
people entered and came out. One went to this place, but one found nothing. This happened during the winter,
not during the summer, before the rising of the sun; many people have been witnesses of it and the account is
perfectly authentic. There was there

[PDF p. 609]

[OF THE TOWN OF ASSOUAN, continued]

all sorts of fruits and all sorts of vegetables, among others samples of vegetables greener than the beet.
Haroun el Raschid had had gathered all the species of fruits harvested at Assouan, a single fruit of each
species. He gathered thus a whole oueïba of fruits that one finds nowhere else than at Assouan.

[PDF p. 610]

CHAPTER XXXIV
OF BILAQ (PHILAE)

Bilaq is the most considerable citadel of the Muslims; it is an island neighboring the cataracts and
surrounded by the Nile. A town is found there which is occupied by a great number of inhabitants. One sees
there also magnificent palms and a mosque that contains a pulpit. It is there that stop the boats of the
Nubians, as well as those of the Muslims who come from Assouan. Between this island and the village of El
Qasr, first bourg of Nubia, there is one mile; four miles separate it from Assouan. Between Assouan and this
island, the river is sown with rocks and one can go up it only by employing all sorts of means and by having
oneself guided by the most adroit of the fishermen who inhabit these parts. At El Qasr is a garrison, for it
is there that is the gate by which one penetrates into Nubia.

[PDF p. 611]

CHAPTER XXXV
OF THE WALL OF THE OLD WOMAN

This wall served formerly as rampart to the country of Egypt which it surrounded entirely; it was furnished
with posts and garrisons, and behind was dug a canal filled with water and on which were thrown bridges. All
that was the work of Daloukah bent Zeba. This rampart, neglected, has fallen into ruins, and there remain of
it only some vestiges near Assouan, on the eastern bank of the Nile. Abou-l Qassem 'Abd el Rahman ben 'Abd
Allah ben 'Abd el Hakem, in his book entitled "Conquests of Egypt," recounts what follows: When Pharaoh and
his army had perished in the floods, there remained in Egypt none of his nobles; there were found there only
the slaves, the mercenaries, and the women. The noble women of Egypt gathered therefore to name a queen, and
their choice fell on the most noble among them, Daloukah bent Zeba, an intelligent, adroit, and energetic
woman. Of the most noble origin, she was also one of the most elevated by rank and counted, at the moment of
her election, a hundred sixty years. As soon as she was proclaimed queen, fearing the attack of the kings of
the earth, she gathered the noble women and said to them: "No one formerly cast on our country an eye of envy,
no one coveted it. But, at present, our chiefs and our nobles have perished; the magicians who made our force
have disappeared. Thus I have resolved to raise a rampart that will surround all our country, and to establish
there posts that will watch all the points of the horizon. For we must distrust those who might bear us envy."
And she built a wall that enveloped all the country of Egypt, fields, towns, and villages. At the foot of
this wall was dug a canal where the water was brought; bridges were thrown on this canal and gates opened in
the wall, and the queen established posts and garrisons from distance to distance; every three miles a post
and an important garrison, and in the intervals, from mile to mile, weaker garrisons. To each post were
assigned salaried men who had order to watch with bells. If they saw come on their side someone who inspired
them some fear, they warned one another by means of these bells, and in this way, at the

[PDF p. 612]

same hour, everyone was warned and knew from what side came the enemy. Thus was established the surveillance
and, thanks to this method, Egypt was protected against those who would have wished to attack it. Daloukah
achieved the construction of her rampart in six months, and it is this rampart that bears in Egypt the name of
"Wall of the Old Woman." There remain important vestiges of it in the Said. And God is the most knowing!

[PDF p. 613]

CHAPTER XXXVI
OF THE TRIBUTE (BAQT)

One calls baqt the quantity of slaves that the Nubians had to bring each year, as tribute, into Egypt. It is
indeed an Arab word and one employs it regarding the soil. [bt] (rental, by means of a due in kind, of a
kitchen-garden or a prairie), that is, a small portion of prairie and, in the circumstance, "a small quantity
of wealth." One employs still this word, for example when one says regarding the Benou Tamim [...] (fraction
of the Rabi'at); there it has the sense of branch, of section; it would signify then a "portion or a fraction
of the goods." From there the expression [...]; piece of land, part of a thing. One calls also [baqt] the
quantity of grains that one gives, the third, the quarter. It is also the name that one gives to the fruits
that, during the gathering, fall beside the basket. In the case that occupies us, the word would signify
therefore "a portion of what the Nubians possess." One received this tribute from the hands of the Nubians,
at the village of El Qasr, situated five miles from Assouan, between Philae and Nubia, and which is a little
port. This due was imposed for the first time on the Nubians, in the time of the emir 'Amr ben El 'As who,
after the conquest of Egypt, had sent into Nubia, in the year 20 [21 December 640 to 9 December 641], or
according to others, in the year 21 [10 December 641 to 29 November 642], Abd allah ben Sa'd ben Abou Sareh
with an army of twenty thousand men. 'Abd allah, after a sojourn fairly long in Nubia, received from 'Amr a
letter ordering him to return. After the death of 'Amr, the Nubians violated the treaty concluded between
them and 'Abd allah ben Sa'd. They made numerous incursions into the Said, devastating and ruining the
country. Abd allah ben Sa'd ben Abou Sareh, then emir of Egypt for the caliph Othman, undertook against them
a second expedition, in the year 31 [24 August 651 to 11 August 652] and besieged them in the town of
Dongola. The siege was conducted roughly and engines of war, unknown to the Nubians, launched against the
town stones that destroyed the church, at the

[PDF p. 614]

[OF THE TRIBUTE (BAQT), continued]

great stupor of the inhabitants; their king Qalidourouth asked for peace; humble, sad, and miserable, he went
to 'Abd allah. The latter came to meet him, raised him up, and, having had him placed near him, concluded
peace under the condition that each year the Nubians would deliver three hundred sixty slaves. 'Abd allah
engaged himself on his side to give him the quantity of grains necessary to the Nubians, for the king had
complained that the dearth desolated his country. And he wrote for them a letter of which here is the copy. We
pass over the salutations: "Convention established by the emir 'Abd allah ben Sa'd ben Abou serah in favor of
the chief of the Nubians and of all the people of his kingdom; this convention concerns all the Nubians,
great and small, from the frontier of the territory of Assouan to the frontier of the country of Alouah. 'Abd
allah ben Sa'd accords them pardon, and a truce will remain between them and the Muslims who neighbor them, as
well those of the Said as the others, as well as the protected persons of Islam. O Nubians, you will be under
the guarantee of God and of his apostle, the prophet Mohammed; we will not make war on you, we will stir up
no war against you, we will make no incursions on your lands as long as you conform to the treaty passed
between us and you: If you enter into our country, you will only pass through it and will not sojourn there;
we likewise, if we enter into your country, will only pass through it and will not sojourn there. You will
have to protect every Muslim or ally of the Muslims who is established in your country or will pass through it
as a traveler, until he has left you. You will be held to return every slave of the Muslims who will have
taken refuge with you; you will bring him back to Muslim land, will not retain him, and will raise no
difficulty on his subject. You will prevent no Muslim from going where it pleases him and from coming back
from it, until he has accomplished his design. You are held to guard the mosque raised by the Muslims in one
of the quarters of your town; you will prevent no one from praying there; you will have it swept, you will
maintain there the necessary lighting, and will make there the indispensable repairs. Each year, you will
deliver to the imam of the Muslims three hundred sixty slaves chosen among the slaves of your country. These
slaves, males and females, must be without any blemish; there must not be found in the number either old man,
or old woman, or child not having reached the age of puberty. These slaves will be remitted to the vali of
Assouan.

[PDF p. 615]

The Muslims will owe you no aid against the enemies who might attack you and will not be held to defend you
against them, and this from the frontiers of the country of Alouah to the frontiers of the territory of
Assouan. If you give asylum to a slave of the Muslims, if you kill a Muslim or an ally of the Muslims, if you
destroy the mosque raised by the Muslims in a quarter of your town, if you retain anyone of the three hundred
slaves, you will lose the benefits of the treaty and of the convention established between us. We refer
ourselves to the decision of God, who is the best of judges, but we take as witness of our engagement God and
his apostle Mohammed. On your side, you attest of the sincerity of your promises, what your religion
designates to you as the most venerable, the Messiah, his disciples, and all those whom your religion orders
you to venerate. May God be still between us and you. Written by 'Amr ben Sharhabil, in the month of Ramadan
of the year 31 [16 April to 15 May 652]."

Before the rupture of the first treaty, the Nubians had, at the moment when they had acquitted themselves of
the due, made a gift to 'Amr of forty slaves; but 'Amr had refused them and had returned the present to the
functionary charged with the baqt, one named Samqous, who, with the money he made of it, bought victuals and
wine that he sent to the Nubians. 'Abdallah ben Sa'd had reach them also what had been agreed in the way of
wheat, barley, lentils, stuffs, and horses. This fashion of proceeding became definitive and was repeated
each year; at the moment of the delivery of the baqt, the Nubians received the supplementary victuals and
sent the forty slaves that they had primitively offered to 'Amr and that the vali of Egypt retained.
According to Abou Khalifah Hamid ben Hesham El Bohtari, the treaty concluded with the Nubians imposed on them
the obligation to deliver three hundred sixty slaves to the Muslims and forty slaves to the sovereign of
Egypt; one remitted them in exchange a thousand ardebs of wheat and three hundred ardebs more for the
delegates of the king of Nubia; same quantities for the barley; a thousand jars of wine for the king and
three hundred jars for his delegates; two horses of the species employed by the emirs; a hundred pieces of
stuff of every kind; four pieces of qabati stuff for the king and three for his delegates; eight pieces of
boqtoriah stuff; five pieces of striped stuff; an embroidered mantle for the king; ten pieces of the stuff
named shirts of Abou-Boqtor and ten pieces of ahas stuff, which

[PDF p. 616]

is of a very thick tissue. Neither in the book of 'Abdallah ben Ouahb, says Abou Khalifah, nor in that of El
Ouaqedi is the detail of these objects given; I found it in Abou Zakaria. Here is what this author says: "I
heard my father 'Amr ben Saleh speak of these things and I retained what I had heard. He recounted to me this:
I was one day present at the Council of the emir 'Abdallah ben Taher, who was governor of Egypt and who said
to me: 'Is it you Othman ben Saleh, of whom we have had information taken on the subject of the baqt of the
Nubians?' 'Yes,' I answered. Mahfouz ben Soliman approached and said: 'Things happen in this country in a
singular fashion; we send them to ask for information on subjects they know, we have also sent to this sheikh
and none of them has been able to enlighten us.' 'May God accord his peace to the emir,' I cried; 'what
interests you on the subject of Nubia, I can tell it to you. I hold this information from old men to whom it
had been given by other old men who were present at the treaty and the convention passed between 'Abdallah ben
Sa'd and the Nubians.' Then I told him all that I had learned myself. As he disapproved of the article of the
wines, I said to him: 'Like you, 'Abd El 'Aziz ben Merwan disapproved of it.'" This reunion took place at
Fostat Masr in the year 211 [13 April 826 to 1 April 827], at the moment when had just been signed the treaty
with 'Abdallah ben El Seri ben El Hakem El Temimi, emir of Egypt before 'Abdallah ben Taher. The emir, added
Othman ben Saleh, sent to seek information at the divan that was then installed outside the mosque of Masr;
one sought there the documents relative to the affairs of Nubia, and one found them such as I had reported
them; the emir was very satisfied with it.

Malek ben Anis is of the opinion that the treaty applies to all Nubia to the country of Alouah, and that it
was consequently forbidden to buy slaves there; his contemporaries, however, such as 'Abdallah ben 'Abd El
Hakem, 'Abdallah ben Ouahl, El Leith ben Sa'd, Yezid ben Abou Habib, and others still among the Egyptian
jurists, are of a different opinion. "We know," says El Leith ben Sa'd, "the peoples of Nubia better than
Malek ben Anis knows them. We have engaged ourselves not to make incursions on their territory, but we must
not aid them against their enemies. All that has been reduced to slavery for the king or that has become
slave following the incursions they make among one another, we can legally

[PDF p. 617]

buy it, but the purchase of slaves carried off by the Muslims is illegal." Many Muslims had then for
concubines Nubian girls. The Nubians therefore paid each year the baqt, and one gave them in exchange what I
have enumerated above; it was thus until the reign of the emir of the believers El Mo'tasem billah Abou Ishaq
ben El Rashid. Nubia was then governed by Zakaria ben Bahnès (Johannès?). At this epoch, the Nubians finding
themselves in the impossibility of acquitting the baqt, the Muslim emirs pushed against them the peoples of
the vicinity and prevented one from furnishing them victuals. Firqi, son of the king Zakaria, made reproaches
to his father for obeying another king, setting forth to him that, moreover, it was impossible to pay the
tribute claimed. "What do you want to do?" asked the father. "Unite ourselves against them," he answered,
"and make war on them." "Our ancestors," said the king, "judged it good to consent to this tribute and I fear
that you will soon, you too, be of the same opinion. Before you undertake the war against the Muslims, I am
going to send you as ambassador to their king. You will be able thus to compare their situation to ours. If
you are of the opinion that we are capable of it, we will make war on them; if not, ask the king to treat us
the best possible." Firqi went therefore to Baghdad. On his passage, the countries adorned themselves with
their ornaments; he traversed the towns. To him had joined himself the cortège of the chief of the Bedjahs
and both went to Mo'tasem. They were marveled at what they saw in Iraq: numerous armies, admirable edifices;
all that surpassed by far all they had seen on the road. Mo'tassem had Firqi come to him, treated him in a
friendly and magnificent manner. He accepted the presents he brought him and made him much more considerable
ones. "Ask me what you want," he said to him. El Firqi asked him the setting at liberty of the prisoners. El
Mo'tassem consented to it, and as Firqi inspired him esteem, he gave him the house where he had lodged in
Iraq; moreover, he had bought for him a house in all the towns where he was to stop on the road, for Firqi
during his voyage had refused to lodge at anyone's home in Egypt. He had reserved for him a house at Ghizeh
and another in the quarter of the Benou Waïl. He assigned him, on the Treasury of Egypt, a salary of seven
hundred dinars, a horse with its saddle and its bridle, a magnificent sword, a robe brocaded with gold, a
turban of silk, a tunic and a mantle of linen, a certain number of robes for the delegates of Nubia, the
whole to be delivered at the moment when the baqt would arrive in Egypt. The functionary charged with

[PDF p. 618]

the reception of the baqt received a robe of honor, and a certain allocation, to be paid by the Nubians, was
attributed to all those who were employed in the reception of this tribute. What these employees received in
surplus was considered as a present, and they were held to make in their turn a present of equal value. El
Mo'tassem examined what the Muslims paid and found that it was worth more than the baqt itself; he refused
therefore to accord the wine, the grains, and the stuffs of which we have given above the enumeration, and
decided that the baqt would be paid every three years; he wrote on this subject a letter that has remained in
the hands of the Nubians. The king of Nubia having complained that some inhabitants of Assouan had bought
domains of his slaves, El Mo'tassem had the affair examined. The vali of the province and a judge, chosen
among the magistrates of the town, had appear the Nubians who had sold the terrains in question and
questioned them on the sale of which their master had complained. But they protested and said: "We are only
his subjects," and the complaint of the king was set aside. This sovereign having asked also that the
garrison established at El Qasr, in Nubian territory, be withdrawn and established at the frontier that
separates Nubia from the country of the Muslims, one refused it him. And the baqt continued to be remitted,
following the new decision, and one paid to the Nubians what El Mo'tassem had decided, until the advent of the
Fatimites in Egypt. That is what the historian of Nubia recounts. For his part, Abou-l Hassan El Masa'oudi
expresses himself thus: The baqt comprises a certain quantity of slaves that are brought each year into Egypt
and represent the tribute imposed on the Nubians by treaty concluded between them and the Muslims: this
tribute is composed of three hundred sixty slaves destined for the Treasury, forty slaves for the emir of
Egypt, twenty slaves for the lieutenant of the emir at Assouan, specially charged with the perception of the
tribute, five for the judge of Assouan who assists the emir in the reception of the baqt, twelve for the
twelve witnesses chosen among the inhabitants of Assouan to assist the judge in the reception of this
tribute; the whole following the regulation established at the beginning of Islamism, at the epoch of the
first convention intervened between the Muslims and the Nubians. In his book of the Conquests, El Baladeri
says: The tribute imposed on the Nubians comprised four hundred slaves; in exchange, one remitted them
victuals -- that is, grains. The emir of the believers El Mahdi Mohammed ben Abou Ga'far El Mansour fixed the
due at three hundred sixty slaves and a giraffe.

[PDF p. 619]

[OF THE TRIBUTE (BAQT), continued]

In the year 694 [27 June 1275 to 14 June 1276], the atrocities committed by Daoud, king of Nubia, multiplied.
He advanced as far as the vicinity of Assouan and burned a crowd of markets, after having ravaged 'Aïdhab.
The vali of Qous marched against him, but could not rejoin him; his cavalry, however, succeeded in seizing a
great number of Nubians. One sent them to the sultan El Melek El Zaher Beïbars El Bondoqdari, at the citadel
of the mountain, where they were sawed between two planks. Skandah, nephew of the king of Nubia, having come
to complain of his uncle Daoud, the sultan sent him with the emir Shams El din Aqsonqor El Faraqani El
Ostadar, the emir 'Az El din Aïbek El Afram, chief of the Treasury, and a numerous army comprising the
regular soldiers, the troops of the provinces, the Bedouins of the South, pikemen, archers, grenade-throwers.
The expedition set out from Cairo the first day of Sha'ban [20 January 1276] and entered into Nubia. The
Nubians went to meet the Egyptian army, mounted on rapid camels, brandishing their javelins and clad in long
black tunics. The two armies delivered each other a fierce combat where the Nubians were put to flight. El
Afram marched rapidly on the citadel of Derr, killed there a great number of inhabitants, and led away a
great quantity of slaves. El Faraqani, on his side, had penetrated into Nubia by land and by water,
massacring or making prisoner all he met, and had carried off a considerable crowd of herds. He stopped in
the island of Mikaïl, at the foot of the cataract, and had his boats conducted across the cataract. The
Nubians fled into the islands. El Faraqani wrote to Qamar el Daoulah, lieutenant of Daoud, king of Nubia, and
accorded him pardon. The latter swore obedience to Skandah and recalled to him the inhabitants of the Maris
and the Nubians, who had taken flight. El Afram, however, had passed the river by ford and put the siege
before a fort situated on the bank of the Nile; he seized it and killed there two hundred men and made
prisoner a brother of Daoud. The latter took flight, pursued for three days by the Egyptians who did not
cease to kill and to make prisoners. Finally the people made their submission; the wife and the sister of
Daoud were prisoners, but Daoud himself had been able to escape. Skandah was named king in the place of
Daoud and took of himself the engagement to give in tribute each year three elephants, three giraffes, five
female leopards, a hundred russet camels, and four hundred oxen of choice. It was established that the
territory

[PDF p. 620]

of Nubia would be divided into two parts, one destined for the sultan and the other reserved for the upkeep
and the guard of the country; the district of the cataracts, immediate neighbor of Assouan and forming about
the quarter of Nubia, would be entirely the property of the sultan who would receive the dates, the cotton,
and the other dues that the district paid since the most ancient time. The inhabitants remaining Christian
were submitted to the capitation; each adult man had to pay per year a dinar of silver cash. One drew up a
formula of solemn oath that was sworn by Skandah and that of another oath sworn by his subjects. The two
emirs destroyed the churches of the Nubians and took what they contained; they had delivered to themselves
twenty Nubian emirs and delivered the Muslims of Assouan and of Aïdhab whom the Nubians retained prisoners.
Skandah placed on his head the royal crown and sat on the throne after having promised and sworn to remit to
the sultan the money and the livestock of Daoud as well as those of the people who had been killed or made
prisoner, the whole at the same time as the ancient established due -- that is, four hundred slaves and a
giraffe, of which three hundred sixty slaves were destined for the caliph and forty for the lieutenant of the
caliph, in exchange for a thousand ardebs of wheat for the king and three hundred ardebs for the royal
delegates.

[PDF p. 621]

CHAPTER XXXVII
OF THE DESERT OF 'AÏDHAB

For more than two hundred years, the pilgrims of Egypt and of the Maghreb followed, to go to Mecca, no other
road than the desert of 'Aïdhab; they went up the course of the Nile from Fostat Masr to Qous, and from Qous
crossed by camel the desert that separates the Nile from 'Aïdhab. There they embarked on ships that
transported them to Djeddah, the port of Mecca. Inversely, the merchants of India, of the Yemen, and of
Abyssinia arrived by sea at 'Aïdhab, traversed the desert to Qous, and from there went to Fostat. This desert
was ceaselessly furrowed by travelers going and coming, by caravans of merchants and of pilgrims. Bales of
merchandise, cinnamon, pepper, or other commodities, were met abandoned there, without the ascending or
descending caravans touching them, and remained thus until their masters came to seek them. The pilgrims
going to Mecca or coming back from it followed this road for more than two hundred years, from the year 450
[28 February 1058 to 16 February 1059] and some to the year 660 [26 November 1261 to 14 November 1262] and
some -- that is, from the time when the scourges that desolated the country, in the time of the caliph El
Mostanser Billah Abou Tamim Mo'add ben El Zaher, had closed the land road to the pilgrims until the epoch when
the sultan El Melek El Zaher Rokn el din Beïbars El Bondoqdari had made a veil and a key for the Kaabah and
sent by land the caravan of the pilgrimage in the year 666 [22 September 1267 to 9 September 1268]. From then,
the pilgrims frequented less and less the road passing through the desert, which however remained the usual
road of the merchants who had their merchandise transported from 'Aïdhab to Qous. In their turn, they
abandoned this itinerary after the year 760 [3 December 1358 to 22 November 1359], and since this epoch, the
situation of Qous declined. The desert in question extends from Qous to 'Aïdhab over a distance of seventeen
days' march; one remains three and even four days without meeting

[PDF p. 622]

water. 'Aïdhab is a town situated on the shore of the sea of Djeddah; it is without walls and most of its
houses are huts of reeds. It counted formerly among the most important ports of the world, because the ships
of India and of the Yemen disembarked there their merchandise and departed again from it, and because the
pilgrims of Mecca set out from this port or landed there on the return. When the ships of India and of the
Yemen had ceased to stop at 'Aïdhab, the most important port became 'Aden, in the country of the Yemen. 'Aden
conserved this supremacy until the year 820 [18 February 1417 to 7 February 1418] and some, epoch when
Djeddah became the most important port of the world, with Harmouz, whose roadstead is considerable. 'Aïdhab is
situated in a desert where grows no plant. All that one eats there is imported, the water even is brought
there from outside. The pilgrimage and the commerce offered formerly to the inhabitants of 'Aïdhab advantages
without number; for each package belonging to the pilgrims and that they transported, they collected a
determined duty; it is from them that the pilgrims rented the boats that were to conduct them to Djeddah and
bring them back from Djeddah to 'Aïdhab. They amassed thus much money, for there was at 'Aïdhab no one who did
not possess one or several boats, according to his means. In the sea of 'Aïdhab, in the vicinity of the town,
are islands where are installed fisheries of pearls. At a certain epoch of the year, the divers go by boat to
these islands and stay there days and days, then they come back with their harvest; at the fishery, the sea
is very little deep. The life of the inhabitants of 'Aïdhab is like the life of the beasts, and they approach
much more, by their nature, the animals than men. The pilgrims who used their boats to cross the sea ran
serious dangers; most of the time the winds pushed them toward ports situated in distant deserts, on the side
of the South. The natives (?) descended from their mountains, to rent them camels, and led them into
solitudes without water; most of these unfortunates died of thirst, and the natives took from them all they
possessed. Some lost their way and died of thirst. Those who managed to escape arrived at 'Aïdhab, similar to
dead drawn from their shrouds, so much was their body emaciated and their face changed. Most of the pilgrims
died

[PDF p. 623]

in these ports; those who had a favorable wind landed at the port of 'Aïdhab, but it was the minority. The
boats destined to transport the pilgrims on the sea were constructed without any nail; the planks were sewn
with qanbar, a thread drawn from the coconut tree, and one caulked them with fiber of date-palm that one
impregnated with grease and oil of castor, or with oil of qorsh; the qorsh is an enormous fish of the sea
that devours the drowned; the sails of these boats are made of leaves of moql. The people of 'Aïdhab treated
the pilgrims in an abominable fashion. They filled the boats and piled the passengers one on top of another,
and this with the aim of gaining more money. If anyone of the pilgrims fell into the sea, they hardly
preoccupied themselves with it and contented themselves with saying: "We watch over the planks, let the
pilgrims watch over the souls!" The inhabitants of 'Aïdhab are Bedjahs of nation and obey a native king; they
have however a vali who governs the country for the sultan of Egypt. I met their cadi at Cairo; he was a
Black. The Bedjahs have neither religion nor justice. Among them, the men and the women are constantly naked
and wear a rag of stuff on their natural parts; many even do not veil these parts. There is at 'Aïdhab a
torrid heat, and there blows there a burning wind, the Simoum.

[PDF p. 624]

CHAPTER XXXVIII
OF THE TOWN OF LOUQSOR

It is one of the important towns of the Said; it is inhabited by the Marisi, and it is from this country that
come the asses named marisiah.

[PDF p. 625]

CHAPTER XXXIX
OF BALIANA

This [town also forms part of the province of the Said]. El Kamal El Edfaoui reports that, difficulties having
arisen between the vali of Qous and the inhabitants of the province, the latter went to Cairo and obtained
the dismissal of the vali and his replacement by another functionary. The imam of Baliana set out with the
former governor who was going to his domain of Erment, and when they arrived there, the population came to
bring him as a gift of welcome sixty different dishes all prepared with milk. "Is it thus in your country?"
asked the former vali of the imam. "At my home," he answered, "one gives also cakes." On arriving at Akhmim,
the imam set out again for Baliana and, at the moment when the vali arrived in this last town, one brought
him sixty dishes of cakes, and sixty other dishes. On a certain feast day, an inhabitant of the place had
composed twenty-five verses in praise of one of the judges of the town, and there were there people who were
not satisfied to hear the cadi praised, and others whom their situation prevented from manifesting their
opinion. There were in this country numerous sugar-presses and the inhabitants distinguished themselves by
their generosity.

[PDF p. 626]

CHAPTER XL
OF SAMHOUD

This town is situated on the western bank of the Nile. El Edfaoui says that there were at Samhoud seventeen
mills for pressing the sugarcane, and one claims that the rats do not attack the canes of the country.

[PDF p. 627]

CHAPTER XLI
OF ARGENOUS

This town forms part of the province of Bahnesa; outside the town is a church that contains a well named
"well of Siros," a well of small dimensions for which is instituted a feast that one celebrates the 25th of
Bashans, one of the months of the Copts. During six hours of the day, the water of the well bubbles and
escapes through the orifice, then takes again its first state. The Christians judge of the altitude that the
flood of the Nile will reach each year according to the height to which the water of this well rises above
the soil, and they claim that the regime and the flood of the Nile are entirely linked to this phenomenon.

[PDF p. 628]

CHAPTER XLII
OF ABOU BAT

This town depends also on the province of Bahnesa. There was found there a minaret constructed in such a
fashion that, when someone went up it, it oscillated to the right and to the left, and from the exterior one
realized very exactly the oscillations, in observing the displacement of the shadow on the soil.

[PDF p. 629]

CHAPTER XLIII
OF MELLAWI

This town is situated on the western bank of the Nile, and its territory is renowned for the cultivation of
the sugarcane; there were found there a great number of mills to crush it. The last who occupied themselves
with this cultivation in the country were the children of Fadil who, in the time of El Naser Mohammed ben
Qalaoun, cultivated a thousand five hundred feddans of canes each year. The inspector of the private Treasury
having come in the year 738 [30 July 1337 to 19 July 1338] to examine what they possessed, found among other
things fourteen thousand qantars of candy sugar that one had carried to the magazine of candy sugar of Masr,
without counting the molasses; he obliged them to bring eight thousand other qantars and held them quit. And
there still remained to them, as goods having escaped the inspection, ten thousand qantars of sugar, without
counting what they possessed in slaves, grains, and other things.

[PDF p. 630]

CHAPTER XLIV
OF THE TOWN OF ANSENA

This town is one of the most ancient of the Said of Egypt; it is filled with marvels and possesses, among
other monuments, a circus that served, it is said, as a nilometer and that had been constructed by Daloukah,
one of the sovereigns of Egypt. It had the form of a Persian bonnet and was surrounded by columns as numerous
as the days of the year; all were of dark red granite, and raised one step from one another. The water of the
Nile, at the moment of the flood, penetrated into this circus through an opening, and when the water reached
the point fixed for this epoch, the land of Egypt was suitably irrigated. The king came to sit in this circus
to attend the event, and the people of the court climbed to the summit of the columns and walked on them,
going and coming, then let themselves fall from the top of the columns into the circus filled with water.
According to Abou 'Obeïd El Bakri, Ansena is a locality well known of Egypt. The concubine of the Prophet, she
who was the mother of his son Ibrahim, was originally from a village named Hafan, depending on this town; it
is from there also that were, it is said, the magicians of Pharaoh; it is from there that he had them come on
the day of the rendezvous fixed to meet with Moses. One claims that the crocodiles do not bite on the shore
of Ansena, thanks to a talisman that one has raised there, and that in skirting its territory these animals
turn over on their backs and remain thus until it has passed it. One claims that the constructor of Ansena was
Ashmoun ben Misraïm ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh; the town rises on the bank of the Nile and possessed
magnificent gardens and villas, the fruits and the dates abounded there; today it is no more than a

[PDF p. 631]

heap of ruins. The bang tree, says Abou Hanifa El Dinouri, grows only at Ansena; it is a wood of which one
makes planks for the boats; it occasions frequently bleedings of the nose to those who saw it. A plank of
this wood sells for fifty dinars or thereabouts. If one joins solidly two of these planks and one leaves them
immersed in the water for six days, they form no more than a single one. Ansena had an old rampart that was
demolished by the sultan Salah el din Youssef ben Ayoub (Saladin); each boat going down the river received as
cargo a certain quantity of stones coming from this wall, and thus it was entirely transported to Cairo.

[PDF p. 632]

CHAPTER XLV
OF EL QEÏS

El Qeïs is a locality situated in the vicinity of Behnesa; one even says currently: El Qeïs and El Behnesa.
'Amr ben el 'As, says Ibn 'Abd el Hakem, sent into the Said Qeïs ben El Hareth, who, having reached El Qeïs,
established himself there and gave it his name. According to Ibn Younes, Qeïs ben El Hareth, surnamed at first
El Moradi, then El Ka'bi, is cited by Omar ben El Khattab as one of the bravest men of his time: Souid ben
Qeïs, otherwise called Shedid ben Qeïs ben Tha'leb, speaks of it equally, as well as 'Asker ben Soudah. It is
he who conquered the town of the Said of Egypt called, after him, El Qeïs. One fabricates in this country
stuffs of wool and garments in goat-hair that one finds only in Egypt. Some Egyptians report that when
Moawiah ben Abou Safian had become old, he could not manage to warm himself, and everyone was in agreement
that he could be warmed only by the garments fabricated in Egypt with the hair of the goats of the country,
washed and dyed. One made for him a certain quantity, but he had need of only a single one. One fabricates
also at Qeïs and at Behnesa carpets and tents that bear the name of these localities; they are the most
beautiful looms (manufactures) of the world. One discovered in the surroundings of Behnesa, in the time of
the sultan El Melek El Kamel Mohammed ben el 'Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub, an underground lake that the governor
of Behnesa wished to examine; for this, he gathered the most adroit swimmers and the most skillful divers --
that is, more than two hundred persons who all descended into the lake, but could not find the bottom of it
nor the banks. The governor then had constructed a boat long and narrow that could be introduced through the
orifice of the underground; one embarked there provisions and men, and one placed there cords attached by one
extremity to posts placed at the opening of the underground; the men were provided with instruments destined
to make them recognize the hours of the day and of the night, a quantity of torches of wax and other objects
proper to give fire and light. Order was given them to go with the boat into the underground until half of
their provisions

[PDF p. 633]

were consumed. They set out therefore with the boat in the darkness, skirting the cords, but without finding,
during the route, the banks of the lake. They did not cease to advance until seeing the victuals diminish,
and they brought back by the oar the boat toward the entrance of the underground, hauling themselves on the
cords to come back to their point of departure; they arrived at last at the entrance of the underground. They
had navigated on the lake for six days of which four had passed in penetrating into the underground and in
seeking the banks of it; the two other days having been employed for the return; and during all this time
they had not been able to reach the extremity of the lake. The emir 'Ala el din El Tanbagha, vali of Behnesa,
addressed a letter on this subject to El Melek El Kamel who was marveled at the thing; but he could not occupy
himself with it more seriously, the attack of Damietta by the Franks having diverted him from it. But when
the Franks had abandoned Damietta and the sultan had returned to Cairo, he went in person to see the
underground in question.

[PDF p. 634]

CHAPTER XLVI
OF DAROUT BILHASSAH

Darout is the name of three localities: Darout Ashmoum, of the province of Ashmounein; Darout Sarian, of the
province of Ashmounein equally; and Darout Bilhassah of the district of Behnesa in the Said. In this last
town is a mosque raised by Ziad ben El Mogheïrah ben Ziad ben 'Amr El 'Alaki, who died in Moharrem of the
year 191 [17 November to 16 December 806] and was buried in this mosque. It is of him that the poet said:

[verses:] Generosity has made an oath to which it has not failed: that God has created no man like Ziad. He
was, during his life, like a beneficent rain for Egypt and a protection in the years of dearth.

His brother Ibrahim ben El Mogheïrah died in 197 [12 September 812 to 31 August 813], and the poet said of
him:

[verses:] Ibrahim ben El Mogheïrah was made of gold and he became more beautiful as the time passed. If he
had possessed all that is on the earth, he would have quickly given it to the poor without hesitating.

At the death of Ahmed ben Ziad ben El Mogheïrah, in Moharrem of the year 256 [15 July to 13 August 850], one
made for him the following verses:

[verses:] Ahmed is dead, glorious and regretted. Indeed, he was praiseworthy and praised. He received the
glory in heritage from his father and his uncle. After him, no one will resemble him.

[PDF p. 635]

CHAPTER XLVII
OF SAKAR

It is a town of the province of Atfiyeh, facing which opens a valley where one sees still at present an
assemblage of stones representing a camel of the greatest size known and of the most beautiful form. It is
standing on its four feet and looks toward the Orient. On its right thigh is traced an inscription of three
lines in characters particular to the people that edified this camel. At about a hundred fifty paces from this
camel is found a second absolutely similar, but looking at the first; this second camel bears no inscription.
Between the two animals a regular (geometric) figure was formerly covered with stuffs that filled forty boxes
of which twenty were placed on one side and twenty on the other; all that was of stone and those who saw it
could hardly suspect that they were bales of stuffs. At a hundred fifty paces from there was a third camel
similar to the two others; it stood turning its back to the second camel and looking at the mountain in which
opens a second valley. This camel bears no inscription. This was recounted to me by a traveler whose accounts
are not suspect.

[PDF p. 636]

CHAPTER XLVIII
OF MINIET EL KHASIB

This town owes its name to Khasib ben 'Abd el Hamid, intendant of the revenues of Egypt for the emir of the
believers Haroun El Rashid.

[PDF p. 637]

CHAPTER XLIX
OF MINIET EL NASEK

This town, situated in the district of Atfiyeh, owes its name to El Nasek, brother of Bahram El Armeni
(the Armenian), vizier of the Caliph El Hafez li din Allah Abou-l Meïmoun 'Abd el Megid ben Mohammed. In 529
[23 October 1134 to 10 October 1135], he had been named, by his brother Bahram, vali of Qous; this valiyah
was at this epoch the best of Egypt. El Nasek showed himself very hard for the Muslims and rendered himself
insupportable by his injustice and his cruelty. Thus, when one learned that Radouan ben Lakhsha had replaced
Bahram, when one knew that the latter was in flight and that another occupied in his place the functions of
vizier, the people of Qous threw themselves on El Nasek (month of Gamadi II of 531 [24 February to 24 March
1137]), killed him, and having attached to his foot a dead dog, dragged him through the town and threw him on
a heap of refuse. This El Nasek was a Christian.

[PDF p. 638]

CHAPTER L
OF GIZEH

The word gizeh, says Ibn Siadat, signifies the direction, the side, and makes in the plural [...]. One names
[...] "the sides of a valley," and it is from there that comes the name of Gizeh, given to an important and
richly constructed locality, situated on the western bank of the Nile, opposite Fostat-Masr. Every Sunday,
there is held there a considerable market where are brought from all sides all sorts of merchandise, and
where gathers a great affluence of people. One meets there numerous mosques. The hafiz Abou Bekr ben Thabet
El Khatîb recounts, among other things, the following tradition that he held from Nabit ben Sharit: "The
prophet of God said: Gizeh is one of the gardens of Paradise, and Egypt is the magazine of God on the earth."
The mosque of Toubah, at Gizeh, contained, it is said, the box in which Moses had been exposed by his mother
on the Nile. It is at Gizeh also that is found the palm under which Mary nursed Jesus; it is the only palm
(of the region) that gives fruits.

Ibn 'Abd el Hakem reports, according to Yezid ben Abou Habib, that Hamadan and the other valis of the region
had a preference for the residence of Gizeh. 'Amr ben El 'As having written to 'Omar ben El Khattab to inform
him of what God had done for the Muslims, of the countries he had opened to them, of what had been done for
the distribution of the lands, and of the preference that Hamadan showed for Gizeh, 'Omar answered him
rendering thanks to God for the situation and adding: "How can you show yourself satisfied to be thus distant
from your companions? You cannot permit any of them to be separated from you by a river. You could not foresee
what may happen to them by surprise, and you would be in the impossibility of rescuing them if a catastrophe
arose. Recall them to you, and, if they refuse to obey you and prefer the sojourn of Gizeh to the security
they would find at your sides, let the true Muslims build them a citadel." 'Amr communicated this letter to
the recalcitrants, but they refused to obey.

[PDF p. 639]

[OF GIZEH, continued]

marveled at the situation they enjoyed at Gizeh: it was the same for the members of their family who had
accompanied them, Yafe' and the others; all preferred what they found there. 'Amr ben El 'As therefore had
the citadel of Gizeh built for them; the construction begun in the year 21 was achieved in the year 22 [30
November 642 to 18 November 643]. According to what is recounted, when 'Amr ben El 'As asked those of Gizeh
to return to Fostat, they would have answered: "We have marched in the vanguard on the road of God; we will
not leave our post for another." And Yafe' installed himself at Gizeh where were already Mobrah ben Shehab,
Hamadan, the Dhu Asbah and, among them, Abou Shamr ben Abrahah and a fraction of the tribe of El Hagar.

According to El Qoda'ï, when 'Amr ben El 'As, returning from Alexandria, stopped at Fostat, he posted a part
of his troops at Gizeh, for he feared on this side an attack of the enemy. In consequence, he established at
Gizeh the family of Dhu Asbah, of the Himyarites, a family very numerous, and Yafe' ben Zeïd, of the
Ra'ïnites. He installed there also Hamadân, as well as a fraction of the Azdis, descendants of El Hagar ben El
Habou ben El Azd, and another fraction of the Habeschat who depended administratively on the Azdis. At his
departure from Gizeh, 'Amr gave the order to all those who were there to leave with him; but this was
disagreeable to them, and they answered: "It is here the point to which we have come in marching in the
vanguard on the road of God; we have established ourselves here and refuse to leave it, for we have been here
for months." 'Amr therefore wrote on this subject to 'Omar ben El Khattab, and informed him of the intention
that Hamadan, the families of Dhu Asbah and of Yafe', and their companions had of staying at Gizeh. To which
'Omar answered: "How can you consent to be separated from your companions and to leave a river between them
and you? It is impossible for you to foresee what unfortunate thing may happen to them, while you would be
incapable of carrying them rescue. Recall them to you and do not remain separated. If they refuse to obey and
prefer to stay where they are, build them a citadel suitable for a troop of Muslims." 'Amr gathered the
interested parties and read them the letter of 'Omar; but they refused to leave Gizeh, and 'Amr gave the
order to build them a citadel. This too displeased them: "We can," they said, "have no better ramparts than
our swords." Hamadan and Yafe' not being

[PDF p. 640]

in agreement, 'Amr drew lots between them, and the lot fell on Yafe' who built them the imposed citadel in
the year 21 and achieved its construction in the year 22. 'Amr then had proceeded with the division of the
lands. The Dhu Asbah of the Himyarites had the portion that extends from the Orient to the Occident to the
plowed and cultivated terrains; they refused to let the citadel be built on their territory. The share of
Yafe' ben el Haretz, of the tribe of Ra'ïn, occupied the center of Gizeh; it was on his terrain that he raised
the citadel; but a part of his tribe, refusing to be thus protected, left the place and went to establish
itself on the territory of Bekil ben Gachem ben Nouf ben Hamadan, to the southeast of Gizeh; Hachet ben
Gachem ben Nouf was established to the northwest. The Giaouyah benou 'Amer ben Bekil and the Benou Hagar ben
Arhab ben Bekil had as their share the portion that faces the qibla. The Benou Ka'b ben Malek ben El Hagar
ben El Habou ben El Azd occupied the free place between Bekil and Yafe'. As for the Habechat, they spread
themselves into the greatest arteries of the town.

The mosque of Gizeh was constructed by Mohammed ben 'Abd allah the Treasurer, in Moharrem of the year 350
[error for 380 -- 20 February to 21 March 961], by order of the emir 'Ali ben El Ikhshid. El Kafour seconded
the Treasurer in his construction and procured the funds necessary for the edification and the upkeep of the
mosque. Previously, the inhabitants of Gizeh did their devotions in the place of prayer of Hamadan which is
the oratory of Morâheq ben 'Amer ben Bekil and where gathered all the inhabitants of Gizeh. The construction
of this mosque was executed concurrently by the Treasurer and by Abou-l Hassan ben Abou Ga'far El Tahaoui. As
one had need of columns for the mosque, the Treasurer went during the night to the church of the province,
removed the columns which he replaced by pillars, and transported them to the mosque. Carried away by zeal,
Ibn El Tahaoui declared that, from then on, it was no longer licit to pray there. According to what El Yemani
reports, Ibn El Tahaoui went to pray in the old mosque of Fostat, of which several columns and several marbles
came from the churches of Alexandria and of the diverse provinces of Egypt. A part of this mosque had been
built by Qosrah ben Sherik, governor delegated by El Oualîd ben Abd el Melek. One recounts that at Gizeh is
found the tomb of Ka'b el Ahbar and that one saw there also stones and plaques of marble on

[PDF p. 641]

which were represented crocodiles; and none of these animals showed itself in the Nile for three miles
upstream and downstream of the town. In 724 [30 December 1323 to 17 December 1324] El Melek El Naser Mohammed
ben Qalaoun forbade his vizier to touch anything of what came from the revenues of Gizeh; all was carried to
the sovereign.

[PDF p. 642]

CHAPTER LI
OF THE PRISON OF JOSEPH

The prison of Joseph, says El Qoda'ï, is at Bousir, in the province of Gizeh; all the instructed Egyptians are
in agreement on this point. One finds in this locality the traces of two prophets: one of them, Joseph, was
imprisoned there for a time estimated at seven years, and it is there that the inspiration descended on him.
The terrace of the prison is known under the name of agabat el da'a (response to the call): it is reported
that Kafour El Ikhshidi having asked Abou Bekr ben El Haddad where was the agabat el da'a to make there the
call, Abou Bekr designated him the terrace of the prison. The other prophet is Moses, but one has raised, on
the vestiges (of the monument recalling) the latter, a mosque that one designates under the name of Mosque of
Moses. Abou-l Hassan Ali ben Ibrahim El Sharfi (he was of El Sharf) recounted to us what follows: "Abou
Mohammed 'Abd allah ben El Ouard, whose sister had died leaving him her heritage, and whose advice we always
followed, found himself at the prison of Joseph at the epoch when it was still a goal of promenade for the
people. Now, one day, he said to us: 'O my friends, here is the time to go to the prison, let us go there
then.' And, taking out ten dinars, he held them out to his companions, adding: 'If you desire something, buy
it.' The companions cited in the account bought what pleased them and we went on Sunday to Gizeh and passed
the night at the mosque of Hamadan. The next morning, we went on foot to the mosque of Moses, which is
situated in the plain and from which one must climb to go to the prison. This is separated from the mosque by
all the height of a considerable hill of sand. The old man then said to us: 'To the one who will carry me and
take me up to the prison, I will tell an account that I will tell no longer to anyone until my soul leaves
this world.' El Sharfi decided himself, took the Sheikh, and carried him to the summit of the hill. As soon
as he was set on the ground, the Sheikh said to him: 'Have you any paper?' 'No,' answered El Sharfi. 'Lead me
near a flagstone,' said the Sheikh. And, taking a coal, he wrote: Yahia ben Ayoub, who held it from Yahia ben

[PDF p. 643]

Bekir, who held it from Zeïd ben Aslam ben Yesar, who held it from Ibn 'Abbas, recounted to me that Gabriel
came to find Joseph in this prison, in this tenebrous sojourn, and that Joseph said to him: 'Who are you?
Since I entered into my prison, I have seen no face more beautiful than yours.' 'I am Gabriel,' answered the
angel, and Joseph set about weeping. 'Why do you weep, O prophet of God?' asked Gabriel. 'What does Gabriel
come to do in the sojourn of the criminals?' 'Do you not know that God purifies such sojourns by means of his
prophets? Through you God has purified the prison and all that touches it. As for me, I will not rise until
the end of the day; only then will I come out of the prison.'" Between Yahia and Zeïd, says el Qoda'ï, a link
is missing. The fiqih Abou Mohammed Ahmed ben Mohammed ben Salamat El Tahaoui, speaking of the prison of
Joseph, says: "If a man comes from Iraq with the aim of visiting it and praying there, I will not reproach him
his voyage." The fiqih Abou Ishaq El Marouzi says: "If a man comes from Iraq to visit it, I will not reproach
him for having undertaken the voyage."

In his chronicle of the month of Rabi' I of the year 415 [13 May to 11 June 1024], El Messihi reports that the
crowd and the populace traversed the markets of Cairo, to the noise of the drums and the trumpets, claiming
from the merchants and the notables of the markets the money necessary to go to the prison of Joseph. And the
merchants refused: "Our situation is too hard," they said, "for us to be able to satisfy you." The victuals,
indeed, sold at exorbitant prices. In consequence, these merchants went to complain to His Purity -- that is,
the emir of the believers El Taher li 'azaz din allah Abou-l Hassan Aly ben Hakem bi 'amr allah, who gave to
the lieutenant of the kingdom, Abou Taher ben Kafi, commander of the lower police, instructions according to
which one was to oblige the merchants to pay the habitual due of each year. At the same time order was given
to the crowd to go to the prison of Joseph, with the promise that they would receive that year an indemnity
equal to that of the preceding years. They set out therefore and on the Saturday, 9th of Gamadi I [19 July
1024], the grand Caïd 'Ezz El Daoulah, escorted by all the Turks and the principal chiefs, traversed the town
and went with his troop to El Sana'at on the dike. From there he passed with all the army to Gizeh and came
to support the troops left there in garrison by the emir. The latter crossed in his turn the river, the

[PDF p. 644]

[OF THE PRISON OF JOSEPH, continued]

Monday 11th of the month [21 July 1024], with four boats and fourteen transport mules. All those who were
with him, particular guard and personnel of the harem, went thus to the prison of Joseph. The emir stayed
there two days, and when the populace that had come to the prison had returned, reciting parables, jokes,
stories, and licentious tales that diverted him much and rendered him very indulgent, he regained his castle
where he reentered the Wednesday 13th of the month [23 July 1024].

The populace of the markets continued for nearly two weeks to traverse the town carrying scarecrows, hideous
objects, statues, and they went thus to Cairo to show them to the emir of the believers. They came back
provided with a firman of the emir prescribing to bring no impediment to their comings and goings, to show
oneself generous toward them, and to protect them. And the promenade did not cease until all had been
gathered. They came back from the prison of Joseph the Saturday 14th of Gemadi I [24 July 1024]. They
traversed the streets with masks, grotesque objects, and recounting stories. That day no one could work nor
earn his living. An enormous crowd pressed into the markets to see them; almost everyone did the same during
all the day. There was given to them all eight thousand dirhems; there were gathered there the people of
twelve markets who all withdrew satisfied.

Outside Gizeh is a locality that bears the name of a certain Abou Harirah. Those who are not informed imagine
that it is a matter there of Abou Harirah El Sahebi (the Companion); it is nothing of the kind; the one that
occupies us is the son of the daughter of the latter.

[PDF p. 645]

CHAPTER LII
OF THE VILLAGE OF TERSA

It is reported, says El Qoda'ï, that El Qasem, son of Obeïd Allah ben El Hagab, intendant of the revenues of
Egypt for Hesham ben 'Abd El Melek, built on the territory of Gizeh a village named Tersâ. And this El Qasem,
having gone to Cairo, was named, after his father Obeïd Allah ben El Hagab El Selouli, vali of the revenues
under the caliphate of El Hesham ben 'Abd El Melek. Then Hesham named him intendant of these same revenues,
when his father was designated to the post of governor of Ifriqiah in the year 116 [10 February 734 to 30
January 735]. He remained there until the year 124 [15 November 741 to 3 November 742], epoch when he left
Masr to join Hafas ben El Oualid with the Arabs and the non-Arabs of the country, and he became vali of the
revenues and of the prayer at once. It is in this village of Tersâ that was delivered the combat against
Haroun ben Mohammed El Ga'edi.

[PDF p. 646]

CHAPTER LIII
OF MINIET ANDOUNAH

It is a village depending on Gizeh, named thus after Andounah, secretary of Ahmed El Modaïni, overseer of the
villages that Mousa ben Bogha possessed in Egypt. Ahmed ben Touloun had this Andounah arrested, who was
Christian and who had to pay fifty thousand dinars.

[PDF p. 647]

CHAPTER LIV
OF OUSIM

According to what Ibn 'Abd El Hakem reports, 'Abd allah ben 'Abd El Melek ben Merwan, emir of Egypt, went to
Ousim, a domain belonging to a Copt. This Copt had asked 'Abd allah to come to visit him at his home,
promising him a hundred thousand dinars, and 'Abd allah ben Merwan had accepted. According to other authors,
it is to the village of Abou-l Nimros that the emir would have gone in the company of a writer named Ibn
Hanzalah. 'Abd allah was destituted and replaced in the valiyah by Qorrat ben Sherik, while he was in this
village. When the news reached him, he rose to put on his underwear and put it on inside out. One says
elsewhere that, when he received the news of his destitution, 'Abd allah gave back the money to his host,
saying: "I am destituted!" 'Abd allah, says another, had gone with his host as far as the ferry and had his
companions pass before him, passing himself last. It is then that was remitted to him the letter announcing
his destitution. The proprietor of the money said then: "By God, you must honor my house; you will be my
guest and you will eat at my table. Certainly, I will keep nothing of this money and will not let you depart."
And he passed with him.

[PDF p. 648]

CHAPTER LV
OF MINIEH 'AQABAH

This village forms part of (the province of) Gizeh and takes its name from 'Aqabah ben 'Amer El Gaheni.
According to the account of 'Abd El Hakem, 'Aqabah ben 'Amer wrote to Mo'awiah ben Abou Sofian, asking him for
a land that he could use, near the village of 'Aqabah. And Mo'awiah accorded him a terrain of a thousand
square cubits. One of the freedmen of 'Aqabah, who was near him, said to him: "God has accorded you a
peaceful land." "It is nothing of the kind," answered 'Aqabah, "for we have six obligations to fulfill: We
must take neither their lands, nor their women, nor their children; we cannot possess more than they; I must
defend them against their enemies and I must watch over it and testify to it." According to another account,
'Aqabah wrote to Mo'awiah, asking him for a terrain in a village to build there houses and dwellings, and
Mo'awiah accorded him a domain of a thousand square cubits. His freedmen and his servants said to him then:
"See the land that suits you, trace it, and build inside it." "That cannot be," answered 'Aqabah; "we must
fulfill six conditions: We can take nothing of their lands; it is not permitted us to possess more than they;
we must not overburden them (with work); one cannot take their children, and one must combat the enemies who
