would wish to attack them from behind." Abou Saïd ben Younes says: This land, given as a fief to 'Aqabah, is
the port known under the name of Minieh 'Aqabah, in the province of Gizeh, facing Fostat-Masr.

'Aqabah ben 'Amer ben 'Eisa ben 'Amr ben 'Adi ben 'Amr ben Refa'ah ben Moudou'ah ben 'Adi ben Rhanam ben El
Rabe'ah ben Rashdan ben Qeïs ben Gahinah, such is his genealogy, according to Abou 'Amr El Kandi. El Hafez
Abou 'Omar ben 'Abd el Barr says: 'Aqabah ben 'Amer ben Hassan El Gahini descends from El Gahinah ben Zeïd
ben Mesa'oud ben Aslam ben 'Amr ben El Haf ben Qoda'ah, but one is not in agreement on this genealogy. He was
surnamed Abou Hamad or Abou Ased or Abou 'Amr or Abou Sa'ad or Abou-l Esoued. Khalifah ben Khiat says that
Abou 'Amr 'Aqabah ben 'Amer [...]

[PDF p. 649]

[OF MINIEH 'AQABAH, continued]

El Gahini was killed as a martyr on the day of Nahrwan in the year 38 [9 June 658 to 28 May 659], but it is an
error on his part, for, in a book published subsequently, he says: In the year 58 [3 November 677 to 22
October 678] died 'Aqabah ben Amer El Gahini. 'Aqabah ben 'Amer inhabited Masr of which he was vali; he had
had a house built for himself there and died toward the end of the caliphate of Mo'awiah. The companions of
the prophet, Gaber, Ibn 'Abbas, Abou Amamah, and Mouslimah ben Mokhallad speak of him. As for the accounts
that those who came after have made of him, they are numerous. Then, says El Kandi, 'Aqabah ben 'Amer was
vali for the account of El Mo'awiah, and he united in his attributions the prayer and the revenues; he put
Hamad at the head of his police. 'Aqabah was a reader of the Koran, a fiqih, a theologian, a poet. He is the
author of the Hegrah (the hijra) and of the Victorious Friendship. He was charged with watching over the
yellow mule of the prophet and led it in his voyages. 'Aqabah was replaced in Egypt by Mouslimah ben
Mokhallad, the 10th of Rabi' I of the year 40 [24 July 660]; he had been vali for two years and three months.
According to Ibn Younas, he died at Masr in the year 58 and was buried in the cemetery of the town, at the
Moqattam. He dyed (his hair) black. May God have pity on him!

[PDF p. 650]

CHAPTER LVI
OF HELOUAN

This town takes, it is said, its name from Halouan ben Babelioun ben 'Amr ben 'Amru-l Qaïs, king of Egypt,
son of Seba ben Yashgab ben Ya'rab ben Qahtan, and this Halouan was in Syria, in the vanguard of Abrah Dhu-l
Mounar, one of the Tobba' kings.

The plague, says Ibn 'Abd el Hakem, ravaged Fostat, and 'Abd el 'Aziz ben Merwan left Fostat and stopped at
Helouan, at the entrance of the desert, in a locality named Abou Qarqourah. It is from there that sets out
the spring dug by 'Abd el 'Aziz ben Merwan and brought by him to the palms he had planted at Helouan. Ibn
Khadig sent each day to 'Abd el 'Aziz the news of what occurred in the country, list of the deaths and the
rest. One day, he dispatched a messenger of whom 'Abd el 'Aziz asked: "What is your name?" "Abou Taleb,"
answered the man. This answer shocked and irritated 'Abd el 'Aziz. "I ask you your name," he cried, "and you
answer me: Abou Taleb (Father of the Seeker)! What is your name?" "Moudrik (the one who reaches/dies)," said
the messenger. The emir found the incident of bad augury; after the departure of the messenger, he fell ill
and died. One transported his body to the river to have it go down to Fostat, but, the cadaver beginning to
decompose, one deposited it in a hut on the bank of Maris. There one washed it, one disembarked the cadaver
and with it the censers of aloes that had served to perfume it at the moment of its decomposition. 'Abd El
'Aziz had recommended to transport him, when he would be dead, to the house of Genab ben Moratted ben Zeïd ben
Hani El Ra'ini, commander of his guard and his devoted friend. But Genab himself had died before 'Abd el
'Aziz, and as one arrived with the body of the latter at the door of Genab, the family of Genab, clad in
black, kept itself before the door, lamenting. It followed the body of 'Abd el 'Aziz to the cemetery. A
certain Nasib had received as a present from 'Abd el 'Aziz a village. During his sickness, he had come to see
him; entered near him and struck by the violence of his ill, he set about saying:

[verses:] We visit our Lord and the Lord of the others; would to heaven that the ill had struck us in his
place!

[PDF p. 651]

[verses:] If it were possible to ransom him by any ransom whatsoever, by the Elect! I would have ransomed him
by what I have and what I have had most dear!

'Abd el 'Aziz, having heard him, opened his eyes and had given to him a thousand dinars. The family of 'Abd
el 'Aziz was joyful at it; it rejoiced with him, then he died.

El Kandi recounts: The plague broke out at Masr in the year 70 [25 June 689 to 15 June 690] and 'Abd el 'Aziz
ben Merwan left from it, directing himself toward the Orient. He stopped at Helouan, found the site superb,
appropriated it to himself, installed himself there, and had come the guards, the servants, and the police
commanded by Genab ben Moratted. 'Abd el 'Aziz raised at Helouan dwellings and a mosque; he spread prosperity
and abundance in the region; he planted there his palms and his vines. Ibn Qeïs El Raqiât said:

[verses:] May Helouan be watered, the country of the vines, and what comes out of it in the way of figs and
grapes! Palms long as lances of Bourni move there all together. Black, they are the sojourn of the pigeons
and ceaselessly the crows attack their dates.

The palms being planted and the dates ripe, 'Abd el 'Aziz had the army come to Helouan. He walked about,
looking at the young plants and the streams that watered them. Yezid ben Arouat El Gamali having said to him:
"O emir, will you not say as the servant (of God) said: 'May God will it! There is no force except in God!'"
"Young man," said 'Abd el 'Aziz, "you remind me that one must be grateful. Say this again: We will not make
Yezid lose the hope of receiving ten dinars."

'Abd el 'Aziz was son of Merwan ben el Hakem ben Abou-l 'As ben Ammyah ben 'Abd Shams ben 'Abd Monaf el
Qoreishi El Amaoui Abou-l Asbagh; his mother was Leïlah, daughter of Zeban ben el Asbagh. This is what El
Kandi reports according to Abou Harirah and 'Aqabah ben 'Amer el Gahini. Aly ben Riah, Bahir ben Dakherah,
'Obeïd Allah ben Malek El Khoulani, Ka'b ben 'Alqamah, Thaqah El Nesaï, and Ibn Sa'd report that, when Merwan
marched on Egypt, he sent his son 'Abd el 'Aziz with an army to Aïlah to penetrate into Egypt from this side.
The emir of Egypt, Ibn Gahdam, sent to meet him an army commanded by Zoheir ben Qeïs El Balaoui; the latter

[PDF p. 652]

met 'Abd el 'Aziz at Besaq, on the plateau of the hill of Aïlah; the combat was engaged and Zoheïr and his
army were put to rout. When Merwan was completely master of Egypt, in Gamadi I of the year 65 [14 December 684
to 12 January 685], he remained two months in the country after having instituted his son intendant of the
prayer and of the revenues. "O emir of the believers," said to him on this occasion 'Abd el 'Aziz, "how to
stay in a country where is found none of the sons of my father?" "My son," answered Merwan, "fill the people
with generosities, they will all become for you sons of your father. Let your face be smiling, and their
affection will be acquired to you. Make each of their chiefs understand that he is dearer to you than the
others: he will become for you the spy of his companions, and his clan will march with you. I have given you
for companion your brother Bechr and for vizier Mousa ben Nasir. Who then prevents you, O my son, from
becoming emir of all the earth? Is that not worth more than making locks for your door and weighing yourself
down in your house?" At the moment of leaving Egypt to return to Syria, he said to him again: "I recommend you
to fear always God in the intimacy of your soul as in your exterior acts, for God is with those who show
themselves pious and do good. Take care not to leave to the crier of God the occasion to have hold over you,
for the Muezzin calls to the execution of the divine prescriptions established by God himself who has said:
The prayer is for the believers an obligation at fixed times (Koran, IV, 104). Make no promises to anyone,
unless you keep them, were you for this to have to make war. Do not hasten in the decisions that regard the
government, but rather take counsel. If God had wished to exempt anyone from this obligation, he would
certainly have exempted first of all his prophet Mohammed from the inspirations he sent him. And moreover, God
has said: Take their counsel in your affairs (Koran, III, 153)."

Merwan came out of Egypt at the new moon of Rageb of the year 65 [11 February 685], leaving his son 'Abd el
'Aziz vali of the prayer and of the revenues, and died at the new moon of Ramadan [11 April 685]. His son
'Abd el Melek was recognized as emir. His brother 'Abd el 'Aziz was maintained in his functions and went to
'Abd el Melek in the year 67 [28 July 686 to 17 July 687], after having put at the head of the guard, of the
cavalry, and of the

[PDF p. 653]

satellites Genab ben Moratted El Ra'ïni. The latter affirmed still more the power of his master and, if
anyone showed malevolence for 'Abd el 'Aziz, Genab and his men went to seize him, struck him, and imprisoned
him. 'Abd el 'Aziz was the first who celebrated the feast of Yarafah in Egypt, in the year 71 [15 June 690 to
3 June 691]. The first, says Yezid ben Abou Habib, who sat in the mosque after the 'asr, on the day of
Yarafah, was 'Abd el 'Aziz ben Merwan.

In the year 72 [4 June 691 to 22 May 692], the army of the sea was sent to Mecca to combat 'Abd allah ben
Zobeïr; it was commanded by Malek ben Sharhabil El Khoulani and composed of three thousand men of whom 'Abd
el Rahman ben Bahnes, freedman of Ibn Abza; it was he who killed Ibn El Zobeïr. In 74 [13 May 693 to 1 May
694], 'Abd el 'Aziz went to Alexandria; in 75 [2 May 694 to 28 April 695], he went to visit his brother 'Abd
el Melek; in 77 [10 April 696 to 29 March 697], he demolished completely the mosque of Fostat which he
enlarged on all sides and had struck dinars with effigy. Ibn 'Afir says: 'Abd el 'Aziz had raised each day
around his palace a table of a thousand covers; in addition, he had sent to the tribes a hundred cauldrons
filled with victuals. 'Abd el Melek having written to him to ask him to renounce the heredity of the valiyat,
in order to be able to designate as his successors El Oualid and Soliman, 'Abd el 'Aziz refused and answered
his father (brother): "If you have a son, I have children, I too. May God judge between us!" 'Abd el Melek
entered into a violent anger, and 'Abd el 'Aziz sent him 'Aty ben Riah to enter into negotiations. The
messenger, at his arrival near 'Abd el Melek, attempted to bring his brother back into grace with him; but
'Abd el Melek only recriminated against 'Abd el 'Aziz and cried: "May God separate us!" Ahy continued to
speak to him and ended by appeasing him. Returned near 'Abd el 'Aziz, he rendered him account of the
situation, of his interview with his brother, and of what the latter had said: "May God separate us!" "I will
separate myself therefore from him," cried 'Abd el 'Aziz; "may God, too, separate himself from him -- he who
has never prayed God without his prayer being granted!" "When I came into Egypt, under the emirate of
Mouslimah ben Mokhallad," said 'Abd el 'Aziz, "I wished three things and obtained them: I wished to be vali of
Egypt; to unite the two wives of Mouslimah; and to have Qeïs ben Kalib for chamberlain!" And Mouslimah being
dead,

[PDF p. 654]

[OF HELOUAN, continued]

'Abd el 'Aziz, come into Egypt, was named vali of it; he took Qeïs for chamberlain and married the two wives
of Mouslimah. His son El Asbagh ben 'Abd el 'Aziz died the 21st of Rabi II of the year 86 [21 April 705]. 'Abd
el 'Aziz fell ill in his turn and died in the night of the Monday 13th of Gamadi II of the same year [11 June
705]. One brought him back by the Nile from Helouan to Fostat where he was buried.

Ibn Abou Malikah reports having seen 'Abd el 'Aziz at the moment of his death. "Would to God," he said, "that
I were nothing at all! Would to God that I had been like a plant of the fields or like a pastor of camels in
the depths of the Hedjaz!" At his death, he possessed for all riches only seven thousand dinars, Helouan,
Qisariah, robes of which one mended, horses, and slaves. He had been vali of Egypt for twenty years, ten
months, and thirteen days, and, in the time of Islam, there had not been before a valiyah longer than his.

There was across the Nile, at Helouan, a dike of stones where the horses passed carrying the travelers and
the merchandise from the eastern bank of Helouan to the western bank. And when [there was...] [lacuna in the
manuscript]

[a digression on the compass:] this is still one of the mysteries of nature; for, if of a metallic body such
as iron, copper, silver, lead, gold, tin, one makes a vase, this vase can contain a weight of water more
considerable than the weight of the vase itself; placed (empty) on the surface of the water, it floats and
can support a certain load without being submerged. Now, the travelers who navigate on the sea of India are
sometimes prevented, during the night, from seeing the stars that could guide them by indicating to them the
direction of the cardinal points; thus they carry constantly with them a hollow iron having the form of a
fish and made of very thin plates; they rub the mouth of the fish with a piece of good magnet, and this fish,
placed on the water, turns and presents its head to the south pole and its tail to the north pole. This too is
a mystery of nature. Knowing the two directions north and south, the navigators find easily the orient and
the occident; indeed, he who faces the south and turns his back to the north has the occident on his right
and the orient on his left. When one has determined the four cardinal points, one knows exactly the countries
that are found in each direction, and one marches toward the point one wishes to reach.

[PDF p. 655]

CHAPTER LVII
OF THE TOWN OF EL 'ARISH

The town of El 'Arish is situated between Palestine and Egypt; it is an ancient town, counting among those
that were founded after the Flood.

Master Ibrahim ben Ouacif Shah, speaking of Misraïm, son of Cham, son of Noah, says: He was a delicate young
boy, and, in arriving in the vicinity of Egypt, one raised for him a hut of branches hung with herbs of the
fields. Then one constructed for him, in the same place, a town that one called Darsân -- that is, "Gate of
Paradise." One cultivated, one planted in trees and gardens the space that extended from Darsân to the sea. It
was only a succession of gardens, of prairies, and of dwellings.

Another says: This name was given to it only because Beïsar, son of Cham, son of Noah, had led with him his
four sons, accompanied by their children to the number of thirty, boys and girls. Masr ben Beïsar marched
straight toward the land of Egypt, crossed the frontier of Syria and, after having wandered at random,
arrived in Egypt at the place where was later El 'Arish. He was harassed with fatigue and fell asleep. In a
dream, he saw someone who spoke to him and announced to him his arrival in the blessed land, country of
prosperity, of royalty, and of glory. He awoke, frightened by his dream, and saw himself under a shelter of
branches surrounded by springs of water. He rendered then thanks to God and prayed him to reunite him with
his father and his brothers, and to accord him his benediction on the earth. God granted him and led to him
his family. Together, they arrived at El 'Arish and stopped there. For them, God made come out of the sea
livestock: horses, asses, oxen, sheep, and camels. They pushed before them this livestock and arrived thus at
the town of Menf (Memphis), where they established themselves and built a town named by the Copts Mafat, a
word that means "the town of the thirty." And the posterity of Beïsar multiplied to the point of peopling the
earth; they devoted themselves to agriculture, and their herds were innumerable. It is they who discovered
the mines. One of them discovered even a piece of emerald so big that he could make of it a great table. They
were able to extract nuggets of gold as big as columns or as a lying camel.

[PDF p. 656]

Ibn Saïd reports, according to El Bihaqi, that the meeting of Joseph with his father and his brothers took
place at El 'Arish, the place where the land of Egypt begins. Joseph, indeed, had set out to meet them as far
as this town, extreme limit of his empire. He had there a throne -- that is, a royal bed -- on which he had
his father sit, and it is for this that this town bore formerly the name of El 'Arsh (the Throne). Later this
name was generally pronounced El 'Arish, which has prevailed. Joseph, it is said, had placed guards at all
the exterior points of Egypt, and, when the drought descended on Syria, the brothers of Joseph, set out to go
to provision themselves in Egypt, arrived at El 'Arish. The chief of the guards of this territory wrote to
Joseph, and informed him that the sons of Jacob the Canaanite desired to penetrate into Egypt following the
drought that desolated their country. While waiting for the answer of Joseph, his brothers built themselves a
shelter to guard themselves from the sun, and the place took thus the name of El 'Arish (the Arbor). Joseph
having written and accorded the authorization to pursue their voyage, there happened to them what is reported
in the Koran, where it is said: "On the throne, etc." (Koran, XII, 100), and this is as you see it. And Ibn
Ouacif Shah is the man who knows best the accounts that concern Egypt.

In 415 [15 March 1024 to 3 March 1025], 'Abd Allah ben Edris El Ga'fari, supported by the Benu-l Garrah,
attacked by night El 'Arish, burned it, and carried off all that was there.

In Gamadi II of the year 577 [12 October to 9 November 1181], says the cadi El Fadil, one received the news
that most of the palms of El 'Arish had been cut down by the Franks who had carried off the trunks of them to
their country, that their territory was now filled with them, and that they had found no one to prevent them
from it. We will report still the passage of Ibn 'Abd el Hakem who asserts that, in the time of the Pharaoh
of Moses, the Gofar entirely was extremely prosperous and covered with water, with towns, with dwellings. The
word of God: "We have overturned what Pharaoh and his people had raised" (Koran, VII, 133) would apply
precisely to the works executed in this very place. The country was peopled from this point to the Yemen, and
it is for this that El 'Arish bore the name of 'Arish. It was, it is said, the extreme point of the country of
Syria, and there ended the prairies where pastured the herds of Abraham. It is there that this patriarch had
built himself a shelter where he kept himself to watch over his livestock. Whence the name of El 'Arish given
to this place. It is reported that Malek ben Da'er ben

[PDF p. 657]

Hagr ben Gadilah ben Lakhm had twenty-four children, among whom El 'Arish ben Malek who gave his name to the
country, for he had stopped there and had built a town there. According to Ka'b el Ahbar, one found at El
'Arish the tombs of ten prophets.

[PDF p. 658]

CHAPTER LVIII
OF THE TOWN OF FARMA

El Farma, says El Bekri, is a town that is found in Egypt. Ibn Khalouya, in his book entitled Leïsa, says that
El Farma takes its name from a brother of Alexander, called El Farma and who was an infidel. It is the country
of the mother of Ismaïl, son of Abraham. This name was borne, it is said, by El Farma ben Filiqous whom one
calls also Ibn Filis or Ibn Bilis. Farma was a flourishing town situated on the lake of Tennis; one sees
there the tomb of the physician Galen. El Moutawakel ala allah raised there, on the shore of the sea, a
citadel whose construction was directed by 'Anbassah ben Ishaq, emir of Egypt: this construction was executed
in 239 [12 June 853 to 1 June 854], at the same time as that of the citadels of Damietta and of Tennis. One
spent there considerable sums. When 'Amr ben El 'As had made himself master of Aïn Shams, he sent against
Farma Abrahah ben El Sabah with whom the inhabitants of the town made peace, by means of 500 dinars of
Heraclius, 408 she-camels, and 1,000 sheep. And 'Anbassah, withdrawing from Farma, marched on El Baqarah.

In 343 [7 May 954 to 26 April 955], the Greeks disembarked there; the inhabitants went to meet them and
killed them two men. The Greeks having made a new descent in Gamadi I of the year 347 [21 July to 19 August
958], the Muslims made a sortie, seized one of their ships of which they massacred the crew and led away ten
prisoners.

According to El Ya'qoubi, Farma is the first town of Egypt on the side of the North: the inhabitants there are
very mixed. Between the town and the Green Sea, there is a distance of three miles.

Here is what Ibn El Kandi says: (Among these towns) is Farma, the richest

[PDF p. 659]

[OF THE TOWN OF FARMA, continued]

in marvels, the most abundant in souvenirs of the past. The Egyptians assert that there existed formerly a
terrestrial route leading from Farma to the island of Cyprus, but that this route has been covered by the
sea. In the part thus covered was found, they say, a quarry of variegated marble (white and black); the
quarry of white marble was in Libya.

I made a reconnaissance at Farma, recounts Yahia ben Othman; from the sea to the town there was about a day's
march; the patrols came out of the town and advanced as far as the huts built on the shore of the sea. But
all this space was one day submerged by the waters. According to the account of Ibn Qadid, Ibn Modabher,
finding himself at Tennis, went to Farma to demolish the gates of stone that are to the east of the citadel;
he had need of these stones to make lime. But he had hardly removed one or two stones when the inhabitants
came out in arms to prevent him from it. "This gate," they cried, "is that of which God said to Jacob: O my
children, enter not by a single gate, but by different gates (Koran, XII, 67)." It is at Farma that is seen
the marvelous palm that gives its fruits when in the rest of the world there are no more dates, neither old
nor new. The fruits begin to appear at the normal time when the bunches form on the other palms. And they do
not cease to renew themselves for four months until the moment when the dates appear -- that is, until the
spring. This phenomenon does not occur in any other region, neither at Basra, nor in the Hedjaz, nor in the
Yemen. The palms of Farma give fruits such that a single date weighs more than twenty drachmas and reaches
the length of a span and a fetr.

In his Events of the year 507 [18 June 1113 to 6 June 1114], Ibn El Mamoun El Bataïhi expresses himself thus:
"Fugitives from Syria arrived bearing the news that Baudoin (Baldwin), king of the Franks, had penetrated
onto the territory of Farma. El Afdal ben Emir el Gioush went at once to find the governor of the province of
Sharqieh and asked him to make depart the Markaziah and the Mouqta'in cantoned in his province and to send at
the same time the foot-soldiers of El 'Atoufiah, prescribing to the governor to march himself in person,
after having given instructions for

[PDF p. 660]

the nomad Arabs to set out in the vanguard, in order to attack the Franks during the night and before the
arrival of the reinforcements. The governor, conforming to all these prescriptions, had the tents brought out,
the men and the servants prepared. The army arrived therefore, preceded by the nomads, and charged the
Franks. Baudoin, their king, informed of the arrival of the army and recognizing himself incapable of
resisting, gave his troops the order to pillage, to destroy, to burn, and to demolish the mosques. The mosque
and the oratories were given to the flames as well as the rest of the town, and Baudoin beat in retreat, but
God seized him and, of himself, he threw himself into the fire (of hell). His companions hid his death and
withdrew after having split the body of Baudoin and having filled it with salt, in order to transport it into
his country, where one buried it. As for the Muslim army, after having made some incursions into the enemy
country and having camped under the walls of Ascalon, it reentered Egypt. A letter was addressed to the emir
Zahir el din Tafadkin (Tughtakin), governor of Damascus, prescribing him to march against the country of the
Franks. He went to Ascalon, where one brought him the presents of hospitality and where spread the news of
his arrival. Tafadkin ordered that one remit to him tents, a great number of horses, of mantles, of banners
and of standards, a sword of gold, a belt of gold, a collar of gold, a garment, a great complete tent, a
royal divan, with its carpets, all its utensils and its accessories of silver; he exacted, for Shams el
Khawas, one of the principal chiefs, a gilded robe, a belt of gold, and a sword; for those of the arrivals
who had distinguished themselves, robes and swords. The whole was remitted to the guard of one of the
chamberlains accompanied by two valets who carried the material of the tents. Tafadkin had the great tent
raised and its carpets spread. The vali of Ascalon, as well as Zahir el din and Shams el Khawas and all the
emirs who were at Ascalon or who went there, were to come to the door of the tent to salute him, then would
advance toward the carpet and toward the divan that would be raised. There, the vali, Zahir el din, Shams el
Khawas, and the other chiefs would sit, while the rest of the assistance would remain standing in sign of
veneration and deference. One would remit a robe of honor to Zahir el din and to Shams el Khawas, one would
have them buckle their belts and would gird them with swords; after which each

[PDF p. 661]

of them would distribute robes of honor to those who had distinguished themselves. Then Zahir el din and the
chiefs, accompanied by the gifts they had received, and preceded by the flags and the standards, would go to
the tents that had been prepared for them. And each day the vali, the two emirs, the chiefs, and the soldiers
would go to the royal tent to converse there of all that would matter to the army. And all that was executed.
One made incursions on the enemy territory, one led away prisoners, one fought, and one made a second
distribution of robes of honor. To Shams el Khawas one accorded, as a particular gift for this expedition, a
sum of ten thousand dinars, and Zahir el din received as a gift the great tent and all it contained. He and
his companions received thus the value of thirty thousand dinars.

In the month of Rageb of the year 545 [24 October to 22 November 1150], the Franks made a descent at Farma,
with a considerable army; they burned the town and pillaged the inhabitants. Finally, the vizier Shaour
destroyed it when its vali Moulhem, brother of El Dourghân, came out of it, in the year [...], and it remained
in ruins without ever having been raised since. There were at Farma, at Baqârah, and at Ouàrâdah Arabs of the
tribe of Gedam called Qate'; they had for chief Géra ben 'Ouf ben Mâlek ben Shenouah ben Badil ben Geshm ben
Gezâm. Among them were 'Abd el 'Aziz ben El Ouazir ben Sâbi ben Mâlek ben 'Amer ben 'Adi ben Harsh ben Baqr
ben Nasr ben El Qate', who died in Safar of the year 205 [17 July to 14 August 820]. The Seraoui and Geraoui
have there legends in abundance, legends that we have reported in the book entitled "The Garland of the
Stones of the Necklace" which treats of the chronicles of the town of Fostat. It is there, says Ibn El Kandi,
that is found the reunion of the two seas -- that is, the separation of which God speaks: "He has separated
the two seas that went to meet one another, and between them is a barrier, and they do not confound
themselves" (Koran, LV, 19, 20), and: "He has placed a barrier between the two seas" (Koran, XXVII, 62).
These two seas are the sea of Roum and the sea of China. The barrier that separates them has a length of a
night's march counted from Qolzoum to Farma. And they are nowhere nearer one to the other than at this point.
Everywhere else, there is between them the distance of a month's march.

[PDF p. 662]

CHAPTER LIX
OF THE TOWN OF QOLZOUM

Qolzoum is a town that was on the shore of the sea of the Yemen, at the point of this sea on the side of
Egypt. It is a town of Egypt that has given its name to the sea of Qolzoum. In the vicinity, Pharaoh was
drowned. Between this town and Masr, there are three days' march. Qolzoum has been destroyed and its site
bears today the name of Suez, facing 'Agroud. At Qolzoum, there is neither water, nor trees, nor cultivation.
The water is brought there from very distant wells. There was there formerly a port common to Syria and to
Egypt where one embarked the merchandise destined for the Hedjaz and the Yemen. Between Qolzoum and Faran one
meets neither towns nor villages, but only some plantations of palms where pass the hunters and the
fishermen; it is the same from Faran and Gilan to Aïlah. The country that bears the name of Qolzoum, says Ibn
El Tawir, has remained standing in great part until our days, and the travelers, who go by sea from Egypt to
the Hedjaz, can ascertain it. It was formerly one of the important beaches of Egypt, and I have been able to
see at the depot of the palace the list of a part of its employees and the budget of the expenses for its
vali, its cadi, its muezzins, its scribes, the army that kept garrison there to protect the town and the
surroundings, for its mosque and its oratories; it was a country very prosperous.

El Messihi, in his Events of the year 387 [14 January 997 to 2 January 998], recounts that in the month of
Ramadan [7 September to 6 October 997], the emir of the believers, El Hakem bi 'amr illah, remitted to the
inhabitants of Qolzoum the amount of the duties on the ships. Ibn Khordadabah says, regarding the merchants:
They embark on the western sea, disembark at Farma, and transport on the backs of men their merchandise to
Qolzoum; between these two towns, there is a distance of twenty-five parasangs. At Qolzoum,

[PDF p. 663]

the merchants reembark on the eastern sea and, after a stopover at the trading-posts of Djeddah, go as far as
the Sind, the Hindus, and China. It is at Qolzoum that one takes the land route to go to Aïlah, where one
arrives after a march of six days, for which one must make provision of water. It is said that between
Qolzoum and the sea of Roum there are three stages and that the space that separates the two points forms
what one calls the barrier of which God spoke: "Between them is a barrier that prevents them from mingling"
(Koran, LV, 20).

[PDF p. 664]

CHAPTER LX
OF EL TIH

It is a region situated in the vicinity of 'Aïlah, from which it is separated by a hill that a cavalier had
great difficulty in crossing, so steep was it. The approach of it was facilitated, in the time of Khamaraouyah
ben Ahmed ben Touloun, and the cavaliers make two stages across the desert of Tih properly speaking to arrive
at the shore of the sea of Farân, there where rose the town of this name; it is there that Pharaoh was
drowned. The Tih has a surface of forty square parasangs; the Israelites wandered there for forty years
without entering a town, nor penetrating into a house, nor changing their garments. Moses died there. The
crossing of the desert of Tih is about six days' march. When the Bahri Mamelukes fled from Cairo in 652 [21
February 1254 to 9 February 1255], it happened that one of their bands passed through the desert of Tih and
wandered there for five days. The sixth day, they perceived from afar a black thing and, having approached,
recognized a magnificent town surrounded by walls and porticoes of green marble. They entered into it, made
the tour of it, and found it invaded by the sand that filled the markets and the houses. They discovered
vases and garments, but, when they wished to gather them, these objects, worn by time, fell into dust. In a
vase that they discovered in a merchant's shop, they found nine dinars bearing the image of a gazelle and a
Hebrew inscription. Having dug at this place, they brought to light a stone that covered a cistern filled
with water, and they drank of this water which was colder than ice. Finally they came out of the town and set
out on the road during the night. A troop of Arabs whom they met led them to the town of Karak where, to pay
some small expenses, they presented their dinars. On these pieces of gold was an inscription stating that
they had been struck in the time of Moses. For each dinar one gave them a hundred dirhems and one said to
them: This town is the Green Town, one of the towns of the Israelites, buried under a deluge of sand that
sometimes increases and sometimes diminishes; this town can be seen only by the lost (those who have lost
their way). And God is the most knowing.

[PDF p. 665]

CHAPTER LXI
OF THE TOWN OF DAMIETTE

Damietta is one of the towns of Egypt; between it and Tennis there are twelve parasangs. This town, it is
said, takes its name from Doumiat, a descendant of Ashmoum ben Misraïm ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh. It is
recounted that Edris was the first man on whom descended He who possesses the force and the valiance and who
said to him: "I am God, the modeler of the towns of the world; by my order and by my art, I have reunited the
sweet and the salty, the fire and the ice, and this, thanks to my power and to the certainty of my science of
the dal, the mim, the alif, and the ta." In Syriac, it is said, this ensemble bears the name of Doumiat.
Doumiat is therefore a Syriac word whose root is damtay, "the force designated by the mixture of the sweet
and the salty." Master Ibrahim ben Ouacif Shah says that Damietta is an ancient town, constructed in the time
of Qlimoun ben Atrib ben Qobtim ben Misraïm, and to which one gave the name of a young man whose mother was
the magician of Qlimoun.

When the Muslims advanced against Egypt, Damietta had for governor a man of the family of the Maqoqos, named
El Hamouk. 'Amr ben el 'As having conquered Egypt, El Hamouk held firm in Damietta and prepared himself for
the resistance. 'Amr ben El 'As sent against the town a troop of Muslims commanded by El Moqdad ben El
Asouad. El Hamouk delivered them battle and his son was killed in the combat. He returned therefore to
Damietta, gathered his companions, and asked them counsel on the situation. A sage, who attended the
deliberation, said to him: "O king, the pearl of intelligence has no price, and it is a profit for no one if
one does not walk in the way of victory and of salvation. These Arabs, since they make war, have lost no
flag. They have conquered the countries, subjugated the peoples; no one can do anything against them. We are
not more powerful than the army of Syria, nor more valiant, nor better fortified than it. The Arabs have
always had the victory and the success; thus, my opinion is that you treat of peace with this people and that
it accord us the aman. We will avoid thus the effusion of blood and will obtain protection for our women. You
do not dispose of more

[PDF p. 666]

men than the Maqoqos." Far from yielding to this discourse, El Hamouk entered into a violent anger and had
the orator killed. The latter had a son, instructed and intelligent, whose house was contiguous to the wall
of the town. He went, during the night, to the Muslims and indicated to them the weak points of the place.
The Muslims seized them and fortified themselves there. El Hamouk came out to deliver battle; but he had had
knowledge of the arrival of the Muslims only when these were already masters of the rampart. The son of El
Hamouk, Sheta, seeing the enemies on the wall, ran at them with a great number of his companions. But this
broke the courage of his father who asked the aman of El Moqdad. The town was therefore rendered to the
Muslims. El Moqdad left there a governor and sent to 'Amr ben El 'As the news of the victory. Sheta, who had
converted to Islamism, went to Bourlos, to Damirat, and to Ashmoum Tenah, gathered the people of these
districts, and marched with them as auxiliary of the Muslims against their enemies; with his troops, he
marched, in concert with the Muslims, to the conquest of Tennis, carried a defiance to the inhabitants, and
delivered them a fierce combat in which he was killed as a martyr after having wounded and killed a great
number of enemies. One removed him from the field of battle and buried him in his domain, which bears his
name, outside Damietta. He was killed in the night of the Friday 15th day of Sha'aban, and it is for this that
each year there was that night a solemnity where gathered the people of the surroundings of Sheta who came to
pass the night there. They do still the same today. Damietta did not cease to belong to the Muslims until the
time when the Greeks disembarked there, in the year 90 of the hijra [20 November 708 to 8 November 709], and
seized Khaled ben Kisan, governor of the maritime region of Damietta. The Greeks sent their prisoner to the
emperor who, in regard to the truce intervened between him and the emir of the believers, restored him to the
latter, the caliph El Oualid ben 'Abd el Melek. Later, under the caliphate of Hesham ben 'Abd el Melek, the
Greeks made a descent at Damietta with three hundred sixty ships, killed and led away into captivity a great
number of inhabitants. It was in the year 121 [18 December 738 to 6 December 739]. At the epoch of the
struggle engaged between the two brothers Mohammed El Amin and Abd allah El Mamoun, discord reigned in the
country of Egypt and the Greeks, wishing to seize the country, disembarked

[PDF p. 667]

at Damietta in 200 and some [between the years 815 and 820]. Later, under the caliphate of the emir of the
believers El Moutawakel ala allah, 'Anbassah ben Ishaq being emir of Egypt, the Greeks disembarked at
Damietta on the day of Arafah of the year 238 [22 May 853]; they seized the town and what was there, killed a
great number of Muslims, and led away into captivity the women, the children, and the protected subjects.
'Anbassah ben Ishaq sent against them, on the day of the Nahr [23 May 853], an army to which had joined
themselves a great number of people; but they could not meet them, and the Greeks went to Tennis and
established themselves at the mouth of the river. 'Anbassah did not pursue them. Thus Yahia ben El Fadil said
to El Moutawakel:

[verses:] Can you admit that your women be taken by force, and that the Muslims be exposed to pillage and to
slaughter? An ass came to Damietta and the Greeks bounded to Tennis within reach of his eyes and nearer
still. They stayed at the mouth of the river, watching to, as formerly, strike Damietta, and preparing the
war. But the ass did not budge a span, thanks to his weakness and to his ignorance of what he should or
should not do. Do not forget that we are in danger of being lost in Egypt, and that the religion has nearly
disappeared.

El Moutawakel gave the order to build the citadel of Damietta and this construction was begun the Monday 3rd
of Ramadan of the year 239 [5 February 854]; at the same epoch, he proceeded to the organization of the
Egyptian fleet. In the year [probably 247, 17 March 861 to 6 March 862], the Greeks attacked Damietta with
about two hundred ships and stayed on the littoral for a month, pillaging, killing, making prisoners, and
delivering some combats to the Muslims. During the troubles that occurred following the death of Kafour El
Ikhshidi, the Greeks attacked Damietta again, the 10th of Rageb of the year 357 [10 June 968], with twenty
and some ships; they killed or made prisoners 150 Muslims.

In the year 408 [30 May 1017 to 19 May 1018], one seized at Damietta an enormous fish measuring

[PDF p. 668]

two hundred sixty cubits in length and a hundred cubits in width. The asses of the salt-works entered all
loaded into the belly of this monster and came out of it. In the skull of the beast kept themselves five men
with shovels to gather the grease that they passed to the crowd. And for a long time the people of the region
fed themselves on its flesh. In the time of the caliph El Faïz bi Nasr allah 'Eïsa, under the vizirate of El
Saleh Talaï' ben Razik, in Gamadi II of the year 550 [2 to 30 August 1155], presented themselves before
Damietta about sixty ships sent by Louis son of Roger, sovereign of Sicily. These enemies gave themselves to
pillage and to murder and made descents at Tennis, Rosetta, and Alexandria which they devastated. Then El
'Aded li din allah having become caliph and the vizirate having been confided for the second time to Shaour
ben Mogir El Sa'idi, the king of the Franks Mori (Amaury) came to besiege Cairo; after having struck the
inhabitants with a tribute, he burned Fostat. During this time, the commander of the Frankish fleet,
attacking Tennis, Ashtoum, and Minieh Ghamr with twenty cargo-ships, gave himself to murder, pillage, and
devastation. Under the vizirate of El Melek El Naser Salah el din Youssef ben Aroub (Saladin), who governed
for the account of El 'Aded, the Franks, mounted on more than twelve hundred ships, arrived at Damietta in
the month of Rabi I of the year 565 [23 November to 22 December 1169]; the Egyptian troops, for whose
equipment one had spent more than a hundred fifty thousand dinars, set out from Cairo; the war, a terrible
war, lasted fifty-five days. And, in so great a calamity, many Egyptians, and of the most noble, had
consented to aid the Franks and to maintain a correspondence with them. El Melek el Naser had them arrested
and put to death. Here is what was the cause of this calamity: The Ghozz, having passed from Syria into Egypt
with Asad el din Shirkawah (Shirkuh), the Franks, who feared that this tribe might seize the country, set out
to make an incursion into Egypt and asked for rescue from their brothers of Sicily. These sent them money and
arms in considerable quantities. The Franks, well provided with munitions and with machines, disembarked at
Damietta in Safar, brought by the number of boats we have said, and surrounded the town by land and by sea.
The sultan sent to Damietta an army under the orders of his nephew Teqi el din 'Omar and of the emir Shehab el
din El Hazemi; both had in abundance money, victuals, and arms. The

[PDF p. 669]

[OF THE TOWN OF DAMIETTE, continued]

situation of Damietta became very precarious, the inhabitants being always on the alert to ward off the
attacks of the Franks. Salah el din sent to ask for rescue from Nour el din Mahmoud ben Zenki, sovereign of
Syria, setting forth to him that he could not leave Cairo to go to Damietta, because he feared an uprising of
the Egyptians. Nour el din, not content with sending to Salah el din reinforcements upon reinforcements, came
out himself from Damascus and marched against the country that the Franks occupied on the littoral, invaded
it, and devastated it. The Franks, who still surrounded Damietta, informed of the attack of Nour el din and
fearing that this prince might make himself master of their territory, left Damietta the 25th of Rabi' I [18
December 1169], after having lost three hundred of their ships which had sunk; a great number of their men had
succumbed to an infectious malady that had broken out in their ranks. They burned moreover all that was too
heavy to transport, the machines and the other heavy objects. "Never," said Salah el din, "have I seen a man
more generous than El 'Aded. During the siege of Damietta by the Franks, he sent me a million dinars, without
counting the garments and the rest." In 577 [17 May 1181 to 6 May 1182], garrisons were established in the two
castles and ships were attached to the chains, so that from these ships one could combat and prevent the
passage between the two castles; the destroyed parts of the rampart were repaired, the breaches were blinded;
one fixed solidly the chain that connected the two castles. These works necessitated an expense of six
million dinars. The rampart was completed and its perimeter measured four thousand six hundred cubits.

In 588 [18 January 1192 to 6 January 1193], one cut, by order of the sultan, the trees of the gardens of
Damietta, one dug the ditches of the town, and one made a dike that ran along the chain of the castle.

In 615 [30 March 1218 to 18 March 1219], took place the great battle of Damietta which had for cause the
following facts: During the year 614 [10 April 1217 to 29 March 1218], the Franks had received rescue from the
great town of Rome, residence of the pope, and from other points of the countries of the Franks, and all had
gone to Acre where took place a great reunion. El 'Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub, informed of what was happening,
set out from Masr with his army and went to Ramleh. The Franks came out of Acre with an army

[PDF p. 670]

considerable and set about pursuing El 'Adel who was on the road for Beïsan. El 'Adel, frightened by the
number of his enemies to whom he could oppose only an insignificant army, turned back and went to Damascus.
The inhabitants of Beïsan and the surroundings, reassured by the presence of the sultan, had not left their
dwellings; but, the sultan hardly departed, the Franks arrived, passed the inhabitants by the edge of the
sword, devastated the country, seized the innumerable riches of the Muslims, and occupied Beïsan, Baïnas, and
all the towns of the region where they stayed three days, after which they returned to the countryside of
Acre with the booty and the captives. A great number of Muslims perished in this affair. The Franks stayed a
certain number of days in the countryside of Acre and, returning a second time, devastated Saïda and El
Shaqif and returned under the walls of Acre where they stayed. All this had happened from the 15th of Ramadan
to the feast of the rupture of the fast [16 December 1217 to 1 January 1218]. The sultan El 'Adel however had
installed himself at Morg el Safar and had sent an army under the orders of his son El Mo'azem 'Eisa to
Naplouse to resist the attacks of the Franks and prevent them from arriving at Jerusalem. The Franks, having
made at Tour a descent that lasted seven days, had returned to Acre and prepared themselves to invade Egypt.
In consequence, all embarked on the sea and set sail for Damietta in Safar. They disembarked there the
Tuesday 4th of Rabi I of the year 615 [31 May 1218] corresponding to the 8th of the month of Haziran. Their
army was composed of about 70,000 cavaliers and 400,000 foot-soldiers. They raised their tent facing Damietta
on the western bank and dug a ditch around the camp; behind, they raised a wall and set about attacking the
castle of Damietta, a solid castle from which set out the chains that barred the Nile and prevented the ships
coming from the sea from going up the river to Damietta. The Nile, indeed, after having watered Fostat,
continues its course toward the North and, arrived at Shatnouf, divides into two arms of which one directs
itself toward the North in the direction of Rosetta, where it throws itself into the sea; the other branch
goes from Shatnouf to Gouger, where it divides into two ramifications; one runs toward Ashmoum and throws
itself into the lake of Tennis; the other continues its course from Gouger to Damietta where is its mouth.
This

[PDF p. 671]

ramification of the river separates the town of Damietta from the western territory to which one has given
the name of island of Damietta, an island, indeed, that is surrounded by the water of the Nile and the sea.
The Franks, installed on the western territory, fabricated tools and cords, and built towers that they placed
on the ships, and these ships were directed toward the castle of the chain of which they wished to make
themselves masters, knowing well that once masters of the castle, they could easily go up the Nile to Cairo
and to Masr. The castle was filled with soldiers, but the Franks imagined a new ruse and, having raised, by
means of long beams, a tower on a great barque, directed it toward the castle, hooked themselves there, came
to blows with the garrison, and finally seized it. The news of the disembarkation of the Franks before
Damietta having reached El Melek El Kamel who then replaced his father in the government of Egypt, this prince
set out with the troops at his disposal, three days after the news had been brought to him by carrier pigeon
-- that is, five days after the beginning of the siege. He gave order to the vali of the Gharbieh to gather
the nomads and set out with a numerous army; the fleet also set itself in movement and stopped below
Damietta. The sultan stopped with his troops at the palace of El 'Adel, near Damietta. The army developed
itself as far as Damietta, to attempt to remove the Franks from the rampart. The struggle prolonged itself
and the castle resisted for four months when El 'Adel sent little by little from Syria his army which came to
rejoin entirely El Melek El Kamel. El 'Adel was very preoccupied with the descent of the Franks at Damietta
and, his disquiet increasing, he set out from Morg el Safar for 'Alefin where he fell ill and died the 7th of
Gamadi II [31 August 1218]. El Melek El Mo'azem 'Eïsa kept this death secret and had the body placed in a
litter escorted on the right and on the left by a servant and a physician. The Sharabdar (the one in charge
of drinks) prepared the potions and remitted them to the servant who drank them. And everyone was persuaded
that the sultan had drunk them. This lasted until the cortège had entered into the citadel of Damascus, where
had been transported the treasures and the coffers of money. There, the news of the death of the sultan was
rendered public, and his son El Melek El Mo'azem, after having entered into possession of all that was under
his hand, buried his father in the citadel; from there he transported him to the School Adeliah, at Damascus
itself. On learning the death of his father, El Melek el

[PDF p. 672]

Kamel, then at the palace of El 'Adel near Damietta, seized the power in Egypt. The Franks, redoubling their
ardor in the struggle, made themselves masters of the castle of the chain, broke the one that was attached to
it, in order to open the passage of the Nile to their ships and to seize the country. But El Kamel, to replace
the chain, had constructed a great dike barring the passage to the Franks; these delivered a fierce combat in
this place and succeeded in making a breach there. The castle and the dike had cost more than 70,000 dinars
and many times a day El Kamel set out on horseback from the palace of El 'Adel to Damietta to watch the work
and to seek by what indirect means he could attack the Franks. He had had sunk in the river a great number of
boats to close to the Franks the passage of the Nile, but these reopened a canal that had formerly served as
bed for the Nile and that bears the name of Azraq; they dug it to a great depth and having thus brought the
water of the Nile to the sea, they made, by this way, their ships go up to Bourah, following the bank of the
island of Damietta, and stopped facing the palace where the sultan resided, in order to repel him from there.
Arrived at Bourah, they watched the palace, attacked it, and attempted on several occasions to invade it, but
their efforts were long useless. This diversion changed nothing in the fate of the inhabitants of Damietta;
the victuals and the reinforcements continued to arrive to them. The Nile still separated them from the army
of the Franks and the gates of the town remained open, and they had in nothing to suffer from the siege. Each
night, the nomads pushed a thrust and carried off some Frankish soldiers; the enemy, disquieted by these
unforeseen attacks, dared not give itself to sleep. Soon the audacity of the nomads became such that they
sought to disquiet the Franks during the day and carried off complete tents with the people who were there;
the Franks put in ambush a large troop that killed a great number of men of the nomads. The winter came and
the swollen river submerged the encampment of the Egyptians and drowned some Muslims. The misfortune became
still greater and the situation worsened, the Franks not ceasing to harass them; little was needed for these
to be altogether victorious, when God raised a wind that broke the anchors of the boat of the Franks, a
marvel, which was carried toward the side of the Muslims and fell into their power. This boat, covered with
plates of iron so that one could not burn it, measured five hundred cubits in length. The Muslims broke it to
pieces and found there nails weighing each twenty-five rotolis. El Kamel

[PDF p. 673]

dispatched on all sides seventy messengers to incite the Muslims to send rescue to their brothers and to make
them understand the danger that would result from the occupation of Egypt by the Franks. Reinforcements were
at once sent from Hamah and from Alep and arrived to El Kamel in Shawal [21 December 1218 to 18 January 1219].
While everyone was attentive to these events, the emir 'Emad el din Ahmed, son of the emir Seïf el din Abou-l
Hassan 'Aly ben Ahmed El Hakari, surnamed Ibn el Mashtoub, at the news of the death of El Melek El 'Adel,
entered into struggle against El Kamel. He had at his discretion and under his orders the most disparate
bands, and bore the title of grand emir, supreme chief of the Hakari Kurds. He enjoyed a great prestige with
the kings and counted himself as one of them. He had moreover vast projects; he was liberal, generous, and
brave, and seemed destined to occupy a throne. He had had resounding adventures when he had filled the
functions of emir under the reign of Salah el din Youssef. He had decided, in an assembly of the army and of
the Kurds, to depose El Kamel and to proclaim in his place his brother El Melek El Faïz Ibrahim, the true
power to remain in the hands of Emad el din. The emirs 'Izz el din El Hamidi, Asad el din El Hakari, and
Mogahed el din, as well as the other emirs, marched in agreement with him. Instructed of this design, El
Kamel presented himself in their assembly while before them was placed the sheet where they were to inscribe
their oath of fidelity to El Faïz. On seeing him, they dispersed, while El Kamel, disquieted for his own
safety, withdrew and shut himself in his palace. It is then that arrived the Saheb Safi el din ben Shoukr,
coming from Amid to rejoin El Kamel who had summoned him after the death of his father. El Kamel went to meet
him, treated him magnificently, set forth to him the situation, and put at his disposition a large sum of
money. The night come, El Kamel mounted on horseback and, leaving the palace of El 'Adel, went alone to
Ashmoum Tenah, where he descended. The next morning, the army no longer had a sultan; each man mounted on
horseback very disquieted, no one preoccupying himself with his father, all throwing their impedimenta, tents,
victuals, arms, and went to the sultan. In the morning, the Franks ran toward Damietta and descended on the
eastern bank the Tuesday 16th of Dhu'l Qa'dah [3 February 1219]; without finding opposition or resistance,
they seized all that the camp of the Muslims contained -- that is,

[PDF p. 674]

[OF THE TOWN OF DAMIETTE, continued]

an indescribable booty. The sultan was plunged into great reflections and little was needed for him to abandon
the country, for he no longer had confidence in anyone of his entourage. The Franks redoubled their audacity
and wished to seize all of Egypt, and they thought indeed to make themselves masters of it. But God came to
the aid of the Muslims and reaffirmed the courage of the sultan. The brother of El Kamel, El Melek El
Mo'azem, came to rejoin him at Ashmoun Tenah and rendered him resolution and energy. Informed of the
intrigues of Ibn El Mashtoub, El Mo'azem engaged himself to put an end to these plots. Indeed, having gone on
horseback to the tent of Ibn el Mashtoub, he invited him to mount on horseback and to come with him. Ibn el
Mashtoub asked only to put on his underclothes and his riding garments, but El Mo'azem did not permit it him
and pressed him. He mounted therefore on horseback and set out with him. Arrived outside the camp of El
Kamel, El Mo'azem said to Ibn el Mashtoub: "O 'Emad el din, this country belongs to you, but I desire that you
cede it to us." And having remitted him a provision for the road, he confided him to a troop of his faithful
to whom he prescribed to lead him through the desert and to leave him free only when he would have left
Syria. Ibn el Mashtoub had to resign himself to obey El Mo'azem, for he was alone and could oppose no
resistance. His escort conducted him to Hamah, whence he set out for the Orient. El Mo'azem, having thus rid
himself of Ibn el Mashtoub, returned to El Kamel and gave the order to his brother El Faïz Ibrahim to go to
the kings of Syria with a letter of El Kamel asking them to declare war on the Franks. El Faïz set out
therefore for Damascus and from there for Hamah where he died poisoned, it is said. Thus El Kamel was
affirmed in his royal power and his spirit was appeased. The Franks however had invested Damietta by land and
by sea and pressed the siege which became very painful for the inhabitants; no reinforcement could arrive to
them. The enemy, who camped around Damietta, had surrounded its camp with a ditch behind which rose a wall.
The inhabitants delivered to the Franks terrible combats and held them at a distance, but they began to suffer
from the dearth, for the victuals were rare. It is then that El Mo'azem left El Kamel to go to Syria, while El
Kamel remained at Damietta to continue the war with the Franks. An officer of the stirrup, named Shemaïl,
asked the authorization to penetrate into Damietta: having thrown himself swimming into the river, he
penetrated into the town and promised the inhabitants the arrival of reinforcements. This trait made him taken
into esteem by El Kamel who went so far as to

[PDF p. 675]

make him vali of Cairo. It is to him that goes back the Khazanah of Shemaïl at Cairo. The situation remained
the same until the beginning of the year 16 [error -- 617, 9 March 1219 to... ; the footnote gives 617]. At
this moment, El Melek El Mansour Mohammed ben 'Amr ben Shahenshah ben Ayoub, sovereign of Hamah, sent his son
El Mozzafar Teqi el din Mahmoud into Egypt with an imposing army that was to aid his uncle El Kamel in his
struggle against the Franks. At his arrival at the camp, he was received by El Kamel who went to meet him and
had him descend at the right wing of the army, a place that his father and his grandfather had occupied in the
time of the sultan Salah el din Youssef. The Franks pushed impetuously the siege, and Damietta was defended by
a garrison of about 20,000 men; but they were decimated by the sickness and the dearth, the victuals were so
rare that an egg sold there for several dinars.

El Hafez 'Abd el 'Azim El Mounzari says he heard the cheikh Abou-l Hassan Aly ben Fadl recount that a rich
man who possessed a cow had killed it and sold it during the siege and had drawn from it eight hundred dinars.
In the book entitled El Mo'agem El Moutargem, the same author reports, according to the account of the emir
Abou Bekr Hassan ben Khasouyam who was at Damietta during the siege, that the sugar sold there for a hundred
forty dinars the rotoli and a chicken thirty dinars. "I bought," said Abou Bekr, "three chickens for
eighty-six dinars and a skin of water forty drachmas. To dig a grave, one asked forty metsqals. Once, my
sister, having split the belly of a camel, had filled it with chickens, fruits, vegetables, and other
objects, and, after having sewn it up, had thrown the beast into the river. At the same time she wrote me: 'I
have done this and that, watch the dead camel and take it.' The cadaver of the animal arrived to us during the
night. We gathered it, and found in the interior an enormous quantity of victuals that I distributed to the
inhabitants. My sister recommenced the experiment three times. At the end, the Franks had suspicions and
seized the dead beasts. The houses and the streets of the town were filled with cadavers; the victuals were
exhausting and the sugar became as rare as the precious stones. Of meat, there was no more; and we had no
means of finding any. Finally one came to the point that there remained in the town only a small quantity of
wheat and of barley." The Franks having scaled the rampart,

[PDF p. 676]

seized the town the Tuesday 24th of Sha'ban [4 November 1220]. The siege had lasted sixteen months and
twenty-two days. At the taking of the town, the Franks passed the women by the edge of the sword, committing
the greatest excesses, massacring and reducing to slavery the inhabitants. There was a considerable number of
victims. The sultan, informed of the event, mounted on horseback two days after the taking of Damietta and
stopped facing Talkha at the point formed by the two branches of the Nile, of which one directs itself toward
Ashmoum and the other toward Damietta. He established his camp at the place that was called later Mansourah
(the Victorious). The Franks fortified the ramparts of Damietta, transformed the mosque into a church, and
sent into the villages of the region detachments that gave themselves to massacre and pillage. The sultan
sent in all directions letters asking that one come to expel the Franks from the kingdom of Egypt; while
waiting, the army was occupied in building houses, hostelries, baths, and markets at Mansourah. For their
part, the Franks, having sent by sea their Muslim prisoners to Acre, came out of Damietta and came to
establish themselves in view of the sultan, facing Mansourah from which they were separated by the two arms of
the Nile, that of Ashmoum and that of Damietta. The enemy army counted two hundred thousand foot-soldiers and
ten thousand cavaliers. The Muslims made advance their ships of war, to the number of a hundred, facing
Mansourah; recruits had gathered, coming from Cairo, from Masr, and from all the region comprised between
Cairo and Assouan; the emir Hassam el din Younas and the fiqih Taqi el din Abou-l Taher Mohammed ben El Hassan
ben 'Abd el Rahman El Mohali made these troops come out of Cairo and Masr, and came to rejoin the bulk of the
army. The emir 'Ala el din Geldak and Gemal el din Ibn Seïram went to make levies in the region that extends
from Cairo to the extremity of the eastern Hauf and gathered an innumerable troop. The sultan established a
thousand cavaliers and several thousand nomads near Sharmesah to occupy the road between the Franks and
Damietta, and the ships, accompanied by an enormous fire-ship, went, under the orders of the emir Badr el din
ben Hassoun, to the point of the canal of Mehallah. Thus one intercepted the provisions that the Franks could
receive either by land or by the river. During this time, a Muslim army, come from the Orient, advanced from
Syria toward Egypt, while the Franks of the maritime countries, in incalculable number,

[PDF p. 677]

came to the rescue of the Franks of Damietta and sought to penetrate into Egypt. Having all gathered at
Damietta, they came out of the town, in serried and numerous ranks, and stopped facing El Kamel, as we have
said above. The reinforcements brought by El Melek El Ashraf Mousa ben El 'Adel, on the insistence of El Melek
El Mo'azem 'Eïsa, arrived to El Kamel, who went to meet them and had them establish themselves near him at
Mansourah, the 23rd of Gamadi II of the year 18 [9 August 1221]. The rescue sent by the various kings
followed, and finally the strength of the Muslim cavalry reached nearly forty thousand men. This army engaged
the combat against the Franks, removed from them six ships by gré or by force, and made them 2,200 prisoners.
A little later, the Muslims removed three other ships from the Franks, who, beaten down by these successive
reverses and feeling the situation critical, sent to ask for peace. But at the same time as their messenger
presented himself, the Alexandrians arrived with 8,000 combatants. The Franks asked, to withdraw from Egypt,
the cession of Jerusalem, of Ascalon, of Tiberias, of Giblah, of Laodicea, and of all the maritime region
conquered by the sultan Salah el din Youssef. The Muslims accorded all they asked, making exception for the
towns of Karak and of Shoubak, but the Franks refused the peace on these conditions, saying that they were to
receive Karak and Shoubak and moreover a sum of 300,000 dinars, in compensation for the part of the ramparts
of Jerusalem that El Melek El Mo'azem 'Eïsa, prince of Damascus, had destroyed. The latter, at the death of
his father El 'Adel, while the Franks occupied Damietta and had established themselves facing Mansourah where
El Kamel resided, feared that a part of the enemies might go by sea to seize Jerusalem and fortify themselves
there; it is for this that he had its ramparts demolished. These ramparts and their towers, very high and very
solid, were completely destroyed, with the exception of the tower of David. A great number of persons left
Jerusalem, where there remained only a small number of inhabitants. El Mo'azem removed from the town all it
contained of arms and instruments of war. The Muslims, having repelled the pretensions of the Franks,
recommenced the war, and a Muslim detachment having crossed the canal of Mehallah, disembarked on the land
that the Franks occupied, and dug an enormous trench in the Nile,

[PDF p. 678]

then at the maximum of its flood; the waters submerged the soil and separated from Damietta the Franks who
found themselves surrounded by the waters and had no longer to reach the town than an extremely narrow road.
At the same time the sultan had a bridge thrown at Ashmoum Tenah, and the army, crossing the river, occupied
the only road that remained to the Franks to fall back on Damietta, in the case where they would have wished
to beat in retreat. The enemy was filled with disquiet, for the land narrowed more and more around it.
Meanwhile, there arrived by sea to the Franks a great ship, escorted by numerous protecting fire-ships, and
filled with arms and provisions. This flotilla was attacked by the Muslim ships which, with the aid of God,
seized it. The Franks, at this news, felt themselves lost; the Muslims overwhelmed them with arrows and threw
themselves on the extremities of their wings. The Franks then overturned their tents, destroyed their
war-machines, and set fire to them, decided to march against the Muslims and to deliver them battle, in order
to be able to withdraw in safety on Damietta. But between them and the town were great heaps of mud and water,
for the Nile had submerged the lands. Thus, fearing in the state of weakness in which they were not to be
able to hold themselves standing, they humbled themselves and asked the aman, offering to abandon Damietta to
the Muslims. The sultan held council, but the opinions were divided; some refused to accord the aman to the
Franks, estimating that one should seize it by force; others consented to accord it to them, for fear of the
other Franks who were still in the islands and elsewhere. This last opinion prevailed. One decided to treat of
peace; the two parties were to take hostages. This happened the 9th of Rageb of the year 18 [29 August 1221].
The Franks sent as hostages to El Kamel twenty of their princes; El Kamel, on his side, sent his own son El
Melek El Saleh Negm el din Ayoub and a certain number of emirs. El Kamel received the princes of the Franks
in pompous ceremony, surrounded by his brothers and the officers of his house. This ceremony was full of
grandeur and of majesty. The priests and the Frankish monks having gone to Damietta, remitted the town to the
Muslims the 19th [8 September 1221]; that day was a great day. The town had just been remitted into the hands
of the Muslims when rescue arrived by sea to the Franks, and it was one of the benefits of God to have brought
them to Damietta only when

[PDF p. 679]

[OF THE TOWN OF DAMIETTE, continued]

the Muslims were already masters of the town. For if this rescue had arrived earlier, the Franks would have
been greatly reinforced by it; indeed, the Muslims had found the town of Damietta admirably fortified by the
Franks and almost impregnable. All being executed, the Franks sent back to the sultan his son and his emirs,
and El Kamel sent back to the Franks the princes he had with him as hostages. A truce of eight years was
signed. Among the conventions accepted for the conclusion of the peace between the Muslims and the Franks, it
had been stipulated that each would return to the other its prisoners. This article having been confirmed by
the sultan and his brothers on one part, and on the other by the Frankish princes, each returned with his
own. The sultan El Kamel reentered Damietta with his brothers and his army, and the day on which he made his
entry has remained a day one likes to recall. The Franks departed for their country, the sultan returned to
the capital of the kingdom and sent back the prisoners among whom were a certain number who were in captivity
since the time of Salah el din Youssef. The princes of Syria returned into their provinces with their troops,
and one spread on all sides the news of the taking of Damietta by the Muslims from the Franks. The Tatars had
already made themselves masters of the Empires of the Orient and the Franks were on the point of removing
Egypt from the Muslims. The duration of the sojourn of the Franks at Damietta until the moment when they had
to abandon it to return home was three years, four months, and nineteen days; during this period of time,
they were effectively masters of the town for one year, ten months, and twenty-four days. In 646 [26 April
1248 to 15 April 1249], the sultan El Saleh Negm el din Ayoub ben El Melek El Kamel Mohammed was struck with a
tumor in the knee that ripened and that one pierced. The operation, very painful, made the sultan ill. In
addition, an ulcer came to him on the chest, and he was obliged to keep the bed. But the ill that afflicted
him could not beat down his energy and, resolved to go from Egypt to Syria, he set out in a litter and
descended to the citadel of Damascus. There, presented himself a messenger of the emperor, king of the German
Franks of the island of Sicily, who, disguised as a merchant, came to teach him secretly

[PDF p. 680]

that Louis, named King of France, had formed the project of marching against Egypt and seizing it. The
sultan, ill, left Damascus in a litter and arrived at Ashmoum Tenah in Moharrem of the year 47 [16 April to
15 May 1249]. He accumulated in Damietta a considerable quantity of victuals, provisions, arms, and
instruments of combat, for he feared that there might arrive at Damietta what had arrived in the time of his
father, the epoch when the town had been taken for lack of provisions. At his arrival at Ashmoum Tenah, the
sultan wrote to Hasam el din Abou Aly El Hadiani, his lieutenant in Egypt, to have the fleet put in state in
the arsenals of the kingdom. Hasam hastened to obey and brought all his care to the execution of these
orders. He provided the ships with men and arms and all that was necessary, and had them depart one after the
other. The sultan, at the same time, dispatched the emir Fakhr el din Youssef ben Sheikh el Shioukh, and with
him the other emirs and the army. Fakhr el din arrived at Damietta, on the western bank, leaving thus the
river between his army and the town. At the second hour of the Friday 21 Safâr [16 May to 13 June 1249], the
fleet of the Frankish sailors arrived, mounted by considerable crews to whom had joined themselves the Franks
of the coast, and anchored facing the Muslims. The Frankish king sent to the sultan a letter thus conceived:
"... You are not ignorant that it is in me that the people of Jesus has put its confidence; I am not ignorant
either that you are the support of the Muslim people. You must know also that I have for neighbor the people
of the islands of Spain who bring me (in tribute) riches and presents; this people, we make it march before
us like a herd of oxen; we have killed the men, we have made the women widows, we have led away captive the
young girls and the young boys, we have made of their country a desert. But I have said enough of it and have
treated you quite as a sincere friend. If you engage yourself by the greatest oaths, if you send me the
priests and the monks, and if you come yourself to me, in sign of obedience to the cross, I will come to you
and will combat you on the terrain you prefer. If the country belongs to me, your riches will remain in my
hand; if the country is yours, if you carry it off, your powerful hand then will extend over me. I make you
know and warn you that the army I command covers the plain and the mountain; it is as numerous as the
pebbles. My soldiers come to you armed with the glaive of divine justice."

[PDF p. 681]

At the reading of this letter, the king, whose ill had aggravated, wept and asked that one answer. The cadi
Boha el din Zoheïr ben Mohammed wrote this answer: "In the name of God the clement and merciful, may his
prayers remain on our lord Mohammed, the apostle of God, on his family and all his companions. We have
received your letter where you menace us with the immense number of your army and the multitude of your
warriors. We, we are the masters of the swords, and none of us has died without our having avenged him on an
enemy. Every unjust man who has unjustly attacked us, we have annihilated him. If your eye, O presumptuous
one, had seen the grandeur of our swords, the space where we have delivered our battles, the citadels and the
shores we have conquered from yourselves, the devastation carried by us into your countries the most distant
and the nearest, you would bite your fingers with repentance; you would cease above all to pursue a day whose
beginning is to us, but whose end is to you. Then you will change opinion on yourself. 'Those who have
committed injustice will see the evil fall back on them' (Koran, XXVI, 128). When you have read this letter,
meditate the beginning of the Sourate El Nahal, where it is said: 'The order of God has come, do not seek to
accelerate it' (Koran, XVI, 1), and the end of the Sourate Sad where it is said: 'In some time you will learn
the news of it' (Koran, XXXVIII, 88). For the rest, we hold to the word of God who is the most veridical of
all those who speak: 'How many times an insignificant troop has vanquished a powerful army with the permission
of God, for God is with those who persevere' (Koran, II, 250). He who commits a transgression, say the sages,
opens a field of battle, and he against whom you have committed the transgression will overturn you and
precipitate you to your loss. Salutation!"

The Saturday [6 June 1249], the Franks disembarked and covered with their tents the greatest part of the
terrain that the Muslim army occupied; the tent of the king of France was red. The Muslims accosted them
boldly. In the encounter, the emir Negm el din, son of the Sheikh el Islam, and the emir Sarem el din Youssef
ben Sheikh el Shioukh were killed for the holy cause. In the evening, at the fall of night, the emir Fakhr el
din Youssef ben Sheikh el Shioukh, dragging the Muslim army, fled cravenly, withdrew with his troops onto the
territory of Damietta, and reached Ashmoum Tenah. The inhabitants of

[PDF p. 682]

Damietta, seized with panic, left the town during the night, without wishing to hear anything and leaving the
place absolutely deserted, rejoined the army at Ashmoum. They went barefoot, without garments, famished,
terrified, with their wives and their little children; they continued to flee as far as Cairo; the brigands,
on the way, stripped of their garments all those who possessed any, and left them naked. The public voice rose
against the emir Fakhr el din, whose flight had unleashed all the calamities on the Muslims. Damietta abounded
with combatants, victuals, arms, etc.; one had feared that it might undergo the same fate as in the time of El
Kamel, when it had succumbed only because of the exiguity of its provisions; yet, despite this inferiority, it
had resisted the Franks for more than a year and until its inhabitants had been annihilated. But God does what
he wills. The next morning, Sunday 23 Safar [7 June 1249], the Franks marched on Damietta, of which they found
the gates open and without defenders; believing in a ruse, the enemy waited to be quite certain of the
abandonment of the town, entered there without obstacle, without resistance, and seized easily all it
contained of victuals, arms, and munitions of war that were there in incalculable number, of riches and
precious objects. Islam and the Muslims received there a terrible blow; without the divine clemency, the name
of Islam would have disappeared from the earth. The inhabitants of Cairo and all the Egyptians were filled
with anguishes, because of the reverses of the Muslims and the sickness of the sultan who could hardly move.
The latter, very irritated against Fakhr el din, asked him: "Could you not, with your army, hold an hour
before the Franks?" And he made him undergo all sorts of bad treatments. But the circumstances counseled him
patience and pardon. However he flew into a rage against the Kénanis who were equally at Damietta, and he
addressed them reproaches. "What could we do," they answered, "since the army of the sultan, with all its
emirs, took flight after having destroyed the depots of arms? How would we not have fled, we too?" But the
sultan ordered that one hang them for having left Damietta without permission. And there were more than fifty
Kénani emirs hanged. Among them was the emir Ganim, who had a superb son and who asked to be executed before
his son; but the sultan ordered that the son be executed before the father, and

[PDF p. 683]

one hanged first the son and the father afterward. This execution, it is said, had been sanctioned by the
fiqihs. The rest of the emirs, seized with fear, thought of revolting against the sultan; but the emir Fakhr
el din explained to them that the health of the sultan was very precarious. "If he dies," he said to them,
"that suffices; if he does not die, he is anyway in your hands." The sultan undertook to fortify the ramparts
of Mansourah and went there in person the 25th of Safar [9 June 1249]; he covered the wall with shelters; the
barques were brought facing Mansourah with their crews complete and the soldiers were employed in the repair
of the constructions. A considerable number of Arabs, of people of the country, and of protected persons was
gathered; these bands set about harassing the Franks; but these covered the walls of Damietta with soldiers
and war-machines. The 1st of Rabi' I [14 June 1249], arrived at Cairo the Frankish prisoners carried off by
the nomads; among them were thirty-six cavaliers; the 5th of Rabi' II [18 July 1249], thirty-nine arrived; the
7th [26 July 1249], twelve; the 10th [29 July 1249], 25, of whom three cavaliers; the 18th of Gamadi I [29
August 1249], fifty. However the state of the sultan worsened and his forces diminished; the physicians
despaired of saving him. The 13th of Rageb [22 October 1249], arrived at Cairo a troop of prisoners
comprising forty-seven foot-soldiers and eleven knights; the Muslims who had managed to approach the place
that the Franks occupied on the river delivered them battle in the surroundings of Nesteraweh. In the night of
the Sunday, 14 Sha'ban [22 November 1249], the king El Saleh died at Mansourah. His death was kept hidden and
