the body transported in a coffer to the citadel of Rodah; the emir Fakhr el din ben Sheikh el Shioukh took the
command of the army. The widow of the sultan, Shagarat el dorr, had, at the death of her husband, summoned the
emir Fakhr el din, the eunuch Gemal el din Mohassen who commanded the Bahrite and Hachite Mamelukes, and
instructed them of the death of the sultan which they kept secret, for fear of the Franks, for these tended
to seize the provinces of Egypt. The direction of affairs was confided to the emir Fakhr el din, and Fâres
Oktai was dispatched to El Melek El Mo'azem Touran Shah, then at

[PDF p. 684]

[OF THE TOWN OF DAMIETTE, continued]

Hosn-Kaifa, in Persia, to hasten his coming. Meanwhile Fakhr el din had the troops swear an oath of fidelity
to the sultan El Melek El Saleh, to his son El Melek El Mo'azem as his successor, and to the emir Fakhr el din
as atabek of the army and lieutenant of the king. This oath was sworn by all the people present at Mansourah
and at Cairo; in this last town, the ceremony took place at the palace of the vizirate, into the hands of the
emir Hasam el din ben Abou Aly, the Thursday 18 Sha'ban [26 November 1249]; the standards were brought out of
the royal residence of Mansourah and transported to Cairo with an autograph of the slave Souhaïl; all those
who saw this writing remained convinced that it had been traced by the very hand of the sultan. The emir Hasam
el din himself suspected nothing. The death of the sultan remained a secret for everyone until the Monday 22
Sha'ban [30 November 1249], the day when reached Cairo the order to say the second prayer in the name of El
Melek El Mo'azem, the first having been made in the name of the sultan (El Saleh); the name of El Mo'azem was
also to be inscribed on the coins. At the news of the death of the sultan, the Franks -- foot-soldiers,
cavaliers, and ships -- came out of Damietta, crossed the river, and stopped at Faraskour the Thursday 25
Sha'ban [5 December 1249]. The Friday [6 December 1249], a letter arrived at Cairo, of which the beginning was
thus conceived: "Dash forth, light and heavy, and apply yourselves, with all your resources and all your
souls, in the road of God. It will be a great good for you to know." There was in this letter an eloquent
exhortation to the holy war. One read it from the pulpit at the mosque of Cairo, where a considerable crowd
had gathered to hear it. The people of Cairo, of Masr, and the surroundings, very disquieted, set about
weeping, lamenting, and groaning, certain to see soon the Franks seize the country, because there was no
longer a king to direct the affairs. However, they did not let themselves be beaten down and hastened from
Cairo, from Masr, and from all the provinces. A considerable crowd was thus gathered. The Tuesday 1st of
Ramadan [8 December 1249], the Muslims and the Franks delivered a combat where perished El 'Alaï, emir of the
council and of the assembly. The Franks arrived as far as Sharmesah; the Monday 7th [15 December 1249], they
were at El Baramoun. Their approach

[PDF p. 685]

spread terror. The Sunday 13th [21 December 1249], they arrived facing Mansourah; there, they were no longer
separated from the Muslims except by the canal of Ashmoum. They dug to protect themselves a ditch that they
backed with a wall protected by numerous shelters, and they raised the machines to launch projectiles against
the Muslims. Their ships were anchored before them on the Nile, while the Muslim ships were in advance of
Mansourah. The struggle became terrible on the land and on the water. The 16th [24 December 1249], arrived to
the Muslims six cavaliers announcing that the Franks were in a critical position. On the day of the feast of
the rupture of the fast [7 January 1250], one made prisoner from the Franks a count, near relative of the
king. All the Muslim warriors put into combating the Franks an extraordinary ardor and made them terrible
wounds, killing them some man at each instant and making them prisoners. They threw themselves into the water,
passed to the bank occupied by the Franks, and sought by all sorts of stratagems to seize some Frankish
soldier. They defied death to such a point that one of them, having hollowed out a watermelon, enclosed his
head in it and, plunging into the river, directed himself toward the Franks: one of these, believing he
perceived a real watermelon, descended into the water to take it, but he was seized and led toward the Muslim
camp. The Wednesday 7 Shawal [13 January 1250], the Muslims removed from the Franks a ship that carried a
count and 100 men. The Thursday 15th of the same month [21 January 1250], the Franks threw themselves on
horseback toward the terrain occupied by the Muslims and engaged the combat, but in the affair they lost forty
cavaliers and sixty-seven foot-soldiers who were sent under good escort to Cairo; among them were three of the
principal secretaries of the king. The Thursday 21st [27 January 1250], the Franks launched on the river an
enormous flaming fire-ship, of which the Muslims made themselves masters. The canal of Ashmoum is fordable on
certain points; a false Muslim indicated the fords to the Franks; these, guided by the traitor, crossed these
fords on horseback in the night of the Tuesday 4th or 5th of Dhu'l Qa'dah [8 February 1250]. The Muslims were
informed of the arrival of the Franks

[PDF p. 686]

only when the enemy hurled itself with impetuosity on their army. The emir Fakhr el din was at the bath when
one came to announce to him the attack of the Franks; quite troubled, for he expected nothing of the kind and
was not on his guard, he sprang on horseback and went in all haste to give the emirs and the troops the order
to mount on horseback and to set out with a detachment of his Mamelukes. A Frankish patrol having met them
attacked them. Those who accompanied Fakhr el din took flight; the emir himself, struck with a blow of lance
in the side, was assailed on all sides with blows of sword and was killed on the spot. It is then that his
Mamelukes went in mass to his palace, broke the coffers and the cases, and seized his money and his precious
objects. The Franks, after the death of Fakhr el din, pushed toward Mansourah; the Muslims, terrified, fled
and dispersed to the right and to the left; the rout was such that little was needed for the Franks to efface
the name of Islam from the land of Egypt. The king of France arrived as far as the door of the palace of the
sultan, and he was going to make himself master of it when God permitted that a troop of Baharite and
Gemdarite Mamelukes, gathered formerly by El Melek El Saleh, and of which Beïbars el Bondoqdari was a part,
threw itself on the Franks and engaged so terrible a melee that it pushed them back from their positions and,
pursuing them without respite with blows of swords and pikes, put them to flight in their turn. The Franks
lost in this battle 150 cavaliers; their infantry had arrived at the dike and prepared to cross the canal. If
the affair had been conducted slackly and had left the Frankish infantry the time to come to blows with the
Muslims, there would have resulted for these last an irreparable misfortune. The collision took place in the
streets and the alleys of the town; if the space had not been so narrow, no Frank would have escaped. Those
who avoided death fled and raised, to protect themselves, a wall that they surrounded with a ditch. Some fell
back on the eastern bank, but the greatest number withdrew into the island contiguous to Damietta. At the
moment of the combat, a note had been confided to the wing of the birds and sent to Cairo where the
inhabitants pushed extraordinary cries; lieutenants and some soldiers arrived at Cairo, of which the gates
remained open during the night of Wednesday. The Wednesday [9 February 1250] the birds fell, bringing the
news of the defeat of the Franks and the figure of their dead. One bedecked the town and one made

[PDF p. 687]

resound at the citadel of the mountain the instruments of good news. El Mo'azem Touran Shah went to Damascus,
where he entered the Saturday, last day of Ramadan [6 February 1250], seizing all that was in the town. The
4th of Shawal [10 January 1250 -- error], arrived by carrier pigeon the news of his entry to Damascus and the
instruments of good news were struck by the troops at Mansourah and at the citadel of the Mountain. Touran
Shah set out from Damascus the antepenultimate day of Shawal [2 February 1250], and the news of his approach
succeeded one another. The emir Hassam el din ben Abou Aly went to meet him and met him at Salahieh the 16th
of Dhu'l Qa'dah [20 February 1250]. It is at this moment that one made known the death of El Melek el Saleh of
which, until then, absolutely no one spoke; the affairs had remained in the state, the palace had undergone no
change, and the dispositions had been taken as customary. Shagarat el dorr, favorite spouse of the sultan,
directed the affairs and, under the pretext that the sultan was ill, permitted no one to approach him. When
Touran Shah left Salahieh, the emirs and the Mamelukes went to meet him. The new sultan installed himself in
the royal palace of Mansourah the Tuesday 19th of Dhu'l Qa'dah [23 February 1250]. The following Monday [1
March 1250], the Muslims conducted barques that they transported on the backs of camels to the canal of
Mehallah where they set them afloat and loaded them with combatants. At the moment when the Frankish barques
crossed the canal of Mehallah, the Muslim barques that had ambushed themselves rushed on them and a combat was
engaged between the two flotillas. The Muslim fleet, arriving from Mansourah, cut the retreat to the Franks,
seized fifty-two of their barques, and killed or made prisoner a thousand men. The way of provisioning of the
Franks was thus cut. The dearth became among them very great, and they were besieged in their turn. The 1st of
Dhu'l Higgah [7 March 1250], the Franks seized seven fire-ships belonging to the flotilla operating in the
canal of Mehallah; the crew was able to escape. On the day of 'Arafah [16 March 1250], the Muslim ships
attacked the barques that brought

[PDF p. 688]

provisions to the Franks and seized thirty-two of these barques, of which nine were loaded with soldiers. The
force of the Franks went weakening, while the dearth augmented. In all haste, they asked a truce of the
Muslims, proposing to render them Damietta, on the condition that one would abandon to them Jerusalem and a
fraction of the countries bordering the sea. But these propositions were repelled. The 27th of Dhu'l Higgah
[2 April 1250], the Franks set fire to all their works of wood and embarked on their ships with the intention
of going to entrench themselves in Damietta. They set out for this town, in the night of the Wednesday 3rd of
Moharrem of the year 648 [5 April 1250]; their ships descended straight before them, with the current. The
Muslims, returned to the bank they occupied, embarked, they too, and threw themselves in pursuit of the
Franks; in the morning of the 4th [8 April 1250], the Muslims had surrounded the Franks, to whom they killed
a great number of men and made numerous prisoners: the number of cavaliers killed above Faraskour exceeded, it
is said, 10,000, and one made prisoners, as much of the cavalry as of the infantry, of the workers and of the
common people, nearly 100,000 men; the booty -- money, munitions, horses, and mules -- was incalculable. The
king of France and the principal lords of the Franks withdrew onto a hill and, asking the aman which was
accorded them, surrendered to the eunuch Gemal el din Mohassem El Salehi; one surrounded them at once and led
them to Mansourah. The king of France was chained and shut in the house that the cadi Fakhr el din Ibrahim
ben Loqman, writer of the bureau of redaction, occupied. One committed to the surveillance the eunuch Sabih El
Mo'azemi; the brother of the king was shut in with him. A daily allowance was served to the king. El Melek El
Mo'azem prescribed to Seif el din Youssef ben El Touri, one of those who had come with him from the Orient, to
occupy himself with the massacre of the prisoners. One made come out each night three hundred of them whom
one killed and whom one threw into the river. This lasted thus until there were no more of them.

Being master of the king of France, El Melek El Mo'azem set out from Mansourah and descended with the royal
court at Faraskour, where he had raised for himself a tower of wood. Delaying his march on Damietta, he wrote
with his hand to the emir Gemal el din ben Yaghmour, his lieutenant at Damascus, and to his son Touran Shah:

[PDF p. 689]

[OF THE TOWN OF DAMIETTE, continued]

"Glory to God who has removed from us the desolation; there is no victory except by the intervention of God.
Today, let the believers rejoice in the divine victory! As for the benefits of your master, you can cite them;
but if one wished to enumerate the benefits of God, that would be impossible. We send to the high council of
El Gemal and to all the Muslims the happy news that God has accorded the Muslims the victory over the enemies
of the religion. These had brought to completion their work, doing us the greatest harm, chasing from the
country the servants (of God), the inhabitants, and the children. It is then that one can cry that one should
not despair of the divine assistance. And on Monday, the 1st day of the blessed year 648, God accomplished his
benediction on Islam; we opened the treasures, we distributed the riches and the arms, we gathered the
nomads, the volunteers, and people whom no one knows, if not God. They came from all the most distant defiles,
from the most far-off countries. Seeing this, the enemies sent to ask peace on the conditions intervened
between them and El Melek El Kamel; but we refused. And in the night of Wednesday, they abandoned their tents,
their riches, their heavy objects, and withdrew toward Damietta. But we pursued them, and the saber did not
cease to strike on their backs during all the night, making fall on them the calamity and the misfortune. In
the morning of Wednesday, we killed them thirty thousand men, without counting those who, of themselves,
threw themselves into the river; as for counting their prisoners, one might as well count the sea. The
Frenchman took refuge in the port and asked the aman. We accorded it to him; we made him prisoner, we treated
him well, and we made ourselves master of Damietta with the aid of God, and thanks to his power, to his
sovereignty, and to his grandeur." And with his letter, he sent the chaperon (hood) of the French king. The
emir Gemal el din put it on his head; this chaperon was of red scarlet, garnished with squirrel-skin. The
Sheikh Negm el din ben Israël said on this subject:

[verses:] The cape of the Frenchman has arrived, and it is truly worthy of the lord of the emirs; it was
white as paper, but our swords have dyed it with blood.

Another said:

[verses:] O chief of all the kings of the time, you have made accomplish the divine promises of victory;

[PDF p. 690]

our master has not ceased to penetrate into the secret country of the enemy, and to clothe, with the robes of
the kings, his slaves.

El Melek El Mo'azem, having become menacing for his stepmother, Shagarat el Dorr, set about asking her for the
treasures of his father. Filled with fear, she wrote to the Mamelukes of El Melek El Saleh to excite them
against El Mo'azem. Now, when Fares Oqtaï had gone to rejoin El Mo'azem at Hosn Kaifa, he had believed that
this prince would accord him an emirate; but it had been nothing of the kind, and El Mo'azem had thus set
against him the Mamelukes of his father. Moreover, he had shown himself brutal vis-à-vis the queen, had
removed from the emir Hassam el din ben Abou Aly the lieutenancy of the kingdom, had obliged him to come
rejoin the army, without occupying himself more with him. He had kept apart the servants of his father and had
replaced them by people come with him from the Orient, whom he had provided with the royal charges. He made of
the eunuch Messour his intendant, and of Sabih, a vigorous Abyssinian slave, his treasurer. To this last, he
had given a cane of gold, considerable riches, and immense fiefs. When he was drunk, he gathered candles of
which he cut the top with his saber, saying: "Thus will I do to the Bahrites." He was foolish, frivolous,
blinded by his love of pleasures; everyone detached himself from him. The situation prolonged itself until the
Monday 29th of Moharrem [13 April]. That day, the sultan was seated on a mat, when one of the Bahrite
Mamelukes presented himself and, striking him with his sword, cut off the fingers of his hand. El Mo'azem
fled and reached the tower, and, pursued by the mutineers with naked sword, took refuge at the summit of the
tower of wood; the Mamelukes launched arrows at him and set fire to the tower; he jumped from the top of the
tower and ran toward the canal: "I want none of your kingdom," he cried; "let me return to El Hosn; O Muslims,
is there no one among you who wishes to rescue me and defend me?" But the soldiers were there standing, armed
with their swords, and no one answered him. The arrows set about raining on him from all sides: he was hacked
with blows of sword and died burned, drowned, massacred the Monday in question. His body was left on the bank
of the river for three days after which one buried it. After the death of El Mo'azem, the people of the
kingdom were of the opinion to name as queen of Egypt Shagarat el Dorr, mother of Khalil, and to give the
command of the army to

[PDF p. 691]

the emir 'Az el din Aybek El Tourkomani El Salehi; everyone swore an oath in this sense, and one dispatched to
the queen 'Az el din El Roumi who, having gone to her at the citadel of the mountain, informed her of what had
happened. The queen was very satisfied with it and affixed on the firmans her paraph which read: "Mother of
Khalil." The prayer was said in her name from the pulpit at Masr and at Cairo. Negotiations had been engaged
with the king of France for the cession of Damietta, and the emir Hassam el din ben Abou Aly El Hadiani had
been charged with the negotiations. The king of France, after many negotiations, consented to this cession, on
condition that one would set him free. He sent therefore to the Franks the order to remit Damietta to the
Muslims; but the cession was made only after long discussions and numerous detours, the Friday 3 Safar [7
May]. One planted the banner of the sultan on the ramparts, and one proclaimed there at last the word of Islam
and the testimony of the truth; the town had remained in the hands of the Franks for eleven months and seven
days. One gave back the liberty to the king of France, to his brother, to his wife, to all those who were
with him. One conducted them to the western bank where they embarked the next day, Saturday 4 Safar [8 May],
and set sail for Acre.

It is regarding these events that the vizier Gemal el din Yahia ben Matrouh said:

[verses:] Say to the Frenchman, if you meet him, this sincere word of a sincere counselor: "May God reward
you for what has happened, thanks to the servants of Jesus the Messiah. You came to Egypt, counting on seizing
it, and imagining, O drum, that it suffices to blow to play the flute. But your destiny pushed you toward the
calamity, and the world, despite its immensity, seemed to you narrow. All your companions are deposited,
thanks to your wise direction, in the bosom of the tombs: of your fifty thousand men one sees no more than
dead or wounded prisoners. May God push you to do the same again! Perhaps thus Jesus will rid himself of you.
If your pope is satisfied with it, it is that (sometimes) the worst counsels come from the best counselors.

[PDF p. 692]

Say to them that, if they wish to return to avenge themselves, still solid is the house of Ibn Loqman in the
same place; that the chains are still there and that the eunuch is still Sabih."

And God decreed that the Frenchman, after having escaped this disaster, gathered again a considerable army and
went to Tunis. Ahmed ben Ismaïl El Zayat, a young Tunisian, said:

[verses:] O Frenchman, this land is the sister of Egypt, prepare yourself for the misfortune that is going to
overwhelm you. Here the house of Ibn Loqman will be for you a tomb, and you will have for eunuch Mounqir and
Nakir (the two angels of death).

These verses were of good augury, for the Frenchman died during the siege of Tunis. The emirs, once masters of
Damietta, sent couriers to Cairo, one made resound the instruments of good news, and one bedecked Cairo and
Masr, and the army arrived, coming from Damietta, the Thursday 9 safar [13 May].

During the reigns of El Ashraf Mousa ben El Melek El Messa'oud Aqsis ben El Melek El Kamel and of El Melek El
Mo'ez 'Az el din El Tourkomani, the troubles accentuated themselves in Egypt, and El Melek El Naser Youssef
ben El 'Aziz made himself master of Damascus. The chiefs of the kingdom -- that is, the Bahrite Mamelukes --
fell in agreement to raze the town of Damietta, where they feared a second descent of the Franks. One sent
there therefore quarrymen and laborers, and the ramparts were attacked the Monday 18 sha'ban 648 [15 October
1250] and demolished completely; there remained nothing more of the town than the mosque. To the south of the
primitive emplacement one built on the shore of the Nile straw-huts where the inhabitants of little vigor
established themselves and to which they gave the name of El Menshieh. The destroyed rampart had been raised
by the emir of the believers El Moutawakel 'ala Allah as we have said above. When, after the murder of El
Melek El Mozaffer Qouttouz, El Melek El Zahir Beïbars El Bondoqdari El Salehi had appropriated to himself the
kingdom of Egypt, he dispatched from Masr, in 659 [6 December 1260 to 15 November 1261], a great number of
quarrymen charged with obstructing the mouth of the river at Damietta. These workers, having cut a great
number of round stones, threw them into the branch of the river that goes to pour itself

[PDF p. 693]

into the sea, to the north of Damietta: the bed of the river narrowed all the more and no longer permitted the
ships to arrive as far as the town. Until present, it is always thus, and the great barques, coming from the
sea, cannot penetrate there; the merchandise brought by the barques is transshipped into special boats on the
Nile that the people of Damietta name guermes (singular guerm). The sea-ships go to stop at the extremity of
the cape that separates the two mouths of the river. Today the inhabitants of Damietta claim that if the
sea-ships cannot go up the river, it is that they are prevented from it by an accident of terrain that
obstructs the mouth, or by an accumulation of sand that has formed in this place. But it is an erroneous
explanation that has for origin the great number of wrecks of shipwrecked vessels that one gathers in this
place, wrecks of which they are ignorant of the origin, not knowing the events that took place. Until present
still, the entry of the river is redoubtable to the ships, and those that are lost there are numerous.

I went to this place to visit it and I recognized that it was one of the most astonishing that men have seen.

As for the Damietta of today, it was formed after the destruction of the ancient town; at the actual
emplacement, huts had been raised, but the place constantly enlarged itself and became in its turn a great
town with markets, baths, mosques, schools, places of prayer. The houses give on the great arm of the Nile;
behind extend gardens that make of this country one of the most beautiful countries of God one can see. The
emir, the vizier El Mouchir El Ostadar Ylbagha El Salemi declared to me never having seen, in his voyage from
Samarcand to Masr, a country more beautiful than this Damietta. I believed his praise exaggerated, but I
visited it, I too, and I found that it was the most beautiful and most agreeable country.

And here is what I say of it:

[verses:] May the rains of spring water Damietta! Salutation to it from the one who has visited it! Its good
memory only increases my desire to see it again. May the south winds not cease to feed its clouds, for it is a
land whose beauty equals that of Paradise. Those who traverse the regions during the night know how sweet it
is, and the beauties that surround it cannot be counted.

[PDF p. 694]

[OF THE TOWN OF DAMIETTE, the praise-poem continued]

[verses:] Indeed, the watercourses that surround its gardens resemble glittering swords or the surface of
cheeks. Its thirsting dust makes it resemble the lover from whom the beloved turns away. Standing on its feet,
the eyes drowned in tears, it watches the stars of the night, plunged in grief. To see it thus standing one
would believe that, despite the length of the waiting, it still hopes in the person of its friend. And then,
these noriahs (water-wheels)! they renew the grief in the heart of the solitary lover. I recount to it my
grief, and it seems to me that it recounts to me its own and pushes the same plaint. It seems to me that it is
a sky whose stars turn always for its good and its happiness. In the white basins, how pretty is the
water-lily! Sweeter, more brilliant in color than the rose -- (one would say) a sky of crystal sown with
stars of marvelous colors and symmetrically arranged. On the bank of the sacred Nile reigns a promenade that
would render youth to the old man weakened by age. There are born winds that dissipate sorrow and sadness, and
nights sweet as the arrival of the beloved. At the meeting of the two rivers are a multitude of marvels that
burst forth and shine from near as from far. When the Nile throws itself into the sea, one would say two kings
marching, surrounded by their army, who present themselves for the combat; the struggle becomes fierce, and
one fights only with the long and flexible lances. They redo what they have already done, and will remain as
they are, magnificent betrothals and in infinite struggle. How many times have I tasted delicious pleasures on
their banks, sweet and thirst-quenching for the one who goes there to drink! How many times have I enjoyed in
these gardens the sweetness of living there in peace and in happiness! On the promontory so frequented how
many times have I wandered alone, and on the side of Shata, to the right of El 'Elm. There, the eye of the
spirit sees all it can embrace of beauty, of goodness, of riches, and of glory. O my God, may your goodness
accord me to return there again, without this time my being called there by misfortune or by pain!

[PDF p. 695]

At Damietta, in the destroyed town, is a mosque, one of the most revered sanctuaries of Islam. One calls it
generally Menged Fatah. It is the oratory founded by the Muslims at Damietta, at the time of the conquest of
the town, when God, for the first time, had Egypt conquered by the hand of 'Amr ben El 'As. On the door is a
Cufic inscription, recalling that it was rebuilt after the year 500 of the Hijra [2 September 1106 to 21
August 1107]. It contains a great number of marble columns, of which some have not their equals. This oratory
bears the name of Gama' Fatah, for the simple reason that a personage called Fâteh sojourned there, which made
the people give it the name of Gama' Fatah. This personage is none other than Fateh ben Othman El Asmar El
Takrouri, who had gone from Merâqesh (Marrakesh) to Damietta, with the aim of detaching himself from the
world. There, he gave water to drink in the markets, without exacting anything from anyone. He sojourned also
outside El Thogr, but being obliged to attend there the prayer in common, he abandoned the world completely
and established himself in the parts of Tounah, on the lake of Tennis, a village ruined for nearly seven
years, of which he repaired the mosque. From Tounah, he went to the mosque of Damietta and dwelt in a hole, at
the foot of the minaret, without seeing anyone, except at the hour of prayer. At that moment, he went to pray
and, after the salutation of the imam, returned to his hole. If one of his neighbors addressed the word to
him, he spoke to him standing, after the termination of the prayer. His life was only union (with God) in the
separation (that is, the world that separates from God), rapprochement in the distancing, communion in the
absence. During the pilgrimage he made, he always walked apart from his companions, and one saw him only at
the moments of the halt. He remained constantly apart from the others and spoke to no one until his return to
Damietta; there, he set about repairing the mosque and cleaned it himself; he thus chased all the bats nested
in the cupolas, he filled the cisterns with water, he paved the court, leveled the terrace with plaster, and
established himself there. Previously, since the destruction of the town, the mosque was open only on Friday.
And one installed there an imam charged with reading the five prayers; this imam dwelt in the house of the
sermon and occupied himself with the direction of those who came there. One named a reader who read the Koran
at dawn and at the setting of the sun; another was

[PDF p. 696]

charged with reading a sermon, to recall to men (the benefits of God) and to instruct them. He said: "If I
knew at Damietta a place more venerable than the mosque, I would go to establish myself there, and if I knew
on the earth a place where the poor man was more miserable than at Damietta, I would go there and stay there."
If some poor man came to find him and he had nothing to give him, he sold one of his garments to be able to
serve him the meal of hospitality. He lay down at night and awoke in the morning, without anyone knowing
anything of him; the eye saw nothing of it, the ear heard nothing of it. He helped in secret the poor and the
indigent. If someone asked him for something, he always received much more than he had asked, and if God made
him obtain something, he employed it in alms. He strove to humble himself, and God made burst forth his virtue
and his benediction without his being for anything in it, and I have known of him many marvelous traits. He
applied himself to follow the example of the ancients who held to the Book and the tradition, kept away from
all discussion, and repelled all pride and all boastfulness. He kept his conduct secret and was full of
restraint in his words and in his acts. No one kept him company during the night; one was ignorant of which
were his days of fasting and which days his fast was broken. Always he employed the expression "if it please
God," there where the others made use of the exclamation "by God!" The cheikh 'Abd El 'Aziz El Damiri having
counseled him to take a wife, affirming that marriage was prescribed by the Sunnah, he married two women
toward the end of his life, but he entered the home of neither of them during the day; never did he eat nor
drink with them. His night was consecrated to prayer; however sometimes he went to them, sometimes he
abstained from visiting them, following the distribution of his time and the exigencies of his religious
practices and of his love of solitude. None of his familiars ever knew which days he fasted and which days he
did not fast. One contented oneself with carrying him his food and depositing it in his particular chamber,
without one ever having seen him eat. He was fond of the poor and affected himself the state of poverty. He
repelled with all his forces oppression and tyranny, remaining humble with the poor and haughty with the
powerful and the rich; he took pleasure in the reading of the Koran and of books, but no one ever saw him
write. He read the Koran with humility and circumspection. He never made use of a carpet for prayer; never did
he affiliate himself with any sect, nor cover his head with the little white bonnet. He never said: "I am a
cheikh,"

[PDF p. 697]

nor: "I am a poor man." Each time the pronoun "I" presented itself in his discourses, he excused himself for
it and asked God pardon for having employed it. Never did he attend a (musical) audition, but he made no
reproaches to whoever attended one. His conduct was perfect, without his seeking to render it perfect. He
showed himself very haughty with the people of the world and very humble with the poor, presenting to these
the food and not presenting it to the rich. If there was at his home some reunion, he put the poor before the
rich, and if a poor man left his house, he accompanied him a few steps, barefoot, without shoe, and remained
standing watching him move away, until he had lost him from view. If some poor man enjoyed the title of
cheikh, he had him sit politely near him, keeping his turban, and preceded him on the road. He said: "I say to
no one: Do this or do not do it. He who wishes to conduct himself well has only to watch his actions. He whom
his own sight does not suffice to conduct will not conduct himself by listening to others." One of his
familiars having said to him: "My lord, pray God that he accord us his benefits, for we are poor," he answered
him: "If you wish God to be generous toward you, keep nothing in your house, and then implore his generosity.
For it is written: Ask nothing of God if you possess only a ring of iron." According to him, the poor man is
like a virgin, and as soon as he implores, he ceases to be one. One of his familiars asked him one day to pray
God to accord him a more ample life, for his was very precarious: "I will not pray God to accord you a more
ample life," he answered; "I will ask him for you a virtue and a perfection greater." Despite his religious
practices and all the time he employed in them, he did not neglect his friends and did not forget their
affairs, to the point that he charged himself with settling them and doing all the necessary for his friends,
and arranging them to the best of their interests. He knew the situation of people according to their
function; he exalted science and showed himself generous toward the orphans; he was full of compassion for
the sickly and the widows. He employed himself to intercede with the judge for affairs general and
particular, without their number rebuffing him or boring him. He multiplied in secret the alms without ever
asking anything for himself. He depreciated what he gave, although it was sometimes considerable; on the
contrary, he made great case of what one gave him, however small the present was, and rewarded the donor by a
gift much more important. Never did he frequent

[PDF p. 698]

an emir or a vizier; but his conduct and his manner of being raised him in humility, glorified him in poverty:
it was the rapprochement in the distancing, the union in the separation, the renunciation in the midst of the
world and of its creatures. He was greater still than his reputation. Here is one of the prayers he made for
himself and for those who asked it of him: "My God, remove us from the world and the people of the world, and
remove them from us." He remained thus until his death, occurred at the end of the night, of which the next
day was the 8th of Rabi II of the year 695 [14 February 1296]. He left two children who had not the means to
live for one night. He owed in addition 2,000 dirhems. One buried him in the vicinity of the Mosque, and,
still today, one visits his tomb.

[End of Chapter LXI.]

[PDF p. 699]

CHAPTER LXII
OF SHATA

Shata, a town situated in the vicinity of Tennis and of Damietta, gives its name to the Shatawiah stuffs. It
itself, it is said, takes its name from Shata ben El Hamouk, whose father was the uncle of El Maqoqos and
commanded at Damietta. When God had had the citadel conquered by the hands of 'Amr ben El 'As and the latter
had made himself master of the land of Egypt, he sent to seize Damietta an army that besieged the town and
seized its ramparts; Shata, with two thousand of his companions, came out of the town and went to join the
Muslims. Already before he loved virtue and had a penchant for Islamism of which he had heard speak. Masters
of Damietta, the Muslims had to struggle against the prince of Tennis. Shata went to Bourlos, to Damirah, and
to Ashmoum Tenah and called the inhabitants to arms. These joined themselves to him to combat the people of
Tennis. Shata set out therefore with these partisans to whom were united the Muslims of Damietta and the
reinforcements dispatched by 'Amr ben El 'As, to deliver battle to the people of Tennis. In the encounter of
the two armies, Shata combated with an admirable courage and killed twelve of the most famous warriors of
Tennis; he died a martyr in the night of Friday the 18th day of Shaaban of the year 21 of the Hijra [19 July
642]. One buried him outside Damietta, at the place where is still today his tomb. One raised him a monument
where the people assemble each year the 15th of the month of Shaaban; one went there in crowds from all the
villages around, and this usage is practiced still at present. It is at Shata that was fabricated the veil of
the Ka'bah. "I saw there," reports El Fakehy, "one of the veils of the emir of the believers Haroun El Rashid,
in qebati stuff of Egypt, bearing this inscription: 'In the name of God, may the benediction of God be on the
servant of God Haroun, emir of the believers. May God prolong his life! This is one of the objects fabricated
by order of El Fadl ben El Rabi', freedman of

[PDF p. 700]

the emir of the believers, in the workshop of tapestry of Shata. It is a veil for the Ka'bah. The year 190
[27 November 805 to 16 November 806].'"

Among other localities very well known of the district of Damietta is Barzakh. It is an oratory raised on the
lake of Damietta. Everyone calls it El Barzakh, but I do not know why. I was there witness of an extraordinary
fact: there is in this mosque a great minaret constructed in bricks; if someone pushes it, it trembles. And
finding myself one day at the summit, there where the muezzin makes the call, I set the minaret in movement,
and I saw its shadow displace itself following its double movement of coming and going. One meets around this
mosque debris of skeletons that seem to be the remains of those who fell as martyrs in the combats against the
Franks. God knows it, and you know nothing.

Dabiq is one of the villages that depended on Damietta. One fabricated there stuffs brocaded with gold,
turbans of dyed linen, and the dabiqi stuffs with designs of gold. It is there also that were made the turbans
of linen with threads of gold; each of these turbans measured a hundred cubits in length and contained
applied pieces woven of gold. The quantity of gold that a turban also contained was worth five hundred dinars,
not counting the price of the silk and the thread. These turbans were inaugurated, as well as other stuffs, in
the time of El Aziz billah ben El Moezz, in the year 365 [10 September 975 to 29 August 976], and employed
until the death of this prince, occurred in Shaba'n of the year 385 [19 August to 16 September 996].

El Nahririah, a village of the province of Gharbieh, was established as a religious donation by the emir Shams
el din Sonqor El Sa'di, lieutenant-general of the army in the time of El Naser Mohammed ben Qalaoun, who
achieved the construction of it. This construction reached in his time the sum of ten thousand dirhems of
silver; this emir left it, and the construction was continued for the sultan; the situation of this village
became more and more prosperous, to such a point that one counted there more than thirty gardens, and the
revenues, thanks to the great number of inhabitants, rose to a thousand dirhems of silver per feddan; then it
became a great town that brought in per year, kharadjî and hilàlï, a sum of 300,000 dirhems of silver, that is

[the footnote: The sense of these expressions will be explained in chapter 94 which treats of the "conversion
of the Coptic kharadjî year into the Arab hilàlï year."]

[PDF p. 701]

fifteen thousand dinars of gold. This Sonqor died in the year 728 [17 November 1327 to 4 November 1328]; it is
to him that is due the school of El Sa'adiah in the quarter of Hadrat el Baqar, outside the gate of Zaouileh.
The island of the Béni Naser takes its name from the children of Naser ben Ma'wiah ben Bekr ben Houazen. Here
is on what subject. The children of Hamas ben Zalem ben Ga'il ben 'Amr ben Darahman ben Nasir ben Ma'wiah ben
Bekr ben Houazen had in Egypt a considerable force and had grown to such a point that they had filled the
Delta and appropriated it to themselves. A tribe of Berbers entered into struggle with them. This tribe was
known under the name of Laouatah; it claimed to descend from Qeïs. It repelled the Béni Naser who dwelt within
walls and resided in a fixed fashion in a place situated in the middle of the Nile that took their name; and
this place is the island of the Béni Naser.

[PDF p. 702]

CHAPTER LXIII
OF THE ROUTE THAT LEADS FROM MASR TO DAMASCUS

The first who established the posts for the horses was the king Dara (Darius), son of Bahman, son of
Kibeshtasf, son of Kihrasf, one of the kings of Persia; in the time of Islam, the first who established the
posts was the emir of the believers El Mahdi Mohammed ben Abou Ga'far El Mansour, who installed between Mecca,
Medina, and the Yemen relays of mules and of camels in the year 166 [15 August 782 to 4 August 783]. The
origin of this term is the word barid zeneb. For Darius having distributed to the relays of the great roads
mounts whose tail had been cut, one called this relay barid zeneb (cut tail). In adopting this expression, the
Arabs cut off the half of it and said simply barid. The great route that the armies, the caravans, and other
travelers follow, setting out from Cairo and directing themselves across the sands toward the town of Gaza, is
not the route that, in antiquity, led from Egypt into Syria. The one that today crosses the desert began to be
employed only after the year 500 of the Hijra, at the moment when was extinguishing itself the dynasty of the
Fatimids. The route that was in use before the Franks had made themselves masters of the maritime country of
Syria was quite other. In his book of the Routes and the Kingdoms, Abou-l Qasem 'Obeïd allah ben 'Abd Allah
ben Khardadabah, in his chapter of the description of the earth, expresses himself thus: The route from
Damascus to El Kesouah is 12 miles; from El Kesouah to Gasem 24 miles; from there to Fiq, 24 miles; then to
Tiberias, town of the Jordan, 6 miles; from Tiberias to El Lagoûn 20 miles; then to El Qolonsouah 20 miles,
then to El Ramleh-Filastin 24 miles; the route from El Ramleh to Azdoud counts 12 miles; from Azdoud to Gaza,
20 miles; from there to El Arish, 24 miles across the sands; from there to El Ouaradah 18 miles; from there to
Omm El Arab 20 miles; from there to El Farma 24 miles, from there to Garir 30 miles; from there to El Qâserah
24 miles; from there to Mesged Qoda'ah 18 miles; from there to Balbeïs, 21 miles; from there to Fostat,
capital of Egypt, 24 miles. This route, as one sees, was quite different from the one

[PDF p. 703]

that one sees today to go from Masr to Damascus. One goes at present from Balbeïs to El Farma across the
regions that one calls actually the country of El Sabakh and that form part of the Hauf; from Farma, a town
neighboring Qatiah, one goes to Omm El Arab, a country today ruined, on the shore of the sea, in the space
comprised between Qatiah and El Ouaradah and where many people practice excavations and find dirhems of pure
silver, very heavy and of great module; from Omm El Arab, one goes to El Ouaradah, a town that occupied
formerly an emplacement different from the one it occupies today, and of which one has spoken in this book.
When the Franks left Constantinople in 490 [19 December 1096 to 8 December 1097] to remove from the Muslims
the country they occupied, Baudoin (Baldwin) seized El Shoubak, previously ruined, and repeopled it in 509 [27
May 1115 to 14 May 1116] and advanced as far as El Arish, a prosperous country at this epoch. The
communications were cut between Egypt and Syria, and one had to follow the land route with the Arabs, for fear
of the Franks. Finally, the sultan Salah el din Yousef ben Ayoub wrested Jerusalem from the Franks in 583 [13
March 1187 to 1 March 1188], redoubled his attacks against them, and removed from them a great number of
countries on the shore of the sea. This route crossed the desert; the travelers have followed it since then
until the reign of El Melek El Saleh Negm el din Ayoub ben El Kamel Mohammed ben El Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub,
who founded in 644 [19 May 1246 to 7 May 1247] in the land of El Sabakh, at the extremity of the desert, a
town known still at present under the name of El Salahieh; it is there that he descended and sojourned, and
after him the kings continued to sojourn there. When he had become sovereign of Egypt, El Melek El Zaher
Beïbars El Bondoqdari established relays in all the directions, so well that a piece of news could be sent
from the Citadel of the Mountain and arrive in four days at Damascus, and vice versa. He received news from
all the points of the Empire twice a week, and, while remaining himself at the Citadel, dispatched through all
the kingdom the destitutions and the nominations. He had to spend considerable sums to achieve the
organization of this relay, which was completely finished in 659 [6 December 1260 to 25 November 1261]. These
posts continued to function between Cairo and

[PDF p. 704]

[OF THE ROUTE THAT LEADS FROM MASR TO DAMASCUS, continued]

Damascus, and in each district one found numerous horses ready to be mounted that one named "post-horses";
with them were grooms and special men named "piqueurs" (drivers) who, if one required it, mounted on the
post-horses, pushed the mount of the traveler, and served him during all the duration of the voyage. No one
could make use of these horses except on an express order of the sultan; sometimes one forbade absolutely the
use of them to any traveler not charged with the service of the sultan; sometimes also some notable procured
this authorization and could then mount them for his voyage. The route of Syria was very frequented, and the
traveler found at each relay all of which he had need, victuals and fodder. And these routes were so safe
that, according to what one has told us, a woman went alone from Cairo into Syria, on horseback or on foot,
without carrying victuals or water. When Timour Lenk (Tamerlane), having seized Damascus in 803 [22 August
1400 to 10 August 1401], had reduced to slavery the inhabitants and burned the town, the post-relays were
abandoned, and the population, desolated by the scourge that overwhelmed the country and the innumerable
calamities that fell on it, could not occupy itself with their re-establishment. The route of Syria was little
by little abandoned, then completely forsaken. It has remained in this state until present -- that is, in the
year 818 [13 March 1415 to 28 February 1416].

[PDF p. 705]

CHAPTER LXIV
OF THE TOWN OF HATEIN

The ruins of this town are seen still between Habouah and El 'Aqoulab, on the territory of this last, in the
region that extends from Qatiah to El 'Arish. Facing it and about a mile distant is a fountain of sweet water
named by the Arabs (fountain) of Abou el 'Arouq; this fountain is to the east of the town. This locality takes
its name from Hateïn, or, according to others, Hatti ben El Melek Abou Gad El Madiani. The inhabitants of
Qatia give today to the region the name of country of Hateïn and country of Gofar. This Hateïn reigned over
Egypt after the death of his father. He was bellicose and violent and resided in a citadel of the mountains of
the Jordan near Tiberias. It is from him that takes its name the town of Hateïn, where one sees the tomb of
Sho'aib, in the vicinity of Safad.

[PDF p. 706]

CHAPTER LXV
OF THE TOWN OF EL RAQAH

This town is one of the localities of Madian, between the sea of Qolzoum and the mountain of El Tour. At the
epoch when Moses made the Israelites come out of Egypt, this town was inhabited by a tribe of Lakhm related to
Pharaoh and that adored the ox. It is to this people that God makes allusion, when he says: "And with the
Israelites we crossed the sea, and they arrived among a people who adore the idols" (Koran, VII, 134); all the
verse concerns them. This tribe of Lakhm, says Qotadah, inhabited El Raqah. They had, it is said, for idol a
statue of an ox; it is for this that the Samaritan produced for them a calf. The traces of this town subsist
still today in what one sees of Faran, of Qolzoum, of Madian, and of Aïlah, regions traversed by the nomads.

[PDF p. 707]

CHAPTER LXVI
OF 'AIN SHAMS

This town formerly was called Ra'msâs, and Aïn Shams was a temple where one went on pilgrimage from all the
points of the horizon; it was one of those ancient temples to which the pilgrims flocked. The Sabeans had
received these temples from 'Ad and Tamoud, according to some; from Seth, son of Adam, and from Hermes the
Ancient or Idris, according to others. This Idris was the first who treated of the supreme essence and of the
celestial movements and built temples to adore God there. One says that, in the times of old, there were
twelve temples: the temple of the First Cause, the temple of the Intelligence, the temple of the Government,
the temple of the Exterior Form, the temple of the Soul; these five temples were of circular form. The sixth
temple was that of Saturn, of hexagonal form; then came the temple of Jupiter of triangular form, that of Mars
of square form; the temple of the Sun, square equally; the temple of Venus, having the form of an elongated
triangle; the temple of Mercury in the form of a triangle and containing in the interior a rectangular
construction; finally the temple of the Moon, of octagonal form. The cult by the temples took a considerable
extension among the Sabeans. For, they claimed, as the Creator of the world is too holy to have been able to
be born, a human creature could not comprehend him, and consequently his adorers, to approach him, had to make
use of the intermediary of those who approached him the most -- that is, the genii who could intercede for
them and serve as mediators between them and the Divinity. By the genii, they understood the angels whom they
supposed charged with the direction of the 7 planets in their firmaments -- that is, in their temples; and
necessarily each spirit had a temple and each temple had a firmament; and between the spirit and the temple
there was a relation similar to that of the soul to the body; and of course there was relation between the
intermediary and the creatures on one part and the Creator on the other, in such a fashion that the creature
has only to turn toward the intermediary spirit to obtain from the Creator what it needs. In

[PDF p. 708]

consequence, they went to the temples where the planets reigned, recognized their emplacements in the
firmament, studied their risings and their settings, their influences nefarious or happy on the days, the
nights, the hours, the persons, the exterior forms, the climates, etc.; finally all that is taught in its
place in the books of astronomy. They named these seven planets "The Lords" and "The Gods," giving to the sun
the title of "God of the Gods" and of "Lord of the Lords"; it was it that distributed its light in the course
of the year where one finds clearly its trace. And they made sacrifices at the temples, offering their gifts
to the genii, so that in their turn these might offer them to the Creator, for they esteemed that the temples
were the bodies of the genii and that all that is offered to a person is offered thus to its soul. To each
planet they addressed their prayers during a day that they regarded as depending on this planet. Their prayers
were made at three determined moments of the day: the first at the rising of the sun, the second at the moment
when this star passes the middle of the sky, and the third at its setting. They invoked Saturn on Saturday,
Jupiter on Sunday, Mars on Monday, the Sun on Tuesday, Venus on Wednesday, Mercury on Thursday, and the Moon
on Friday. There existed, it is said, at Balkh a temple raised by the Himyarites to the Moon to rival the
Ka'bah. The Persians came there on pilgrimage and had hung it with silk. This temple was called Nou bahr. When
they had embraced the religion of the Magi, the Persians made of it a temple of fire whose overseer bore the
title of Barmak -- that is, Vali of Mecca. The function of Barmak continued until the grandfather of Khaled,
grandfather of Ga'far ben Yahia ben Khaled, who embraced Islamism into the hands of Hesham ben 'Abd el Melek
and took the name of Abd Allah. The temple was destroyed by Qeis ben El Heisham at the beginning of the
caliphate of Mo'awiah in the year 41 [7 May 661 to 25 April 662]. It was a colossal construction surrounded by
porticoes and 360 chambers where lodged the servants of the temple. There was formerly at Sanaa the palace of
Rhamdân, one of the monuments raised by El Dahak. It was a temple dedicated to the Moon and that was destroyed
under the caliphate of Othman ben 'Afan. In Spain, in the mountain of El Fareq that separates the peninsula
from the continent, existed a temple of Jupiter built by Cleopatra daughter of Ptolemy. At Farghanah, there
was a

[PDF p. 709]

[OF 'AIN SHAMS, continued]

monument called Colousan and that was a temple of the Sun built by one of the first kings of Persia; it was
destroyed by El Mo'tasem. One is not in agreement on the constructor of the temple of 'Aïn Shams; but I will
reunite on this temple a quantity of accounts that one finds gathered in no other book.

When, says Ibn Ouasif Shah, the king Menqâous mounted on horseback, one made before him the most astonishing
representations (spectacles); the crowd pressed to admire the execution of them. This king had built for
himself for prayer a particular temple, in which he placed a cupola containing the image of the sun and of the
planets, and which he surrounded with statues and marvelous objects. There he went on horseback and stayed for
seven days; he raised there two columns on which he inscribed the date of the construction, and these two
columns exist still at present; it is the place that one calls 'Aïn Shams. He had transported treasures,
talismans, drugs, and marvelous objects that he buried at 'Aïn Shams and in the surroundings. After a reign of
91 years, this king died of the plague according to some, of poison according to others; one dug him a tomb
in the desert of the Occident or, according to another version, to the Occident of Qous; one buried with him
books of science and of art, statues of gold, precious stones, a considerable quantity of coined gold. At the
same time one buried the statue of the genie of the Sun in brilliant gold with two wings of emeralds, and the
image of his wife: he loved her much and, when she died, he had her statue placed in all the temples. This
statue was of gold with two black tresses and bore a mantle of precious stones disposed with art; the woman
was represented seated on a throne, and the king had her placed before him everywhere he sat himself, to try
to console himself for her loss. This statue was buried with him and placed at his feet, as if it addressed
the word to him.

The virtuous sage Ahmed ben Khalifat, in his book entitled "Essences of the news regarding the categories of
medicines," reports this: Pythagoras, ardently desiring to unite himself with the priests who were in Egypt,
went to the people of the town of the Sun, called today 'Aïn Shams, who received him reluctantly and put him
long to the test without finding him either defect or insufficiency. They conducted him therefore to the
priests of Memphis who were to complete his examination; these received him also with repugnance and examined
him

[PDF p. 710]

minutely without finding anything to reproach him, nor catching him at fault; they sent him to the
inhabitants of Diosos to have him examined. But these last could not catch him at fault nor refute his
arguments. They imposed on him difficult tests, so that he could not realize them and that they might succeed
thus in setting him aside and rejecting him, in imposing on him tests different from the Greek tests.
Pythagoras accepted and executed them. The priests had for him a great veneration and the rumor of the piety
of Pythagoras spread in Egypt and reached the king Amasis. This prince accorded him a right on the tariffs of
the sacrifices made to the gods as well as on all the offerings, which was forbidden to foreigners. It is
reported that the seven planets had temples where one came on pilgrimage from all points of the earth; these
temples had been raised by the workers who had edified for each planet a temple in one of the regions of the
world. One thought that the first temple was the Kaaba, of which the pilgrimage was prescribed by Idris whom
the Egyptians name Hermes the Ancient, the Trismegistus. This temple, one believes, was dedicated to Saturn.
The second temple was that of Mars, raised at Tyre on the coast of Syria. The third, raised to Jupiter, had
been constructed at Damascus by Giroun ben Sa'd ben 'Ad; it is on its emplacement that rises today the mosque
of the Umayyads. The fourth temple, that of the Sun, was in Egypt; it was, it is said, one of the monuments
constructed by Harshik, one of the kings of the first Persian dynasty; this temple is the one that one calls
'Aïn Shams. The fifth temple, raised to Venus, was at Mantih; the sixth, that of Mercury, was at Saïda on the
coast of Syria; the seventh finally, that of the Moon, was at Harran, of which it is, it is said, the Citadel
and that one calls the circular; it remained standing until the arrival of the Tatars, who overturned it; it
was, as one claims, the greatest temple of the Sabeans.

Shafé ben Aly, in his book entitled "Marvels of the countries," says that 'Aïn Shams is a small town of which
the wall of enclosure, half ruined, is still seen; one recognizes clearly that it was a temple of adoration
where were terrible idols of monstrous form carved in the stone; each statue was thirty cubits high and the
body was carved proportionally to this colossal height. All these statues were raised on pedestals, of which
some of a marvelous plan and admirable dispositions. The gate of the town

[PDF p. 711]

is seen still today. On these immense stones are drawn figures of men and animals and engraved numerous texts,
in unknown characters. One does not meet a single stone that does not bear either writing or a drawing. In
this town are the two well-known obelisks that one calls the obelisks of the Pharaoh. The obelisk reposes on a
pedestal of square form of a vertical section of 10 square cubits and of about 10 cubits in width; this
vertical base is posed on foundations solidly established in the soil, supports in its turn a triangular (?)
and conical column measuring more than a hundred cubits in height, of a diameter of five cubits at the base
and terminating in a point. The summit was covered with a chaperon of copper of a height of about three cubits
in the form of a funnel; but it has been oxidized by the rains and the duration of the ages; it has become
green, and this color has run on the faces of the obelisk. These faces are covered with writings in unknown
characters. The two obelisks were formerly standing, but one of them has fallen and has been broken in two
because of its enormous weight; one has taken the copper of the summit. Around were innumerable statues whose
height reached or nearly the half of the height of the obelisk. Rarely, among these small obelisks, does one
meet some that are of a single piece. They are on the contrary formed of superposed courses. Most have been
destroyed, and there remains of them only the pedestal.

Mohammed ben Ibrahim El Gazari reports, in his History, that the 4th of Ramadan of the year 656 [4 September
1258] one of the obelisks of the Pharaoh of the district of Matarieh in the surroundings of Cairo fell, and
one found in the interior 200 qantars of copper, and from the cap of the summit one withdrew 10,000 dinars.

One says that 'Aïn Shams was built by El Oualid ben Douma, one of the Amalecite kings; according to others the
foundation of it would be due to El Rian ben El Oualid, of whom it was the capital. The Persians claim that
its founder was Harshik.

The height of the two columns is, according to certain authors, 100 cubits, according to others, 84 or even
50; one claims that it was Bokht Nasar (Nebuchadnezzar) who destroyed Heliopolis, at the time of his entry
into Egypt. 'Aïn

[PDF p. 712]

Shams, says El Qoda'i, is the temple of the Sun, where rise the two columns so marvelous that one has never
seen anything more beautiful, nor even anything that approaches it. They are about 50 cubits high and are
posed on the surface of the soil. Between the two of them stands the statue of a man mounted on a courser.
They are terminated by two points of copper. When the Nile rises, one sees distinctly the water seep drop by
drop from their summit, descend until it flows in moving away from their foot; at their base grow brambles and
other plants. At the moment when the sun penetrates the first minute of the sign of Capricorn -- that is, the
shortest day of the year -- this star reaches the most southern of the two obelisks and culminates at its
summit; when it reaches the first minute of the sign of Cancer -- that is, the longest day of the year -- it
reaches the northern obelisk and culminates at its summit. These two obelisks form therefore the two extreme
points of the solar balancing, and the line of the equator (sic) passes exactly between the two of them. The
going and coming of the year is therefore comprised between these two obelisks; it is at least what the
competent scholars say.

Ibn Sa'id, in the work entitled "The Occident," asserts that in antiquity 'Aïn Shams was a town very long and
very wide, and that extended to the constructions of ancient Masr, there where is today Fostat. During his
expedition, 'Amr ben El 'As had stopped at 'Aïn Shams and, thanks to the army he had gathered, seized it.

The compiler of the History of the Toulounides reports that there was at 'Aïn Shams a statue tall as a man of
medium stature, in white stone of Keddan (limestone) and of a perfect workmanship; it seemed to whoever saw it
endowed with speech. One spoke of it to Ahmed ben Touloun, who was desirous to see it at leisure; but
Nadoussah attempted to prevent him from it and said to him: "Never has a vali seen it without having been
overturned." He went there nevertheless on horseback. It was in the year 258 [18 November 871 to 6 November
872]; he examined it, then returned to give the order to the stone-cutters to remove it from the earth and to
leave no trace of it, then he said to Nadoussah, his treasurer: "O Nadoussah, who, of the statue or of me, has
overturned the master?" "It is you, O emir," answered Nadoussah. And Ahmed lived still 12 years as emir.

[PDF p. 713]

El 'Aziz billah Nezar ben El Mo'ezz constructed palaces at Aïn Shams. Aïn Shams, says Abou 'Obeïd Bakri, is a
source of water well known. 'Aïn Shams, says Mohammed ben Habib, is where Pharaoh built the citadel. The
people are of the opinion that 'Aïn Shams owes its name to this water, and the first who gave it this name was
Seba ben Yashgeb. According to El Kalbi, Shams is the name of an antique idol. The two columns of 'Aïn Shams in
Egypt, says Ibn Khardadabeh, are the remains of the columns that were there. At their summit was a cap of
copper; one of these columns let seep from under this cap a water that flowed slowly to the middle of the
column without passing it, and this stillation interrupted itself neither night nor day. The trace of the
water on the column is of a humid green, but does not extend to the soil. It is one of the monuments raised by
Aushenk.

Mohammed ben Abd el Rahim, in his book entitled "Gift to the spirits," says: These minarets are square and a
hundred cubits high and of a single piece sharpened at the summit and posed on a pedestal of stone. On the
summit of these minarets is an envelope of copper similar to gold, where is the image of a man seated on a
throne turned toward the Orient. From this envelope of copper escapes a thread of water that descends to ten
cubits (from the summit) and that makes grow some herbs, such as the talhab. This water shows itself in all
times, summer and winter, and nothing of it descends to the soil. At 'Aïn Shams grows a sort of plant, the
balsam, from which one draws the oil of balsam and that grows only in this place. One employs for this the
bark of this plant. It has a certain savor hot and pungent very agreeable. In the region of Matarieh, in the
vicinity of 'Aïn Shams, grows the balsam, a sort of small shrub watered by the water of a well that is in the
region. This well is held in great consideration by the Christians, who go to wash themselves there and to ask
for healing. The harvest is made at the wished moment by employees whom the sultan designates. One keeps it to
carry it to the magazines of the sultan whence one sends it to the citadels of Syria and into the hospitals to
heal the feverish. It is impossible to procure any elsewhere than at the royal magazines and with a special
permission. The Christian kings -- Abyssinian, Greek, and Frankish -- prized it

[PDF p. 714]

[OF 'AIN SHAMS, continued]

at a very high price and made presents to the king of Egypt to obtain some of it, and they esteemed that no
one among them was truly Christian if this balsam was not mixed with the water of baptism, and believed firmly
that one had to add to the water of baptism a little of the essence of balsam that they named miroun. In
antiquity, when a piece of news came from Syria, it arrived first to the master of 'Aïn Shams, then from there
set out again for the citadel that one named Qasr El Shama', there where is now the town of Masr, from the
citadel to Memphis, capital of the kingdom. The cause of the veneration of the Christians for the essence of
balsam is exposed in the Synaxar, the book that contains the accounts of the Christians. When Mary and Joseph
the carpenter left Jerusalem to flee Herod, king of the Jews, the first town of Egypt where they stopped was
Bosta. It was the 24th of Bachans. The inhabitants refusing to receive them, they had to establish themselves
outside the town and stayed there a long time, then they directed themselves toward Samanoud where they
crossed the Nile, and, arrived on the western bank, took the direction of Ashmounein. On the culminating point
of the town rose then an image of copper representing a horse posed on four columns and that neighed when
another approached it, and the inhabitants ran to see which were the strangers who arrived; and when Mary
arrived with the Messiah near the town, the copper horse fell and broke into pieces. The mother having entered
with the child, a prodigy manifested itself at Ashmouneïn: five loaded camels obstructing their passage, the
Messiah invoked (God) against them at Ashmouneïn and the animals were changed into stones. From there, the
travelers set out and stopped a long time in a village named Files which they left then to go to the town of
Qos and Qâm, today El Qoussiah. The demon spoke by the mouth of the idols of the town and announced to the
inhabitants that a woman had come with her child to destroy the temple of their gods. About a hundred men came
out in arms to repel the travelers, who withdrew toward Mirah, to the west of El Qoussiah, and stopped at the
place called today Deïr el Moharraq, where they remained six months and some days. There, Joseph had a dream
and heard someone who announced to him the death of Herod and ordered him to return to Jerusalem with the
Messiah. They left therefore Mirah and, arrived at the place named today Qasr El Shama, in the town of Masr,
stopped in a grotto that

[PDF p. 715]

bears now the name of Church of Bou Sergah (Saint Serge) and went from there to 'Aïn Shams. They made a halt
in this place near a fountain where Mary washed the garments of the Messiah. After having wrung the linens,
she spread them on the soil, where God made grow the balsam that grew then in the Jordan, whence it
disappeared to be found no more than on this territory, and the well that one sees there today filled itself
with the water of which Mary had made use to wash the garments of the Messiah. And one has recounted to me
that even today still, if one looks closely there, the water of this well is formed by a source that springs
in its depths. Such is the cause of the veneration that the Christians have for this well and for the balsam
that is brought only by this water. And God is the most knowing.

[PDF p. 716]

CHAPTER LXVII
EL MANSOURAH

This locality is situated at the point of the branch of Ashmoum, facing the district of Talkha. It was founded
by the sultan El Kamel Nasr el din Mohammed ben El Melek El 'Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub in the year 616 [19
March 1219 to 7 March 1220], at the epoch when the Franks had made themselves masters of Damietta. The sultan,
having made a halt in this place, planted there his tents, built there a palace, and ordered all those who
were with him, emirs and soldiers, to construct; and one edified numerous houses, one established there
markets, the whole was protected on the side of the river by a wall that one garnished with war-machines and
shelters; the new town was named El Mansourah. The sultan resided there until the retaking of Damietta, as we
have said above in the chapter of this book that treats of the town of Damietta. El Mansourah became a
considerable town with baths, hostelries, and markets. El Melek el Kamel having retaken Damietta from the
Franks, these having departed for their country, the sultan held session in his palace of Mansourah with his
brothers El Melek El Mo'azem 'Eïsa, prince of Damascus, and El Melek El Ashraf Mousa, prince of the countries
of the Orient, and other personages of his family and of his house. On an order given by El Melek El Ashraf to
one of his slaves, she set about singing to her lute:

[verses:] When Pharaoh and his people, filled with pride, came toward Egypt to devastate the land, Mousa
(Moses) advanced toward them, a staff in his hand, and drowned them in the sea, one on top of another.

El Ashraf, transported with joy, cried: "In the name of God, repeat," but this displeased El Melek El Kamel
who imposed silence on him and said to his slave: "Sing, you." And she, having taken her lute, sang:

[verses:] O sectaries of an impious religion, rise up and look at what has happened and has renewed itself in
our time.

[PDF p. 717]

[verses:] Servants of Eisa (Jesus), Eisa and his partisans, and Mousa (Moses), all have carried rescue to
Mohammed.

This distich is drawn from the Qasidah of Sharaf el din ben Habarah, which begins thus:

[verses:] My love permits me only to keep vigil.

El Melek El Kamel, full of admiration, had given to the two slaves 500 dinars. The cadi, the most illustrious
chief, the chief Habbah Allah ben Mohassen, cadi of Gaza, who was among the assistants, rose standing and set
about reciting:

[verses:] Be happy, for the happiness has come to stay always. The Clement has accomplished his promise of
victory. The Creator has accorded us a victory brilliant, and has filled us with benefits and with an eternal
glory. The face of the earth, before morose, sets itself again to smile, and the visage of the impious has
been rendered black by their crimes. The sea was swollen by the great number of infidels it carried, and the
waves broke foaming against their ships. There rose then for our religion a man who handled it as one handles
a cutting sword. There remained on the field of battle only the bodies cut by the sword, or the prisoners with
bound hands. The Creation entire cried out, raising the voice on the two faces of the Universe and singing:
Servants of Eisa (Jesus), Eisa and his partisans, and Mousa (Moses), all have carried rescue to Mohammed.

This night, passed at Mansourah, was one of the most beautiful that ever a king passed. In reciting these
verses, the cadi Habbah Allah, in pronouncing the name of Eïsa, designated with his finger Eisa El Mo'azem, in
pronouncing the name of Mousa, he designated Mousa El Ashraf, and in pronouncing the name of Mohammed, he
designated the sultan El Melek El Kamel. According to another version, the one who recited these verses was
Rageh El Mohali, the poet.

[PDF p. 718]

CHAPTER LXVIII
EL 'ABBASSAH

This locality is situated between Balbeïs and Salahieh in the country of Sedir. It was always a place of
pleasure for the kings. It is there that was born El Abbas ben Ahmed ben Touloun, it is for this that his
father gave him this name; it is there also that was born El Melek El Amgad Taqi el din 'Abbas ben El 'Adel
Abou Bekr ben Ayoub. El Melek El Kamel Mohammed ben Adel sojourned there much. "This land," he said, "is
preferable to Masr; when I reside there I can hunt there the birds of the sky, the fish of the waters, the
beasts of the plains. From the citadel of the mountain one brings me the bread to my residence, and it is
still hot." He had constructed there a palace, belvederes, gardens; his emirs built there also quantity of
houses in the gardens. 'Abbassah remained thus until the moment when El Melek El Saleh Negm el din Ayoub ben
El Kamel raised his residence of Salahieh; from then on 'Abbassah was neglected; its belvederes were destroyed
under the reign of El Melek El Mo'ezz Aïbek. And when arrived the reign of El Melek El Zaher Rokn El din
Bïebars, this prince, passing at Sedir at the mouth of the valley, was marveled at it and had built in a
chosen place a village that he named Zaherieh; he founded there a mosque, and that, in the year 666 [22
September 1267 to 10 September 1268].

This town takes its name from Abbassah, daughter of Ahmed ben Touloun, for this princess went to this place to
make her farewells to her niece Qotr el Nada, daughter of Khamaraouyah ben Ahmed ben Touloun, at the epoch when
the latter was sent to the caliph Mo'taded. There, 'Abbassah planted her tents, constructed a village, and
gave it her name.

[PDF p. 719]

CHAPTER LXIX
OF THE TOWN OF QOFT IN THE SAID OF EGYPT

This town owes its name to Qaftarim ben Qobtim ben Misraïm ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh. It was formerly an
(important) town of the climes, but it began to decline after the year 400 of the Hijra of the Prophet [25
August 1019 to 15 August 1020]. After the year 700 of the Hijra [19 September 1300 to 5 September 1301], there
remained of it no more than forty sugar-works and six presses for canes. There, it is said, the houses were
surmounted by cupolas, and the inhabitants who possessed (at least) ten thousand dinars were recognized by the
cupola that surmounted their house. In the vicinity of Qoft are quarries of emeralds that have been abandoned
only since a short time. Qaftarim took the power after his father Qobtim. He was, says Ibn Ouacif Shah, the
eldest and the most cherished of the children of his father. He was bold, and of great stature, and it is he
who threw the foundations of the pyramids of Dahchour and elsewhere. He built also the town of Dendérah and
the town of the Idols. At the end of his reign, 'Ad was destroyed by the wind. He obtained in the mines more
metals than any of his predecessors. He had extracted ingots of gold as big as the millstones, emeralds
enormous as pillars, and in the desert of the Occident blocks of ceruse big as donjons. He made a quantity of
marvelous things. He raised on the mountain of Qoft a tower from which one saw the Eastern sea, and he
discovered in this same mountain mines of mercury of which he made statues tall as mountains that did not
disaggregate nor liquefy. He had also dug the pond that one calls Siadat El Teïr (the hunter of birds): if a
bird passed above this pond, it fell into it and could not budge until one had taken it. This pond, it is
said, exists still today. As for the tower, it has collapsed. The king had executed numerous marvels, and it
is from his time that began the cult of the idols that were drowned by the Flood and that the demon had, by
perfidy, made adored by the peoples. This prince, it is said, founded also the towns of

[PDF p. 720]

the interior and placed there marvelous objects; to the west of the Nile, beyond the oases of the interior, he
built towns that he provided with numerous marvels to which were attached protecting genii; no one could
approach these towns nor enter there without first making his offering to these spirits. Qaftarim reigned 480
years, and the greatest part of the marvelous objects were executed by him and by his son Boudsir. Thus the
Said possessed more marvels than the Delta; Qaftarim resided there. When death approached, the prince had made
for himself a naos in the western mountain, near the town of the priests, in a subterranean corridor backed on
vaults descending to the soil. He carved in the mountain a vast palace surrounded by niches hollowed in the
wall; he reserved in the ceiling a corridor for the passage of the air, and he had the soil and the rest of
the edifice paved with marble. In the middle of the chamber, he had raised a bench posed on eight feet and
covered with fused crystal of diverse colors; in the ceiling were placed luminous stones and at each angle of
the bench statues of gold holding in hand trumpets into which they blew. Under the cupola, another bench
plated with gold and mounted with emeralds; on the bench a bed of silk where his body was placed after having
been coated with preservative aromatics. Near him were deposited the censers of camphor, and the body was
clothed in robes lamé with gold, the face remaining uncovered. He was crowned with the royal crown, and near
the bench stood four statues of hollow glass representing women provided with fans of gold. On his chest, and
over the garments, was deposited a precious sword with a hilt of emerald. One deposited in the magazines the
treasures of the king, ingots of gold, crowns, precious stones, hieroglyphs treating of the sciences, and all
sorts of drugs and talismans, and books of science in innumerable quantity. On the door one fixed a cock of
gold perched on a pedestal of green glass, the wings extended; on this cock were engraved preservative
formulas. At the entrance of each of the vaults one had raised two statues of copper holding in hand swords
and the feet posed on flagstones under which was hidden a mechanism. Whoever approached these statues was
struck by their swords and died. At the ceiling of each vault was suspended a ball coated with a prepared
unguent that remained luminous indefinitely. The door of the vaults was closed by blocks of lead; above were
deposited enormous flagstones, and the interstices were filled with sand. At the door of the corridor one
wrote: "This is

[PDF p. 721]

the entrance that leads to the body of the superb, redoubted, generous, and vigorous king Qaftarim, endowed
with valiance and with power, with force and with victory. His star has eclipsed itself, but his memory and
his souvenir have remained. And no one will be able to penetrate to him nor reach by any means before there
have been accomplished seven hundred seventy revolutions of years."

The mine of emerald, says El Masa'oudi, is found in the upper Said, in the district of Qoft. It is from this
town that one goes to the mine, which is situated at the place that bears the name of El Kharbah, an ensemble
