of valleys and of mountains. The Bedjahs are charged with the guard of El Kharbah. They serve, by means of a
salary, as escort to those who wish to go to dig the soil to find emeralds. Experienced people of the Said who
had frequented this mine and knew well this sort of stone claim that it is either more abundant or more rare
according to the seasons of the year; it is more abundant when the state of the air is firmer and more stable
and when blows a certain one of the four winds; the green color of the stone becomes more frank and its
brilliance more luminous in the first days of the month; this brilliance reaches its maximum at the moment of
the full moon. Between El Kharbah, there where is found the mine of emeralds, and the nearest inhabited
locality, there are seven days' march. These localities are Qoft, Qous, and other towns of the Said. Qous is
situated on the bank of the Nile; as for Qoft, it is distant from the river by about two miles.

There are on the two towns of Qoft and of Qous marvelous accounts that treat of their foundation. In the
Chronicles of the Copts, one recounts that already at this epoch Qoft began to decline, while Qous was more
prosperous and more peopled. There was at Qoft a temple placed under the guard of a genie in the form of a
young black girl carrying a small black child; one affirms even having seen her several times. The mine of
emerald was situated on the shore of the Nile where is found also Assouan; there was for this mine a special
divan with employees and accountants. This divan pays the workers who work there as well as the expenses
necessitated for the excavations and the extraction of the emerald. This mine is found in sandy mountains: the
sand in which one digs has many times collapsed, killing a certain number of workers. After having gathered
the product of the mine, one dispatched it to Fostat, whence one dispatched it into all the countries. The
people put eight days of average march to go from Qous to the mine of emerald;

[PDF p. 722]

all around and in proximity resided the Bedjahs who were held to watch over and guard the mines. These are
situated in a mountain that runs to the east of the Nile, to the north of an enormous massif that forms part
of this mountain and that one names Aqarshandat; there is not in the region a higher mountain. The mine is in
a part of the territory where is found no dwelling; the place itself and its surroundings are absolutely
deserted. The water itself is at more than a half-day's march; this water is furnished only by the rains and
deposits itself in a sort of pool that augments when the rains are strong and diminishes when they are weak.
The mine is in the middle of a long gorge formed of a white stone, from which one extracts the emerald. This
white stone is of three sorts: the talk of camphor, the talk of silver, and the geraoui stone. One strikes on
this stone until comes out the emerald that is there as if drowned. There are several species of emeralds:
one, the riani emerald, is little abundant and is found only rarely. As soon as it is extracted, one throws it
into hot oil, then one puts it into cotton, and one envelops the whole in a piece of rag or of any stuff
whatsoever. The surveillance exercised in these mines is very severe; the workers are examined each day at the
exit, and the most secret parts of their body do not escape the examination. Despite this, they succeed, by
means of their own, in stealing some stones. One continued to extract emeralds from this mine until the moment
when the vizier El Saheb 'Alam el din 'Abd Allah ben Zanbour suspended the works there, in the time of El
Melek El Naser Hassan ben Mohammed ben Qalaoun, in the year 760 [3 December 1358 to 22 November 1359] and some.

In the year 572 [10 July 1176 to 29 June 1177], there was at Qoft a great uprising: a missionary (da'i) of the
tribe of the Benou Abd El Qaoui, having passed himself off as Daoud ben El 'Adhed (the last Fatimid caliph),
had gathered around him a crowd of people. The sultan Salah el din Youssef ben Ayoub sent a troop on the
orders of his brother El Melek El 'Adel Abou Bekr ben Ayoub who made perish nearly 3,000 inhabitants of Qoft;
they were hanged from the trees outside the town, by means of their turbans and their robes.

[PDF p. 723]

CHAPTER LXX
OF THE TOWN OF DENDERAH

It is one of the antique towns of the upper Said, built by Qaftarim ben Misraïm ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh.
There was found there a magnificent temple provided with a hundred eighty windows through each of which
entered each day the sun until it had arrived at the last; from there it retrograded to its point of
departure. The spirit that watched over this temple appeared in the form of a man with a lion's head and two
horns. There was there also a tree that one called "the tree of Abbas." This tree, of ordinary size, had green
and round leaves. If, in passing near it, someone said: "O tree of Abbas, the axe comes on you," its leaves
folded back and faded at once and returned then to their primitive state. Between Denderah and Qous, there is
the distance of a barid. The temple of Denderah was more beautiful than that of Akhmim.

[PDF p. 724]

CHAPTER LXXI
OF THE OASES OF THE INTERIOR

The oases are separated lands situated in the Southwest; they form part of no vilayet nor of any province, and
no vali administers them on behalf of the Sultan; he who administers them does it for the account of the one
who has received them in fief.

The region of the oases is comprised between Masr, Alexandria, the Said, Nubia, and Ethiopia; the oases are
situated one behind the other. They form a country living by itself, without being linked to any other and
without having need of any other. It is a land abundant in alum, in vitriol, in acid springs whose water is
employed like vinegar, in springs whose taste presents at once a savor acid, astringent, and salty. Each of
these waters has its special utility. One divides these oases into two categories: the oases of the interior
and the oases of the exterior, the whole forming four oases. They saw born, it is said, Haouil ben Koush ben
Kana'an ben Ham ben Nouh; then came Seba ben Koush, the father of the Abyssinians; Abou Shanba ben Koush, the
father of the Zaghaouah; and Abou Shefabiah ben Koush, the father of the Ramram Abyssinians.

One recounts, says Ibn Ouacif Shah, that Qaftarim constructed the towns of the interior and did there
marvelous things, among others, a water that held itself standing in the form of a column without
disaggregating nor flowing; from him also is the pond named Falesthin -- that is, the taker of birds; indeed,
if a bird passed above this pond, it fell into it and could no longer come out until one came to take it. He
made also a column of stone surmounted by the image of a bird; if lions, serpents, or other malevolent beasts
approached the town, the bird pushed a strident whistle that put these beasts to flight. At the four gates of
this town, he had raised four statues of copper of which a stranger could not approach without being seized
with a profound sleep; he fell asleep near the statue and could awaken only if the people of the town came to
blow on his face to

[PDF p. 725]

recall him to himself. If they neglected to do it, the sleeper continued his sleep near the statue, and ended
it only at death. This same prince constructed an elegant turret of colored glass, posed on a pedestal of
copper and surmounted by a statue made of a great number of mixed substances and holding in hand a bow from
which it seemed to launch arrows. If a stranger carried his eyes on the statue, he remained fixed in his place
until the people of the town came to him. This statue placed itself by itself in the direction of the four
winds. It is there still today, it is said, but one abstains from going to this town, despite the considerable
quantity of treasures and marvels that one meets there, for fear of this statue, for one dreads to let one's
eyes fall on it. It remained standing until it destroyed itself. A certain king wished to throw it down, but
he could not succeed, and in this attempt, a great number of people perished. One recounts that Qaftarim
raised in one of the towns of the interior a mirror where one could see all that one asked of it; he built
also to the west of the Nile and beyond the oases of the interior, towns where he executed numerous marvels;
he charged with watching over them spirits that defended the approach of them, and no one could either
approach or enter there without having first carried offerings to these spirits. One can still go today to
this town, and one takes there what one wishes of the treasures without obstacle and without difficulty. The
king Sa ben El Sad, or, according to others, Sa ben Marqounos, had constructed, in the interior of the oases,
a town that he had surrounded with plantations of numerous palms. This king resided at Memphis and reigned
over all the provinces; he made marvelous objects and talismans, and rendered to the priests their rank,
chased the people of vice and of debauchery who had been the companions of El Sad ben Marqounos. He posted at
the extreme points of Egypt messengers charged with informing him of what happened at their frontiers, and he
had raised, to the west of the Nile, towers on which one lit fires if something occurred or if someone
advanced from this side. When he was master of his country entire, he gathered around him the sages, and
examined the stars, an art in which he was very skilled. He saw there that his country would be infallibly
drowned by the overflowing of its Nile and that it would be ruined by a man who would come from the side of
Syria. He gathered therefore all the workers of Egypt and had built, in the extreme oasis, a town whose
rampart reached fifty cubits in height, and he gathered there the sciences and the riches. It is this town
that Mousa

[PDF p. 726]

ben Nouseïr met, in the time of the Umayyads, when he came from the Magreb; when he penetrated into Egypt, he
sought to find the extreme oasis of which he had heard speak; he remained seven days wandering in the sands,
between the West and the South; finally a town appeared to him provided with a rampart and gates of iron. It
was impossible for him to open the gates; some men, having mounted on the ramparts, had no sooner looked at
the interior of the town than they threw themselves into it. Not being able to come to the end of the mystery
of this town, Mousa passed on after having lost a great number of his companions. In this desert, many people
had houses of pleasure, marvelous villas, and treasures; but all that has been covered by the sands, although
all the kings strove to construct, against the sand, talismans whose virtue has obliterated itself with time.
No one could fail to recognize the enormous quantity of the constructions of these peoples, or of their towns,
or of all the magnificent monuments they founded, for this people had a boldness that no other has had. And
traces of it are still manifest, like the pyramids, the stelae, Alexandria, the vestiges that one meets in the
desert of the Orient, the mountains they hollowed to deposit their treasures there, the valleys cut by the
hand of man, and all that one can see in the Said in the way of temples, and all that they engraved in
testimony of their science. Let one say to all the kings of the earth to construct two monuments similar to
the two pyramids, they will not arrive at it; similarly, were they to wish to engrave a temple, the time would
flow, and they could not succeed at it.

One recounts that a troop of masons of the village of the West, to escape the vexations of one of their
governors, had taken refuge, with provisions, in the desert of the West, until, their affair being arranged,
they could return. Now, after the first day's march and a part of the second, they had directed themselves
toward the foot of a mountain and had found there a domestic ass that had come out of a path. One of them
followed it and ended at dwellings with trees, palms, and running waters. There, men guarded herds and had
their dwellings. He spoke to them and was surprised at what he heard; he went to seek his companions and with
them returned to these people who interrogated them on their situation. They informed them and stayed with
them until their affairs were arranged. They set out then to go seek their families and their herds and to
return to install themselves among the unknown people. But they had much marched

[PDF p. 727]

a very long time, they could not find again the road nor return to the town glimpsed, which they bitterly
repented having left.

Others, having strayed from their route on the side of the Occident, fell on a flourishing town, abounding in
population, in herds, in palms, and in diverse trees. One gave them hospitality there, one had them eat and
drink, and they passed the night in a mill where they got drunk and fell asleep; they awoke only in the ardor
of the sun, and they found themselves in a town ruined and deserted. All thinned out, they set out and marched
all the day until the evening: another town appeared to them, larger, more prosperous than the first, richer
in population, in trees, and in herds. They conversed with the inhabitants and recounted to them the history
of the first town; the inhabitants set about exclaiming and laughing at them, then they led them to a meal at
the home of one of the inhabitants of the town. They ate, drank, and passed thus the time until they were
drunk. The next day, on awakening, they found themselves in an immense town, without any inhabitant and
surrounded by palms whose fruits had fallen and piled up. They came out, the breath charged with the odor of
the drinks and the reek of the wines; all the day they marched, and in the evening, of a shepherd who pastured
his ewes, they asked their route, and on his indications, they marched during a part of the day of the next
day and arrived at the town of Ashmounein in the Said.

The towns of these peoples are the ancient towns of the interior of which the Genii have made themselves
masters. Among them, there are some that are veiled to the eyes and that no one can see. One says that in the
time of El Boudair ben Qaftarim ben Qobtim ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh one raised, in the western desert,
towers and places of pleasure where this prince sent a crowd of people of his house who peopled the region and
multiplied to such a point that all the country was inhabited. They remained thus a long time. Then the
Berbers mingled with them by marriages. Later, there was misunderstanding; there were between them wars during
which these regions were ruined; the population disappeared, except some points that one calls the oases.

[PDF p. 728]

CHAPTER LXXII
OF THE TOWN OF SANTARIAH

The town of Santariah forms part of the Oases and was built by Minaqioush, the constructor of the town of
Akhmim, one of the ancient kings of the Copts. He had, says Ibn Ouacif Shah, the resolution and the firmness
of his father and was admired by the Egyptians. It was he who, the first, constructed riding-grounds (manèges)
and who ordered his companions to exercise themselves there. The first, he constructed a hospital for the
people stricken with acute and chronic afflictions: he provided it with remedies and with physicians whom he
paid largely, and placed there administrators. He established for himself a feast in which the people gathered
near him; he called it the "feast of the king": it took place on a certain day of the year; one ate and drank
for seven days, and the king watched, seated on a throne posed on columns, clothed in collars of gold and in
garments magnificent and brocaded with gold. Above the king rose a cupola plated in the interior with marble,
with glass, and with gold. It is in the time of this king that was built Santariah in the desert of the Oases.
He made it of white square stones; in each wall opened a gate from which set out a boulevard leading to the
opposite wall. Each boulevard to the right and to the left was provided with gates giving on streets leading
to the middle of the town. There extended a circus around which ran seven rows of tiers, surmounted by a
cupola of varnished wood reposing on magnificent columns of marble. In the middle of the circus rose a tower
of marble surmounted by a statue of black granite that turned at the same time as the sun. On all sides under
the cupola were suspended statuettes that whistled and spoke in different languages. The king took place on the
highest tier of the circus, having near him his sons, his relatives, and the princes; on the second tier sat
the chiefs of the priests and the viziers; on the third, the chiefs of the army; on the fourth, the
philosophers, the astronomers, the physicians, and the masters of science; on the fifth, the architects; on
the sixth, the chiefs of corporation, and on the seventh, the crowd. And each of the categories had for
instruction to

[PDF p. 729]

[OF THE TOWN OF SANTARIAH, continued]

look at those who were below it and not those who were above it, for never would it manage to equal them" --
and that is the best line of conduct. The wife of Minaqioush killed him with a blow of knife, and he died
after a reign of sixty years. Today Santariah is a very small country where dwell barely six hundred persons
originating from the cultivated lands: one calls them Syouah; their dialect is the Syouy which approaches that
of Zenata. One sees there orchards of palms, of fig-trees, of olive-trees, and other trees; the vines abound
there. There are there today nearly twenty springs that spread their sweet waters on the soil. From Santariah
to Alexandria, the distance is eleven days; it is fourteen from Santariah to Ghizeh-Misr. The inhabitants are
frequently stricken with the fever. The fruits of the country are excellent. The genii (djinns) afflict the
population of this village; whoever is isolated is carried off by them. One hears there distinctly the whistle
of the Djinns.

[PDF p. 730]

CHAPTER LXXIII
OF THE OASES OF THE EXTERIOR

They were constructed by one of the first kings of the Copts, named El Boudsir ben Qoftim ben Qobtim ben
Misraïm ben Beïsar ben Ham ben Nouh. "El Boudsir," says Ibn Ouacif Shah, "wished to go to the Occident, in
order to see what was found there; he fell on an immense territory furrowed with waters and with springs and
covered with herbage. He built there towers and houses of pleasure, and established there a great number of
people of his house who cultivated the region and built there so well that all the land of the Occident was
peopled. It remained thus a long time. Then came the Berbers who mingled with the inhabitants by marriages;
then burst forth the misunderstanding and the discord; wars came that ruined the country, and the population
disappeared, except on some points that one calls the Oases."

As for the countries of the Oases, says El Mas'oudi, they are situated between Masr, Alexandria, the Said of
Egypt, the Occident, and the land of the Ethiopians of Nubia, etc. There is found a land saturated with alum
and another saturated with vitriol, acid springs and others potable. The master of the Oases, in our epoch --
that is, in the year 332 [4 September 943 to 23 August 944] -- is Abd el Melek ben Merwan, of the tribe of the
Laouata, but of the Merwanite religious sect; he commands several thousand men who mount on horseback or on
camel. Between his country and that of the Ethiopians, there are about six days' march; it is also the
distance that separates it from all the inhabited places of which we have spoken. In his land are met things
particular and marvelous. This country subsists by itself, being linked to no other and having need of no
other. It produces dates, dried grapes (raisins), and jujubes.

The intendant of Abou-l Sherkh El Mo'ezz Hossam ed din 'Amr ben Mohammed ben Zenki El Shahrzouri recounted to
me having heard said, in the country of the Oases, that there was found there an orange-tree that produced in
a single

[PDF p. 731]

year fourteen thousand yellow fruits, without counting those that fell or remained green. But, added El
Shahrzouri, this seemed to me so extraordinary that I could not believe it, and I stayed in the country until
I had seen this tree: it was of the size of the greatest sycamore of Egypt, perhaps larger. I interrogated on
its subject the moustaufi (chief of the accounting) of the country, who, having had the registers of the
accounts brought, leafed through them and showed there the passage saying that, in such a year, such an
orange-tree had produced fourteen thousand ripe and yellow fruits, without counting what remained on the tree
of green ones and what had fallen from it, which was little.

At the Oases, the white alum is found in a valley that faces the town of Edfou. In the time of El Melek El
Kamel Mohammed ben El Adel Abou Bekr, and of his son El Saleh Negm el din Ayyoub, one brought each year from
the quarries of the Oases to Cairo a thousand qantars of white alum; in exchange, one exonerated the
inhabitants from the tax for the lands of the Oases; then this custom was less and less observed and ceased
completely.

In the year 339 [20 June 950 to 8 June 951], the king of Nubia advanced with a numerous army as far as the
Oases and fell unexpectedly on the inhabitants, of whom he killed and made prisoners a great number.

[PDF p. 732]

CHAPTER LXXIV
OF THE TOWN OF QOUS

Qous is the largest town of the Said; it is situated on the Nile. It was built after Qoft in the time of one
of the first Coptic kings named Sedan ben Adim ben El Boudsir ben Qaftarim; it took, it is said, its name from
Qous ben Qoft ben Akhmim ben Sifat ben Ashman ben Masr. Sedan ben Adim, reports Ibn Ouacif Shah, is the one
who built the pyramids of Dahchour with the stones cut in the time of his father. It is he who made the books
of the Nirandjâts (?) and the temple of Erment. He raised also a temple at Antinoé, a town of the interior;
he established his residence at Athrib and constructed a temple to the east of Alexandria. On the eastern bank
of the river, he founded towns. It is from his time that was built Qous, the elevated town, where was
installed a whole people of scholars and of artists. The Ethiopians and the Blacks having invaded the
country, he sent against them his son Minqaous at the head of a considerable army. He killed and took a
certain number of them and reduced to slavery those he had taken. This way of acting became for them a
traditional custom. He had opened the mines of gold of the country and charged his prisoners to work there and
to bring him the gold. He was the first who took a taste for the hunt, captured the animals of prey, and
obtained the race of the sloughi dogs by the crossing of wolves and domestic dogs. He executed talismans and
marvels of all sorts in incalculable number.

In his history of the Said, El Edfaoui says: Qous is neighbor to Qoft. A writer has recounted that Qous had
begun to prosper and that Qoft had begun to decline from the year 400 [25 August 1009 to 14 August 1010]. One
recounts that the Cadi of Qous, having gone to Assouan, four hundred cavaliers mounted on mules went to meet
him.

In the month of Ramadan of the year 662 [27 June to 26 July 1264] one brought to El Melek El Zahir Beïbars
small coins (fels) found at Qous where they were buried. One

[PDF p. 733]

examined one of them; on one face was the image of a king standing holding in the right hand a balance and in
the left a sword; on the other face a head with very long ears, the eye open; around the piece was an
inscription that a Greek monk read, and whose date on the day when it was deciphered went back two thousand
three hundred years. The sense of it was: "I, Ghaliath the king, I have the balance of justice and of
generosity in my right hand for those who obey, in my left hand the sword for the one who disobeys." On the
other face: "I, Ghaliath the king, my ear is open to hear the oppressed; my eye is open to watch over the good
state of my Empire." The scorpions and the great lizards abound at Qous; one meets there a species of scorpion
whose sting is mortal, to such a point that Qous is called "the pasture of the scorpions," for there is no
hope for whoever has been stung by a reptile. Once, on a summer day, there accumulated on the wall of the
mosque seventy great lizards in a single row. During the summer, if some inhabitant walks during the night
outside his house, he carries in one hand a lamp to light himself and in the other an iron spit to pierce the
scorpions.

From the year 800 [24 September 1397 to 12 September 1398] Qous has done nothing but decline; in 806 [21 July
1403 to 9 July 1404], at the epoch of the calamities and the scourges, there died at Qous seventeen thousand
persons. It was before so prosperous that at the epoch of the drought, in the year 776 [12 June 1374 to 1 June
1375], one had to abandon a hundred fifty parks, in the eastern part of the country. One calls there a "park"
a garden of twenty feddans at least, that possesses a saqiah with four channels of flow. And that without
counting a quantity of other gardens of a lesser extent that were also abandoned.

[PDF p. 734]

CHAPTER LXXV
OF THE TOWN OF ESNE

It is reported, says El Edfaoui, that one year this town produced forty thousand ardebs of dates, twelve
thousand ardebs of dried grapes (raisins). Esné is composed of about thirteen thousand houses; formerly, it is
said, there were there seventy boulevards.

[PDF p. 735]

CHAPTER LXXVI
OF THE TOWN OF EDFOU

The name of the town of Edfou is written sometimes with a d, sometimes with a t. El Edfaoui says: The perfect
preacher Abou Bekr, preacher of the town of Edfou, recounted to me that a palm projected three branches each
producing a single date; that he had pulled up this palm with the roots and had weighed it; the total weight
had risen to twenty-five dirhems, branches and trunk comprised; this tree was at Edfou. After the year 700 [16
September 1300 to 5 September 1301], brick-makers who were digging the soil brought to light a statue of stone
representing a woman seated on a throne and enveloped in a sort of net. On the back was a stele covered with
Greek writing. I saw it in this state in the town of Edfou.

[PDF p. 736]

CHAPTER LXXVII
OF THE TOWN OF AHNAS

It is one of the towns of the Said. One says that Jesus son of Mary was born there and that the palm of Mary
of which God speaks in this passage: "Shake the trunk of the palm, there will fall for you ripe dates" (Koran,
XIX, 25) continued to be seen there until the end of the dynasty of the Umayyads. But the general opinion is
that Jesus Christ was born at the borough of Bethlehem, a village depending on Jerusalem. At Ahnas, one finds
the Bang tree.

[PDF p. 737]

CHAPTER LXXVIII
OF THE TOWN OF EL BAHNASA

This town is situated to the west of the Nile; it is there that one fabricates the hangings named Bahnasyah,
that one weaves the stuffs with embroideries, the royal stuffs, the tents of great dimensions, and the robes
with white and black stripes. One fabricated there hangings of which a single piece measured thirty cubits
and of which the pair was worth two hundred methqals of gold. When one has fabricated there a curtain, a
carpet, or a robe of wool or of cotton, one always inscribes there the name of the one who is to receive the
object. It is a custom that has transmitted itself from age to age.

The Copts are in agreement to recognize that the Messiah and his mother Mary sojourned at Bahnasa, whence they
would have gone to Jerusalem.

According to a commentator of the Koran, in the passage relative to Jesus and to his mother: "We gave to them
both hospitality on a hill peaceful and abundant in springs" (Koran, XXIII, 52), the term of hill designates
Bahnasa. This town was built by a king of the Copts named Minaoush ben Minqâoush.

Here is what Ibn Ouacif Shah says of it: "Minaoush reigned in his turn and sought wisdom like his father. He
had its books brought to light, showed himself generous toward those who cultivate them, and filled them with
presents. He sought to attain the highest degree of perfection in the execution of marvelous objects; each of
their kings, moreover, had applied himself to make for himself things that none of his predecessors had made.
He affirmed himself in the knowledge of their books and had engraved on the stone their annals." Minaoush was
also the first, among the Egyptians, who adored the ox, here on what occasion: he had been stricken with a
sickness so grave that one despaired of him when, in a dream, he saw a gigantic genie who said to him: "You
will heal of your ill only if you consent to adore the ox; for the constellation that presided over your
horoscope is that of the bull with two horns." And Minaoush did what the genie asked; he had brought to him a

[PDF p. 738]

variegated bull of beautiful forms and had prepared for it in his palace a hall surmounted by a gilded cupola
and that one perfumed with incense. A special guardian was charged to keep himself near it, and to clean its
litter; and the king who came to adore it, unknown to his subjects, healed of his sickness. He was the first
who made use of chariots, and that during his sickness. These chariots were surmounted by houses with cupolas
of wood, and those of his servants and his women who desired it could do the same, and the ox dragged the
chariot from place to place and from one place of pleasure to another. When he arrived in an agreeable place,
the king stopped there, and each time he passed by some ruined place, he had it restored. One recounts that,
having seen that the bull that dragged his chariot was variegated and of an admirable form, he promised to
give it special cares and to make it walk before him, so much it pleased him; he had it covered with a
caparison of brocade. One day, finding himself in an isolated place, far from his slaves and his servants, he
approached the bull which remained standing; and behold, the animal spoke and said to him: "If the king
dispenses me from walking, puts me in a temple, and adores me, if he orders his subjects to adore me, I will
accomplish for him all he will exact; I will help him in his enterprises, I will render him strong in his
kingdom, and will set aside from him all calamity." The king, frightened, ordered that the bull be washed,
perfumed, placed in a temple, and that it be adored. Long was this bull thus adored. Marvelous thing! the
animal neither urinated nor dropped dung; it ate only the extremity of the green leaves of the reeds once a
month. It is this that confounded the spirit of the people. Such was the origin of the cult of the ox.
Menaoush constructed reduits where he buried treasures, and over which he raised stelae. In the desert of the
Occident, he built a town named Dîmas in which he raised a tower and buried around it the heroes. This town,
it is said, is still standing, and people who came from the Occident and had strayed have heard there the
whistle of the Djinns and have seen a brightness reflected there. In the [Egyptian] books one recounts that
this bull, which one adored since a long time, ordered them to execute its image in hollow gold, to gather
hairs of its head and of its tail and the powder of its horns and of its hoofs so that one might place them in
the statue; then it announced to them that it returned whence it had come, and prescribed them to place its
body in a sarcophagus of red stone and to bury it in the temple, raising its statue on the sarcophagus at the
moment when Saturn would be at its apogee and in opposition with the Sun in

[PDF p. 739]

[OF THE TOWN OF EL BAHNASA, continued]

the third quarter of the moon, while this star is in its greatest brilliance; one was to engrave again on the
statue the signs of the seven planets. One did thus, and the statue was adorned with all sorts of precious
stones, and in the place of the eyes, one put two enormous pearls. After having deposited it in the
sarcophagus, one planted a tree on its body in the temple; and one built a tower, eighty cubits high, that
during a week changed color each day to return every seven days to the first color. The temple was hung with
all sorts of hangings, and one brought a canal from the Nile to the temple. Around the sarcophagus one placed
talismanic statues with a monkey's head and a human body, each to set aside an evil and procure a good. At the
four gates of the temple were placed four idols, under each of which were buried all sorts of treasures; for
each statue one fixed offerings and incensings, and these statues were placed in the tree. The town was known
under the name of town of the Tree, and from this tree came all the species of trees. Minaoush is the first
who celebrated the Nourouz (New Year) in Egypt, and in his time was built Bahnasa. He raised there pillars
supporting a hall of yellow glass surmounted by a gilded cupola that, at the rising of the sun, sent back its
rays on the town. Minaoush reigned, it is said, over the Copts for 830 years, and was buried in one of the
small pyramids of the South, or, according to others, to the west of Ashmounein. With him were buried a great
quantity of silver, of precious stones, and of marvelous objects, the images (?) of the seven planets that
see the dead and the living (?), a thousand lamps of gold and of silver, ten thousand cups and vases of gold,
silver, and glass, and a thousand ingredients useful in all sorts of arts; and on his tomb one engraved his
name, the duration of his reign, and the epoch of his death.

In the year 734 [12 September 1333 to 31 August 1334], one discovered at Ashmouneïn, in a valley hollowed
between two mountains, square basins filled with a sweet and limpid water. People who followed their banks for
a whole day and a whole night could not reach the extremity of them. One says that these basins are the work
of Sourid, the constructor of the pyramids, who had made them to serve as a relief against the deluge of fire
that had been announced. Later, this valley was filled, because one feared that men might perish there.

[PDF p. 740]

The cheïkh, the imam Mohammed ben Ahmed El Ghariani says: "Ali ben Hassan ben Khaled El Sha'eri recounted to
me three times, without ever varying in his accounts, the following fact: A man of the tribe of the Fezarah
who dwell at Bahnasa said to me: I had set out with one of my friends, to visit the countries and earn our
living through the world; it was after the year 810 [8 June 1407 to 26 May 1408]; we had crossed the western
mountain on the side of Bahnasa, and we went at the grace of God. For days we marched thus, from the West to
the South, when we arrived all at once in a valley filled with trees, herbs, water, and fodder, but not a
human being. The valley was very extended in length and width: about a day (of march) in length and a day in
width; it was nothing but springs, plantations of palms and of olive-trees, and in great number, camels,
goats, jackals, and hyenas. The camels were there in the wild state, as well as the goats which, after having
been domesticated, had returned to the wild state. But in all the valley, one saw circulating no human being.
He told me then that they had stayed about two to three months in this place and had seen in the middle of the
valley a powerful town, fortified, with high walls and magnificent palaces; in approaching the walls, they had
heard a frightful noise and terrible and dreadful cries; they had seen a smoke rise into the sky and cover
little by little the town and all it contained. The wild camels, having approached the domestic camels they
rode, had attacked and killed them. The two Fezaris then had recourse to ruse; they plaited cords and made a
net of palm-fibers and seized these wild camels; then, having gathered stalks of palm, they fabricated baskets
of palm and panniers of reeds to put their provisions there. They filled them with dates and, making use of
the wild camels in the place of their tamed beasts, mounted them and took the direction of the Orient,
carrying with them a certain number of palm-stalks to mark out the road from the town, in order to be able to
return there. When they passed over a hillock, they planted there two of these stalks. They arrived finally at
the mountain that borders Egypt to the west. Arrived at Bahnasa, they recounted their adventures to their
fellow-citizens and set out again with their families. But, having reached the summit

[PDF p. 741]

of the western mountain, they found there, gathered in a single heap, all the palm-stalks they had planted on
the hillocks of the road. They had therefore to return, with their families and their companions, to Bahnasa.
That is what one recounted to me, but God is the most knowing."

[PDF p. 742]

CHAPTER LXXIX
OF THE TOWN OF ASHMOUNEIN

It was one of the greatest towns of the Said; it was, it is said, built by Ashmoun ben Masr ben Beïsar ben Ham
ben Nouh.

Ashmoun, says Ibn Ouacif Shah, was the most just of the children of his father, and the most desirous to
execute durable works capable of perpetuating his memory. It is he who constructed the halls plated with
colored glass in the middle of the Nile, and, according to the Copts, it is he who dug a subterranean passage
that led from Ashmouneïn to Antinoë passing under the Nile. According to what is reported, he dug it and
constructed it for his daughters who went thus to the temple of the sun. This subterranean passage was plated,
on the floor, the ground, and the ceiling, with thick and colored glass. Ashmoun, it is said, reigned longer
than his brothers: according to the historians, he reigned 800 years. After the 600th year of his reign, the
people of 'Ad took from him the kingdom which they kept 70 years, after which it withdrew through the Hedjaz
to El Dathimah and to the Ouadi-l Qora which it cultivated, and where it constructed dwellings and workshops.
It is then that God made the calamity fall on this people and destroyed it, and the government of Egypt
returned to Ashmoun. One recounts that this prince placed at the gate of Ashmouneïn a goose of copper that, if
some stranger came to enter into the town, pushed a cry while agitating its wings; thus one was warned of the
coming of the stranger, and one could, at will, send him away or let him enter. In his time, the serpents
having multiplied, one made the hunt of them and, of their flesh, one prepared medicines and remedies. Then,
with the aid of magic, one repelled them to the valley of the serpents in the mountains of Libya and of
Maraqiah where they remained imprisoned.

It is said, in the book of Orosius, that Ashmoun ben Qobt was the first king of the Egyptians and that he
lived in the time of Sharouh ben Raghou ben Falagh ben 'Aber ben Shalekh ben Arfakhshad ben Sam ben Nouh; that
the years of the world, until the time of Sharouh, were 2905, which carries back to 663 years after the
Flood.

[PDF p. 743]

There, the horses, the mules, and the asses were renowned for their agility, and one fabricated there red
hangings similar to the hangings of Armenia. A great number of clans of the Béni Ga'far ben Abou Taleb had
established themselves at Ashmouneïn; they were nomads and very powerful. With them were the Benou Mousallimah
ben 'Abd el Melek ben Merwan, their allies, and another tribe, the Benou 'Asker, whose father was, it is said,
a freedman of 'Abd el Melek ben Merwan. They descend, as one claims, from the Umayyads through the males.
There were still with them, as allies, the Benou Khaled ben Yezid ben Moawiah ben Abou Sofian, who had fixed
themselves in the land of Dalgah, near Ashmoun.

[PDF p. 744]

CHAPTER LXXX
OF THE TOWN OF AKHMIM

El Bakri orthographs it thus, of the form ifîl (whence: Ikhmîm). It is a town situated on the eastern bank of
the Nile, and that was built by Minaqioush, one of the first kings of the Copts.

This prince, reports Ibn Ouacif Shah, was patient and resolute. He began by applying himself to the
cultivations, built villages, raised stelae, gathered the works of science and the books left by the kings and
the sages; he fabricated marvelous objects and built himself a town where he withdrew. This town was
surrounded by a rampart on which were raised four stelae, one at each angle; between the stelae were placed
eighty statues of copper, holding in hand diverse arms and bearing on the chest an inscription mentioning his
virtues. There was at Memphis a man of the caste of the priests, one of the men most versed in magic, who
taught them to take the crocodiles and the wild beasts; he taught magic to the young people, and when these
had become skilled at it, he taught it to others. The king had a town constructed to install this priest
there, and this town is Akhmîm. Minaqioush reigned over the Egyptians a little more than forty years; then he
died and was buried in the pyramid situated facing El Atfih, and with him were buried considerable treasures,
precious stones, vases, and statues. On the tomb, one engraved the name of the king and the epoch of his
death. The people of Akhmîm recount that an individual, come from the Orient, had attached himself to the
temple; that he came each day to perfume it with incense and saffron, addressing above all his perfumes and
his incense to an image placed beside the door; and each day he found under this image a dinner that he took,
after which he went away. He had done this a number of times, but finally he was denounced by one of his
slaves to the governor of the country. One arrested him, but having given some money, he was able to leave the
country.

[PDF p. 745]

The temple of Akhmîm was one of the most admirable and most considerable. The Egyptians had constructed it to
store their wheat, for they had been warned in advance of the arrival of the Flood. But they were not in
agreement on its subject; according to some, it was to be a fire that would burn all that was found on the
surface of the earth; according to others, it would be an inundation. They constructed therefore this temple
before the Flood. One saw there the portraits of the kings who were to reign over Egypt. It was built of
blocks of marble, each measuring five cubits in width by two cubits in thickness. It comprised seven halls
covered with stones each eighteen cubits long and five wide; these stones were covered with paintings the
color of lapis and other shades, and for the one who saw them, these paintings seemed to have been executed
the very day, so perfect were they. Each of the halls bore the name of one of the seven planets, and on all
the walls were engraved images of forms and sizes different, accompanied by signs explaining the sciences of
the Copts -- the chemistry, the cosmography, the art of talismans, the medicine, the astronomy, the geometry,
etc., that these images represented.

Ibn Djoubeir recounts, in his voyage, that the length of this temple was six hundred twenty cubits and its
width a hundred seventy cubits; it reposed on forty columns, independently of the walls. Each column measured
fifty spans of circumference, and from one column to another, the space was thirty spans. Their capitals were
enormous. They were engraved from the base to the summit. From one capital to another went an enormous
flagstone of sculpted stone, fifty-six spans long, on a thickness of ten spans and a height of eight. The
ceiling, in flagstones of stone equally, seemed of a single piece, and one saw there, on the interior and the
exterior, extraordinary designs and marvelous colors, representing birds, men, and other objects. The wall of
the temple, eighteen spans wide, was of stones well cemented. Thus measured it Ibn Djoubeir in the year 578 [7
May 1182 to 25 April 1183]. One says that it is there that Dhou-l Noun (Jonas) learned the chemistry. This
temple remained standing until the year 780 [30 April 1378 to 18 April 1379]. A man of Akhmîm, the preacher
Gamal el din ben Bakr el Khatib 'Alam el din 'Ali, demolished it and drew from it much money: but his life was
short, and he died (a short time after). Since then, Akhmîm went declining and finished by being ruined. Many
recount that

[PDF p. 746]

the temple of Akhmîm was incarnated (?) in a beardless and naked young man. One day when people were hidden in
the temple, this young man had followed them and had struck them with redoubled blows, so that they came out
of it precipitately. One recounts the same fact regarding a man who had entered into the pyramids.

One recounted to me that an individual having stuck wax on one of the images of the temple of Akhmîm and having
left it in place, the scorpions flocked there, and that this wax having been put in a box, the scorpions
gathered around it. One recounts that there was in the temple of Akhmîm a demon that held itself standing on a
single leg and that had only one hand, which it held raised in the air; on its forehead and on its flanks were
engraved characters. It had a phallus very in evidence, adherent to the wall, and one claimed that whoever
would be adroit enough to cut the wall around this phallus and to withdraw it without breaking it would have
only to suspend it at his side to be constantly in erection as long as he had not withdrawn it; that he could
thus unite himself with her whom he loved and that he would not weaken as long as the stone phallus remained
suspended at his belt. One of the valis of Akhmîm having removed it experienced some of these marvelous
properties. The carpets of beast-skins came from Akhmîm, where one prepared them. One recounts that in this
town were gathered twelve thousand scholars versed in magic; it is there also that was met the bang tree. One
affirms that the one who built the temple of Akhmîm was named Doumaria and that he made it to serve as a model
to the peoples who would come after him. He retraced there the history of the peoples and the ages, the
exploits of which they are proud; he represented there the prophets and the sages, and engraved there the
names of the kings who were to reign until the end of times. At the moment of the construction of the temple,
the eagle was in the sign of the Ram (Aries), and, according to them, the eagle stays three thousand years in
each of the signs of the Zodiac. Now, today, the eagle is found at the end of the sign of Capricorn; there
would be therefore, according to this calculation, nearly thirty thousand years that this temple has been
constructed.

Abou 'Abdallah Mohammed ben 'Abd el Rahim el Qeïti, in his book "Gift to the Spirits," recounts that this
temple was of square form and constructed in cut stone; that it had four gates leading each to an edifice
provided equally with four dark gates leading to edifices whose disposition imitated that of the leaves of a
tree.

[PDF p. 747]

CHAPTER LXXXI
OF THE TOWN OF EL 'OQAB

The town of El 'Oqâb (in Arabic: the eagle), says Mas'oudi, is situated to the west of the pyramids of
Abousir, near Gizeh, at five days and five nights' march for a solid cavalier. The route of it has been filled
in, and the trace of the path that led there effaced. In this town are marvelous constructions, precious
stones, and riches.

Here is what Ibn Ouacif Shah recounts: El Oualid ben Douma the Amalecite had set out with a considerable army
traversing the regions and subduing the kings. Arrived in Syria, he sent one of his slaves, named 'Oun, who
directed himself toward Egypt and subdued it. Then El Oualid set out in his turn, rejoined 'Oun, who had gone
to meet him, and entered into Egypt of which he treated the inhabitants according to his good pleasure. Having
formed the project of going to the sources of the Nile, he set out with a numerous army, leaving the
government of Egypt to 'Oun, and remained forty years in his expedition. Now, 'Oun, after seven years of
government, became proud and had himself proclaimed king, refusing to recognize himself slave of El Oualid and
saying that he was his brother. Thanks to magic, he imposed himself, he carried off the free women, and
everyone attached himself to him. Every woman descending from the kings of Egypt, he married her; every
fortune, he seized it, having the proprietor die, and yet, he honored the priests and respected the temples.
One day, he saw in a dream El Oualid. The latter said to him: "Who permitted you to take the title of king?
You are not ignorant that it is a crime that merits death; you have united yourself with the daughters of the
kings and you have taken riches without having any right to them." Then he had a cauldron filled with oil
which was heated until boiling, and tore off his garments to throw him there. Then an eagle swooped on 'Oun,
seized him, carried him off into the airs, and deposited him at the edge of a precipice at the summit of a
mountain, whence he fell into a valley filled with a stinking mire. He awoke startled and recounted his vision
to the priests who said to him: "We will deliver you from El Oualid if you wish to fabricate an eagle and
adore it, for it is it that delivered you in your dream." "I

[PDF p. 748]

recognize it," answered 'Oun, "and the eagle said to me: Recognize this place and do not forget it." And he
made an eagle of gold, having two precious stones in the place of the eyes; he put on it a belt of precious
stones and made it a beautiful temple hung with silk. There one came to incense it and to make it offerings.
At the end, the eagle spoke. And 'Oun prostrated himself and adored it and invited his subjects to imitate
him, which they consented to do. On the orders of 'Oun all the workers of Egypt were gathered, and 'Oun led
all his partisans toward the western desert in search of a terrain vast and even where one could penetrate
only by difficult passages and abrupt mountains: pools of water spread in the vicinity. It is today the
Fayoum which was then only a marsh formed by the waters of the Nile and which remained thus until the moment
when Joseph brought the waters of the river to Medinet (el Fayoum). They set out therefore and remained a
month turning before finding the object of their desires. And there remained in Egypt neither worker, nor
engineer, nor whoever was skilled in construction, in the cutting of stones, or in sculpture: all went there.
He led there a thousand men of the army and seven hundred magicians to aid the constructors, and with them
tools and victuals on chariots, and the trace of these chariots is still visible in the desert of the Occident
as far as the Fayoum behind the Pyramids. When all the necessary stones were cut, one traced the enclosure of
the town, a square of two parasangs to the side; in the middle, one dug a well into which one descended the
image of a pig made of copper mixed with other materials, that one placed on a pedestal of copper, the face
turned toward the Orient, and that, at the moment of the rising of the house of Saturn, at the hour of its
apogee. One immolated a pig; with its blood one coated the face of the statue, one burned some of its hairs,
and one filled the interior with the blood, the hairs, the bones, the flesh, and the gall; a little gall was
put in the ears, and the rest of the pig was burned and the ashes deposited in a phial of copper before the
statue; one engraved there the virtues of Saturn. At the bottom of the well, one dug, in four directions, four
subterranean passages leading to the walls of the town, and at each extremity were made openings for the
circulation of the air; then the well was closed and surmounted by a cupola posed on columns raised on the
walls of the town. One traced boulevards, each boulevard ending at one of the gates of the town, which was
divided into streets and into houses. Around the cupola, one set statues of copper representing cavaliers
holding in hand javelins and the face turned toward the gates. The foundations

[PDF p. 749]

[OF THE TOWN OF EL 'OQAB, continued]

of the town were made of black stone, over it red stone, then yellow stone, green, and over the whole white
transparent stone, the whole cemented with lead poured into the joints. At the center of each stone was a rod
of iron, as in the construction of the pyramids. One made the rampart sixty cubits high and twenty wide. At
the summit of each of the gates of the rampart was a great eagle made of an alloy of copper, the wings
extended, and hollow. At each angle, a cavalier held in hand a javelin, the face turned toward the exit of the
town. The water, brought to the eastern gate, flowed across the town toward the western gate and poured itself
into cisterns; likewise from the South gate to the North gate. One sacrificed to the eagle the male eagles;
one brought the winds to the mouth of the statues that made heard shrill voices. 'Oun attached to each of them
a genie that was to prevent any individual, with the exception of the inhabitants, from entering into the
town. Then the eagle to which one rendered a cult was placed under the cupola in the middle of the town on a
pedestal with four angles; at each angle was the figure of a demon. The whole reposed on a column that turned;
the angle turned with it and remained in each direction (of the cardinal points) the quarter of the year.
Finally, all that achieved, 'Oun transported into this town the precious stones and the riches of Egypt, royal
objects, statues, works of sciences, silver powder, aromatics, arms. He installed there the great magicians,
the priests, the industrialists, the merchants, and divided among them the dwellings. The people of each trade
mingled only among themselves. He built a suburb for the artisans and the cultivators; on the canals, he put
bridges where passed those who penetrated into the town. The water flowed around the suburb. 'Oun raised
signals and established guards. Behind the town, on the side of the desert, he planted vines, palms, and all
sorts of trees, in distinct lots. Behind extended on all sides the cultivations of cereals. And all that was
created for fear of El Oualid.

Between this town and Memphis there were three days' march. One stayed there or went there, then returned to
Memphis. There were celebrated four feasts per year, at the four epochs when the eagle changed position.
Having admired all that, 'Oun felt his heart more reassured, until he received from Nubia a letter of El
Oualid prescribing him to bring him victuals and to prepare the markets. 'Oun sent him back by land and by
water what he asked and gathered in the town his partisans and those he had chosen from the daughters of the
kings

[PDF p. 750]

and of the great. El Oualid having approached, 'Oun went in his turn to the town, and fortified himself there,
having left a substitute at Memphis. El Oualid, advancing and having learned all that 'Oun had done, entered
into fury and thought of sending against him an army, but, better informed on the state of the town, on the
fortifications and the magicians that defended it, he wrote to 'Oun to come to him, menacing him with the
consequences that his disobedience could entail. 'Oun answered him: "On my part, there is no wounding word
against the king, no attack, no hostile act against his country: I am his servant and hold myself in this
place to repel any enemy coming from the West; and I cannot go to him because of the terror that he inspires
in me. Let the king therefore leave me where I am in quality of governor, and I will serve him all the taxes
and all the presents he will exact." And he sent him considerable treasures and precious stones. And El Oualid
renounced attacking him, and he remained in Egypt until his death.

[PDF p. 751]

CHAPTER LXXXII
OF THE TOWN OF EL FAYOUM

The emplacement of Fayoum was the outlet of the waters of the Nile; when the lord Joseph the Veridical took
the government of Egypt, he put it into cultivation.

Then, says Ibn Ouacif Shah, reigned El Rian ben El Oualid, who was the Pharaoh of Joseph; the Copts name him
Nahraoush. When he mounted on the throne, he was a prince of an admirable character, beautiful of visage, wise
and reflective, and who promised to be amiable. He discharged his people from the tax for three years and
divided the treasures among his particular friends and his subjects. He called to the government of the
country a man of his family named Atfeïn, the same that the traditionists name El Aziz. The king had raised
for him in the palace a throne of silver on which Atfeïn held himself and that he left only to go to the door
of the king. The latter remitted to his vizier the authority over the officers and the writers, and Nahraoush
occupied himself no more than with what passed behind the curtain (that is, outside the harem). Atfeïn
accumulating all his authority and relegating him to his pleasures, Nahraoush plunged himself into his
frivolity, neglecting the affairs, no longer showing himself to the people; but the country was prosperous and
the king asked no more. One constructed for him salons of colored glass, surrounded by water where the fish
lived freely, and of crystals of color where was produced, when the rays of the sun struck them, a marvelous
reflection. One constructed for him also pavilions of pleasure in number equal to that of the days of the
year, and each day he walked in one of them. Each pavilion was hung and furnished with furniture and hangings
different. However the rumor spread among the kings of the vicinity that Nahraoush occupied himself only with
pleasure and that the care of affairs reposed on Atfeïn. The king of the Amalecites, Abou Qabous 'Aqer ben
Yanhoum, marched on Egypt and directed himself toward its frontiers. El Aziz raised to resist him

[PDF p. 752]

an army whose general was named Barianis; he struggled for three years; but the Amalecite took the upper hand,
killed Barianis, razed the towers and the fortresses, and his yoke weighed on the country. The people then
went in crowds to the palace of the king and implored his protection. Nahraoush appeared, reviewed his army,
and with 600,000 combatants, without counting the valets, he set out on the march. The two armies met beyond
Houf and delivered a fierce combat. The Amalecite was defeated, and Nahraoush pursued him to the frontiers of
Syria, killed him a great number of men, destroyed the harvests and the trees, burned, hanged, and raised at
the places where he had arrived stelae on which he engraved these words: "He who passes beyond this limit, I
await him." He reached, it is said, Mossoul, struck Syria with a tribute, built near El 'Arich a magnificent
town, left a garrison, and returned to Egypt, where, having gathered an army from all the provinces, he
prepared to attack the king of the Occident. He set out therefore with 700,000 men, crossed the country of the
Berbers of which he subjugated the greatest part, and had depart from Raqodah, on a fleet, a general who was
to go to the islands of the children of Iafeth (Japheth) and devastate them. As for him, following the route
of land, he took the direction of the country of the Berbers, delivered them battle, and, by treaty, imposed
on them the tribute; from there he pursued his route on Ifriqiah and Carthage (?), concluded peace with these
countries by means of tribute and, continuing his route, reached the place where the green river throws itself
into the sea of Roum; it is there that are raised the statues of copper. He raised there in his turn a statue
on which he engraved his name and the account of his campaign, and imposed a tribute on the inhabitants of the
region. Then, making an elbow on the great land, he reached Spain whose king combated him for long days, then
treated, by means of tribute and a promise to defend Egypt against the aggression of the neighbors. After
that, he set out, but not by sea, and directed himself toward the Orient across the country of the Berbers.
All the peoples he met had to submit to him. From there, he marched toward the South, combated a number of
peoples, and sent a general to a town situated on the Black Sea. The king of this town came out to meet the
general who taught him what El Raïan was and the fashion in which he treated the kings. "Never has anyone,"
said the king, "spoken to us of that." The general then posed him some questions on the subject of the sea.
"Has no one ever navigated it?" he asked. "That is impossible for whoever it may be," answered the king,
"because of the shadow that the clouds project there and that prevents seeing."

[PDF p. 753]

El Raïan having arrived, one brought him presents -- fruits, bananas for the most part, and a black stone
that, put in the water, became white. The king, directing himself toward the countries of the Soudan, arrived
at the kingdom of the anthropophagous (cannibal) Damdams who went to meet him entirely naked. He vanquished
them, subjugated them, and took the route of the Obscure sea; but, as fogs rose from it, he returned toward
the North and arrived near a statue of red stone that, with the hand, made a sign to turn back and that bore
this inscription on the chest: "There is nothing behind me." From there he marched toward the town of Copper,
but could not reach it; he found the Tenebrous valley where one heard great noises without seeing anyone,
because of the thickness of the shadows. He went from there to the valley of the Sands and, on his route, met
statues bearing names of kings. He raised near them another statue on which he engraved his name. Having taken
knowledge of the desert, he crossed it to ruins that extend along the Obscure sea, and where he saw lions that
roared one against the other. Judging that beyond there was for him no ruin, he came back on his steps,
regained the valley of the Sands, and crossed the land of the Scorpions where he lost some of his men; the
rest of the army preserved itself from harm thanks to conjurations. Having crossed this region, he arrived at
the town of the Sages, more known under the name of town of Kand, whose inhabitants fled before him to the
mountain. He remained there a long time and his army was on the point of dying there of thirst. At the end,
from the mountain descended one of the most virtuous and of the sages, whose body was all covered with hairs:
"What do you want," he said to the king, "O stranger, too happy and too favored, why lose yourself and your
army? Does what you possess not suffice you, and have you not confidence in your Creator? Seek the repose,
abandon the fatigues and the error, for that is all you can acquire thus." The king, surprised at these words,
asked him for water. The other having indicated some to him, the king interrogated him on his country. "Our
country," he answered, "no one before you has reached it." "Of what do you live?" "Of the roots of the plants;
that suffices us, for we content ourselves with little." "And what do you drink?" "The rain and the snow."
"Why have you fled at our approach?" "We have little desire to frequent you, but we had no subject to fear
you." "What do you do when the sun becomes burning?" "We withdraw into grottoes hollowed in the mountain."
"Have you need of money? I will leave you some."

[PDF p. 754]

[OF THE TOWN OF EL FAYOUM, continued]

"Only the civilized (policed) people have need of money; we would not know what to do with it. We content
ourselves with what suffices us; moreover, we have so much that, if you saw it, you would despise your
riches." "Show it to me," said the king. The man then led the king and some men of his suite toward a land
situated at the foot of the mountain; there were found there ingots of gold in quantity. Their guide showed
them also a valley whose two banks were sown with emeralds and with sapphires. Nahraoush ordered his
companions to take some of the largest of these stones, which they did. The sage, seeing that the suite of the
king adored a statue that one transported in the expedition, invited the king not to sojourn longer on their
land and inspired in him some fear on the subject of the adoration of the idols. Nahraoush, having taken
leave, set out, and among all the peoples he met, he left traces of his passage. He arrived finally in Nubia,
imposed by treaty the tribute on this country, and raised at Dongola a statue on which he engraved his name
and the account of his expedition. Then he took the route of Memphis; and in each town of Egypt, the
inhabitants, filled with joy and gladness, came to meet him carrying flowers and perfumes. Finally he arrived
at Memphis; the people of the town, led by El 'Aziz, came to meet him laden with flowers and perfumes of all
sorts. El 'Aziz had had prepared for him a pavilion of colored glass, adorned with the richest hangings.
Around were planted trees and flowers, and one had dug a basin filled with blue glass in the thickness of
which were seen images of fish in white glass. The king descended in this pavilion, and the people stayed days
and days drinking and eating. Then Nahraoush reviewed his army and ascertained that he had lost 70,000 of his
men; on the other hand, he brought back more than 50,000 prisoners. His expedition, outside Egypt, had lasted
eleven years.

The kings, informed of his return, were full of respect for him, and his power affirmed itself. He
constructed, on the eastern bank, palaces of marble surmounted by towers. He gave orders for the amelioration
of the country, had the dikes repaired and the soil cultivated, so well that the yield of the tax rose to a
hundred million dinars.

It is in his time that entered into Egypt a young man of Syria whom his brothers had sold by ruse. The
caravans stopped then at the place that one calls today El Maouqef (the halt). The young man was brought there
and was put up for auction. It was Joseph the Veridical, the son of Jacob, son of Abraham the cherished of
God.

[PDF p. 755]

Atfeïn bought him to make a present of him to the king. But when he arrived with him at his palace, his wife
Zuleikha, who was at the same time his cousin, having seen the new slave, said to her husband: "Let us keep
him, we will raise him, and he will serve us." And there happened to him what God recounts in the Koran. She
dissimulated her love until the day when she was vanquished by it. Then, having withdrawn aside with Joseph,
she adorned herself for him and avowed to him that she loved him, adding that if he consented to satisfy her
desires, she would fill him with riches. But, as he refused, she promised herself to make him yield. She set
about praying him, and he, always resisted, until at the end her husband appeared. On seeing him, Joseph drew
away from Zuleikha. Now, El 'Aziz was impotent and could not approach women. And as Joseph attempted to excuse
himself to El 'Aziz: "I was asleep," said Zuleikha, "when this one came to abuse me." But some of her people
appeared and testified against his wife. "Leave that," said Atfeïn to Joseph -- that is, "leave the excuses" --
and addressing himself to his wife: "Ask me pardon for your sin," he said. The rumor of the adventure reached
Nahraoush, but he had returned to his pleasures and lived apart from men. The women of high society, put au
courant of the story, mocked Zuleikha; she invited some of them to a collation and had prepared two gilded
halls that one hung with brocade, golden yellow. Between the two halls she had hung curtains of brocade, and
she ordered the hairdressers to adorn Joseph and to make him come out by the hall that faced the one where she
would be with the women. This hall faced the sun. The hairdressers took therefore Joseph with them, and
adorned his hair with all sorts of precious stones; they clothed him in a robe of yellow brocade brocaded with
red disks incrusted with gold where one saw little green birds; the robe was lined with green. Under the robe,
Joseph wore a red tunic, and on his head was placed a crown of pearls and of precious stones. The hairdressers
made pass under the crown the extremity of the hairs that fell thus on the forehead, they brought the curls
onto his chest, uncovered the forehead, and placed there the crown. At his ears, they put two earrings of
precious stones; behind the collar of his caftan, they let hang between his shoulders his hairs intermingled
with precious stones and gold; at his neck one suspended a collar of gold incrusted with red stones and
splendid pearls. At his waist was attached a belt of gold with clasps of colored stones and with chiseled
pendants.

[PDF p. 756]

One shod him with white shoes with green embroideries on a ground of gold; and the bottom of his caftan was
bordered with braids and galloons, and one sewed there a number of green stones. On each cheek one made curl a
lock of hair, one enlivened his eyes with kohl, and one put in his hand a fan of green feathers. The women
having finished eating and drinking, Zuleikha remitted to them knives with handles of precious stones to cut
the fruits; these fruits were, it is said, oranges, and while her guests peeled them, Zuleikha said to them:
"One has reported to me that you spoke of me and of my slave." "How," they cried, "can one have told you that?
you are of a race too elevated for such a thing to exist; a person of your quality is placed higher than the
very sons of the kings by her beauty and her nobility. How could you have contented yourself with your slave?"
"One has not told you the truth," replied Zuleikha, "and he is at my home for another service." Then she made
a sign to the hairdressers, these lifted the curtain that separated the hall where they held themselves from
the other, and Joseph appeared lit by the sun full in the face; and the hall and all it contained was lit by
the face of Joseph. The latter advanced, the fan in hand, and the women looked at him furtively. Arrived near
Zuleikha, Joseph stopped and with his fan kept away the flies from the head of his mistress. The women, all
occupied in looking at him, and marveled at his beauty, cut their fingers believing they cut their fruits, and
pronounced not a word. "What have you then?" Zuleikha asked them, "you no longer speak and you look at my
slave." "God forbid!" they answered; "that one is not your slave; it is a magnificent angel." And there was
among them none who was not seized with desires and did not burn with love for him. "It is that one," said
Zuleikha, "for which one makes me so many reproaches." "No one," answered the women, "can address you the least
blame on his subject. Whoever would blame you would be wrong. Take him then." "I have tried," said Zuleikha,
"but he refused me. Speak to him for me." Then each set about speaking to Joseph, trying in secret to convince
him for her own account and offering herself to him, but he, always refused. Hoping to have themselves
accepted, they spoke for Zuleikha and said to him: "Your mistress loves you and you hate her. You have not the
right to disobey her." "It matters little to me," said Joseph. Finally, judging all persuasion useless, they
attempted to take him by force. "No," said Zuleikha, "that would not be suitable; but since he refuses me, I
will put him aside from all pleasure; I will have him

[PDF p. 757]

imprisoned and will withdraw from him all I have given him." Joseph answered: "The prison is preferable to
what one exacts of me." And she swore by her god, which was a statue of green emerald named Atared (Mercury),
that if he persisted, she would put her menace into execution on the spot. And she had him stripped of his
garments, had him clothed in coarse cloth, and asked El 'Aziz to put his prison at her disposal in order to
make cease the calumnious rumors that circulated about her. El 'Aziz consented, and Joseph was thrown into
prison. The king saw in a dream someone who said to him: "Such and such have formed the project of killing
you." And he designated the officer of the mouth (chief cook) and the cup-bearer of the king. On his
awakening, the king had them come, interrogated them, and they avowed. According to certain authors, only one
of them avowed and the other denied energetically. The king had them imprisoned. The officer of the mouth was
named Rasan and the cup-bearer Mortos. Joseph was equally in the same prison, consoling those who were there
and promising them liberty. The two officers recounted to him their dreams, as God reports in his book, and
the event was accomplished as Joseph had announced. Later, the king had the vision of the cows and that of the
ears (of grain); it is then that the cup-bearer spoke to him of Joseph, went to the captive, recounted to him
the dreams of the king, and returned to the prince who cried: "Let him come!" "I will not come out," said
Joseph, "before one has cleared up the affair of the women for which I was imprisoned." All was discovered
then, and Zuleikha made complete avowals. One sent therefore to seek Joseph, one washed him, one rid him of
the impurities of the prison, and one had him clothe the garments that suit those who present themselves
before the kings. On seeing him, the king felt his heart fill with affection for him; he filled him with
favors and interrogated him on his dreams, which Joseph explained, as God has recounted. "Who will come to my
aid?" asked the king. "I," answered Joseph. And the king gave him a royal garment, put on his head a crown,
and had him paraded through the town, escorted by the army, and brought back to the palace where the king had
him sit on the throne of El 'Aziz, of whom he took at the same time the functions of regent. One reports that
after the death of El 'Aziz, the king gave his widow in marriage to Joseph. "This is better than what you
wished of me," Joseph said to her. "Pardon me," answered Zuleikha; "my husband was impotent, and no woman can
see you without her heart being filled with love for you because of your beauty." The years of abundance
having come in Egypt, Joseph gathered from all sides the grains, stored them, and gathered a

[PDF p. 758]

great quantity. And when came the years of famine, when the Nile began to decrease and its level lowered from
year to year, the country was desolated to such a point that the wheat sold for fortunes, jewels, livestock,
garments, dishes (of price), lands. One would have abandoned Egypt, if Joseph had not been at the head of
affairs. Syria too was desolated by the scourge, and the brothers of Joseph came to Egypt as God has reported.
Joseph sent to seek his father who transported himself to Egypt with all his family. Joseph, carrying with him
wheat of Egypt, went to meet him and presented him to the king. Jacob was then a venerable old man whom the
king treated with respect. He interrogated him on his age, his state, and his religion. "I am a hundred twenty
years old," answered Jacob; "for my state, I possess sheep that I pasture and of which I make use. I adore the
master of the world, your creator and mine. He is the God of my fathers, your God, and the God of all things."
Among the people of the suite of the king was a priest, very powerful, who said to the king: "I fear that the
ruin of Egypt may come by the hand of the children of this man." "How to assure ourselves of it?" asked the
king. Then the priest said to Jacob: "Show me your God, O old man." "My God," said Jacob, "is too great for one
to see him." "We others, we see our gods." "Certainly," said Jacob, "your gods are of gold, of silver, of
stone, of precious stones, of copper, and of wood put into work by the sons of Adam who are the slaves of my
God. There is no God but him, he is the sublime and the wise." "A thing that one cannot see with the eyes does
not exist," replied the priest. Jacob, irritated, gave him a contradiction: "God," he said, "is not a thing
like the other things; he is the creator of all that exists; there is no God but him." "Describe him to us,"
asked the priest. "The creatures alone," said Jacob, "can be described; but he, he is the Unique creator, the
Ancient, the Wise, the Eternal; he sees, but one does not see him." And Jacob rose in anger. The king had him
sit down again and ordered the priest to be silent. "We have found in the books," said again the priest to the
king, "that the ruin of Egypt will come by the hand of these people." "Will it be accomplished in our time?"
asked the king. "No," said the priest, "nor for a long time yet. But the best would be to have him die and to
leave subsisting no one of his race." "Even though," replied the king, "the thing were such as you say, it is
not possible for us to prevent it, and we cannot make these people die." And he gave as a place of sojourn to
Jacob and to his companions the valley of El Sedir, where Jacob remained

[PDF p. 759]

[OF THE TOWN OF EL FAYOUM, continued]

until his last day. At his death, one transported him to the village of Abraham, and one buried him near him.
Nahraoush, it is said, was a believer, but he dissimulated his faith, fearing that his authority might suffer
from it. He reigned 120 years, and, under his reign, Joseph created the Fayoum. The Egyptians had spoken ill
of him to the king: "He has become old," they said, "his intelligence darkens; put it to the test." And the
king said to Joseph: "I have given this region to my daughter; it is only an outlet for the waters; put it in
state for her." And Joseph set to work; he managed to make the waters disappear, had the muds removed, dug the
Menha, and built Allahoun; he divided the waters and distributed them; and all that in four months. Everyone
was astonished at his ability.

He was, it is said, the first who, in Egypt, practiced the art of the engineer. At the death of Nahraoush, his
son Darmagoush succeeded him. It is the same who bears among the historians the name of Darem ben El-Rian; it
is the fourth Pharaoh of the Egyptians. This prince followed a line of conduct quite different from that his
father had followed. Joseph was his lieutenant, but if, in certain affairs, he adopted his opinions, in
certain others, he took no account of them. It is in his time that Joseph died; one buried him and deposited
his body in a sarcophagus of marble that one buried on the western bank of the Nile; and this bank became more
and more fertile, while the eastern bank remained sterile. The sarcophagus was then transported to the
Orient, and this region became fertile in its turn, while the fertility of the western bank decreased. One
decided therefore to place the body one year on the eastern bank and one year on the western bank. Then one
resolved to attach the sarcophagus in the middle of the river by means of solid chains, and the two banks of
the river became fertile both.

Then, says Ibn el Hakam, reigned El Raisan ben El Oualid ben Douma; it is he who was the sovereign of the
prophet Joseph. Joseph having explained the dreams the king had had, the latter sent to seek him and had him
come out of prison. On arriving near Joseph, recounts Ibn 'Abbas, the messenger said to him: "Throw far from
you the garments of the prisoner, clothe yourself in new garments, rise, and go to the king." And the other
prisoners invoked God in favor of Joseph. He was then thirty years old, and when he was in the presence of the
king, the latter, surprised at his youth, cried: "How could this young man explain dreams that neither the
magicians nor the priests could understand!" However he had him sit near him. "Fear nothing,"

[PDF p. 760]

he said to him, and when he had conversed with him, Joseph grew in his eyes. He transmitted to him his
authority, remitted to him his seal, and charged him with all that passed behind his door (that is, all public
affairs, as opposed to the private affairs that pass inside the palace). He made him a gift of a collar of
gold, of garments of silk, of a horse harnessed and adorned like the mount of the king himself, and had
