proclaimed at the sound of the drum through all Egypt that Joseph was the lieutenant of the king.

According to 'Akramah, Pharaoh said to Joseph: "I have given you the empire, but I desire that my throne be
four fingers higher than yours." "Good," said Joseph. And the king, having had him sit on the throne,
withdrew into his apartments with his women and remitted to Joseph the direction of all the affairs of Egypt.
Thus, for having explained the dream of the king, Joseph reigned over Egypt.

Here is what El Leith ben S'ad reports: Old men of our country reported to me the following tradition: The
dearth was so great in Egypt that the inhabitants bought what to eat with gold; the gold exhausted, they paid
with silver; the silver exhausted in its turn, they paid with sheep, and the sheep too were exhausted. And
Joseph continued to sell victuals until there remained to the Egyptians neither silver, nor gold, nor ewes,
nor oxen, which happened in the first two years. The following year, the third, they came to find Joseph:
"There remains to us no more," they said to him, "than ourselves, our families, and our lands." And Joseph
bought all their lands for Pharaoh, then he gave them grains to sow these lands, on condition that the fifth
of the harvest belong to the king.

Regarding the foundation of the town of El Fayoum by Joseph, one recounts that, after having been for thirty
years the vizier of Pharaoh, Joseph was destituted. "Why have you deposed me?" asked Joseph. "I do not depose
you by discontent," answered him the king, "and I do not forget your blessed influence; but my fathers
recommended me not to keep a vizier more than thirty years, and I would fear (that in staying longer) the
vizier might take root and end by prevailing over the king." "I have been for you," replied Joseph, "a
faithful counselor who has made you possessor of all the country of Egypt; give me in your turn a land that
will serve as a residence for me, my family, and my descendants." "Choose the land you wish," said Pharaoh to
him. And Joseph walked in the desert and arrived at the land of Fayoum. There was a mountain;

[PDF p. 761]

the plain extended from this mountain to the river, and after having examined the state of the waters of the
river, he recognized that the Nile would come to cover all the region. He pierced the mountain and made the
water pass there, which spread through the Fayoum, watering the soil; on the two banks of the water he raised
three hundred sixty villages, according to the number of the days of the year, filled them with the grains and
the harvests that he gathered. And when the Nile diminished and the dearth fell on Egypt, he sold each day
what a village of the Fayoum contained, so well that he was in his turn proprietor of all Egypt, as he had
before made the king master of it. The fortune of Joseph became immense, his riches accumulated, and, a short
time after, the king made him again vizier, a function he exercised until his death. By his testament, he
recommended to transport his body toward the Holy Land, and Haroun, son of Ephraïm, son of Joseph, led it away
with an escort of ten thousand Israelites. But the great of Egypt opposed his departure and vanquished him in
the desert that is between Egypt and Syria. The greatest part of his companions having perished, Haroun had to
return with the others to Egypt where they remained until the moment when God sent Moses, son of Amran, as
messenger to Pharaoh. Moses, having made the Israelites come out of Egypt, led away with him the body of
Joseph; at this epoch, the Fayoum was in full prosperity. The cause of the putting into cultivation of the
Fayoum, according to another version, was the following: Joseph governed in Egypt and enjoyed with Pharaoh a
magnificent situation; he was then a hundred years old, and the viziers of the king came to declare to their
master that the intelligence of Joseph was weakening, that his spirit was darkening, and that his wisdom was
diminishing. Pharaoh received them very badly, contradicted their assertions, and maltreated them. They were
silent for two years, then returned to the charge and held the same discourse. "Imagine something that may
permit me to put him to the test," said Pharaoh. The Fayoum was named then El Goubah (the pit) and served as
an outlet for the overflow and the excess of the waters of the Said. The viziers agreed to decide that it
would be the point that would serve as a test for Joseph. They said therefore to Pharaoh: "Ask Joseph to
exhaust the water of El Goubah and to rid it of it, thus you will add a domain to your domains and revenues to
your revenues." The pharaoh summoned Joseph and said to him: "You know how much I love my daughter such-and-
such; I have resolved, at her majority, to seek her a land, and I have found nothing better for her than El
Goubah. It is indeed a country

[PDF p. 762]

at once distant and near that one can perceive, in whatever direction it may be, only by a defile or by the
desert; likewise one can go there from Egypt only by a defile or by the desert. The Fayoum is the center of
Egypt as Egypt is the center of the other countries, for one can approach Egypt only by a defile or by the
desert. I have made a gift of this land to my daughter, therefore neglect neither means nor study for the
success of it." "Good," said Joseph. "When you wish it, send to seek me, and, if it please God, I will
accomplish what you ask." "It is what I desire most ardently," said the king, "and the thing is quite
pressing." And he recommended to Joseph to dig three canals, one leading from the south to the Said at such or
such place; another to the Orient, going from such to such point, and a third to the Occident from such place
to such other. Joseph put the workers to work and dug El Manha which sets out from the Nile, a little to the
south of Ashmoun, and goes to Al Lahoun; order was given to the masons to dig Al Lahoun; he dug the canal of
the Fayoum which is the eastern canal, and another canal passing at Benhamat, one of the villages of the
western Fayoum; the water coming out by the eastern canal poured itself into the Nile, that which came out by
the western canal poured itself into the desert of Benhamat, toward the West: there remained no more water in
El Goubah. He then made the workers enter there: one tore up the reeds and the aquatic plants that were there,
one carried them outside. The water of the Nile then for the first time became running, and the lands of El
Goubah excellent for cultivation; the water of the Nile, rising, entered by the water-intake of El Manha, ran
in the canal until it arrived at Al Lahoun which it crossed to the Fayoum whose canal it filled, and which it
watered, making of the region a lake of the Nile. The king went there with his viziers. The work had lasted
only seventy days. At the sight of the result, the king said to his viziers: "It is there the work of a
thousand days (elf youm)." And the region took the name of El Fayoum. One cultivated it in the same fashion as
the plains of Egypt.

I have heard recounted in another fashion the creation of Fayoum. When Joseph took the government of Egypt, he
was aged thirty years; he remained forty years at the head of affairs, and the Egyptians murmured: "There he
is become old, his wisdom diminishes," and they deposed him: "Choose yourself," they said to him, "among the
fallow lands a domain that you will take for yourself and that you will arrange as you understand it. If we
ascertain that you are still

[PDF p. 763]

skilled and wise, we will be convinced that you are in the force of intelligence, and we will give you back
the power." Joseph therefore traversed the desert of Egypt and chose the emplacement of the Fayoum which was
conceded to him. He dug there the canal of El Manha which set out from the Nile and brought the waters of it
into the Fayoum, and the work was achieved in a year.

One recounted to me, says Yezid ben Abou Nabib, that Joseph had accomplished this work by divine inspiration,
and that he had been powerfully aided by the multitude of the workers and the laborers. When one saw the
result of this work, one recognized that the work accomplished at the Fayoum by Joseph had not its equal in
all Egypt. The people were of the opinion that never had Joseph shown more prudence, ability, and wisdom, and
one gave him back the power that he exercised still for sixty years, in all for a hundred years, until he died
at the age of 130 years. Joseph, having been informed of the conversations that had taken place between the
viziers and the king, and knowing that all that had been accomplished had been only a test, said to the king:
"I have other projects and other plans than all you have seen." "What are they?" said the king. "I will give
as inhabitants to the Fayoum a family drawn from each of the villages of Egypt, and each family will build
itself a village; in this way, the number of the villages of the Fayoum will be equal to that of the villages
of Egypt. And when these villages are built, I will distribute to each of them the quantity of water
necessary, neither more nor less. I will give water to each village only when the Nile no longer reaches it.
For the elevated terrains, I will make the water rise from below and will make it descend from above for the
depressed terrains, and that at every instant of the day and of the night; each village will receive a
quantity of water wisely measured, without ever having less than what will be necessary to it nor more than
what it will need." "That," said Pharaoh, "will be similar to the celestial kingdom." "Yes, certainly," said
Joseph. And having set to work, he ordered the construction of the villages of which he himself fixed the
limits. The first village that was built at the Fayoum was the village of Sanah; it is there that resided the
daughter of Pharaoh. Then, according to his orders, one dug the canal and one built bridges, and when the
whole was achieved, the land was measured as well as the water. It is since this time that the art of the
engineer exists; no one before knew it. Joseph was also the first who measured the flood of the Nile and who
constructed a nilometer at Memphis.

The author says: "The Bible reports that Pharaoh constrained the Israelites

[PDF p. 764]

[OF THE TOWN OF EL FAYOUM, continued]

to build and to make bricks; they built him a quantity of towns, such as among others Fithom and 'Aramsîs. A
commentator claims that by these two towns one must understand the Fayoum and the Houf-Ramsis. In the time of
El Raisan ben El Oualid, Jacob and his children entered into Egypt; they were then in all seventy-three
persons, men and women, and Joseph gave them for sojourn the territory comprised between Aïn Shams and Farma,
a fertile and prosperous land. In approaching Egypt, Jacob sent Juda to Joseph. The latter went to meet him,
clasped him on his chest, and wept. And when Jacob was brought into the presence of Pharaoh, the king
addressed the word to him. Jacob was then a venerable old man, beautiful of visage, with a magnificent beard,
with a powerful voice. "O old man," Pharaoh said to him, "what age are you?" "120 years," said Jacob. Now,
Bahman, magician of Pharaoh, had given in his book the description of Jacob, of Joseph, and of Moses: he knew
that the loss and the destruction of Egypt would come by their hands. Thus he left berabi (temple) texts and
images of those who were to be the cause of the destruction of Egypt. When he saw Jacob, he rose in the
council, and the first question he posed him was this one: "Whom do you adore, O old man?" "I adore God,"
answered Jacob, "the God of all things." "And how do you adore what you do not see?" "God is too great and too
powerful for one to see him." "We others, we see our gods," said Bahman. "Your gods," answered Jacob, "are
made by the sons of Adam who die and dissolve; but my God is higher and greater, and he is nearer to man than
his jugular vein." Then Bahman, turning toward Pharaoh: "Here," he said to him, "is the one by whose hand must
come the loss of our country." "Will that take place in our time," asked Pharaoh, "or in another than ours?"
"Neither in your time, nor in the time of your sons," said Bahman. "Have you found that in the decrees of your
God?" "Yes." "And how could you kill the one whom his God wishes to make the instrument of the ruin of his
people? It is not fitting to speak thus."

According to Ka'b, Jacob lived in Egypt sixteen years and, when death approached,

[PDF p. 765]

he said to Joseph: "Do not bury me in Egypt, but when I am dead, carry off my body and bury it in the grotto
of Hebron. Hebron is the oratory of Abraham and is situated eighteen miles from Jerusalem." When Jacob was
dead, one embalmed him with aloes and myrrh, and one deposited his body in a coffin of plane-wood. It took for
this forty days. Then Joseph spoke to Pharaoh and informed him of the death of his father and of the desire he
had expressed to be inhumed in the land of Canaan. The king authorized the translation of the body; the
cortège was accompanied by the great of Egypt, who, after having attended the inhumation, returned to their
country. One knows however that Jacob was first buried in Egypt and that it is only at the end of three years
that he was carried to Jerusalem, as he had recommended in dying. El Raisan ben El Oualid died next and was
replaced on the throne by his son Darem ben El Raisan; it is under the reign of this last that Joseph died.
"One day," said this patriarch on his deathbed, "one day you will come out of Egypt to return to the country
of your fathers. Take with you my bones." When he was dead, one deposited his body in a sarcophagus that one
buried on one of the banks of the river; and this bank became fertile, while the opposite bank became sterile.
The body was therefore transported to the other bank which became fertile in its turn while the first became
sterile again. Seeing this, one gathered the bones of Joseph which one put in a coffer of iron provided with a
chain. One raised on the bank of the river a column at the base of which one fixed a wedge of iron; to this
wedge one adjusted the chain, and the coffer was thrown into the middle of the Nile. And the banks of the
river became fertile both.

Here is on what occasion the bones of Joseph were transported from Egypt to Syria: Sarah, daughter of Aser,
son of Jacob, had lived to a certain old age and had lost her sight when Moses came out of Egypt with the
Israelites. They were enveloped in a cloud that interposed itself between them and the road which he no longer
saw. And a voice made itself heard that said to Moses: "You will not pass unless you have with you the bones of
Joseph." "Who knows where these bones are?" asked Moses. And one said to him: "An old blind woman whom we have
left in Egypt." Moses returned on his steps, and Sarah, having heard his approach, asked: "Why do you return?"
"I have received the order," said Moses, "to lead away the bones of Joseph." "You cannot," replied the old
woman, "if I am not with you." "Indicate to me where are the bones of Joseph," replied Moses.

[PDF p. 766]

Sarah indicated them to him, and Moses carried off the bones of Joseph with him into the desert of Tih.

Joseph, son of Jacob, son of Isaac, son of Abraham the cherished of God, is one of the twelve sibts (a term
applied to the descendants of illustrious families, particularly to the sons of Jacob and by extension to the
twelve tribes of Israel). He was born in the land of Canaan, a region of Syria; he saw the eleven stars, the
sun, and the moon prostrating themselves before him; he was then seventeen years old. This vision rendered
jealous his brothers, who sold him to people of Madian. These led him to Egypt and ceded him to a general of
Pharaoh in whose house he remained twelve months, after which the wife of El 'Aziz asked him to satisfy her
desires. Joseph having refused it, was falsely accused, and thrown into prison where he remained ten years.
One says other things still. He remained in prison until Pharaoh and the baker of the king had the two dreams
(that one knows); Joseph explained them; the two officers came out, but the cup-bearer forgot Joseph for two
years, until the time when Pharaoh saw in a dream the cows and the ears. The cup-bearer then spoke of Joseph
to the king who had him come and recounted to him his dreams. Joseph having explained them, one had him come
out of prison; he was then thirty years old, and the king named him vizier. From that moment to the arrival
of Jacob in Egypt, there elapsed nine years, comprising the seven years of abundance and two of the years of
dearth. At his arrival in Egypt, Jacob had 130 years, and his family was composed of seventy persons: from his
arrival to the birth of Moses, there passed 130 other years; Jacob had died seventeen years after his entry
into Egypt, at the age of 147 years. The sibts, dreading the resentment of Joseph, said to him: "Your father
asked that you pardon your brothers, for your brothers and you are the servants of God, of the God of your
father." "Have no disquiet," answered Joseph, weeping, and he made them generous promises that he fulfilled.
And Joseph died at the age of 110 years, and God is the most knowing.

[PDF p. 767]

CHAPTER LXXXIII
OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID OF THE FAYOUM, OF ITS CANALS, AND OF ITS VILLAGES

Formerly, says El Ya'qoubi, one said "Egypt and the Fayoum," because of the importance of the Fayoum and the
great number of its inhabitants; it is from there that came the best wheat, and one fabricated there the
kheïch (a coarse light linen cloth). According to El Mas'oudi, the word El Fayoum signifies a thousand days
(alf youm).

The Fayoum, says El Qoda'ï, is a town founded by the prophet Joseph by divine inspiration. It contained three
hundred sixty villages of which each could provision Egypt for one day; the entire province could therefore
provide for the needs of Egypt for the whole year. A flood of twelve cubits sufficed to water it; the surplus
could cause no damage, for Joseph had regulated the course of the water and had taken his measures in such a
fashion that the water penetrated there without interruption, contained by means of dikes of piled stones; it
is in this aim that he constructed Allahoun.

In the Fayoum, says Ibn Radouan, one stores the water of the Nile, and the region can be sown several times per
year. Thus, you see that this water, when it is released, alters the color and the taste of the (rest of the)
Nile; this state of things is particularly remarkable in the lake that exists at the height of summer at Saft
and at Nahia and higher still to the confines of the Fayoum. This state of things is very prejudicial to the
inhabitants of the town -- that is, of Fostat -- above all when the wind of the South blows; for the Fayoum is
to the south and at a distance rather far from Fostat. In his book "Guide for the science of the tax," the
cadi Abou-l Hanay Aly, son of the Cadi al Moutamin Thiqat el daulat Abou 'Amr Othman ben Youssef El Qoraïshi
El Makhoumi,

[PDF p. 768]

explains himself thus: These districts form what there is most beautiful for the ordering, their (cultivable)
land is of the most extended, and the quality of their soil of the best; some of them however have become
sterile following the abandonment of the inhabitants and the invasion of the sands that have covered the
greatest part of them. I have had under my eyes a register drawn up by Abou Ishaq Ibrahim ben Gafar ben el
Hanay ben Ishaq, in which he had inscribed the canals of the provinces that had been neglected and the
villages that rose on their banks. I report it here, although some have disappeared, others have changed name,
others finally so well disappeared that one no longer knows the emplacement of them; I give it so that one may
realize what is cultivation today, and that whoever would desire to put back into cultivation as much as he
could of what has become sterile and would wish to make good administration may inform himself there to learn
what the locality would absorb of water. Here is the copy of it:

Register where is exposed the situation of the principal canals of Medinet El Fayoum, their emplacement, the
water that each village absorbs of them, the regulations concerning the closing and the opening of the dikes,
the distribution and the regulation of the waters, and the fixed epoch. Made in Djoumada II of the year 422
[26 May to 24 June 1031]. We begin with the aid of God and his benevolent assistance by recalling the state of
the principal branch from which are derived these canals, then we will recall there what is indispensable for
its good upkeep.

Great Canal of Fayoum. The water is brought to this canal by the little branch (of the Nile) named El Manha of
the stone of Joseph. The branch is above (the canal), near a mountain named seat of the sorceress in the
province of Achmouneïn. It waters some of the villages of Ashmoun, of Qeïs, and of Ahnas; on its two banks are
numerous villages that draw their water there with which they water the vines that grow there.

The stone of Joseph is a wall constructed of bricks and of that lime that the ancients named sâroûg; it is a
compound of lime and of oil. The construction of it is oriented from north to south, and ends by its southern
extremity at another wall constructed in the same fashion and directed exactly from the west to the east. Two
buttresses, detaching themselves from it, form for it a belt (that is, for the second wall) at its extremity:
its length is two hundred

[PDF p. 769]

[OF WHAT HAS BEEN SAID OF THE FAYOUM, continued]

practical cubits. The junction with this wall takes place over a length of eighty cubits on the west side by
the southern extremity of the great wall. The establishment of the great wall serves to throw back the
waters, when the level of them reaches twelve cubits, onto the town of Fayoum. The length of the junction of
the wall, which goes from the west to the east, then rejoins the buttress, then lowers from this symmetrical
buttress that faces it to the south, is fifty cubits; the part that comes after the interval comprised between
these two buttresses, which is the lowered part, is a hundred ten cubits; the extent of the lowered part is
four cubits; this lowered part is barred by a dike made of grass called labsh; the width of the region where
the water runs, which comprises the place where the labsh is and the terrain that faces it on the east side,
is forty cubits; there is the second labsh; the junction with this buttress toward the south side is made over
a length of three hundred seventy-two cubits, then on the extremity of this length connects a wall that
follows the same direction to the stone of Joseph, built of stone, whose length on the eastern line is a
hundred cubits, then it lowers equally at the point of junction with this wall, over a length of twenty
cubits, the lowered part of it is two cubits; this lowered part is equally barred by a dike of grasses, called
lokbad; the length of the rest of the wall on the north side is a hundred thirty-six cubits; facing it over
all the length is a paving. There were aqueducts on arches constructed of stone that formerly sent back the
waters into the Fayoum by the old canal today obstructed; these arch-aqueducts were provided with gates; they
were formerly to the number of ten. The length of the great wall is in total about nine hundred seventy-two
practical cubits, not counting the wall that extends from the west to the east. The great wall extends without
interruption on the two sides and goes to join the mountain, and one finds traces of it at the height of
summer, but these traces do not form a straight line.

[PDF p. 770]

As for the width of this wall, it is variable, and diminishes in approaching the summit. The upper part as well
as what one sees of the lower part has a width of sixteen cubits. Openings are made there for the flow of the
waters; these openings are formed of tubes of colored glass similar to blue enamel or souleïmânî. This wall is
a splendid marvel by the grandeur and the ability of its construction. It is indeed a construction that
rivals the tower of Alexandria and the Pyramids. The most surprising is that the Nile makes its waters pass
there since the time of Joseph until present, and that its solidity has not been shaken. Today, the waters are
carried from the river to Médinet el Fayoum, by means of the great canal of the Fayoum which passes between
the territories of the two villages of Damounah and of Al Lahoun and waters the fields of these two villages
and of many others. One irrigates the vines by means of machines set in movement by oxen. When the waters of
the Nile are too low to cover the lands, it is again the oxen that raise the water necessary for the
cultivations. The water passes from the great canal to the canal of El Aouasa which is closed and opened
without determined rule, and whose waters are distributed without fixed plan. This canal passes at the village
of Bayad and fills the pond that is in this place and other ponds. From these set out canals of derivation,
each of which receives the water necessary for the irrigation of the terrains they cross; the canal then
continues and reaches the village of El Aousiah El Koubra, whence derive two canals special to the locality
and whose intake is regulated. The palms and the other trees of the region are watered by this canal, and on
its banks rises a mill actuated by the water. Farther, are formed three canals of derivation that end at the
village of Martinah; one of them is special to this village, the second waters a great number of domains, and
the third goes to carry its waters to a nursery of palms where are found sakiehs (irrigation machines) and
gardens that have been destroyed, and where is an enclosure of sycamores; houses rose in the alleys of palms.
The canal then passes to a second nursery similar to the first and arrives at the village of Goubah whose
reservoir it fills; there it forms three canals of derivation end to end above which is an abandoned canal;
they water a great number of villages. The water brought by the canal arrives finally at Bâtas where it
terminates. On the banks of the great canal, beyond the canal of El Fayoum, extend plains of silt that are
watered by the waters flowing from the great canal itself,

[PDF p. 771]

thanks to special water-intakes. At the moment of the lowering of the Nile, one stretches nets at these
water-intakes for the fishing. The great canal then arrives, to the right of whoever directs himself toward El
Fayoum, at a canal named:

CANAL OF SAMASTOUS. It waters Samastous and other villages as well as numerous domains that extend to the
desert to the east and to the south, and cover the space comprised between this canal and the canal of El
Avasa. Farther, the great canal continues to the:

CANAL OF DAHALAH. This canal waters a great number of villages; on its banks one cultivates the rice and other
cereals. Then the great canal forms three other canals and arrives at the:

CANAL OF BEINTAWAH. There are found there three ancient gates from the time of Joseph, each two practical
cubits wide; the water after having crossed the first gate ends again at two gates from the time of Joseph.
The rule is to close this canal and all the derived ones from the second to the last day of Hathor; one opens
it from the 1st to the 20th of Kihak to close it again until the 10th of Toubah, to reopen it on the eve of
the feast of the Baptism until the end of Toubah; one closes it again from the 1st to the 2nd of Amchir; one
reopens it until the 10th of Barmahat; then one leaves it open until the 10th of Barmoudah, the day on which
one distributes the waters; the cultivations that bordered the northern part of this canal are abandoned; it
waters a great number of villages. For this canal one has cut under the mountain a vaulted conduit by which the
waters flowed when they were too abundant. Then the great canal arrives at the:

CANAL OF DALAH, one of the derived ones, which is opened and closed and whose waters are distributed and
managed following the rule indicated above; it is to the left of whoever directs himself toward the town (of
the Fayoum). This canal has two gates of stone built in the time of Joseph and each two cubits and a quarter
wide. It waters a great number of villages, central ones or others. In the middle of this canal is a spillway
that one opens at the time of the flood to permit the waters to flow into the great reservoir; at the
extremity of this is another spillway provided with gates, which were, it is said, formerly of iron. When

[PDF p. 772]

the water is too abundant, one opens the gates and the water flows toward the west and goes, it is said, to
Santariah. On the banks of its two canals were gardens and numerous vines that one watered by means of the
ox-machines. Then the great canal arrives at the:

CANAL OF EL MAGNOUNAH. One has given it this name because of the enormous quantity of water it receives (El
Magnounah means "the mad woman"). For the closing and the rest, one follows the rules already reported. It
waters numerous villages and makes turn numerous mills. The surplus of the waters of the villages of the South
pours itself into the canal and into the lake situated at the extremity of the Fayoum, in the vicinity of the
mountain of Abou Qitrân; into this lake also pour the waters coming from the villages of the North; it is the
one that one calls the great lake. Then the great canal continues its route and arrives at the:

CANAL OF TELALAH. This canal has two gates dating from Joseph, built solidly of stones and each two cubits and
two thirds wide; there is no regulation touching the closing or the opening of this canal, nor for the
distribution and the repartition of the waters; when the flood is insufficient, one contents oneself with
establishing a dike of grasses; some quarters of the town (of the Fayoum) feed themselves on this canal as
well as a great quantity of lands and numerous villages; it is there that is found the water-intake of the
canal of El Batash where goes the excess of the waters; it is provided with gates that one closes until the
water has reached a determined level above the elevated lands. If the closing-dike undergoes some damage, it
is repaired proportionally by the villages that this canal waters. Then the great canal arrives at two other
canals that set out from its two banks to the north and to the south, after which it reaches:

The CANAL OF SAMOUAH, situated to the right of whoever directs himself toward the town of the Fayoum. It is
one of the derived ones: it is provided with two gates from the time of Joseph, each two cubits and a half
wide. It follows the rules given previously; it waters numerous domains and a great quantity of villages. Then
there detach from it four canals of derivation provided with gates and different canals that water a great
number of villages.

CANAL OF TABDOUD. In the bed of this canal springs a source of sweet water

[PDF p. 773]

with which one waters the neighboring lands when the canal is closed. One discovered this source one year when
the water was lacking, and when one was digging at this place to make a well; it is then that the source
appeared and sufficed for the needs. Then the great canal arrives at different canals from which detach
secondary branches dating from the time of Joseph. These canals have gates of the same epoch, and for the
opening and the closing of which there are established rules; numerous villages feed themselves there. The
regulation of the canals requires that all be closed from the 10th of Hathor to the end of this month; one
opens them for twenty days from the 1st of Kihak; they are closed from the 21st of Kihak to the eve of the
feast of the Baptism; on the day of the feast, one opens them until the end of the month of Tobah; one closes
them from the 1st to the 20th of Amchir; on the 21st, one opens them until the 20th of Barnahat; one opens them
again during the first ten days of Barmoudah; one puts them in state, then one occupies oneself with the
repartition of the waters; each district receives the quantity of water that suits it following rules
perfectly known to the inhabitants. I have abridged the name of the villages reported in the register, because
most of them are ruined. And God is the most knowing.

[PDF p. 774]

CHAPTER LXXXIV
OF THE CONQUEST OF THE FAYOUM, OF THE AMOUNT OF ITS REVENUES, AND OF THE ADVANTAGES IT PRESENTS

Ibn 'Abdel Hakem recounts that when the Muslims had achieved the conquest, 'Amr ben El 'As sent troops of
cavaliers toward the neighboring villages, but the Muslims were a whole year without knowing the emplacement
of the Fayoum, when a man came to speak to them of it. 'Amr sent with him Rabi'at ben Habeish ben 'Arfatah El
Sadfi. The expedition, after a very long march in the desert, having met nothing, had decided to return on its
steps, but their guides said to them: "Do not hasten to leave; if one has lied to you, it will always be
possible for you to do what you wish." They advanced therefore a little more, and all at once there surged
before them the countryside of the Fayoum; they penetrated there, and without there being combat, the
province fell into their hands. One says also: Malek ben Na'mak El Sadafi, the same that one calls the man
with the chestnut horse, set out one day on his mount into the desert without knowing that beyond extended the
Fayoum, but when he had seen the countryside, he returned to inform 'Amr of it. One says again: 'Amr ben El
'As had sent into the Said Qeïs ben El Hareth, who marched until he arrived at El Qeïs, a village where he
stopped and to which he gave his name. Remaining without news of him, 'Amr was disquieted, and Rabi'ah ben
Habeïch proposed himself to go to the discovery. He set out therefore on his mare and, crossing the river,
learned what he desired to know. He had set out, one said, on the side of the Orient and had not stopped until
the Fayoum. His mare was named the Blind One. And God is the most knowing.

In his book "The Merits of Egypt," El Kandi expresses himself thus: Among the provinces of Egypt is found the
province of the Fayoum which comprises three hundred sixty villages, a number answering to the number of the
days

[PDF p. 775]

of the year; all these villages are always watered by a sufficient quantity of water. If there comes a year
when the Nile is insufficient, each village can provide for one day for the needs of the country of Masr.
There is not in the world another country than this province that has been built by (divine) inspiration, nor
that is more precious, nor more abundant in goods, nor more furrowed with canals. If one compares to the
canals of the Fayoum those of Basra and of Damascus, the advantage remains to the first. A great number of
intelligent and instructed people have sought what were the revenues and the riches of the Fayoum, but they
were so considerable that they had to abandon the researches. One has made the count of the lands that in this
province belong to no Muslim nor to any of their tributaries and of which the rich and the poor people can
equally make use, and one has found more than seventy categories of these terrains.

According to Ibn Zoulaq cited by El Kandi in his book of the Documents relative to the emirs of Egypt, the
Fayoum, that year -- that is, in the year 366 -- brought to Kafour El Ikhshidi six hundred twenty thousand and
some dinars.

[PDF p. 776]

CHAPTER LXXXV
OF THE TOWN OF EL NAHRIRIEH

It was a fief constituted to ten soldiers of the halqah (the royal guard of the Ayyubid and Mameluke sultans),
one of whom was Chems addîn Sonqor al Sa'dî; he had removed a part of the terrain from cultivation to
establish there a stable for his beasts and his equipages; his co-beneficiaries complained of it to the
sultan Al Malik al Mansour Qalaoun who interrogated him on this subject. He answered: I wish to establish
there a mosque where the Khotbah will be made; the sultan granted him the authorization of it; and the
construction of it was begun toward the end of the year 683 and finished in 685; the sultan had a minbar made
there; the (Friday) assembly was held there, and that until our days; Al Sa'dî created shops along the mosque;
he remained proprietor of them until his death; the inheritance of them passed to his sons 'Izz eddin Khalil
and Rokn eddin 'Omar, who sold them some time after to the emir Cheïkhou al 'Omarî. The latter had them enter
into the waqf that he constituted to the khânakâh and to the mosque that he created at the Khatt Salibeh of
the mosque of Ibn Touloun outside Cairo. The construction of the mosque brought other constructions in the
region which peopled itself and became one of the towns of the country of Egypt where were even installed
workshops of weaving of silk. Sonqor rose by degrees in the service (of the sultan) until being part of the
emirs, became lieutenant of the mamluks of the sultan. It is he who created the sa'idiah madrasah outside
Cairo near Hadarat al baqar, "the hall of the oxen," in the space comprised between the citadel of the
mountain and Birkat el fil, "the pond of the elephant," in the year 715; he constructed also a ribât for the
women; he had a pronounced taste for constructions, loved also the cultivations; he possessed great goods, and
his exterior manifested opulence. Later, he withdrew to Tripoli, where he died in the year 728.

[END OF THE SECOND PART.]
